    (\pi(g)E_{mn}\pi(g^{-1}))_{ij}=\textstyle\sum_{a,b}\pi(g)_{ia}(E_{mn})_{ab}\pi(g^{-1})_{bj}=\pi(g)_{im}\,\pi(g^{-1})_{nj}.
Comparing with (\lambda\operatorname{id})_{ij}=\lambda\delta_{ij} yields the first orthogonality relation for matrix coefficients
    \sum_{g\in G}\pi(g)_{im}\,\pi(g^{-1})_{nj}=\frac{|G|}{d}\,\delta_{mn}\delta_{ij}.   (\dagger)

2c. Two consequences. (i) Set m:=i and n:=j in (\dagger) and sum over all i,j\in\{1,\dots,d\}. The left side becomes
    \sum_g\sum_{i,j}\pi(g)_{ii}\pi(g^{-1})_{jj}=\sum_g\Big(\sum_i\pi(g)_{ii}\Big)\Big(\sum_j\pi(g^{-1})_{jj}\Big)=\sum_g\chi(g)\chi(g^{-1)},
while the right side becomes (|G|/d)\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ij}\delta_{ij}=(|G|/d)\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ij}=(|G|/d)\cdot d=|G|, because \sum_{i,j}\delta_{ij} counts the d pairs with i=j. Hence
    \sum_{g\in G}\chi(g^{-1})\chi(g)=|G|.   (\ddagger)
(Here, and below, all sums are over g\in G; note that the cross terms i\neq j are correctly accounted for because the factorisation into \chi(g)\cdot\chi(g^{-1}) is performed *after* summing over i and j.)

(ii) Non-isomorphic case. Let (\theta,U) be simple with character \psi\neq\chi, and let A_0:U\to W be any k'-linear map. Then S:=\sum_g\pi(g)A_0\theta(g^{-1}) satisfies \pi(h)S=S\theta(h) for all h (identical reindexing argument as in 2b), i.e. S\in Hom_A(U,W)=0 by Schur's lemma applied to non-isomorphic simples (any nonzero intertwiner would be an isomorphism). Taking A_0=E_{mn}:U\to W the matrix unit relative to fixed bases, the (i,j)-entry of S is \sum_g\pi(g)_{im}\theta(g^{-1})_{nj}=0 for all i,j,m,n. Setting m:=i, n:=j and summing over i,j gives
    \sum_g\Big(\sum_i\pi(g)_{ii}\Big)\Big(\sum_j\theta(g^{-1})_{jj}\Big)=\sum_g\chi(g)\psi(g^{-1})=0,
and since g\mapsto g^{-1} is a bijection of G (equivalently, apply the displayed identity with the roles of (\pi,W) and (\theta,U) interchanged),
    \sum_{g\in G}\chi(g^{-1})\psi(g)=0\qquad(\chi\neq\psi).   (\ddagger\ddagger)

2d. The elements e_\chi. For each irreducible \chi define
    e_\chi:=\frac{\chi(1)}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g^{-1})\,g\ \in k'[G].
This makes sense: \chi(1)=d\in\mathbb N and |G|^{-1}\in k'.

CENTRALITY. g\mapsto\chi(g^{-1}) is a class function, since for h\in G, \chi((hgh^{-1})^{-1})=\chi(hg^{-1}h^{-1})=\chi(g^{-1}). For a class function a:G\to k', the element \sum_g a(g)g is central: h(\sum_g a(g)g)h^{-1}=\sum_g a(g)hgh^{-1}=\sum_{g'}a(h^{-1}g'h)g'=\sum_{g'}a(g')g'. Hence e_\chi is central in A.

ACTION ON SIMPLES. Let (\pi,W) have character \chi, d=\chi(1). Since e_\chi is central, \pi(e_\chi)\in End_A(W)=k'\operatorname{id} by Schur, say \pi(e_\chi)=\mu\operatorname{id}_W. Taking traces,
    \mu d=\operatorname{Tr}\pi(e_\chi)=\frac{d}{|G|}\sum_g\chi(g^{-1})\operatorname{Tr}\pi(g)=\frac{d}{|G|}\sum_g\chi(g^{-1})\chi(g)=\frac{d}{|G|}\cdot|G|=d
by (\ddagger); hence \mu=1, i.e. \pi(e_\chi)=\operatorname{id}_W.
If instead (\theta,U) is simple with character \psi\neq\chi, the same argument (centrality \Rightarrow scalar, then trace) gives \theta(e_\chi)=\nu\operatorname{id}_U with \nu\dim U=\frac{d}{|G|}\sum_g\chi(g^{-1})\psi(g)=0 by (\ddagger\ddagger), so \theta(e_\chi)=0.

IDEMPOTENCE, ORTHOGONALITY, COMPLETENESS. Consider the element e_\chi^2-e_\chi\in A. For any simple module M\cong W_\theta we have computed \theta(e_\chi)=\operatorname{id} if \theta=\chi and 0 otherwise, so \theta(e_\chi^2-e_\chi)=\theta(e_\chi)^2-\theta(e_\chi)=0 in every case, i.e. e_\chi^2-e_\chi annihilates every simple A-module. Writing A=\bigoplus_{\theta}W_\theta^{\oplus m_\theta} as a left A-module (Maschke, applied to A itself), the annihilator of the collection of all simples is a left ideal containing no nonzero element a, since a=a\cdot 1\in A and a would annihilate 1\in A. Hence e_\chi^2=e_\chi: each e_\chi is an idempotent. Identically, for \chi\neq\psi the element e_\chi e_\psi annihilates every simple (\theta(e_\chi)\theta(e_\psi)=0 since at most one of \chi,\psi equals \theta), so e_\chi e_\psi=0; and \sum_\chi e_\chi-1 annihilates every simple (\sum_\theta' \theta(e_{\theta'}) = \operatorname{id} on W_\theta), hence equals 0. Thus
    e_\chi e_\psi=\delta_{\chi\psi}e_\chi\quad\text{and}\quad \sum_{\chi}e_\chi=1_{k'[G]},
with a finite sum. (Each e_\chi is central by the above; we do not assert primitivity, which is neither needed nor claimed.) We also note, for later reference, that e_\chi need not lie in \mathbb Q_\ell[G]: only the scalar factor \chi(1)/|G|\in\mathbb Q_\ell is canonical; the values \chi(g^{-1}) live in k'. The only property of |G| used anywhere above is invertibility in k'.

=====================================================================
STEP 3. The isotypic pieces are F-stable and give a direct decomposition.

Fix n\ge0 and put W_n:=V_n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}k'. This is a finite-dimensional k'-vector space (dim_{k'}W_n=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_n<\infty by Step 0). Let F_W:=F\otimes\operatorname{id}_{k'} and \rho_W(g):=\rho(g)\otimes\operatorname{id}_{k'}. Both are k'-linear, F_W is invertible, and by Step 1 they commute: F_W\rho_W(g)=\rho_W(g)F_W. Hence for any a=\sum_g a_g\rho_W(g)\in k'[G], k'-linearity of F_W gives F_W a=\sum_g a_g\rho_W(g)F_W=a\,F_W; that is, F_W commutes with the whole k'[G]-action on W_n.

(i) F-stability. Define W_{n,\chi}:=e_\chi(W_n)=\operatorname{im}(\rho_W(e_\chi))\subset W_n. If w=e_\chi(v)\in W_{n,\chi} then F_W(w)=F_We_\chi(v)=e_\chi F_W(v)\in W_{n,\chi}, so F_W(W_{n,\chi})\subseteq W_{n,\chi}. Since F_W^{-1} also commutes with the k'[G]-action (F commutes with each \rho(g), hence so does F^{-1}), the same argument gives F_W^{-1}(W_{n,\chi})\subseteq W_{n,\chi}. Thus W_{n,\chi} is F_W-stable and F_W restricts to an automorphism of W_{n,\chi}.

(ii) Direct sum decomposition. Because \sum_\chi e_\chi=1 in k'[G], every w\in W_n satisfies w=\sum_\chi e_\chi w with e_\chi w\in W_{n,\chi}, so W_n=\sum_\chi W_{n,\chi}. Because e_\chi e_\psi=\delta_{\chi\psi}e_\chi, the sum is direct: if \sum_\chi w_\chi=0 with w_\chi=e_\chi v_\chi, applying e_\psi gives w_\psi=e_\psi e_\psi v_\psi=0. Hence
    W_n=\bigoplus_{\chi}W_{n,\chi},
a finite direct sum (finitely many irreducible characters, Step 2a). Each W_{n,\chi} is the image of a projector, hence a k'[G]- and F_W-stable direct summand of W_n.

(iii) Identification as isotypic components (for terminology, not for the logic). By Maschke, W_n=\bigoplus_j M_j as k'[G]-modules with each M_j simple; e_\chi acts as \operatorname{id} on those M_j\cong W_\chi and as 0 on the others by Step 2d, so W_{n,\chi}=\bigoplus_{M_j\cong W_\chi}M_j is exactly the \chi-isotypic component of W_n.

=====================================================================
STEP 4. A linear-algebra claim on direct sums.

Claim. Let K be a field, W a finite-dimensional K-vector space, T\in\operatorname{GL}(W), and W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}W_i a FINITE direct sum of T-stable subspaces. Then T is semisimple on W if and only if T|_{W_i} is semisimple on W_i for each i.

Definition used. For an operator on a finite-dimensional space over a field, "semisimple" means: the minimal polynomial is squarefree. Over K=\mathbb Q_\ell this coincides with the notion of lemma_5/lemma_4 by lemma_60(ii). Over K=k'=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell (algebraically closed, characteristic 0) it coincides with diagonalizability: if \mu_T=\prod_{j=1}^{s}(t-\lambda_j) with the \lambda_j distinct, the ideals ((t-\lambda_j))\subset k'[t] are pairwise comaximal, so the Chinese remainder theorem identifies k'[t]/(\mu_T)\cong\prod_j k'[t]/(t-\lambda_j); as W is a k'[t]/(\mu_T)-module on which t acts as T, this yields W=\bigoplus_j\ker(T-\lambda_j), a decomposition into eigenspaces, i.e. T is diagonalizable; conversely a diagonalizable T with distinct eigenvalues \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s has \mu_T=\prod_j(t-\lambda_j), squarefree. (This is the only place where the characteristic-0/algebraically-closed nature of k' is used; no module-theoretic "stable subspace has stable complement" argument is needed, and none is given.)

Proof of the Claim. Let \mu_i\in K[t] be the minimal polynomial of T|_{W_i} and \mu_T that of T. Since W=\bigoplus_iW_i with each W_i stable, an annihilating polynomial for T is the same thing as an annihilating polynomial for every T|_{W_i}: indeed \mu_T(T)=0 on W forces \mu_T(T|_{W_i})=0, so \mu_i\mid\mu_T for all i, hence \operatorname{lcm}(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r)\mid\mu_T; conversely P:=\operatorname{lcm}(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r) satisfies P(T)|_{W_i}=0 for each i, hence P(T)=0 on the sum W, so \mu_T\mid P. Thus
    \mu_T=\operatorname{lcm}(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r)\quad\text{in the UFD }K[t].
(\Leftarrow) If every \mu_i is squarefree, write \mu_i=\prod_{f\in S_i}f with S_i a set of distinct monic irreducibles; then \operatorname{lcm}_i\mu_i=\prod_{f\in\cup_iS_i}f, again with each irreducible occurring to the first power, so \mu_T is squarefree.
(\Rightarrow) Each \mu_i divides \mu_T, and a divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree.
This proves the Claim. (Equivalently, in the diagonalizable language over k': (\Leftarrow) the union of eigenbases of the W_i is an eigenbasis of W; (\Rightarrow) the spectral projection onto the \lambda-eigenspace is a polynomial in T, hence preserves every T-stable W_i, so W_i=\bigoplus_\lambda(W_i\cap E_\lambda).)

=====================================================================
STEP 5. The equivalence for F, and the consequence for the conjecture.

Applying the Claim in Step 4 with K=k', W=W_n, T=F_W, and the finite decomposition W_n=\bigoplus_\chi W_{n,\chi} of Step 3(ii) (finite by Step 2a, stable by Step 3(i)):
    F_W is semisimple (diagonalizable) on W_n \iff F_W|_{W_{n,\chi}} is semisimple on W_{n,\chi} for every \chi.   (1)
On the other hand, lemma_5 applied to the finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-space V_n and the operator F gives
    F is semisimple on V_n \iff F_W=F\otimes\operatorname{id} is semisimple (diagonalizable) on V_n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=W_n.   (2)
Combining (1) and (2) yields, for every n\ge0:
    F is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \iff F is semisimple on every isotypic piece W_{n,\chi},
which is the asserted "consequently".

Finally, assume F is semisimple on every isotypic piece W_{n,\chi} for every n\ge0. By the equivalence just proved, F=F_{\mathrm{ar}} is semisimple on V_n for every n. By lemma_6a, the geometric Frobenius on V_n is F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1} (this uses the finite-dimensionality of V_n from Step 0, which guarantees invertibility and that lemma_6a applies). By lemma_4 (semisimplicity is invariant under inversion for an invertible operator on a finite-dimensional space over a field), F_{\mathrm{geo}} is semisimple on V_n. By lemma_5 applied to F_{\mathrm{geo}}, its extension to V_n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable. Since this holds for every n\ge0, X satisfies the conjecture: geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for all n, equivalently diagonably on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. This completes the proof of the lemma. \hfill\qedsymbol

Remark. The argument used only that |G| is invertible in k'=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell (guaranteed by (|G|,\ell)=1); it did not use that the e_\chi are defined over \mathbb Q_\ell, and indeed they generally are not, which is precisely why the isotypic decomposition is stated over H^n\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell rather than over H^n itself.

lemma_86.statement: Let \ell be a prime, let V be a finite-dimensional \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector space, and let T\in\mathrm{GL}(V) be semisimple. Then for every n\ge 1 the automorphisms induced by T on the tensor power \otimes^n V, on the exterior power \wedge^n V, and on the symmetric power \mathrm{Sym}^n V are semisimple; more generally, for every partition \lambda of n the automorphism induced on the corresponding Schur functor S_\lambda(V)\subset \otimes^n V is semisimple, and the same holds for every \mathbb{Q}_\ell[G]-submodule of a tensor construction on V that is a direct summand as a \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector space and stable under the diagonal action of T.
lemma_86.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_86.

NOTATION AND CONVENTIONS. Write $K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and for $m\ge 1$ write $A_m:=\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$ for the group algebra. If $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $W$ is any tensor construction on $V$, $T_W$ denotes the automorphism induced by the *diagonal* action of $T$ (the same operator $T$ on every tensor factor, the contragredient $T^{-1}$ on every dual factor). We use 'semisimple' in the module-theoretic sense: an operator $U$ on a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $X$ is semisimple iff $X$ is a semisimple $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$-module via $t\cdot x=Ux$, equivalently (lemma_60(ii), which we do not need to reprove) iff the minimal polynomial of $U$ is squarefree. The only external inputs are lemma_5 (semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is equivalent to diagonalisability after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$), lemma_35(i)-(ii), lemma_9, and lemma_64(iv) (semisimplicity passes to duals and to inverses).

EDGE CASES. If $V=0$ then $\otimes^n V=\wedge^n V=\mathrm{Sym}^n V=0$ for every $n\ge 1$, and every assertion is vacuous (the identity on the zero space is semisimple). If $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=d<n$ then $\wedge^n V=0$, again vacuous. Henceforth assume $V\ne 0$, and put $d:=\dim V$.

STEP 1 (tensor powers). By hypothesis $T$ is semisimple on $V$. Lemma_35(i) states that if $T_1$ (resp. $T_2$) is semisimple on $V_1$ (resp. $V_2$) then $T_1\otimes T_2$ is semisimple on $V_1\otimes V_2$. Inducting on $n$: the case $n=1$ is the hypothesis; if $T^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is semisimple on $\otimes^{n-1}V$, then identifying $\otimes^n V\simeq(\otimes^{n-1}V)\otimes V$, the operator $T^{\otimes n}=T^{\otimes(n-1)}\otimes T$ is semisimple by lemma_35(i). This proves the first assertion for $\otimes^n V$.

STEP 2 ($S_n$ commutes with the diagonal $T$). Let $M:=\otimes^n V$ and define the left $S_n$-action $\rho(\sigma)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n):=v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}$ (this is a left action since $\rho(\sigma)\rho(\sigma')=\rho(\sigma\sigma')$). Then for a pure tensor,
$T^{\otimes n}\rho(\sigma)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=Tv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}=\rho(\sigma)(Tv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_n)=\rho(\sigma)T^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$,
because the entries $Tv_i$ are permuted by the same $\sigma$. Pure tensors span $M$, so $T^{\otimes n}\circ\rho(\sigma)=\rho(\sigma)\circ T^{\otimes n}$ for all $\sigma$, hence $T^{\otimes n}$ is $A_n$-linear: it commutes with every element of $A_n=\mathbb Q_\ell[S_n]$ acting through $\rho$, extended linearly.

STEP 3 (images of idempotents of $A_n$ inherit semisimplicity). Let $e\in A_n$ be an idempotent, $e^2=e$, acting on $M$ through $\rho$. Then $M=eM\oplus(1-e)M$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces: every $x\in M$ is $x=ex+(1-e)x$ with $ex\in eM$, $(1-e)x\in(1-e)M$; and if $x=ey=(1-e)z$ then $x=ex=e(1-e)z=(e-e^2)z=0$. Thus $eM$ is a direct summand as a vector space. By Step 2, $T^{\otimes n}(eM)=e\,T^{\otimes n}(M)=eM$, so $eM$ is $T^{\otimes n}$-stable. By Step 1, $T^{\otimes n}$ is semisimple on $M$, so lemma_35(ii) (a stable direct summand of a semisimple operator is semisimple) gives: **$T^{\otimes n}|_{eM}$ is semisimple for every idempotent $e\in A_n$.** All the remaining assertions for subspaces of $\otimes^nV$ will be instances of this.

STEP 4 (Maschke, proved inline). For any finite group $G$, any field $F$ with $\mathrm{char}F\nmid |G|$, and any $F[G]$-submodule $N\subset X$, choose an $F$-linear projection $p:X\twoheadrightarrow N$ and average it: $\bar p(x):=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g^{-1}p(gx)$. This is $F$-linear, maps into $N$ (as $N$ is $G$-stable), restricts to the identity on $N$, and satisfies $\bar p(hx)=h\bar p(x)$ (reindex the sum by $g\mapsto gh$). Hence $X=N\oplus\ker\bar p$ as $F[G]$-modules. So $F[G]$ is semisimple, and every $F[G]$-submodule is an $F[G]$-direct summand, in particular an $F$-vector-space direct summand. We apply this with $F=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (characteristic $0$) and $G=S_n$ or any finite group of permutations of tensor factors.

STEP 5 (exterior powers). In $A_n$ put $\mathrm{Alt}:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\,\sigma$; division by $n!$ is legitimate since $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$. Compute:
$\mathrm{Alt}^2=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_{\sigma,\tau}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\mathrm{sgn}(\tau)\,\sigma\tau=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_{\rho\in S_n}\Big(\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma^{-1}\rho)\Big)\rho=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_{\rho}(n!\,\mathrm{sgn}(\rho))\rho=\mathrm{Alt},$
so $\mathrm{Alt}$ is an idempotent. By Step 3, $W_{\mathrm{Alt}}:=\mathrm{Alt}(M)$ is a $T^{\otimes n}$-stable direct summand of $M$ on which $T$ is semisimple.
Now consider the composite $\wedge^n V\xleftarrow{\;q\;}M\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{Alt}\;}M$, where $q$ is the quotient map. First, $\mathrm{Alt}\circ q$ factors through $\wedge^n V$: for $\tau=(r\,r{+}1)$ one has $\mathrm{Alt}\cdot\tau=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma\tau=\frac1{n!}\sum_\rho\mathrm{sgn}(\rho\tau^{-1})\rho=-\mathrm{Alt}$ in $A_n$, so if $x=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ has $v_r=v_{r+1}$ (a defining relation of $\wedge^nV$), then $\rho(\tau)x=x$ and $\mathrm{Alt}(x)=\mathrm{Alt}(\rho(\tau)x)=\rho(\tau)\mathrm{Alt}(x)=(\tau\,\mathrm{Alt})(x)=-\mathrm{Alt}(x)$, whence $\mathrm{Alt}(x)=0$ (characteristic $\ne2$). Thus there is a well-defined map $\mathrm{alt}:\wedge^nV\to M$ with $\mathrm{alt}(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)=\mathrm{Alt}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$; its image is exactly $W_{\mathrm{Alt}}$. It is $T$-equivariant: $\mathrm{alt}(Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_n)=\mathrm{Alt}(Tv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_n)=T^{\otimes n}\mathrm{Alt}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=T^{\otimes n}\mathrm{alt}(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)$.
Injectivity: fix a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $V$; then $\{e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}:i_1<\cdots<i_n\}$ is a basis of $\wedge^nV$, and $\{e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n}\}$ is a basis of $M$. If the multi-index $I=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$ has a repeated entry, $\mathrm{Alt}(e_I)=0$ by the relation argument above. If $I$ is strictly increasing, $\mathrm{Alt}(e_I)=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)e_{\sigma I}$ is a nonzero signed sum of the $n!$ *distinct* basis tensors in the $S_n$-orbit of $e_I$ (the stabiliser of $e_I$ is trivial because the entries are distinct). Distinct increasing $I,I'$ have disjoint $S_n$-orbits (an orbit determines its increasing rearrangement), so the vectors $\mathrm{Alt}(e_I)$, $i_1<\cdots<i_n$, are linearly independent. Hence $\mathrm{alt}$ is injective, and it identifies $\wedge^nV$ $T$-equivariantly with $W_{\mathrm{Alt}}$, on which $T$ is semisimple by Step 3. This proves the assertion for $\wedge^nV$.

STEP 6 (symmetric powers). Put $\mathrm{Sym}:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\in A_n$; the computation of Step 5 without signs gives $\mathrm{Sym}^2=\mathrm{Sym}$, so $\mathrm{Sym}$ is an idempotent and $W_{\mathrm{Sym}}:=\mathrm{Sym}(M)$ is a $T^{\otimes n}$-stable direct summand with semisimple $T$ (Step 3). Since $\mathrm{Sym}\cdot\tau=\mathrm{Sym}$ for every transposition, $\mathrm{Sym}(x)$ is invariant under permuting the tensor factors of $x$; hence $\mathrm{Sym}$ factors through $\mathrm{Sym}^nV$: there is a well-defined $\mathrm{mult}:\mathrm{Sym}^nV\to M$ with $\mathrm{mult}(v_1\cdots v_n)=\mathrm{Sym}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, of image $W_{\mathrm{Sym}}$, and $T$-equivariant by the same computation as in Step 5. Injectivity: $\mathrm{Sym}^nV$ has basis $\{e_1^{a_1}\cdots e_d^{a_d}:a_1+\cdots+a_d=n\}$, and $\mathrm{mult}(e^a)=\frac{a_1!\cdots a_d!}{n!}\sum e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n}$, the sum over the distinct arrangements of the multiset containing $a_i$ copies of $i$; this is nonzero, and different $a$ have disjoint supports in the tensor basis, so the images are linearly independent. Thus $\mathrm{mult}$ identifies $\mathrm{Sym}^nV$ $T$-equivariantly with $W_{\mathrm{Sym}}$, on which $T$ is semisimple.

STEP 7 (Schur functors). Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding irreducible $A_n$-module (Specht module). By Step 4, $A_n$ is semisimple, so $S^\lambda$ is a direct summand of the regular module $A_n$; equivalently there is a *primitive* idempotent $e_\lambda\in A_n$ with $A_ne_\lambda\simeq S^\lambda$ as left $A_n$-modules. (Concretely, for the standard tableau of shape $\lambda$ with row group $R$ and column group $C$, the Young symmetrizer $c_\lambda=(\sum_{p\in R}p)(\sum_{q\in C}\mathrm{sgn}(q)q)$ satisfies the classical identity $c_\lambda^2=\frac{n!}{f^\lambda}c_\lambda$ with $f^\lambda=\dim S^\lambda$, so $e_\lambda=\frac{f^\lambda}{n!}c_\lambda$ is such an idempotent; we shall only use that $e_\lambda$ is an idempotent of $A_n$.)
Define $S_\lambda(V):=e_\lambda(M)\subset\otimes^nV$. By Step 3 this is a $T^{\otimes n}$-stable direct summand of $M$, hence $T$ is semisimple on it. It remains to check this is the usual Schur functor, i.e. that the definition is the standard one and is independent of choices:
(a) For any left $A_n$-module $M$ and any idempotent $e$, the map $\mathrm{Hom}_{A_n}(A_ne,M)\to eM$, $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(e)$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. Indeed $\varphi(e)=\varphi(e\cdot e)=e\varphi(e)\in eM$; injectivity holds because $A_ne$ is generated by $e$; and for $m=em\in eM$ the rule $\varphi(ae):=am$ is well defined since $ae=0\Rightarrow am=a(em)=(ae)m=0$.
(b) Taking $e=e_\lambda$ and $M=\otimes^nV$ gives $S_\lambda(V)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{A_n}(S^\lambda,\otimes^nV)$, the standard characteristic-zero definition of the Schur functor; and under (a) the restriction of $T^{\otimes n}$ to $e_\lambda M$ corresponds exactly to post-composition with the $A_n$-linear automorphism $T^{\otimes n}$, i.e. to the automorphism $S_\lambda(T)$ functorially induced by $T$. So the operator in the statement is the one proved semisimple.
(c) Independence of the choice of $e_\lambda$: if $e'$ is another primitive idempotent with $A_ne'\simeq S^\lambda$, then (a) and precomposition with an $A_n$-isomorphism $A_ne\to A_ne'$ give a $T$-equivariant isomorphism $eM\simeq e'M$ (the $T$-action on $\mathrm{Hom}_{A_n}(-,M)$ is by post-composition and hence commutes with precomposition). So the $T$-module isomorphism class depends only on $\lambda$.
(d) Compatibility with scalar extension, needed below: $e_\lambda$ has coefficients in $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and for an idempotent endomorphism $p$ of a finite free module, $\mathrm{rank}(p)=\mathrm{tr}(p)$ because the space splits as $\mathrm{im}\,p\oplus\ker p$ with $p$ the identity on the first and $0$ on the second. Trace is computed from matrix entries, hence unchanged by $\mathbb Q_\ell\hookrightarrow K$. Therefore $\dim_K e_\lambda(\otimes^n_K V_K)=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}e_\lambda(\otimes^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)$, and the natural map $S_\lambda(V)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\to S_\lambda(V_K)$ is an isomorphism, intertwining $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ with $T_{K}$-Schur. The same basis argument applies to $\otimes^n$, $\wedge^n$, $\mathrm{Sym}^n$.

STEP 8 (general tensor constructions and the $G$-submodule clause). Call a pair $(W,T_W)$ a *tensor construction on $(V,T)$* if it is obtained from $(V,T)$ by finitely many operations of the following types: (i) finite direct sums $W=W_1\oplus W_2$, $T_W=T_{W_1}\oplus T_{W_2}$; (ii) tensor products $W=W_1\otimes W_2$, $T_W=T_{W_1}\otimes T_{W_2}$; (iii) duals $W=W_1^{\vee}$, $T_W=(T_{W_1}^{-1})^{t}$; (iv) passage to a $T$-stable direct summand as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space; (v) the operations of Steps 5-7, i.e. images of idempotents of $\mathbb Q_\ell[G]$ for a finite group $G$ acting by permutations of tensor factors (more generally by any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms commuting with $T_W$). We claim $T_W$ is semisimple for every such $W$. Induct on the number of operations. The initial case is $(V,T)$, semisimple by hypothesis. (i) is lemma_9 (a direct sum of operators is semisimple iff each summand is). (ii) is lemma_35(i). (iii) is lemma_64(iv), which states that semisimplicity passes to duals (and to $T^{-1}$ and to nonzero scalar multiples $cT$). (iv) and (v) are lemma_35(ii), using for (v) that the image of an idempotent is a direct summand (Step 3's splitting $W=eW\oplus(1-e)W$) and is $T$-stable because $T_W$ commutes with the idempotent. This covers, in particular, $V^{\otimes a}\otimes(V^{\vee})^{\otimes b}$, all Schur functors $S_\lambda(V)$, $\wedge^n$, $\mathrm{Sym}^n$, divided powers $\Gamma^n$ (in characteristic $0$ these are $\mathrm{Sym}^n$ or its dual, and in any case images of idempotents in $A_n$), Weyl functors, and kernels and images of contraction/pairing maps (which split, hence are direct summands).
Now let $G$ be a group acting on a tensor construction $W$ by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms commuting with $T_W$, and let $U\subset W$ be a $\mathbb Q_\ell[G]$-submodule which is a direct summand as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space and is stable under $T_W$. Then $U$ is a $T_W$-stable direct summand of $W$, and $T_W$ is semisimple on $W$ by the claim, so lemma_35(ii) gives that $T_W|_U$ is semisimple. This is the last assertion of the statement. (When $G$ is finite, the direct-summand hypothesis is automatic by Step 4; $T_W$-stability, however, is a genuine extra hypothesis for an arbitrary $G$-submodule, and is used as stated. In Steps 5-7 stability holds because the subspaces there are images of idempotents of the commutant algebra $\mathbb Q_\ell[G]$.)

STEP 9 (explicit eigenbasis verification, and the eigenvalue descriptions). This gives an independent proof of Steps 1, 5, 6, 7 and identifies the eigenvalues. Let $V_K:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ and $T_K:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$. By lemma_5, $T$ semisimple on $V$ implies $T_K$ semisimple, equivalently diagonalisable, on $V_K$. Every eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $T_K$ is nonzero: $T_Kv=\alpha v$ with $v\ne0$ and $T_K$ invertible force $\alpha\ne0$. Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $V_K$ with $T_Ke_i=\alpha_ie_i$, $\alpha_i\in K^{*}$.
(a) $\otimes^n_KV_K$: the $d^n$ tensors $E_I=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ form a basis and $T_K^{\otimes n}E_I=(\prod_{j=1}^n\alpha_{i_j})E_I$; so $T_K^{\otimes n}$ is diagonalisable. Via the canonical identification $(\otimes^nV)\otimes K\simeq\otimes^n_KV_K$ (both sides have the same indexed basis), lemma_5 applied in the reverse direction gives that $T^{\otimes n}$ is semisimple on $\otimes^nV$ (recovering Step 1), with eigenvalues the products $\prod_j\alpha_{i_j}$.
(b) $\wedge^n_KV_K$: the wedges $e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}$, $i_1<\cdots<i_n$, form a basis, and $T_K^{\wedge n}$ multiplies them by $\prod_j\alpha_{i_j}$; these are exactly the vectors $\mathrm{alt}^{-1}(\mathrm{Alt}(E_I))$ of Step 5, confirming that construction. Likewise $\mathrm{Sym}^n_KV_K$ has the eigenbasis $\{e_1^{a_1}\cdots e_d^{a_d}:\sum a_i=n\}$ with eigenvalues $\prod_i\alpha_i^{a_i}$. Lemma_5 then descends both statements to $\mathbb Q_\ell$.
(c) $S_\lambda(V_K)=e_\lambda(\otimes^n_KV_K)$ by Step 7(d). For each basis tensor $E_I$, every $\sigma E_I$ is again a basis tensor whose index multiset equals that of $I$, hence an eigenvector of $T_K^{\otimes n}$ for the *same* eigenvalue $\prod_j\alpha_{i_j}$. Therefore $e_\lambda(E_I)=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\,\sigma E_I$ ($c_\sigma\in\mathbb Q_\ell\subset K$) is either $0$ or an eigenvector for that eigenvalue. Since the $e_\lambda(E_I)$ span $e_\lambda(\otimes^n_KV_K)$, this space is spanned by eigenvectors, i.e. $T_K$ is diagonalisable on $S_\lambda(V_K)$. By Step 7(d) and lemma_5, $T$ is semisimple on $S_\lambda(V)$; moreover its eigenvalues are precisely the products $\prod_{(r,c)\in\lambda}\alpha_{T(r,c)}$ for the tableaux $T$ of shape $\lambda$ for which the corresponding symmetrised tensor is nonzero (in particular, each is a product of $n$ eigenvalues of $T$).
(d) $V^{\vee}$: the dual basis $e_i^{\vee}$ satisfies $T_{V^{\vee}}e_i^{\vee}=\alpha_i^{-1}e_i^{\vee}$, since $(T^{-1})^te_i^{\vee}(e_j)=e_i^{\vee}(T^{-1}e_j)=\alpha_j^{-1}\delta_{ij}=\alpha_i^{-1}e_i^{\vee}(e_j)$; so $T_{V^{\vee}}$ is diagonalisable on $V_K^{\vee}=(V^{\vee})\otimes K$, and lemma_5 gives semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (independently of the citation of lemma_64(iv) in Step 8).

STEP 10 (conclusion). Steps 1, 5, 6 and 7 establish the semisimplicity of the automorphisms induced by $T$ on $\otimes^nV$, $\wedge^nV$, $\mathrm{Sym}^nV$ and on each Schur functor $S_\lambda(V)\subset\otimes^nV$; Step 8 establishes the general statement for every $\mathbb Q_\ell[G]$-submodule of a tensor construction that is a vector-space direct summand and is $T$-stable; Step 9 verifies all of these by explicit eigenbases and records the eigenvalues. All edge cases ($V=0$, $d<n$) were disposed of at the start. This completes the proof.

REMARK (relation with the conjecture, not used above). Since lemma_64(iv) also gives that semisimplicity passes to $T^{-1}$, the same conclusions hold for the inverse operator; in geometric applications (e.g. together with lemma_6a, which identifies geometric with the inverse of arithmetic Frobenius) this means the tensor constructions of $H^i_{\acute et}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)$ — exterior, symmetric and Schur powers, and the pieces cut out by Chow-K\"unneth idempotents, which are images of idempotents in the commutant algebra as in Step 3 — inherit semisimplicity of Frobenius from $H^i$ itself.

lemma_78.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective variety over F_q of pure dimension d, let k=\overline{F}_q, let l\neq p be prime, and let F be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of X_k. For each j\ge 0 let cl: CH^j(X) \to H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_l(j)) be the l-adic cycle class map, and let F_* denote the induced \mathbb{Q}_l-linear automorphism of H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_l(j)) coming from the arithmetic Frobenius structures on X_k and on \mathbb{Q}_l(j), on which F acts as multiplication by q^{-j}. Then F_*(cl(z))=cl(z) for every codimension-j cycle z on X defined over F_q. Equivalently, for any nonzero \xi \in \mathbb{Q}_l(j) and any such z, writing c_z \in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_l) for the unique vector with cl(z)=c_z\otimes\xi under the identification H^{2j}(\mathbb{Q}_l(j))=H^{2j}(\mathbb{Q}_l)\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}_l}\mathbb{Q}_l(j), one has F_*c_z=q^{j}c_z.
lemma_78.proof:
Proof. Let k = Fbar_q and let sigma:k->k be sigma(t)=t^q. Write Lambda=Q_l. Let p:X_k->X be the projection. The q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of X_k is F=id_X times sigma; by lemma_6a this is the arithmetic Frobenius operator on etale cohomology. We use the convention stated in the lemma that the arithmetic Frobenius structure on Lambda(j) on X_k acts on every geometric fiber as multiplication by q^{-j}. By lemma_45_finite_frob, any arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism phi:F^*K->K on a bounded constructible complex K on X_k induces a canonical Lambda-linear automorphism F_* on H^n(X_k,K).

1. A formal fixedness lemma. Let G be a Lambda-sheaf on X and put G_k=p^*G on X_k. Since p o F = p, there is a canonical descent isomorphism theta_G:F^*G_k = F^*p^*G -> (p o F)^*G = p^*G = G_k. For G=Lambda(j), theta_G is the arithmetic Frobenius structure whose fiber action is q^{-j}; for G=Lambda it is the identity. We claim that for every n and every alpha in H^n(X,G), the base-changed class p^*alpha in H^n(X_k,G_k) satisfies F_*(p^*alpha)=p^*alpha.

To prove the claim, describe cohomology by morphisms in the derived category. H^n(X,G)=Hom_{D(X)}(Lambda_X,G[n]) and H^n(X_k,G_k)=Hom_{D(X_k)}(Lambda_{X_k},G_k[n]). If alpha is represented by u:Lambda_X->G[n], then p^*alpha is represented by p^*u:Lambda_{X_k}->G_k[n]. By lemma_45_finite_frob, the Frobenius automorphism associated with theta_G sends a class v:Lambda_{X_k}->G_k[n] to the class represented by theta_G o F^*v o theta_Lambda^{-1}. Taking v=p^*u gives theta_G o F^*p^*u o theta_Lambda^{-1}. The canonical isomorphism F^*p^* -> (p o F)^* = p^* is exactly theta_G on coefficients and theta_Lambda on the constant sheaf. Functoriality of pullback therefore identifies theta_G o F^*p^*u o theta_Lambda^{-1} with p^*u. Hence F_*(p^*alpha)=p^*alpha.

2. Application to cycle classes. Let cl_X:CH^j(X)->H^{2j}(X,Lambda(j)) be the absolute l-adic cycle class map. For an integral closed subscheme Z subset X of codimension j with closed immersion i:Z->X, cl_X([Z])=i_*(1_Z), where i_*:H^0(Z,Lambda)->H^{2j}(X,Lambda(j)) is the Gysin map; for a general cycle extend linearly. The geometric cycle class cl in the statement is the base change of cl_X. Indeed, if p_Z:Z_k->Z and i_k:Z_k->X_k, the square
Z_k -> X_k
|      |
p_Z    p
v      v
Z -> X
is cartesian, p is flat (a field extension), and Gysin maps are compatible with flat base change, so p^*i_*(1_Z)=i_{k,*}p_Z^*(1_Z)=i_{k,*}(1_{Z_k}), which is the usual geometric cycle class of Z_k. Thus cl=p^* o cl_X.

Apply the fixedness claim with G=Lambda(j), n=2j, and alpha=cl_X(z). Since z is a cycle on X, i.e. defined over F_q, cl(z)=p^*cl_X(z), and therefore F_*cl(z)=F_*p^*cl_X(z)=p^*cl_X(z)=cl(z). This proves the first assertion.

3. The untwisted formulation. Let V=H^{2j}(X_k,Lambda) and W=Lambda(j). Since W is a one-dimensional Lambda-vector space, there is a natural isomorphism V tensor W -> H^{2j}(X_k,Lambda(j)). Under this isomorphism the arithmetic Frobenius operator on the right is F_V tensor F_W, where F_V is the operator on V coming from the identity structure on Lambda and F_W is multiplication by q^{-j} on W. This follows by choosing a basis of W: the constant sheaf with fiber W is a direct sum of copies of Lambda, and the Frobenius structure is the direct sum of the given structures; in rank one it is the scalar q^{-j}.

Fix a nonzero xi in W and write cl(z)=c_z tensor xi. Then
F_*cl(z) = (F_V c_z) tensor (q^{-j} xi).
If F_*cl(z)=cl(z), then ((F_V c_z)-q^j c_z) tensor xi=0. Because xi is nonzero, choose a linear functional lambda:W->Lambda with lambda(xi)=1; applying id_V tensor lambda gives F_V c_z - q^j c_z=0. Conversely, if F_V c_z=q^j c_z, then F_*cl(z)=c_z tensor xi=cl(z). The statement denotes F_V by F_*. Hence the equivalent formulation holds.

4. Edge cases. For j=0, W=Lambda and q^{-0}=1, so the same argument gives F_*cl(z)=cl(z) and F_*c_z=c_z. The proof uses only that z is a cycle on X, hence defined over F_q; it does not require the components of z to be smooth or geometrically integral. If z is a sum of integral cycles, linearity of cl and of F_* reduces the statement to the integral case.

Thus every codimension-j cycle on X defined over F_q has a fixed class in H^{2j}_et(X_k,Q_l(j)) under arithmetic Frobenius, and its untwisted coefficient is an eigenvector of arithmetic Frobenius with eigenvalue q^j.

lemma_90.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, \(V\) a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), \(m\ge1\) an integer and \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\). Suppose \(V\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by vectors \(v\) satisfying \(T^{m}v=c\,v\). Then \(T^{m}=c\,\mathrm{id}_V\); hence the minimal polynomial \(\mu_T\) divides \(t^{m}-c\), which is squarefree in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) because \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) has characteristic \(0\) and \(c\neq0\); and \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\). No basis of eigenvectors and no permutation of a basis is assumed; a spanning set of \(T^m\)-eigenvectors for one common eigenvalue suffices.
lemma_90.proof:
We work over k := \mathbb Q_\ell. Write \operatorname{id} for the identity of V and, for a polynomial P=\sum_j p_j t^j\in k[t], write P(T):=\sum_j p_j T^{j}\in\operatorname{End}_k(V).

**Step 0 (the zero space).** If V=0 then T=\operatorname{id}_0=0 and c\operatorname{id}_0=0, so T^m=c\operatorname{id}_V holds, and T is semisimple on V (the zero module is the empty direct sum of simple modules, and its minimal polynomial is 1, which is squarefree). Henceforth assume V\neq 0.

**Step 1 (the spanning hypothesis forces a scalar power).** Put S := T^{m}-c\operatorname{id}_V\in\operatorname{End}_k(V); S is k-linear. Let \Sigma:=\{v\in V: T^{m}v=cv\}=\ker S, which by hypothesis spans V. Take any v\in V. Since \Sigma spans, there are finitely many v_1,\dots,v_r\in\Sigma and scalars \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\in k with v=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i v_i. By k-linearity of S,
Sv=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\,S v_i=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\cdot 0=0.
Thus S vanishes on all of V, i.e.
\[\qquad T^{m}=c\,\operatorname{id}_V.\]
Note that no linear independence of the spanning vectors was used, and no basis of eigenvectors nor any permutation of a basis is involved: a single common eigenvalue c for the single operator T^m suffices. (Consistency check: since c\neq 0, the identity above gives T\circ(c^{-1}T^{m-1})=(c^{-1}T^{m-1})\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V, so T is indeed invertible, in agreement with the hypothesis T\in\operatorname{GL}(V).)

**Step 2 (the minimal polynomial divides t^m-c).** Let \mu_T\in k[t] be the monic minimal polynomial of T, i.e. the monic generator of the ideal \mathfrak a:=\{P\in k[t]:P(T)=0\}. This ideal is nonzero (it contains the characteristic polynomial by Cayley\textendash Hamilton, and in any case it contains t^m-c by Step 1), and k[t] is a Euclidean domain, so \mathfrak a=(\mu_T). The polynomial g(t):=t^{m}-c is nonzero (it is monic of degree m\ge 1) and satisfies g(T)=T^{m}-c\operatorname{id}_V=0 by Step 1; hence g\in\mathfrak a=(\mu_T), which means precisely
\[\qquad \mu_T\ \text{divides}\ t^{m}-c\ \text{in}\ \mathbb Q_\ell[t].\]

**Step 3 (t^m-c is squarefree over \mathbb Q_\ell).** We use the criterion of lemma_64(ii): over a field of characteristic 0, a nonzero polynomial h is squarefree if and only if \gcd(h,h')=1. Take h=g=t^{m}-c. Then g'=m\,t^{m-1}.
- If m=1, then g=t-c and g'=1, so \gcd(g,g')=1.
- If m\ge 2: the integer m is nonzero in k because \operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0, so g'=m t^{m-1} is a nonzero polynomial of degree m-1\ge 1. Suppose d\in k[t] is a common divisor of g and g' of positive degree. Since \overline{k}=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is algebraically closed, d acquires a root \alpha\in\overline{k}; then g'(\alpha)=0 and g(\alpha)=0. From g'(\alpha)=m\alpha^{m-1}=0 and m\neq 0 in \overline k we get \alpha=0, and then 0=g(0)=-c, contradicting c\in k^{\times}. Hence no such d exists, so \gcd(g,g')=1 in k[t] (the Euclidean algorithm computes this gcd inside k[t], so computing in \overline k[t] cannot produce a smaller gcd; equivalently, any common divisor in k[t] is a common divisor in \overline k[t]).
By the quoted criterion, g=t^{m}-c is squarefree in \mathbb Q_\ell[t]. (This is exactly where characteristic 0 is used: in characteristic p>0 dividing m, the derivative of t^m-c is 0 and the statement fails, e.g. t^{p}-c=(t-\gamma)^{p} over a field containing a p-th root \gamma of c; see the warning in lemma_64(ii).)

**Step 4 (\mu_T is squarefree).** Factor g into monic irreducibles in the UFD k[t]: g=\prod_{i\in I} f_i^{e_i}. Squarefreeness of g (Step 3) is equivalent to e_i=1 for all i, so g=\prod_{i\in I}f_i with the f_i pairwise distinct and irreducible. Since \mu_T is a monic divisor of g (Step 2), unique factorisation gives \mu_T=\prod_{i\in J}f_i for some subset J\subseteq I; in particular \mu_T is a product of pairwise distinct irreducibles, i.e. \mu_T is squarefree in \mathbb Q_\ell[t].

**Step 5 (semisimplicity).** By lemma_60(ii) applied to the nonzero finite-dimensional k-space V and T\in\operatorname{GL}(V), T is semisimple on V if and only if \mu_T is squarefree in k[t]. Step 4 gives exactly this, so
\[\qquad T\ \text{is semisimple on}\ V.\]

**Step 6 (equivalent formulation over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and the diagonalisability statement).** For completeness we verify the same conclusion by the route of lemma_5, which also exhibits the eigenspace decomposition after scalar extension. Let V^{\sim}:=V\otimes_k\overline k and T^{\sim}:=T\otimes\operatorname{id}. By Step 1, (T^{\sim})^{m}=c\operatorname{id}_{V^{\sim}}, and by lemma_64(i) the minimal polynomial of T^{\sim} is \mu_T viewed in \overline k[t], hence still divides t^{m}-c. The polynomial t^{m}-c has exactly m roots in \overline k and they are pairwise distinct: choosing one root \alpha (so \alpha^{m}=c, and \alpha\neq 0 since c\neq 0), every root is of the form \alpha\zeta with \zeta^{m}=1, and X^{m}-1 has m distinct roots in \overline k because its derivative mX^{m-1} does not vanish at any of them (\zeta\neq 0 and m\neq0 in \overline k). Write \{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_s\} for the distinct roots of \mu_T in \overline k (s\ge 1 since \mu_T is nonconstant: V^{\sim}\neq 0); these are among the roots of t^m-c, so they are pairwise distinct and \mu_{T^{\sim}}=\prod_{j=1}^{s}(t-\alpha_j) is a product of pairwise coprime factors. The Chinese remainder theorem in \overline k[t] gives \overline k[t]/(\mu_{T^{\sim}})\cong\prod_j\overline k[t]/(t-\alpha_j); since V^{\sim} is a module over \overline k[t]/(\mu_{T^{\sim}}) on which t acts as T^{\sim}, we obtain the decomposition
\[\qquad V^{\sim}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{s}\ker\bigl(T^{\sim}-\alpha_j\operatorname{id}\bigr),\]
sending w\in V^{\sim} to its components via the idempotents of the product decomposition (explicitly, w=\sum_j e_j(T^{\sim})w with e_j the idempotent mapping to 1 in the j-th factor and to 0 in the others; each e_j(T^{\sim})w lies in \ker(T^{\sim}-\alpha_j) because (t-\alpha_j) annihilates the j-th factor, and \sum_j e_j=1 in the product). Each summand is an honest eigenspace of T^{\sim}, so T^{\sim} is diagonalisable on V^{\sim}. By lemma_5, T is semisimple on V if and only if T^{\sim} is diagonalisable on V^{\sim}; this again yields Step 5. (Equivalently, one may invoke lemma_64(iii) with k\subseteq\overline k, which is the same statement phrased via squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial.)

**Conclusion.** We have shown: (a) the spanning hypothesis implies T^{m}=c\operatorname{id}_V; (b) consequently \mu_T\mid t^{m}-c in \mathbb Q_\ell[t]; (c) t^{m}-c is squarefree in \mathbb Q_\ell[t] because \operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0 and c\neq 0 (Step 3, using lemma_64(ii)); (d) hence \mu_T is squarefree; and (e) by lemma_60(ii) (equivalently, by the eigenspace decomposition over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell together with lemma_5) T is semisimple on V. This proves all the claims of the lemma, including the edge case V=0 handled in Step 0 and the case m=1 (where the hypothesis already says T=c\operatorname{id}_V, which is semisimple with \mu_T=t-c). \hfill\blacksquare

lemma_83.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective variety over F_q, let k=\overline{F}_q, let l\neq p be prime, and let \Delta:X_k\to (X\times_{F_q}X)_k and \mathrm{pr}_1:(X\times_{F_q}X)_k\to X_k be the diagonal and the first projection. For every n\ge 0 the composite \Delta^*\circ \mathrm{pr}_1^* of \acute etale cohomology pullbacks is the identity of H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_l), both maps commute with the q-power arithmetic Frobenius, and the image of \mathrm{pr}_1^* is a Frobenius-stable direct summand of H^n_{\acute et}((X\times_{F_q}X)_k,\mathbb Q_l) on which Frobenius is identified with its action on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_l). Consequently, if arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on H^n_{\acute et}((X\times_{F_q}X)_k,\mathbb Q_l) for every n, then it acts semisimply on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_l) for every n.
lemma_83.proof:
Write $Y:=X\times_{\mathbf F_q}X$, and $\sigma:k\to k$, $a\mapsto a^q$, for the $q$-power automorphism of $k=\overline{\mathbf F}_q$. For any $\mathbf F_q$-scheme $Z$ of finite type put $Z_k:=Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$ and
$$\mathrm F_Z:=\mathrm{id}_Z\times\sigma:Z_k\longrightarrow Z_k ,\qquad \Phi_Z:=(\mathrm F_Z)^*:H^n(Z_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(Z_k,\mathbf Q_\ell).$$
By lemma_6a (applied to $Z$ over $\mathbf F_q$) $\Phi_Z$ is exactly the operator called the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius on $H^n_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, it is $\mathbf Q_\ell$-linear and invertible, and its inverse $\Phi_Z^{-1}$ is the geometric Frobenius. So proving the statement for $\Phi$ proves it for the arithmetic Frobenius as named in the lemma.

**Step 0 (finite-dimensionality).** $X$ is proper over $\mathbf F_q$, and $Y=X\times_{\mathbf F_q}X$ is proper over $\mathbf F_q$ as well: $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ is proper, hence so is the base change $Y\to X$, and the composite $Y\to X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ of proper morphisms is proper. Take $K=\mathbf Q_{\ell,Z_k}$, which lies in $D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:\mathrm F_Z^*\mathbf Q_{\ell,Z_k}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf Q_{\ell,Z_k}$. Lemma_45_finite_frob then gives, for $Z=X$ and $Z=Y$, that $H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ and $H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q_\ell$-vector spaces for every $n\ge 0$. All vector spaces below are finite-dimensional, so the linear-algebra lemmas we quote apply.

**Step 1 (the two geometric maps are base changes of $\mathbf F_q$-morphisms).** Let $p_1:Y\to X$ be the first projection, an $\mathbf F_q$-morphism, and let $\delta:X\to Y$, $\delta=(\mathrm{id}_X,\mathrm{id}_X)$, be the relative diagonal over $\mathbf F_q$ (a morphism over $\mathbf F_q$ because $Y$ is the fibre product of $X$ with itself over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$). Under the canonical identification $Y_k=(X\times_{\mathbf F_q}X)\times_{\mathbf F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k\simeq X_k\times_k X_k$ (which on $T$-points, for a $k$-scheme $T$, is the bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf F_q}(T,X)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf F_q}(T,X)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf F_q}(T,X\times_{\mathbf F_q}X)$ given by the universal property of the fibre product), the morphisms of the statement are
$$\mathrm{pr}_1=p_1\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k}:Y_k\to X_k,\qquad \Delta=\delta\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k}:X_k\to Y_k.$$
Indeed, the first projection of $X_k\times_kX_k$ restricts to $p_1$ on the $X$-factors and to the identity on the $\operatorname{Spec}k$-factor; and base change preserves diagonals, so the diagonal of $X_k\times_kX_k$ over $k$ is $\delta\times\mathrm{id}$. We shall use twice the elementary rule for composites of base-changed morphisms: for $\mathbf F_q$-morphisms $Z'\xrightarrow{g}Z\xrightarrow{f}Z''$ one has $(f\times\mathrm{id})\circ(g\times\mathrm{id})=(f\circ g)\times\mathrm{id}$, and for any $\mathbf F_q$-morphism $f:Z'\to Z$,
$$(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\sigma)\circ(f\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k})=f\times\sigma=(f\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{Z'}\times\sigma),\tag{$*$}$$
both composites being the morphism $Z'_k\to Z_k$ which on a $T$-point $(a:T\to Z,\;b:T\to\operatorname{Spec}k)$ gives $(a,\sigma\circ b)$.

**Step 2 ($\Delta^*\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*=\mathrm{id}$).** From the universal property of the fibre product, $p_1\circ\delta=\mathrm{id}_X$ (the first component of $(\mathrm{id}_X,\mathrm{id}_X)$ is $\mathrm{id}_X$). Base-changing to $k$ and using the composition rule of Step 1 gives $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\Delta=(p_1\circ\delta)\times\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k}=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}$. Étale cohomology with $\mathbf Q_\ell$-coefficients is a contravariant functor on the category of $k$-schemes: for composable morphisms $A\xrightarrow{u}B\xrightarrow{v}C$ one has $(v\circ u)^*=u^*\circ v^*$, and $\mathrm{id}^*=\mathrm{id}$. Hence on $H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$,
$$\Delta^*\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*=(\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\Delta)^*=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}^*=\mathrm{id}.$$
In particular $\mathrm{pr}_1^*$ is injective and $\Delta^*$ is surjective.

**Step 3 (both pullbacks commute with Frobenius).** Using $(*)$ with $f=p_1$ and with $f=\delta$:
$$\mathrm{pr}_1\circ \mathrm F_Y=(p_1\times\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\sigma)=p_1\times\sigma=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)\circ(p_1\times\mathrm{id})=\mathrm F_X\circ\mathrm{pr}_1,$$
$$\mathrm F_Y\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\sigma)\circ(\delta\times\mathrm{id})=\delta\times\sigma=(\delta\times\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)=\Delta\circ \mathrm F_X.$$
Taking contravariant pullbacks on $H^n(-,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ (all four composites are morphisms $Y_k\to X_k$ resp. $X_k\to Y_k$) yields, for every $n\ge0$,
$$\Phi_Y\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Phi_X\qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta^*\circ\Phi_Y=\Phi_X\circ\Delta^*.\tag{3.1}$$
Thus $\mathrm{pr}_1^*:H^n(X_k)\to H^n(Y_k)$ and $\Delta^*:H^n(Y_k)\to H^n(X_k)$ are $\Phi$-equivariant; this is precisely the assertion that "both maps commute with the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius". (Since $\Phi_X,\Phi_Y$ are automorphisms by lemma_6a, the same relations with $\Phi^{-1}$ show the analogous statement for geometric Frobenius.)

**Step 4 (the image of $\mathrm{pr}_1^*$ is a direct summand).** Set $e:=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Delta^*\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf Q_\ell}(H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell))$. By Step 2,
$$e^2=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ(\Delta^*\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*)\circ\Delta^*=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\mathrm{id}\circ\Delta^*=e,$$
so $e$ is an idempotent, and $H^n(Y_k)=\mathrm{im}(e)\oplus\ker(e)$ (every $x$ decomposes as $x=ex+(x-ex)$, with $ex\in\mathrm{im}(e)$, $x-ex\in\ker(e)$, and $\mathrm{im}(e)\cap\ker(e)=0$ because $e$ acts as the identity on its image). We identify $\mathrm{im}(e)$ with $\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$: clearly $\mathrm{im}(e)\subseteq\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$; conversely if $x=\mathrm{pr}_1^*(y)$ then $ex=\mathrm{pr}_1^*(\Delta^*\mathrm{pr}_1^*y)=\mathrm{pr}_1^*(y)=x$ by Step 2, so $x\in\mathrm{im}(e)$. Hence
$$\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)=\mathrm{im}(e)$$
is a $\mathbf Q_\ell$-vector-space direct summand of $H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, with complement $\ker(e)$, and $\mathrm{pr}_1^*:H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$ is an isomorphism (injectivity is Step 2, surjectivity onto the image is by definition).

**Step 5 (the summand is Frobenius-stable).** Using (3.1) twice,
$$\Phi_Y\circ e=\Phi_Y\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Delta^*=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Phi_X\circ\Delta^*=\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Delta^*\circ\Phi_Y=e\circ\Phi_Y.$$
So $\Phi_Y$ commutes with the projector $e$; therefore $\Phi_Y(\mathrm{im}e)\subseteq\mathrm{im}e$ (if $x=ey$ then $\Phi_Yx=\Phi_Yey=e\Phi_Yy$) and also $\Phi_Y(\ker e)\subseteq\ker e$. Since $\Phi_Y$ is invertible and $\Phi_Y^{-1}$ commutes with $e$ as well, $\Phi_Y(\mathrm{im}e)=\mathrm{im}e$: the summand $\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$ is Frobenius-stable, and $\Phi_Y$ restricts to an automorphism of it.

**Step 6 (the Frobenius on the summand is the Frobenius of $X$).** The isomorphism $\mathrm{pr}_1^*:H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)\subseteq H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ satisfies $\mathrm{pr}_1^*\circ\Phi_X=\Phi_Y\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^*$ by (3.1); i.e. it is an isomorphism of $\mathbf Q_\ell$-vector spaces intertwining $\Phi_X$ with the restriction $\Phi_Y|_{\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)}$. This is the claimed identification of Frobenius on the summand with Frobenius on $H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$.

**Step 7 (consequence for semisimplicity).** Assume that for every $n\ge0$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $\Phi_Y$ acts semisimply on $H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)=H^n_{\acute et}((X\times_{\mathbf F_q}X)_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$. Fix $n\ge0$. By Step 5, $U:=\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$ is a $\Phi_Y$-stable direct summand of the finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q_\ell$-space $H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, so lemma_35(ii) (with $V=H^n(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, $T=\Phi_Y$, $U$ as in Step 5) gives that $\Phi_Y|_U$ is semisimple on $U$. By Step 6 the spaces $(H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell),\Phi_X)$ and $(U,\Phi_Y|_U)$ are isomorphic as vector spaces with an invertible operator, so lemma_8 applies and yields that $\Phi_X$ is semisimple on $H^n(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$. As $n$ was arbitrary, the arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on $H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

*Remark (not used above).* The same argument with the roles reversed shows that $\Phi_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n(Y_k)$ if and only if it is semisimple on $\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$ and on $\ker(e)$ simultaneously (lemma_9 applied to the Frobenius-module decomposition of Step 5); the lemma only needs the direction that transfers semisimplicity from $\mathrm{im}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*)$ back to $H^n(X_k)$.

lemma_95.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective variety over \mathbb F_q, let k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q, let \ell\neq p be prime, and let G be a finite abelian group of \mathbb F_q-automorphisms of X whose order is prime to \ell. Fix n\ge 0 and suppose that every character space of G on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is at most one-dimensional, i.e. for each homomorphism \chi:G\to\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{*} the subspace on which g\in G acts as \chi(g) has dimension \le 1. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
lemma_95.proof:
We prove that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on V := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ), under the stated multiplicity-one hypothesis for the G-character spaces. The argument is: (i) the G-representation Vbar := V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Qbar_ℓ splits as a direct sum of its character spaces M_χ (pure character theory for a finite abelian group, done by explicit idempotent computations); (ii) Frobenius preserves each M_χ because it commutes with G; (iii) each M_χ has dimension ≤ 1 by hypothesis, so a choice of nonzero vector in each nonzero M_χ is a basis of Vbar consisting of Frobenius eigenvectors, i.e. Frob is diagonalisable over Qbar_ℓ; (iv) descend to Q_ℓ.

STEP 0 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of F).
The variety X is smooth projective over F_q, hence proper. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to K = Q_{ℓ,X_k}, the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism ψ: F_X^* Q_{ℓ,X_k} →~ Q_{ℓ,X_k}: it gives that H^n(X_k, Q_ℓ) = V is finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ, and equips it with a canonical Q_ℓ-linear automorphism, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F. Concretely (and consistently with the notation of lemma_6a) F = F_ar = (id_X × σ)^*, where σ: k → k, a ↦ a^q; lemma_6a asserts that this is a Q_ℓ-linear automorphism of V (with inverse the geometric Frobenius). Put Vbar := V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Qbar_ℓ, a finite-dimensional Qbar_ℓ-vector space, and Fbar := F ⊗ id_{Qbar_ℓ} ∈ GL(Vbar).

STEP 1 (the G-action, and its commutation with F).
For g ∈ G let g_k := g ×_{F_q} id_k: X_k → X_k; since g is an F_q-automorphism of X, g_k is a well-defined k-morphism, and g_k is an automorphism with (g^{-1})_k = (g_k)^{-1}. We take the G-action on V used in lemma_82, namely g · v := (g_k)^*(v), and we extend it Qbar_ℓ-linearly to Vbar; thus M := Vbar is a Qbar_ℓ[G]-module. Because g is defined over F_q, the squares commute as morphisms X_k → X_k: (id_X × σ) ∘ g_k = g_k ∘ (id_X × σ) (both are the map (x, a) ↦ (g x, a^q)). Since pullback is contravariant, this gives (g_k)^* ∘ F = F ∘ (g_k)^* on V, i.e. F(gv) = g(Fv) for all g ∈ G, v ∈ V; this is exactly the first statement of lemma_82, which we cite (it also needs gcd(|G|, ℓ) = 1, which is part of our hypotheses). Extending scalars, Fbar(gv) = g(Fbar v) for all g ∈ G, v ∈ Vbar. We note once and for all that the choice of convention is immaterial: had we used g ↦ ((g^{-1})_k)^* = (g_k)^{-1*}, the operator attached to g would be inverted, which replaces a character χ by χ^{-1}; this is a bijection of the character group, so the hypothesis "each character space has dimension ≤ 1" and the conclusion are unchanged. Henceforth we work with the convention above.

STEP 2 (character theory of the finite abelian group G over Qbar_ℓ).
Let X(G) := Hom(G, Qbar_ℓ^{×}) be the group of characters, under pointwise multiplication; the identity element is the trivial character 1, and χ^{-1}(g) = χ(g)^{-1}. Since Qbar_ℓ has characteristic 0, for every m ≥ 1 the polynomial t^m − 1 is separable (its derivative m t^{m−1} is nonzero and coprime to t^m − 1), and Qbar_ℓ being algebraically closed gives μ_m(Qbar_ℓ) a cyclic group of order m; in particular μ_{|G|}(Qbar_ℓ) ≅ Z/|G|, and every character takes values in μ_{|G|} because g^{|G|} = 1 forces χ(g)^{|G|} = 1.

(2a) Separation of points. For every g ∈ G with g ≠ 1 there exists χ ∈ X(G) with χ(g) ≠ 1. If G = {1} the statement is vacuous; note also that then X(G) = {1}, so |X(G)| = |G| = 1, and everything below reduces to M = M_1. Assume G ≠ {1}. By the structure theorem for finite abelian groups, write G ≅ ⊕_{i=1}^{s} Z/m_i with integers m_i ≥ 2 (we normalise so that no factor m_i = 1 is listed; the decomposition is empty only when G = {1}, already treated). Write the image of g as (g_1, …, g_s) with g_i ∈ Z/m_i; since g ≠ 1, some index i_0 has g_{i_0} ≢ 0 (mod m_{i_0}). Choose a primitive m_{i_0}-th root of unity ζ_{i_0} ∈ Qbar_ℓ^{×} (exists by the preceding paragraph) and define χ_0: G → Qbar_ℓ^{×} by χ_0(h) := ζ_{i_0}^{h_{i_0}}, where h_{i_0} ∈ {0, …, m_{i_0}−1} is the i_0-th coordinate of h. This is a homomorphism (coordinates add mod m_{i_0}, and ζ_{i_0}^{m_{i_0}} = 1). Now χ_0(g) = ζ_{i_0}^{g_{i_0}}, and the order of ζ_{i_0}^{g_{i_0}} in the cyclic group ⟨ζ_{i_0}⟩ of order m_{i_0} equals m_{i_0}/gcd(m_{i_0}, g_{i_0}). Since g_{i_0} ≢ 0 (mod m_{i_0}), gcd(m_{i_0}, g_{i_0}) < m_{i_0}, so this order is ≥ 2; hence χ_0(g) ≠ 1. This is the required character (χ := χ_0 suffices).

(2a') Cardinality. |X(G)| = |G|. Indeed X(G) = Hom(G, Qbar_ℓ^{×}) = Hom(G, μ_{|G|}) ≅ ∏_{i=1}^{s} Hom(Z/m_i, μ_{|G|}), and Hom(Z/m, μ_{|G|}) ≅ μ_m (a homomorphism is determined by the image of 1, which may be any element of order dividing m), of order m. Hence |X(G)| = ∏_i m_i = |G|. (For G = {1} this reads 1 = 1.)

(2b) First orthogonality. For g ∈ G, ∑_{χ ∈ X(G)} χ(g) = |G| if g = 1 and 0 otherwise. If g = 1, every χ(g) = χ(1) = 1 because χ is a homomorphism into a multiplicative group, and the sum has |X(G)| = |G| terms by (2a'). If g ≠ 1, choose χ_0 ∈ X(G) with χ_0(g) ≠ 1 by (2a). Left-multiplication by χ_0 is a bijection of the finite set X(G) (inverse: multiplication by χ_0^{-1}), so with S := ∑_χ χ(g),
S = ∑_{χ ∈ X(G)} (χ_0 χ)(g) = ∑_{χ ∈ X(G)} χ_0(g) χ(g) = χ_0(g) S.
Thus (1 − χ_0(g)) S = 0 in Qbar_ℓ, and 1 − χ_0(g) ≠ 0, so S = 0.

(2b') Second orthogonality. For χ, ψ ∈ X(G), ∑_{g ∈ G} χ(g)^{-1} ψ(g) = |G| if χ = ψ and 0 otherwise. Indeed the summand is (ψχ^{-1})(g), and applying (2b) to the element g and the character group written additively is not what we need here; rather, apply (2b)'s proof verbatim to the character φ := ψχ^{-1} ∈ X(G): ∑_g φ(g) = |G| if φ(g) = 1 for all g, and 0 otherwise. Now φ(g) = 1 for all g ⇔ ψ(g) = χ(g) for all g ⇔ χ = ψ as functions (hence as characters). For the vanishing case, if φ ≠ 1 as a function there is g_0 with φ(g_0) ≠ 1, and the same bijection argument as in (2b) (multiplying X(G) by φ, which is a bijection with inverse multiplication by φ^{-1}) gives ∑_g φ(g) = φ(g_0) ∑_g φ(g), forcing the sum to be 0. Note that no separation input is needed here: distinctness of χ and ψ is by definition the existence of a point where the functions differ.

(2c) The idempotents. For χ ∈ X(G) set e_χ := (1/|G|) ∑_{g ∈ G} χ(g)^{-1} g ∈ Qbar_ℓ[G] (|G| is invertible in Qbar_ℓ since char Qbar_ℓ = 0). These agree with the elements of lemma_82 in the abelian case: for an abelian group every irreducible character has degree χ(1) = 1, since χ is a homomorphism into the multiplicative group Qbar_ℓ^{×}, so the idempotent of lemma_82 attached to χ is exactly e_χ. We verify the needed properties by direct computation, not quoting any representation theory.
• Eigenproperty: for h ∈ G,
  h e_χ = (1/|G|) ∑_{g} χ(g)^{-1} h g = (1/|G|) ∑_{a} χ(h^{-1}a)^{-1} a  (a := hg)
      = (1/|G|) ∑_{a} χ(h) χ(a)^{-1} a = χ(h) e_χ.
  Hence also e_χ h = χ(h) e_χ (G is abelian).
• Orthogonality of idempotents:
  e_χ e_ψ = (1/|G|^2) ∑_{g,h} χ(g)^{-1} ψ(h)^{-1} g h = (1/|G|^2) ∑_{a,h'} ψ(h')^{-1} h' ∑_{g} χ(g)^{-1} ψ(g),
  where we set a := g h, so h = g^{-1}a and ψ(h)^{-1} = ψ(g^{-1}a)^{-1} = ψ(g)ψ(a)^{-1}; regrouping gives
  e_χ e_ψ = (1/|G|^2) (∑_{a} ψ(a)^{-1} a)(∑_{g} (ψχ^{-1})(g)) = (1/|G|^2) (|G| e_ψ)(|G| δ_{χ,ψ}) = δ_{χ,ψ} e_χ,
  using ∑_a ψ(a)^{-1} a = |G| e_ψ (definition) and ∑_g (ψχ^{-1})(g) = |G| δ_{χ,ψ} (by (2b') multiplied by nothing — precisely, (2b') with the pair (χ, ψ) gives ∑_g χ(g)^{-1}ψ(g) = |G| δ_{χ,ψ}).
• Completeness: ∑_{χ ∈ X(G)} e_χ = (1/|G|) ∑_{g} (∑_χ χ(g)^{-1}) g = (1/|G|)(|G| · 1) = 1, since t ↦ t^{-1} is a bijection of X(G) and (2b) gives ∑_χ χ(g)^{-1} = ∑_χ χ(g) = |G| δ_{g,1}.

(2d) Identification of the character spaces. For χ ∈ X(G) let M_χ := {v ∈ M : g v = χ(g) v for all g ∈ G}, the subspace appearing in the hypothesis of the lemma, and e_χ M := {e_χ v : v ∈ M}. If v = e_χ w then g v = g e_χ w = χ(g) e_χ w = χ(g) v by the eigenproperty, so e_χ M ⊆ M_χ. Conversely, if v ∈ M_χ then
  e_χ v = (1/|G|) ∑_{g} χ(g)^{-1} g v = (1/|G|) ∑_{g} χ(g)^{-1} χ(g) v = (1/|G|) |G| v = v,
so v ∈ e_χ M. Hence M_χ = e_χ M for every χ. Since ∑_χ e_χ = 1 we have M = ∑_χ M_χ, and the sum is direct: if ∑_χ m_χ = 0 with m_χ ∈ M_χ = e_χ M (so e_χ m_χ = m_χ and e_ψ m_χ = 0 for ψ ≠ χ by (2c)), applying e_ψ yields m_ψ = 0. Thus
  M = V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Qbar_ℓ = ⊕_{χ ∈ X(G)} M_χ  as Qbar_ℓ-vector spaces (and as Qbar_ℓ[G]-modules).

STEP 3 (each M_χ is Fbar-stable). Let v ∈ M_χ and g ∈ G. By Step 1, g(Fbar v) = Fbar(g v) = Fbar(χ(g) v) = χ(g) Fbar v, the last equality using Qbar_ℓ-linearity of Fbar. Hence Fbar v ∈ M_χ. So each M_χ is an Fbar-stable subspace of M.

STEP 4 (diagonalisability of Fbar over Qbar_ℓ). By hypothesis, dim_{Qbar_ℓ} M_χ ≤ 1 for every χ. For each χ with M_χ ≠ 0 choose a nonzero v_χ ∈ M_χ. By Step 3, Fbar v_χ ∈ M_χ = Qbar_ℓ v_χ, so there is a unique λ_χ ∈ Qbar_ℓ with Fbar v_χ = λ_χ v_χ (necessarily λ_χ ≠ 0, since Fbar is invertible by Step 0). The family (v_χ)_χ is linearly independent because its members lie in distinct summands of the direct sum of Step 2(d), and it spans M because M = ⊕_χ M_χ and each nonzero summand is Qbar_ℓ v_χ. Hence (v_χ)_χ is a basis of M consisting of Fbar-eigenvectors, which means exactly that Fbar = F ⊗ id_{Qbar_ℓ} is diagonalisable, hence semisimple, on V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Qbar_ℓ. (In the edge case G = {1}: X(G) = {1}, M = M_1 has dimension ≤ 1 by hypothesis, and any operator on a space of dimension ≤ 1 is diagonalisable, so the same conclusion holds.)

STEP 5 (descent to Q_ℓ). By Step 0, V is a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space and F ∈ GL(V). By Step 4, F ⊗ id_{Qbar_ℓ} is diagonalisable on V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Qbar_ℓ. Lemma_5 (semisimplicity over Q_ℓ is equivalent to diagonalisability after scalar extension to Qbar_ℓ) now gives that F is semisimple on V = H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). This is exactly the required conclusion. ∎

lemma_92.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let m\ge 1, let B be a simple abelian variety over \mathbb F_{q^m}, let \pi\in\mathrm{End}(B) be its q^m-power Frobenius endomorphism, and let \ell\neq p be a prime. Write V_\ell(B):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(B) for the rational \ell-adic Tate module, on which \pi acts \mathbb Q_\ell-linearly. Then the minimal polynomial of \pi on V_\ell(B) is squarefree in \mathbb Q_\ell[t]; equivalently, \pi acts semisimply on V_\ell(B).
lemma_92.proof:
**Notation.** Write $k_0:=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $\bar k:=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $g:=\dim B\ge 1$ (a simple abelian variety is nonzero by definition), $\pi:=\mathrm{Frob}_{B/k_0}\in \mathrm{End}_{k_0}(B)$ for the $q^m$-power Frobenius endomorphism, $T_\ell(B):=\varprojlim_n B[\ell^n](\bar k)$ and $V:=V_\ell(B)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(B)$. It is classical that $T_\ell(B)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2g$, so $V$ is a **nonzero** finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space ($\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=2g\ge 2$). All endomorphism rings below are taken in the category of abelian varieties over $k_0$, and $\mathrm{End}^0(B):=\mathrm{End}(B)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$.

**Step 1: $\mathbb Q[\pi]$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra.**
We use the standard theorem of the theory of abelian varieties that $\mathrm{End}(B)$ is a finitely generated free $\mathbb Z$-module. (Reason, as an input theorem: $\alpha\mapsto[\Gamma_\alpha]$ embeds $\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ into the N\'eron--Severi group $\mathrm{NS}(B\times B)$ — a homomorphism is recovered from its graph, and additivity of the class of the graph follows from the theorem of the cube — and the theorem of the base says $\mathrm{NS}(B\times B)$ is a finitely generated abelian group; a subgroup of a f.g. abelian group is f.g. Torsion-freeness is immediate: if $n\alpha=0$ with $n\ge1$, then $\alpha(B)\subseteq B[n]$; $\alpha(B)$ is a closed connected subvariety (image of a proper connected variety) of the finite scheme $B[n]$, hence a point, so $\alpha=0$.)

$\mathbb Z[\pi]=\sum_{r\ge0}\mathbb Z\,\pi^r$ is a $\mathbb Z$-submodule of the finitely generated free $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathrm{End}(B)$; since $\mathbb Z$ is a PID, submodules of finitely generated free modules are finitely generated, so $\mathbb Z[\pi]\cong\mathbb Z^{s}$ for some $s\le \mathrm{rank}\,\mathrm{End}(B)$, generated by $\pi^{r_1},\dots,\pi^{r_s}$. Hence $K:=\mathbb Q[\pi]=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z[\pi]$ is spanned over $\mathbb Q$ by $\pi^{r_1},\dots,\pi^{r_s}$: $K$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $\mathbb Q$-subalgebra of $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ (equivalently, $\pi$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$).

**Step 2: $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ is a division ring, so $K$ is a number field and $m_\pi$ is irreducible and separable.**
Let $0\ne\varphi\in\mathrm{End}(B)$. The scheme-theoretic image $\mathrm{im}(\varphi)$ of a homomorphism of abelian varieties over $k_0$ is a closed connected group scheme over $k_0$, i.e. an abelian subvariety of $B$ defined over $k_0$. Since $B$ is **simple** over $k_0$ and $\varphi\ne0$ (so $\mathrm{im}(\varphi)\ne\{0\}$), $\mathrm{im}(\varphi)=B$: $\varphi$ is surjective. All fibres of $\varphi$ are translates of $\ker\varphi$, so $\dim\ker\varphi=\dim B-\dim B=0$, i.e. $\varphi$ is an *isogeny*. By the standard isogeny theory there is $\psi\in\mathrm{End}(B)$ with $\psi\varphi=[\deg\varphi]=\varphi\psi$ (the dual isogeny). Thus in $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ the element $\varphi\otimes1$ is invertible, with inverse $\psi\otimes(1/\deg\varphi)$. Every nonzero element of $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ is therefore invertible: $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ is a division ring (a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-algebra).

The Frobenius $\pi$ is nonzero and an isogeny: on $\bar k$-points $\pi$ is $x\mapsto x^{q^m}$, a bijection of $B(\bar k)$ (as $\bar k$ is perfect) and a group homomorphism, so $\mathrm{im}(\pi)=B$, and $\dim\ker\pi=0$. In particular $\pi\in\mathrm{End}^0(B)^\times$.

Now $K=\mathbb Q[\pi]$ is a commutative subring of a division ring, hence has no zero divisors, and is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$. For $0\ne x\in K$ the $\mathbb Q$-linear map $\mu_x:K\to K$, $y\mapsto xy$ is injective (no zero divisors), hence surjective by finite dimensionality, so $xy=1$ for some $y\in K$: $K$ is a **field**. Let $m_\pi\in\mathbb Q[t]$ be the monic generator of the kernel of the evaluation map $\mathrm{ev}_\pi:\mathbb Q[t]\twoheadrightarrow K$, $t\mapsto\pi$; the kernel is nonzero because $K$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$ (so $1,\pi,\dots,\pi^{N}$ are linearly dependent for some $N$). Then $K\cong\mathbb Q[t]/(m_\pi)$, and since $K$ is a field, $m_\pi$ is **irreducible**. As $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q=0$, every irreducible polynomial is separable, so $m_\pi$ is separable, i.e. **squarefree in $\mathbb Q[t]$**.

**Step 3: The $\ell$-adic representation, and $\mu_\pi\mid m_\pi$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$.**
Functoriality of the Tate module gives a ring homomorphism $\rho_0:\mathrm{End}(B)\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(T_\ell(B))$, and extension of scalars gives $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(T_\ell(B))\hookrightarrow\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, $u\mapsto\mathrm{id}\otimes u$ (this last map is injective because $V=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes T_\ell(B)$ and a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear map is zero iff its scalar extension is zero; we will not need this). Composing, $\rho_0$ is a unital ring map $\mathrm{End}(B)\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ sending an integer $n$ to $n\cdot\mathrm{id}_V$, which is a unit of $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ for $n\ne0$ (as $V\ne0$). Since $\mathrm{End}^0(B)=S^{-1}\mathrm{End}(B)$ with $S=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, the universal property of localisation extends $\rho_0$ uniquely to a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$$\rho:\mathrm{End}^0(B)\longrightarrow \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V),\qquad \rho\!\big(\varphi\otimes \tfrac ab\big)=\tfrac ab\,\rho_0(\varphi).$$
(Concretely, the defining relation $\varphi\otimes1=(n\varphi)\otimes\frac1n$ is respected because $\rho_0(n\varphi)=n\,\rho_0(\varphi)$.) **No injectivity of $\rho$ is asserted or used.**

Put $\pi_V:=\rho(\pi)=\mathrm{id}\otimes T_\ell(\pi)\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$. Because $m_\pi(\pi)=0$ in $K\subset\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ and $\rho$ is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism,
$$0=\rho\big(m_\pi(\pi)\big)=m_\pi\big(\rho(\pi)\big)=m_\pi(\pi_V)\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V),$$\nwriting $m_\pi(t)=\sum_j a_jt^j$ and using $\rho(\sum_j a_j\pi^j)=\sum_j a_j\pi_V^j$.
Since $V\ne0$ is finite dimensional, the kernel of $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, $t\mapsto\pi_V$, is a nonzero ideal generated by a unique monic polynomial $\mu_\pi$, the minimal polynomial of $\pi_V$; the relation $m_\pi(\pi_V)=0$ says $m_\pi$ lies in that kernel, hence
$$\mu_\pi\ \big|\ m_\pi\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q_\ell[t].$$
Finally $\pi_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$: $\pi$ is an isogeny with dual $\hat\pi$ satisfying $\hat\pi\pi=[\deg\pi]=\pi\hat\pi$ in $\mathrm{End}(B)$, so $\rho(\pi)\,\rho(\hat\pi/\deg\pi)=\mathrm{id}_V=\rho(\hat\pi/\deg\pi)\,\rho(\pi)$.

**Step 4: Squarefreeness of $\mu_\pi$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.**
Apply **lemma_64(ii)** with $k=\mathbb Q$ and $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (a field extension of the characteristic-$0$ field $\mathbb Q$): a nonzero $g\in\mathbb Q[t]$ is squarefree iff $\gcd(g,g')=1$, and this gcd is unchanged after the scalar extension $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$, because the B\'ezout coefficients expressing $\gcd(g,g')$ are produced by the Euclidean algorithm inside $\mathbb Q[t]$. Taking $g=m_\pi$, Step 2 gives $m_\pi$ squarefree in $\mathbb Q[t]$, hence $m_\pi$ is **squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$**. (The characteristic-$0$ hypothesis is genuinely used, exactly as lemma_64 warns.)
Now factor $m_\pi=\prod_{i=1}^{s}g_i$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ into pairwise distinct monic irreducibles. Since $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ is a PID/UFD and $\mu_\pi\mid m_\pi$, unique factorisation gives $\mu_\pi=\prod_{i\in I}g_i$ for some subset $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,s\}$: every irreducible occurs with exponent $0$ or $1$. Hence $\mu_\pi$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. This proves the first assertion of the lemma.

**Step 5: Semisimplicity, and the equivalence.**
Apply **lemma_60** to the nonzero finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $V=V_\ell(B)$ and the element $T=\pi_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ (invertibility shown at the end of Step 3). Its equivalence (ii) states: $T$ is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial $\mu_T=\mu_\pi$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. Step 4 gives the right-hand side, so $\pi_V$ is semisimple, i.e. $\pi$ acts semisimply on $V_\ell(B)$; and the same equivalence (ii) is exactly the "equivalently" in the statement of the lemma.

**Remark on what was *not* used.** The argument never compares $\mu_\pi$ with $m_\pi$: only the divisibility $\mu_\pi\mid m_\pi$ is used, which is formal from the existence of the representation $\rho$. In particular no injectivity of $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q[\pi]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(B))$ is claimed (that statement is the deferred, genuinely deep part requiring the Weil-polynomial theorem), no faithfulness of $\mathrm{End}^0(B)$ on $T_\ell(B)$ is invoked, and no purity/weight input is used (cf. the warning in lemma_62 that purity alone never yields semisimplicity).

lemma_101.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\) of pure dimension \(d\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(r\ge 1\). Suppose that (i) \(H^{2j+1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(j\ge 0\), and (ii) for every \(j\ge 0\) the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space \(H^{2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\) is spanned by the cycle classes \(\mathrm{cl}(z)\) of codimension-\(j\) cycles \(z\) on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on \(H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(i\ge 0\). No basis of cycle classes and no permutation of a spanning set by Frobenius is required.
lemma_101.proof:
Notation. Put $H^i:=H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $i\ge0$, and write $\sigma:k\to k$, $a\mapsto a^q$, for the $q$-power field automorphism. By lemma_6a the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius is the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism $F:=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)^*$ of $H^i$, with inverse $(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^{-1})^*$; in particular $F\in \mathrm{GL}(H^i)$. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the proper $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$ and the constant sheaf $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}\in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (with its standard structure $\psi$), each $H^i$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. We must prove that $F$ is semisimple on $H^i$ for every $i$.

Step 1: reduction to even degrees. Let $i\ge0$.
If $i$ is odd, write $i=2j+1$; hypothesis (i) gives $H^i=0$, and every operator on the zero space is semisimple (there are no nonzero subspaces to complement; equivalently the minimal polynomial is $1$, which is squarefree).
Henceforth fix $j\ge0$ and set $V:=H^{2j}$, $W:=H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)):=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$. We prove that $F|_V$ is semisimple.

Step 2: the ground-field extension $\mathbb F_{q^r}$. Put $Q:=q^r=p^{ar}$, a prime power, and let $X':=X\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{Q}$. Smoothness, projectivity and purity of dimension are preserved by arbitrary base change, so $X'$ is a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb F_Q$ of pure dimension $d$. Since $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ is also an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_Q$, the universal property of the fibre product gives a canonical isomorphism over both base fields
$$\iota:X'_k:=X'\times_{\mathbb F_Q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k \;=\; X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_Q\times_{\mathbb F_Q}k \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; X\times_{\mathbb F_q}k=X_k,\qquad (x,\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto (x,\lambda\mu).$$
Under $\iota$ the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $X'_k$, namely $\mathrm{id}_{X'}\times\sigma^r$ (because $a\mapsto a^Q$ is $\sigma^r$), becomes $\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^r$: indeed $\iota$ intertwines $(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id},\sigma^r)$ with $(\mathrm{id},\nu)\mapsto(\mathrm{id},\sigma^r\nu)$, using $\sigma^r\lambda=\lambda$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb F_Q\subset k$. By functoriality of pullback, $(\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^r)^*=((\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)^*)^r$, since $(g\circ h)^*=h^*\circ g^*$ and here $g=h=\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma$; induction on $r$ gives the equality. Thus, transported along the identification $H^{2j}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V$ induced by $\iota$, the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on $H^{2j}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is exactly $F^r$.

Step 3: reading hypothesis (ii) as a statement about cycles on $X'$. A codimension-$j$ cycle on $X$ "defined over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$" is by definition an element of $\mathrm{CH}^j(X')$ (a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of integral closed subschemes of $X'$ of codimension $j$, equivalently a cycle of $X_k$ whose support is $\sigma^r$-stable with Galois-invariant multiplicities); its class $\mathrm{cl}(z)\in W$ is computed after base change to $k$, and the class map is compatible with the isomorphism $\iota$ by functoriality of $\ell$-adic cycle classes for $k$-morphisms (flat pull-back of cycles and the Gysin/cycle-class construction commute with base change to $k$). Hypothesis (ii) therefore says:
$$\text{the classes }\mathrm{cl}(z),\ z\in\mathrm{CH}^j(X'),\ \text{span } W=H^{2j}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)) \text{ over }\mathbb Q_\ell.$$
(For $j>d$ there are no integral closed subschemes of $X'$ of codimension $j$, because such a subscheme would have dimension $\le d-j<0$; then $\mathrm{CH}^j(X')=0$ and (ii) forces $W=0$, which is the trivial case treated in Step 6 below. So there is no consistency issue in high degrees, and no external vanishing theorem for $H^{>2d}$ is needed.)

Step 4: apply lemma_78 over $\mathbb F_Q$. Lemma_78 applied to the prime power $Q=p^{ar}$, the smooth projective pure-dimensional $\mathbb F_Q$-variety $X'$, the prime $\ell\ne p$, and the codimension $j$, says the following. Let $F_{Q,*}$ denote the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^{2j}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ induced by the arithmetic Frobenius structures on $X'_k$ and on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, on which the $Q$-power Frobenius acts as multiplication by $Q^{-j}$. Then
$$F_{Q,*}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=\mathrm{cl}(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathrm{CH}^j(X').$$
Transporting to $V$ via Step 2 and the canonical identification $W=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, the automorphism $F_{Q,*}$ is $F^r\otimes m_{Q^{-j}}$, where $m_{Q^{-j}}$ is multiplication by the scalar $Q^{-j}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$ on the one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ (this is exactly the description of the Frobenius structure on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ recalled in lemma_78, with $q$ replaced by $Q$; note $Q^{-j}=(q^{-j})^r$, so this is the $r$-th power of the $q$-power action, as it must be).

Step 5: untwisting. Fix any nonzero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$; the map $\theta:V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W$, $w\mapsto w\otimes\xi$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. For each $z\in\mathrm{CH}^j(X')$ let $c_z:=\theta^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}(z))\in V$, so $\mathrm{cl}(z)=c_z\otimes\xi$. Then
$$c_z\otimes\xi=\mathrm{cl}(z)=F_{Q,*}\mathrm{cl}(z)=(F^rc_z)\otimes Q^{-j}\xi=\big(Q^{-j}F^rc_z\big)\otimes\xi.$$
Since $\theta$ is injective, $c_z=Q^{-j}F^rc_z$, i.e.
$$F^r c_z=Q^{j}c_z=q^{rj}c_z\qquad\text{for all }z\in\mathrm{CH}^j(X').$$
This is the "equivalently" clause of lemma_78 with $q$ replaced by $Q$. Because the $\mathrm{cl}(z)$ span $W$ by Step 3 and $\theta$ is an isomorphism, the vectors $c_z$ span $V$.

Step 6: the linear-algebra conclusion. If $V=0$ there is nothing to prove, so suppose $V\ne0$. We have: $V$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space (Step 1), $F\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ (Step 1), $m:=r\ge1$, $c:=q^{rj}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$ (a positive rational number, hence nonzero in $\mathbb Q_\ell$), and $V$ is spanned by vectors $c_z$ satisfying $F^{m}c_z=c\,c_z$ (Step 5). By lemma_90 (with $T=F$) we conclude: $F^r=q^{rj}\mathrm{id}_V$; the minimal polynomial $\mu_F$ divides $t^r-q^{rj}$, which is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ because $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$ and $q^{rj}\ne0$ (explicitly, $\tfrac{d}{dt}(t^r-q^{rj})=rt^{r-1}$ vanishes only at $0$, and $0$ is not a root of $t^r-q^{rj}$, so $\gcd(t^r-q^{rj},\,r t^{r-1})=1$); and $F$ is semisimple on $V$.

Step 7: assembly. Step 6 gives semisimplicity of the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius on $H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $j\ge0$, and Step 1 gives it on $H^{2j+1}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every $j\ge0$.
