Since every $i\ge0$ is of one of these two forms, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on $H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $i\ge0$, which is exactly the claim.

Remark on the route. Only hypothesis (ii) as stated was used: the classes need not form a basis, and $F^r$ need not permute any chosen spanning set. Indeed the argument produces a single eigenvalue $q^{rj}$ for $F^r$ on the whole of $H^{2j}$ (because every generator is fixed by $F_{Q,*}$ on the twisted group, the twist contributing the same scalar $Q^{-j}$ to all of them), and lemma_90 turns a spanning set of $F^r$-eigenvectors for one common eigenvalue directly into semisimplicity. Thus the stronger lemma_85 (which asks for a Frobenius-permuted basis of cycle classes) is not invoked. Nor is any duality, purity, or positivity input used.

lemma_102.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, let R be a finite-dimensional semisimple unital k-algebra, let V be a finite-dimensional left R-module, and let c be an element of the centre Z(R). Then the k-linear endomorphism v \mapsto c v of V is semisimple, i.e. its minimal polynomial over k is squarefree and it is diagonalizable over \bar k. Equivalently: a central element of a semisimple algebra over a field of characteristic 0 acts semisimply on every finite-dimensional module.
lemma_102.proof:
We prove: for char k = 0, R a finite-dimensional semisimple unital k-algebra, V a finite-dimensional left R-module and c ∈ Z(R), the k-endomorphism T: V → V, v ↦ c v, has squarefree minimal polynomial over k and becomes diagonalizable over k̄.

STEP 0 (trivial cases; the meaning of "semisimple"). If R = 0 then 1_R = 0 and, V being unital (1_R v = v), V = 0; then T = id_0 = 0 on the zero space, its minimal polynomial is 1 (squarefree) and it is diagonalizable with the empty eigenbasis. Likewise if V = 0 there is nothing to prove. Henceforth assume R ≠ 0 (so 1_R ≠ 0) and V ≠ 0.

We use the standard, mutually equivalent meanings of "semisimple finite-dimensional k-algebra": (a) R is a semisimple object of the category of left R-modules, i.e. every left ideal of R is a direct summand of R as a left ideal; (b) Jac(R) = 0; (c) Artin–Wedderburn: R ≅ ∏_{i=1}^t M_{n_i}(D_i) with the D_i finite-dimensional division k-algebras. We will only need (a). For completeness we check that (c) implies (a): as a left module over itself, M_n(D) = C_1 ⊕ ··· ⊕ C_n where C_j is the set of matrices supported in the j-th column; left multiplication by matrices acts column-wise, so C_j ≅ D^n (column vectors) with the usual action, and D^n is simple because D is a division ring (any nonzero vector can be moved to any other nonzero vector by an invertible matrix, so every nonzero submodule contains every standard basis vector). A finite product of rings that are semisimple over themselves is semisimple over itself (a module over ∏ R_i is the direct sum of its e_i-parts, and submodules decompose accordingly). Thus (c) ⟹ (a), and (a) ⟺ (b) is the classical theorem (Jac(R) = 0 iff the regular module is semisimple). So in all cases: **every left ideal of R is a direct summand of R.**

STEP 1 (T is k-linear). Write λ·v for the scalar action of λ ∈ k, identified with λ1_R ∈ R. Since R is a k-algebra, multiplication R × R → R is k-bilinear, and λ1_R is central, so for v,w ∈ V and λ,μ ∈ k: T(λv + μw) = c(λv + μw) = λ(cv) + μ(cw) = λT(v) + μT(w). Thus T ∈ End_k(V). Also T is well defined and V is finite-dimensional over k by hypothesis, so T has a minimal polynomial μ_T ∈ k[t].

STEP 2 (the algebraic relation of c). Consider the k-algebra homomorphism ev_c: k[t] → R, P ↦ P(c) (well defined because k[t] is commutative and free on 1,t,t²,…; it is a homomorphism since c commutes with itself and with k·1_R). Since R is finite-dimensional over k, the vectors 1, c, c², … are linearly dependent, so ker(ev_c) ≠ 0. As k[t] is a principal ideal domain, ker(ev_c) = (g) for a unique monic polynomial g = t^d + a_{d-1}t^{d-1} + ··· + a_0, d ≥ 1 (d ≥ 1 because 1 ∉ ker(ev_c): g = constant would mean 1_R = 0). Thus g(c) = 0 in R, and P(c) = 0 in R ⟺ g | P in k[t]; equivalently k[c] := im(ev_c) ≅ k[t]/(g) as k-algebras, and g is the unique monic polynomial of least degree annihilating c.

STEP 3 (R has no nonzero central nilpotent element). Let n ∈ Z(R) with n^m = 0 for some m ≥ 1. Consider the left ideal Rn = {rn : r ∈ R}. Because n is central, Rn is a two-sided ideal: (rn)r' = r(nr') = r(r'n) = (rr')n ∈ Rn. By Step 0, Rn is a direct summand of R as a left ideal: R = Rn ⊕ I. Write 1 = e + f with e ∈ Rn, f ∈ I. For any x ∈ Rn we have x = x·1 = xe + xf, where xe ∈ Rn since Rn is a right ideal, and xf ∈ Rn ∩ I = 0 since Rn is a right ideal and I is only a left ideal — careful: xf with x ∈ Rn ⊂ R and f ∈ R need not lie in I a priori. Fix this by noting instead that Rn being a two-sided ideal gives xe ∈ Rn, and we must check xf ∈ I: write x = rn with r ∈ R; then xf = r(nf) = r(fn) (n central) = (rf)n, and rf ∈ R since R is a ring; so xf ∈ Rn. To see xf ∈ I we use that I is a left ideal and f ∈ I: xf = (rn)f — this is a right multiple, not a left multiple, so it need not be in I. We therefore argue differently and more robustly: since R = Rn ⊕ I as LEFT ideals and Rn is a two-sided ideal, the projection π: R → Rn along I is R-linear (π is left multiplication by e: for r ∈ R, r = r e + r f with re ∈ Rn (two-sided ideal) and rf ∈ I (left ideal), so π(r) = re). Then π(1) = e, and for r ∈ Rn, r = π(r) = re, i.e. e is a right identity of the ideal Rn. In particular e² = e. Now Rn is a nilpotent ideal: a product of m elements of Rn has the form (∏ r_i) n^m = 0, using centrality of n to collect the n's: (r_1n)(r_2n) = r_1(n r_2)n = r_1(r_2 n)n = (r_1r_2)n², inductively. Hence e^m = 0 as e ∈ Rn, and since e is idempotent, e = e² = e³ = ··· = e^m = 0. Thus Rn = Re = 0, and finally n = 1·n ∈ Rn = 0. This proves: a central nilpotent element of R is zero. (Equivalently, in the language of Step 0(b): a nilpotent two-sided ideal is contained in Jac(R) = 0, since for any simple left module S, IS = S would force I^mS = S ≠ 0.)

STEP 4 (g is squarefree). Suppose not. Factor g = ∏_{j=1}^s p_j^{e_j} in the UFD k[t], with the p_j distinct monic irreducibles, e_j ≥ 1, and some e_j ≥ 2. Set h := ∏_{j=1}^s p_j and e := max_j e_j ≥ 2. Then deg h = Σ_j deg p_j < Σ_j e_j deg p_j = deg g (strict because some e_j ≥ 2), and deg h ≥ 1. We claim h(c) ≠ 0: otherwise g | h by Step 2, forcing deg g ≤ deg h, contradiction. But h^e = ∏_j p_j^e is divisible by g in the UFD k[t] (as e ≥ e_j for all j), so h(c)^e = 0 in R by Step 2. Thus n := h(c) is a nonzero nilpotent element of R. It is central: for r ∈ R, r h(c) = h applied to c with r commuting past each power of c (c ∈ Z(R) ⟹ c^m ∈ Z(R) ⟹ P(c) ∈ Z(R) for all P). This contradicts Step 3. Hence g is squarefree: g = ∏_{j=1}^s p_j with the p_j distinct monic irreducibles.

STEP 5 (the minimal polynomial of T is squarefree). For every v ∈ V, g(T)v = g(c)v = 0 because g(c) = 0 in R; hence g(T) = 0 in End_k(V). Divide g by μ_T: g = q μ_T + r with r = 0 or deg r < deg μ_T; evaluating at T gives r(T) = 0, so r = 0 by minimality of μ_T. Therefore μ_T | g in k[t]. Since g = ∏_{j=1}^s p_j is a product of distinct irreducibles, every divisor of g is of the form ∏_{j∈J} p_j for some J ⊆ {1,…,s}; thus μ_T = ∏_{j∈J} p_j is squarefree. This is the first required conclusion. (Edge check: V ≠ 0 so μ_T ≠ 1; the case μ_T = t, i.e. cV = 0, is squarefree and handled below with J = {index of p = t}.)

STEP 6 (diagonalizability over k̄). Because char k = 0, every irreducible polynomial in k[t] is separable: if p ∈ k[t] is monic irreducible and p' were divisible by p, then p' = 0, i.e. p ∈ k[t^p], impossible for p = 0 the characteristic; so deg p' ≥ 0 < deg p and gcd(p,p') = 1 by irreducibility. Hence each p_j splits in k̄[t] as a product of distinct linear factors, and so does μ_T = ∏_{ℓ=1}^u (t - α_ℓ) with α_ℓ ∈ k̄ pairwise distinct (u = Σ_{j∈J} deg p_j ≥ 1). Set V̄ := V ⊗_k k̄ and T̄ := T ⊗ id_{k̄}. Then μ_T(T̄) = μ_T(T) ⊗ id = 0, so V̄ is a module over the k̄-algebra k̄[t]/(μ_T), with t acting as T̄. By the Chinese remainder theorem applied to the pairwise coprime factors (t - α_ℓ),
  k̄[t]/(μ_T) ≅ ∏_{ℓ=1}^u k̄[t]/(t - α_ℓ) ≅ k̄^u.
Let ε_ℓ ∈ k̄[t]/(μ_T) be the preimage of the ℓ-th standard idempotent; explicitly, in terms of the operator,
  ε_ℓ = ∏_{m ≠ ℓ} (T̄ - α_m id)/(α_ℓ - α_m),
which is a genuine polynomial expression in T̄ because the denominators α_ℓ - α_m are nonzero (the α's are distinct). These satisfy Σ_ℓ ε_ℓ = id_{V̄}, ε_ℓ ε_m = 0 for ℓ ≠ m (these are the images of the orthogonal idempotents of k̄^u, or a direct computation), and (T̄ - α_ℓ id) ε_ℓ = 0 because (t - α_ℓ)·∏_{m≠ℓ}(t-α_m) = μ_T ≡ 0 modulo (μ_T), up to the nonzero scalar ∏_{m≠ℓ}(α_ℓ-α_m). Hence V̄ = ⊕_{ℓ=1}^u ε_ℓ V̄ (using Σ ε_ℓ = id for the spanning statement and orthogonality for the directness), and ε_ℓ V̄ ⊆ ker(T̄ - α_ℓ id), the α_ℓ-eigenspace. So V̄ is a direct sum of eigenspaces of T̄, i.e. T̄ = T ⊗_k id_{k̄} is diagonalizable over k̄. This is the second required conclusion.

Steps 5 and 6 together say exactly that T is semisimple, proving the lemma.

REMARK 1 (rephrasing, i.e. the "equivalently" in the statement). The argument shows more: the subalgebra k[c] ⊂ Z(R) is a finite-dimensional commutative semisimple k-algebra, isomorphic to k[t]/(g) ≅ ∏_{j=1}^s k[t]/(p_j) by CRT, a product of finite separable field extensions of k; every element of such an algebra has squarefree minimal polynomial, and hence acts semisimply on every finite-dimensional module. Concretely, via Artin–Wedderburn R ≅ ∏_i M_{n_i}(D_i) one has Z(R) ≅ ∏_i Z(D_i) (the centre of M_n(D) is the ring of scalar matrices with entries in Z(D): a matrix commuting with all matrix units E_{pq} is diagonal with all diagonal entries equal, and commuting with all matrices then forces that entry into Z(D)), a product of fields, so Z(R) itself has no nonzero nilpotents and c = (c_i) has minimal polynomial lcm_i(minpoly of c_i over k), a lcm of irreducible (hence separable, char 0) polynomials, therefore squarefree — an independent proof of Step 4.

REMARK 2 (characteristic 0 is essential; cf. the analogous warning for scalar extension). Let k = F_p(s) with s transcendental, and R = k[x]/(x^p - s). The polynomial x^p - s is irreducible over k by Eisenstein at the prime (s) ⊂ F_p[s] (s divides the constant term, s² does not), so R is a field, hence a semisimple k-algebra, commutative, so every c ∈ R is central. Take c = x̄ and V = R as a module over itself (dimension p). Then the minimal polynomial of the k-endomorphism v ↦ cv is x^p - s = (x - α)^p in k̄[x] (α = s^{1/p}), which is not squarefree, and over k̄ the operator is multiplication by x̄ on k̄[x]/((x-α)^p), a single Jordan block of size p, not diagonalizable. Thus the conclusion fails in characteristic p, and the use of char k = 0 in Step 6 (separability of irreducibles) — equivalently, in Step 4 via the fact that a field extension generated by one element is separable — is genuinely required.

lemma_104.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, m\ge 1, Q=q^m, let A be an abelian variety over \mathbb F_Q with Q-power Frobenius endomorphism \pi, let \ell\neq p be prime and V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A). Let \lambda:A\to A^\vee be a polarization defined over \mathbb F_Q, let e_\ell:T_\ell(A)\times T_\ell(A^\vee)\to \mathbb Z_\ell(1) be the \ell-adic Weil pairing with \mathbb Z_\ell(1)=\varprojlim_n \mu_{\ell^n}, and set E_\lambda(x,y)=e_\ell(x,\lambda y), extended \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinearly to V_\ell(A)\times V_\ell(A)\to \mathbb Q_\ell(1). Then E_\lambda is alternating and perfect, and E_\lambda(\pi v,\pi w)=Q\,E_\lambda(v,w) for all v,w\in V_\ell(A), where Q acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(1) by scalar multiplication.
lemma_104.proof:
Proof. Let k=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q and g=\dim A. We write the Tate twists \mathbb Z_\ell(1) and \mathbb Q_\ell(1) additively, although at finite level the values lie in \mu_{\ell^r} multiplicatively.

1. Finite-level Weil pairing. For n prime to p, the Poincare biextension on A \times A^\vee gives a canonical Cartier-duality isomorphism
A^\vee[n] \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}(A[n],\mu_n).
Define e_n^A(x,\eta) by evaluating the character corresponding to \eta at x. We use the following properties, which are part of the Poincare-biextension construction.
WP1 (bihomomorphism): e_n^A(x+x',\eta)=e_n^A(x,\eta)e_n^A(x',\eta) and similarly in \eta.
WP2 (functoriality): if f:A\to B is a homomorphism, then e_n^B(fx,\eta)=e_n^A(x,f^\vee\eta).
WP3 (skew under biduality): e_n^{A^\vee}(y,\iota_A x)=e_n^A(x,y)^{-1}.
WP4 (perfectness): the map A^\vee[n](k)\to \operatorname{Hom}(A[n](k),\mu_n(k)) is an isomorphism.
WP5 (Galois equivariance): for \sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb F_Q), e_n^A(\sigma x,\sigma \eta)=\sigma(e_n^A(x,\eta)).
WP6 (level compatibility): for x'\in A[\ell^r](k), y\in A^\vee[\ell^{r+1}](k),
e_{\ell^{r+1}}(x',y)=e_{\ell^r}(x',[\ell]y),
and for x,y\in A[\ell^{r+1}](k),
e_{\ell^{r+1}}([\ell]x,y)=e_{\ell^{r+1}}(x,[\ell]y).
Indeed the first identity is the compatibility of the Cartier-duality identifications with the transition maps: the dual of the inclusion A[\ell^r]\hookrightarrow A[\ell^{r+1}] is [\ell]:A^\vee[\ell^{r+1}]\to A^\vee[\ell^r]. This is one of the biextension identities ([\ell]\times \operatorname{id})^*P\cong \operatorname{pr}_2^*P^{\otimes \ell}\cong (\operatorname{id}\times [\ell])^*P. The second identity is WP2 applied to [\ell]:A\to A, whose dual on A^\vee is again [\ell]. From these two identities and WP1 we obtain, for x,y\in A[\ell^{r+1}](k),
e_{\ell^r}([\ell]x,[\ell]y)=e_{\ell^{r+1}}(x,[\ell]y)=e_{\ell^{r+1}}(x,y)^\ell.

2. The \ell-adic Weil pairing. Put
T_\ell(A)=\varprojlim_r A[\ell^r](k), \quad \mathbb Z_\ell(1)=\varprojlim_r \mu_{\ell^r}(k),
where the transition maps are [\ell] on the torsion groups and \zeta\mapsto\zeta^\ell on roots of unity. For v=(v_r)\in T_\ell(A) and w=(w_r)\in T_\ell(A^\vee), define
e_\ell(v,w)=(e_{\ell^r}(v_r,w_r))_{r\ge1}.
The compatibility just proved says exactly that this is an element of \mathbb Z_\ell(1): since v_r=[\ell]v_{r+1} and w_r=[\ell]w_{r+1},
e_{\ell^r}(v_r,w_r)=e_{\ell^r}([\ell]v_{r+1},[\ell]w_{r+1})=e_{\ell^{r+1}}(v_{r+1},w_{r+1})^\ell.
The action of a\in\mathbb Z_\ell on T_\ell(A) is given componentwise by a_r=[a\bmod \ell^r]; WP1 then gives
e_\ell(av,w)=(e_{\ell^r}(v_r,w_r)^{a_r})_r=a e_\ell(v,w),
and similarly in the second variable. Thus e_\ell is \mathbb Z_\ell-bilinear.

3. Perfectness of e_\ell. Let M=T_\ell(A), N=T_\ell(A^\vee), L=\mathbb Z_\ell(1). Since \ell\neq p, A[\ell^r](k) is a free \mathbb Z/\ell^r\mathbb Z-module of rank 2g. The maps [\ell]:A[\ell^{r+1}](k)\to A[\ell^r](k) are surjective, because [\ell]:A(k)\to A(k) is surjective over the algebraically closed field k. The projection M\to A[\ell](k) is therefore surjective. Its kernel is exactly \ell M: if v=(v_r) has v_1=0, then u=(u_r) with u_r=v_{r+1} lies in M, because [\ell]^r v_{r+1}=v_1=0, and \ell u=v; the converse is immediate. Hence
M/\ell M\cong A[\ell](k)\cong(\mathbb F_\ell)^{2g}.
Lifting an \mathbb F_\ell-basis of M/\ell M gives a \mathbb Z_\ell-linear map \mathbb Z_\ell^{2g}\to M which is surjective by the usual \ell-adic approximation, since the projections M\to A[\ell^n] are surjective. Thus M is finitely generated. Moreover M is torsion-free: if \ell^s v=0 and r is arbitrary, choose N large with N-r\ge s; then v_r=[\ell]^{N-r}v_N=0 because [\ell]^s v_N=0. Hence M is a finitely generated torsion-free \mathbb Z_\ell-module, so it is free of rank 2g. The same argument applies to N, and L is free of rank 1.
Consider the adjoint maps
\alpha:M\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(N,L),\quad \alpha(v)(w)=e_\ell(v,w),
\beta:N\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(M,L),\quad \beta(w)(v)=e_\ell(v,w).
Choose bases and write the pairing matrix G. The maps \alpha and \beta are represented by G and G^t. Reducing modulo \ell identifies M/\ell M, N/\ell N, and L/\ell L with A[\ell](k), A^\vee[\ell](k), and \mu_\ell(k), and the reduced pairing is e_\ell^A, which is perfect by WP4. Therefore G is invertible modulo \ell, hence invertible over the local ring \mathbb Z_\ell. Thus \alpha and \beta are isomorphisms; e_\ell is perfect on Tate modules. Tensoring with \mathbb Q_\ell gives a perfect pairing
V_\ell(A)\times V_\ell(A^\vee)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(1),
where V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}M and similarly for A^\vee.

4. Alternality of E_\lambda. A polarization is symmetric: under the canonical biduality \iota_A:A\xrightarrow{\sim}A^{\vee\vee}, one has
\lambda^\vee\circ\iota_A=\lambda.
For \lambda=\lambda_L this follows from \lambda_L^\vee\circ\iota_A=\lambda_{(-1)^*L} and the theorem of the square, which gives \lambda_{(-1)^*L}=\lambda_L.
For x,y\in A[n](k), set E_{\lambda,n}(x,y)=e_n^A(x,\lambda y). Using WP2 with f=\lambda and WP3, we compute
E_{\lambda,n}(x,y)
=e_n^A(x,\lambda y)
=e_n^{A^\vee}(\lambda x,\iota_A y)
=e_n^A(y,\lambda x)^{-1}
=E_{\lambda,n}(y,x)^{-1}.
Passing to T_\ell(A) and writing the target additively gives
E_\ell(v,w):=e_\ell(v,T_\ell(\lambda)w)=-E_\ell(w,v).
Since L=\mathbb Z_\ell(1) is torsion-free, E_\ell(v,v)=0 for all v\in T_\ell(A). The \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinear extension to V_\ell(A) is therefore alternating.

5. Perfectness of E_\lambda on V_\ell(A). Let
\rho:V_\ell(A^\vee)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A),\mathbb Q_\ell(1)),\quad \rho(\eta)(v)=e_\ell(v,\eta).
By Step 3, \rho is an isomorphism. Let \Lambda=V_\ell(\lambda):V_\ell(A)\to V_\ell(A^\vee). Since \lambda is an isogeny, there is an isogeny \mu:A^\vee\to A with \mu\lambda=[d] for some d>0; after tensoring with \mathbb Q_\ell this gives \Lambda^{-1}=d^{-1}V_\ell(\mu), so \Lambda is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism.
Define the two adjoints of E_\lambda by
\Phi_1(v)(w)=E_\lambda(v,w),\qquad \Phi_2(w)(v)=E_\lambda(v,w).
Then
\Phi_2=\rho\circ\Lambda,
so \Phi_2 is an isomorphism. By alternality,
\Phi_1(v)(w)=E_\lambda(v,w)=-E_\lambda(w,v)=-\Phi_2(v)(w),
hence \Phi_1 is also an isomorphism. Thus E_\lambda is perfect.

6. Frobenius similitude. We use the convention that the Q-power Frobenius endomorphism \pi_A of A is the relative Frobenius over \mathbb F_Q; on k-points it is
\pi_A(P)=\sigma_Q(P),
where \sigma_Q(c)=c^Q. The same convention is used on A^\vee. Since \lambda is defined over \mathbb F_Q, it commutes with Frobenius:
\lambda\circ\pi_A=\pi_{A^\vee}\circ\lambda.
For v,w\in T_\ell(A), the r-th component of E_\ell(\pi v,\pi w) is
 e_{\ell^r}(\sigma_Q v_r,\lambda(\sigma_Q w_r))
= e_{\ell^r}(\sigma_Q v_r,\sigma_Q(\lambda w_r))
= \sigma_Q(e_{\ell^r}(v_r,\lambda w_r))
= e_{\ell^r}(v_r,\lambda w_r)^Q.
In additive notation on \mathbb Z_\ell(1), the last expression is the r-th component of Q E_\ell(v,w). Hence
E_\ell(\pi v,\pi w)=Q E_\ell(v,w)
for all v,w\in T_\ell(A). Since \pi is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear on V_\ell(A) and E_\lambda is \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinear, the same identity holds for all v,w\in V_\ell(A). This proves the required three properties.

7. Closing remark. If V_\ell(A) is nonzero, choose any \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell. By lemma_69(0), the perfect alternating pairing E_\lambda defines a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear anti-involution a\mapsto a^\dagger on \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A)) by E_\lambda(av,w)=E_\lambda(v,a^\dagger w). The similitude relation gives
E_\lambda(v,\pi^\dagger\pi w)=E_\lambda(\pi v,\pi w)=Q E_\lambda(v,w),
so by perfectness \pi^\dagger\pi=Q\operatorname{id}. Since \pi is an isogeny, \pi is invertible on V_\ell(A), and therefore \pi^\dagger=Q\pi^{-1}. This consequence is not part of the statement.

lemma_mult_pic0.statement: Let k be a field, let A be an abelian variety over k with identity element e, let L be a line bundle on A whose class lies in Pic^0(A)(k), and let [m]: A -> A denote the multiplication-by-m morphism for an integer m >= 1. Then there is an isomorphism of line bundles [m]^*L \simeq L^{\otimes m}. Equivalently, for the addition morphism \sigma: A \times_k A -> A one first has \sigma^*L \simeq \mathrm{pr}_1^*L \otimes \mathrm{pr}_2^*L.
lemma_mult_pic0.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_mult_pic0",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove the two displayed isomorphisms. The addition formula (the second one) is established in Steps 2–4 via the see‑saw principle with a reduced base, and the multiplication formula (the first one) follows from it by induction in Step 5. Step 1 supplies the only property of Pic⁰ that is used: translation invariance.

CONVENTIONS AND NOTATION. For a field extension Ω/k we write X_Ω := X ×_k Spec Ω and M_Ω for the pullback of a line bundle M. For a line bundle M we write M^{-1} := M^∨ = M^{⊗(-1)}. The identity of A is e: Spec k → A; for a ∈ A(Ω), t_a: A_Ω → A_Ω is the translation x ↦ a + x; σ: A ×_k A → A is the addition morphism and pr_1, pr_2 the projections. An abelian variety is proper, smooth and geometrically connected over k, and its group law is commutative. For x ∈ X a point of a k‑scheme, κ(x) is its residue field and X_x := Spec κ(x) ×_X (X ×_k Y) = Y_{κ(x)} the scheme‑theoretic fibre of p = pr_X.

STEP 1. TRANSLATION INVARIANCE OF Pic⁰.
Claim 1. Let L be a line bundle on A whose class [L] lies in Pic⁰(A)(k). Then for every field extension Ω/k and every a ∈ A(Ω) there is an isomorphism of line bundles on A_Ω,
    t_a^* L_Ω ≅ L_Ω.      (1.1)
Proof. (1a) *The characterisation over an algebraically closed field.* Let K be algebraically closed and B/K an abelian variety. The Picard scheme Pic_{B/K} exists (B is projective, flat and of finite presentation over K): it represents the fppf sheaf T ↦ Pic(B_T)/pr^*Pic(T), it is a group scheme locally of finite type with group law induced by ⊗, and its identity component Pic⁰(B) is open and closed, of finite type, and is an abelian variety (the dual variety B̂). Over an algebraically closed field one has the standard identification
    Pic⁰(B)(K) = { M ∈ Pic(B) : t_b^*M ≅ M for all b ∈ B(K) }.      (1.2)
We record the ingredients, since only the inclusion "⊆" is used. For each M the family σ^*M ⊗ pr_2^*M^{-1} on B ×_K B, viewed as a family over B via pr_1, is classified by a K‑morphism φ_M: B → Pic_{B/K} which on K‑points is b ↦ [t_b^*M ⊗ M^{-1}]. The *theorem of the square* says φ_M is a homomorphism of group schemes; its image is connected and contains 0, hence lands in Pic⁰(B) = B̂. The theorem of the square is a consequence of the rigidity lemma: the "defect" F: B × B → B̂, (x,y) ↦ φ_M(x+y) − φ_M(x) − φ_M(y), is a morphism from a product of complete varieties which is constant on {0} × B and on B × {0} (both restrictions equal −φ_M(0) = 0), hence is constant by the rigidity lemma, which is itself a formal consequence of the see‑saw principle proved in Step 2 (apply Step 2 to the line bundle on X × Y classified by the composed map to the affine space of a projective embedding of the target; equivalently, use the standard proof of the rigidity lemma via the Stein factorisation and Step 2(a)). The assignment M ↦ φ_M is a group homomorphism Pic(B) → Hom_K(B, B̂) (φ_{M⊗M'} = φ_M + φ_{M'}, which is again the theorem of the square), its kernel is by definition the right‑hand side of (1.2), and the induced map NS(B) = Pic(B)/Pic⁰(B)(K) → Hom_K(B,B̂) is injective with image the symmetric homomorphisms (this is the standard description of the Néron–Severi group of an abelian variety via the first Chern class: the kernel of M ↦ φ_M consists of the numerically trivial line bundles, and over an algebraically closed field the numerically trivial line bundles are exactly Pic⁰(B)(K)). Combining these two sentences gives (1.2). 

(1b) *Base change of the hypothesis.* Let Ω/k be any field extension. Formation of the Picard scheme commutes with extension of the ground field for a smooth projective geometrically integral variety, so Pic_{A/k} ×_k Ω ≅ Pic_{A_Ω/Ω} as group schemes, and under this isomorphism the class of L_Ω is the image of [L]. Since Pic⁰(A) = Â is an abelian variety it is geometrically connected, so (Pic⁰ A)_Ω is connected; the base change of the open immersion Pic⁰(A) → Pic_{A/k} is again an open immersion, and its image is a connected subscheme of Pic_{A_Ω/Ω} containing the identity, hence is contained in Pic⁰(A_Ω). Therefore [L] ∈ Pic⁰(A)(k) implies [L_Ω] ∈ Pic⁰(A_Ω)(Ω).

(1c) *Descent of the isomorphism.* Fix Ω and a ∈ A(Ω), and put F := t_a^*L_Ω, G := L_Ω on A_Ω. By (1b) and (1.2) applied to the algebraically closed field Ω̄, we have an isomorphism F_{Ω̄} ≅ G_{Ω̄}. The functor Isom(F,G) is represented by a G_m‑torsor I → Spec Ω (the bundle of trivialisations of the invertible sheaf Hom(F,G)), and Isom commutes with extension of scalars, so I ×_Ω Ω̄ ≅ Isom(F_{Ω̄},G_{Ω̄}) has an Ω̄‑point. STEP 2. THE SEE‑SAW PRINCIPLE WITH REDUCED BASE.
