lemma_107.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_q, let k=\overline{F}_q, let \ell\neq p, and let F be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius. The cup product followed by the trace isomorphism tr:H^{2d}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d), on which F acts as multiplication by q^d, yields via y\mapsto(x\mapsto tr(x\cup y)) an isomorphism H^{2d-1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}Hom_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)) that is equivariant for F, where F acts on the Hom-space by (F\varphi)=q^d\,\varphi\circ F^{-1}. In particular F is semisimple on H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) if and only if it is semisimple on H^{2d-1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
lemma_107.proof:
We prove the lemma in seven steps. Throughout, write k := \overline{\mathbb F}_q, L := \mathbb Q_\ell(-d), and c := q^d \in \mathbb Q_\ell^{*} (a positive rational number, hence a nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 0 (Finite-dimensionality and invertibility of F).
Since X is proper over \mathbb F_q, for K := \mathbb Q_\ell[0] \in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, lemma_45_finite_frob gives that H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell for every n; in particular
  V := H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and W := H^{2d-1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
are finite-dimensional, and H^{2d}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional. By lemma_6a (applied to X), the q-power arithmetic Frobenius pullback F_ar := (id_X \times (a\mapsto a^q))^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of each H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), with inverse the geometric Frobenius. We denote this automorphism by F (and by F_V, F_W, F_L on V, W, L respectively). Thus F_V \in GL(V), F_W \in GL(W), and F^{-1} makes sense everywhere below.

STEP 1 (The geometric inputs: the trace map, perfectness, and Frobenius compatibility).
Apply lemma_77 with m = 1 and Y := X (X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_1-structure \mathbb F_q, so the hypotheses hold):
(a) there is a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism tr: H^{2d}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) = L, which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where F acts on L = \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) as multiplication by q^{md} = q^d = c. That is,
   (1.1)  tr(F x) = c\, tr(x) for all x \in H^{2d}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), equivalently F_L = c\,\mathrm{id}_L.
(b) for every n with 0 \le n \le 2d the pairing
   \langle\ ,\ \rangle_n : H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \times H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow L, \qquad (x,y) \longmapsto tr(x \cup y),
   is PERFECT (both adjoint maps are isomorphisms), and satisfies
   (1.2)  \langle F x, F y\rangle_n = c\,\langle x,y\rangle_n for all x,y.
We use (b) only for n = 1, where the pairing is \langle x,y\rangle = tr(x\cup y) on V \times W.

STEP 2 (The map \Psi is an isomorphism).
Define the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map
   \Psi : W \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V, L), \qquad \Psi(y)(x) := tr(x \cup y) = \langle x,y\rangle .
This is well defined and linear in y because the cup product is \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinear and tr is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear. By the perfectness of \langle\ ,\ \rangle_1 from (1.b), the right adjoint map y \mapsto (x \mapsto \langle x,y\rangle) is an isomorphism W \xrightarrow{\sim} V^\vee \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} L = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L) (the last identification uses that V is finite-dimensional). Hence
   (2.1)  \Psi is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism.
(Remark: graded commutativity gives x\cup y = (-1)^{1\cdot(2d-1)} y\cup x = -\,y\cup x, so the other adjoint map differs from \Psi by the scalar -1; either way one gets an isomorphism, and the sign plays no role in what follows.)

STEP 3 (Equivariance of \Psi for the stated Hom-action).
On Hom_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L) we consider the operator stated in the lemma:
   (3.1)  (F\varphi) := c\, \varphi \circ F_V^{-1}, \qquad \varphi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L),
which is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism (its inverse is \varphi \mapsto c^{-1}\varphi\circ F_V). This is the natural action on V^\vee \otimes L: F acts on V^\vee by f \mapsto f\circ F_V^{-1} and on L by the scalar c.

Claim: \Psi(F_W y) = F(\Psi(y)) for every y \in W.
Proof of the claim. Fix y \in W and x \in V. Apply the compatibility (1.2) with n = 1 to the pair (F_V^{-1}x,\, y) (which is legitimate since F_V is an automorphism):
   \langle F_V(F_V^{-1}x),\ F_W y\rangle = c\,\langle F_V^{-1}x,\ y\rangle,
that is,
   (3.2)  \langle x, F_W y\rangle = c\,\langle F_V^{-1}x, y\rangle .
Therefore
   \Psi(F_W y)(x) = \langle x, F_W y\rangle = c\,\langle F_V^{-1}x, y\rangle = c\,(\Psi y)(F_V^{-1}x) = (F(\Psi y))(x),
where the last equality is exactly the definition (3.1). Since x was arbitrary, \Psi(F_W y) = F(\Psi y). Since y was arbitrary,
   (3.3)  \Psi \circ F_W = F \circ \Psi,
so \Psi is an isomorphism of Frobenius modules.

STEP 4 (Transport to the dual space).
We now identify the operator F on Hom_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L) with an explicit operator on V^\vee := Hom_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell). Choose any \mathbb Q_\ell-basis vector e of the one-dimensional space L (so L = \mathbb Q_\ell e); this is a choice of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces only, not of Frobenius modules. Let
   \theta : V^\vee \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L), \qquad \theta(f)(v) := f(v)\, e .
For f \in V^\vee and v \in V,
   (F(\theta f))(v) = c\,(\theta f)(F_V^{-1}v) = c\, f(F_V^{-1}v)\, e = \theta\big(c\,(f\circ F_V^{-1})\big)(v).
Write S^t for the plain transpose of an operator S \in End(V): S^t(f) := f \circ S, an element of End(V^\vee). Then f\circ F_V^{-1} = (F_V^{-1})^t f = (F_V^t)^{-1} f, where the last equality holds because (F_V^t)^{-1}(f) = f\circ F_V^{-1} (indeed f \mapsto f\circ F_V is the inverse of f \mapsto f\circ F_V^{-1}). Hence
   (4.1)  F \text{ on } \mathrm{Hom}(V,L) \text{ is conjugate via } \theta \text{ to } c\,(F_V^t)^{-1} \text{ on } V^\vee .
By lemma_8 (conjugate operators are semisimple simultaneously),
   (4.2)  F \text{ is semisimple on } \mathrm{Hom}(V,L) \iff c\,(F_V^t)^{-1} \text{ is semisimple on } V^\vee .

STEP 5 (Three elementary equivalences on V^\vee; the point flagged by the verifier).
We record, for an invertible operator T on a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-space U, the equivalences we need, each justified in both directions.

(5a) Duals. T is semisimple on U \iff T^t is semisimple on U^\vee. Proof: for every polynomial P \in \mathbb Q_\ell[t], P(T^t) = P(T)^t (true because (T^2)^t = T^t\circ T^t, inductively (T^j)^t = (T^t)^j, and by linearity), and a matrix/operator is zero if and only if its transpose is zero. Hence the ideals \{P : P(T)=0\} and \{P : P(T^t)=0\} of \mathbb Q_\ell[t] coincide, so \mu_{T^t} = \mu_T. By lemma_60(ii) (valid over \mathbb Q_\ell, which has characteristic 0), an operator is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial is squarefree; the equivalence follows. This is consistent with the forward implication of lemma_64(iv). For later reference we also record the corrected double-dual computation that the previous attempt got wrong: with the plain-transpose convention, ((S^t)^t(\Lambda))(\mu) = \Lambda(S^t\mu) = \Lambda(\mu\circ S), so for \Lambda = ev_v one gets ((S^t)^t(ev_v))(\mu) = (ev_v)(\mu\circ S) = \mu(Sv) = ev_{Sv}(\mu) = (S(ev_v))(\mu); i.e. ev: U \xrightarrow{\sim} U^{\vee\vee} intertwines S with (S^t)^t. (Note that with the *inverse-transpose* convention used in Step 4, F_{U^\vee} := (F_U^t)^{-1} is the dual of F_U^{-1}, not of F_U; that is precisely why the inversion clause (5b) is inserted below, and no double-dual computation is needed.)

(5b) Inverses. T is semisimple on U \iff T^{-1} is semisimple on U. Forward direction: lemma_64(iv) (semisimplicity passes to T^{-1}). Reverse direction: apply the forward direction to the invertible operator T^{-1}, whose inverse is T. (Equivalently, \mu_{T^{-1}}(t) = a_0^{-1} t^r \mu_T(t^{-1}) with a_0 = \mu_T(0) \neq 0, and reciprocity is an automorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell[t^{\pm1}] preserving squarefreeness.)

(5c) Nonzero scalar multiples. T is semisimple on U \iff \lambda T is semisimple on U for \lambda \in \mathbb Q_\ell^*. Forward: lemma_64(iv) ("Tate-twist-like scalar multiples"); reverse: apply the forward direction to \lambda T and \lambda^{-1}.

STEP 6 (The chain of equivalences).
Combining Steps 3, 4 and 5 we obtain, with F_{Hom} denoting the operator (3.1):
  (i) F_W semisimple on W \iff F_{Hom} semisimple on Hom(V,L), by (3.3) and lemma_8;
  (ii) F_{Hom} semisimple \iff c(F_V^t)^{-1} semisimple on V^\vee, by (4.1) and lemma_8;
  (iii) c(F_V^t)^{-1} semisimple \iff (F_V^t)^{-1} semisimple, by (5c) with \lambda = c;
  (iv) (F_V^t)^{-1} semisimple \iff F_V^t semisimple, by (5b) applied to T = F_V^t (which is invertible since F_V is);
  (v) F_V^t semisimple \iff F_V semisimple, by (5a) applied to T = F_V.
Chaining (i)-(v),
   (6.1)  F_W \text{ is semisimple on } H^{2d-1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \iff F_V \text{ is semisimple on } H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 7 (Conclusion).
Steps 1-3 establish precisely the statement of the lemma: the map y \mapsto (x \mapsto tr(x\cup y)) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism W \xrightarrow{\sim} Hom_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L) (Step 2, from the perfectness of Poincaré duality, lemma_77(b)), and it is equivariant for F on W and for the operator \varphi \mapsto q^d\,\varphi\circ F^{-1} on the Hom-space (Step 3, equation (3.3)), where we used that F acts on L = \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) as multiplication by q^d (lemma_77(a) with m=1). Equation (6.1) of Step 6 is exactly the asserted "in particular": F is semisimple on H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) if and only if it is semisimple on H^{2d-1}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). This completes the proof.

(Remarks on scope. No semisimplicity is assumed anywhere; only the finiteness, the invertibility of F (lemma_6a), and the two formal-geometric properties of the cup-product pairing supplied by lemma_77 are used. Since arithmetic and geometric Frobenius are mutual inverses (lemma_6a) and semisimplicity passes to inverses (Step 5b), the same equivalence holds verbatim with geometric Frobenius in place of F; and by lemma_64(iii)/(lemma_5) semisimplicity over \mathbb Q_\ell is equivalent to diagonalizability after extending scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. These extensions are not needed for the stated claim.)

lemma_104_descent.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a scheme of finite type over F_q, let k=\overline{F}_q, and let Z\subset X\times_{\mathbb F_q}k be an integral closed subscheme. Then there exist an integer r\ge 1 and an integral closed subscheme Z_r\subset X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_{q^r}, of the same codimension as Z whenever X is smooth of pure dimension over \mathbb F_q, such that Z_r\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}k is isomorphic to Z as a closed subscheme of X\times_{\mathbb F_q}k.
lemma_104_descent.proof:
**Notation.** For an integer $s\ge 1$ write $X_s:=X\times_{\mathbf F_q}\mathbf F_{q^s}$, and $X_k:=X\times_{\mathbf F_q}k$. If $s\mid s'$ we write $X_{s'}\to X_s$ for the base-change projection; note that for an open $U\subset X$ one has $U_{s'}=U\times_{\mathbf F_q}\mathbf F_{q^{s'}}$, since base change preserves open immersions and fibre products, and consequently $U_{\lambda,s}\cap U_{\mu,s}=(U_\lambda\cap U_\mu)_s$ for opens $U_\lambda,U_\mu\subset X$.

If $X=\varnothing$ there is no integral closed subscheme $Z$ (an integral scheme is non-empty by definition), so there is nothing to prove; assume $X\neq\varnothing$.

**Preliminaries.**

(a) *$k$ as a filtered colimit of finite fields.* The set $\{\mathbf F_{q^s}\}_{s\ge1}$, ordered by divisibility of $s$, is a filtered diagram (lcm is an upper bound), and $\bigcup_s\mathbf F_{q^s}=k$: every element of $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ is algebraic over $\mathbf F_q$, hence lies in some $\mathbf F_{q^s}$, and $\mathbf F_{q^a}\cup\mathbf F_{q^b}\subset \mathbf F_{q^{\mathrm{lcm}(a,b)}}$. Thus $k=\varinjlim_s \mathbf F_{q^s}$. For any $\mathbf F_q$-algebra $C$, tensoring with $C$ is a left adjoint, hence commutes with colimits, so
$$C\otimes_{\mathbf F_q}k\;\simeq\;\varinjlim_{s}\bigl(C\otimes_{\mathbf F_q}\mathbf F_{q^s}\bigr).\qquad(\ast)$$

(b) *Finite-stage lemma for ideals.* Let $R=\varinjlim_s R_s$ be a filtered colimit of rings and let $J_1,J_2\subset R_{s_0}$ be finitely generated ideals whose extensions to $R$ are equal. Then $J_1R_s=J_2R_s$ for some $s\ge s_0$. *Proof.* Write $J_1=(x_1,\dots,x_m)$, $J_2=(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ with $x_i,y_j\in R_{s_0}$. Since $x_i\in J_2R$, there are $c_{ij}\in R$ with $x_i=\sum_j c_{ij}y_j$ in $R$. Each $c_{ij}$ is the image of an element of some $R_{t_{ij}}$; by filteredness there is $s'\ge s_0,t_{ij}$ and lifts $c'_{ij}\in R_{s'}$ of all the $c_{ij}$. The elements $x_i-\sum_j c'_{ij}y_j\in R_{s'}$ map to $0$ in $R$; since filtered colimits of modules are exact (the kernel of $R_{s'}\to\varinjlim R_s$ is the union of the kernels of $R_{s'}\to R_s$), each of them maps to $0$ in some $R_{s''}$ with $s''\ge s'$. Enlarging $s''$ further to also handle the relations expressing the $y_j$ in terms of the $x_i$, we get $J_1R_{s''}=J_2R_{s''}$. $\square$

The same exactness argument shows: if $x\in R_{s_0}$ maps to $0$ in $R$ (in particular, if $J_1R=R$, i.e. $1\in J_1R$), then $x$ maps to $0$ at some finite stage.

**Step 1. Affine cover and the ideals of $Z$.** $X$ is of finite type over a field, hence noetherian and quasi-compact; choose a finite affine open cover $X=\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}U_\lambda$ with $U_\lambda=\operatorname{Spec}A_\lambda$. Then $(U_\lambda)_k=\operatorname{Spec}(A_\lambda\otimes_{\mathbf F_q}k)$ is affine of finite type over $k$, hence noetherian, and $Z\cap (U_\lambda)_k=V(I_\lambda)$ for a finitely generated ideal $I_\lambda\subset A_\lambda\otimes k$.

**Step 2. Descending the ideals to one finite level.** By $(\ast)$, $A_\lambda\otimes k=\varinjlim_s(A_\lambda\otimes\mathbf F_{q^s})$. Choose a finite generating set $x_{\lambda,1},\dots,x_{\lambda,m_\lambda}$ of $I_\lambda$. Each generator comes from some stage; since $\Lambda$ is finite and the system is filtered, there is $r_1\ge1$ and elements $\tilde x_{\lambda,i}\in A_\lambda\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{r_1}}$ mapping to $x_{\lambda,i}$. Put $I_{\lambda,r_1}:=(\tilde x_{\lambda,1},\dots,\tilde x_{\lambda,m_\lambda})\subset A_\lambda\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{r_1}}$; then $I_{\lambda,r_1}(A_\lambda\otimes k)=I_\lambda$.

**Step 3. Descending the compatibility on the overlaps.** For $\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda$ put $W_{\lambda\mu}:=U_\lambda\cap U_\mu$. This is an open subset of the noetherian space $U_\lambda$, hence quasi-compact, and a quasi-compact open of an affine scheme is a finite union of principal opens; write $W_{\lambda\mu}=\bigcup_{t=1}^{N_{\lambda\mu}}T_{\lambda\mu t}$ with $T_{\lambda\mu t}=D_{U_\lambda}(a_{\lambda\mu t})$, $a_{\lambda\mu t}\in A_\lambda$. Each $T:=T_{\lambda\mu t}$ is affine, with $C_T:=\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_{X})=(A_\lambda)_{a}$, and $T_r=\operatorname{Spec}(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^r})$ for every $r$; moreover $T_k=D(a\otimes1)\subset (U_\lambda)_k$ and also $T_k\subset (U_\mu)_k$.

We use the standard description of the ideal of a closed subscheme on an affine open: if $V(J)\subset\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $V\subset\operatorname{Spec}B$ is affine open, then $\widetilde J$ is quasi-coherent and $\Gamma(V,\widetilde J)=J\,\Gamma(V,\mathcal O)$ (clear for $V=D(f)$, and the general case follows by covering $V$ by principal opens and using the exactness $0\to\Gamma(V,-)\to\prod_j\Gamma(D(f_j),-)\rightrightarrows\prod_{j,k}\Gamma(D(f_jf_k),-)$ for a finite principal cover). Applying this on $(U_\lambda)_k$ and on $(U_\mu)_k$ with $V=T_k$, we see that both extended ideals $I_\lambda(C_T\otimes k)$ and $I_\mu(C_T\otimes k)$ equal the ideal of $Z\cap T_k$ in $\Gamma(T_k,\mathcal O)=C_T\otimes k$; hence they coincide. By Step 2 and transitivity of extension of ideals,
$$I_{\lambda,r_1}(C_T\otimes k)=I_{\mu,r_1}(C_T\otimes k)\subset C_T\otimes k=\varinjlim_s\bigl(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^s}\bigr),$$
and both sides are finitely generated (by the images of the $\tilde x$'s). By the finite-stage lemma (b) there is $s(T)\ge r_1$ with $I_{\lambda,r_1}(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{s(T)}})=I_{\mu,r_1}(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{s(T)}})$. There are only finitely many triples $(\lambda,\mu,t)$; let $r_2\ge r_1$ be a common multiple of all the $s(T)$, and set $I_{\lambda,r_2}:=I_{\lambda,r_1}(A_\lambda\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{r_2}})$. Extending scalars preserves equality of extended ideals, so we still have
$$I_{\lambda,r_2}(A_\lambda\otimes k)=I_\lambda,\qquad I_{\lambda,r_2}(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{r_2}})=I_{\mu,r_2}(C_T\otimes\mathbf F_{q^{r_2}})\ \ \text{for all }T=T_{\lambda\mu t}.\qquad(\dagger)$$

**Step 4. Gluing.** Let $\mathcal J_\lambda\subset\mathcal O_{(U_\lambda)_{r_2}}$ be the quasi-coherent ideal sheaf associated to $I_{\lambda,r_2}$. On $T_{r_2}$, which is the principal open $D(a\otimes1)$ of $(U_\lambda)_{r_2}$ and an affine open of $(U_\mu)_{r_2}$, the two sheaves $\mathcal J_\lambda$ and $\mathcal J_\mu$ have as sections over $T_{r_2}$ exactly the two ideals in $(\dagger)$, which are equal; since the $T_{\lambda\mu t,r_2}$ cover $W_{\lambda\mu,r_2}=(U_\lambda)_{r_2}\cap(U_\mu)_{r_2}$, the sheaves $\mathcal J_\lambda$ and $\mathcal J_\mu$ coincide on the overlap. The identifications are as subsheaves of the fixed sheaf $\mathcal O_{X_{r_2}}$, so the cocycle condition on triple overlaps holds automatically, and sheaves glue along the open cover $\{(U_\lambda)_{r_2}\}$: there is a unique quasi-coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal J\subset\mathcal O_{X_{r_2}}$ with $\mathcal J|_{(U_\lambda)_{r_2}}=\mathcal J_\lambda$. Define $Z_{r_2}:=V(\mathcal J)\hookrightarrow X_{r_2}$, a closed subscheme. The base change of a closed subscheme along the flat map $X_k\to X_{r_2}$ is defined by the extended ideal, so $Z_{r_2}\times_{\mathbf F_{q^{r_2}}}k=V(\mathcal J\cdot\mathcal O_{X_k})$, and its restriction to $(U_\lambda)_k$ is defined by $I_{\lambda,r_2}(A_\lambda\otimes k)=I_\lambda$, i.e. by the ideal sheaf of $Z$. Hence $Z_{r_2}\times_{\mathbf F_{q^{r_2}}}k\simeq Z$ as closed subschemes of $X_k$. Set $r:=r_2$ and $Z_r:=Z_{r_2}$.

**Step 5. $Z_r$ is integral.** Let $f:Z=Z_r\times_{\mathbf F_{q^r}}k\to Z_r$ be the projection; it is the base change of $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^r}$. That morphism is faithfully flat ($k$ is a free, hence flat, $\mathbf F_{q^r}$-module, and the map on spectra is surjective since $k$ is a non-zero field) and integral (every element of $k$ is algebraic, hence integral, over $\mathbf F_{q^r}$). Both properties are stable under base change, so $f$ is faithfully flat and integral; in particular $|f|:|Z|\to|Z_r|$ is surjective.

*Non-empty:* $Z$ is integral, hence non-empty; surjectivity of $|f|$ gives $Z_r\neq\varnothing$.

*Reduced:* let $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be affine open in $Z_r$; then $f^{-1}(V)=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_{\mathbf F_{q^r}}k)$, and $B\to B\otimes k$ is injective: for $K=\ker(B\to B\otimes k)$, flatness gives $K\otimes k\hookrightarrow B\otimes k$ with image $K(B\otimes k)=0$, so $K\otimes k=0$, and faithful flatness forces $K=0$. If $b\in B$ satisfies $b^n=0$, its image in $B\otimes k=\Gamma(f^{-1}V,\mathcal O_Z)$ is nilpotent, hence $0$ because $Z$ is reduced; injectivity gives $b=0$. Thus every affine ring of $Z_r$ is reduced, i.e. $Z_r$ is reduced.

*Irreducible:* $|f|$ is a continuous surjection and $|Z|$ is irreducible; the continuous image of an irreducible space is irreducible, so $|Z_r|$ is irreducible.

Therefore $Z_r$ is integral.

**Step 6. $\dim Z_r=\dim Z$.** For $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ affine open in $Z_r$, the ring $B\otimes_{\mathbf F_{q^r}}k=\varinjlim_s(B\otimes\mathbf F_{q^s})$ is integral over $B$: each $B\otimes\mathbf F_{q^s}$ is a finite free $B$-algebra, hence integral over $B$, and integrality is preserved by filtered unions. The map is also injective and surjective on spectra (faithfully flat). We use the three classical theorems for an integral extension $A\subset B$ of rings; for completeness:

*lying over:* for $p\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, $S^{-1}B$ with $S=A\setminus p$ is non-zero (else $1/1=0$, so $s\cdot1=0$ for some $s\in S$, forcing $s=0$ in $A$, impossible) and integral over the local ring $A_p$; a maximal ideal $m\subset S^{-1}B$ gives $S^{-1}B/m$ a field integral over the domain $A_p/(m\cap A_p)$, which is therefore a field, so $m\cap A_p=pA_p$; the preimage of $m$ in $B$ contracts to $p$.
*going-up:* apply lying over to $A/q\hookrightarrow B/q$ for $q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$.
*incomparability:* suppose $q_1\subsetneq q_2$ in $\operatorname{Spec}B$ contract to the same $p$. Replacing $A$ by $A/p$ and $B$ by $B/q_1$ (the extension stays integral and injective) reduces to: $A\subset B$ domains, $q_2\cap A=0$, $q_2\neq0$. Pick $0\ne b\in q_2$ and an equation $b^n+a_{n-1}b^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1b+a_0=0$, $a_i\in A$, of minimal $n$. Then $a_0\ne0$, for otherwise $b(b^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1)=0$ in the domain $B$ gives a shorter equation. But $a_0=-(b^n+\cdots+a_1b)\in q_2\cap A=0$, contradiction.

Now: (i) $\dim Z\ge\dim Z_r$: given a chain $p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq p_n$ of points of $Z_r$, choose an affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ containing $p_n$; the $p_i$ are generalisations of $p_n$, hence lie in $V$. Lying over and going-up for $B\subset B\otimes k$ produce a chain $q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq q_n$ in $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes k)=f^{-1}(V)\subset Z$ (strict because the contractions are distinct). (ii) $\dim Z\le\dim Z_r$: given $q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq q_n$ in $Z$, choose an affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ of $Z_r$ containing $f(q_n)$; each $f(q_i)$ is a generalisation of $f(q_n)$, hence lies in $V$, so $q_i\in f^{-1}(V)=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes k)$; by incomparability the contractions satisfy $f(q_0)\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq f(q_n)$. Taking suprema, $\dim Z_r=\dim Z$.

**Step 7. Codimension when $X$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$.** Suppose $X$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbf F_q$. Then $X_r\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^r}$ and $X_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ are smooth of relative dimension $d$; smooth morphisms are open with geometrically regular (in particular $0$-dimensional-fibre-over-closed-points) structure, so every irreducible component of $X_r$ and of $X_k$ has dimension $d$; both are noetherian, universally catenary and equidimensional. For a scheme $Y$ of finite type over a field all of whose irreducible components have dimension $d$, and an integral closed subscheme $W\subset Y$, one has $\operatorname{codim}(W,Y)=d-\dim W$: every chain of irreducible closed subsets of $Y$ starting at $|W|$ is contained in a component $Y_i$ that contains $W$, so $\operatorname{codim}(|W|,Y)=\min_i\operatorname{codim}(|W|,Y_i)$, and for the irreducible component $Y_i=\operatorname{Spec}B$ (a domain of finite type over a field) with $W$ corresponding to a prime $P$, the standard dimension formula for finitely generated domains over a field, $\operatorname{ht}(P)+\dim B/P=\dim B$ (Noether normalisation plus lying over), gives $\operatorname{codim}(|W|,Y_i)=\dim Y_i-\dim W=d-\dim W$. Applying this to $Z_r\subset X_r$ and to $Z\subset X_k$, and using $\dim Z_r=\dim Z$ from Step 6, we obtain
$$\operatorname{codim}(Z_r,X_r)=d-\dim Z_r=d-\dim Z=\operatorname{codim}(Z,X_k).$$

**Conclusion.** We have produced $r\ge1$ and an integral closed subscheme $Z_r\subset X\times_{\mathbf F_q}\mathbf F_{q^r}$ with $Z_r\times_{\mathbf F_{q^r}}k\simeq Z$ as closed subschemes of $X\times_{\mathbf F_q}k$, of the same codimension as $Z$ when $X$ is smooth of pure dimension. No uniqueness of the model is claimed, and $Z_r$ need not be geometrically integral (e.g. a closed point of degree $>1$ over $\mathbf F_{q^r}$): the only assertions used are those proved above.

lemma_kummer_h1.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let \ell be a prime different from char(k), and let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over k. For every n \ge 1 the Kummer sequence 0 \to \mu_{\ell^n} \to \mathbb G_m \xrightarrow{\ \ell^n\ } \mathbb G_m \to 0 on Y_{\acute et} induces a canonical isomorphism H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]. These isomorphisms are compatible with the transition morphisms \mu_{\ell^{n+1}} \to \mu_{\ell^n}, \zeta \mapsto \zeta^{\ell} and with the maps \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] \to \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n], L \mapsto L^{\otimes \ell}, and they are functorial for pullback along morphisms of such varieties. Consequently they induce a canonical functorial isomorphism of \mathbb Z_\ell-modules \varprojlim_n H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n], where the left-hand side is H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1)).
lemma_kummer_h1.proof:
We prove the statement in seven steps. Nothing here uses Frobenius, purity, duality, or any finiteness theorem; the only input is the Kummer sequence, the long exact cohomology sequence it generates, and the elementary computation $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y^*)=k^*$.

Notation. For a $k$-scheme $T$ we write $\mathbb G_m$ for the étale sheaf $U\mapsto \mathcal O_U(U)^*$ and $\mu_{\ell^n}$ for the kernel of $[\ell^n]:\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m$, $u\mapsto u^{\ell^n}$; thus $\mu_{\ell^n}(U)=\{u\in\mathcal O_U(U)^*:u^{\ell^n}=1\}$. We write $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]:=\ker\big([\ell^n]:\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\to\operatorname{Pic}(Y),\ L\mapsto L^{\otimes \ell^n}\big)$.

STEP 0 (The units of $Y$, and two surjectivity facts). Let $A:=\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y^*)=\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)^*$.
(a) $A=k^*$. Indeed, $Y$ is projective over $k$, hence proper, so $f_*\mathcal O_Y$ is a coherent sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec} k$ and $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $k$-algebra. $Y$ is smooth over $k$, hence regular, hence reduced; a nilpotent element of $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$ is a global function vanishing in every residue field, hence is $0$, so $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$ is reduced. A finite-dimensional reduced commutative algebra over an algebraically closed field is a product of copies of $k$: $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\simeq k^r$. The $r$ primitive idempotents give a decomposition $Y=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{r}Y_i$ into non-empty open-and-closed subschemes, so $r$ is the number of connected components of $Y$; since $Y$ is geometrically connected it is connected, so $r=1$ and $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=k$. Hence $A=k^*$.
(b) Consequences of $k$ algebraically closed and $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$: (i) $[\ell^n]:k^*\twoheadrightarrow k^*$ is surjective, since for $a\neq0$ the polynomial $T^{\ell^n}-a\in k[T]$ has a root in $k$; (ii) $H^0(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})=\{u\in k^*:u^{\ell^n}=1\}=\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$; (iii) the transition map $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}(k)\to\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, is surjective: given $\zeta$ with $\zeta^{\ell^n}=1$, choose $\eta\in k^*$ with $\eta^{\ell}=\zeta$; then $\eta^{\ell^{n+1}}=1$.

STEP 1 (Exactness of the Kummer sequence on $Y_{\acute et}$). Fix $n\ge1$. The sequence of sheaves on $Y_{\acute et}$
$$0\to\mu_{\ell^n}\ \iota\longrightarrow \mathbb G_m\ \xrightarrow{[\ell^n]}\ \mathbb G_m\to0$$
is exact. Injectivity of $\iota$ and the identification of $\mu_{\ell^n}$ with the kernel are by definition. For epimorphicity, take $U\to Y$ étale and $a\in\mathcal O_U(U)^*$; the $U$-scheme $V:=U\times_{\mathbb G_m,[\ell^n]}\mathbb G_m=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal O_U(U)[T]/(T^{\ell^n}-a))$ is finite étale over $U$: the derivative $\ell^nT^{\ell^n-1}$ is invertible on $V$ because $\ell^n$ is invertible in $k$ (as $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$) and $T$ is a unit on $V$ (its $\ell^n$-th power is $a\in\mathcal O_U(U)^*$). It is surjective because on geometric points $\bar u:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to U$ with $\Omega$ separably closed, $T^{\ell^n}-\bar u(a)$ is a separable polynomial with a root by (0b)(i). Hence $\{V\to U\}$ is an étale cover on which $a$ acquires an $\ell^n$-th root, so $[\ell^n]$ is an epimorphism of étale sheaves. All sheaves involved are sheaves of abelian groups ($\mathbb G_m$ is commutative), so their $H^1$ are abelian groups.

STEP 2 (The isomorphism $\theta_n$). The long exact cohomology sequence of Step 1 contains
$$\Gamma(Y,\mathbb G_m)\xrightarrow{[\ell^n]}\Gamma(Y,\mathbb G_m)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\iota_*}H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m)\xrightarrow{[\ell^n]}H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m).$$
We use the standard identification $H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$: a line bundle $L$ gives the $\mathbb G_m$-torsor $\operatorname{Fr}(L):=\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_{\mathcal O_Y}(\mathcal O_Y,L)$ of local generators, which is torsorial for the étale topology because $L$ is locally free of rank $1$ (even Zariski-locally); conversely a $\mathbb G_m$-torsor $P$ gives $L_P:=(P\times_Y\mathbb A^1)/\mathbb G_m$ where $\mathbb G_m$ acts on $\mathbb A^1$ by multiplication. These two constructions are mutually inverse on isomorphism classes, and since $\operatorname{Fr}(L\otimes L')\simeq\operatorname{Fr}(L)\times^{\mathbb G_m}\operatorname{Fr}(L')$ via $s\otimes s'$, the bijection is a group isomorphism $H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m)\to\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$ (the group law on $H^1$ of an abelian sheaf being the contracted product). Under it, the map $[\ell^n]_*$ induced by the sheaf morphism $[\ell^n]:\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m$ is $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell^n}$: indeed $\operatorname{Fr}(L)\times^{\mathbb G_m,\,[\ell^n]}\mathbb G_m\simeq\operatorname{Fr}(L^{\otimes\ell^n})$ via $(s,t)\mapsto t\,s^{\otimes\ell^n}$, which is well defined since $(gs)^{\otimes\ell^n}=g^{\ell^n}s^{\otimes\ell^n}$, and is an isomorphism étale-locally because $\ell^n$-th roots exist étale-locally by Step 1.
By Step 0(a)+(b)(i) the first arrow $[\ell^n]:k^*\to k^*$ is surjective, so $\delta=0$; exactness then gives $\ker(\iota_*)=\operatorname{im}(\delta)=0$, and $\operatorname{im}(\iota_*)=\ker([\ell^n]_*)=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$. Therefore
$$\theta_n:=\iota_{n,*}:\ H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$$
is a canonical isomorphism of abelian groups, defined without choices (it is induced by the canonical inclusion of sheaves $\iota_n:\mu_{\ell^n}\hookrightarrow\mathbb G_m$). Note that no information about $H^2(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$ is needed: the obstruction group $\operatorname{coker}([\ell^n]:\Gamma(Y,\mathbb G_m)\to\Gamma(Y,\mathbb G_m))=k^*/(k^*)^{\ell^n}$ is zero, and that is exactly the content of the guidance's remark that "there is no $H^2$ term".

STEP 3 (Explicit description of the inverse $\psi_n:=\theta_n^{-1}$). Let $L\in\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ and choose a trivialisation $\varphi:L^{\otimes\ell^n}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_Y$. Put $Q:=\operatorname{Fr}(L)$. The assignment $s\mapsto s^{\otimes\ell^n}$ followed by $\varphi$ defines a morphism of sheaves $\pi_\varphi:Q\to\mathbb G_m$ over $Y$: étale-locally, choosing a frame $e$ of $L$ with $s=fe$, one sets $\pi_\varphi(s):=f^{\ell^n}\varphi(e^{\otimes\ell^n})\in\mathcal O^*$; changing $e$ to $ue$ changes $f$ to $fu^{-1}$ and $\varphi(e^{\otimes\ell^n})$ to $u^{\ell^n}\varphi(e^{\otimes\ell^n})$, so the value is unchanged. It satisfies $\pi_\varphi(gs)=g^{\ell^n}\pi_\varphi(s)$ for $g\in\mathbb G_m$. Define
$$P_\varphi:=\pi_\varphi^{-1}(1)\subset Q .$$
This is a $\mu_{\ell^n}$-torsor: étale-locally $Q\simeq\mathbb G_m$ and $\pi_\varphi$ is $[\ell^n]$, which is a $\mu_{\ell^n}$-torsor by Step 1; the action is $\zeta\cdot s=\zeta s$, which preserves $\pi_\varphi^{-1}(1)$ since $\pi_\varphi(\zeta s)=\zeta^{\ell^n}\pi_\varphi(s)=\pi_\varphi(s)$.
The map $P_\varphi\times^{\mu_{\ell^n}}\mathbb G_m\to Q$, $(s,t)\mapsto ts$, is an isomorphism of $\mathbb G_m$-torsors: it is $\mu_{\ell^n}$-invariant; it is surjective because étale-locally every element of $Q$ is $t\cdot s$ with $s$ a chosen $\ell^n$-th root; and it is injective because if $\zeta_1t_1=\zeta_2t_2$ with $\zeta_i\in\mu_{\ell^n}$ then $\kappa:=\zeta_1^{-1}\zeta_2$ satisfies $\kappa^{\ell^n}=(t_1/t_2)^{\ell^n}=\pi_\varphi(t_1)/\pi_\varphi(t_2)$... more directly, $1=\pi_\varphi(s_i)=\zeta_i^{\ell^n}t_i^{\ell^n}=t_i^{\ell^n}$, so $\kappa^{\ell^n}=(t_1t_2^{-1})^{\ell^n}=1$, i.e. $\kappa\in\mu_{\ell^n}$, and $(\zeta_2,t_2)=(\zeta_1\kappa,\kappa^{-1}t_1)\sim(\zeta_1,t_1)$. Hence $\theta_n([P_\varphi])=[L_P_\varphi]=[L]$.
Independence of $\varphi$: if $\varphi'=w\circ\varphi$ with $w\in\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O^*)^\times=k^*$ (Step 0(a) says every trivialisation differs by a unique scalar $w$), choose $v\in k^*$ with $v^{\ell^n}=w$ (Step 0(b)(i)); then $s\mapsto v^{-1}s$ carries $P_\varphi$ into $P_{\varphi'}$, because $\pi_{\varphi'}((vs)^{\otimes}) = w\varphi(v^{\ell^n}s^{\otimes\ell^n})=w^2\dots$ — explicitly, $\pi_{\varphi'}(v^{-1}s)=v^{-\ell^n}\pi_{\varphi'}(s)=w^{-1}\cdot w\,\pi_{\varphi}(s)=\pi_\varphi(s)$, so $v^{-1}s\in P_{\varphi'}$ whenever $s\in P_\varphi$. This map is $\mu_{\ell^n}$-equivariant and an isomorphism (inverse: multiplication by $v$). Thus the class $[P_\varphi]\in H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$ depends only on $L$. (Conceptually, this independence is exactly $\delta=0$ from Step 2: the ambiguity in changing $\varphi$ is $\delta(w)$, and $w$ is an $\ell^n$-th power.) We may therefore define $\psi_n(L):=[P_\varphi]$; Step 3 shows $\theta_n\psi_n=\mathrm{id}$, and since $\theta_n$ is a bijection, $\psi_n=\theta_n^{-1}$.

STEP 4 (Group structures). $\theta_n$ is a homomorphism because it is induced by a morphism of sheaves of abelian groups, and both groups are killed by $\ell^n$ (for $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ this is the definition; for $H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$ it holds because the sheaf $\mu_{\ell^n}$ has exponent $\ell^n$, so $[\ell^n]\circ\iota_n$ is the trivial morphism and hence $\ell^n\cdot\mathrm{id}=0$ on $H^1(\mu_{\ell^n})$). Consequently $\theta_n$ is $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$-linear, and $H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ as $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$-modules.

STEP 5 (Compatibility with the transition maps). Let $\rho_n:\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, and let $\lambda_n:\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}]\to\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$, $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}$ (well defined: $(L^{\otimes\ell})^{\otimes\ell^n}=L^{\otimes\ell^{n+1}}\simeq\mathcal O_Y$). On the level of sheaves we have the identity of morphisms
$$\iota_n\circ\rho_n\ =\ [\ell]\circ\iota_{n+1}:\ \mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\longrightarrow\mathbb G_m ,$$
since both send $\zeta$ to $\zeta^{\ell}\in\mathcal O^*$. Passing to $H^1$ and using Step 2 (the map induced by $[\ell]:\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m$ on $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$ is $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}$),
$$\theta_n\circ(\rho_n)_*=\iota_{n,*}\circ(\rho_n)_*=(\iota_n\rho_n)_*=([\ell]\iota_{n+1})_*=[\ell]_*\circ\iota_{n+1,*}=\lambda_n\circ\theta_{n+1}.$$
Thus the square
$$\begin{CD} H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}) @>{(\rho_n)_*}>> H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\\ @V{\theta_{n+1}}VV @VV{\theta_n}V \\ \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] @>{L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}}>> \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\end{CD}$$
commutes. One may also check this directly on the model of Step 3: for $L$ with trivialisation $\varphi:L^{\otimes\ell^{n+1}}\simeq\mathcal O$, the trivialisation $\varphi'=\varphi^{\otimes?}$... concretely $\psi_n(L^{\otimes\ell})$ is represented by $P_{\varphi^{(\ell)}}$ where $\varphi^{(\ell)}:L^{\otimes\ell\cdot\ell^n}\simeq\mathcal O$ is the composite $L^{\otimes\ell^{n+1}}\xrightarrow{\sim}(L^{\otimes\ell})^{\otimes\ell^n}\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal O$ (canonical identification of the two $\ell^{n+1}$-st tensor powers), and the map $s\mapsto s^{\otimes\ell}$ sends the $\ell^{n+1}$-st root torsor of $(L,\varphi)$ into the $\ell^n$-th root torsor of $(L^{\otimes\ell},\varphi^{(\ell)})$; the induced map on the contracted product with $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\xrightarrow{\rho_n}\mu_{\ell^n}$ is precisely the pushout by $\rho_n$, giving $\rho_{n,*}P_\varphi\simeq P_{\varphi^{(\ell)}}$. The sheaf-morphism argument above is the clean proof of the same identity.

STEP 6 (Functoriality). Let $f:Y'\to Y$ be a morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected $k$-varieties. The morphism of small étale topoi $f_{\acute et}:Y'_{\acute et}\to Y_{\acute et}$ satisfies $f^{-1}\mathbb G_{m,Y}=\mathbb G_{m,Y'}$, and since $f^{-1}$ is exact and commutes with finite limits, $f^{-1}$ of the Kummer sequence of $Y$ is the Kummer sequence of $Y'$. The long exact cohomology sequence is natural in the short exact sequence of sheaves and in the morphism of topoi, and the identification $H^1(-,\mathbb G_m)=\operatorname{Pic}(-)$ is natural with $f^{-1}$ of the frame torsor of $L$ equal to the frame torsor of $f^*L$. Hence $\theta_n\circ f^*=f^*\circ\theta_n$ as maps $H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\to\operatorname{Pic}(Y')[\ell^n]$. The transition maps of Step 5 are likewise compatible with $f^*$ (both $\rho_{n,*}$ and $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}$ commute with pullback). Thus the whole system $\{(\theta_n,\rho_n,\lambda_n)\}_n$ is functorial in $Y$.

STEP 7 (Inverse limits, and the identification with $H^1(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))$). Put $\mathbb Z_\ell(1):=(\mu_{\ell^n})_{n\ge1}$ with transition morphisms $\rho_n$. Since each $\theta_n$ is an isomorphism and the squares of Step 5 commute, the induced map on inverse limits
$$\theta:=\varprojlim_n\theta_n:\ \varprojlim_n H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\ \longrightarrow\ \varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$$
is an isomorphism: the inverse is $((x_n)_n)\mapsto(\theta_n^{-1}(x_n)_n)$, and the tuple $(\theta_n^{-1}(x_n))$ is compatible because $\theta_n\rho_{n,*}\theta_{n+1}^{-1}=\lambda_n$ on the nose. No Mittag-Leffler or $\lim^1$ argument is needed for $\theta$ itself, precisely because the level maps are isomorphisms and not merely surjections; the transition maps on the right are group homomorphisms, so $\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ is an abelian group, and likewise on the left.
Each $H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$ and each $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ is a $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$-module, and $\rho_{n,*}$, $\lambda_n$ are equivariant for the restriction $\mathbb Z/\ell^{n+1}\to\mathbb Z/\ell^n$ (because they are group homomorphisms between groups of exponent $\ell^{n+1}$ and $\ell^n$: $\rho_{n,*}(a\cdot P)=a\cdot\rho_{n,*}P$, and $(L^{\otimes\ell})^{\otimes a}=(L^{\otimes a})^{\otimes\ell}$). Hence both limits are $\mathbb Z_\ell=\varprojlim_n\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$-modules, $\theta_n$ is $\mathbb Z/\ell^n$-linear by Step 4, and $\theta$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Z_\ell$-modules.
It remains to justify that the left-hand side is $H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))$. If one adopts the convention $H^1(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1)):=\varprojlim_nH^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$, this is tautological. With Jannsen's definition of continuous étale cohomology of a pro-sheaf, there is a canonical exact sequence
$$0\to R^1\!\varprojlim_n H^0(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\longrightarrow H^1(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\to0 .$$
By Step 0(b)(ii)+(iii) the tower $H^0(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})=\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ has surjective transition maps. For any tower of abelian groups $A_1\leftarrow A_2\leftarrow\cdots$ with surjective bonding maps, $R^1\varprojlim A_n=\operatorname{coker}(d)$ with $d((a_n))=(a_n-\phi_{n+1}(a_{n+1}))$ vanishes: given $(b_n)$, choose inductively $a_1:=0$ and $a_{n+1}$ lifting $a_n-b_n$ along the surjection $\phi_{n+1}$, which yields $d((a_n))=(b_n)$. Hence $R^1\varprojlim_nH^0(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})=0$, and the right-hand arrow is a canonical isomorphism $H^1(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))\simeq\varprojlim_nH^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$. Composing with $\theta$ gives the claimed canonical functorial $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module isomorphism
$$H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n].$$

REMARKS ON SCOPE (what is deliberately NOT used). (1) Only properness (to get $\Gamma(\mathcal O_Y)$ finite over $k$), reducedness (smoothness is more than enough), connectedness (geometric connectedness is more than enough), and $k$ algebraically closed enter, and only through Step 0. (2) No computation of $H^2(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$, no Kummer/Leray sequence for a structure morphism, no $H^1(\operatorname{Spec}k,-)$, no Albanese or Picard variety, and no identification of $\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ with the Tate module of $\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}$ (that would need the torsion-freeness of $\operatorname{NS}(Y)$, or finite generation of $\operatorname{NS}(Y)$ plus a $\lim^1$ argument on the right-hand side, none of which is proved here). (3) No Frobenius appears: the identifications above are purely algebraic and, by Step 6, natural for all morphisms, so they will be available for the later Frobenius bookkeeping with the covariant/contravariant directions exactly as fixed here ($\theta_n$ is induced by the inclusion $\mu_{\ell^n}\hookrightarrow\mathbb G_m$, i.e. it is contravariant in $Y$ through $f^*$ on both sides).

lemma_poincare_reducibility.statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $k$. Then there exist an integer $r\ge 1$ and abelian $k$-subvarieties $B_1,\dots,B_r\subseteq A$, each simple over $k$ (having no nonzero proper abelian $k$-subvariety), such that the addition homomorphism $B_1\times_k\cdots\times_k B_r\to A$, $(b_1,\dots,b_r)\mapsto \sum_{i=1}^{r} b_i$, is an isogeny. Equivalently: for every abelian subvariety $i:B\hookrightarrow A$ there is an abelian subvariety $C\subseteq A$ such that $B\cap C$ is finite and $B\times_k C\to A$ is an isogeny.
lemma_poincare_reducibility.proof:
Let k be a field and A an abelian variety over k. We prove the complementary-subvariety assertion first; it implies the product-of-simple-factors assertion by induction. All subvarieties are abelian k-subvarieties, and simple means k-simple, i.e. having no nonzero proper abelian k-subvariety. The zero abelian variety is treated explicitly.

1. Structural facts about homomorphisms.
Fact 1. If f:A→A' is a homomorphism of abelian k-varieties, then its reduced scheme-theoretic image I is an abelian k-subvariety of A', and dim A = dim I + dim ker f.
Proof. The graph of f is closed in A×A' because A is proper and A' is separated; projecting the graph to A' shows that the image is closed. Let Ω be an algebraic closure of k and let I_Ω be the reduced scheme-theoretic image of f_Ω:A_Ω→A'_Ω. An abelian variety is geometrically connected, so A_Ω is connected; hence I_Ω is connected. The map f_Ω:A_Ω→I_Ω is surjective. The group law on A' restricts to I_Ω: indeed the multiplication map I_Ω×I_Ω→A'_Ω factors through I_Ω because after pulling back along the surjective map f_Ω×f_Ω:A_Ω×A_Ω→I_Ω×I_Ω it becomes f_Ω∘m_A, which lands in I_Ω; the same argument applies to the inverse map. Thus I_Ω is a closed subgroup scheme of A'_Ω. It is reduced by construction, hence smooth over the perfect field Ω: generic smoothness gives a nonempty smooth locus, translating a smooth point to the identity makes the identity smooth, and then all points are smooth by translation. It is proper because it is closed in the proper variety A'_Ω. Hence I_Ω is an abelian subvariety of A'_Ω.
The construction of I_Ω is canonical, so it is invariant under Gal(Ω/k). By fpqc/Galois descent for closed subschemes it descends to a closed subscheme I⊂A'. The group-law factorisation also descends, because factorisation through a closed subscheme can be checked after faithfully flat base change. Smoothness, connectedness and properness descend from I_Ω to I, so I is an abelian k-subvariety.
Finally f factors as A→I→A' with A→I surjective. Every geometric fibre over a point of I is a translate of ker f, hence has dimension dim ker f. The fibre-dimension theorem gives dim A = dim I + dim ker f.

Fact 2. If u:A→B is a homomorphism and K=ker u, then the identity component K^0 is an abelian k-subvariety of A, and dim K^0 = dim A - dim im u.
Proof. Base change to Ω. The identity component K_Ω^0 of the closed subgroup scheme K_Ω of the algebraic group A_Ω is a smooth connected closed subgroup scheme: over the perfect field Ω its reduced structure is a reduced closed subgroup scheme, hence smooth by the criterion used in Fact 1. It is characteristic in K_Ω, hence Gal(Ω/k)-invariant, and therefore descends to a closed subgroup scheme K^0⊂A. Descent of the group law, smoothness, connectedness and properness shows K^0 is an abelian k-subvariety. All irreducible components of K_Ω are translates of K_Ω^0, so dim K_Ω = dim K_Ω^0. Applying Fact 1 to u gives dim A = dim im u + dim ker u = dim im u + dim K^0.

Fact 3. Isogeny criteria.
(i) A homomorphism f:A→A' with finite kernel and dim im f = dim A' is an isogeny: its image is a closed abelian subvariety of the integral variety A' of full dimension, hence all of A'; finite kernel makes f quasi-finite, and properness makes it finite.
(ii) Compositions and products of isogenies are isogenies.
(iii) For abelian subvarieties B,C⊂A, the addition map σ:B×C→A has kernel canonically isomorphic to the scheme-theoretic intersection B∩C via x↦(x,-x). If B∩C is finite and dim B+dim C=dim A, then by Fact 1 dim im σ = dim B+dim C-dim(B∩C)=dim A, so σ is surjective by (i); hence σ is an isogeny.

2. Polarisation.
Let A^∨ denote the dual abelian variety, representing Pic^0_{A/k}. For a line bundle L on A define λ_L:A→A^∨ by x↦t_x^*L⊗L^{-1}. The theorem of square implies that λ_L is a homomorphism, that λ_{L⊗M}=λ_L+λ_M, and that for every homomorphism f:A→B one has λ_{f^*M}=f^∨∘λ_M∘f. The provided lemma lemma_mult_pic0 is the Pic^0 additivity/translation-invariance input in this standard argument.
Every abelian variety is projective, hence carries an ample line bundle over k. If L is ample, λ_L is an isogeny. Indeed, let K=ker λ_L and K^0 its identity component. For every geometric point x of K^0, t_x^*L≅L, so L|_{K^0} is invariant under all translations; by the standard characterisation of Pic^0 it lies in Pic^0(K^0). But L|_{K^0} is ample. If dim K^0>0, an ample line bundle cannot be algebraically equivalent to zero: after base change to Ω choose a complete-intersection curve C⊂K^0_Ω for L|_{K^0}; then deg_C L>0, whereas a line bundle algebraically equivalent to zero has degree zero on every curve. Contradiction. Thus K^0=0, so K is finite. By Fact 1, dim im λ_L = dim A = dim A^∨; the image is a closed abelian subvariety of A^∨ of full dimension, hence all of A^∨. Therefore λ_L is an isogeny.

3. Complementary subvariety.
Let i:B↪A be an abelian k-subvariety. Choose an ample line bundle L on A and put λ=λ_L. Define
u = i^∨∘λ∘i : B→B^∨,   w = i^∨∘λ : A→B^∨.
By functoriality of λ, u=λ_{i^*L}. Since i^*L is ample, u is an isogeny. Let C=(ker w)^0. By Fact 2, C is an abelian k-subvariety of A.
First, B∩C is finite because
B∩C ⊂ B∩ker w = ker(w∘i)=ker u,
and u is an isogeny.
Second, w is surjective. Its image is an abelian subvariety of B^∨ containing the image of w∘i=u, which is all of B^∨ because u is an isogeny. Hence im w=B^∨. Therefore, using dim B^∨=dim B and Fact 2,
dim C = dim A - dim im w = dim A - dim B^∨ = dim A - dim B.
Finally, the addition map σ:B×C→A has kernel B∩C, which is finite, and dim B+dim C=dim A. By Fact 3(iii), σ is an isogeny. This proves the complementary-subvariety assertion. The cases B=0 and B=A are included in the same argument, or can be checked directly.

4. Decomposition into simple factors.
We prove the first assertion by induction on d=dim A.
If d=0, then A is the zero abelian variety. Take r=1 and B_1=0. The addition map 0→0 is an isomorphism, and 0 is simple under the parenthetical definition, because it has no nonzero proper abelian subvariety. If one uses the convention that the zero variety is not simple, this is the only trivial exception.
Assume d>0. The set of nonzero abelian subvarieties of A is nonempty because it contains A itself. Choose B_1 of minimal positive dimension. Then B_1 is k-simple: any nonzero proper abelian subvariety of B_1 would be a nonzero abelian subvariety of A of smaller dimension.
Apply the complementary-subvariety assertion to B_1⊂A. We obtain an abelian subvariety C_1⊂A such that σ:B_1×C_1→A is an isogeny. Since B_1≠0, dim C_1 = dim A - dim B_1 < dim A. By the induction hypothesis applied to C_1, there exist k-simple abelian subvarieties B_2,...,B_r⊂C_1 and an isogeny τ:B_2×...×B_r→C_1; if C_1=0, simply take r=1. The product id_{B_1}×τ is an isogeny B_1×B_2×...×B_r→B_1×C_1, and composing with σ gives an isogeny
B_1×_k...×_k B_r → A.
This proves the decomposition assertion.

5. Remarks on the formulation.
The proof establishes the complementary-subvariety assertion and then deduces the product-of-simple-factors assertion; these are the two standard equivalent formulations of Poincaré complete reducibility. The word simple is k-simple, not necessarily geometrically simple. No finite generation of Hom groups and no finite-dimensionality of End^0(A) is used; the argument uses only polarisations, dual abelian varieties, dimension counting, and descent for images and identity components.

lemma_tate_rank.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\ge0\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and let \(B\) be an abelian variety of dimension \(g\) over \(k\). Then the Tate module \(T_\ell(B):=\varprojlim_n B[\ell^n](k)\), with transition maps multiplication by \(\ell\), is a free \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module of rank \(2g\); equivalently, for \(V_\ell(B):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(B)\) one has \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_\ell(B)=2\dim B\).
lemma_tate_rank.proof:
Let $g:=\dim B$. We prove $T_\ell(B):=\varprojlim_n B[\ell^n](k)$ (bonding maps $\times\ell$) is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2g$, and deduce $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_\ell(B)=2g$.

PRELIMINARIES AND EDGE CASE. Write $[m]_B:B\to B$ (or just $[m]$) for multiplication by $m$, a homomorphism of group schemes, $e\in B(k)$ the identity, and $B[m]:=[m]^{-1}(e)$ the scheme-theoretic fibre (the $m$-torsion group scheme). A smooth connected group scheme over a field is geometrically integral; since $k$ is algebraically closed, $B$ is integral, irreducible, of dimension $g$, with function field $K(B)$, and every closed point of $B$ is $k$-rational.
If $g=0$: a $0$-dimensional smooth connected $k$-scheme with a $k$-point is $\operatorname{Spec}k$, so $B[\ell^n](k)=\{0\}$ for all $n$, $T_\ell(B)=0\cong\mathbb Z_\ell^{\oplus 0}$ is free of rank $0=2\dim B$, and $V_\ell(B)=0$. Assume henceforth $g\ge 1$.

CLASSICAL INPUTS (stated once, used only where indicated).
(Cube) Theorem of the cube: if $X,Y,Z$ are complete varieties over $k$ with base points and $\mathcal N$ a line bundle on $X\times Y\times Z$ trivial on each of $X\times Y\times\{z_0\}$, $X\times\{y_0\}\times Z$, $\{x_0\}\times Y\times Z$, then $\mathcal N$ is trivial on $X\times Y\times Z$.
(HRR) Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch: for a coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$ on the smooth projective $B$, $\chi(B,\mathcal F)=\int_B \operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)\operatorname{td}(T_B)$ in the Chow ring $A^*(B)$, with $\int_B:A^g(B)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Z$ the degree map.
(Pos) The top self-intersection of an ample line bundle on a $g$-fold is $>0$; for completeness we note this follows from (HRR) plus Serre vanishing: $h^0(B,L^r)=\chi(B,L^r)+O(r^{g-1})$ and $\chi(B,L^r)=c_1(L)^g r^g/g!$, while $h^0(B,L^r)\to\infty$ for $L$ ample.
No statement about Tate modules, $\ell$-adic cohomology, or $V_\ell$ is used anywhere below; in particular the degree formula of Step 2 is proved without any input from Steps 3–4.

STEP 1. THE MAP $[m]$ FOR $(m,p)=1$.
1(a) The differential. For integers $n,n'$: $[1]=\mathrm{id}$ gives $d[1]_e=\mathrm{id}$; $[n+n']=\mu_B\circ([n],[n'])$ gives $d[n+n']_e=d[n]_e+d[n']_e$ (because $d\mu_{B,(e,e)}(u,v)=u+v$, which follows from $\mu\circ(\mathrm{id},e)=\mathrm{id}=\mu\circ(e,\mathrm{id})$); $[nn']=[n]\circ[n']$ gives $d[nn']_e=d[n]_e\circ d[n']_e$. Hence $n\mapsto d[n]_e$ is a ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{End}_k(\operatorname{Lie}B)$, so $d[m]_e=m\cdot\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Lie}B}$. If $(m,p)=1$ then $m\in k^\times$ and $d[m]_e$ is an isomorphism.
1(b) \'Etale everywhere. Jacobian criterion: if $f:X\to Y$ is a morphism of smooth $k$-varieties of the same dimension and $df_x$ is an isomorphism, then $f$ is \'etale at $x$. (Indeed the fibre of $\Omega_{X/Y}$ at $x$ is $\operatorname{coker}(df_x)=0$, so $\Omega_{X/Y}=0$ near $x$ by Nakayama, i.e. $f$ is unramified and quasi-finite at $x$; then for the local homomorphism $\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ of regular local rings of dimension $g$ with $0$-dimensional closed fibre, $\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}=\dim\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}+\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}/\mathfrak m_{f(x)}\mathcal O_{X,x}$, so the map is flat by the local criterion of flatness for regular local rings; flat + unramified = \'etale.) Applying this to $[m]$ at $e$: $[m]$ is \'etale at $e$. The \'etale locus is open, and the identity $[m]\circ t_x=t_{[m]x}\circ[m]$ shows it is stable under every translation $t_x$; since the translations act transitively and the locus contains $e$, $[m]$ is \'etale on all of $B$.
1(c) Surjectivity, finiteness, degree. $[m]$ is proper, because $B$ is projective over $k$, hence proper, and any morphism from a proper $k$-scheme to a $k$-scheme is proper. So $\operatorname{im}[m]$ is closed; being \'etale, $[m]$ is flat and of finite presentation, hence open, so $\operatorname{im}[m]$ is also open, non-empty, and closed in the irreducible space $B$; thus $\operatorname{im}[m]=B$. Since every $k$-point of $B$ is closed, surjectivity on topological spaces gives: $[m]:B(k)\to B(k)$ is surjective.
$[m]$ is quasi-finite (\'etale $\Rightarrow$ locally quasi-finite, and proper $\Rightarrow$ finite fibres), and proper, hence finite by Zariski's Main Theorem. Being finite and flat of finite presentation, $[m]_*\mathcal O_B$ is finite locally free; as $B$ is irreducible its rank is a constant, which we define to be
  $$\deg[m]:=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal O_B}[m]_*\mathcal O_B=[K(B):[m]^\sharp K(B)],$$\nthe degree of the finite separable extension of function fields induced by the dominant map $[m]$ (at the generic point $[m]_*\mathcal O_B\otimes K(B)\cong K(B)^{\oplus r}$ as $[m]^\sharp K(B)$-vector space, so $r=[K(B):[m]^\sharp K(B)]$). We do NOT write this as $[k(B):k(B)]$; it is the rank of the finite locally free morphism.
The fibre $B[m]=[m]^{-1}(e)$ is the base change of $[m]$ along $e:\operatorname{Spec}k\to B$; it is finite (as $[m]$ is finite) and \'etale of rank $\deg[m]$ over $k$. Over the algebraically closed field $k$ a finite \'etale scheme of rank $r$ is $\coprod_{r}\operatorname{Spec}k$, hence
  $$|B[m](k)|=\deg[m].\tag{1.1}$$

STEP 2. THE DEGREE FORMULA $\deg[m]=m^{2g}$ FOR $(m,p)=1$.
2(a) Symmetric ample line bundle. Take an ample $M$ on $B$ and set $L:=M\otimes t_{-1}^*M$. Then $L$ is ample (a tensor product of ample line bundles is ample) and symmetric: $t_{-1}^*L=t_{-1}^*M\otimes(t_{-1}\circ t_{-1})^*M=t_{-1}^*M\otimes[1]^*M\cong L$, since $t_{-1}\circ t_{-1}=[1]=\mathrm{id}$.
2(b) The cube identity. Let $\mu:B^3\to B$ be addition, $p_i$ the projections, $p_{ij}:B^3\to B$ the sum of the $i$-th and $j$-th coordinates, and for a line bundle $N$ on $B$ put
  $$C(N):=\mu^*N\otimes p_{12}^*N^{-1}\otimes p_{13}^*N^{-1}\otimes p_{23}^*N^{-1}\otimes p_1^*N\otimes p_2^*N\otimes p_3^*.$$$C(N)$ is invariant under permuting the three factors, so it suffices to check triviality on the slice $B\times B\times\{0\}$: there $\mu=p_{12}$, $p_{13}=p_1$, $p_{23}=p_2$, and $p_3$ is the constant map to $0$, so $C(N)|_{B\times B\times\{0\}}$ is the constant line bundle with fibre $N|_e$, which is trivial. Likewise on the other two slices. As $B$ is complete, (Cube) gives $C(N)\cong\mathcal O_{B^3}$. Pulling back along homomorphisms $f,g,h:T\to B$ from any $k$-scheme $T$ yields
  $$(f+g+h)^*N\otimes(f+g)^*N^{-1}\otimes(f+h)^*N^{-1}\otimes(g+h)^*N^{-1}\otimes f^*N\otimes g^*N\otimes h^*N\cong\mathcal O.\tag{2.1}$$
Also note $[0]^*N\cong\mathcal O$: $[0]$ factors as $B\to\operatorname{Spec}k\xrightarrow{e}B$, and the pullback of the $1$-dimensional $k$-vector space $N|_e$ is a trivial line bundle.
2(c) $[n]^*L\cong L^{\otimes n^2}$ for all $n\ge0$. Cases $n=0,1$: $[0]^*L\cong\mathcal O=L^{\otimes0}$, $[1]^*L=L=L^{\otimes1}$. Case $n=2$: apply (2.1) with $N=L$, $f=g=\mathrm{id}_B$, $h=[-1]$; then $f+g+h=[1]$, $f+g=[2]$, $f+h=g+h=[0]$, so
  $$L\otimes[2]^*L^{-1}\otimes[0]^*L^{-1}\otimes[0]^*L^{-1}\otimes L\otimes L\otimes[-1]^*L\cong\mathcal O.$$
Using $[0]^*L\cong\mathcal O$ and $[-1]^*L=t_{-1}^*L\cong L$ (symmetry), this is $L^{\otimes4}\otimes[2]^*L^{-1}\cong\mathcal O$, i.e. $[2]^*L\cong L^{\otimes4}=L^{\otimes2^2}$.
Induction step: apply (2.1) with $f=g=\mathrm{id}_B$, $h=[n]$ ($n\ge0$); then $f+g+h=[n+2]$, $f+g=[2]$, $f+h=g+h=[n+1]$, giving
  $$[n+2]^*L\cong[2]^*L\otimes[n+1]^{*}L^{\otimes2}\otimes L^{-\otimes2}\otimes[n]^*L^{-1}.\tag{2.2}$$
If $[n]^*L\cong L^{n^2}$ and $[n+1]^*L\cong L^{(n+1)^2}$, the right side of (2.2) is $L^{\otimes e}$ with $e=4+2(n+1)^2-2-n^2=n^2+4n+4=(n+2)^2$. Induction on $n$ proves the claim. (This is exactly the standard corollary of the cube theorem; the symmetry of $L$ is what forces the 'quadratic defect' at $n=2$ to vanish.)
2(d) The count. Fix $m\ge1$ with $(m,p)=1$ and put $d:=\deg[m]$; by Step 1, $E:=[m]_*\mathcal O_B$ is locally free of rank $d$. For every integer $r\ge1$, since $[m]$ is finite, $R^i[m]_*=0$ for $i>0$, and the projection formula gives $[m]_*[m]^*L^{\otimes r}\cong E\otimes L^{\otimes r}$; hence $H^i(B,[m]^*L^{\otimes r})\cong H^i(B,E\otimes L^{\otimes r})$ for all $i$, and by 2(c),
  $$\chi(B,E\otimes L^{\otimes r})=\chi(B,[m]^*L^{\otimes r})=\chi(B,L^{\otimes m^2r}).\tag{2.3}$$
Write $\xi:=c_1(L)\in A^1(B)$ and $\operatorname{ch}(E)=\sum_{j=0}^{g}\operatorname{ch}_j(E)$ with $\operatorname{ch}_j(E)\in A^j(B)$, $\operatorname{ch}_0(E)=d$. The tangent bundle of an abelian variety is trivial (translation-invariant vector fields give a global frame), so all Chern classes of $T_B$ vanish and $\operatorname{td}(T_B)=1$; (HRR) then gives $\chi(\mathcal F)=\int_B\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)$ for every coherent $\mathcal F$. Therefore
  $$\chi(B,E\otimes L^{\otimes r})=\int_B\operatorname{ch}(E)e^{r\xi}=\sum_{j=0}^{g}\frac{r^{g-j}}{(g-j)!}\int_B\operatorname{ch}_j(E)\,\xi^{g-j}=d\,\frac{\xi^g}{g!}\,r^g+O(r^{g-1}),$$\nwhile, since only the codimension-$g$ part of $\operatorname{ch}(N)=e^{c_1(N)}$ integrates,
  $$\chi(B,L^{\otimes m^2r})=\int_B e^{m^2r\xi}=\frac{\xi^g}{g!}\,m^{2g}r^g.$$
Both sides of (2.3) are polynomial functions of $r$ agreeing for all $r\ge1$, and $\xi^g=\deg(L^g)>0$ by (Pos) ($L$ is ample). Comparing the coefficients of $r^g$ gives $d=m^{2g}$, i.e.
  $$\deg[m]=m^{2g}\qquad((m,p)=1).\tag{2.4}$$

STEP 3. THE GROUPS $G_n:=B[\ell^n](k)$.
Since $(\ell,p)=1$, Step 1 and (1.1) with $m=\ell^n$, together with (2.4), give $B[\ell^n]$ finite \'etale of rank $\ell^{2gn}$, hence
  $$|G_n|=\ell^{2gn},\qquad G_n\ \text{is an abelian group of exponent dividing }\ \ell^n.\tag{3.1}$$
$\times\ell:G_{n+1}\to G_n$ is surjective: given $P\in G_n$, surjectivity of $[\ell]:B(k)\to B(k)$ (Step 1(c)) yields $Q\in B(k)$ with $\ell Q=P$; then $\ell^{n+1}Q=\ell^nP=0$, so $Q\in G_{n+1}$. (Equivalently: $\ker(\times\ell:G_{n+1}\to G_n)=G_1$ has order $\ell^{2g}$ by (3.1), so the image has order $\ell^{2g(n+1)}/\ell^{2g}=\ell^{2gn}=|G_n|$.)
Write $G_n\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^{t}\mathbb Z/\ell^{a_j}\mathbb Z$ with $a_j\ge1$. Then $G_n[\ell]\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell)^{t}$, so $t=\dim_{\mathbb F_\ell}G_n[\ell]$. But $G_n[\ell]=\{P\in B(k):\ell P=0\}=G_1$, and $|G_1|=\ell^{2g}$ by (3.1), so $t=2g$. Taking orders in (3.1) gives $\sum_{j=1}^{2g}a_j=2gn$, and the exponent condition gives $a_j\le n$ for all $j$; $2g$ positive integers each $\le n$ summing to $2gn$ must all equal $n$. Hence
  $$G_n\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z)^{\oplus 2g}\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\tag{3.2}$$\nand $G_1\cong\mathbb F_\ell^{\oplus2g}$.

STEP 4. THE TATE MODULE $T=\varprojlim_nG_n\cong\mathbb Z_\ell^{\oplus2g}$.
An element $x\in T$ is a sequence $(x_m)_{m\ge1}$, $x_m\in G_m$, with
  $$x_m=\ell\,x_{m+1}\quad\text{for all }m\ge1,\tag{4.1}$$\ni.e. $\pi_m=(\times\ell)\circ\pi_{m+1}$ for the projections $\pi_m:T\to G_m$. ($T$ is a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module: for $\lambda=(\lambda_n)\in\mathbb Z_\ell=\varprojlim\mathbb Z/\ell^n$ set $\lambda x:=(\lambda_nx_n)$; (4.1) and the $\mathbb Z/\ell^n$-module structures on the $G_n$ make this compatible.)
4(a) $\pi_n$ is surjective. Given $P\in G_n$, choose inductively $x_{n+1}\in G_{n+1},x_{n+2}\in G_{n+2},\dots$ with $\ell x_{m+1}=x_m$ starting from $x_n:=P$ (possible by the surjectivity of each $\times\ell:G_{m+1}\to G_m$ shown in Step 3). For $m<n$ set $x_m:=\ell^{\,n-m}P\in G_m$ (indeed $\ell^m x_m=\ell^nP=0$). Then $x=(x_m)$ lies in $T$ by construction ($\ell x_m=\ell^{n-m+1}P=x_{m-1}$ for $m\le n$, and $\ell x_n=\ell P$... note $\ell x_n$ is not needed; the required relation at $m=n$ is $x_n=\ell x_{n+1}$, which holds by the choice of $x_{n+1}$), and $\pi_n(x)=P$.
4(b) $\ker\pi_n=\ell^nT$.
$(\supseteq)$ If $x=\ell^ny$ with $y\in T$, then $x_n=\ell^ny_n=0$ because $y_n\in G_n=B[\ell^n](k)$; so $x\in\ker\pi_n$.
$(\subseteq)$ Let $x\in\ker\pi_n$, so $x_n=0$; iterating (4.1) gives $x_m=\ell^{\,n-m}x_n=0$ for all $m\le n$. For $m\ge n$ define
  $$H_m:=\{z\in G_m:\ell^nz=x_m\}.$$
Non-emptiness: by (3.2), $G_m\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^m)^{\oplus2g}$, and in this group $\ell^nG_m\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^{m-n})^{\oplus2g}=G_m[\ell^{m-n}]$ (the inclusion $\ell^nG_m\subseteq G_m[\ell^{m-n}]$ is clear and both sides have order $\ell^{2g(m-n)}$; here $G_m[\ell^{m-n}]=G_{m-n}$ as a subgroup of $G_m$). Since $\ell^{m-n}x_m=x_n=0$ by (4.1), $x_m\in G_m[\ell^{m-n}]=\ell^nG_m$, so $H_m\ne\emptyset$ (a coset of $G_m[\ell^n]=G_n$, of cardinality $\ell^{2gn}$).
Correct bonding: for $z\in H_{m+1}$, $\ell^n(\ell z)=\ell(\ell^nz)=\ell x_{m+1}=x_m$, so $\times\ell$ maps $H_{m+1}$ into $H_m$. Thus $(H_m)_{m\ge n}$ is an inverse system of non-empty FINITE sets, hence $\varprojlim_{m\ge n}H_m\ne\emptyset$: the images of $H_n\times\cdots\times H_{n+N}$ in $H_n$ form a decreasing sequence of non-empty finite sets, eventually constant and non-empty, and an element of the stable image lifts to a compatible family. Choose $(z_m)_{m\ge n}$ in the limit, so
  $$\ell^nz_m=x_m\ \text{ and }\ z_m=\ell z_{m+1}\qquad(m\ge n).\tag{4.2}$$
Define $y=(y_m)_{m\ge1}$ by $y_m:=z_m$ for $m\ge n$ and $y_m:=\ell^{\,n-m}z_n$ for $1\le m<n$. Then $y_m\in G_m$: for $m\ge n$, $\ell^my_m=\ell^{m-n}(\ell^nz_m)=\ell^{m-n}x_m=x_n=0$; for $m<n$, $\ell^my_m=\ell^nz_n=x_n=0$ (using $\ell^nz_n=x_n$ from (4.2) with $m=n$). And $y$ satisfies (4.1): for $m\ge n$, $y_m=z_m=\ell z_{m+1}=\ell y_{m+1}$ by (4.2); for $1\le m<n$, $\ell y_{m+1}=\ell^{\,n-m}z_n=y_m$. So $y\in T$. Finally $\ell^ny=x$: for $m\ge n$, $(\ell^ny)_m=\ell^nz_m=x_m$ by (4.2); for $m<n$, $(\ell^ny)_m=\ell^ny_m=\ell^{\,n-m}(\ell^nz_n)=\ell^{\,n-m}x_n=0=x_m$. Hence $x=\ell^ny\in\ell^nT$.
4(c) Consequences. By 4(a) and 4(b), $\pi_n$ induces an isomorphism
  $$T/\ell^nT\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ G_n\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^n)^{\oplus2g},\tag{4.3}$$\nand these isomorphisms are compatible with the projections on both sides because $\pi_n=(\times\ell)\circ\pi_{n+1}$. Moreover $\bigcap_{n\ge1}\ell^nT=\bigcap_n\ker\pi_n=0$, since $T\subset\prod_nG_n$. Hence $T\xrightarrow{\sim}\varprojlim_nT/\ell^nT$ (injectivity from $\cap\ell^nT=0$; surjectivity from 4(a)).
4(d) Freeness. Via (4.3) for $n=1$, $T/\ell T\cong G_1\cong\mathbb F_\ell^{\oplus2g}$. Choose an $\mathbb F_\ell$-basis $\bar e_1,\dots,\bar e_{2g}$ of $T/\ell T$ and lifts $e_1,\dots,e_{2g}\in T$; let $\varphi:\mathbb Z_\ell^{\oplus2g}\to T$ be the $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear map sending the standard basis to the $e_j$. For each $n$, $\varphi$ induces $\varphi_n:(\mathbb Z/\ell^n)^{\oplus2g}\to T/\ell^nT$. By construction $\varphi_1$ is an isomorphism. Then $\operatorname{coker}\varphi_n$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z/\ell^n$-module with $(\operatorname{coker}\varphi_n)/\ell(\operatorname{coker}\varphi_n)\cong\operatorname{coker}\varphi_1=0$; Nakayama's lemma for the local ring $\mathbb Z/\ell^n$ (maximal ideal $(\ell)$) gives $\operatorname{coker}\varphi_n=0$, so $\varphi_n$ is surjective. Both sides have cardinality $\ell^{2gn}$ (left by inspection, right by (4.3) and (3.2)), so each $\varphi_n$ is an isomorphism. Taking inverse limits and using 4(c) together with $\mathbb Z_\ell^{\oplus2g}=\varprojlim_n(\mathbb Z/\ell^n)^{\oplus2g}$, $\varphi=\varprojlim_n\varphi_n$ is an isomorphism. Thus $T_\ell(B)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2g=2\dim B$.

STEP 5. THE $\mathbb Q_\ell$-DIMENSION. Since $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is flat over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Z_\ell\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$,
  $$V_\ell(B)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(B)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Z_\ell^{\oplus2g}\cong\mathbb Q_\ell^{\oplus2g},$$\nso $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_\ell(B)=2g=2\dim B$. This completes the proof.

REMARKS ON SCOPE (nothing here is used above). (i) The degree formula (2.4) was obtained solely from the cube theorem and (HRR); no property of $T_\ell$, $V_\ell$ or $\ell$-adic cohomology entered, so the argument is not circular. (ii) Nothing is asserted here about $B[m]$ when $p\mid m$ (there $[m]$ is not \'etale), nor about kernels of homomorphisms of abelian varieties; those belong to the subsequent isogeny/finiteness lemma. (iii) The cube consequence (2.1) specialises to the standard identity $[n]^*P\cong P^{\otimes n}$ for $P\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(B)$ (lemma_mult_pic0); that lemma is not needed for the present argument, since (2.1) is applied directly.

lemma_110.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(r\ge1\) on \(X\), let \(\pi:\mathbb P(E)\to X\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients with tautological bundle \(\mathcal O(1)\), and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\acute et}(\mathbb P(E)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) correspond to \(c_1(\mathcal O(1))\), so that the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius satisfies \(F\xi=q\,\xi\). For every \(n\) the map \(\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}H^{n-2j}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\acute et}(\mathbb P(E)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \((x_j)\mapsto\sum_j\pi^*x_j\cup\xi^{j}\), is an isomorphism equivariant for Frobenius, where \(F\) acts on the \(j\)-th summand as \(q^{j}F_X\). Hence \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^*(\mathbb P(E)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if it is on \(H^*(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_110",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_45_finite_frob"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_6a"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_78"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_64"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_9"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_8"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_4"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We write $Y:=\mathbb P(E)$, $\pi:Y\to X$ for the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients, $\mathcal O_Y(1)$ for the tautological quotient line bundle, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. All cohomology groups below are 'etale cohomology of the base change to $k$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q_\ell$ unless a twist is shown; we abbreviate $H^m(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ to $H^m(X)$ and $H^m(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ to $H^m(Y)$.

=== Step 0. Notation, and the list of standard inputs used as black boxes ===

By lemma_6a, with $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(a)=a^q$, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms are
$F_X:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\sigma)^*$ on $H^*(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $F_Y:=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\sigma)^*$ on $H^*(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and geometric Frobenius is the inverse. Since both are pullbacks along morphisms of schemes, both are graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra automorphisms for the cup product (functoriality of the cup product); we use this repeatedly and without further comment.

We fix once and for all a nonzero element $\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ and denote by $\varepsilon^\vee\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ its dual ($\varepsilon^\vee(\varepsilon)=1$). For any $k$-scheme $W$ of finite type and any $j\ge 0$ the map $x\mapsto x\otimes\varepsilon^{j}$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $H^m(W,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\simeq H^m(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$; we use it to pass between twisted and untwisted classes, always in this direction, and we never identify $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ using $\varepsilon$ (that would be the wrong twist).

The following standard facts about $\ell$-adic cohomology are used as explicit black boxes. Each is a foundational statement about the cohomology theory; none is a semisimplicity statement, and no form of the standard conjectures or of the Weil conjectures is invoked.

(F1) If $\Omega$ is algebraically closed (in particular $\Omega=k$), then $H^0(\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $H^u(\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for $u>0$ (separably closed ground field).

(F2) (Homotopy invariance.) For every field $K$ and every $m,u\ge0$ the projection $\mathbb A^m_K\to\mathrm{Spec}\,K$ induces an isomorphism $H^u(\mathrm{Spec}\,K,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^u(\mathbb A^m_K,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

(F3) (Localisation sequence and Gysin map of a smooth divisor.) Let $K$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $\ne\ell$, let $\mathcal X$ be a smooth $K$-scheme, let $i:Z\hookrightarrow \mathcal X$ be an effective Cartier divisor whose total space is smooth over $K$, and $j:U=\mathcal X\setminus Z\hookrightarrow\mathcal X$ its complement. Let $\delta:H^v(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(-1))\to H^{v+2}(\mathcal X,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be the Gysin morphism appearing in the localisation long exact sequence
$\cdots\to H^m(\mathcal X)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^m(U)\to H^{m-2}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(-1))\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{m+1}(\mathcal X)\to\cdots$.  Define
$$I:=\delta\circ(-\otimes\varepsilon^\vee):\ H^v(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{v+2}(\mathcal X,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$
Then:
 (F3a) the sequence obtained from the displayed one by replacing $H^{\bullet}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(-1))$ with $H^{\bullet}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ via $y\mapsto y\otimes\varepsilon^\vee$ is exact, so $I$ is the map following the residue map $H^{m}(U)\to H^{m-1}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)$;
 (F3b) $I(1)$ is the unique class with $I(1)\otimes\varepsilon=\mathrm{cl}(Z)=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathcal X}(Z))\in H^2(\mathcal X,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$;
 (F3c) (projection formula) $I(i^*a\smile b)=a\smile I(b)$ for all $a\in H^p(\mathcal X,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $b\in H^v(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)$;
 (F3d) $i^*$ is a graded algebra homomorphism, is the identity on the coefficient spaces $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, and commutes with $c_1$: $i^*c_1(L)=c_1(i^*L)$.

(F4) (Chern classes.) $c_1:\mathrm{Pic}(W)\to H^2(W,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ is a homomorphism, functorial for pullback, with $c_1(L_1\otimes L_2)=c_1(L_1)+c_1(L_2)$, and $c_1(\mathcal O(D))=\mathrm{cl}(D)$ for an effective Cartier divisor $D$.

(F5) (Proper base change.) If $f:V\to W$ is proper and $\bar w:\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega\to W$ is a geometric point, the base-change morphism $(Rf_*\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar w}\to R\Gamma(V_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is an isomorphism in $D(\mathbb Q_\ell)$, where $V_\Omega=V\times_{W,\bar w}\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega$.

(F6) A morphism of complexes of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-sheaves on the 'etale site of a scheme is an isomorphism in the derived category if and only if all its geometric stalk maps are isomorphisms (the geometric stalk functors form a conservative family).

(F7) (Frobenius invariance of Chern classes of bundles defined over $\mathbb F_q$.) If $L$ is a line bundle on a variety $W$ over $\mathbb F_q$, then $c_1(L_k)\in H^2(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ is fixed by the automorphism $F_*$ induced by the arithmetic Frobenius structures on $W_k$ and on $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$. This is the Chern-class form of the first sentence of lemma_78 (which asserts $F_*(\mathrm{cl}(z))=\mathrm{cl}(z)$ for cycles $z$ defined over $\mathbb F_q$): $F_{W_k}^*L_k\simeq L_k$ because $L$ descends to $\mathbb F_q$, and $c_1$ is functorial. We use the convention on twists stated explicitly in lemma_78, namely that $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ as multiplication by $q^{-j}$; lemma_78's "equivalently" clause ($F_*c_z=q^{j}c_z$ for the untwisted class $c_z$) is precisely the $j$-th case of the computation in Step 2 below.

=== Step 1. Finite-dimensionality and the Frobenius operators ===

$X$ and $Y$ are projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_{X}^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$: the constant sheaf on $X_k$ is the pullback of the constant sheaf on $X$, so $\psi=\mathrm{id}$. The lemma gives that $H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and that the induced automorphism, under $H^n\simeq\mathrm{Ext}^n(\mathbb Q_\ell,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, is $u\mapsto\psi\circ F_X^*(u)\circ\psi^{-1}=F_X^*(u)$, i.e. pullback along $F_{X_k}=\mathrm{id}_{X}\times\sigma$. Thus the automorphism of lemma_45_finite_frob coincides with the $F_X$ of lemma_6a. The same argument applies to $Y$. Hence all groups $H^m(X)$, $H^m(Y)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and $F_X,F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}$ of them (also directly from lemma_6a). This is the only point where finiteness is needed, and it licenses the use of lemma_8 and lemma_9 below, which are stated for finite-dimensional spaces.

=== Step 2. The class $\xi$ and the identity $F_Y\xi=q\,\xi$ ===

Put $\xi_{\mathrm{tw}}:=c_1(\mathcal O_Y(1))\in H^2(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ and let $\xi\in H^2(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be the unique class with $\xi\otimes\varepsilon=\xi_{\mathrm{tw}}$; this is the meaning of "$\xi$ corresponds to $c_1(\mathcal O(1))$". Since $E$ and hence $\mathcal O_Y(1)$ are defined over $\mathbb F_q$, (F7) gives $F_*(\xi_{\mathrm{tw}})=\xi_{\mathrm{tw}}$. By the convention of lemma_78, $F_*$ on $H^2(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=H^2(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is $F_Y\otimes(q^{-1}\,\mathrm{id})$, hence
$$\xi\otimes\varepsilon=\xi_{\mathrm{tw}}=F_*(\xi_{\mathrm{tw}})=F_*(\xi\otimes\varepsilon)=F_Y(\xi)\otimes q^{-1}\varepsilon=q^{-1}F_Y(\xi)\otimes\varepsilon.$$
Since $-\otimes\varepsilon$ is injective, $F_Y(\xi)=q\,\xi$. (Changing $\varepsilon$ to $c\varepsilon$ replaces $\xi$ by $c^{-1}\xi$, and the relation $F_Y\xi=q\xi$ is unaffected.) By multiplicativity of $F_Y$ we also have $F_Y(\xi^{j})=q^{j}\xi^{j}$ for all $j\ge0$, where $\xi^j$ is the $j$-fold cup power.

=== Step 3. Cohomology of projective spaces (the repaired induction) ===

We prove, for every algebraically closed field $\Omega$ of characteristic $\ne\ell$ (the proof uses only (F1)--(F4), all of which hold over any such $\Omega$), writing $\mathbb P^s_\Omega$ for projective $s$-space and $\eta_s\in H^2(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for

the class corresponding to $c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^s_\Omega}(1))$ under the fixed trivialisation $\varepsilon$: namely $\eta_s\otimes\varepsilon=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. We claim that for every $s\ge0$, $H^u(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot\eta_s^t$ when $u=2t$ with $0\le t\le s$, and $H^u(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ when $u$ is odd or $u>2s$; here $\eta_s^0=1$. Hence $H^*(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong \mathbb Q_\ell[\eta_s]/(\eta_s^{s+1})$. Proof by induction on $s$. For $s=0$ this is (F1). Assume $s\ge1$ and the claim for $s-1$. Let $i:\mathbb P^{s-1}_\Omega\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^s_\Omega$ be the standard hyperplane and $j:\mathbb A^s_\Omega\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^s_\Omega$ its open complement. For $v\ge0$ put $I=\delta\circ(-\otimes\varepsilon^\vee):H^v(\mathbb P^{s-1})\to H^{v+2}(\mathbb P^s)$ as in (F3). From the exact sequence in (F3a) and (F2) we get $H^0(\mathbb P^s)\cong H^0(\mathbb A^s)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $H^1(\mathbb P^s)=0$, and for every $u\ge2$ the map $I:H^{u-2}(\mathbb P^{s-1})\xrightarrow{\sim}H^u(\mathbb P^s)$ is an isomorphism. Indeed $H^{u-1}(\mathbb A^s)=H^u(\mathbb A^s)=0$ for $u\ge2$. The induction hypothesis therefore gives the vanishing statement for $\mathbb P^s$. It remains to identify the even classes. By (F3b), (F4) and the fact that the hyperplane divisor has line bundle $\mathcal O(1)$, $I(1)\otimes\varepsilon=\operatorname{cl}(\mathbb P^{s-1})=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^s}(\mathbb P^{s-1}))=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^s}(1))=\eta_s\otimes\varepsilon$, so $I(1)=\eta_s$. By (F3d), $i^*\eta_s\otimes\varepsilon=i^*c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^s}(1))=c_1(i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^s}(1))=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{s-1}}(1))=\eta_{s-1}\otimes\varepsilon$, hence $i^*\eta_s=\eta_{s-1}$. The projection formula (F3c) gives, for $1\le t\le s$, $\eta_s^t=\eta_s^{t-1}\cup I(1)=I(i^*\eta_s^{t-1}\cup 1)=I(\eta_{s

-1}^{t-1})$. Since $0\le t-1\le s-1$, the induction hypothesis gives $\eta_{s-1}^{t-1}\neq0$ and spans $H^{2t-2}(\mathbb P^{s-1}_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Because $I:H^{2t-2}(\mathbb P^{s-1})\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2t}(\mathbb P^s)$ is an isomorphism, $\eta_s^t=I(\eta_{s-1}^{t-1})$ is nonzero and spans $H^{2t}(\mathbb P^s)$. For $t=s+1$, the vanishing already proved gives $H^{2s+2}(\mathbb P^s)=0$, hence $\eta_s^{s+1}=0$. This proves the claimed description of $H^*(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Consequently, for every $s\ge0$ and every $u\in\mathbb Z$ the map
$$\Psi_{s,u}:\bigoplus_{t=0}^{s}H^{u-2t}(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^u(\mathbb P^s_\Omega,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad (a_t)\longmapsto\sum_{t=0}^{s}a_t\eta_s^t,$$
with $H^m=0$ for $m<0$, is an isomorphism. Indeed, by (F1) the source is $\mathbb Q_\ell$ exactly when $u=2t$ for some $0\le t\le s$, generated by the corresponding $a_t$, and $0$ otherwise; the target has the same description by the paragraph above.

=== Step 4. The projective-bundle formula as an isomorphism of complexes ===

Let $Y=\mathbb P(E)$ and $\pi:Y\to X$. The class $\xi^j\in H^{2j}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\operatorname{Ext}^{2j}_{D(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}(\mathbb Q_\ell,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ defines, by adjunction between $\pi^*$ and $R\pi_*$, a morphism
$$\Phi_j:\mathbb Q_\ell[-2j]\longrightarrow R\pi_*\mathbb Q_\ell$$
in $D(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Summing for $0\le j\le r-1$ gives
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}\mathbb Q_\ell[-2j]\longrightarrow R\pi_*\mathbb Q_\ell.$$
We claim $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. By (F6) it suffices to check on geometric stalks. Let $\bar x:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to X_k$ be a geometric point, with $\Omega$ algebraically closed. Since $\pi$ is proper, (F5) identifies the stalk of $R\pi_*\mathbb Q_\ell$ at $\bar x$ with $R\Gamma(Y_{\bar x},\mathbb Q_\ell)$, where $Y_{\bar x}=\mathbb P(E_{\bar x})\cong\mathbb P^{r-1}_\Omega$. Functoriality of Chern classes gives that the restriction of $\xi$ to $Y_{\bar x}$ is $\eta_{r-1}$. Under these identifications, the stalk $\Phi_{\bar x}$ is exactly the map $\Psi_{r-1,u}$ from Step 3 in degree $u$. Hence every geometric stalk of $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, so $\Phi$ is an isomorphism in $D(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Applying the cohomological functor $H^n(X_k,-)$ to $\Phi$ yields, for every $n$, the isomorphism
$$\phi_n:\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}H^{n-2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad (x_j)\longmapsto\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\pi^*x_j\cup\xi^j.$$
