This is the desired projective-bundle isomorphism.

=== Step 5. Frobenius equivariance of $\phi_n$ ===

Because $\pi$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, the arithmetic Frobenius morphisms commute with $\pi$:
$$(\operatorname{id}_X\times\sigma)\circ\pi_k=\pi_k\circ(\operatorname{id}_Y\times\sigma).$$
Taking pullbacks and using lemma_6a gives
$$F_Y\circ\pi^*=\pi^*\circ F_X.$$
Let $W^n:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}H^{n-2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and let
$$\Psi_n:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r-1}q^jF_X:W^n\to W^n.$$
For $(x_j)\in W^n$, using Step 2 and the fact that $F_Y$ is a graded algebra automorphism,
$$F_Y(\phi_n(x_j))=F_Y\left(\sum_j\pi^*x_j\cup\xi^j\right)=\sum_jF_Y(\pi^*x_j)\cup F_Y(\xi^j)=\sum_j\pi^*(F_Xx_j)\cup q^j\xi^j=\phi_n\left(\sum_j q^jF_Xx_j\right)=\phi_n(\Psi_n(x_j)).$$
Thus $F_Y\circ\phi_n=\phi_n\circ\Psi_n$, i.e. $\phi_n$ is equivariant from the $j$-th summand with Frobenius $q^jF_X$ to $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with Frobenius $F_Y$.

=== Step 6. Transfer of semisimplicity ===

All spaces are finite-dimensional by Step 1. Suppose first that $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^m(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $m$. Fix $n$. For each $j$, $q^j\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$, so $q^jF_X$ is semisimple on $H^{n-2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ by lemma_64(iv). By lemma_9, $\Psi_n=\bigoplus_j q^jF_X$ is semisimple on $W^n$. Since $\phi_n$ is an isomorphism and $F_Y\phi_n=\phi_n\Psi_n$, lemma_8 implies $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This proves the forward implication.

Conversely, suppose $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n$. Fix $n$. Again by lemma_8, $\Psi_n$ is semisimple on $W^n$. The operator $\Psi_n$ is the direct sum of its blocks $q^jF_X$ on $H^{n-2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. By lemma_9, semisimplicity of a direct sum is equivalent to semisimplicity of each block; in particular the $j=0$ block, which is $F_X$ on $H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, is semisimple. Hence $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n$. This proves the equivalence for arithmetic Frobenius.

Finally, by lemma_6a geometric Frobenius is the inverse of arithmetic Frobenius, and by lemma_4 semisimplicity is preserved under inversion. Therefore the same equivalence holds for geometric Frobenius. Under the inverse Frobenius the equivariance factor becomes $q^{-j}$, since $\Psi_n^{-1}=\bigoplus_j q^{-j}F_X^{-1}$.

This proves the lemma."}

lemma_108a.statement: Let Q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be prime, let (A,\lambda) be a polarized abelian variety over \mathbb F_Q, let x\mapsto x^\dagger be the Rosati involution of \operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A):=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A) attached to \lambda, and for an abelian variety B over \mathbb F_Q write \tau_B(y):=\operatorname{Tr}_{V_\ell(B)}(y). For m\ge 1 let \lambda_m:=\lambda\times\cdots\times\lambda be the product polarization of A^m, and identify \operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A^m) with M_m(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)) by X\mapsto(X_{ij}) with X_{ij}=\mathrm{pr}_i\circ X\circ\iota_j. Then the Rosati involution of (A^m,\lambda_m) is the conjugate transpose (X_{ij})\mapsto(X_{ji}^\dagger), and \tau_{A^m}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tau_A(X_{ii}).
lemma_108a.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_108a.

===============================================================
0. CONVENTIONS AND NOTATION
===============================================================
Throughout, $Q=p^{a}$, $\ell\neq p$ is prime, $A$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ and $\lambda:A\to A^{\vee}$ is a polarization defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$. We write $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B,C)$ for the abelian group of $\mathbb F_{Q}$-rational homomorphisms of abelian varieties, $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B,B)$, and $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B):=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B)$, a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-algebra. For $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B,C)$ we write $f^{\vee}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(C^{\vee},B^{\vee})$ for the dual homomorphism; the dual is defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ because dualisation is functorial over the ground field.

The Rosati involution attached to a polarization $\mu:B\to B^{\vee}$ on an abelian variety $B/\mathbb F_{Q}$ is the $\mathbb Q$-linear map on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B)$ given on integral elements by
   $x^{\dagger_{\mu}}:=\mu^{-1}\circ x^{\vee}\circ\mu\ \in\ \operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B)$,
since $\mu$ is an isogeny and hence invertible in $\operatorname{End}^{0}$; it extends $\mathbb Q$-linearly. We write $\dagger$ for $\dagger_{\lambda}$ on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$ (as in the statement) and $\dagger_{m}$ for $\dagger_{\lambda_{m}}$ on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$.

For an abelian variety $B/\mathbb F_{Q}$, $V_{\ell}(B):=\mathbb Q_{\ell}\otimes_{\mathbb Z_{\ell}}T_{\ell}(B)$, and the $\ell$-adic representation $\rho_{B}:\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(B)\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_{\ell}}(V_{\ell}(B))$ is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism; $\tau_{B}(y):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{B}(y))$. Both $y\mapsto\rho_{B}(y)$ and $y\mapsto\tau_{B}(y)$ are $\mathbb Q$-linear.

Fix $m\ge 1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ let $\iota_{j}:A\to A^{m}$ be the homomorphism into the $j$-th factor (the identity in the $j$-th component, the zero morphism elsewhere), and $\operatorname{pr}_{i}:A^{m}\to A$ the $i$-th projection. All these morphisms are defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$. The same symbols $\iota_{\bullet},\operatorname{pr}_{\bullet}$ will denote the inclusions and projections of the product $(A^{\vee})^{m}$; the factors involved will always make the meaning clear.

===============================================================
1. MATRIX CALCULUS FOR HOMOMORPHISMS BETWEEN PRODUCTS
===============================================================
1.1. (The partition-of-unity identity.) For any product $C=C_{1}\times\cdots\times C_{r}$ over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ with inclusions $\iota_{i}:C_{i}\to C$ and projections $\operatorname{pr}_{i}:C\to C_{i}$,
   $\sum_{i=1}^{r}\iota_{i}\circ\operatorname{pr}_{i}=\operatorname{id}_{C}$ in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(C)$.
Proof: both sides are $\mathbb F_{Q}$-homomorphisms $C\to C$, so it suffices to check equality on geometric points over $\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$. Using that the group law on $C$ is componentwise, $\big(\sum_{i}\iota_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i}\big)(c_{1},\dots,c_{r})=\sum_{i}(0,\dots,c_{i},\dots,0)=(c_{1},\dots,c_{r})$. A homomorphism of abelian varieties determined by its values on geometric points, so the identity holds. $\square$

1.2. (Entries and the product rule.) Let $B=\prod_{a=1}^{n}B_{a}$, $C=\prod_{i=1}^{p}C_{i}$, $D=\prod_{b=1}^{q}D_{b}$ and $f:B\to C$, $g:C\to D$ be homomorphisms. Define the entries $f_{ia}:=\operatorname{pr}_{i}\circ f\circ\iota_{a}\in\operatorname{Hom}(B_{a},C_{i})$ and $g_{bi}:=\operatorname{pr}_{b}\circ g\circ\iota_{i}\in\operatorname{Hom}(C_{i},D_{b})$. Then, inserting 1.1 for $C$ on both sides,
   $f=\sum_{i,a}\iota_{i}f_{ia}\operatorname{pr}_{a}$,  and  $(g\circ f)_{ba}=\operatorname{pr}_{b}g\big(\sum_{i}\iota_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i}\big)f\iota_{a}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}g_{bi}\circ f_{ia}$.   (1.2.1)
Note that the sum over $i$ is a genuine sum: there is no Kronecker delta anywhere in (1.2.1); deltas appear only from the relations $\operatorname{pr}_{i}\iota_{s}=\delta_{is}\operatorname{id}$ when they are explicitly evaluated.

1.3. (The isomorphism for $A^{m}$.) Take $B=C=D=A^{m}$ and $f=X\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$, and put $X_{ij}:=\operatorname{pr}_{i}\circ X\circ\iota_{j}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$. Define
   $\Phi:\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})\longrightarrow M_{m}(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)),\quad \Phi(X)=(X_{ij})$,
   $\Psi:M_{m}(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A))\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m}),\quad \Psi((u_{ij}))=\sum_{i,j}\iota_{i}u_{ij}\operatorname{pr}_{j}$.
Both are homomorphisms of abelian groups. Using $\operatorname{pr}_{a}\iota_{i}=\delta_{ai}$ and $\operatorname{pr}_{j}\iota_{b}=\delta_{jb}$,
   $(\Phi\Psi((u_{ij})))_{ab}=\operatorname{pr}_{a}\big(\sum_{i,j}\iota_{i}u_{ij}\operatorname{pr}_{j}\big)\iota_{b}=\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ai}\delta_{jb}u_{ij}=u_{ab}$,
and by 1.2, $\Psi\Phi(X)=\sum_{i,j}\iota_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i}X\iota_{j}\operatorname{pr}_{j}=(\sum_{i}\iota_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i})X(\sum_{j}\iota_{j}\operatorname{pr}_{j})=X$ by 1.1. So $\Phi,\Psi$ are mutually inverse bijections. By the product rule (1.2.1), $(XY)_{ij}=\sum_{k}X_{ik}Y_{kj}$ and $(\operatorname{id})_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\operatorname{id}_{A}$; hence $\Phi$ is a ring isomorphism. Tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ (using $M_{m}(\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A))=M_{m}(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A))\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$) gives a $\mathbb Q$-algebra isomorphism
   $\Phi^{0}:\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})\ \tilde\longrightarrow\ M_{m}(\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A))$.   (1.3.1)
In particular $\Phi^{0}$ is injective, so two elements of $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ are equal as soon as their $(i,j)$-entries $\operatorname{pr}_{i}(\cdot)\iota_{j}$ agree for all $i,j$.

===============================================================
2. THE DUAL OF A PRODUCT
===============================================================
2.1. (Standard facts, cf. Milne, Abelian Varieties, §16: the dual is contravariantly functorial and carries finite products to finite products; the proof is the theorem of the cube applied to the Poincaré bundle.) Let $P_{B}\in\operatorname{Pic}(B\times B^{\vee})$ denote the rigidified Poincaré bundle. The representing property says: for every $\mathbb F_{Q}$-scheme $T$, $h\mapsto(\operatorname{id}_{B}\times h)^{*}P_{B}$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(T,B^{\vee})$ onto the group of rigidified line bundles on $B\times T$ algebraically equivalent to zero along the $B$-fibres. Consequently two homomorphisms $h,h':T\to B^{\vee}$ are equal iff $(\operatorname{id}\times h)^{*}P_{B}\simeq(\operatorname{id}\times h')^{*}P_{B}$ rigidified. Also, $f^{\vee}$ is characterised by
   $(f\times\operatorname{id}_{C^{\vee}})^{*}P_{C}\ \simeq\ (\operatorname{id}_{B}\times f^{\vee})^{*}P_{B}$   (2.1.1)
as rigidified line bundles on $B\times C^{\vee}$, and the formation of the dual is a homomorphism of abelian groups, contravariant for composition:
   $\operatorname{id}^{\vee}=\operatorname{id},\quad(f\circ g)^{\vee}=g^{\vee}\circ f^{\vee},\quad(f+g)^{\vee}=f^{\vee}+g^{\vee}$.   (2.1.2)
(The last identity is the statement that the Poincaré bundle is a biextension: addition $B\times B\to B$ pulls $P_{B}$ back to $\operatorname{pr}_{1}^{*}P_{B}\otimes\operatorname{pr}_{2}^{*}P_{B}$ on $B\times B\times B^{\vee}$.)

2.2. (The isomorphism $\theta_{m}$.) There is a canonical isomorphism
   $\theta_{m}:(A^{\vee})^{m}\ \tilde\longrightarrow\ (A^{m})^{\vee}$
characterised by
   $(\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}}\times\theta_{m})^{*}P_{A^{m}}\ \simeq\ \bigotimes_{r=1}^{m}(\operatorname{pr}_{r},\operatorname{pr}'_{r})^{*}P_{A}$   (2.2.1)
as rigidified line bundles on $A^{m}\times(A^{\vee})^{m}$, where $\operatorname{pr}_{r}:A^{m}\to A$ and $\operatorname{pr}'_{r}:(A^{\vee})^{m}\to A^{\vee}$ are the $r$-th projections. Equivalently, on geometric points $\theta_{m}(L_{1},\dots,L_{m})=\bigotimes_{r}\operatorname{pr}_{r}^{*}L_{r}$. Existence of $\theta_{m}$ follows from (2.2.1) and the representing property, since the right-hand side is rigidified and algebraically equivalent to zero along the $A^{m}$-fibres (external tensor products of such bundles are such). That $\theta_{m}$ is an isomorphism is the standard identification $(B\times C)^{\vee}\simeq B^{\vee}\times C^{\vee}$, proved by the theorem of the cube: the maps $N\mapsto(\iota_{1}^{*}N,\dots,\iota_{m}^{*}N)$ and $(L_{1},\dots,L_{m})\mapsto\bigotimes_{r}\operatorname{pr}_{r}^{*}L_{r}$ are mutually inverse isomorphisms $\operatorname{Pic}^{0}_{A^{m}/S}\simeq\prod_{r}\operatorname{Pic}^{0}_{A/S}$ (the composite in one direction is the identity because $\operatorname{pr}_{r}\iota_{s}=\delta_{rs}$, and in the other direction the theorem of the cube kills the cross terms of a bundle algebraically equivalent to zero which is trivial on every coordinate subvariety); applying the representing property identifies this with $\theta_{m}$ being an isomorphism. All morphisms involved are defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$, so $\theta_{m}$ is an $\mathbb F_{Q}$-isomorphism.

2.3. (Projections and inclusions dualise to inclusions and projections.) For all $i,j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$,
   $\operatorname{pr}_{i}^{\vee}=\theta_{m}\circ\iota_{i}\quad(\text{maps }A^{\vee}\to(A^{m})^{\vee}),\qquad \iota_{j}^{\vee}=\operatorname{pr}'_{j}\circ\theta_{m}^{-1}\quad(\text{maps }(A^{m})^{\vee}\to A^{\vee})$.   (2.3.1)
Proof of the first identity. By the criterion of 2.1 applied with $B=A^{m}$, $T=A^{\vee}$, it suffices to compare the rigidified bundles $(\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}}\times\operatorname{pr}_{i}^{\vee})^{*}P_{A^{m}}$ and $(\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}}\times\theta_{m}\iota_{i})^{*}P_{A^{m}}$ on $A^{m}\times A^{\vee}$. The first one equals $(\operatorname{pr}_{i}\times\operatorname{id}_{A^{\vee}})^{*}P_{A}$ by (2.1.1) applied to $f=\operatorname{pr}_{i}:A^{m}\to A$. For the second, pull (2.2.1) back along $(\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}},\iota_{i}):A^{m}\times A^{\vee}\to A^{m}\times(A^{\vee})^{m}$; it gives $\bigotimes_{r}(\operatorname{pr}_{r}\iota_{i},\operatorname{pr}'_{r}\iota_{i})^{*}P_{r}}^{*}P_{A}=\bigotimes_{r}(\delta_{ri}\operatorname{id},\delta_{ri}\operatorname{id})^{*}P_{A}$. For $r\neq i$ the map $(\operatorname{pr}_{r}\iota_{i},\operatorname{pr}'_{r}\iota_{i})=(\text{constant }0,\text{constant }0)$ factors through the zero section, and the rigidified pullback of $P_{A}$ along such a map is trivial; the term $r=i$ is $P_{A}$. Hence the second bundle is also $(\operatorname{pr}_{i}\times\operatorname{id})^{*}P_{A}$, and $\operatorname{pr}_{i}^{\vee}=\theta_{m}\iota_{i}$.
Proof of the second identity. It is equivalent to $\iota_{j}^{\vee}\circ\theta_{m}=\operatorname{pr}'_{j}$ as maps $(A^{\vee})^{m}\to A^{\vee}$; by the criterion of 2.1 with $B=A$, $T=(A^{\vee})^{m}$ we compare $(\operatorname{id}_{A}\times\iota_{j}^{\vee}\theta_{m})^{*}P_{A}$ and $(\operatorname{id}_{A}\times\operatorname{pr}'_{j})^{*}P_{A}$ on $A\times(A^{\vee})^{m}$. By (2.1.1) applied to $f=\iota_{j}:A\to A^{m}$ one has $(\iota_{j}\times\operatorname{id}_{(A^{m})^{\vee}})^{*}P_{A^{m}}\simeq(\operatorname{id}_{A}\times\iota_{j}^{\vee})^{*}P_{A}$; pulling this back by $(\operatorname{id}_{A},\theta_{m})$ gives $(\operatorname{id}_{A}\times\iota_{j}^{\vee}\theta_{m})^{*}P_{A}\simeq(\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}}\times\theta_{m})^{*}P_{A^{m}}$ pulled back by $(\iota_{j},\operatorname{id}_{(A^{\vee})^{m}})$, which by (2.2.1) is $\bigotimes_{r}(\operatorname{pr}_{r}\iota_{j},\operatorname{pr}'_{r})^{*}P_{A}=\bigotimes_{r}(\delta_{rj}\operatorname{id},\operatorname{pr}'_{r})^{*}P_{A}$; again all factors with $r\neq j$ are trivial rigidified bundles (first component constant $0$), leaving $(\operatorname{id},\operatorname{pr}'_{j})^{*}P_{A}$. Hence $\iota_{j}^{\vee}\theta_{m}=\operatorname{pr}'_{j}$. $\square$

2.4. LEMMA (the dual transposes the matrix). Let $X\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ with entries $X_{ij}=\operatorname{pr}_{i}X\iota_{j}$. Then $\theta_{m}^{-1}\circ X^{\vee}\circ\theta_{m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}((A^{\vee})^{m})$ has entries
   $\operatorname{pr}'_{i}\circ(\theta_{m}^{-1}X^{\vee}\theta_{m})\circ\iota_{i}'=(X_{ji})^{\vee}\quad\text{for every pair }(i,j),\text{ including }i\neq j.$   (2.4.1)
Proof. By 1.2, $X=\sum_{a,b}\iota_{a}X_{ab}\operatorname{pr}_{b}$. Using (2.1.2) (additivity and contravariance) and then (2.3.1),
   $X^{\vee}=\sum_{a,b}(\iota_{a}X_{ab}\operatorname{pr}_{b})^{\vee}=\sum_{a,b}\operatorname{pr}_{b}^{\vee}\,X_{ab}^{\vee}\,\iota_{a}^{\vee}=\sum_{a,b}\theta_{m}\iota_{b}'\,X_{ab}^{\vee}\,\operatorname{pr}'_{a}\theta_{m}^{-1}=\theta_{m}\Big(\sum_{a,b}\iota_{b}'X_{ab}^{\vee}\operatorname{pr}'_{a}\Big)\theta_{m}^{-1}$,
so $\theta_{m}^{-1}X^{\vee}\theta_{m}=\sum_{a,b}\iota_{b}'X_{ab}^{\vee}\operatorname{pr}'_{a}$, and taking the $(i,j)$-entry with the product rule (1.2.1) (or directly) gives $\sum_{a,b}\operatorname{pr}'_{i}\iota'_{b}X^{\vee}_{ab}\operatorname{pr}'_{a}\iota'_{j}=\sum_{a,b}\delta_{ib}\delta_{aj}X^{\vee}_{ab}=X^{\vee}_{ji}$. Here the only deltas come from $\operatorname{pr}'\iota'=\delta$; the sum over $(a,b)$ is otherwise unrestricted. $\square$

===============================================================
3. THE PRODUCT POLARIZATION
===============================================================
3.1. The product polarization of $(A^{m})$ attached to $\lambda$ is
   $\lambda_{m}:=\theta_{m}\circ(\lambda\times\cdots\times\lambda):A^{m}\longrightarrow(A^{m})^{\vee}$,
where $(\lambda\times\cdots\times\lambda)((a_{1},\dots,a_{m}))=(\lambda a_{1},\dots,\lambda a_{m})$. Thus, as a matrix of homomorphisms $A\to A^{\vee}$,
   $D:=\theta_{m}^{-1}\circ\lambda_{m}\ \ \text{has entries}\ \ D_{lj}=\delta_{lj}\,\lambda.$   (3.1.1)
This is the usual product polarization: writing $\lambda=\varphi_{L}$ for an ample line bundle $L$ on $A$, the additivity of $\varphi$ and the behaviour of $\varphi$ under external tensor products give $\varphi_{\boxtimes_{i}L}=\varphi_{\bigotimes_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i}^{*}L}=\theta_{m}\circ\prod_{i}\varphi_{L}=\lambda_{m}$; and $\bigotimes_{i}\operatorname{pr}_{i}^{*}L$ is ample on $A^{m}$ (pullback of ample is ample, tensor product of ample line bundles is ample), so $\lambda_{m}$ is a polarization. In particular $\lambda_{m}$ is an $\mathbb F_{Q}$-isogeny, hence invertible in $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$, and by (3.1.1) its inverse is
   $\lambda_{m}^{-1}=D^{-1}\circ\theta_{m}^{-1},\qquad (D^{-1})_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\,\lambda^{-1}\in\operatorname{Hom}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{\vee},A),$   (3.1.2)
where $\lambda^{-1}$ denotes the inverse isogeny in $\operatorname{Hom}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{\vee},A)$; indeed $\sum_{k}(D^{-1})_{ik}D_{kj}=\delta_{ij}\lambda^{-1}\lambda=\delta_{ij}\operatorname{id}$ and symmetrically, so $D^{-1}D=\operatorname{id}$ and $DD^{-1}=\operatorname{id}$ by the product rule 1.2. Both $\theta_{m}$ and $\lambda$ are defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$, so $\lambda_{m}$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ and $\dagger_{m}$ preserves $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$.

===============================================================
4. THE ROSATI INVOLUTION IS THE CONJUGATE TRANSPOSE
===============================================================
Let $X\in\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ and write $\Phi^{0}(X)=(X_{ij})$. Both sides of the claimed identity are $\mathbb Q$-linear in $X$ (dualisation and composition are $\mathbb Q$-bilinear after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$, and $\dagger$, $\dagger_{m}$ are $\mathbb Q$-linear), so it suffices to treat $X\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$; the general case then follows by $\mathbb Q$-linearity.

By definition and (3.1.2),
   $X^{\dagger_{m}}=\lambda_{m}^{-1}\circ X^{\vee}\circ\lambda_{m}=D^{-1}\circ\theta_{m}^{-1}\circ X^{\vee}\circ\theta_{m}\circ D.$
Put $F:=\theta_{m}^{-1}X^{\vee}\theta_{m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}((A^{\vee})^{m})$; by Lemma 2.4 its entries are
   $F_{kl}=(X_{lk})^{\vee}\quad\text{for EVERY pair }(k,l).$   (4.1)
In particular $F$ is not diagonal when $X$ is not: no Kronecker delta occurs in (4.1). Now apply the product rule (1.2.1) twice. For each fixed pair $(i,j)$,
   $(X^{\dagger_{m}})_{ij}=\sum_{k,l}(D^{-1})_{ik}\circ F_{kl}\circ D_{lj}
   =\sum_{k,l}\delta_{ik}\,\delta_{lj}\circ\big(\lambda^{-1}\circ(X_{lk})^{\vee}\circ\lambda\big)$
   $=\lambda^{-1}\circ(X_{ji})^{\vee}\circ\lambda=(X_{ji})^{\dagger}.$   (4.2)
Explanation of the middle step: the two Kronecker deltas come ONLY from $D^{-1}$ and $D$ as displayed in (3.1.1)–(3.1.2); there is no $\delta_{kl}$ factor coming from $F$, and one must not insert one. The summation is then trivial: $\delta_{ik}$ kills the $k$-sum at $k=i$ and $\delta_{lj}$ kills the $l$-sum at $l=j$, leaving $F_{ij}=(X_{ji})^{\vee}$ — this is exactly the transposition of the matrix — and the outer $\lambda^{-1},\lambda$ perform the dualisation (Rosati) on $A$.

Type check: $D_{lj}:A\to A^{\vee}$, $F_{kl}:A^{\vee}\to A^{\vee}$, $(D^{-1})_{ik}:A^{\vee}\to A$ (in $\operatorname{End}^{0}$), so the composite $\lambda^{-1}(X_{lk})^{\vee}\lambda$ is an element of $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$, and the last equality in (4.2) is precisely the definition of $\dagger$ on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$.

Equation (4.2) holds for all $i,j$, in particular for $i\neq j$. Since $\Phi^{0}$ is injective (1.3.1), entrywise equality yields
   $\Phi^{0}\big(X^{\dagger_{m}}\big)=\big(X_{ji}^{\dagger}\big)_{i,j},\qquad\text{i.e. }\ X\longmapsto X^{\dagger_{m}}\ \text{is}\ (X_{ij})\longmapsto (X_{ji}^{\dagger}).$   (4.3)
This proves the first assertion; it is manifestly a $\mathbb Q$-linear anti-automorphism of order two, since $\dagger$ is one on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$ and matrix transposition reverses products (consistency check: applying (4.3) twice gives $((X_{ji}^{\dagger})_{ji})^{\dagger}=(X_{ij}^{\dagger\dagger})=(X_{ij})$, using $\dagger^{2}=\operatorname{id}$).

Off-diagonal sanity check (independent of the index bookkeeping above). Take $X=\iota_{a}\circ x\circ\operatorname{pr}_{b}$ with $x\in\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$, $a\neq b$; then $\Phi^{0}(X)=x\,e_{ab}$ ($x$ in position $(a,b)$, zero elsewhere). By (2.1.2) and (2.3.1), $X^{\vee}=\operatorname{pr}_{b}^{\vee}x^{\vee}\iota_{a}^{\vee}=\theta_{m}\iota'_{b}x^{\vee}\operatorname{pr}'_{a}\theta_{m}^{-1}$, so $F=\theta_{m}^{-1}X^{\vee}\theta_{m}=\iota'_{b}x^{\vee}\operatorname{pr}'_{a}$, i.e. $x^{\vee}$ in position $(b,a)$ and zero elsewhere; then (4.2) gives $\lambda^{-1}x^{\vee}\lambda=x^{\dagger}$ in position $(b,a)$ and $0$ elsewhere, which is the conjugate transpose $x^{\dagger}e_{ba}$. A spurious extra factor $\delta_{kl}$ in the sum would have forced $k=l$ and hence $i=j$, producing $0$ at the position $(b,a)$ with $b\neq a$ — plainly wrong, since $X\neq0$ while a Rosati involution is a bijection. So the computation is genuinely off-diagonal and not diagonal-only.

===============================================================
5. THE TRACE FORMULA
===============================================================
5.1. (Tate modules of products.) For every $n\ge1$, $(A^{m})[\ell^{n}]=A[\ell^{n}]^{m}$ as abelian groups (the $\ell^{n}$-torsion of a product is the product of the $\ell^{n}$-torsion subgroups, since the group law is componentwise), and these identifications are compatible with the transition maps $[\ell]$. Passing to the inverse limit gives a canonical isomorphism of $\mathbb Z_{\ell}$-modules
   $T_{\ell}(A^{m})\ \tilde\longrightarrow\ T_{\ell}(A)^{m}$   (5.1.1)
and, after $\otimes_{\mathbb Z_{\ell}}\mathbb Q_{\ell}$, $V_{\ell}(A^{m})\simeq V_{\ell}(A)^{m}$. Under (5.1.1), $T_{\ell}(\operatorname{pr}_{i})$ is the $i$-th projection and $T_{\ell}(\iota_{j})$ is the $j$-th coordinate inclusion, because $\operatorname{pr}_{i}\iota_{j}=\delta_{ij}\operatorname{id}_{A}$ and $\sum_{j}\iota_{j}\operatorname{pr}_{j}=\operatorname{id}_{A^{m}}$, and $T_{\ell}$ is a covariant functor which is a homomorphism on Hom-groups (on $\ell^{n}$-torsion points, $T_{\ell}(f+g)$ is given by $x\mapsto f(x)+g(x)=T_{\ell}(f)(x)+T_{\ell}(g)(x)$).

5.2. (Block form of $\rho_{A^{m}}(X)$.) The functoriality and additivity just recalled, applied to the decomposition $X=\sum_{i,j}\iota_{i}X_{ij}\operatorname{pr}_{j}$ of 1.2, give
   $T_{\ell}(X)=\sum_{i,j}T_{\ell}(\iota_{i})\,T_{\ell}(X_{ij})\,T_{\ell}(\operatorname{pr}_{j})=(T_{\ell}(X_{ij}))_{i,j}$
as a block matrix acting on column vectors $(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})^{t}\in T_{\ell}(A)^{m}$ by $\big(\sum_{j}T_{\ell}(X_{1j})v_{j},\dots,\sum_{j}T_{\ell}(X_{mj})v_{j}\big)^{t}$. Tensoring with $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$ (which is flat over $\mathbb Z_{\ell}$, and the identification (5.1.1) is $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-linear) the same holds for $\rho_{A^{m}}(X)=(\rho_{A}(X_{ij}))_{i,j}$ on $V_{\ell}(A)^{m}$.

5.3. (Trace of a block matrix.) Let $d:=\dim_{\mathbb Q_{\ell}}V_{\ell}(A)=2\dim A$ and choose a $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-basis $e_{1},\dots,e_{d}$ of $V_{\ell}(A)$. For $r\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, $s\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ let $E^{(r)}_{s}$ be the vector of $V_{\ell}(A)^{m}$ with $e_{s}$ in the $r$-th slot and $0$ elsewhere; $(E^{(r)}_{s})$ is a basis, ordered lexicographically in $(r,s)$. Write $\rho_{A}(X_{ir})e_{s}=\sum_{t}c^{(ir)}_{ts}e_{t}$. Then
   $\rho_{A^{m}}(X)E^{(r)}_{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\iota_{i}\big(\rho_{A}(X_{ir})e_{s}\big)=\sum_{i,t}c^{(ir)}_{ts}\,E^{(i)}_{t}$,
so the matrix coefficient in row $((i,t))$, column $((r,s))$, is $c^{(ir)}_{ts}$. The diagonal coefficients are those with $i=r$ and $t=s$, namely $c^{(ii)}_{tt}$. Hence
   $\tau_{A^{m}}(X)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{A^{m}}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{t=1}^{d}c^{(ii)}_{tt}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{A}(X_{ii})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tau_{A}(X_{ii}).$   (5.3.1)
5.4. Both $X\mapsto\tau_{A^{m}}(X)$ and $X\mapsto\sum_{i}\tau_{A}(X_{ii})$ are $\mathbb Q$-linear maps on $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ (the entries $X\mapsto X_{ii}$ are $\mathbb Q$-linear by 1.3, and $\tau$ is $\mathbb Q$-linear because $\rho$ is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra map and trace is $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-linear). Since every element of $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})=\mathbb Q\otimes\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of integral endomorphisms, (5.3.1) extends verbatim from $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ to $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$. This proves the second assertion.

===============================================================
6. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK VIA ADJOINTS AND GRAM MATRICES
===============================================================
This section re-derives (4.3) by a different route, to make the off-diagonal terms visibly correct. By lemma_104, $E_{\lambda}(x,y)=e_{\ell}(x,\lambda y)$ is a perfect alternating $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-bilinear pairing on $V_{\ell}(A)$. The compatibility of the Weil pairing with products and with duals gives, for $v=(v_{i}),w=(w_{i})\in V_{\ell}(A)^{m}=V_{\ell}(A^{m})$,
   $E_{\lambda_{m}}(v,w)=e_{\ell}^{A^{m}}\big((v_{i}),(\lambda w_{i})\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}e_{\ell}^{A}(v_{i},\lambda w_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E_{\lambda}(v_{i},w_{i})$,
i.e. $E_{\lambda_{m}}$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the $E_{\lambda}$ (off-diagonal blocks vanish because $\lambda_{m}$ is block diagonal, (3.1.1)). Moreover Rosati is the adjoint for $E_{\lambda}$: for $x\in\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$ and all $v,w$,
   $E_{\lambda}(xv,w)=e_{\ell}(xv,\lambda w)=e_{\ell}(v,x^{\vee}\lambda w)=e_{\ell}\big(v,\lambda(\lambda^{-1}x^{\vee}\lambda)w\big)=E_{\lambda}(v,x^{\dagger}w)$,
using the functoriality $e_{\ell}^{B}(xu,\psi)=e_{\ell}^{A}(u,x^{\vee}\psi)$; the same computation with $\lambda_{m}$ shows $X^{\dagger_{m}}$ is the adjoint of $X$ for $E_{\lambda_{m}}$. Now apply lemma_69(0) to the perfect pairing $E_{\lambda_{m}}$ on $V_{\ell}(A)^{m}$ with the basis of 5.3: the Gram matrix is block diagonal, $G=\operatorname{diag}(G_{0},\dots,G_{0})$ with $G_{0}$ the (invertible) Gram matrix of $E_{\lambda}$, and lemma_69(0) gives $[X^{\dagger_{m}}]=G^{-1}[X]^{t}G$, where $[X]^{t}$ is the full scalar transpose. Writing $[X]=(M_{ij})$ with $M_{ij}=[\rho_{A}(X_{ij})]\in M_{d}(\mathbb Q_{\ell})$, the $(i,j)$ block of $[X]^{t}$ is ${}^{t}M_{ji}$, so the $(i,j)$ block of $G^{-1}[X]^{t}G$ is $G_{0}^{-1}\,{}^{t}M_{ji}\,G_{0}=[\,(X_{ji})^{\dagger}\,]$ by lemma_69(0) applied on $A$. Hence $[X^{\dagger_{m}}]$ is the conjugate transpose of $[X]$, in agreement with (4.3), and again the off-diagonal blocks are $[(X_{ji})^{\dagger}]$, not zero. (This section is a check only; §1–§5 are independent of it.)

===============================================================
7. CONCLUSION AND EDGE CASES
===============================================================
Equations (4.3) and (5.3.1) are exactly the two assertions of the lemma: under $\Phi^{0}:\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})\simeq M_{m}(\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A))$, $X\mapsto(X_{ij})$ with $X_{ij}=\operatorname{pr}_{i}X\iota_{j}$, the Rosati involution of $(A^{m},\lambda_{m})$ is the conjugate transpose $(X_{ij})\mapsto(X_{ji}^{\dagger})$, and $\tau_{A^{m}}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tau_{A}(X_{ii})$.

Edge cases and hypotheses checked: (i) $m=1$: $\theta_{1}=\operatorname{id}$, $\lambda_{1}=\lambda$, $\Phi^{0}=\operatorname{id}$, and both formulas reduce to $X^{\dagger_{1}}=X^{\dagger}$ and $\tau_{A}(X)=\tau_{A}(X)$, as they must. (ii) The formulas are stated for $\mathbb F_{Q}$-rational endomorphisms; this is legitimate because $\iota_{j},\operatorname{pr}_{i},\theta_{m},\lambda_{m}$ are all defined over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ and the dual of an $\mathbb F_{Q}$-homomorphism is an $\mathbb F_{Q}$-homomorphism, so $\dagger_{m}$ maps $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A^{m})$ into itself and the entries $X_{ij}$ lie in $\operatorname{End}^{0}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}(A)$. (iii) $\lambda$ being a polarization is used only through the fact that it is an $\mathbb F_{Q}$-isogeny, so that $\lambda^{-1}$ and $\lambda_{m}^{-1}$ exist in $\operatorname{End}^{0}$ (and, for §6, that $E_{\lambda}$ is perfect, lemma_104). (iv) No statement about positivity of $\tau$, about characteristic polynomials, or about semisimplicity is used or asserted here; those belong to later lemmas.

lemma_114.statement: Let \(Q=q^m\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_Q\), let \(\pi\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) be its \(Q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A)\). If the \(\mathbb Q\)-subalgebra \(\mathbb Q[\pi]\subset\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A):=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) is reduced, equivalently if the minimal polynomial of \(\pi\) as an element of the \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) is squarefree in \(\mathbb Q[t]\), then \(\pi\) acts semisimply on \(V_\ell(A)\).
lemma_114.proof:
Let $g:=\dim A$, let $k:=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q$ (an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p\neq\ell$), and write $V:=V_\ell(A):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A)$, where $T_\ell(A):=\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n](k)$ with transition maps $[\ell]$. Write $T:=V_\ell(\pi):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes T_\ell(\pi)\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ for the operator whose semisimplicity is to be proved.

**Step 1: $V$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.** Applying lemma_tate_rank to the abelian variety $A_k$ over the algebraically closed field $k$ (with $\ell\neq p=\mathrm{char}(k)$) gives that $T_\ell(A_k)=T_\ell(A)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2g$; hence $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=2g<\infty$. If $g=0$ then $V=0$ and there is nothing to prove, so assume $g\ge1$, i.e. $V\neq0$.

**Step 2: the $\ell$-adic action is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism $\rho:\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$.** Functoriality of the Tate module: for $f\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$ the map on $k$-points $x\mapsto f(x)$ carries $A[\ell^n]$ into $A[\ell^n]$ and commutes with $[\ell]$, so it induces a group endomorphism $T_\ell(f)$ of $T_\ell(A)$; $T_\ell(f)$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear because $f$ commutes with $[m]$ for every integer $m$. For $f,f'\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$ one has $(f+f')(x)=f(x)+f'(x)$ in the group $A(k)$ (definition of the sum of homomorphisms via the group law), hence $T_\ell(f+f')=T_\ell(f)+T_\ell(f')$, and clearly $T_\ell(f\circ f')=T_\ell(f)\circ T_\ell(f')$, $T_\ell(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $f\mapsto T_\ell(f)$ is a unital ring homomorphism $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(T_\ell(A))$. Since $T_\ell(A)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of finite rank, $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(T_\ell(A))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, so $f\mapsto V_\ell(f):=\mathrm{id}\otimes T_\ell(f)$ is a ring homomorphism $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ sending an integer $m$ to $m\cdot\mathrm{id}_V$. Every nonzero integer $n$ acts invertibly on $V$ (as $n\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$), so by the universal property of the localisation $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}(-)$ there is a unique ring map
$$\rho:\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\longrightarrow \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V),\qquad \rho\!\big(\tfrac1n\otimes f\big)=\tfrac1n V_\ell(f).$$
Well-definedness is explicit: if $f/n=f'/n'$ in $\mathbb Q\otimes\mathrm{End}(A)$ then $n'f=nf'$ in $\mathrm{End}(A)$ (localisation is exact over the PID $\mathbb Z$, and $\mathrm{End}(A)$ is torsion-free), so $n'V_\ell(f)=nV_\ell(f')$ in $\mathrm{End}(V)$, hence $n^{-1}V_\ell(f)=n'^{-1}V_\ell(f')$. Being a ring map out of a $\mathbb Q$-algebra that is the identity on $\mathbb Q$ (integers go to scalar multiplications, hence $\mathbb Q$ to $\mathbb Q\cdot\mathrm{id}_V$), $\rho$ is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism. In particular $\rho(\pi)=T$.

**Step 3: the two forms of the hypothesis are equivalent.** Let $\mu\in\mathbb Q[t]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\pi$ as an element of the $\mathbb Q$-algebra $\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$, i.e. the monic generator of $\ker(\mathrm{ev}_\pi)$ where $\mathrm{ev}_\pi:\mathbb Q[t]\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Q[\pi]$, $t\mapsto\pi$. Then $\mathbb Q[\pi]\simeq\mathbb Q[t]/(\mu)$. Write $\mu=\prod_{i=1}^{s} f_i^{e_i}$ with the $f_i$ distinct monic irreducibles in the PID $\mathbb Q[t]$ and $e_i\ge1$. By the Chinese remainder theorem $\mathbb Q[t]/(\mu)\simeq\prod_i \mathbb Q[t]/(f_i^{e_i})$. A finite product of rings is reduced iff each factor is; and $\mathbb Q[t]/(f_i^{e_i})$ is reduced iff $e_i=1$, because for $e_i\ge2$ the nonzero class of $f_i$ satisfies $(f_i)^{e_i}=0$ (nilpotent), while for $e_i=1$ the quotient is a field. Hence $\mathbb Q[\pi]$ is reduced $\iff$ every $e_i=1$ $\iff$ $\mu$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q[t]$. We shall therefore use the hypothesis in the form:
$$(*)\qquad \mu\ \text{is squarefree in }\mathbb Q[t].$$

**Step 4: $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$.** Let $F_{A/\mathbb F_Q}:A\to A^{(Q)}$ be the relative (i.e. $Q$-power) Frobenius morphism and $V_{A/\mathbb F_Q}:A^{(Q)}\to A$ the Verschiebung; for abelian varieties in characteristic $p$ these satisfy $V_{A/\mathbb F_Q}\circ F_{A/\mathbb F_Q}=[Q]_A$ and $F_{A/\mathbb F_Q}\circ V_{A/\mathbb F_Q}=[Q]_{A^{(Q)}}$ (both compositions are the multiplication-by-$Q$ map, since on $k$-points they are $x\mapsto x^{Q}\mapsto (x^{Q})^{1/Q}\cdot$-product over conjugates $=x^{Q\cdot 1}$... concretely: the Verschiebung is by definition the unique homomorphism with $V\circ F=[Q]$, and one checks $F\circ V=[Q]$ by comparing on $k$-points and using that $F$ is faithfully flat). Because $A$ is defined over $\mathbb F_Q$, the canonical isomorphism $A^{(Q)}\simeq A$ identifies $F_{A/\mathbb F_Q}$ with the $Q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$; under this identification the Verschiebung becomes an endomorphism $\pi':=V_{A/\mathbb F_Q}\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$ with
$$\pi'\circ\pi=[Q]_A\quad\text{in }\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A).$$
Applying the ring homomorphism $\rho$ of Step 2 gives $\rho(\pi')\,\rho(\pi)=\rho([Q])=Q\cdot\mathrm{id}_V$. Since $\ell\neq p$, $Q=p^{am}$ is a unit of $\mathbb Z_\ell$, hence $Q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. Thus $T=\rho(\pi)$ is invertible with inverse $T^{-1}=\rho(\pi')/Q\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$. (This also shows $\mu(0)\ne0$, since $\pi$ is a unit of $\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$: $\pi\cdot(\pi'/Q)=1$.)

**Step 5: the minimal polynomial of $T$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ divides $\mu$.** Since $\mu(\pi)=0$ in $\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$ and $\rho$ is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism, $\mu(T)=\rho(\mu(\pi))=0$ in $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$. Let $m\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ be the minimal polynomial of $T$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, the monic generator of the ideal $\ker(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V))$, which is nonzero (it contains $\mu$) and principal since $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ is a PID. As $\mu$ (viewed in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$) lies in that kernel, $m\mid\mu$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$.

**Step 6: $m$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$.** First, $\mu$ remains squarefree after the extension $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$: both fields have characteristic $0$, and by lemma_64(ii) a nonzero $g\in\mathbb Q[t]$ is squarefree iff $\gcd(g,g')=1$, with the gcd (and Bézout coefficients, produced by the Euclidean algorithm inside $\mathbb Q[t]$) unchanged in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. Applying this to $g=\mu$ and using $(*)$, $\mu$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. Second, a divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree: write $\mu=m\,h$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$; then $\mu'=m'h+mh'$, so any common divisor $d=\gcd(m,m')$ divides $\mu$ and $\mu'$, hence divides $\gcd(\mu,\mu')=1$; thus $d=1$ and $m$ is squarefree by lemma_64(ii) again. (Equivalently: in the UFD $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, $\mu$ is a product of distinct irreducibles, so any monic divisor is a product of a sub-collection of them.)

**Step 7: conclusion.** We have $V\ne0$ finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ (Step 4), and the minimal polynomial $\mu_T=m$ of $T$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ (Step 6). By lemma_60, equivalence (i)$\iff$(ii), $T=V_\ell(\pi)$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(A)$. This is exactly the required statement.

**Step 8: two supplementary consequences (not needed for the statement, recorded for use downstream).** (a) By lemma_64(iv), semisimplicity passes to inverses, so the geometric Frobenius $T^{-1}=V_\ell(\pi')/Q$ is also semisimple on $V_\ell(A)$; and by lemma_64(iii) with $k=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (characteristic $0$), $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable, on $V_\ell(A)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.
(b) The argument used nothing specific to $\pi$ except invertibility in $\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$: the same proof shows that any $u\in\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)^{\times}$ whose minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ is squarefree acts semisimply on $V_\ell(A)$. Conversely, the reverse implication (semisimple on $V_\ell(A)$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb Q[\pi]$ reduced) would need injectivity of $\rho$, which is not used here and is not claimed.

Remark on the role of the hypothesis: the point of the lemma is that semisimplicity on the $\ell$-adic realisation is a *formal* consequence of squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial **inside** $\mathrm{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)$, because the operator's minimal polynomial can only get smaller (divide) when one passes from the abstract $\mathbb Q$-algebra to its image in $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$, and squarefreeness survives the ground-field change $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$ in characteristic $0$ (this is precisely where lemma_64(ii) is used; in positive characteristic the analogue fails, as lemma_64 warns with $x^p-t$ over $\mathbb F_p(t)$).

lemma_113.statement: Let \(Q=q^m\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_Q\), let \(\lambda:A\to A^\vee\) be a polarization defined over \(\mathbb F_Q\), let \(\pi\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) be the \(Q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(E_\lambda:V_\ell(A)\times V_\ell(A)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) be the perfect alternating Weil pairing of \(\lambda\) on \(V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A)\). Write \(x\mapsto x^{\dagger_\lambda}\) for the Rosati involution of \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A):=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\) attached to \(\lambda\), and for \(u\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))\) write \(u^*\) for the adjoint defined by \(E_\lambda(uv,w)=E_\lambda(v,u^*w)\). Then \(*\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear anti-involution of \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))\), it extends \(\dagger_\lambda\) on \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)\), and \(\pi^*=Q\,\pi^{-1}\); consequently \(\mathbb Q_\ell[\pi]=\mathbb Q_\ell[\pi,\pi^{-1}]\) is \(*\)-stable and \(*|_{\mathbb Q_\ell[\pi]}\) is the anti-involution induced on \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t^{\pm1}]\) by \(t\mapsto Qt^{-1}\).
lemma_113.proof: Let V=V_ℓ(A) and E=E_λ. If A is the zero abelian variety, then V=0 and all assertions are immediate; assume dim A>0. By lemma_104, E is a perfect alternating Q_ℓ-bilinear pairing V×V→Q_ℓ(1), E(x,y)=e_ℓ(x,λy), and E(πv,πw)=Q E(v,w), where Q acts on Q_ℓ(1) by scalar multiplication. Since ℓ≠p, Q is a unit in Q_ℓ. By lemma_tate_rank, V is finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ. The space Q_ℓ(1) is one-dimensional over Q_ℓ: choosing compatible primitive ℓ^r-th roots of unity in F̄_Q identifies Z_ℓ(1)=lim μ_{ℓ^r} with Z_ℓ. Choose a nonzero ξ∈Q_ℓ(1) and write E(v,w)=<v,w>_ξ ξ. Then <,>_ξ is a perfect alternating Q_ℓ-valued pairing, and for u∈End_{Q_ℓ}(V) the equation E(uv,w)=E(v,u^*w) is equivalent to <uv,w>_ξ=<v,u^*w>_ξ. Thus u^* is the adjoint of u for <,>_ξ. By lemma_69(0), u↦u^* is Q_ℓ-linear and anti-multiplicative. It is an involution: for all v,w, E(u^*v,w)=E(v,(u^*)^*w) by the definition of the adjoint of u^*; also E(u^*v,w)=-E(w,u^*v)=-E(uw,v)=E(v,uw), where the middle equality uses E(uw,v)=E(w,u^*v). Hence E(v,(u^*)^*w)=E(v,uw) for all v,w, and perfectness gives (u^*)^*=u. Therefore * is a Q_ℓ-linear anti-involution of End_{Q_ℓ}(V). To see that π is invertible, suppose πv=0. Then for every w, Q E(v,w)=E(πv,πw)=0, so E(v,w)=0 for every w; perfectness gives v=0. Thus π is injective, and by lemma_tate_rank V is finite-dimensional, so π is bijective. For v,w∈V, E(πv,w)=E(πv,π(π^{-1}w))=Q E(v,π^{-1}w)=E(v,Qπ^{-1}w). By uniqueness of the adjoint, π^*=Qπ^{-1}. Apply lemma_69(1) to k=Q_ℓ, the vector space V, T=π, c=Q, the perfect pairing <,>_ξ, and its adjoint *. Its hypotheses are satisfied because π∈GL(V) and π^*=Qπ^{-1}. It yields π^{-1}∈Q_ℓ[π], hence Q_ℓ[π]=Q_ℓ[π,π^{-1}], and * stabilizes this subalgebra. Moreover (π^j)^*=Q^jπ^{-j} for every j∈Z. Consequently, for any Laurent polynomial P(t)=∑_j p_j t^j with p_j∈Q_ℓ, P(π)^*=∑_j p_j Q^j π^{-j}; equivalently *|_{Q_ℓ[π]} is the anti-involution induced on Q_ℓ[t^{±1}] by t↦Qt^{-1}. It remains to prove that * extends the Rosati involution. We first prove functoriality of the ℓ-adic Weil pairing. Let f:A→B be a homomorphism over F̄_Q. For n=ℓ^r, let P_A be the rigidified Poincaré bundle on A×A^∨. In the standard construction of the Weil pairing, P_A restricted to A[n]×A^∨[n] is a μ_n-valued biextension, and e_n^A is the pairing associated with this biextension: for x∈A[n] and y∈A^∨[n], the fiber P_A(x,y)^{⊗ n} has two canonical trivializations, one coming from the fact that x is killed by n together with the rigidification on {0}×A^∨, and the other coming from the fact that y is killed by n together with the rigidification on A×{0}; e_n^A(x,y) is the ratio of these two trivializations. The dual homomorphism f^∨:B^∨→A^∨ is characterized by the canonical isomorphism of rigidified biextensions (f×id)^*P_B≅(id×f^∨)^*P_A on A[n]×B^∨[n]. Under this isomorphism the two trivializations defining e_n^B(fx,η) correspond to the two trivializations defining e_n^A(x,f^∨η), so e_n^B(fx,η)=e_n^A(x,f^∨η). Passing to the inverse limit over r and tensoring with Q_ℓ gives e_ℓ^B(fx,η)=e_ℓ^A(x,f^∨η) for all x∈V_ℓ(A) and η∈V_ℓ(B^∨). Now take f∈End_{F_Q}(A). The Rosati involution attached to λ is f^{†_λ}=λ^{-1}f^∨λ in End^0(A). Since λ is a polarization, it is an isogeny, hence its action on V_ℓ(A) is invertible, and f^{†_λ} acts on V_ℓ(A). For v,w∈V, using lemma_104 and the functoriality just proved, E(fv,w)=e_ℓ(fv,λw)=e_ℓ(v,f^∨λw)=e_ℓ(v,λ(λ^{-1}f^∨λw))=E(v,f^{†_λ}w). By uniqueness of the adjoint, f^*=f^{†_λ}. Both sides are linear over Q in f, and * is Q_ℓ-linear on End_{Q_ℓ}(V), so the same equality holds for every element of End^0_{F_Q}(A). Thus * extends the Rosati involution. This proves all assertions.

lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let A be an abelian variety over F_q, let k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q, and let \ell\neq p be prime. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^1_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is semisimple.
lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple.proof:
Proof. Let k = bar(F_q) and let sigma:k -> k be sigma(x)=x^q. Let F denote the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^1_et(A_k,Q_l); by lemma_6a it is the pullback (id_A x sigma)^*. If A is the zero abelian variety, then H^1_et(A_k,Q_l)=0 and there is nothing to prove. Assume dim A > 0.

Step 1: Kummer theory identifies H^1(A_k,Q_l(1)) with the rational Tate module of the dual.
For each n >= 1, lemma_kummer_h1 applied to the smooth projective geometrically connected variety A_k over k gives a canonical isomorphism
kappa_n: H^1_et(A_k,mu_{l^n}) -> Pic(A_k)[l^n],
and these isomorphisms are compatible with the transition maps mu_{l^{n+1}} -> mu_{l^n}, zeta -> zeta^l, and Pic(A_k)[l^{n+1}] -> Pic(A_k)[l^n], L -> L^{tensor l}. Passing to inverse limits gives
kappa: H^1_et(A_k,Z_l(1)) -> lim_n Pic(A_k)[l^n].

We identify the inverse limit on the right with T_l(A^vee). First, the Néron-Severi group of A_k is torsion-free. Let NS(A_k)=Pic(A_k)/Pic^0(A_k). The standard construction of the dual abelian variety gives a homomorphism
Phi: Pic(A_k) -> Hom(A_k,A_k^vee),   L -> (x -> t_x^*L tensor L^{-1}),
whose kernel is exactly Pic^0(A_k). Hence Phi induces an injection NS(A_k) -> Hom(A_k,A_k^vee). The group Hom(A_k,A_k^vee) is torsion-free: if n f = 0 for f in Hom(A_k,A_k^vee), then [n]_{A_k^vee} o f = 0, so f factors through the finite kernel A_k^vee[n]; since A_k is connected and reduced and the underlying topological space of A_k^vee[n] is finite, any such morphism is constant, and because f(0)=0 we get f=0. Thus NS(A_k) is torsion-free.
Therefore every l^n-torsion line bundle on A_k lies in Pic^0(A_k). By definition of the dual abelian variety, Pic^0(A_k) = A^vee(k) as groups, and under this identification tensoring a line bundle by l corresponds to multiplication by l on A^vee(k). Consequently
lim_n Pic(A_k)[l^n] = lim_n A^vee(k)[l^n] = T_l(A^vee),
where the transition maps are multiplication by l, matching the convention of lemma_tate_rank. Lemma_tate_rank also shows that T_l(A^vee) is a finite free Z_l-module, hence V_l(A^vee) is finite-dimensional over Q_l. Tensoring the Kummer isomorphism with Q_l yields a canonical Q_l-linear isomorphism
kappa_Q: H^1_et(A_k,Q_l(1)) -> V_l(A^vee).

Step 2: The arithmetic Frobenius on H^1(A_k,Q_l(1)) is a scalar multiple of Frobenius on V_l(A^vee).
Let B=A^vee and let pi_B be the q-power Frobenius endomorphism of B over F_q. We use the convention for Tate twists in lemma_78: arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_l(1) by the nonzero scalar lambda = q^{-1}. The exact value of lambda is not important below; only that lambda is in Q_l^*.

The Kummer isomorphism is functorial for morphisms of varieties and for endomorphisms of the coefficient sheaf. At the finite level, the arithmetic Frobenius structure on mu_{l^n} is the composition of pullback by F_ar = id_A x sigma on the scheme and multiplication by lambda on the coefficient sheaf mu_{l^n}. At level n, lambda is represented by an integer m_n prime to l. Under kappa_n, pullback by F_ar sends a line bundle L to F_ar^*L, while multiplication by m_n on mu_{l^n} sends L to L^{tensor m_n}.

We claim that, under Pic^0(A_k)=B(k), the map L -> F_ar^*L is exactly pi_B. Indeed, B represents Pic^0_{A/F_q}; the isomorphism Pic^0_{A/F_q} = B is defined over F_q and is compatible with base change. The morphism F_ar is the base change to k of the sigma-semilinear q-power Frobenius on the F_q-scheme A. Applying the relative Picard functor therefore gives the sigma-semilinear q-power Frobenius on B, which on k-points is x -> x^q = pi_B(x). Thus, on B[l^n], the combined operation is multiplication by m_n followed by pi_B, i.e. m_n pi_B. Passing to the inverse limit and then tensoring with Q_l gives
kappa_Q o F_{tw} = lambda pi_B o kappa_Q,
where F_{tw} is the arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^1_et(A_k,Q_l(1)).

Now H^1_et(A_k,Q_l(1)) is canonically H^1_et(A_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(1), and the arithmetic Frobenius on the tensor product is F tensor lambda. Hence, under kappa_Q, the untwisted arithmetic Frobenius F on H^1_et(A_k,Q_l) corresponds to pi_B. In any case, even if one uses the opposite convention for the Frobenius structure on mu_{l^n}, F corresponds to a nonzero scalar multiple of pi_B. By lemma_64(iv), semisimplicity is preserved under multiplication by a nonzero scalar. Therefore it suffices to prove that pi_B acts semisimply on V_l(B).

Step 3: Frobenius is semisimple on the rational Tate module of B=A^vee.
Apply lemma_poincare_reducibility to the abelian variety B over F_q. It gives an integer r >= 1, simple abelian F_q-subvarieties B_1,...,B_r of B, and an F_q-isogeny
f: C := B_1 x ... x B_r -> B
(the addition map). For each i, lemma_92 with m=1 says that the q-power Frobenius pi_i of B_i acts semisimply on V_l(B_i).

For the product C we have C[l^n] = B_1[l^n] x ... x B_r[l^n], hence T_l(C) = direct sum_i T_l(B_i) and V_l(C) = direct sum_i V_l(B_i). The q-power Frobenius pi_C is componentwise, so pi_C = direct sum_i pi_i. By lemma_9, pi_C is semisimple on V_l(C).

Because f is an isogeny, there exist an integer n >= 1 and an F_q-isogeny g:B -> C with f o g = [n]_B and g o f = [m]_C for some m >= 1. Applying V_l gives V_l(f) o V_l(g) = n id and V_l(g) o V_l(f) = m id; since n and m are nonzero in Q_l, V_l(f) is a Q_l-linear isomorphism. Since f is defined over F_q, it commutes with the q-power Frobenius endomorphisms: f o pi_C = pi_B o f. Applying V_l, the isomorphism V_l(f):V_l(C) -> V_l(B) intertwines pi_C and pi_B. By lemma_8, semisimplicity transfers along such an intertwining isomorphism. Hence pi_B is semisimple on V_l(B).

Combining Steps 2 and 3, the arithmetic Frobenius F on H^1_et(A_k,Q_l) is semisimple. This proves the lemma.

lemma_faithful_tate.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let A be an abelian variety over k, let \ell be a prime different from char(k), and let T_\ell(A):=\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n](k) and V_\ell(A):=\mathbb{Q}_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}T_\ell(A). Then the natural homomorphism of \mathbb{Q}-algebras \mathbb{Q}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{End}_k(A) \to \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}(V_\ell(A)), sending a\otimes\varphi to a\,V_\ell(\varphi), is injective.
lemma_faithful_tate.proof:
Let $E:=\operatorname{End}_k(A)$, let $S:=A[\ell^{\infty}](k)=\bigcup_{n\ge1}A[\ell^n](k)\subset A(k)$, and for $C$ any abelian variety over $k$ write $T_\ell(C)=\varprojlim_n C[\ell^n](k)$ (transition maps multiplication by $\ell$) and $V_\ell(C)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(C)$. If $\dim A=0$ then $A$ is the trivial group scheme, $E=0$ and $V_\ell(A)=0$, so the map $0\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0)=0$ is injective; assume henceforth $\dim A=g\ge1$. By lemma_tate_rank (applicable since $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $p\ge0$ and $\ell\ne p$), $T_\ell(C)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2\dim C$ for every abelian variety $C/k$; in particular $V_\ell(C)$ is finite dimensional of dimension $2\dim C$, so $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$ is a unital $\mathbb Q$-algebra.

STEP 1. $\ell$-DIVISIBILITY FACTS.
(1a) For every abelian variety $C/k$, $[\ell]:C\to C$ is finite étale and surjective. Indeed, the differential $d_0[\ell]$ on $\operatorname{Lie}(C)$ is multiplication by $\ell$, which is invertible in $k$ since $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$; because $[\ell]$ is a homomorphism, translations show it is étale at every point, hence smooth of relative dimension $0$, in particular quasi-finite. A morphism from a proper $k$-scheme to a separated $k$-scheme is proper, so $[\ell]$ is proper and quasi-finite, hence finite (Zariski's main theorem). Étale morphisms are open, so $\operatorname{im}[\ell]$ is open in $C$, and finite morphisms are closed, so it is also closed; it is non-empty (it contains $0$) and $C$ is connected, so $\operatorname{im}[\ell]=C$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, every non-empty closed subscheme of finite type over $k$ has a $k$-point, so the surjective map on underlying spaces gives a surjection $[\ell]:C(k)\twoheadrightarrow C(k)$; the same holds for every power $[\ell^n]$.
(1b) Each transition map $C[\ell^{n+1}]\twoheadrightarrow C[\ell^n]$, $Q\mapsto \ell Q$, is surjective: given $P\in C[\ell^n](k)$ choose $Q\in C(k)$ with $\ell Q=P$ by (1a); then $\ell^{n+1}Q=\ell^n P=0$, so $Q\in C[\ell^{n+1}](k)$.
(1c) Each projection $p_n:T_\ell(C)\twoheadrightarrow C[\ell^n](k)$ is surjective: by (1b) one lifts $P\in C[\ell^n](k)$ inductively to a compatible sequence $(P_m)_{m\ge1}$ with $P_m\in C[\ell^m](k)$, $\ell P_{m+1}=P_m$, and $p_n((P_m))=P$.
(1d) The sequence $0\to T_\ell(C)\xrightarrow{\ \ell^n\ }T_\ell(C)\xrightarrow{\ p_n\ }C[\ell^n](k)\to0$ is exact. Injectivity of $\ell^n$ holds because $T_\ell(C)$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-free (lemma_tate_rank). $\operatorname{im}(\ell^n)\subseteq\ker p_n$ is clear. Conversely, if $(P_m)\in\ker p_n$ put $Q_m:=P_{m+n}$; then $\ell Q_m=\ell P_{m+n}=P_{m+n-1}=Q_{m-1}$, so $(Q_m)\in T_\ell(C)$ and $\ell^n(Q)=P$. Hence $C[\ell^n](k)\cong T_\ell(C)/\ell^nT_\ell(C)\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z)^{2\dim C}$, and in particular $\#C[\ell^n]=\ell^{2n\dim C}$ (again using the freeness from lemma_tate_rank).

STEP 2. THE GROUP $S$ OF $\ell$-POWER TORSION POINTS IS ZARISKI DENSE IN $A$.
(2a) Let $H\subset A$ be the reduced closed subscheme whose underlying set is the Zariski closure of $S$. Then $H$ is a closed subgroup scheme. For $s\in S$, the translation $t_s:A\xrightarrow\sim A$, $x\mapsto x+s$, is an automorphism of varieties with $t_s(S)=S$; hence $t_s$ carries the closure of $S$ onto itself, i.e. $t_s(H)=H$ as reduced closed subschemes, so $s+H\subseteq H$. Thus $S(k)\times H(k)\subseteq m^{-1}(|H|)$, where $m:H\times H\to A$ is the addition. Since $S(k)$ is dense in $H$ and $k$ is algebraically closed, $S(k)\times H(k)$ is dense in $H\times H$; $m^{-1}(|H|)$ is closed because $m$ is continuous and $H$ is closed in $A$; hence $m(H\times H)\subseteq H$. The inversion map similarly preserves $H$ (it preserves $S$). So $H$ is a closed subgroup scheme.
(2b) $H$ is smooth over $k$: a reduced group scheme of finite type over a perfect field is smooth (the local ring at the identity is geometrically reduced over $k$, hence regular, and translations spread regularity). Its identity component $H^0$ is open and closed in $H$ (the complement is a union of open cosets), hence a closed subscheme of $A$, therefore proper over $k$; it is connected, smooth and a group variety, so by the standard theorem that a smooth proper connected group scheme over a field is an abelian variety, $H^0$ is an abelian variety, and the closed immersion $H^0\hookrightarrow A$ makes it an abelian subvariety.
(2c) By the standard existence theorem for quotients of abelian varieties by abelian subvarieties, there is an abelian variety $B:=A/H^0$ and a faithfully flat homomorphism $\pi:A\to B$ with kernel $H^0$; $\pi$ is surjective on $k$-points (faithfully flat of finite type over an algebraically closed field), and $\dim B=\dim A-\dim H^0$. The map $\pi$ is proper, so $\pi(H)$ is closed in $B$; the induced homomorphism $H/H^0\xrightarrow\sim\pi(H)$ is an isomorphism, and $H/H^0$ is the finite component group of the noetherian scheme $H$ (finitely many irreducible components, each coset of $H^0$ being open). Hence $\pi(H)(k)$ is a finite set.
(2d) For every $n\ge1$, $\pi(A[\ell^n](k))=B[\ell^n](k)$. The inclusion $\subseteq$ is clear. For the reverse, take $P\in B[\ell^n](k)$ and lift it to $Q\in A(k)$. Then $\ell^nQ\in\ker\pi=H^0(k)$, and by (1a) applied to $H^0$ there is $R\in H^0(k)$ with $\ell^nR=-\ell^nQ$. Then $Q':=Q+R$ satisfies $\ell^{n}Q'=0$ and $\pi(Q')=P$.
(2e) Since $A[\ell^n](k)\subseteq S\subseteq H(k)$, (2d) gives $B[\ell^n](k)=\pi(A[\ell^n](k))\subseteq\pi(H)(k)$, a set of uniformly bounded finite cardinality. But by (1d), $\#B[\ell^n]=\ell^{2n\dim B}$. If $\dim B\ge1$ these numbers are unbounded in $n$, a contradiction. Hence $\dim B=0$, so $B$ is the trivial abelian variety, $H^0=A$, and therefore $H=A$. Thus $\overline{S}^{\,Zar}=A$: the $\ell$-power torsion points are Zariski dense in $A$.

STEP 3. FAITHFULNESS ON $\operatorname{End}_k(A)$.
Let $\varphi\in E$ with $V_\ell(\varphi)=0$. The natural map $T_\ell(A)\to V_\ell(A)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A)$ has kernel equal to the $\mathbb Z_\ell$-torsion submodule of $T_\ell(A)$, which is $0$ because $T_\ell(A)$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-free (lemma_tate_rank). Hence $T_\ell(\varphi)=0$. Functoriality of the projections says $\varphi\circ p_n=p_n\circ T_\ell(\varphi)$ as maps $T_\ell(A)\to A[\ell^n](k)$, so $\varphi\circ p_n=0$; by surjectivity of $p_n$ (1c), $\varphi$ vanishes on all of $A[\ell^n](k)$, for every $n$. Thus $\varphi$ and the zero morphism $0:A\to A$ agree on $S$, which is Zariski dense in $A$ by Step 2. Since $A$ is separated over $k$, the equaliser of $\varphi$ and $0$ is a closed subscheme of $A$ whose underlying set is all of $|A|$; as $A$ is reduced, that equaliser is all of $A$, so $\varphi=0$. Therefore $\varphi\mapsto V_\ell(\varphi)$ is injective on $E$.

STEP 4. PASSAGE TO $\mathbb Q$.
First, $E$ is torsion-free as an abelian group: if $m\varphi=0$ for some integer $m\ne0$, then $m\,V_\ell(\varphi)=V_\ell(m\varphi)=V_\ell(0)=0$ in the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$, and multiplication by $m\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ is invertible, so $V_\ell(\varphi)=0$; Step 3 gives $\varphi=0$. Consequently the localisation map $E\to S_0^{-1}E$, $\psi\mapsto\psi/1$ (with $S_0=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$) is injective, and the canonical isomorphism $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E\xrightarrow\sim S_0^{-1}E$, $a\otimes\psi\mapsto a\psi/1$, identifies $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E$ with the ring of fractions of $E$; every element is of the form $\psi/m$ with $\psi\in E$, $m\ge1$.
The assignment $\varphi\mapsto V_\ell(\varphi)$ is a unital ring homomorphism $E\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$: functoriality of $T_\ell$ gives $T_\ell(\varphi\psi)=T_\ell(\varphi)T_\ell(\psi)$ and $T_\ell(\varphi+\psi)=T_\ell(\varphi)+T_\ell(\psi)$ (a group homomorphism of abelian varieties commutes with every $[r]$, so $T_\ell(\varphi)$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear), and $V_\ell(-)$ is obtained by applying the additive functor $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(-)$, with $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$ a $\mathbb Q$-algebra since $V_\ell(A)$ is finite dimensional. Hence there is a unique unital $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$$\theta:\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A)),\qquad a\otimes\varphi\longmapsto a\,V_\ell(\varphi),$$
which is exactly the map of the statement (it sends $\psi/m$ to $\tfrac1m V_\ell(\psi)$).
Injectivity: let $u\in\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}E$ with $\theta(u)=0$. Write $u=\psi/m$ with $\psi\in E$, $m\ge1$. Then $0=\theta(u)=\tfrac1m V_\ell(\psi)$, so $V_\ell(\psi)=0$, so $\psi=0$ by Step 3, and then $u=0$ in $S_0^{-1}E$. Thus $\theta$ is injective.

This completes the proof that $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_k(A)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(A))$ is injective. (Note that no semisimplicity statement, and no finiteness of $\operatorname{End}_k(A)$ as a $\mathbb Z$-module, is used anywhere above; the only external input from the proved list is lemma_tate_rank, used for the freeness of $T_\ell$ and for $\#C[\ell^n]=\ell^{2n\dim C}$.)

lemma_118.statement: Let $p$ be a prime, let $Q$ be a power of $p$, let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\mathbb{F}_Q$, and let $\pi_A:A\to A$ denote its $Q$-power Frobenius endomorphism. Then $\pi_A\circ f=f\circ \pi_A$ for every endomorphism $f\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_Q}(A)$. Consequently the image of $\pi_A$ in $\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb{F}_Q}(A):=\mathbb{Q}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_Q}(A)$ lies in the centre of that $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. (Route: the graph of $f$ is an $\mathbb{F}_Q$-rational closed subscheme of $A\times A$, hence stable under the $Q$-power absolute Frobenius of $A\times A$, which is $\pi_A\times\pi_A$.)
lemma_118.proof:
We prove the statement from the functoriality of the absolute Frobenius; no external lemma from the provided list is needed (the reviser's guidance confirms, and none of the proved lemmas concerns absolute Frobenius on schemes).

=== Step 0. Setup and the exponent b ===
Write Q = p^b with b \ge 0. Since the hypothesis says that A is an abelian variety over \mathbb F_Q, the ring \mathbb F_Q must be a field, which forces b \ge 1 (there is no field with p^0 = 1 element). Thus Q = p^b with b \ge 1, Q \ge p, and we put k := \mathbb F_Q. Every k-scheme is in particular an \mathbb F_p-scheme, via the structure morphism A \to \operatorname{Spec} k \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p.

We record a basic fact that will be used repeatedly: the structure morphism of an \mathbb F_p-scheme is unique. Indeed, morphisms X \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p are in bijection with ring homomorphisms \mathbb F_p \to \Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X), and there is exactly one such homomorphism. Consequently, if X and Y are \mathbb F_p-schemes with structure morphisms a_X, a_Y and g: X \to Y is ANY morphism of schemes, then a_Y \circ g and a_X are both morphisms X \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p, hence are equal by uniqueness; so g is automatically a morphism over \mathbb F_p. In particular every k-morphism of k-schemes (in particular every f \in \operatorname{End}_k(A), and the projections, multiplication, inverse and identity section of A) is a morphism of schemes over \mathbb F_p.

=== Step 1. The absolute Frobenius and its iterates ===
Let X be a scheme over \mathbb F_p; then every ring \mathcal O_X(V) is a commutative \mathbb F_p-algebra, so for each open V the map F^{\#}_{X,V}: \mathcal O_X(V) \to \mathcal O_X(V), s \mapsto s^p, is a ring homomorphism: (st)^p = s^p t^p by commutativity, (s+t)^p = s^p + t^p because all intermediate binomial coefficients \binom{p}{j} (0<j<p) vanish in characteristic p, 1^p = 1, and 0^p = 0. These maps are compatible with restriction, so they define a homomorphism of sheaves of rings \mathcal O_X \to \mathcal O_X (equivalently, of sheaves on the space |X|, since the map on the underlying topological space will be the identity).

Define F_X: X \to X to be the morphism of locally ringed spaces whose underlying continuous map is the identity of |X| and whose comorphism is the sheaf map above. This is a morphism of locally ringed spaces: on the stalk at x the induced map \mathcal O_{X,x} \to \mathcal O_{X,x} is s \mapsto s^p, and its inverse image of the maximal ideal \mathfrak m_x is {s : s^p \in \mathfrak m_x} = \mathfrak m_x, the inclusion \subseteq being the primeness of \mathfrak m_x and \supseteq being trivial. Hence it is a local homomorphism, so F_X is a well-defined morphism of schemes (the absolute Frobenius). It is a morphism over \mathbb F_p: by uniqueness of Step 0, the structure morphism a: X \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p satisfies a \circ F_X = a.

Iterate. For b \ge 1 let F_X^b denote the b-fold composite F_X \circ \cdots \circ F_X. We claim:
  (1a) the underlying map |F_X^b| is the identity of |X|;
  (1b) for every open V \subseteq X, the comorphism (F_X^b)^{\#}_V: \mathcal O_X(V) \to \mathcal O_X(V) is s \mapsto s^{p^b} = s^Q.
Both are proved simultaneously by induction on b. For b = 1 they are the definition. Assume them for b; then |F_X^{b+1}| = |F_X| \circ |F_X^b| = id. For sections, using the rule (g \circ f)^{\#}_W = f^{\#}_{g^{-1}W} \circ g^{\#}_W for f, g: X \to X and W open (and g^{-1}W = W since |g| = id):
  (F_X^{b+1})^{\#}_W(s) = (F_X^{b})^{\#}_W\big((F_X)^{\#}_W(s)\big) = (F_X^{b})^{\#}_W(s^p) = (s^p)^{p^b} = s^{p^{b+1}},
where the second equality is the induction hypothesis applied to the section s^p. This proves (1a), (1b). In particular F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p}^b = id, since every element of \mathbb F_p satisfies x^p = x (Fermat), so x^{p^b} = x.

=== Step 2. Functoriality (naturality) of the absolute Frobenius — no affine charts ===
Claim. Let g: X \to Y be a morphism of schemes over \mathbb F_p and b \ge 1, Q = p^b. Then
  (2\star)   g \circ F_X^b = F_Y^b \circ g.
Proof. A morphism of schemes is a morphism of locally ringed spaces, so two morphisms X \rightrightarrows Y are equal as soon as (i) their underlying continuous maps coincide and (ii) for every open V \subseteq Y the induced homomorphisms \mathcal O_Y(V) \to \mathcal O_X(g^{-1}V) coincide. We check both.
(i) By (1a), F_X^b and F_Y^b are the identity on the underlying topological spaces, so |g \circ F_X^b| = |g| \circ id = |g| = id \circ |g| = |F_Y^b \circ g|.
(ii) Fix an open V \subseteq Y and s \in \mathcal O_Y(V). Using (g \circ f)^{\#}_V = f^{\#}_{g^{-1}V} \circ g^{\#}_V:
  - the comorphism of g \circ F_X^b sends s to (F_X^b)^{\#}_{g^{-1}V}\big(g^{\#}_V(s)\big) = g^{\#}_V(s)^{Q}, by (1b);
  - the comorphism of F_Y^b \circ g sends s to g^{\#}_V\big((F_Y^b)^{\#}_V(s)\big) = g^{\#}_V(s^{Q}), by (1b) applied to Y.
Now g^{\#}_V: \mathcal O_Y(V) \to \mathcal O_X(g^{-1}V) is a homomorphism of rings, hence of \mathbb F_p-algebras, so it commutes with taking Q-th powers: g^{\#}_V(s^Q) = g^{\#}_V(s)^Q. The two maps agree for every V and s, so (ii) holds. This proves (2\star). \qed

Note that this argument never requires g^{-1}(V) to be affine: it compares the two sheaf homomorphisms \mathcal O_Y(V) \to \mathcal O_X(g^{-1}V) for arbitrary open V. (This is precisely the point where an affine-chart proof would break down, e.g. for \operatorname{pr}_1^{-1}(V) = V \times_k A with \dim A > 0.)

=== Step 3. The Q-power Frobenius endomorphism of A is F_A^b ===
Let a: A \to \operatorname{Spec} k be the structure morphism. Applying (2\star) to a (a morphism of \mathbb F_p-schemes) gives a \circ F_A^b = F_k^b \circ a, where F_k := F_{\operatorname{Spec} k} is the p-power absolute Frobenius of \operatorname{Spec} k. Hence (F_A^b, a) is a cone over X \xrightarrow{a} \operatorname{Spec} k \xleftarrow{F_k^b} \operatorname{Spec} k, and by the universal property of the fibre product it induces a unique k-morphism (k acting through the second factor)
  F^{(Q)}_{A/k}: A \longrightarrow A^{(Q)} := A \times_{\operatorname{Spec} k,\, F_k^b} \operatorname{Spec} k,   \qquad \operatorname{pr}_1 \circ F^{(Q)}_{A/k} = F_A^b,\quad \operatorname{pr}_2 \circ F^{(Q)}_{A/k} = a.
This is the Q-power relative Frobenius. (Equivalently, on an affine open U = \operatorname{Spec} R of A the comorphism of the fibre product is R \otimes_{k,\,x\mapsto x^Q} k \to R, r \otimes \lambda \mapsto r^{Q}\lambda; since the b-th iterate of x \mapsto x^p on k is x \mapsto x^{p^b} = x^{Q} by (1b), and every element of k = \mathbb F_Q satisfies x^Q = x, this is r \otimes \lambda \mapsto r^{Q}\lambda with \lambda^{Q}=\lambda, i.e. r \mapsto r^Q after identifying R \otimes_{k,\mathrm{id}} k with R. This is exactly the comorphism of F_A^b by (1b).)

Since k = \mathbb F_Q, the map F_k^b: \operatorname{Spec} k \to \operatorname{Spec} k is the identity (on points, and on functions x \mapsto x^Q = \mathrm{id}_k by Fermat's theorem for \mathbb F_Q). Therefore A^{(Q)} = A \times_{\operatorname{Spec} k,\,\mathrm{id}} \operatorname{Spec} k = A and \operatorname{pr}_1: A^{(Q)} \xrightarrow{\sim} A is the identity. Under this identification the relation \operatorname{pr}_1 \circ F^{(Q)}_{A/k} = F_A^b reads
  (3\star)   \pi_A = F_A^b
as morphisms A \to A, where \pi_A denotes the Q-power Frobenius endomorphism of A.

For completeness we check that \pi_A is a homomorphism of group schemes (the statement calls it an endomorphism). First, the Q-power absolute Frobenius of the product A \times_k A equals \pi_A \times \pi_A: by (2\star) applied to the projections \operatorname{pr}_i: A \times_k A \to A (morphisms of \mathbb F_p-schemes by Step 0),
  \operatorname{pr}_i \circ F^{b}_{A\times_k A} = F^{b}_{A} \circ \operatorname{pr}_i = \pi_A \circ \operatorname{pr}_i = \operatorname{pr}_i \circ (\pi_A \times \pi_A) \quad (i=1,2),
and a morphism into a product is determined by its two components. Second, by (2\star) applied to the multiplication m: A \times_k A \to A,
  m \circ (\pi_A \times \pi_A) = m \circ F^{b}_{A\times_k A} = F^{b}_{A} \circ m = \pi_A \circ m,
so \pi_A is compatible with the group law; similarly (2\star) applied to the identity section e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to A gives \pi_A \circ e = e \circ F_k^b = e, and to the inverse morphism gives \pi_A \circ \mathrm{inv} = \mathrm{inv} \circ \pi_A. Thus \pi_A \in \operatorname{End}_k(A), as claimed.

=== Step 4. \pi_A commutes with every k-endomorphism of A ===
Let f \in \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_Q}(A) = \operatorname{End}_k(A). As a morphism of schemes f: A \to A between \mathbb F_p-schemes, Step 0 shows it is a morphism over \mathbb F_p, so (2\star) with X = Y = A and b as above gives
  f \circ F_A^b = F_A^b \circ f.
By (3\star) this is exactly f \circ \pi_A = \pi_A \circ f, i.e. \pi_A \circ f = f \circ \pi_A. This proves the first assertion. (Remark: the argument used only that f is a k-morphism of the underlying schemes, so \pi_A in fact commutes with every k-endomorphism of the scheme A, not just with group endomorphisms.)

Scheme-theoretic form via the graph (the route suggested in the statement; it is the same functoriality, spelled out on the graph). Let \Gamma_f \subset A \times_k A be the graph of f, with closed immersion \iota: \Gamma_f \hookrightarrow A\times_k A, and write (\mathrm{id},f) = \iota \circ j with j: A \xrightarrow{\sim} \Gamma_f an isomorphism. By Step 3, F^{b}_{A\times_k A} = \pi_A \times \pi_A. Applying (2\star) to \iota (a morphism of \mathbb F_p-schemes) gives (\pi_A\times\pi_A)\circ\iota = \iota\circ F^{b}_{\Gamma_f}. Hence, with h := j^{-1}\circ F^{b}_{\Gamma_f}\circ j \in \operatorname{End}_k(A),
  (\pi_A,\,\pi_A\circ f) = (\pi_A\times\pi_A)\circ(\mathrm{id},f) = (\pi_A\times\pi_A)\circ\iota\circ j = \iota\circ F^{b}_{\Gamma_f}\circ j = \iota\circ j\circ h = (\mathrm{id},f)\circ h = (h,\,f\circ h).
Comparing components gives h = \pi_A and then \pi_A\circ f = f\circ\pi_A. (The point is that the graph is preserved by the absolute Frobenius of A\times A because the Frobenius is functorial for the closed immersion \iota; the content of "\mathbb F_p-rationality" is exactly that the restriction of F^{b}_{A\times A} to \Gamma_f is F^{b}_{\Gamma_f}, which is naturality, and no descent of A to \mathbb F_p is required.)

=== Step 5. Centrality in \operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A) ===
The ring \operatorname{End}_k(A) is a \mathbb Z-algebra: the image of n \in \mathbb Z is n\cdot\mathrm{id}_A = \underbrace{\mathrm{id}_A+\cdots+\mathrm{id}_A}_{n}, and (n\cdot\mathrm{id}_A)\circ f = \underbrace{f+\cdots+f}_{n} = f\circ(n\cdot\mathrm{id}_A) for all f, so \mathbb Z maps into the centre of \operatorname{End}_k(A). Hence the extension of scalars
  \operatorname{End}^0_k(A) := \mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\operatorname{End}_k(A)
is a \mathbb Q-algebra with multiplication given on simple tensors by (\alpha\otimes f)(\beta\otimes g) = (\alpha\beta)\otimes(f\circ g) and extended additively; this is well defined because the two \mathbb Z-actions commute and the bilinear map (\alpha\otimes f, \beta\otimes g) \mapsto \alpha\beta\otimes f\circ g is \mathbb Z-balanced in the middle variables.
Every element of \operatorname{End}^0_k(A) is a finite sum \sum_i \alpha_i\otimes f_i of simple tensors. For each summand, Step 4 gives \pi_A\circ f_i = f_i\circ\pi_A, hence
  (1\otimes\pi_A)(\alpha_i\otimes f_i) = \alpha_i\otimes(\pi_A\circ f_i) = \alpha_i\otimes(f_i\circ\pi_A) = (\alpha_i\otimes f_i)(1\otimes\pi_A),
and summing over i yields (1\otimes\pi_A)\,x = x\,(1\otimes\pi_A) for every x \in \operatorname{End}^0_k(A). The image of \pi_A under the canonical homomorphism f \mapsto 1\otimes f is precisely 1\otimes\pi_A, so it lies in the centre Z(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb F_Q}(A)).

This completes the proof of both assertions of the lemma.

lemma_translations_trivial.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(n\ge 0\). For every point \(a\in A(k)\), the translation \(t_a:A_k\to A_k\), \(x\mapsto x+a\), acts as the identity on \(H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_translations_trivial.proof:
We prove that for every $a\in A(k)$ the pullback $t_a^*:\,H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the identity. The whole argument is formal once one knows the Künneth decomposition of the pullback by the addition map; no Frobenius and no homotopy input is used.

**Step 0: The point $a$ is defined over a finite field.**
Since $A$ is of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, the functor $R\mapsto A(R)$ commutes with filtered colimits of $\mathbb F_q$-algebras. As $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\varinjlim_{r\ge 1}\mathbb F_{q^r}$ is a filtered colimit of the finite fields $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, every element of $A(k)=\varinjlim_r A(\mathbb F_{q^r})$ lies in $A(\mathbb F_{q^r})$ for some $r\ge 1$. Fix such an $r$, and write $A'$ for the base change of $A$ to $\mathbb F_{q^r}$; then $A'_k=A_k$ (base change is transitive and $\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^r}$), $A'$ is smooth and projective over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, and $a$ is the base change of an $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-rational point, still denoted $a:A'\to\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (equivalently a section of $A'\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^r}$).

**Step 1: The addition map and its Künneth decomposition.**
Let $m:A'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}A'\to A'$ be the addition morphism, and let $\bar m=(A'\times A')_k\to A_k$ be its base change to $k$; via the canonical identification $(A'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}A')_k\simeq A_k\times_k A_k$, $\bar m$ is the addition map of the abelian variety $A_k$. Write $\mathrm{pr}_1,\mathrm{pr}_2:A_k\times_k A_k\to A_k$ for the projections.

By lemma_81 applied to $X=Y=A'$ over the finite field $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (i.e. with $q$ replaced by $q^r$), for every $n\ge0$ the cross product
$$\kappa:\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^q_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n_{\acute et}((A'\times A')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad u\otimes v\longmapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*u\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*v,$$
is an isomorphism (this is precisely the Künneth isomorphism of lemma_81, which is induced by that cup-product cross product).

Fix $x\in H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Because $\kappa$ is an isomorphism, $\bar m^*x$ has a **unique** expansion
$$\bar m^*x=\sum_{p+q=n}\xi_{p,q},\qquad \xi_{p,q}\in\kappa\big(H^p(A_k)\otimes H^q(A_k)\big).$$
Write $\xi_{p,q}=\sum_i \mathrm{pr}_1^*u_{p,q,i}\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*v_{p,q,i}$ with $u_{p,q,i}\in H^p_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $v_{p,q,i}\in H^q_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Note that the classes $\xi_{p,q}$ depend on $x$ but **not** on $a$.

**Step 2: The slice morphism.**
Define $s_a:A_k\to A_k\times_k A_k$ by $y\mapsto(a,y)$; explicitly $s_a=(c_a,\mathrm{id})$, where $c_a:A_k\to A_k$ is the constant morphism with value $a$, i.e. the composite $A_k\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathrm{Spec}\,k\xrightarrow{\ i_a\ }A_k$ with $\pi$ the structure morphism and $i_a$ the $k$-point obtained from the $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-point $a$ by base change. Then
$$\mathrm{pr}_1\circ s_a=c_a,\qquad \mathrm{pr}_2\circ s_a=\mathrm{id}_{A_k},\qquad \bar m\circ s_a=t_a,$$
the last identity holding because $\bar m(a,y)=a+y=t_a(y)$ as morphisms of $k$-schemes. Hence by contravariance of pullback, $t_a^*=s_a^*\circ\bar m^*$.

**Step 3: Effect of $s_a^*$ on the Künneth pieces.**
For each summand,
$$s_a^*\big(\mathrm{pr}_1^*u\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*v\big)=(\mathrm{pr}_1\circ s_a)^*u\cup(\mathrm{pr}_2\circ s_a)^*v=c_a^*u\cup v,$$
using functoriality of pullback and its compatibility with the cup product.

We claim:
(a) if $p>0$ then $c_a^*u=0$ for all $u\in H^p_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$;
(b) if $p=0$ then $c_a^*u=u$ for all $u\in H^0_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Proof of (a): $c_a^*u=\pi^*i_a^*u$ with $i_a^*:H^p_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^p_{\acute et}(\mathrm{Spec}\,k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Since $k$ is separably closed, every $k$-scheme étale over $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is a disjoint union of copies of $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$, so $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ has no higher cohomology: $H^p_{\acute et}(\mathrm{Spec}\,k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for $p>0$. Thus $i_a^*u=0$ and so $c_a^*u=0$.

Proof of (b): $A$ is an abelian variety, hence proper, smooth and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$; therefore $A_k$ is connected (indeed geometrically integral). For a connected locally noetherian scheme $Y$, $H^0_{\acute et}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\Gamma(Y_{\acute et},\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell})$ is the group of locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued functions on the underlying topological space of $Y$, which is just $\mathbb Q_\ell$ because $Y$ is connected. So $H^0_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell=H^0_{\acute et}(\mathrm{Spec}\,k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and for any morphism $f:Y\to Z$ between such schemes, $f^*$ is given by precomposition with $|f|$ on locally constant functions, hence sends the constant function $\lambda$ to the constant function $\lambda$. Applying this to $\pi:A_k\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ and to $i_a:\mathrm{Spec}\,k\to A_k$ (both have connected source and target) shows $\pi^*$ and $i_a^*$ are the identity $\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell$, whence $c_a^*=\pi^*\circ i_a^*=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^0_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Combining: $s_a^*\xi_{p,q}=0$ for $p>0$, and $s_a^*\xi_{0,n}=\sum_i u_{0,n,i}\cup v_{0,n,i}=\xi_{0,n}$.

**Step 4: $t_a^*x$ is the $(0,n)$-component.**
By Steps 2 and 3,
$$t_a^*x=s_a^*\bar m^*x=\sum_{p+q=n}s_a^*\xi_{p,q}=\xi_{0,n}.\tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 5: Identification of $\xi_{0,n}$ with $x$.**
Take $a=0$, the origin of $A$, which is $\mathbb F_q$-rational. Then $s_0(y)=(0,y)$ and $\bar m\circ s_0=\mathrm{id}_{A_k}$, since $0+y=y$. Hence $s_0^*\bar m^*=(\bar m\circ s_0)^*=\mathrm{id}$, so $x=s_0^*\bar m^*x$. But by the computation of Step 3 applied to $a=0$ (which applies verbatim, the origin being a $k$-point), $s_0^*\bar m^*x=\xi_{0,n}$. Thus
$$\xi_{0,n}=x.\tag{$\ast\ast$}$$

**Step 6: Conclusion.**
From $(\ast)$ and $(\ast\ast)$ we obtain $t_a^*x=\xi_{0,n}=x$. Since $x\in H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $a\in A(k)$ were arbitrary, $t_a^*=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$.

(Remark on the case $n=0$: the argument covers it, since then $\bar m^*x=\xi_{0,0}$ automatically and $t_a^*x=x$ by Step 3(b); this is consistent with the fact that every endomorphism of the connected scheme $A_k$ acts as the identity on $H^0=\mathbb Q_\ell$.)
