(4a) *Universal property used.* The Jacobian $J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}$ is, by definition, the open-and-closed subscheme $\deg^{-1}(0)$ of the scheme $\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}$ representing the fppf sheafification $\mathcal Q^{+}$ of the presheaf $\mathcal Q(T)=\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)/\mathrm{pr}_T^{*}\operatorname{Pic}(T)$, where $C_T:=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}T$. (Representability applies since $C\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ is proper, flat, of finite presentation with geometrically integral fibres: $\mathbb F_q$ is perfect, so $C$ is geometrically reduced, and geometrically reduced $+$ geometrically connected $\Rightarrow$ geometrically integral.) Composition with sheafification gives, for each $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $T$, a map
$$\rho_T:\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)\longrightarrow \mathcal Q(T)\longrightarrow \mathcal Q^{+}(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_q}(T,\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}),$$
natural in $T$: for $u:T'\to T$, $\rho_{T'}(u^{*}L)=\rho_T(L)\circ u$. The degree of the fibres defines a morphism $\deg:\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}\to\underline{\mathbb Z}$: for $L\in\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)$ the function $t\mapsto\deg(L_t)$ is locally constant on $T$, because $t\mapsto\chi(C_t,L_t)$ is locally constant for a flat proper morphism with a $T$-flat sheaf, and $\deg(L_t)=\chi(L_t)-1+p_a(C_t)$ with $p_a(C_t)=g$ constant. By construction $\rho_T(L)$ factors through $J=\deg^{-1}(0)$ if and only if all geometric fibre degrees of $L$ are $0$. In particular $J$ is an abelian variety, hence of finite type and separated over $\mathbb F_q$.

(4b) *Construction.* On $C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C$ (factors $1,2,3$) let $\Delta_{13}=p_{13}^{-1}(\Delta)$, $\Delta_{23}=p_{23}^{-1}(\Delta)$, where $\Delta\subset C\times C$ is the diagonal. Since $C/\mathbb F_q$ is smooth of relative dimension $1$, $\Delta\hookrightarrow C\times C$ is a regular immersion of codimension $1$, hence an effective Cartier divisor; by base change so are $\Delta_{13},\Delta_{23}$. Thus
$$\mathcal M:=\mathcal O(\Delta_{13})\otimes\mathcal O(\Delta_{23})^{\vee}$$
is a line bundle on $C\times C\times C$, which we view as a line bundle on $C_T$ for $T:=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C$ (curve factor $=3$, base $=$ factors $1,2$). For a geometric point $t=(x,y):\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ ($\Omega$ a field) the restriction is $\mathcal M_t=\mathcal O(x)\otimes\mathcal O(y)^{\vee}=\mathcal O(x-y)$ on $C_\Omega$, of degree $1-1=0$. Hence $\mathrm{div}:=\rho_T(\mathcal M):T\to\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}$ factors through $J$, giving an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism
$$\mathrm{div}:C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\longrightarrow J .$$

(4c) *Values on points.* For every field $\Omega/\mathbb F_q$ and every $(x,y)\in C(\Omega)^2$, writing $t_{x,y}:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to C\times C$ for the corresponding point,
$$\mathrm{div}\circ t_{x,y}=[\mathcal O(x-y)]\in J(\Omega),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the image of $\operatorname{Pic}(C_\Omega)\to J(\Omega)$.
*Proof.* By naturality of $\rho$, $\mathrm{div}\circ t_{x,y}=\rho_\Omega(t_{x,y}^{*}\mathcal M)$. Base-changing the Cartier divisors along $t_{x,y}\times\mathrm{id}_{C}:C_\Omega\to C_{C\times C}$ gives $\Delta_{13}\times_{C\times C}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega=\{(c,x,y):c=x\}=$ graph of $x$, whose line bundle is $\mathcal O(x)$, and similarly $\Delta_{23}$ gives $\mathcal O(y)$. So $t_{x,y}^{*}\mathcal M=\mathcal O(x-y)$. $\square$

---

**Preliminary 5 (Frobenius on $X\times_S X$).** Let $\tau:X\times_S X\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C)_k$ be the canonical isomorphism (the flip $C\times_{\mathbb F_q}S\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\ \tilde\to\ C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\times_{\mathbb F_q}S$), characterised by
$$q_1\circ\tau=p\circ\mathrm{pr}_1,\qquad q_2\circ\tau=p\circ\mathrm{pr}_2,\qquad \pi'\circ\tau=\pi\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=\pi\circ\mathrm{pr}_2=:\Pi .$$
Define $F\times^{k}F:X\times_S X\to X\times_S X$ to be the **unique morphism with $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ(F\times^{k}F)=F\circ\mathrm{pr}_i$** for $i=1,2$. It exists because the two maps $F\circ\mathrm{pr}_i:X\times_SX\to X$ have the same $S$-component: $\pi\circ F\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\pi\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\Pi=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\pi\circ\mathrm{pr}_2=\pi\circ F\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$. (This is the correct replacement for the ill-formed expression $F_{C,k}\times_kF_{C,k}$, since $F_{C,k}$ is not a $k$-morphism.) Then
$$F_{(C\times C),k}\circ\tau=\tau\circ(F\times^{k}F).$$
*Proof.* A morphism into $(C\times C)_k=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\times_{\mathbb F_q}S$ is determined by its three components $q_1,q_2,\pi'$.
$q_1$: $q_1\circ F_{(C\times C),k}\circ\tau=q_1\circ\tau=p\circ\mathrm{pr}_1$ (as $q_1\circ F_{(C\times C),k}=q_1$ by Prelim 1(i)), and $q_1\circ\tau\circ(F\times^{k}F)=p\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(F\times^{k}F)=p\circ F\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=p\circ\mathrm{pr}_1$ (as $p\circ F=p$). Equal.
$q_2$: identical.
$\pi'$: $\pi'\circ F_{(C\times C),k}\circ\tau=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\pi'\circ\tau=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\Pi$, and $\pi'\circ\tau\circ(F\times^{k}F)=\Pi\circ(F\times^{k}F)=\pi\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(F\times^{k}F)=\pi\circ F\circ\mathrm{pr}_1=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\Pi$. Equal. $\square$

---

**Step 1 (identification of $\varphi_y$).** Set $\mathrm{Div}:=\mathrm{div}_k\circ\tau:X\times_SX\to J_k$ (a $k$-morphism, being a composition of $k$-morphisms: $\mathrm{div}_k=\mathrm{div}\times\mathrm{id}_S$ is the base change of an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism, hence an $S$-morphism, and $\tau$ is an $S$-isomorphism), and define
$$\psi_y:=\mathrm{Div}\circ(\mathrm{id}_X,c_y):X\longrightarrow J_k .$$
This is a well-defined $k$-morphism: $\pi\circ c_y=\pi\circ s_y\circ\pi=\pi$, so $(\mathrm{id}_X,c_y)$ lands in the $S$-fibre product $X\times_SX$.

*Claim.* For every $x\in C(k)$, $\psi_y\circ s_x$ is the $S$-point of $J_k$ attached to $[\mathcal O(x-y)]\in J(k)$.
Indeed $c_y\circ s_x=s_y\circ\pi\circ s_x=s_y$, hence $\psi_y\circ s_x=\mathrm{Div}\circ(s_x,s_y)$. The morphism $\tau\circ(s_x,s_y):S\to(C\times C)_k$ has components $q_1=p\circ s_x=x$, $q_2=p\circ s_y=y$, $\pi'=\pi\circ s_x=\mathrm{id}_S$; i.e. it is the $S$-point of $(C\times C)_k$ attached to the $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $(x,y):S\to C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C$. Therefore $\psi_y\circ s_x=\mathrm{div}_k\circ(x,y)$ is the $S$-point of $J_k$ attached to $\mathrm{div}\circ(x,y):S\to J$, which equals $[\mathcal O(x-y)]$ by Preliminary 4(c) with $\Omega=k$.

Since $X=C_k$ is reduced of finite type over $k$ ($C$ is smooth) and $J_k$ is of finite type and separated over $k$ ($J$ is an abelian variety), Preliminary 3 shows $\psi_y$ is the **unique** $k$-morphism $C_k\to J_k$ with these point-values. By the statement's description of $\varphi_y$ we may (and do) identify
$$\varphi_y=\mathrm{Div}\circ(\mathrm{id}_X,c_y).\qquad(\ast)$$

---

**Step 2 (moving Frobenius across).** Starting from $(\ast)$ and using Preliminary 1(ii) for the $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $\mathrm{div}:C\times C\to J$ (which gives $F_{J,k}\circ\mathrm{div}_k=\mathrm{div}_k\circ F_{(C\times C),k}$), then Preliminary 5:
$$F_{J,k}\circ\varphi_y=F_{J,k}\circ\mathrm{div}_k\circ\tau\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y)=\mathrm{div}_k\circ F_{(C\times C),k}\circ\tau\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y)=\mathrm{div}_k\circ\tau\circ(F\times^{k}F)\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y)=\mathrm{Div}\circ(F\times^{k}F)\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y).$$
Next, the two morphisms $(F\times^{k}F)\circ(\mathrm{id}_X,c_y)$ and $(\mathrm{id}_X,c_{F(y)})\circ F$ from $X$ to $X\times_SX$ are equal, by the universal property of the fibre product (the map $\operatorname{Hom}(T,X\times_SX)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)\times\operatorname{Hom}(T,X)$ is injective), since their components agree:
$$\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(F\times^{k}F)\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y)=F\circ\mathrm{id}_X=F=\mathrm{id}_X\circ F=\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(\mathrm{id},c_{F(y)})\circ F,$$
$$\mathrm{pr}_2\circ(F\times^{k}F)\circ(\mathrm{id},c_y)=F\circ c_y\overset{2(b)}{=}c_{F(y)}\circ F=\mathrm{pr}_2\circ(\mathrm{id},c_{F(y)})\circ F.$$
Substituting,
$$F_{J,k}\circ\varphi_y=\mathrm{Div}\circ(\mathrm{id}_X,c_{F(y)})\circ F=\psi_{F(y)}\circ F_{C,k}=\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}\circ F_{C,k},$$
where the last equality uses Step 1 for the base point $F(y)$ and Preliminary 2(c) to read $F(y)$ as the image under $F_{C,k}$ of the closed point $y$, i.e. $F_{C,k}(y)$. This is the required identity of morphisms $C_k\to J_k$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Remark (genus $0$).** No case distinction is needed. If $g=0$ then $C\simeq\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_q}$ (a genus-$0$ curve over a finite field has an $\mathbb F_q$-point by Hasse–Weil: $\#C(\mathbb F_q)\ge q+1-2\sqrt q>0$), $J=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$, $\mathrm{div}$ is the structure morphism, and the chain of equalities above still reads literally; both sides are the structure morphism $C_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k=J_k$, so the statement is immediate in that case as well.

lemma_132.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F\) denote the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Suppose that for every \(n\ge 0\) the \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-module \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is a direct summand, as a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, of a finite direct sum of Schur functors \(S_\lambda\!\left(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\right)\), where \(F\) acts on each \(S_\lambda(H^1)\) through its action on \(H^1\). Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge 0\), and geometric Frobenius acts semisimply there, its extension of scalars to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) being diagonalizable.
lemma_132.proof:
**Notation and reading of the hypothesis.** Put $V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and write $F$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius. For a partition $\lambda$ of $m$ write $S_\lambda(V)$ for the corresponding Schur functor and $S_\lambda(F)$ for the operator induced by $F$ (this is what \"$F$ acts on $S_\lambda(H^1)$ through its action on $H^1$\" means: $S_\lambda$ is a covariant functor, so $S_\lambda(F):S_\lambda(V)\to S_\lambda(V)$). For each $n\ge0$ set
$$W_n:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_n}S_\lambda(V),\qquad F_{W_n}:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_n}S_\lambda(F),$$
with $\Lambda_n$ a finite set of partitions. The statement \"the $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-module $H^n$ is a direct summand of $W_n$\" is read in the category of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules, i.e. there are $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-linear maps $\iota:H^n\to W_n$ and $\pi:W_n\to H^n$ with $\pi\circ\iota=\mathrm{id}$; equivalently $W_n=\iota(H^n)\oplus\ker\pi$ as $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspaces (the words \"as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space\" only stress that the splitting is a splitting of the underlying vector spaces; no semisimplicity of the group ring $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$ is used or claimed). Under the weaker reading in which $\iota,\pi$ are merely $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear the hypothesis would carry no information about $F$, so the above is the only sensible interpretation.

**Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility).** An abelian variety is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, so lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $X=A$, $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell}$ with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_A^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ shows that $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $n$; in particular $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$. By lemma_6a, $F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\sigma)^*$ (with $\sigma(u)=u^q$) is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of every $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and the geometric Frobenius is $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F^{-1}$.

**Step 2 ($F$ is semisimple on $V=H^1$).** This is exactly lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple: for $A/\mathbb F_q$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is semisimple.

**Step 3 (tensor powers preserve semisimplicity).** Let $T\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ be a semisimple operator on a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $U$, and let $m\ge1$. Then $T^{\otimes m}\in\mathrm{GL}(U^{\otimes m})$ is semisimple. Indeed, by lemma_5 it suffices to prove semisimplicity after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ the operator $T_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}$ is diagonalizable, so $U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}$ has a basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ with $Te_i=\alpha_ie_i$, $\alpha_i\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\,\times}$ (non-zero because $T$ is invertible). The $r^m$ tensors $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_m}$ form a basis of $U^{\otimes m}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\cong(U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell})^{\otimes m}$ and are eigenvectors of $T^{\otimes m}$ with eigenvalues $\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_m}$. Hence $T^{\otimes m}$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and lemma_5 (applied to $T^{\otimes m}$ on $U^{\otimes m}$) gives semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. Combined with Step 2, $F^{\otimes m}$ is semisimple on $V^{\otimes m}$ for every $m\ge1$ (and $F^{\otimes m}$ is invertible, with inverse $(F^{-1})^{\otimes m}$).

**Step 4 (Schur functors are $F$-equivariant direct summands of tensor powers).** Let $\lambda\vdash m$. The symmetric group $S_m$ acts on $V^{\otimes m}$ on the right by permuting tensor factors:
$$(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_m)\cdot\sigma:=v_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma(m)}.$$
This is a right action, since writing $w=v\cdot\sigma$ one has $(w\cdot\tau)_i=w_{\tau(i)}=v_{\sigma(\tau(i))}$, i.e. $(v\cdot\sigma)\cdot\tau=v\cdot(\sigma\circ\tau)$. Because $F^{\otimes m}(v\cdot\sigma)=Fv_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Fv_{\sigma(m)}=(F^{\otimes m}v)\cdot\sigma$, the operator $F^{\otimes m}$ commutes with the $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$-action, and so does every polynomial in it.

Let $\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$ be the irreducible (Specht) $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$-module labelled by $\lambda$. Since $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q_\ell=0$, Maschke's theorem applies: for any short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$-modules, a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear section $s:C\to B$ averages to a $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$-linear one, $s'(c):=\frac{1}{m!}\sum_{g\in S_m}g\,s(g^{-1}c)$, so the sequence splits. Taking $C=\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$ and $B=\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$ (surjecting onto $\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$ by $u\mapsto uw$ for any non-zero $w\in\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$), we obtain a decomposition $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]=\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda\oplus M_\lambda$ of left $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$-modules; equivalently there is an idempotent $e_\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$ (concretely $e_\lambda=\gamma^{-1}c_\lambda$, where $c_\lambda=a_t b_t$ is a Young symmetrizer of a tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb Q^{\times}$ is the classical scalar $c_\lambda^2=\gamma c_\lambda$, namely $\gamma=m!/\dim\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda\ne0$) with $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]e_\lambda^{\mathrm{op}}\cong\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$.

Define the Schur functor in characteristic $0$ by the classical Schur construction
$$S_\lambda(V):=V^{\otimes m}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]}\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda ,\qquad S_\lambda(T):=T^{\otimes m}\otimes\mathrm{id}.$$
This is the usual Schur functor: $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ acts on $V^{\otimes m}$ by $g^{\otimes m}$, which commutes with the $S_m$-action, hence acts on $S_\lambda(V)$; the resulting polynomial $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-module has character $s_\lambda$, i.e. it is $S_\lambda(V)$ in any of the standard equivalent senses (image of a Young symmetrizer, or Weyl construction modulo relations), and over characteristic $0$ all these models are naturally isomorphic functors on $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Two edge cases: for $\lambda=\varnothing$ ($m=0$) one gets $S_\varnothing(V)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ with the identity operator; if the number of non-zero parts of $\lambda$ exceeds $\dim V$ then $S_\lambda(V)=0$.

From the splitting $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]=\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda\oplus M_\lambda$ and the canonical isomorphism $\mu:V^{\otimes m}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]}\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]\xrightarrow{\sim}V^{\otimes m}$, $x\otimes u\mapsto x\cdot u$ (inverse $y\mapsto y\otimes 1$), we get a decomposition of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
$$V^{\otimes m}=\underbrace{\mu\big(V^{\otimes m}\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda\big)}_{=:\,I_\lambda}\;\oplus\;\underbrace{\mu\big(V^{\otimes m}\otimes M_\lambda\big)}_{=:\,J_\lambda},\qquad I_\lambda\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }S_\lambda(V).$$
The projections onto $I_\lambda$ and $J_\lambda$ are right multiplication by the idempotents $e_\lambda$ and $1-e_\lambda$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell[S_m]$, hence commute with $F^{\otimes m}$. Therefore $I_\lambda$ is $F^{\otimes m}$-stable, $J_\lambda$ is $F^{\otimes m}$-stable, and the induced operator on $I_\lambda$ is carried by the isomorphism $I_\lambda\cong S_\lambda(V)$ exactly onto $S_\lambda(F)$. In other words $S_\lambda(F)$ is conjugate (equivalently, isomorphic as a $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$-module via $t\mapsto$ the operator) to the restriction of $F^{\otimes m}$ to the stable direct summand $I_\lambda$.

**Step 5 ($S_\lambda(F)$ is semisimple).** By Step 3, $F^{\otimes m}$ is semisimple on $V^{\otimes m}$. The decomposition $V^{\otimes m}=I_\lambda\oplus J_\lambda$ from Step 4 expresses $F^{\otimes m}$ as a direct sum of the invertible operators $F^{\otimes m}|_{I_\lambda}$ and $F^{\otimes m}|_{J_\lambda}$ on finite-dimensional spaces. By lemma_9 (the \"only if\" direction), $F^{\otimes m}|_{I_\lambda}$ is semisimple. Finally, $S_\lambda(F)$ is transported from $F^{\otimes m}|_{I_\lambda}$ by the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $I_\lambda\xrightarrow{\sim}S_\lambda(V)$ intertwining the two operators, so lemma_8 gives that $S_\lambda(F)$ is semisimple on $S_\lambda(V)$. (If $S_\lambda(V)=0$ there is nothing to prove; the empty direct sum is handled below.)

**Step 6 (assembly for $W_n$).** $\Lambda_n$ is finite, so by Step 5 and lemma_9 (the \"if\" direction) applied to the family $\{S_\lambda(V)\}_{\lambda\in\Lambda_n}$ of finite-dimensional spaces with the invertible operators $S_\lambda(F)$, the operator $F_{W_n}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_n}S_\lambda(F)$ is semisimple on $W_n$.

**Step 7 (descent to the summand $H^n$).** By the hypothesis (as interpreted above), $W_n=\iota(H^n)\oplus\ker\pi$ with both summands stable under $F_{W_n}$, and $\iota:(H^n,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}(\iota(H^n),F_{W_n}|)$ an isomorphism of operators. Since $F_{W_n}$ is invertible and preserves each summand, its restrictions to $\iota(H^n)$ and to $\ker\pi$ are invertible; both summands are finite-dimensional (subspaces of the finite-dimensional $W_n$). Applying lemma_9 (the \"only if\" direction) to $F_{W_n}=F|_{\iota(H^n)}\oplus F|_{\ker\pi}$ and using Step 6, $F|_{\iota(H^n)}$ is semisimple. By lemma_8 applied to the intertwining isomorphism $\iota$, $F$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This holds for every $n\ge0$, which is the first claim.

**Step 8 (geometric Frobenius and scalar extension).** By Step 1, $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F^{-1}$ on each $H^n$. Lemma_4 (valid for any finite-dimensional space and invertible operator) gives that $F^{-1}$ is semisimple because $F$ is; hence geometric Frobenius acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n$. Finally, by lemma_5 applied to the semisimple operator $F_{\mathrm{geo}}$ on the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, the scalar extension $F_{\mathrm{geo}}\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable, on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. This is the equivalent formulation in the conjecture (geometric Frobenius being the inverse of $x\mapsto x^q$, as in lemma_6a).

All cases are covered: $n=0$ and $\lambda=\varnothing$ (trivial one-dimensional operator), partitions $\lambda$ with more than $\dim V$ non-zero parts (zero space), the empty/zero summands of $W_n$, and the complement $\ker\pi$. Every step is justified by the cited lemmas and by the explicit linear algebra of Steps 3 and 4. This completes the proof.

lemma_end0_simple_division.statement: Let \(k\) be a field and let \(B\) be a simple abelian variety over \(k\), that is, an abelian variety with no nonzero proper abelian \(k\)-subvariety. Then every nonzero element of \(\operatorname{End}^0_k(B):=\mathbb{Q}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\operatorname{End}_k(B)\) is invertible; equivalently, \(\operatorname{End}^0_k(B)\) is a division ring.
lemma_end0_simple_division.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_end0_simple_division",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_120"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_tate_rank"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_faithful_tate"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "PROOF. Let R := End_k(B), the ring of k-endomorphisms of B, with addition the group law of homomorphisms and multiplication composition. Then End^0_k(B) := Q ⊗_Z R is a unital associative (generally noncommutative) Q-algebra with (a ⊗ f)(b ⊗ g) = (ab) ⊗ (f ∘ g) and unit 1 ⊗ id_B.

=== 0. Formalities about Q ⊗_Z R ===
Since Q = S^{-1}Z for S = Z \ {0}, the canonical map S^{-1}R → Q ⊗_Z R, f/m ↦ (1/m) ⊗ f, is an isomorphism of rings (localisation commutes with tensor products: S^{-1}R ≅ (S^{-1}Z) ⊗_Z R). We write elements as f/m. Three consequences we use repeatedly:
(0a) every element of End^0_k(B) is of the form f/m with f ∈ R and m ≥ 1;
(0b) f/m = 0 in S^{-1}R iff there is t ≥ 1 with t·f = 0 in R (i.e. iff f is torsion);
(0c) (f/m)(g/n) = (f ∘ g)/(mn), and [m]_B = m·id_B in R: in the endomorphism ring of a commutative group scheme the sum id + ⋯ + id (m times) is precisely the multiplication-by-m morphism, because addition of homomorphisms is A ↦ (x ↦ φ(x) + ψ(x)) and the group law on B restricts on the diagonal to the m-fold sum.

=== 1. The trivial case ===
If dim B = 0 then B is the trivial abelian variety Spec k, R is the zero ring (its single endomorphism is both 0 and id), End^0_k(B) = 0 has no nonzero elements, and the assertion \"every nonzero element is invertible\" holds vacuously. Henceforth assume dim B ≥ 1.

=== 2. Claim 1 (image of a homomorphism of abelian varieties) ===
Statement: if φ: A → A' is a homomorphism of abelian varieties over k and Z ⊂ A' is the scheme-theoretic image of φ, then Z is an abelian subvariety of A' and the induced φ̄: A → Z is surjective.
Proof.
(a) φ is proper: A → Spec k is proper and A' → Spec k is separated, so any k-morphism A → A' is proper. Hence Z := Spec_{A'}(im(O_{A'} → φ_*O_A)) is a closed subscheme of finite type (φ_*O_A is coherent), O_Z → φ_*O_A is injective, and φ = i ∘ φ̄ with i: Z ↪ A' and φ̄: A → Z schematically dominant (O_Z → φ̄_*O_A injective, since φ_*O_A = φ̄_*O_A).
(b) Z is a closed subgroup scheme. We use the standard fact that formation of the scheme-theoretic image of a quasi-compact morphism commutes with flat base change; for the reader's convenience: with Y = Spec R affine, X covered by finitely many affines U_i with all U_i ∩ U_j affine (true when X → Y is separated, as here), the kernel of O_Y → f_*O_X is computed as the kernel of R → ∏ Γ(U_i,O) of a Cech complex, and tensoring the exact sequence 0 → I → O_Y → f_*O_X with a flat R-algebra R' keeps it exact at the left because Tor_1^R(R', O_Y/I) = 0, which is exactly the statement for Y' = Spec R'. Applying this, the product φ̄ × φ̄: A × A → Z × Z is schematically dominant (it is the composite of the flat base changes A × A → Z × A and Z × A → Z × Z of φ̄). Now the multiplication m_{A'} satisfies m_{A'} ∘ (i × i) ∘ (φ̄ × φ̄) = m_{A'} ∘ (φ × φ) = φ ∘ m_A = i ∘ (φ̄ ∘ m_A), so m_{A'}|_{Z×Z} composed with the schematically dominant map φ̄ × φ̄ factors through i; a morphism out of Z × Z factors through the closed subscheme Z iff the quasi-coherent ideal ker(O_{A'} → i_*O_Z) pulls back to 0, and schematic dominance forces that pullback to vanish. Hence m_{A'}(Z × Z) ⊂ Z. The identical argument applied to the inverse morphism and to the identity section Spec k → A' (which factors through Z because A' is the image of the identity of A) shows Z is a closed subgroup scheme of A'.
(c) Let k̄ be an algebraic closure. By (b) and flat base change, Z_{k̄} is a closed subgroup scheme of A'_{k̄} and is the scheme-theoretic image of φ_{k̄}; hence O_{Z_{k̄}} → (φ_{k̄})_*O_{A_{k̄}}} is injective. Since A is geometrically reduced, every ring O_{A_{k̄}}(V) is reduced, and a subsheaf of a sheaf of reduced rings is reduced; so Z_{k̄} is reduced.
(d) k̄ is perfect, and a group scheme of finite type over a perfect field which is reduced is smooth (over a perfect field reduced finite type ⇒ geometrically reduced; the smooth locus of a group scheme is open and contains the identity, and translations cover the scheme by it). Thus Z_{k̄} is smooth over k̄.
(e) A_{k̄} is connected (an abelian variety is geometrically integral). The map A_{k̄} → Z_{k̄} is proper, so its set-theoretic image is closed; it is also scheme-theoretically dense by (c), and a scheme-theoretically dense map into a reduced target is set-theoretically dense (otherwise the nonzero ideal of the reduced closed image would pull back to 0). Hence A_{k̄} → Z_{k̄} is surjective, and Z_{k̄} is connected as the continuous image of a connected space. Being a closed subscheme of the proper A'_{k̄}, it is proper. A smooth, connected, proper group scheme over a field is an abelian variety; embedded as a closed subgroup scheme of A'_{k̄}, it is an abelian subvariety.
(f) Finally Z itself is an abelian subvariety of A': smoothness and geometric connectedness descend fpqc along Spec k̄ → Spec k, properness is already known, and the subgroup structure is given. Surjectivity of φ̄ descends similarly (surjectivity of a finite type morphism is fpqc-local on the target). ∎(Claim 1)

=== 3. Claim 2 (dimension formula for a surjective homomorphism) ===
Statement: if ψ: G → H is a surjective homomorphism of abelian varieties over k, then dim G = dim H + dim ker ψ (Krull dimension of the closed subscheme ker ψ).
Proof. Surjectivity is preserved by extension of the ground field for morphisms of finite type over a field: every fibre of ψ is a non-empty scheme of finite type over its residue field, and base change to a field extension is faithfully flat, hence cannot make a non-zero ring zero. Dimensions of finite type schemes over a field are unchanged by field extension. So we may replace k by k̄ and assume k algebraically closed; then G and H are integral. Let η ∈ H be the generic point with residue field K = k(H). The generic fibre X_η := G ×_H Spec K is a torsor under the group scheme K_0 := (ker ψ) ×_k K over K. Base change further to an algebraic closure K̄ of K: X_η ×_K K̄ is a non-empty scheme of finite type over the algebraically closed field K̄ (non-empty because X_η is non-empty and K̄/K is faithfully flat), hence has a K̄-rational point; a torsor with a rational point is trivial, so X_η ×_K K̄ ≅ (ker ψ) ×_k K̄ and therefore dim X_η = dim(X_η ×_K K̄) = dim(ker ψ) (dimension is invariant under field extension).
It remains to recall the standard theorem that for a dominant morphism of integral schemes of finite type over a field, dim G = dim H + dim X_η. For completeness: take affine opens U = Spec A ⊂ G, V = Spec R ⊂ H with U → V dominant. By Noether normalisation over the field k(H), A ⊗_R k(H) is finite over k(H)[t_1,…,t_s] with s = dim X_η. Clearing denominators and using generic freeness, there is 0 ≠ g ∈ R such that A_g is finite over R_g[t_1,…,t_s]. Finite integral extensions preserve dimension (going-up), and R_g[t_1,…,t_s] has dimension dim R_g + s because R_g is a finitely generated domain over a field. Thus dim U = dim A = dim A_g = dim R_g + s = dim V + s, i.e. dim G = dim H + dim X_η. Combining gives dim ker ψ = dim G − dim H. ∎(Claim 2)

=== 4. Nonzero endomorphisms of B are isogenies ===
Let 0 ≠ f ∈ R.
(a) By Claim 1, Z := im(f) is an abelian subvariety of B and f̄: B → Z is surjective. Since f ≠ 0, Z ≠ 0: if Z were the trivial group scheme, f would factor through the identity section Spec k → B, i.e. f would be the zero homomorphism. As B is simple (no nonzero proper abelian k-subvariety), Z = B, and f: B → B is surjective.
(b) By Claim 2 applied to f, dim ker f = dim B − dim B = 0. (The kernel is a closed subscheme because B is separated over k: ker f = B ×_{(f,f), B×B, Δ} B.)
(c) ker f is finite over k. Indeed it is a scheme of finite type over k of Krull dimension 0; cover it by the finitely many affine opens Spec A_i with each A_i a finitely generated k-algebra of dimension 0, hence Artinian, hence a finite-dimensional k-vector space; so each Spec A_i → Spec k is finite, in particular its image is closed in ker f; a noetherian space covered by finitely many open-and-closed affines is their finite disjoint union, hence affine with Artinian ring, i.e. finite over k. Note that we do NOT claim ker f is reduced (e.g. kernels of relative Frobenius are non-reduced); only finiteness as a group scheme is needed.
(d) Every geometric fibre of f is a coset of ker f_{k̄}, hence finite, so f is quasi-finite; f is proper as in 2(a); proper + quasi-finite ⇒ finite. Thus f is surjective with finite kernel, i.e. f is an isogeny.

=== 5. Inverting f in End^0_k(B) ===
Choose a prime ℓ ≠ char k; then ℓ is invertible in k. Apply lemma_120 to the isogeny f: B → B of abelian varieties over k: it yields a homomorphism g: B → B, i.e. g ∈ R, and an integer n ≥ 1 with f ∘ g = [n]_B and g ∘ f = [n]_B. In End^0_k(B), using (0c) and [n]_B = n·id_B:
   (f/1)·(g/n) = (f ∘ g)/n = [n]_B/n = (n·id_B)/n = id_B/1,
   (g/n)·(f/1) = (g ∘ f)/n = [n]_B/n = id_B/1.
So f/1 is a unit of End^0_k(B), with two-sided inverse g/n.

=== 6. General nonzero element ===
Let 0 ≠ α ∈ End^0_k(B). By (0a) write α = f/m with f ∈ R, m ≥ 1. By (0b), α ≠ 0 means f is not torsion, in particular f ≠ 0. Step 5 then makes f/1 a unit, and since 1/m ∈ Q^× ⊂ End^0_k(B)^×, α = (f/1)·(1/m) is a unit with inverse m·(g/n). Hence every nonzero element of End^0_k(B) is invertible.

=== 7. The ring is not the zero ring (division-ring convention) ===
Since dim B ≥ 1, the Tate module V_ℓ(B_{k̄}) is a non-zero Q_ℓ-vector space: by lemma_tate_rank (applied over the algebraically closed field k̄) T_ℓ(B_{k̄}) is free of rank 2 dim B ≥ 2, so dim_{Q_ℓ} V_ℓ(B_{k̄}) = 2 dim B > 0. By lemma_faithful_tate (again over k̄) the map Q ⊗_Z End_{k̄}(B_{k̄}) → End_{Q_ℓ}(V_ℓ(B_{k̄})) is injective. If t ≥ 1 satisfied t·id_B = 0 in R, then base change gives t·id_{B_{k̄}} = 0 in End_{k̄}(B_{k̄}) (morphisms are determined after the faithfully flat base change k → k̄), hence t·id = 0 on V_ℓ(B_{k̄}), forcing t = 0 as V_ℓ(B_{k̄}) ≠ 0 — contradiction. Thus Z → R, t ↦ [t]_B, is injective, and 1 ≠ 0 in End^0_k(B). Together with Step 6 this says End^0_k(B) is a division ring (skew field).

=== 8. Conclusion ===
In the case dim B = 0 the assertion \"every nonzero element is invertible\" is vacuous (Step 1); in the case dim B ≥ 1 Steps 6 and 7 show that End^0_k(B) is a nonzero ring in which every nonzero element has a two-sided inverse. This is exactly the statement that every nonzero element of End^0_k(B) := Q ⊗_Z End_k(B) is invertible, equivalently that End^0_k(B) is a division ring. ∎"
}

lemma_curve_in_abelian.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\) of positive dimension. Then there exist a smooth projective geometrically connected curve \(C\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), a point \(c\in C(\mathbb F_q)\), and a nonconstant \(\mathbb F_q\)-morphism \(f:C\to A\) with \(f(c)=0\).
lemma_curve_in_abelian.proof:
We prove the lemma by the elementary construction indicated: cut out a curve germ at 0 which is *regular* at 0, take its closure, and normalise. No Bertini/Poonen input, no generation claim about f(C), and no function-field composita are used.

=====================================================================
Step 0. Three standard commutative-algebra facts (proved for completeness).

(F1) Dimension of local rings at maximal ideals of a finitely generated domain. Let B be a finitely generated domain over a field k, let d := trdeg_k Frac(B). Then dim B = d, every maximal ideal n ⊂ B has height d, and dim B_n = d.
Proof. By Noether normalization there are algebraically independent u_1,...,u_d ∈ B such that B is finite (hence integral) over A := k[u_1,...,u_d] ≅ k[T_1,...,T_d]. First dim A = d: the chain (0) ⊊ (u_1) ⊊ (u_1,u_2) ⊊ ... ⊊ (u_1,...,u_d) gives dim A ≥ d; conversely, if m ⊂ A is maximal, then A/m is a field finite over k (Zariski's lemma), so each u_i is algebraic over k modulo m, and there are monic f_i ∈ k[T_i] with f_i(u_i) ∈ m; then A/(f_1(u_1),...,f_d(u_d)) is finite over k, hence artinian, so m is minimal over an ideal generated by d elements, and Krull's generalised principal ideal theorem gives ht m ≤ d. Thus every maximal ideal of A has height ≤ d and dim A = d. Next, integrality of B over A gives dim B = dim A = d (lying over gives ≥, incomparability plus going-up gives ≤: chains in B contract to chains in A of the same length). Finally, for a maximal n ⊂ B, n' := n ∩ A is maximal (A/n' ⊂ B/n is integral and B/n is a field, so A/n' is a field), and lifting the chain of primes below n' of length d via lying over gives ht n ≥ d; since ht n ≤ dim B = d, ht n = d. As dim B_n = ht n, this is the claim. ∎

(F2) Regular local rings are domains, and initial segments of a regular system of parameters generate prime ideals of the expected height. Let (S, n) be regular local of dimension r, so n = (x_1,...,x_r) with r = dim S. Then S is a domain, and for each 0 ≤ i ≤ r, S_i := S/(x_1,...,x_i) is regular local of dimension r − i (hence a domain, and (x_1,...,x_i) is prime of height i).
Proof. (a) S is a domain: the associated graded ring gr_n(S) = ⊕_{k≥0} n^k/n^{k+1} is the polynomial ring (S/n)[T_1,...,T_r] over the field S/n, since the images of x_1,...,x_r form a basis of n/n^2 and dim n/n^2 = r = dim S means these r elements minimally generate n; in particular gr_n(S) is a domain. If a,b ∈ S are nonzero with ab = 0, put ord(a) := max{k : a ∈ n^k}, which is finite because ∩_k n^k = 0 by Krull's intersection theorem; the initial forms ā ∈ n^{ord a}/n^{ord a+1} and b̄ are nonzero, and ā·b̄ is the class of ab = 0 in n^{ord a+ord b}/n^{ord a+ord b+1}, contradicting that gr_n(S) is a domain. (b) Induction on i: S_0 = S is a domain, so x_1 ≠ 0 is a nonzerodivisor. S_1 is local with maximal ideal generated by the images of x_2,...,x_r, so dim S_1 ≤ r−1 by Krull's height theorem, while dim S_1 ≥ dim S − 1 = r−1 by the principal ideal theorem; hence dim S_1 = r−1 and S_1 is regular local. By induction S_1 is a domain, so (x_1) is prime and x_2 is a nonzerodivisor on S_1, and the same argument continues. At the end, ht(x_1,...,x_i) = i because the chain (0) ⊊ (x_1) ⊊ ... ⊊ (x_1,...,x_i) consists of distinct primes (distinctness: the class of x_{j+1} is nonzero in n_j \ n_j^2, where n_j is the maximal ideal of S_j, since S_j is regular of dimension r−j ≥ 1 for j < i). ∎

(F3) A nonempty scheme which is regular, connected and locally noetherian is irreducible. Proof: at a point of a regular local ring (a domain, by (F2)) there is a unique minimal prime, so no point of the scheme lies on two irreducible components; irreducible components are therefore pairwise disjoint closed subsets, and if there are finitely many (e.g. the scheme is noetherian) each is also open; a decomposition into ≥ 2 disjoint nonempty open-and-closed pieces contradicts connectedness. ∎

=====================================================================
Step 1. Setup: the local ring at the origin.
Let g := dim A ≥ 1 and let 0 ∈ A(F_q) be the identity element (image of the identity section). A is smooth over F_q, hence regular, and connected by definition of an abelian variety; by (F3) A is irreducible, and being regular it is reduced, so A is integral. Hence every open subset of A is integral.
Choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec R of 0 in A. Since A is of finite type over F_q, R is a finitely generated F_q-algebra; since U is integral, R is a domain. Let m ⊂ R be the maximal ideal of the point 0; because 0 is F_q-rational, R/m = F_q. The local ring O_{A,0} = R_m (localisation at S := R \ m) is regular (A is smooth over a field) and, applying (F1) to the finitely generated F_q-domain R (whose fraction field is the function field of A, of transcendence degree g), dim R_m = g. Choose a regular system of parameters x_1,...,x_g ∈ R_m of R_m.

=====================================================================
Step 2. The germ ideal q ⊂ R_m.
By (F2), for each i the quotient R_m/(x_1,...,x_i) is regular local of dimension g − i, hence a domain. Put q := (x_1,...,x_{g−1}) R_m. Then
   R_m/q is regular local of dimension 1, hence a discrete valuation ring;  (∗)
in particular R_m/q is not the zero ring, so q ⊊ m R_m. Also q is a prime ideal of R_m (R_m/q is a domain), and q ⊆ m R_m.

=====================================================================
Step 3. Descent to R; the affine curve Y.
Let p := q ∩ R (contraction along R → R_m). The map P ↦ S^{-1}P is an order-preserving bijection from the set of primes of R contained in m onto the set of primes of R_m, with inverse the contraction Q ↦ Q ∩ R. Since q is prime with q ⊆ m R_m, it follows that p is a prime ideal of R with p ⊆ m and p R_m = q.
Consequences:
 (a) R/p is a finitely generated domain over F_q, and Y := Spec(R/p) is an integral affine scheme, of finite type over F_q.
 (b) The localisation map R/p → S^{-1}(R/p) is injective: S ∩ p = ∅ because p ⊆ m, so S maps to nonzero elements of the domain R/p, and inverting nonzero elements of a domain is injective. Identifying S^{-1}(R/p) = S^{-1}R/S^{-1}p = R_m/q, we obtain an INJECTION
        R/p  ↪  R_m/q,
     i.e. Y is an open subscheme... no: more precisely the natural map from the coordinate ring into the local ring at y_0 below is injective.
 (c) Since p ⊆ m, the ideal m/p is a maximal ideal of R/p; call the corresponding point y_0 := m/p ∈ Y. Its residue field is (R/p)/(m/p) = R/m = F_q, so y_0 is an F_q-rational closed point of Y, and its image in U = Spec R is m, i.e. the point 0 of A.
 (d) The local ring of Y at y_0 is
         O_{Y,y_0} = (R/p)_{m/p} ≅ S^{-1}(R/p) = R_m/q,
     a DVR by (∗); thus Y is regular (normal) at y_0. Let K := Frac(R/p), the function field of Y. Localising a domain at a multiplicative set does not change its fraction field, so Frac((R/p)_{m/p}) = K; hence O_{Y,y_0} is a DVR with fraction field K, and O_{Y,y_0} ⊂ K (a localisation of a domain sits inside its fraction field). [This is the correct direction of the inclusion.]
 (e) Dimension of Y. Apply (F1) to the finitely generated F_q-domain B := R/p and its maximal ideal n := m/p: it gives dim Y = dim B = ht n = dim B_n = dim (R/p)_{m/p} = dim R_m/q = 1 by (∗). So Y is an integral affine curve over F_q. (No appeal to heights of non-maximal primes, and hence no catenarity statement, is needed.)

=====================================================================
Step 4. The projective closure \bar Y.
Y is closed in U and U is open in A, so Y is locally closed in A; let j: Y → A be the corresponding immersion and let \bar Y ⊂ A be the scheme-theoretic closure of Y, i.e. the closed subscheme defined by the quasi-coherent ideal I := ker(O_A → j_*O_Y).
 (a) \bar Y ∩ U = Y as schemes: for the open immersion ι: U ↪ A one has I|_U = ker(O_U → (j_*O_Y)|_U) = ker(O_U → j_{U*}O_Y) where j_U: Y ↪ U is the given closed immersion (because U ∩ Y = Y), and that kernel is the ideal of Y in U.
     Hence Y is an OPEN subscheme of \bar Y, and consequently O_{\bar Y,0} = O_{Y,y_0} = R_m/q is a DVR: \bar Y is regular and normal at 0.
 (b) \bar Y is integral. It is irreducible because Y is dense in it and Y is irreducible. It is reduced: for any nonempty open W ⊆ \bar Y, the map O_{\bar Y}(W) → O_Y(W ∩ Y) is injective (as O_{\bar Y} = O_A/I ⊂ j_*O_Y by definition of I) and W ∩ Y ≠ ∅ by density, while O_Y(W ∩ Y) is a subring of the domain K because Y is integral; so O_{\bar Y}(W) is a domain, in particular has no nonzero nilpotents.
 (c) \bar Y is a projective integral curve over F_q: it is a closed subscheme of the projective F_q-scheme A, hence of finite type and projective over F_q; it is integral with function field K (as Y ⊂ \bar Y is dense open), so by (F1) dim \bar Y = trdeg_{F_q} K = 1. The point 0 is a closed point of \bar Y with residue field F_q (it is closed in A because A is separated over F_q and 0 is rational).

=====================================================================
Step 5. Normalisation ν: C → \bar Y, and its basic properties.
Let \bar O be the integral closure of O_{\bar Y} in K and set C := Spec_{\bar Y} \bar O.
 (a) \bar O is a coherent O_{\bar Y}-algebra (ν is finite). Check on an affine open Spec B ⊂ \bar Y: B is a finitely generated F_q-domain with Frac B = K, of dimension 1 by Step 4(c). By Noether normalization there is t ∈ B transcendental over F_q such that B is finite over A_0 := F_q[t]; then K is a finite extension of F_q(t). The integral closure A_1 of the PID F_q[t] in the finite extension K/F_q(t) is a finite F_q[t]-module (Dedekind's theorem on integral closures in global fields; equivalently: in the separable case A_1 is contained in the dual lattice for the trace pairing, and a purely inseparable step of exponent 1 adjoining x with x^p ∈ A_1 is generated by 1,x,...,x^{p−1}). The integral closure B_1 of B in K satisfies A_1 ⊂ B_1 (transitivity of integrality) and B_1 ⊂ A_1 (an element of K integral over B is integral over A_0, as B is finite over A_0), so B_1 = A_1 is finite over B. Thus ν is finite.
 (b) C is integral with function field K: \bar O is a subsheaf of the constant sheaf K (integral closure inside a field), so C is integral; Frac(B_1) = K because B ⊂ B_1 ⊂ K and Frac B = K.
 (c) ν is surjective and dim C = 1: finite morphisms are integral, so lying over gives surjectivity, and lying over plus incomparability give dim C = dim \bar Y = 1.
 (d) C is regular, hence smooth over F_q. C is normal by construction; a noetherian normal local ring of dimension 1 is a DVR (every nonzero prime is maximal and height one, and the local ring is integrally closed noetherian of dimension 1), so all local rings of C are DVRs or fields: C is regular. C is of finite type over F_q (finite over \bar Y, which is of finite type over F_q). A finite-type scheme over the perfect field F_q which is regular is smooth (regular implies geometrically regular over a perfect field).
 (e) C is projective over F_q. We show ν is projective (a finite morphism is projective), and compose with the projective morphism \bar Y → Spec F_q. For the finite morphism ν, write \mathcal A := ν_*O_C, a coherent O_{\bar Y}-algebra with C = Spec_{\bar Y} \mathcal A. Since \bar Y is projective over F_q, there is a very ample line bundle O(1); for n ≫ 0 the sheaf \mathcal A(n) is globally generated, so there is a surjection of O_{\bar Y}-modules E := O(−n)^{⊕N} ↠ \mathcal A. A set of O-module generators of an O-algebra generates it as an O-algebra, so Sym_O E ↠ \mathcal A is a surjection of O_{\bar Y}-algebras, hence a CLOSED immersion C ↪ V(E) := Spec_{\bar Y}(Sym_O E) over \bar Y. Since E is locally free of finite rank, V(E) is the open subscheme P(E ⊕ O) \ P(E) of the projective bundle P(E ⊕ O) (quotient convention for P, where the projective bundle represents one-dimensional quotients; the embedding V(E) ↪ P(E⊕O) is the standard open of points where the O-summand does not vanish). Thus we have a closed immersion C ↪ V(E) and V(E) is an open subscheme of the \bar Y-scheme P := P(E⊕O), so the composite i: C → P is an immersion. Now C is proper over \bar Y (ν finite) and P is separated over \bar Y (projective), so the \bar Y-morphism i is proper: indeed, C → P factors as C → P ×_{\bar Y} C = graph(i), which is a closed immersion because P → \bar Y is separated, followed by the projection P ×_{\bar Y} C → P, which is proper since C → \bar Y is proper. A proper immersion is a closed immersion: i is a monomorphism of finite type, it is universally closed, so its base change to its scheme-theoretic image \bar i(C) is a proper monomorphism of finite type which is a universal homeomorphism onto a closed subscheme, and the induced map C → \bar i(C) is an immersion which is also proper, hence a closed immersion (equivalently: an immersion which is a closed map has closed image, and the induced map onto that closed subscheme is an open immersion and a closed map, hence an isomorphism). Therefore C is a closed subscheme of P, i.e. C → \bar Y is projective. Composing with the closed immersion \bar Y ↪ A and A → Spec F_q projective, we get that C → Spec F_q is projective (compositions of projective morphisms are projective).
 (f) The fibre over 0. Since ν is finite, \bar O is coherent, and for the local ring O := O_{\bar Y,0} (a DVR, hence integrally closed in K) we have (ν^{-1}(0)) = Spec(\bar O ⊗_{O_{\bar Y}} κ(0)) = Spec(\bar O_0 / m_0 \bar O_0) because formation of the fibre of a finite morphism commutes with localisation; here \bar O_0 is the integral closure of O_0 = O_{\bar Y,0} in K (integral closure commutes with localisation: S^{-1}\bar O is the integral closure of S^{-1}O in S^{-1}K = K). As O is a DVR it is integrally closed in K, so \bar O_0 = O, and
        ν^{-1}(0) = Spec(O/m) = Spec F_q.
     Thus there is exactly one point c ∈ C above 0, its residue field is κ(c) = F_q, i.e. c ∈ C(F_q), and ν(c) = 0; moreover O_{C,c} = O_{\bar Y,0} = R_m/q and κ(c) = F_q.

Summary so far: C is integral, separated (projective), of finite type and of dimension 1 over F_q — a curve — smooth, projective, with an F_q-rational point c, and there is a finite F_q-morphism ν: C → \bar Y with ν(c) = 0.

=====================================================================
Step 6. C is geometrically connected.
 (a) Γ(C, O_C) = F_q. Since C is integral, Γ(C,O_C) is a subring of K, hence a domain. Since C is proper over the noetherian ring Spec F_q and O_C is coherent, Grothendieck's finiteness theorem gives that Γ(C,O_C) is a finite-dimensional F_q-vector space; a finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective, hence surjective, F_q-linear endomorphism). So Γ(C,O_C) = k' is a finite field extension of F_q. The F_q-rational point c gives an F_q-algebra homomorphism ev_c: Γ(C,O_C) → κ(c) = F_q (the pullback along c: Spec F_q → C); the composite F_q → Γ(C,O_C) → F_q is the identity because C → Spec F_q ∘ c = id, so ev_c is surjective, and being a nonzero map of fields it is an isomorphism. Hence k' = F_q.
 (b) Let kbar = \overline{F}_q. Flat base change for H^0 of the quasi-compact quasi-separated morphism C → Spec F_q gives Γ(C_{kbar}, O) = kbar ⊗_{F_q} Γ(C,O_C) = kbar.
 (c) C_{kbar} is smooth over kbar, hence regular; it is noetherian, so by the argument of (F3) its irreducible components are pairwise disjoint; being of finite type over kbar it has finitely many, so each is also open. If C_{kbar} had ≥ 2 irreducible components, it would be a disjoint union Z_1 ⊔ Z_2 of two nonempty open-and-closed subschemes, and then Γ(C_{kbar},O) = Γ(Z_1,O) × Γ(Z_2,O) would contain a nontrivial idempotent, contradicting (b). So C_{kbar} is irreducible; it is reduced because it is regular; hence C_{kbar} is integral. In particular C is geometrically integral, hence geometrically connected.

=====================================================================
Step 7. The morphism f and its nonconstancy.
Define f: C → \bar Y ↪ A, the composite of ν with the closed immersion, and set c as in Step 5(f). Then:
 • f is an F_q-morphism (ν and \bar Y ↪ A are defined over F_q),
 • f(c) = 0 by construction,
 • C is a smooth, projective, geometrically connected curve over F_q (Steps 5(d),(e), 6),
 • f is NONCONSTANT: ν is integral and surjective (Step 5(c)), so set-theoretically f(C) = ν(C) = |\bar Y|. The scheme \bar Y is integral of dimension 1 (Step 4(c)), so it has a generic point η and the closed point 0, and η ≠ 0 because dim \bar Y = 1 > 0 (a one-point scheme is the spectrum of a field, of dimension 0). Hence the image of f contains the two distinct points η and 0 = f(c); a constant morphism has a single-point image, so f is not constant. (Equivalently: the point c ∈ C maps to 0, while the generic point of C — whose image under ν is the generic point of \bar Y, since Frac(\bar O) = K — maps to η ≠ 0.)

This produces exactly the required C, c and f. ∎

=====================================================================
Remarks on scope. As instructed, nothing is claimed about the image f(C) generating A, about the induced homomorphism Pic^0_{C/F_q} → A, or about tangent directions spanning T_0 A: a smooth curve germ at 0 has a single tangent line and may well sit inside a proper abelian subvariety. The proof uses only: regularity of O_{A,0} (smoothness), the prime correspondence under localisation, the dimension theorem for maximal ideals of finitely generated algebras over a field (Noether normalization, (F1)), finiteness of normalisation of a curve over a field, the fact that a finite morphism is projective (proved above by an honest closed immersion into P(E ⊕ O)), and the standard identification of geometric integrality with H^0 = base field for smooth proper varieties.

lemma_isogeny_cohom_finite_field.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be prime, let k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q, and let f:A\to B be an isogeny of abelian varieties over \mathbb F_q. Then for every n\ge 0 the pullback f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.
lemma_isogeny_cohom_finite_field.proof:
Throughout, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and an "isogeny" means a surjective homomorphism of abelian varieties with finite kernel; an "abelian variety over F_q" means a group scheme over F_q that is smooth, proper and geometrically connected of finite type.

STEP 1. A and B are smooth projective geometrically connected F_q-varieties.

Smoothness, properness and geometric connectedness hold by definition. Projectivity is the standard theorem that every abelian variety carries an ample line bundle, so A and B are projective over F_q. It remains to check (geometric) integrality, since lemma_36 applies to varieties.

Let K/F_q be any field extension. Then A_K is smooth over K, hence locally Noetherian with regular local rings, and A_K is connected because A is geometrically connected. We show: a connected regular locally Noetherian scheme X is integral.
 (i) A regular local ring is a domain (standard commutative algebra: its associated graded ring for the maximal-ideal filtration is a polynomial ring over the residue field, hence a domain, which forces the local ring to be a domain).
 (ii) In a locally Noetherian scheme the irreducible components passing through a point x are in bijection with the minimal prime ideals of O_{X,x}. By (i) there is exactly one such minimal prime, so through each x passes a unique irreducible component Z(x).
 (iii) Every irreducible component Z of X is open. Indeed, take x \in Z; the unique component through x is Z. Choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec R of x with R Noetherian; U meets only finitely many irreducible components Z = Z_1, Z_2, ..., Z_r of X (a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes, and the components meeting U are the closures of those of U). Each Z_i \cap U is closed in U, so V := U \setminus \bigcup_{i\ge 2}(Z_i \cap U) is open in U, hence in X; it contains x and meets no irreducible component of X except Z, so V \subseteq Z. Thus Z is a neighbourhood of each of its points, i.e. open.
 By (iii) Z is non-empty clopen, so connectedness forces Z = X; hence X is irreducible, and (i) gives reducedness. Irreducible + reduced = integral.
Applying this to X = A_K for every extension K/F_q shows A is geometrically integral; the same argument applies to B. Hence A and B are integral, separated, of finite type, smooth and projective over F_q with geometrically connected fibres, i.e. smooth projective geometrically connected varieties as required by lemma_36.

STEP 2. f is finite, surjective, of positive degree.

Write p_A: A -> Spec F_q and p_1, p_2 for the projections of A \times_{\mathbb F_q} B.
(a) The graph \Gamma_f := (\mathrm{id}_A, f): A -> A \times B is a closed immersion. Namely, \Gamma_f is the base change of the diagonal \Delta_B: B -> B \times B along the morphism (f \circ p_1, p_2): A \times B -> B \times B: the fibre product is {(a,b) : f(a) = b}, canonically isomorphic to A via a \mapsto (a, f(a)). The diagonal is a closed immersion because B is separated over F_q (proper implies separated), and closed immersions are stable under base change.
(b) p_2: A \times B -> B is proper and of finite type, being the base change of p_A, which is proper and of finite type.
(c) f = p_2 \circ \Gamma_f is a composite of a closed immersion (closed immersions are proper, being finite) with a proper morphism, hence proper; it is of finite type as a composite of finite-type morphisms.
(d) Geometric fibres. Let \Omega/F_q be a field and b: Spec \Omega -> B a point whose fibre A_b := A \times_{B,b} Spec \Omega is non-empty; choose \tilde a \in A(\Omega) with f \circ \tilde a = b. Let \mu: A_\Omega \times_\Omega A_\Omega -> A_\Omega be the group law and \iota the inverse. Define u: A_b -> (\ker f)_\Omega by u(a) = a - \tilde a (i.e. \mu \circ (\mathrm{pr}, \tilde a \circ \pi) with \pi: A_b -> Spec \Omega) and v: (\ker f)_\Omega -> A_b by v(t) = t + \tilde a. Since f is a homomorphism, f \circ \mu = \mu_B \circ (f \times f) as morphisms A \times A -> B, so f(u(a)) = f(a) - f(\tilde a) = b - b = 0 as morphisms A_b -> B (the composite A_b -> B is b \circ \pi by the defining property of the fibre product, and b \circ \pi = f \circ \tilde a \circ \pi); hence u factors through (\ker f)_\Omega. Similarly f \circ v = 0 + b = b, so v lands in the fibre A_b. The composites are v \circ u = a - \tilde a + \tilde a = a and u \circ v = t + \tilde a - \tilde a = t, identities of morphisms because they hold functorially on T-valued points for all \Omega-schemes T (translation by \tilde a and by -\tilde a are inverse automorphisms of A_\Omega). Thus A_b \simeq (\ker f)_\Omega. Since \ker f is finite over F_q, (\ker f)_\Omega is finite over \Omega, so A_b is a finite \Omega-scheme; its coordinate ring is Artinian, so |A_b| is a finite discrete space. (Empty fibres are trivially finite.)
(e) f is quasi-finite: f is of finite type by (c), and by (d) every point of every fibre is an isolated point of that fibre; the standard characterisation of quasi-finiteness for finite-type morphisms (f is quasi-finite at x iff x is isolated in its fibre) gives quasi-finiteness.
(f) A proper quasi-finite morphism is finite (Zariski's Main Theorem in this form). So f is finite.
(g) f is surjective by the definition of isogeny. Since A and B are integral, f is dominant, and F_q(B) \hookrightarrow F_q(A). Let \eta be the generic point of B. Because f is integral, incomparability holds: any x \in A with f(x) = \eta is a minimal point of A, hence x = the generic point \xi of A. Thus f^{-1}(\eta) = {\xi}, and (f_* O_A)_\eta is a finite F_q(B)-algebra (finite, as f is finite) with unique prime and residue field \kappa(\xi) = F_q(A). Therefore d := [F_q(A) : F_q(B)] < \infty, and d \ge 1 since f_*O_A \ne 0. This is the degree of the finite surjective morphism f.

STEP 3. Apply lemma_36 to f.

f: Y = A -> X = B is a finite surjective morphism of degree d \ge 1 between smooth projective geometrically connected F_q-varieties (Steps 1-2). By lemma_36, for every n \ge 0 the pullback
   f^*: H^n_{\acute et}(B_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) -> H^n_{\acute et}(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell)
is injective (indeed it is Frobenius-equivariant and has the retraction (1/d) f_*).

STEP 4. An isogeny in the opposite direction.

Apply lemma_120 with ground field k_0 = \mathbb F_q (the prime \ell \ne p is invertible in \mathbb F_q; only its conclusion on the existence of g is used). There exist a homomorphism g: B -> A over \mathbb F_q and an integer m \ge 1 with g \circ f = [m]_A and f \circ g = [m]_B.

STEP 5. g is an isogeny.

Finiteness of \ker g. The identity sections e_A: Spec F_q -> A and e_B: Spec F_q -> B are closed immersions: e_A is the equaliser of \mathrm{id}_A and the constant morphism e_A \circ p_A, i.e. the base change of the diagonal \Delta_A along (\mathrm{id}_A, e_A \circ p_A): A -> A \times A, and \Delta_A is a closed immersion since A is separated over F_q; likewise for e_B. Since f is a homomorphism, f \circ e_B = e_B, so e_B factors through the closed immersion \ker f -> B. Base changing along g: B -> A gives a morphism
   \ker g = B \times_{A, e_B} Spec F_q  ->  B \times_{A, \ker f} A = (f \circ g)^{-1}(e_B) = [m]_B^{-1}(e_B) = \ker[m]_B.
This morphism is a closed immersion: both \ker g -> B and \ker[m]_B -> B are immersions, the triangle over B commutes, \ker[m]_B -> B is a monomorphism (base change of the immersion Spec F_q -> B), and a monomorphism is stable under base change, so the square with \ker g -> B is cartesian and \ker g -> \ker[m]_B is the base change of the closed immersion \ker g -> B. Now [m]_B is a finite morphism (standard theorem: on a g-dimensional abelian variety, [m] is finite locally free of degree m^{2g}), so \ker[m]_B, being the base change of [m]_B along e_B, is finite over F_q. A closed subscheme of a scheme finite over a field is finite (if Y = Spec R with R a finite k-module, a closed subscheme is Spec R/I with R/I finite over k). Hence \ker g is finite over F_q.

Surjectivity of g. The morphism [m]_A is finite locally free of rank m^{2\dim A} > 0, hence surjective; for a \in A(k) the fibre [m]_A^{-1}(a) is a non-empty finite k-scheme, and since k is algebraically closed every non-zero finite k-algebra has a maximal ideal with residue field k, so the fibre contains a k-rational point. Thus [m]_A: A(k) -> A(k) is surjective. As [m]_A = g \circ f, the map g: B(k) -> A(k) is surjective. Steps 2(a)-(c) applied to the homomorphism g show that g is proper, hence |g_{\bar k}|: |B_k| -> |A_k| is a closed map; its image is closed and contains all k-rational points of A_k, i.e. all closed points of A_k, which are dense because A_k is of finite type over a field (Jacobson). Therefore |g_k| is surjective, and since Spec k -> Spec F_q is integral (algebraic), hence |A_k| -> |A| is surjective by lying over, |g| is surjective. So g is a surjective homomorphism with finite kernel: an isogeny.

STEP 6. Apply lemma_36 to g.

Repeating Steps 2 and 3 verbatim with f replaced by g: g is proper, quasi-finite (its geometric fibres are torsors under the finite group scheme \ker g, by the same translation argument as in Step 2(d)), hence finite and surjective, of degree d' := [F_q(B) : F_q(A)] \ge 1 between smooth projective geometrically connected F_q-varieties. Lemma_36 then gives, for every n \ge 0, an injective map
   g^*: H^n_{\acute et}(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) -> H^n_{\acute et}(B_k, \mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 7. Finite-dimensionality.

A and B are proper over F_q. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob with X = A, K = \mathbb Q_\ell the constant sheaf on A_k, and \varphi = \psi its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism F_A^* \mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell: for every n the hypercohomology H^n(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) = H^n_{\acute et}(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. The same with X = B gives finite-dimensionality of H^n_{\acute et}(B_k, \mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 8. Dimension count.

Fix n \ge 0 and put V := H^n_{\acute et}(B_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) and W := H^n_{\acute et}(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell), both finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell by Step 7. By Steps 3 and 6 there are injective \mathbb Q_\ell-linear maps f^*: V \hookrightarrow W and g^*: W \hookrightarrow V. Injectivity of f^* gives \dim V \le \dim W, injectivity of g^* gives \dim W \le \dim V, hence \dim V = \dim W =: N < \infty. The image f^*(V) is an N-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-subspace of the N-dimensional space W, so f^*(V) = W; combined with injectivity, f^* is an isomorphism. As n was arbitrary, f^*: H^n_{\acute et}(B_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) -> H^n_{\acute et}(A_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every n \ge 0. \blacksquare

(Remark, not needed above: by the Frobenius-equivariance supplied by lemma_36 the map f^* is in fact an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell[F]-modules, so lemma_8 shows arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) if and only if it is on H^n_{\acute et}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).)

lemma_139.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let A be an abelian variety over F_q, let k=overline(F_q), let l≠p be prime, and let P be a smooth projective variety over F_q which is an étale torsor under A. For p∈P(k), let t_p:A_k→P_k be a↦a+p, and for Y=P,A let F_Y=(id_Y×Spec sigma)^*, where sigma:k→k is c↦c^q. Then for every n≥0 the pullback t_p^*:H^n_et(P_k,Q_l)→H^n_et(A_k,Q_l) is a p-independent F_P-F_A-equivariant isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces.
lemma_139.proof:
We fix the following data: a prime power q=p^a, an abelian variety A over F_q, an étale A-torsor P over F_q (so the action map m:A×_{F_q}P→P, (a,p)↦a+p, makes the map α:A×_{F_q}P→P×_{F_q}P, (a,p)↦(a+p,p), an isomorphism), k=\bar F_q, σ:k→k, c↦c^q, ℓ≠p, and for Y∈{A,P} the morphism F_{Y,k}:=id_Y×Spec(σ):Y_k→Y_k together with F_Y:=F_{Y,k}^* on étale cohomology. For y∈Y(k) we write \tilde y:A_k? — more precisely, for a k-point y of an F_q-scheme Y we denote by y:Spec k→Y_k the corresponding section and by \bar y:Y_k→Spec k? No: we denote by π_{Y,k}:Y_k→Spec k the structure morphism, and for a point y∈Y(k) we write c_y:Z_k→Y_k for the constant morphism Z_k→^{π}Spec k→^{y}Y_k attached to any F_q-scheme Z. Note π_{Y,k}∘F_{Y,k}=Spec(σ)∘π_{Y,k}, since F_{Y,k}=id×Spec(σ) and π is the second projection.

The proof has three steps: (1) t_p is an isomorphism; (2) t_p^* does not depend on p; (3) t_p^* intertwines F_P and F_A.

=== Step 1: t_p is an isomorphism of k-schemes ===
Base-changing the torsor isomorphism α to k gives an isomorphism
   α_k:(A×_{F_q}P)_k=A_k×_kP_k ⟶ P_k×_kP_k,  (a,p)↦(a+p,p),
where we use the canonical identification (A×_{F_q}P)×_{Spec F_q}Spec k ≅ A_k×_kP_k (on affine rings: (R⊗_{F_q}S)⊗_{F_q}k → (R⊗_{F_q}k)⊗_k(S⊗_{F_q}k), (r⊗s)⊗c↦(r⊗c)⊗(s⊗1), with inverse (r⊗c)⊗(s⊗d)↦(rs⊗1)⊗cd; both are easily checked to be mutually inverse k-algebra isomorphisms).
Define s:P_k→A_k by s:=pr_1∘α_k^{-1}∘(id_{P_k},c_p): that is, p'↦p'−p, and t_p:A_k→P_k by t_p:=m_k∘(id_{A_k},c_p), i.e. a↦a+p, where m_k:(A×P)_k→P_k is the base change of the action m. On the level of the functor of points (or by pasting the displayed morphisms through the universal property of the fibre product) one computes
   t_p∘s(p') = t_p(p'−p) = (p'−p)+p = p',   s∘t_p(a) = s(a+p) = (a+p)−p = a,
using the associativity and unit axioms of the action, which hold as identities of morphisms since they hold for the group scheme action. Hence t_p is an isomorphism with inverse s. (Concretely: α_k^{-1}(p',p)=(p'−p,p) by definition of the inverse of the simply-transitive action map, so t_p∘s = pr_1∘α_k∘(α_k^{-1}(id,c_p)×...) = id, etc.)
Étale cohomology is contravariantly functorial for morphisms of schemes, and an isomorphism induces an isomorphism; therefore for every n≥0
   t_p^*:H^n_ét(P_k,Q_ℓ) ⟶ H^n_ét(A_k,Q_ℓ)
is a Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism (inverse (t_p^{-1})^* = s^*). This proves the "isomorphism" part of the statement.

=== Step 2: independence of p ===
Let p,p'∈P(k). Since α_k is an isomorphism, it is bijective on k-points, so there is a unique a∈A(k) with a+p=p'. Let τ_a:A_k→A_k denote translation by a, x↦x+a. We claim t_{p'}=t_p∘τ_a. Write i_a:Spec k→A_k for the section of a and \bar a:=c_{a}=i_a∘π_{A,k}:A_k→A_k for the constant map. Since τ_a=m_{A,k}∘(id,\bar a) (m_A:A×A→A the group law),
   t_p∘τ_a = m_k∘(id,c_p)∘m_{A,k}∘(id,\bar a) = m_k∘(m_{A,k}∘(id,\bar a), c_p) = m_k∘(m_{A,k}×id_{P_k})∘((id,\bar a),c_p),
where ((id,\bar a),c_p):A_k→A_k×_kA_k×_kP_k. By associativity of the action, m∘(m_A×id_P)=m∘(id_A×m) as morphisms A×A×P→P over F_q; base-changing to k and composing with ((id,\bar a),c_p) gives
   t_p∘τ_a = m_k∘(id_{A_k}, m_k∘(\bar a,c_p)).
Now m_k∘(\bar a,c_p) = m_k∘(i_a,p)∘π_{A,k} = c_{a+p} = c_{p'}, because the sum of two sections i_a,p:Spec k→(A×P)_k is the section a+p, and a+p=p' by the choice of a. Hence t_p∘τ_a = m_k∘(id,c_{p'}) = t_{p'}. Applying (g∘f)^*=f^*∘g^* and then lemma_translations_trivial (translation by any k-point of A acts as the identity on H^n_ét(A_k,Q_ℓ), for every n≥0),
   t_{p'}^* = τ_a^*∘t_p^* = id∘t_p^* = t_p^*.
Thus the map t_p^* is independent of p∈P(k). This also applies to the special point q∈P(k) constructed in Step 3.

=== Step 3: equivariance ===
First record two formal facts about F.
(a) The action m is a morphism over F_q, hence its base change along Spec(σ) commutes with F: as morphisms (A×_{F_q}P)_k→P_k over Spec F_q,
   m_k∘(id_{A×P}×Spec σ) = (m∘id_{A×P})×(id_k∘Spec σ) = m×Spec σ = (id_P∘m)×(Spec σ∘id_k) = (id_P×Spec σ)∘m_k,
using (f∘g)×(f'∘g')=(f×f')∘(g×g') for products over Spec F_q. Under the identification (A×P)_k≅A_k×_kP_k of Step 1, the morphism id_{A×P}×Spec σ corresponds to F_{A,k}×_kF_{P,k}: indeed on affine rings (R⊗_{F_q}S)⊗_{F_q}k→(R⊗_{F_q}S)⊗_{F_q}k, (r⊗s)⊗c↦(r⊗s)⊗σ(c) is carried by the displayed isomorphism to (r⊗c)⊗(s⊗d)↦(r⊗σ(c))⊗(s⊗σ(d)), which is exactly (id⊗σ)⊗_k(id⊗σ). Hence
   F_{P,k}∘m_k = m_k∘(F_{A,k}×_kF_{P,k})   as morphisms A_k×_kP_k→P_k over Spec F_q.
(b) For the given p∈P(k), the composite F_{P,k}∘p:Spec k→P_k satisfies π_{P,k}∘F_{P,k}∘p=Spec(σ), so it is not a section. Define
   q := F_{P,k}∘p∘Spec(σ^{-1}) ∈ P(k).
This is a section: π_{P,k}∘q = Spec(σ)∘π_{P,k}∘p∘Spec(σ^{-1}) = Spec(σ)∘Spec(σ^{-1}) = Spec(σ^{-1}∘σ)=id. Uniquely, q is the only k-point with F_{P,k}∘p = q∘Spec(σ) (compose with Spec(σ^{-1}) on the right to recover q). By construction the constant morphisms satisfy
   F_{P,k}∘c_p = F_{P,k}∘p∘π_{A,k} = q∘Spec(σ)∘π_{A,k} = q∘π_{A,k}∘F_{A,k} = c_q∘F_{A,k},
specifying at π_{A,k}∘F_{A,k}=Spec(σ)∘π_{A,k}.
Now compute, in the category of schemes over Spec F_q, using (a) and (b):
   F_{P,k}∘t_p = F_{P,k}∘m_k∘(id_{A_k},c_p)
              = m_k∘(F_{A,k}×_kF_{P,k})∘(id_{A_k},c_p)
              = m_k∘(F_{A,k}, F_{P,k}∘c_p)
              = m_k∘(F_{A,k}, c_q∘F_{A,k})
              = m_k∘(id_{A_k},c_q)∘F_{A,k}
              = t_q∘F_{A,k}.
(The fourth equality is the universal property of the fibre product A_k×_kP_k: (id,c_q)∘F_{A,k}=(F_{A,k},c_q∘F_{A,k}); both sides land in the fibre product because π_{A,k}∘F_{A,k}=Spec(σ)∘π_{A,k}=π_{P,k}∘c_q∘F_{A,k}.)
Passing to cohomology and using contravariance (F_Y denotes F_{Y,k}^*),
   t_p^*∘F_P = (F_{P,k}∘t_p)^* = (t_q∘F_{A,k})^* = F_A∘t_q^*.
By Step 2 applied to the two k-points p and q of P we have t_q^*=t_p^*. Therefore
   t_p^*∘F_P = F_A∘t_p^*,
which is exactly F_P–F_A-equivariance of t_p^*:H^n_ét(P_k,Q_ℓ)→H^n_ét(A_k,Q_ℓ).

=== Conclusion ===
Steps 1–3 hold for every n≥0 (Step 1 uses only functoriality of H^n_ét(-,Q_ℓ); Step 2 uses lemma_translations_trivial, which is stated for every n≥0; Step 3 is a statement about morphisms, hence valid in every degree). Hence for every n≥0 the map t_p^* is a Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism, independent of the choice of p∈P(k), and intertwining F_P with F_A. (For n=0 this says in particular that the canonical identification Q_ℓ=H^0(P_k,Q_ℓ)≅H^0(A_k,Q_ℓ)=Q_ℓ is F-equivariant, both operators being the identity, in agreement with the general argument.) This completes the proof.

lemma_etale_fibrewise_iso.statement: Let B be a ring and let f: S \to A be a homomorphism of étale B-algebras. Suppose that for every prime ideal \mathfrak p \subset B the induced homomorphism S \otimes_B \kappa(\mathfrak p) \to A \otimes_B \kappa(\mathfrak p) is an isomorphism. Then f is an isomorphism.
lemma_etale_fibrewise_iso.proof:
CONVENTION. All rings are commutative with 1 and all homomorphisms preserve 1. For a ring R and a prime 𝔭, κ(𝔭) is the residue field Frac(R/𝔭); for s ∈ R, R[1/s] is the localisation. Following the convention of the statement, an R-algebra C is called ÉTALE if it is flat, of finite presentation, and Ω_{C/R} = 0. No result outside elementary commutative algebra is used; none of the supplied lemmas is needed.

=====================================================================
PART 0 — PRELIMINARY FACTS
=====================================================================

F1 (determinant trick ⇒ idempotent). Let I = (x_1,…,x_n) be a finitely generated ideal of a ring C with I = I². Then I = (e) with e² = e.
Proof. Since I = I², x_i = Σ_j a_{ij} x_j with a_{ij} ∈ I. The matrix M = (δ_{ij} − a_{ij}) ∈ M_n(C) satisfies M·(x_1,…,x_n)^t = 0, hence adj(M)·M·x = det(M)·x = 0, so det(M)·x_j = 0 for every j. Expanding det(M) shows det(M) = 1 − e' with e' ∈ I, so e'x_j = x_j for all j. Every z ∈ I has z = Σ c_j x_j, hence (1−e')z = Σ c_j(1−e')x_j = 0; taking z = e' ∈ I gives e' = e'². Finally (x_1,…,x_n) ⊂ (e') because e'x_j = x_j, and e' ∈ I gives the reverse inclusion, so I = (e'). ∎

F2 (differentials of a presentation). Let C = R[X_1,…,X_n]/(h_1,…,h_m) and let x_i be the image of X_i. Then Ω_{C/R} ≅ coker(u) where u: C^m → C^n sends e_j to (a_{ji})_{i=1..n} with a_{ji} := (∂h_j/∂X_i)(x) ∈ C. Hence Ω_{C/R} = 0 iff u is surjective; since C^n is free, this is equivalent to the existence of a matrix Λ = (λ_{ij}) ∈ M_{n×m}(C) with Σ_{j=1}^m λ_{ij} a_{ji'} = δ_{ii'} for all i,i'.
Proof. For a C-module M, an R-derivation D: C → M is the same as an R-derivation P := R[X] → M vanishing on J := (h_1,…,h_m); derivations P → M are parametrised freely by (D(X_1),…,D(X_n)) ∈ M^n, and the vanishing condition is 0 = D(h_j) = Σ_i (∂h_j/∂X_i)(x)·D(X_i) for all j. Thus Der_R(C,−) ≅ Hom_C(coker u, −); comparing with Der_R(C,−) ≅ Hom_C(Ω_{C/R},−) and applying Yoneda gives the claim. ∎

F3 (Taylor expansion at a rational point). For h ∈ R[X_1,…,X_n] and r = (r_1,…,r_n) ∈ R^n, putting Y_i = X_i − r_i, one has in R[X]
  h = h(r) + Σ_i (∂h/∂X_i)(r)·Y_i + Σ_{|α| ≥ 2} c_α Y^α,  c_α ∈ R.
Proof. Rewrite h as a polynomial in the variables Y_i (X_i = Y_i + r_i); the constant term is h(r) and the coefficient of Y_i is the partial derivative evaluated at Y = 0, i.e. at X = r. ∎

F4 (base change of differentials). For a B-algebra A and any B-algebra B′, the natural map B′ ⊗_A Ω_{A/B} → Ω_{(A⊗_B B′)/B′}, λ ⊗ da ↦ (1⊗λ)·d(a⊗1), is an isomorphism.
Proof. For an (A⊗_B B′)-module M, restriction along a ↦ a⊗1 is a bijection Der_{B′}(A⊗_B B′, M) → Der_B(A, M). The inverse sends a B-derivation d: A → M to D(Σ_i a_i ⊗ λ_i) = Σ_i λ_i d(a_i): this is well defined because on the balancing relation (ab)⊗λ = a⊗bλ (b ∈ B) the two sides give λ d(ab) = λ(a d(b) + b d(a)) = aλ d(b) + bλ d(a) and λ b d(a); these agree since d(b) = 0 for a B-derivation. Then Der_B(A,M) = Hom_A(Ω_{A/B},M) = Hom_{A⊗_B B′}(B′⊗_A Ω_{A/B}, M), and Yoneda concludes. ∎

F5 (fundamental exact sequence). For R → S′ → S″ there is an exact sequence S″ ⊗_{S′} Ω_{S′/R} → Ω_{S″/R} → Ω_{S″/S′} → 0.
Proof. An S″-module-valued R-derivation of S″ kills d(s′) for all s′ ∈ S′ iff it is an S′-derivation; hence Ω_{S″/S′} = Ω_{S″/R}/N where N is the S″-submodule generated by the images of d(s′). The map S′ → N, s′ ↦ d(s′), is an R-derivation, so it factors through Ω_{S′/R}, and the induced S″-linear map S″⊗_{S′}Ω_{S′/R} → Ω_{S″/R} has image exactly N. ∎

F6 (stability of étale maps). (i) If A is étale over B and B → B′ is any map, then A⊗_B B′ is étale over B′. (ii) Étale maps are closed under composition.
Proof. (i) Finite presentation: A = B[x_1,…,x_n]/(g_1,…,g_m) ⇒ A⊗_B B′ = B′[x_1,…,x_n]/(g_1,…,g_m). Flatness: for an injection N′ ↪ N of B′-modules, N′⊗_{B′}(B′⊗_B A) ≅ N′⊗_B A ↪ N⊗_B A ≅ N⊗_{B′}(B′⊗_B A), using that A is B-flat (the isomorphism is n′⊗(b′⊗a) ↦ n′b′ ⊗_B a, inverse n′⊗a ↦ n′⊗(1⊗a)). Differentials: F4 gives Ω_{(A⊗_B B′)/B′} ≅ (A⊗_B B′)⊗_A Ω_{A/B} = 0. (ii) Flatness is transitive. Finite presentation is transitive: with C = S[y_1,…,y_n]/(f_1,…,f_p) and A = C[z_1,…,z_m]/(g_1,…,g_q), choose lifts G_k ∈ S[y,z] of g_k; then A = S[y,z]/(f_1,…,f_p,G_1,…,G_q), for if H maps to 0 in A then in C[z] we have H̄ = Σ h̄_k g_k, lift h̄_k to H_k, and H − Σ H_k G_k maps to 0 in C[z], hence lies in (f_1,…,f_p). Differentials: F5 gives A⊗_C Ω_{C/S} → Ω_{A/S} → Ω_{A/C} → 0 with both outer terms 0. ∎

F7 (faithfully flat criterion). Let M be a flat R-module with M ⊗_R κ(𝔭) ≠ 0 for every 𝔭 ∈ Spec R. Then for every R-module N, M ⊗_R N = 0 ⇒ N = 0.
Proof. If N ≠ 0, choose 0 ≠ x ∈ N and a maximal ideal 𝔪 of Ann(x) ⊊ R; then 𝔪 is prime and N_𝔪 ≠ 0. Pick 0 ≠ y ∈ N_𝔪, I := Ann_{R_𝔪}(y) ⊊ R_𝔪, so I ⊂ 𝔪R_𝔪 and R_𝔪/I embeds into N_𝔪. Flatness of M_𝔪 gives an injection M_𝔪/IM_𝔪 = M_𝔪⊗_{R_𝔪}(R_𝔪/I) ↪ M_𝔪⊗_{R_𝔪}N_𝔪. Since I ⊂ 𝔪R_𝔪, the quotient M_𝔪/IM_𝔪 surjects onto M_𝔪⊗_{R_𝔪}κ(𝔪), and M_𝔪⊗_{R_𝔪}κ(𝔪) = S^{−1}(M⊗_R κ(𝔪)) = M⊗_Rκ(𝔪) ≠ 0 because S = R∖𝔪 acts invertibly on the κ(𝔪)-vector space M⊗_Rκ(𝔪). Hence (M⊗_R N)_𝔪 ≠ 0, so M⊗_R N ≠ 0. ∎

F8. Every nonzero unital ring has a maximal ideal (Zorn's lemma).

=====================================================================
PART 1 — STEP 1: A RETRACTION OF AN ÉTALE MAP
=====================================================================

Let R → C be étale with structure map ι: R → C, and let ρ: C → R be an R-algebra map with ρ∘ι = id_R. Put I := ker ρ.

(1a) Presentation of I. Write C = R[X_1,…,X_n]/(h_1,…,h_m) (possible: finite presentation). Let r_i := ρ(x_i) ∈ R and y_i := x_i − ι(r_i) ∈ I. Then I = (y_1,…,y_n): for c = P(x) ∈ C one has c − ι(ρ(c)) = P(x) − P(r) ∈ (y_1,…,y_n), since P(X) − P(r) lies in the ideal (X_i − r_i) of R[X] (identity P(X) − P(r) = Σ_i (X_i − r_i)Q_i(X,r)). Also, since ρ is an R-algebra map and h_j(x) = 0,
  h_j(r_1,…,r_n) = ρ(h_j(x)) = 0  in R  for every j.   (∗)

(1b) I = I². By F2, Ω_{C/R} = 0 means there are λ_{ij} ∈ C with Σ_j λ_{ij} a_{ji'} = δ_{ii'} for all i,i', where a_{ji} = (∂h_j/∂X_i)(x). Put b_{ji} := (∂h_j/∂X_i)(r) ∈ R. F3 applied to h_j at the point r gives in R[X]
  h_j = h_j(r) + Σ_i b_{ji}(X_i − r_i) + Σ_{|α|≥2} c_{jα}(X−r)^α.
Evaluating X_i ↦ x_i in C, and using h_j(x) = 0 together with (∗):
  Σ_i b_{ji} y_i = − Σ_{|α|≥2} c_{jα}(x−r)^α ∈ I²   for every j,            (†)
as each monomial (x−r)^α with |α| ≥ 2 is a product of at least two of the generators y_i of I. Applying ρ to Σ_j λ_{ij}a_{ji'} = δ_{ii'} and using that ρ is an R-algebra homomorphism, so ρ(a_{ji'}) = (∂h_j/∂X_{i'})(ρ(x_1),…,ρ(x_n)) = b_{ji'}, we obtain, with λ̄_{ij} := ρ(λ_{ij}) ∈ R,
  Σ_j λ̄_{ij} b_{ji'} = δ_{ii'}  in R  for all i,i'.
Therefore, using (†),
  y_i = Σ_{i'} δ_{ii'} y_{i'} = Σ_{i'} (Σ_j λ̄_{ij} b_{ji'}) y_{i'} = Σ_j λ̄_{ij} (Σ_{i'} b_{ji'} y_{i'}) ∈ I²,
so I = I².

(1c) Conclusion. By (1a) and F1, I = (t) with t² = t. Then C ≅ R × I as R-algebras via c ↦ (ρ(c), c − ιρ(c)) with inverse (r,x) ↦ ι(r)+x: indeed I is a ring with unit t (for x = ct ∈ I, xt = ct² = ct = x), and ι(r)ι(r′)+ι(r)x′+ι(r′)x+xx′ multiplies to (rr′, xx′+rx′+r′x). In particular C/(t) ≅ R through ρ.

(1d) ρ is itself étale. Let e := 1 − t; then ρ(e) = 1. In C[1/e] we have t/1 = 0 because te = 0 and e is invertible, so C[1/e] ≅ C/(t) ≅ R as C-algebras, and this C-algebra is exactly ρ: C → R. The map C → C[1/e] is étale: C[1/e] ≅ C[T]/(eT−1) is of finite presentation, is flat (localisation), and Ω_{C[1/e]/C} = C[1/e]·dT/(e·dT) = 0 since e is a unit there. Hence ρ: C → R is étale. ∎

=====================================================================
PART 2 — STEP 2: f IS ÉTALE
=====================================================================

Assume first S ≠ 0 (the case S = 0 is disposed of in Part 6). Set C := A ⊗_B S, and define
  σ: A → C,  a ↦ a⊗1        (A-algebra structure on C, first factor),
  ρ: C → A,  a⊗s ↦ a·f(s)   (A-linear for σ, since ρ((aa_1)⊗s) = aa_1f(s) = aρ(a_1⊗s)),
so ρ∘σ = id_A because ρ(a⊗1) = a f(1) = a.

• C is étale over A: it is the base change along B → A of the étale B-algebra S, by F6(i).
• By Step 1 (1d) applied with R = A, ρ: C → A is étale (and ker ρ = (t), C ≅ A × tC as A-algebras).
• σ_S: S → C, s ↦ 1⊗s, is étale: it is the base change along B → S of the étale B-algebra A, by F6(i).
• f = ρ ∘ σ_S, since ρ(σ_S(s)) = ρ(1⊗s) = f(s).
By F6(ii), f: S → A is étale. Thus A is flat over S, of finite presentation over S, and Ω_{A/S} = 0.

=====================================================================
PART 3 — STEP 3: FIBRES OVER Spec S
=====================================================================

Let s ∈ Spec S and p := s ∩ B. There is a natural map S⊗_B κ(p) → κ(s), hence κ(s) is an (S⊗_B κ(p))-algebra. We compute A⊗_S κ(s). First, the A⊗_S(S⊗_Bκ(p))-algebra A⊗_Bκ(p) are isomorphic: the map a⊗(s⊗c) ↦ a f(s) ⊗ c is well defined (S-balanced: a f(s)⊗(s′⊗c) ↦ a f(ss′)⊗c and aa′…) with inverse a⊗c ↦ a⊗(1⊗c), which is B-balanced because (ab)⊗c ↦ ab⊗(1⊗c) = a⊗(b⊗c) = a⊗(1⊗bc) = a⊗(1⊗bc) ↦ a⊗bc. Hence, by associativity of ⊗,
  A⊗_S κ(s) ≅ (A⊗_B κ(p)) ⊗_{S⊗_B κ(p)} κ(s).                              (‡)
Under (‡) the map induced by f is f_p ⊗ id. By hypothesis f_p: S⊗_Bκ(p) → A⊗_Bκ(p) is an isomorphism of S⊗_Bκ(p)-ALGEBRAS (it is a ring map and f_p((s⊗c)(a⊗c′)) = f_p(sa⊗cc′) = f(s)a⊗cc′ = (s⊗c)f_p(a⊗c′)), so base change along S⊗_Bκ(p) → κ(s) is an isomorphism
  θ_s: A⊗_S κ(s) ≅ (S⊗_Bκ(p)) ⊗_{S⊗_Bκ(p)} κ(s) = κ(s),
which is a κ(s)-algebra map for the structure on A⊗_Sκ(s) through the second factor.

Consequences.
(i) A⊗_S κ(s) ≠ 0 for all s ∈ Spec S. Together with the flatness of A over S (Part 2), F7 says A is FAITHFULLY FLAT over S: for every S-module N, A⊗_S N = 0 ⇒ N = 0.
(ii) Spec(A⊗_Sκ(s)) = Spec κ(s) is a single point; hence over each s there is exactly one s′ ∈ Spec A, and its residue field satisfies κ(s′) = κ(s). Consequently, for every s′ ∈ Spec A, using (‡)-type associativity and (i)-type computation,
  A⊗_S κ(s′) ≅ (A⊗_S κ(s)) ⊗_{κ(s)} κ(s′) ≅ κ(s) ⊗_{κ(s)} κ(s′) = κ(s′),
and this composite θ_{s′} is a κ(s′)-algebra isomorphism (structure through the second factor).

=====================================================================
PART 4 — STEP 4: THE MULTIPLICATION MAP μ: A⊗_S A → A IS AN ISOMORPHISM
=====================================================================

Let C′ := A ⊗_S A, with A-algebra structure σ′: A → C′, a ↦ a⊗1 (first factor), and μ: C′ → A, a⊗b ↦ ab. Then μ is an A-algebra map and μ∘σ′ = id_A. By Part 2, A is étale over S, so C′ = A ⊗_{S,f} A is étale over A by F6(i) (base change of the S-algebra A along f: S → A). Step 1 applies with R = A: ker μ = (t′) with t′² = t′, and C′ ≅ A × D′ as A-algebras, where D′ := t′C′ (unit t′).

Fix s′ ∈ Spec A and form C′ ⊗_{A,1} κ(s′). The map
  Φ: C′⊗_{A,1}κ(s′) → A⊗_Sκ(s′),   (a⊗b)⊗λ ↦ b ⊗ āλ     (ā = image of a in κ(s′))
is a well-defined isomorphism: A-balanced since ((aα)⊗b)⊗λ ↦ b⊗āα̅λ and (a⊗b)⊗α̅λ ↦ b⊗āα̅λ; S-balanced since (a⊗f(s)b)⊗λ ↦ f(s)b⊗āλ = b⊗ s̅ ā λ and (af(s)⊗b)⊗λ ↦ b⊗ ā s̅ λ (the S-module structure on κ(s′) is S → A → κ(s′)). Its inverse is b⊗μ ↦ (1⊗b)⊗μ. Moreover
  (μ⊗id)((a⊗b)⊗λ) = (ab)̅ λ = m(b⊗āλ) = (m∘Φ)((a⊗b)⊗λ),
where m: A⊗_Sκ(s′) → κ(s′), c⊗λ ↦ c̅λ, is the multiplication map. Both m and θ_{s′} (Part 3(ii)) are κ(s′)-ALGEBRA homomorphisms A⊗_Sκ(s′) → κ(s′) (each sends 1⊗λ to λ). Hence m∘θ_{s′}^{−1} is a κ(s′)-algebra endomorphism of the field κ(s′), i.e. the identity; so m = θ_{s′} is an isomorphism, and therefore μ⊗id = m∘Φ is an isomorphism.
