(d) The map $i:W\to U$ is a $k$-linear isomorphism (Step 1) satisfying $(T|_U)\circ i=i\circ S$; by lemma_8, semisimplicity transfers along such an intertwining isomorphism, so $S$ is semisimple. (Note that $S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ is part of the hypotheses, so $T|_U\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ as required by lemma_145 is consistent: indeed $r\circ T=S\circ r$ also shows $\ker r$ is $T$-stable, so $T$ is the direct sum of $T|_U$ and $T|_{\ker r}$.)

Both proofs are complete; either alone establishes the lemma. In the intended application (Frobenius semisimplicity), $V$ is a cohomology group of a variety, $W$ that of another, $T,S$ the Frobenius automorphisms, and $i,r$ a pullback/trace pair with $r\circ i=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ for a degree $d\neq0$: after dividing $i$ (or $r$) by $d$, exactly the hypotheses proved above hold, so semisimplicity passes to Frobenius-equivariant direct summands.

lemma_155.statement: Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{End}_k(V)\) be an endomorphism whose characteristic polynomial \(\chi_T\in k[t]\) is squarefree, that is, is not divisible by the square of any nonconstant polynomial in \(k[t]\). Then \(T\) is semisimple: its minimal polynomial \(\mu_T\) is squarefree in \(k[t]\), and \(T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalisable on \(V\otimes_k\bar k\). In particular, for a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space and \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), squarefreeness of the characteristic polynomial implies semisimplicity of \(T\), of \(T^{-1}\), and of \(cT\) for every \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\,*}\).
lemma_155.proof:
Throughout, a nonzero polynomial is called *squarefree* if it is not divisible by the square of any nonconstant polynomial. Since $k[t]$ is a unique factorisation domain, for a polynomial of positive degree this is equivalent to saying that no monic irreducible factor occurs with multiplicity $\ge 2$.

**Step 0 (the derivative criterion in characteristic $0$, and its stability under field extension).** Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $f\in K[t]$ have $\deg f\ge 1$, and let $f'$ be the formal derivative. Then
$$f\text{ squarefree in }K[t]\iff \gcd(f,f')=1. \qquad (\dagger)$$
Proof of $(\dagger)$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $f=g^2h$ with $g$ nonconstant, take a monic irreducible $p\mid g$; then $f'=2gg'h+g^2h'$ is divisible by $p$, and so is $f$, hence $p\mid\gcd(f,f')$, contradiction. ($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $d=\gcd(f,f')$ is nonconstant and let $p$ be a monic irreducible divisor of $d$. Write $f=p^{m}u$ with $m\ge1$ and $p\nmid u$. Then $f'=p^{m-1}\big(m\,p'u+pu'\big)$. If $m\ge2$ then $p^2\mid f$, contradicting squarefreeness, so $m=1$; but $p\mid f'=p'u+pu'$ and $p\nmid u$ force $p\mid p'$ by Euclid's lemma. In characteristic $0$, $p'\neq0$ and $\deg p'=\deg p-1<\deg p$ (the leading term $a_dt^{d}$ of $p$, $d\ge1$, gives $p'=da_dt^{d-1}+\cdots$ with $da_d\neq0$), so $p\nmid p'$, a contradiction. Hence $d$ is constant, proving $(\dagger)$.

Because $K[t]$ is Euclidean, $\gcd(f,f')=1$ is equivalent to the existence of a Bézout identity $af+bf'=1$ with $a,b\in K[t]$. Such an identity remains valid in $L[t]$ for every extension $L/K$. We record:
$$\text{if }f\in K[t]\text{ is squarefree and }K\text{ has characteristic }0,\text{ then }f\text{ is squarefree in }L[t]\ (\ast)$$
for every extension field $L/K$: indeed $(\dagger)$ gives $af+bf'=1$ in $K[t]$, hence in $L[t]$, so $\gcd(f,f')=1$ in $L[t]$ (any common divisor divides $1$), and $(\dagger)$ over $L$ (valid since $\mathrm{char}\,L=0$) gives squarefreeness in $L[t]$.

**Step 1: $\mu_T$ is squarefree in $k[t]$.** If $V=0$ then $\chi_T=1$ is squarefree, $\mu_T=1$ is squarefree, and $V\otimes_k\bar k=0$ is trivially diagonalisable; assume from now on $n:=\dim_kV\ge1$. By the Cayley--Hamilton theorem $\chi_T(T)=0$. The set $\mathfrak a:=\{f\in k[t]:f(T)=0\}$ is an ideal of $k[t]$: it is clearly an additive subgroup and $f(T)=0\Rightarrow (hf)(T)=h(T)f(T)=0$. Its monic generator is $\mu_T$: for $f\in\mathfrak a$ write $f=q\mu_T+r$ with $\deg r<\deg\mu_T$; then $r(T)=f(T)-q(T)\mu_T(T)=0$, so minimality of $\mu_T$ forces $r=0$. Thus $\mathfrak a=(\mu_T)$ and, as $\chi_T\in\mathfrak a$, $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$. If $\mu_T$ were divisible by $g^2$ for some nonconstant $g$, then so would $\chi_T$ be; since $\chi_T$ is squarefree, $\mu_T$ is squarefree. (Also $\deg\mu_T\ge1$, for $\mu_T=1$ would give $\mathrm{id}_V=0$, i.e. $V=0$.)

**Step 2: primary decomposition; $T$ is semisimple as a $k[t]$-module.** By Step 1 we can write $\mu_T=p_1\cdots p_r$ with the $p_i$ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles ($r\ge1$). The ideals $(p_i)$ are pairwise comaximal, since for $i\ne j$ the sum $(p_i)+(p_j)$ is an ideal strictly containing the maximal ideal... more elementarily, $p_i,p_j$ are coprime in the PID $k[t]$, so $(p_i)+(p_j)=k[t]$. By the Chinese remainder theorem there are polynomials $q_1,\dots,q_r\in k[t]$ with $q_i\equiv1\pmod{p_i}$ and $q_i\equiv0\pmod{p_j}$ for all $j\ne i$. Set $e_i:=q_i(T)\in\mathrm{End}_k(V)$ and $W_i:=\mathrm{im}(e_i)$.

*The $e_i$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents summing to the identity.* For $i\ne j$, $q_iq_j$ is divisible by every $p_\nu$, hence by $\mu_T$, so $e_ie_j=q_i(T)q_j(T)=0$. Also $\sum_i q_i\equiv1\pmod{p_i}$ for every $i$, hence $\sum_iq_i-1\in(\mu_T)$ and $\sum_ie_i=\mathrm{id}_V$; taking $i=j$ above gives $e_i^2=e_i$.

*The $W_i$ are $T$-stable, and $V=\bigoplus_iW_i$.* Each $e_i$ is a polynomial in $T$, so $T$ commutes with $e_i$ and $\mathrm{im}(e_i)$ is $T$-stable. Every $v=\sum_ie_iv$ lies in $\sum_iW_i$; if $w_i\in W_i$ and $\sum_iw_i=0$, applying $e_j$ gives $w_j=0$.

*Each $W_i$ is nonzero and $\mu_{T|W_i}=p_i$.* Since $p_iq_i$ is divisible by $p_\nu$ for every $\nu$, $p_iq_i\in(\mu_T)$, so $p_i(T)e_i=0$; thus $p_i(T)|_{W_i}=0$ and $\mu_{T|W_i}\mid p_i$. If $W_i=0$ then $e_i=0$, so $\mathrm{id}_V=\sum_{j\ne i}e_j$. Put $m=\prod_{j\ne i}p_j$ (the empty product $1$ if $r=1$). For $j\ne i$, $m$ is divisible by $p_j$, so $m(T)e_j=0$ because $p_j(T)e_j=0$; hence $m(T)=m(T)\mathrm{id}_V=\sum_{j\ne i}m(T)e_j=0$. But $m$ is a proper monic divisor of $\mu_T$ (or $m=1$, which would give $\mathrm{id}_V=0$, impossible as $V\ne0$), contradicting the minimality of $\mu_T$. So $W_i\ne0$ and $\mu_{T|W_i}=p_i$.

*Simple-module decomposition.* The $k[t]$-action on $W_i$ factors through the field $K_i:=k[t]/(p_i)$, and the $K_i$-scalar multiplication is given by polynomials in $T|_{W_i}$; consequently the $k[t]$-submodules of $W_i$ are exactly the $T|_{W_i}$-stable $k$-subspaces, which are exactly the $K_i$-subspaces. Choosing a $K_i$-basis of $W_i$ exhibits $W_i\cong K_i^{\oplus m_i}$ as $k[t]$-module, a direct sum of simple $k[t]$-modules. Hence $V\cong\bigoplus_iK_i^{\oplus m_i}$ is a semisimple $k[t]$-module: $T$ is semisimple.

**Step 3: $\bar T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable on $\bar V:=V\otimes_k\bar k$.** Since $\mu_T(T)=0$, applying $-\otimes_k\bar k$ gives $\mu_T(\bar T)=\mu_T(T)\otimes\mathrm{id}=0$; therefore the minimal polynomial $\mu_{\bar T}\in\bar k[t]$ divides $\mu_T$. By Step 1, $\mu_T$ is squarefree in $k[t]$, and by $(\ast)$ (with $K=k$, $L=\bar k$; $k$ has characteristic $0$, so $\bar k$ too) $\mu_T$ is squarefree in $\bar k[t]$. A divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree, so $\mu_{\bar T}$ is squarefree. As $\bar k$ is algebraically closed, $\mu_{\bar T}=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(t-\lambda_i)$ with $\lambda_i\in\bar k$ pairwise distinct ($s\ge1$ because $\bar V\ne0$). We repeat the argument of Step 2 over $\bar k$: let $\rho_i(t):=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{t-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}$, so $\rho_i\equiv1\pmod{t-\lambda_i}$ and $\rho_i\equiv0\pmod{t-\lambda_j}$ for $j\ne i$. Then $\Pi_i:=\rho_i(\bar T)$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_i\Pi_i=\mathrm{id}_{\bar V}$, and $(\bar T-\lambda_i)\Pi_i=0$ because $(t-\lambda_i)\rho_i\in(\mu_{\bar T})$. Thus $\mathrm{im}(\Pi_i)\subseteq\ker(\bar T-\lambda_i)$. Conversely, if $\bar Tv=\lambda_iv$ then $\rho_j(\bar T)v=\rho_j(\lambda_i)v=\delta_{ij}v$, so $v=\Pi_iv\in\mathrm{im}(\Pi_i)$. Hence $\mathrm{im}(\Pi_i)=\ker(\bar T-\lambda_i)$ and $\bar V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}\ker(\bar T-\lambda_i)$: $\bar T$ is diagonalisable. Steps 1--3 prove the main assertion.

**Step 4: the $\mathbb Q_\ell$ case.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and suppose $\chi_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ is squarefree. Since $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q_\ell=0$, Steps 1--3 applied to $T$ show $\mu_T$ is squarefree, $T$ is semisimple, and $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. It remains to treat $cT$ ($c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{*}$) and $T^{-1}$; we check that their characteristic polynomials are squarefree and then apply Steps 1--3 again.

*(a) $cT$.* With $n=\dim V$ and $\chi_T(t)=\sum_{j=0}^na_jt^j$ ($a_n=1$),
$$\chi_{cT}(t)=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}-cT)=c^{\,n}\det(c^{-1}t\,\mathrm{id}-T)=c^{\,n}\chi_T(c^{-1}t),$$
using $\det(cA)=c^{n}\det A$. If $\chi_{cT}=g^{2}h$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ with $g$ nonconstant, then $\chi_T(t)=c^{-n}\chi_{cT}(ct)=c^{-n}g(ct)^{2}h(ct)$, and $g(ct)$ is nonconstant of degree $\deg g\ge1$, contradicting squarefreeness of $\chi_T$. Hence $\chi_{cT}$ is squarefree; since $c\ne0$ and $T$ is invertible, $cT\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and Steps 1--3 give semisimplicity of $cT$ (and diagonalisability of $(cT)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$).

*(b) $T^{-1}$.* First, $a_0=\chi_T(0)=\det(-T)=(-1)^n\det T\ne0$. For $t\ne0$,
$$\det(\mathrm{id}-tT)=t^{n}\det(t^{-1}\mathrm{id}-T)=t^{n}\chi_T(t^{-1}),$$
and both sides are polynomials in $t$: writing $\chi_T(t)=\sum_j a_jt^j$, the right side is $\chi_T^{*}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}a_jt^{n-j}$, which involves no negative powers. Since $\mathbb Q_\ell^{*}$ is infinite, the two polynomials agree identically. Now
$$\chi_{T^{-1}}(t)=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}-T^{-1})=\det(T^{-1})\det(tT-\mathrm{id})=(-1)^n(\det T)^{-1}\det(\mathrm{id}-tT)=(-1)^n(\det T)^{-1}\chi_T^{*}(t).$$
It suffices to prove $\chi_T^{*}$ squarefree. Factor $\chi_T(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(t-\lambda_i)$ in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$; by $(\ast)$, $\chi_T$ is squarefree over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, so the $\lambda_i$ are pairwise distinct, and $a_0=(-1)^n\prod_i\lambda_i\ne0$ shows every $\lambda_i\ne0$. Then
$$\chi_T^{*}(t)=t^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(t^{-1}-\lambda_i\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-\lambda_it)=\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n(-\lambda_i)\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(t-\lambda_i^{-1}\bigr)=a_0\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(t-\lambda_i^{-1}\bigr),$$
whose roots $\lambda_i^{-1}$ are pairwise distinct. So $\chi_T^{*}$ has no repeated root in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, hence is squarefree in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$, and therefore squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ (a factorisation $\chi_T^{*}=g^2h$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ with $g$ nonconstant would also be one in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$). Being a nonzero scalar multiple of $\chi_T^{*}$, the polynomial $\chi_{T^{-1}}$ is squarefree, and Steps 1--3 applied to $T^{-1}\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ give its semisimplicity and the diagonalisability of $T^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

This completes the proof of all the claims: squarefreeness of $\chi_T$ over a characteristic-$0$ field forces $\mu_T$ to be squarefree and $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ to be diagonalisable over an algebraic closure, and over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ the same holds for $T$, $T^{-1}$ and $cT$ ($c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{*}$).

lemma_159.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\), and let \(b:V\times W\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be a perfect bilinear pairing. If there exists a scalar \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) such that \(b(Tv,Sw)=c\,b(v,w)\) for all \(v\in V\) and \(w\in W\), then \(T\) is semisimple if and only if \(S\) is semisimple.
lemma_159.proof:
Let $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\bar K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; all vector spaces are finite-dimensional over $K$. For a $K$-vector space $X$ and an endomorphism $A$ of $X$, write $A^\vee:X^\vee\to X^\vee$, $\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ A$, for the dual (transpose) endomorphism.

**Step 0 (criterion for semisimplicity that we use).** Following the convention of the provided lemmas (cf. the parenthetical definition in lemma_147 and the formulation of lemma_155), an operator $A\in\mathrm{GL}(X)$ is *semisimple* iff its minimal polynomial $\mu_A\in K[t]$ is squarefree; by lemma_5 this is equivalent to $A\otimes\mathrm{id}$ being diagonalisable on $X\otimes_K\bar K$. For completeness, here is the justification of the equivalence of these two conditions: $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$, so $\mu_A$ is squarefree iff $\gcd(\mu_A,\mu_A')=1$ in $K[t]$; the Euclidean algorithm computing this gcd is unchanged by the flat extension $K[t]\hookrightarrow\bar K[t]$, so $\mu_A$ is squarefree over $K$ iff it has no repeated root in $\bar K$; and over the algebraically closed field $\bar K$, the operator is diagonalisable iff its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct linear factors (primary decomposition of the $\bar K[t]$-module $X\otimes\bar K$). We shall therefore prove the statement by comparing minimal polynomials.

If $\dim V=0$, the existence of a perfect pairing forces $\dim W=0$, and $T$ and $S$ are both the identity of the zero space, whose minimal polynomial is $1$; both are semisimple and the claim is trivial. We may suppose $\dim V\ge 1$ (in fact every computation below is also valid in dimension $0$).

**Step 1 (the isomorphisms attached to $b$).** Define $K$-linear maps
$$\psi:W\longrightarrow V^\vee,\qquad \psi(w)=b(-,w),\qquad\qquad \chi:V\longrightarrow W^\vee,\qquad \chi(v)=b(v,-).$$
Both are isomorphisms. Indeed, if \"perfect\" is taken to mean precisely that these two maps are isomorphisms there is nothing to prove; if instead it means non-degeneracy on both sides, then $\psi$ is injective (if $\psi(w)=0$ then $b(v,w)=0$ for all $v$, hence $w=0$) and $\chi$ is injective, so $\dim W\le\dim V$ and $\dim V\le\dim W$; thus $\dim V=\dim W=:n$ and both maps are isomorphisms by a dimension count.

**Step 2 (rewriting the hypothesis as an intertwining identity).** For all $v\in V$, $w\in W$,
$$(T^\vee\circ\psi\circ S)(w)(v)\;=\;\big(T^\vee(\psi(Sw))\big)(v)\;=\;\psi(Sw)(Tv)\;=\;b(Tv,Sw)\;=\;c\,b(v,w)\;=\;c\,\psi(w)(v),$$
where the fourth equality is exactly the hypothesis on $b$. Since this holds for every $v$, $T^\vee\circ\psi\circ S=c\,\psi$ as maps $W\to V^\vee$.

Because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the dual $T^\vee$ is invertible with inverse $(T^{-1})^\vee$: using $(B\circ C)^\vee=C^\vee\circ B^\vee$, one gets $T^\vee\circ(T^{-1})^\vee=(T^{-1}\circ T)^\vee=\mathrm{id}$ and likewise in the other order. Composing the identity $T^\vee\psi S=c\psi$ on the left by $(T^\vee)^{-1}$ (the scalar $c$ commutes with everything) gives
$$\psi\circ S=c\,(T^\vee)^{-1}\circ\psi.\tag{$*$}$$
Equivalently, composing on the left by $\psi^{-1}$,
$$S=c\,\psi^{-1}(T^\vee)^{-1}\psi,\qquad\text{and}\qquad (T^\vee)^{-1}=c^{-1}\psi S\psi^{-1},$$
the latter using $c\in K^{\times}$.

**Step 3 (four elementary facts about semisimplicity).**

*(F1) Conjugate operators.* Let $\alpha:X\to Y$ be a $K$-linear isomorphism with $\alpha A=B\alpha$. Then inductively $\alpha A^{k}=B^{k}\alpha$ for all $k\ge0$ (since $\alpha A^{k+1}=(\alpha A^{k})A=B^{k}\alpha A=B^{k+1}\alpha$), hence $\alpha\,p(A)=p(B)\,\alpha$ for every $p\in K[t]$. As $\alpha$ is invertible, $p(A)=0\iff p(B)=0$, so the two operators have the same annihilator ideal and therefore the same monic generator $\mu_A=\mu_B$. Thus $A$ is semisimple iff $B$ is. (This is exactly the content of lemma_8, which we cite; the argument is repeated for completeness.)

*(F2) Inverses.* For $A\in\mathrm{GL}(X)$, $A$ is semisimple iff $A^{-1}$ is: this is lemma_4. Concretely, $\mu_A(0)\ne0$ (otherwise $\mu_A=t\,\nu$ and $0=\mu_A(A)=A\nu(A)$ would force $\nu(A)=0$ since $A$ is invertible, contradicting minimality); and with $d=\deg\mu_A$ the reciprocal polynomial $\mu_A^{*}(t):=\mu_A(0)^{-1}t^{d}\mu_A(1/t)$ is monic of degree $d$ and satisfies $\mu_A^{*}(A^{-1})=\mu_A(0)^{-1}A^{-d}\mu_A(A)=0$. The correspondence $p\mapsto p^{*}$ is an involution on monic polynomials with nonzero constant term, so $\mu_{A^{-1}}=\mu_A^{*}$; the roots of $\mu_A^{*}$ in $\bar K$ are the inverses of those of $\mu_A$, so $\mu_A^{*}$ is squarefree iff $\mu_A$ is.

*(F3) Nonzero scalar multiples.* Let $c\in K^{\times}$ and $A\in\mathrm{GL}(X)$. Then $A$ is semisimple iff $cA$ is. Write $\mu_A(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_it^{i}$ with $a_d=1$, and set $\nu(t):=c^{d}\mu_A(c^{-1}t)=\sum_i a_ic^{d-i}t^{i}$, which is monic of degree $d$. Then $\nu(cA)=c^{d}\mu_A(A)=0$, so $\mu_{cA}\mid\nu$ and $e:=\deg\mu_{cA}\le d$. Conversely, for a monic $p(t)=\sum_i b_it^{i}$ of degree $e$ put $p^{\natural}(t):=c^{-e}p(ct)=\sum_i b_ic^{i-e}t^{i}$, monic of degree $e$; then $\mu_{cA}^{\natural}(A)=c^{-e}\mu_{cA}(cA)=0$, so $\mu_A\mid\mu_{cA}^{\natural}$ and $d\le e$. Hence $d=e$ and, as monic divisors of the same degree, $\mu_{cA}=\nu$. Finally, $t\mapsto c^{-1}t$ induces a $K$-algebra automorphism $\sigma$ of $K[t]$ (inverse: $t\mapsto ct$), and $\sigma(\mu_A)=c^{-d}\nu$, $\sigma(\mu_A')=c^{1-d}\nu'$ because $\nu'(t)=c^{d-1}\mu_A'(c^{-1}t)$. Automorphisms preserve coprimeness up to units, so $\gcd(\mu_A,\mu_A')=1\iff\gcd(\nu,\nu')=1$. Thus $\mu_A$ is squarefree iff $\mu_{cA}$ is.

*(F4) Duals.* $\mu_{A^\vee}=\mu_A$, hence $A$ is semisimple iff $A^\vee$ is. Indeed, $(A^{\vee})^{k}=(A^{k})^{\vee}$ for all $k\ge1$ (induction using $(B\circ C)^\vee=C^\vee\circ B^\vee$), so for every $p(t)=\sum a_it^{i}\in K[t]$,
$$p(A^\vee)=\textstyle\sum_i a_i (A^{i})^{\vee}=\big(\sum_i a_iA^{i}\big)^{\vee}=p(A)^{\vee}.$$
A linear map $L$ is zero iff its dual $L^\vee$ is zero: if $L\ne0$ pick $x$ with $Lx\ne0$, extend $Lx$ to a basis of $X$ and choose $\varphi\in X^\vee$ with $\varphi(Lx)=1$, so $L^\vee\varphi=\varphi\circ L\ne0$; the converse is immediate. Hence $p(A)=0\iff p(A^\vee)=0$, the annihilator ideals coincide, and their monic generators are equal: $\mu_{A^\vee}=\mu_A$.

**Step 4 (conclusion).** Applying the four facts in sequence to $A=T$ we obtain a chain of equivalences:
$$T\ \text{semisimple}\;\overset{(\mathrm{F4})}{\Longleftrightarrow}\;T^\vee\ \text{semisimple}\;\overset{(\mathrm{F2})}{\Longleftrightarrow}\;(T^\vee)^{-1}\ \text{semisimple}\;\overset{(\mathrm{F3})}{\Longleftrightarrow}\;c\,(T^\vee)^{-1}\ \text{semisimple}\;\overset{(\mathrm{F1})}{\Longleftrightarrow}\;S\ \text{semisimple},$$
where the last equivalence is (F1) — equivalently lemma_8 — applied to the isomorphism $\psi:W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^\vee$ and the intertwining relation $(*)$: $\psi\circ S=\big(c(T^\vee)^{-1}\big)\circ\psi$, both operators being invertible ($c(T^\vee)^{-1}$ because $c\ne0$ and $T^\vee$ is invertible). Reading the chain left-to-right gives \"$T$ semisimple $\Rightarrow$ $S$ semisimple\"; reading it right-to-left gives the converse. (Concretely, for the converse one may also argue directly from $(T^\vee)^{-1}=c^{-1}\psi S\psi^{-1}$: by (F1) $c^{-1}S$ is semisimple, by (F3) so is $S$, by (F2) so is $S^{-1}$, by (F1) so is $c^{-1}\psi S^{-1}\psi^{-1}=(T^\vee)^{-1}$... which is the same chain reversed.) This proves the lemma.

**Step 5 (consistency check / interpretation).** Suppose $T$ is semisimple, and let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\in\bar K^{\times}$ be its eigenvalues with multiplicity. Then $T^\vee\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $V^\vee\otimes\bar K$ is diagonalisable with the same eigenvalues (the dual basis of eigenfunctionals), $(T^\vee)^{-1}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^{-1}$, and by $(*)$ the operator $S$, being conjugate over $K$ to $c(T^\vee)^{-1}$, is diagonalisable over $\bar K$ with eigenvalues $c\lambda_1^{-1},\dots,c\lambda_n^{-1}$. This is exactly the forward implication, and lemma_5 identifies it with semisimplicity; the reverse implication is the same statement with the roles of $T$ and $S$ exchanged through the relation $T^\vee=c\,\psi S^{-1}\psi^{-1}$ obtained from $(*)$ by inverting both sides.

lemma_158.statement: Let \(q=p^{a}\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_{q}\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^{*}\), \(\sigma(u)=u^{q}\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let \(j\ge 0\), let \(m\ge 1\), and suppose that \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell}(j))\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\) by the cycle classes \(\mathrm{cl}(z)\) of codimension-\(j\) cycles \(z\) on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m}}}\) that are defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m}}\). Then \(F^{m}\) acts as the identity on \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell}(j))\), and \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell}(j))\) and on \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\).
lemma_158.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_158",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_45_finite_frob"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_6a"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_5"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Notation. Write $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(u)=u^q$, and $F_{X,k}^{(r)}:=\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^r:X_k\to X_k$, so that $F=(F_{X,k}^{(1)})^*$ and, by functoriality of pullback and $\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma\circ\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma=\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^2$, one has $F^r=(F_{X,k}^{(r)})^*$ for all $r\ge1$ (the same formula on cohomology with coefficients in any lisse sheaf defined over $\mathbb F_q$, using its Weil structure). Put
\[ V:=H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)),\]
and denote by $F_V,F_W$ the restrictions of $F$ to these spaces.

STEP 0 (finite dimensionality). $X$ is projective, hence proper over $\mathbb F_q$. The sheaves $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ on $X_k$ are lisse of rank $1$, hence belong to $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and each carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism ($\psi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $\psi_j$ below). By lemma_45_finite_frob, $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By lemma_6a (and the identical argument for the coefficients $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, since $F_{X,k}$ is an isomorphism of schemes with inverse $\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1}$) $F_V$ and $F_W$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms.

STEP 1 ($F^m=\mathrm{id}$ on $W$). Let $z$ be a codimension-$j$ cycle on $X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ which is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, and let $\pi:X_k=X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\to X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}=X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^m}$ be the projection. The class $\mathrm{cl}(z)$ is defined as $\pi^*\mathrm{cl}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}(z)$ where $\mathrm{cl}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}(z)\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}},\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$; this is exactly the meaning of the hypothesis, since on the level of cycles $\pi^*z=z$. The morphism $F_{X,k}^{(m)}=\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^m$ satisfies $\pi\circ F_{X,k}^{(m)}=\pi$: on the second factor this says that the two inclusions $\mathbb F_{q^m}\hookrightarrow k$, namely $a\mapsto a$ and $a\mapsto a^{q^m}$, agree, which is true because every element of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ is fixed by $u\mapsto u^{q^m}$. Hence, by contravariance of pullback,
\[ F^m\,\mathrm{cl}(z)=(F_{X,k}^{(m)})^*\pi^*\mathrm{cl}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}(z)=(\pi\circ F_{X,k}^{(m)})^*\mathrm{cl}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}(

z)=\pi^*\mathrm{cl}_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}(z)=\mathrm{cl}(z).
Since the hypothesis says that the classes $\mathrm{cl}(z)$, with $z$ ranging over codimension-$j$ cycles on $X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, span $W$, the preceding identity implies $F_W^m=\mathrm{id}_W$. This proves the first assertion of the lemma.

STEP 2 (semisimplicity on $W$). Let $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and put $U=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $T=F_W\otimes 1_U$. From $F_W^m=\mathrm{id}$ we have $T^m=1$. The polynomial $P(X)=X^m-1$ is squarefree in $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$: its derivative is $mX^{m-1}$, which has no common root with $P$ because $\operatorname{char}\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0$ and the roots of $P$ are nonzero. Let $\mu_m$ be its set of roots. For each $\zeta\in\mu_m$ define
\[
e_\zeta=\prod_{\eta\in\mu_m,\,\eta\ne\zeta}\frac{T-\eta}{\zeta-\eta}.
\]
Since $\prod_{\eta\in\mu_m}(T-\eta)=P(T)=0$, the usual Chinese remainder theorem argument gives $\sum_\zeta e_\zeta=1$, $e_\zeta e_\eta=0$ for $\zeta\ne\eta$, and $e_\zeta^2=e_\zeta$. Moreover $(T-\zeta)e_\zeta=0$, so $e_\zeta U$ is contained in the $\zeta$-eigenspace of $T$. Hence
\[
U=\bigoplus_{\zeta\in\mu_m} e_\zeta U
\]
is a direct sum of eigenspaces, and $T$ is diagonalisable over $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By lemma_5, diagonalisability of $F_W\otimes1$ over $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is equivalent to semisimplicity of $F_W$ on $W$. Thus $F_W$ is semisimple.

STEP 3 (comparison with untwisted cohomology). Since $k$ is separably closed, the lisse sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ on $X_k$ is the constant sheaf attached to the one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$. For any finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $A$, the cochain complex computing $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,A)$ is $C^*(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}A$; because $A$ is flat over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, taking cohomology gives a functorial isomorphism
\[
\theta_A:H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}A\xrightarrow{\sim}H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,A).
\]
Apply this with $A=\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ and $*=2j$.

The arithmetic Frobenius $F_W$ on $W$ is obtained from two pieces. The geometric part is the pullback along $F_{X,k}=\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\sigma$ acting on $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; this is $F_V$. The coefficient part is the Weil structure on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$. Because $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, this Weil structure is multiplication by a single scalar $\varphi_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$; it is invertible because it is a descent isomorphism for a sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec}k$ with respect to the automorphism $\sigma$ of $k$. Therefore, under $\theta_{\mathbb Q_\ell(j)}$,
\[
F_W\circ\theta_{\mathbb Q_\ell(j)}=\theta_{\mathbb Q_\ell(j)}\circ(F_V\otimes\varphi_j).
\]
Choose a basis vector $e$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ and let $\iota_e:V\to W$ be $v\mapsto\theta_{\mathbb Q_\ell(j)}(v\otimes e)$. Then $\iota_e$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism and
\[
F_W\circ\iota_e=\iota_e\circ(\varphi_j F_V).
\]
The exact value of $\varphi_j$ is a matter of the usual Tate-twist convention; the argument below uses only that $\varphi_j\ne0$.

STEP 4 (semisimplicity on $V$). From Step 1, $F_W^m=\mathrm{id}_W$. Conjugating by $\iota_e$ gives
\[
(\varphi_j F_V)^m=\mathrm{id}_V.
\]
Since $\varphi_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$, this is equivalent to
\[
F_V^m=\varphi_j^{-m}\,\mathrm{id}_V.
\]
Let $U'=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $T'=F_V\otimes1$. Choose $d\in\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell^\times$ with $d^m=\varphi_j^{-m}$ (possible because $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is algebraically closed). Put $S=d^{-1}T'$. Then
\[
S^m=d^{-m}T'^m=d^{-m}\varphi_j^{-m}=1.
\]
By the diagonalisation argument of Step 2, $S$ is diagonalisable over $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar $d$ preserves the eigenspace decomposition, so $T'=dS$ is also diagonalisable over $\bar{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Lemma_5 now implies that $F_V$ is semisimple on $V$.

This proves that $F^m$ acts as the identity on $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$, that $F$ acts semisimply on $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$, and that $F$ acts semisimply on $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$."
}

lemma_160.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\) of pure dimension \(d\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. For every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2d\), the operator \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if it acts semisimply on \(H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_160.proof:
We prove that for every n with 0 \le n \le 2d, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F is semisimple on H^n := H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) if and only if it is semisimple on H^{2d-n}. The whole content is: (i) semisimplicity for a disconnected X is checked geometrically connected component by geometrically connected component, with powers of F whose exponents do not depend on the degree (lemma_27), and (ii) on a geometrically connected smooth projective variety, Poincar\'e duality identifies the two degrees n and 2d-n by a Frobenius-equivariant perfect pairing up to the scalar q^{md}, to which the linear-algebra criterion lemma_159 applies.

STEP 0 (Notation, finiteness, invertibility).
Write k = \overline{\mathbf F}_q and \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(u)=u^q, so F = (\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*. If X = \varnothing then all cohomology groups H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) vanish and every statement below is vacuous; we assume X \neq \varnothing, so d \ge 0. For every i \ge 0 the group H^i := H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbf Q_\ell: X is proper over \mathbf F_q, and applying lemma_45_finite_frob to the constant complex \mathbf Q_\ell on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism F_X^*\mathbf Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf Q_\ell gives that H^i(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional. By lemma_6a, F is a \mathbf Q_\ell-linear automorphism of each H^i (its inverse is the geometric Frobenius (\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*); the same lemma applied with the field \mathbf F_{q^m} and the automorphism c\mapsto c^{q^m} in place of \mathbf F_q and \sigma shows that for every m \ge 1 the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is likewise an invertible operator on the cohomology of any \mathbf F_{q^m}-scheme.

STEP 1 (Reduction to geometrically connected varieties).
Let C_1,\dots,C_m be the geometric connected components of X_k. (Since X is smooth of pure dimension d over \mathbf F_q, X_k is smooth of pure dimension d over k; in particular its local rings are regular, hence domains, so X_k is locally integral, and being noetherian its finitely many connected components C_j are open and closed. Each C_j is therefore projective (closed in X_k) and smooth of pure dimension d over k.) Let O_1,\dots,O_r be the orbits of the permutation induced by F on the finite set \{C_1,\dots,C_m\}, choose a representative C_s in O_s, and let m_s := |O_s|.

Crucially, the components C_1,\dots,C_m, the orbits O_s, the representatives C_s and the lengths m_s are determined by the action of \mathrm{Gal}(k/\mathbf F_q) = \langle\sigma\rangle on the topological space of X_k; they do NOT depend on the cohomological degree. Hence the same list (C_s, m_s)_{s=1}^r is obtained whether we apply the analysis to degree i = n or to degree i = 2d-n.

By the stabiliser description, C_s is invariant under \sigma^{m_s} and under no smaller positive power of \sigma. By Galois descent for quasi-projective schemes (effective descent along \mathrm{Spec}\,k \to \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbf F_{q^{m_s}}), using the semilinear \sigma^{m_s}-action on C_s coming from its invariance, C_s descends to a scheme Y_s over \mathbf F_{q^{m_s}} with (Y_s)_k \simeq C_s; this is the F_{q^{m_s}}-model referred to in the last sentence of lemma_27. Because (Y_s)_k = C_s is connected, Y_s is geometrically connected; smoothness, projectivity and purity of dimension d hold for Y_s because they can be checked after the faithfully flat (indeed fpqc) base change k/\mathbf F_{q^{m_s}}. Under the identification (Y_s)_k = C_s, the q^{m_s}-power arithmetic Frobenius \Phi_s := (\mathrm{id}_{Y_s}\times\mathrm{Spec}(c\mapsto c^{q^{m_s}}))^* of H^i((Y_s)_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) coincides with the restriction F^{m_s}|_{H^i(C_s,\mathbf Q_\ell)}: this is precisely the assertion made in the "Equivalently" clause of lemma_27. By Step 0 applied over \mathbf F_{q^{m_s}}, each H^i((Y_s)_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional and \Phi_s is invertible.

Now lemma_27 (applied in degree i, with the data (C_s,m_s) above) gives, for each i \ge 0,
  (1.1)  F is semisimple on H^i(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) \Longleftrightarrow for every s = 1,\dots,r, \Phi_s = F^{m_s} is semisimple on H^i(C_s,\mathbf Q_\ell) = H^i((Y_s)_k,\mathbf Q_\ell).
Indeed, lemma_27 identifies H^i(X_k) with \bigoplus_j H^i(C_j) as an F-permutation of summands and asserts exactly this equivalence.

Therefore, once we prove in Step 2 that for each s the operator \Phi_s is semisimple on H^n((Y_s)_k) if and only if it is semisimple on H^{2d-n}((Y_s)_k), the two applications of (1.1) with i = n and i = 2d-n (using the same s-index set, the same components and the same exponents m_s) chain together:
  F ss on H^n(X_k) \overset{(1.1)}{\Longleftrightarrow} (\forall s)\ \Phi_s \text{ ss on } H^n((Y_s)_k) \Longleftrightarrow (\forall s)\ \Phi_s \text{ ss on } H^{2d-n}((Y_s)_k) \overset{(1.1)}{\Longleftrightarrow} F \text{ ss on } H^{2d-n}(X_k),
which is the desired statement. This reduces everything to the following claim.

CLAIM. Let m \ge 1, let Q := q^m, let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \mathbf F_Q of pure dimension d, let k = \overline{\mathbf F}_q, and let \Phi denote the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}(c\mapsto c^{Q}))^*. Then for every n with 0 \le n \le 2d, \Phi is semisimple on V := H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) if and only if it is semisimple on W := H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell).

PROOF OF THE CLAIM. By Step 0 (over \mathbf F_Q), V and W are finite-dimensional \mathbf Q_\ell-vector spaces and T := \Phi|_V \in \mathrm{GL}(V), S := \Phi|_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W).

(2a) The duality pairing. Since Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbf F_Q = \mathbf F_{q^m}, lemma_77 applies with that m and with F = \Phi. Its part (b) gives, for each n with 0 \le n \le 2d (which is our hypothesis; then automatically 0 \le 2d-n \le 2d as well), a PERFECT pairing of \mathbf Q_\ell-vector spaces
  \langle -, - \rangle : V \times W \longrightarrow \mathbf Q_\ell(-d), \qquad \langle x, y \rangle = \mathrm{tr}(x \cup y),
where \mathrm{tr}: H^{2d}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf Q_\ell(-d) is the Frobenius-equivariant trace isomorphism of lemma_77(a), and satisfying
  (2a.1)  \langle \Phi x, \Phi y \rangle = Q^{d}\, \langle x, y \rangle = q^{md}\,\langle x,y\rangle \quad \text{for all } x\in V,\ y\in W.

(2b) The degenerate case. Suppose V = 0. Perfectness of \langle-,-\rangle means the induced map W \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf Q_\ell}(V, \mathbf Q_\ell(-d)) is an isomorphism; the target is 0, so W = 0. Conversely, symmetry of the pairing (equivalently, applying (2a) to 2d-n in place of n) gives W = 0 \Rightarrow V = 0. On the zero space there is a unique endomorphism, and it is semisimple (the space is the direct sum of the empty family of eigenspaces; equivalently its minimal polynomial is 1, which is squarefree). Hence in this case both T and S are semisimple and the claimed equivalence holds trivially. We now assume V \neq 0 (and then W \neq 0), so that the criterion of lemma_159, which is stated for finite-dimensional spaces, is applied to nonzero spaces.

(2c) Reduction of the pairing to a \mathbf Q_\ell-valued one. The \mathbf Q_\ell(-d) is a one-dimensional \mathbf Q_\ell-vector space; choose any \mathbf Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \lambda: \mathbf Q_\ell(-d) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf Q_\ell (such a \lambda exists by picking a nonzero element of the dual of \mathbf Q_\ell(-d)). Define
  b : V \times W \longrightarrow \mathbf Q_\ell, \qquad b(x,y) := \lambda(\langle x, y\rangle).
Because \lambda is an isomorphism and \langle-,-\rangle is perfect, b is a perfect pairing: the induced maps V \xrightarrow{\sim} W^\vee and W \xrightarrow{\sim} V^\vee are isomorphisms. Moreover, using \mathbf Q_\ell-linearity of \lambda and (2a.1), with c := Q^{d} = q^{md} \in \mathbf Q_\ell^{\times} (a positive rational number, hence nonzero in \mathbf Q_\ell),
  (2c.1)  b(Tx, Sy) = \lambda(\langle \Phi x, \Phi y\rangle) = \lambda(Q^{d}\langle x,y\rangle) = Q^{d}\,\lambda(\langle x,y\rangle) = c\, b(x,y) \quad \forall x\in V,\ y\in W.

(2d) Application of the criterion. The data (V, T), (W, S), b, c now satisfy exactly the hypotheses of lemma_159: V and W are finite-dimensional \mathbf Q_\ell-vector spaces, T \in \mathrm{GL}(V) and S \in \mathrm{GL}(W) (Step 0 / lemma_6a), b: V \times W \to \mathbf Q_\ell is a perfect bilinear pairing (2c), and b(Tv,Sw) = c\,b(v,w) with c = Q^d \in \mathbf Q_\ell^{\times} (2c.1). Lemma 159 concludes that T is semisimple if and only if S is semisimple, which is exactly the claim. (For orientation: the mechanism of lemma_159 is that b identifies W with the dual V^\vee up to the scalar c, and semisimplicity is preserved under duality, under inversion, and under multiplication by a nonzero scalar — the content of lemma_159, which we use as proved and do not reprove here.) Note that the equivalence of lemma_159 is symmetric in the two factors (its hypothesis b(Tv,Sw)=cb(v,w) is unchanged on swapping (V,T) with (W,S) and using b'(w,v):=b(v,w)), so it gives both implications required. This proves the claim. \hfill \square(\text{Claim})

STEP 2 concludes with the claim; STEP 1 shows the claim for each s = 1,\dots,r implies the theorem for X, because the components C_s, their models Y_s over \mathbf F_{q^{m_s}} and the exponents m_s are the same for the two degrees n and 2d-n, and because lemma_27 gives the equivalence (1.1) in each degree separately.

STEP 3 (Verification of the hypotheses of the claim for each Y_s, and edge conditions).
For each s: Y_s is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbf F_{q^{m_s}} (Step 1), m_s \ge 1, and \Phi_s = F^{m_s} is the q^{m_s}-power arithmetic Frobenius of H^i((Y_s)_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) = H^i(C_s,\mathbf Q_\ell) (lemma_27). The numerical hypothesis of lemma_77(b), namely 0 \le i \le 2d, is satisfied for i = n and for i = 2d-n precisely because 0 \le n \le 2d is assumed in the statement of this lemma; this is the only place where that hypothesis on n is used, and it is essential (Poincar\'e duality pairs H^i with H^{2d-i}, so no such statement can hold for i outside [0,2d]).

Edge conditions already covered: (a) X = \varnothing — Step 0; (b) d = 0 — then n = 0 = 2d-n and the statement is tautological, and indeed the proof applies verbatim (the components Y_s are \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbf F_{q^{m_s}}, V = W = \mathbf Q_\ell, \Phi = \mathrm{id}, c = Q^0 = 1); (c) V = 0 with W = 0 — Step 2b; (d) invertibility of F and of \Phi_s, needed to regard T and S as elements of \mathrm{GL} — Step 0 via lemma_6a; (e) finite-dimensionality, needed for lemma_159 and for the notion of semisimplicity used in lemma_27 — Step 0 via lemma_45_finite_frob.

Combining Steps 0--3 we obtain, for every 0 \le n \le 2d,
  F \text{ acts semisimply on } H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell) \Longleftrightarrow F \text{ acts semisimply on } H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbf Q_\ell),
which is the required statement.

lemma_166.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Under the Frobenius-equivariant trace isomorphism \(\operatorname{tr}:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\) that sends the class of a closed point \(x\) to \([k(x):\mathbb F_q]\), the operator \(F\) corresponds to multiplication by \(q\) on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\).
lemma_166.proof:
We prove the statement by instantiating clause (a) of the proved lemma_77 (Frobenius-equivariant Poincaré duality) in the case of a curve over the ground field itself, and then checking that the normalisation in lemma_77 is exactly the normalisation demanded here, and that it determines the trace isomorphism uniquely.

STEP 0 (Notation). Let q = p^a be a prime power, C a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_q, k = \bar{F}_q, \ell \neq p a prime, and F = (id_C \times Spec\,\sigma)^* with \sigma(c) = c^q the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell). By definition of the Tate twist, Q_\ell(-1) := Hom_{Q_\ell}(Q_\ell(1), Q_\ell) with Q_\ell(1) = (lim_\leftarrow \mu_{\ell^n}(k)) \otimes_{Z_\ell} Q_\ell; in particular Q_\ell(-1) is a one-dimensional Q_\ell-vector space, and F acts on it Q_\ell-linearly (through the cyclotomic character).

STEP 1 (Verification of the hypotheses of lemma_77). Lemma_77 requires: a prime power q = p^a; an integer m \ge 1; a smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y over F_{q^m} of pure dimension d; k = \bar F_q; a prime \ell \neq p; and F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of Y_k. Take
  m := 1,   Y := C,   d := 1.
Then:
  (1a) m = 1 \ge 1, and F_{q^m} = F_{q^1} = F_q, so "Y a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^m}" is precisely our hypothesis "C a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_q".
  (1b) A curve is, by definition, of pure dimension 1, and C is non-empty (it has dimension 1), so d = 1 is correct.
  (1c) The algebraic closure used in lemma_77 is \bar{F}_q for the prime power q^m = q, which is the same field k as here.
  (1d) The prime \ell \neq p is the same.
  (1e) The operator F of lemma_77 is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, i.e. (id_Y \times Spec\,\sigma_m)^* with \sigma_m(c) = c^{q^m} = c^q for m = 1; this is literally the operator F in the present statement.
All hypotheses of lemma_77 are therefore satisfied.

STEP 2 (Application of lemma_77(a)). Clause (a) of lemma_77, applied to Y = C, m = 1, d = 1, asserts the following. For the structure morphism f : C \to Spec F_q, the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism Q_\ell(1)[2] \to Rf^! Q_\ell induces a canonical isomorphism of Q_\ell-vector spaces
   tr : H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Q_\ell(-1),
normalised by tr(cl(x)) = [k(x) : F_{q^m}] = [k(x) : F_q] for every closed point x of C, and this tr is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where F acts on Q_\ell(-1) as multiplication by the positive rational number q^{md} = q^{1\cdot 1} = q.

STEP 3 (Unpacking the equivariance). "tr is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, with F acting on Q_\ell(-1) as multiplication by q" means precisely that for every \alpha \in H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell),
   tr(F\alpha) = q \cdot tr(\alpha).
Equivalently, the square
   H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell) --F--> H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell)
        | tr                        | tr
        v                           v
   Q_\ell(-1) --(\times q)--> Q_\ell(-1)
commutes. Since tr is an isomorphism, this says exactly that the conjugate operator tr \circ F \circ tr^{-1} of End_{Q_\ell}(Q_\ell(-1)) is multiplication by q; i.e. under tr the operator F corresponds to multiplication by q. This is the desired conclusion, once we know that the tr of Step 2 is "the" trace isomorphism referred to in the statement.

STEP 4 (Uniqueness of the normalised trace isomorphism; identification with the one in the statement). We show that there is at most one Q_\ell-linear map tr' : H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell) \to Q_\ell(-1) satisfying tr'(cl(x)) = [k(x):F_q] for all closed points x.
  (4a) H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell) is one-dimensional over Q_\ell: by Step 2 it is isomorphic via tr to Q_\ell(-1), which is one-dimensional (Step 0).
  (4b) C has a closed point: C is a non-empty scheme of finite type over the field F_q, hence has closed points, and for a closed point x of a finite-type F_q-scheme the extension k(x)/F_q is finite; write deg(x) := [k(x):F_q] \in Z_{>0}.
  (4c) Fix one closed point x of C. Then tr(cl(x)) = deg(x), which is a positive integer, hence a non-zero (indeed invertible) element of Q_\ell. Thus cl(x) \neq 0, and by (4a) cl(x) is a Q_\ell-basis of H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell).
  (4d) If tr' is any Q_\ell-linear map with tr'(cl(y)) = deg(y) for every closed point y, then in particular tr'(cl(x)) = deg(x) = tr(cl(x)); since cl(x) is a basis of the source and the target is a Q_\ell-vector space, a linear map out of a one-dimensional space is determined by its value on a basis, so tr' = tr. Hence the normalised trace isomorphism is unique, and the map called "the Frobenius-equivariant trace isomorphism ... that sends the class of a closed point x to [k(x):F_q]" in the present statement is necessarily the tr constructed in Step 2.

STEP 5 (Conclusion). Combining Steps 3 and 4: for the (unique) normalised trace isomorphism tr : H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} Q_\ell(-1), one has tr \circ F = (\times q) \circ tr, i.e. F corresponds under tr to multiplication by q on Q_\ell(-1). This is exactly the claim of lemma_166.

REMARK (convention check, not used in the argument above). The scalar q is consistent with the standard conventions: arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_\ell(1) by q^{-1} (it raises each \ell^n-th root of unity to its q-th power, which is multiplication by q on the inverse-limit lattice in the pullback convention used for F^*, hence by q^{-1} on Q_\ell(1) as an operator, and dually by q on Q_\ell(-1)); correspondingly F acts trivially on H^2_et(C_k, Q_\ell(1)) \cong Q_\ell, since the class of a closed point of C_k is F-fixed there and its trace is 1. Thus the assertion of lemma_77(a) used above, and hence of lemma_166, is the statement that the top cohomology of a curve is the Tate motive Q_\ell(-1) with its cyclotomic Frobenius action.

lemma_168.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). For every \(n\ge 1\) the cup-product map \(\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) satisfies \(F(x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_n)=Fx_1\cup\cdots\cup Fx_n\), that is, it intertwines \(F\) with the \(n\)-th exterior power of its action on \(H^1\). Consequently, whenever this cup-product map is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, it is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules.
lemma_168.proof:
Fix n >= 1 and write, for brevity, V := H^1_et(X_k, Q_l) and H^m := H^m_et(X_k, Q_l) for m >= 0, where l denotes the given prime ell. Let
   f := id_X x Spec(sigma) : X_k -> X_k ,   sigma(c) = c^q .
Since sigma is an F_q-algebra automorphism of k, f is a well defined morphism of schemes, and by the definition in the statement F = f^* on ⊕_m H^m.

STEP 0 (finite-dimensionality, invertibility, degree preservation).
The variety X is projective over F_q, hence proper. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to Y = X and to K = Q_l (the constant sheaf on X_k) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism psi : F_X^* Q_l -> Q_l: it gives that H^n(X_k, Q_l) = H^n(X_k, K) is finite-dimensional over Q_l for every n. In particular V is finite-dimensional. By lemma_6a, applied to the scheme X over F_q, the pullback F_ar = (id_X x sigma)^* = f^* is a Q_l-linear automorphism of each H^m (with inverse the geometric Frobenius (id_X x sigma^{-1})^*). Thus F preserves each degree and F|_V lies in GL(V), and F|_{H^n} lies in GL(H^n).

STEP 1 (the cup-product map on the exterior power).
Recall the standard properties of the etale cup product with Q_l coefficients: it is Q_l-bilinear, associative, graded-commutative (for alpha in H^r, beta in H^s one has alpha cup beta = (-1)^{rs} beta cup alpha), and unital. For completeness we recall the reason for the sign rule, since we use it: H^* is the cohomology of the differential graded Q_l-algebra RGamma(X_k, Q_l); the product is induced by the derived tensor product otimes^L together with Q_l otimes^L Q_l = Q_l, and the symmetry constraint A otimes^L B -> B otimes^L A of the symmetric monoidal derived category of sheaves of Q_l-vector spaces is computed on complexes of Q_l-vector spaces by the Koszul-sign rule a otimes b |-> (-1)^{|a||b|} b otimes a. Naturality of RGamma with respect to these identifications gives the stated sign rule in cohomology.

For x_1,...,x_n in V the iterated product x_1 cup ... cup x_n is well defined (associativity, independently of bracketing) and lies in H^n (degrees add). By bilinearity the assignment (x_1,...,x_n) |-> x_1 cup ... cup x_n is n-linear, so it induces a Q_l-linear map
   m_n : V^{otimes n} -> H^n ,  x_1 otimes ... otimes x_n |-> x_1 cup ... cup x_n .
Since elements of V have degree 1, graded commutativity gives x cup y = - y cup x for x,y in V. Using associativity, interchanging two adjacent tensor factors changes the sign of m_n: for any decomposition of the tensor positions as (xi, x, y, eta) one has m_n(xi otimes x otimes y otimes eta) = - m_n(xi otimes y otimes x otimes eta), hence m_n vanishes on xi otimes x otimes y otimes eta + xi otimes y otimes x otimes eta. Let R'_n be the Q_l-subspace of V^{otimes n} spanned by these elements; then R'_n subset ker(m_n).

We claim V^{otimes n}/R'_n is the usual exterior power ∧^n V. Indeed, let U_n be the subspace spanned by tensors x_1 otimes ... otimes x_n with x_i = x_j for some i < j. Each generator of R'_n lies in U_n because xi otimes (x otimes y + y otimes x) otimes eta = xi otimes (x+y) otimes (x+y) otimes eta - xi otimes x otimes x otimes eta - xi otimes y otimes y otimes eta. Conversely, in the quotient V^{otimes n}/R'_n the adjacent transposition s_p acts as multiplication by -1 for every p, and since the s_p generate the symmetric group S_n with the sign character, every permutation acts by its sign; a tensor with x_i = x_j (i < j) is fixed by the transposition (i j) (the two entries being equal vectors) yet is multiplied by -1 by it, so it is zero in the quotient, as 2 != 0 in Q_l. Hence U_n subset R'_n, and the two quotients coincide. We identify ∧^n V := V^{otimes n}/R'_n and write x_1 wedge ... wedge x_n for the class of x_1 otimes ... otimes x_n.

Since R'_n subset ker(m_n), the map m_n descends to a well defined Q_l-linear map
   cup_n : ∧^n V -> H^n ,  x_1 wedge ... wedge x_n |-> x_1 cup ... cup x_n .
This is the cup-product map of the statement (for n = 1 it is the identity of V, and the assertions below are then immediate).

STEP 2 (pullback is multiplicative).
For any morphism of schemes g : Y -> Z, the pullback g^* : H^*_et(Z, Q_l) -> H^*_et(Y, Q_l) is a homomorphism of graded Q_l-algebras: g^*(alpha cup beta) = g^* alpha cup g^* beta. Justification: g^* is exact on etale sheaves, there are natural isomorphisms g^*(A otimes^L B) = g^*A otimes^L g^*B and g^* Q_l = Q_l which are compatible with the associativity, unit and symmetry constraints (they come from the fact that g^* is a symmetric monoidal functor, being a left adjoint which is exact), and the cup product is defined as the composite
   RGamma(Z,A) otimes^L RGamma(Z,B) -> RGamma(Z, A otimes^L B) ;
the naturality square for the map RGamma(Z,-) -> RGamma(Y, g^* -) against these tensor-product identifications is precisely the multiplicativity statement. Iterating over n factors by induction on n (using associativity) gives, for all x_1,...,x_n in V,
   F(x_1 cup ... cup x_n) = f^*(x_1 cup ... cup x_n) = f^*x_1 cup ... cup f^*x_n = Fx_1 cup ... cup Fx_n .   (2.1)

STEP 3 (intertwining with the n-th exterior power).
Because F|_V is Q_l-linear, (F|_V)^{otimes n} maps R'_n into R'_n: it sends the generator xi otimes x otimes y otimes eta + xi otimes y otimes x otimes eta to Fxi otimes Fx otimes Fy otimes Feta + Fxi otimes Fy otimes Fx otimes Feta, again a generator. Hence (F|_V)^{otimes n} descends to a Q_l-linear automorphism of ∧^n V, denoted ∧^n F, characterised by
   (∧^n F)(x_1 wedge ... wedge x_n) = Fx_1 wedge ... wedge Fx_n ,
and it is invertible with inverse ∧^n(F^{-1}) (apply the same construction to the Q_l-linear map F^{-1}|_V; the two are mutually inverse since (F^{otimes n})^{-1} = (F^{-1})^{otimes n}).
Now compute, for a decomposable wedge, using the definition of cup_n, then (2.1):
   cup_n( (∧^n F)(x_1 wedge ... wedge x_n) ) = cup_n(Fx_1 wedge ... wedge Fx_n)
   = Fx_1 cup ... cup Fx_n = F(x_1 cup ... cup x_n) = F( cup_n(x_1 wedge ... wedge x_n) ).
Decomposable wedges span ∧^n V, and both sides are Q_l-linear in the wedge argument, so the two linear maps cup_n o (∧^n F) and F o cup_n from ∧^n V to H^n coincide:
   cup_n o (∧^n F) = F o cup_n .
This is exactly the assertion that the cup-product map intertwines F with the n-th exterior power of its action on H^1.

STEP 4 (isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules).
Both ∧^n V and H^n are Q_l[F]-modules: H^n via the automorphism F|_{H^n}, and ∧^n V via the automorphism ∧^n F; concretely P(t) in Q_l[t] acts by P(F|_{H^n}) and by P(∧^n F) respectively (in fact both are Q_l[t,t^{-1}]-modules, since the operators are invertible by Step 0). A Q_l[F]-module homomorphism is the same thing as a Q_l-linear map commuting with F. The map cup_n is Q_l-linear (Step 1) and commutes with F (Step 3), hence is a Q_l[F]-module homomorphism.
Assume now that cup_n is an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces. Its inverse is then also a module homomorphism: writing F_1 := ∧^n F and F_2 := F|_{H^n}, the identity cup_n o F_1 = F_2 o cup_n with cup_n bijective gives F_2 = cup_n o F_1 o cup_n^{-1}, hence cup_n^{-1} o F_2 = F_1 o cup_n^{-1}. Thus cup_n is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules, which completes the proof of the statement.

STEP 5 (consequence for semisimplicity, recorded for later use).
Suppose F|_V is semisimple. Iterating lemma_147 (tensor product of semisimple automorphisms is semisimple) shows that F^{otimes n} is semisimple on V^{otimes n}. The subspace R'_n is stable under F^{otimes n} by Step 3, so lemma_145 applied to (V^{otimes n}, F^{otimes n}, R'_n) gives that the induced automorphism on the quotient V^{otimes n}/R'_n = ∧^n V, which is ∧^n F, is semisimple. If moreover cup_n is surjective, its kernel is stable under ∧^n F by the intertwining of Step 3, and lemma_145 applied to (∧^n V, ∧^n F, ker cup_n) shows the induced automorphism on H^n = ∧^n V/ker cup_n, which is F|_{H^n}, is semisimple. Conversely, when cup_n is an isomorphism, lemma_8 (conjugate operators have the same semisimplicity behaviour, both spaces being finite-dimensional by Step 0 and both operators invertible) gives: F|_{H^n} semisimple if and only if ∧^n F semisimple. In particular, under the hypothesis that the cup-product map ∧^n H^1 -> H^n is an isomorphism, semisimplicity of Frobenius on H^1 implies semisimplicity on H^n.

lemma_170.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety of dimension \(g\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts on \(H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as multiplication by \(q^g\); in particular \(F\) and geometric Frobenius act semisimply on it.
lemma_170.proof:
We prove that the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, acts on $V:=H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as the scalar $q^g$, and deduce the semisimplicity of $F$ and of geometric Frobenius.

**Step 1 — Hypotheses of the trace theorem.** An abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$ of dimension $g$ is by definition proper, smooth and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$; since $\mathbb F_q$ is perfect and $A$ is smooth, connected and a group scheme, $A$ is geometrically integral, hence in particular geometrically connected, and it is of pure dimension $g$. Thus $A$ satisfies all the hypotheses of lemma_77 with $Y:=A$, with the extension degree $m:=1$ (so $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q$), with $d:=g$, with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and with the prime $\ell\neq p$.

**Step 2 — The Frobenius-equivariant trace isomorphism.** Applying lemma_77(a) to $Y=A$, $m=1$, $d=g$, we obtain a canonical isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
\[
\operatorname{tr}:H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-g),
\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[k(x):\mathbb F_q]\ \ \text{for every closed point }x\in A,
\]
which is equivariant for arithmetic Frobenius, where $F$ acts on the target $\mathbb Q_\ell(-g)$ as multiplication by the positive rational number $q^{mg}=q^{1\cdot g}=q^g$. Concretely, equivariance says that for all $v\in V$,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(Fv)=q^g\cdot \operatorname{tr}(v).
\]

**Step 3 — $F$ is the scalar $q^g$.** Since $\operatorname{tr}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, $q^g\cdot\operatorname{tr}(v)=\operatorname{tr}(q^g v)$. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(Fv-q^gv)=0$ for every $v\in V$. The map $\operatorname{tr}$ is an isomorphism, in particular injective, so $Fv-q^gv=0$, i.e.
\[
Fv=q^g v\qquad\text{for all }v\in V,
\]
which is exactly the first claim: $F=q^g\cdot\mathrm{id}_V$ on $H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Note $q^g\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ (a prime power is non-zero in $\mathbb Q_\ell$), so this operator is invertible, consistently with lemma_6a.

**Step 4 — The edge case $g=0$.** If $g=0$, then $A\simeq\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ is the trivial abelian variety, $V=H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathrm{Spec}\,k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ because $k$ is separably closed (the étale topos of $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is trivial), and $F$ acts as the identity, which is multiplication by $q^0=1$. So the statement holds also in this case; alternatively, lemma_77 applied with $d=0$ gives the same conclusion, since then $\operatorname{tr}(1)=\mathrm{cl}([k:\mathbb F_q])$-normalised identity and $q^{0}=1$.

**Step 5 — Dimension (for later use).** Since $V\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell(-g)$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and $\mathbb Q_\ell(-g)$ is a free $\mathbb Q_\ell$-module of rank $1$, $V$ is one-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$; in particular every $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism of $V$ is a scalar, and $V$ is finite-dimensional as required in the statements of the linear-algebra lemmas we invoke.

**Step 6 — Semisimplicity of $F$.** The operator $F=q^g\mathrm{id}_V$ is annihilated by the polynomial $t-q^g\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. Its minimal polynomial $\mu_F$ divides $t-q^g$; since $F$ is invertible (lemma_6a), $F\neq 0$, so $\mu_F$ is not constant, hence $\mu_F=t-q^g$. This polynomial is linear, its derivative is $1$, so $\gcd(\mu_F,\mu_F')=1$ and $\mu_F$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$. By the criterion of lemma_155 (squarefree characteristic/minimal polynomial implies semisimplicity), $F$ is semisimple on $V$. Explicitly and independently: choose $0\neq v_0\in V$; then $V=\mathbb Q_\ell v_0$ is a direct sum of $1$-dimensional $F$-eigenspaces with eigenvalue $q^g$, so $F$ is diagonalisable over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ already. Tensoring with $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, the operator $F\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is again the scalar $q^g$ on the $1$-dimensional $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-space $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, hence diagonal (any non-zero vector is an eigenvector); this agrees with lemma_5, which identifies semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ with diagonalisability after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 7 — Semisimplicity of geometric Frobenius.** By lemma_6a, the geometric Frobenius $F_{\mathrm{geo}}:=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}$ on $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $i$. Therefore on $V$ we have
\[
F_{\mathrm{geo}}=(q^g\mathrm{id}_V)^{-1}=q^{-g}\mathrm{id}_V,
\]
a scalar automorphism. Its minimal polynomial is $t-q^{-g}$, linear and squarefree, so by the same argument as in Step 6 (or by lemma_4, which states that $T$ is semisimple if and only if $T^{-1}$ is semisimple, applied to $T=F$) $F_{\mathrm{geo}}$ acts semisimply on $V$, and $F_{\mathrm{geo}}\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 8 — Conclusion.** We have shown $F=q^g\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{2g}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (Steps 2–4), that this operator is semisimple (Step 6), and that geometric Frobenius, equal to $q^{-g}\cdot\mathrm{id}$, is likewise semisimple (Step 7). This is precisely the statement of the lemma. (Remark: the case $g=1$ recovers the curve statement of lemma_166, where the target is $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ and $F$ acts as $q$; and applying the same argument with $\sigma^m$ in place of $\sigma$ gives $F^m=q^{gm}\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{2g}$.)

lemma_173.statement:
Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\), let \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\) be prime, and let \(n\ge 1\). Write \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k}\) for the identity component of the Picard scheme, \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X):=P(k)\) for the group of line bundles on \(X\) algebraically equivalent to zero, and \(\operatorname{NS}(X):=\operatorname{Pic}(X)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\). For an abelian group \(A\) let \(A[\ell^n]\) denote the kernel of multiplication by \(\ell^n\). Then the natural sequence
\[0\longrightarrow P[\ell^n](k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0\]
is exact.
lemma_173.proof:
PROOF OF LEMMA 173.

We prove that for every algebraically closed field $k$, every smooth projective geometrically connected $k$-variety $X$, every prime $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)$ and every $n\ge 1$, the natural sequence
\[0\longrightarrow P[\ell^n](k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0\]
is exact, where $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k}$ and $\operatorname{NS}(X):=\operatorname{Pic}(X)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$. The proof has four steps: (1) the definitional short exact sequence $0\to P(k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\operatorname{NS}(X)\to 0$; (2) the identification $P[\ell^n](k)=(P(k))[\ell^n]$; (3) divisibility of $P(k)$; (4) an abstract group-theoretic snake-lemma/element chase. No $\ell$-adic cohomology and no Frobenius enter anywhere.

NOTATION AND THE TWO MAPS. Write $\mathcal P:=\operatorname{Pic}_{X/k}$ for the Picard scheme of $X$ over $k$, and let $\iota:P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k}\hookrightarrow\mathcal P$ be the inclusion of the identity component (an open, in particular a monomorphism, immersion of group schemes). Both arrows of the asserted sequence come from homomorphisms commuting with $[\ell^n]$:
(i) $\iota$ is a homomorphism, so $\iota\circ[\ell^n]_P=[\ell^n]_{\mathcal P}\circ\iota$, hence it restricts to a map $P[\ell^n](k)\to\mathcal P[\ell^n](k)$, which under the isomorphism $\mathcal P(k)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ of Step 1 is the first arrow;
(ii) the quotient homomorphism $q:\operatorname{Pic}(X)\twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$ satisfies $q(\ell^n L)=\ell^n q(L)$, so it restricts to $\operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]\to\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]$, the second arrow. Thus both arrows are well defined group homomorphisms and $q\circ\iota=0$ on $\ell^n$-torsion, i.e. the sequence is a complex.

STEP 1: THE DEFINITIONAL SHORT EXACT SEQUENCE.
(1a) $\mathcal P(k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Pic}(X)$. The relative Picard functor is $\mathcal P=R^1f_{*,\mathrm{fppf}}\mathbf G_m$ for $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; the Leray five-term exact sequence for $f_{\mathrm{fppf}}$ and $\mathbf G_m$ gives
\[0\to \operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)\to\mathcal P(k)\to H^2_{\mathrm{fppf}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbf G_m).\]
Now $\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}k)=0$ because every line bundle over a field is a free module, of rank $1$ iff invertible as an $\mathcal O$-module of rank one, hence trivial. Also $H^2_{\mathrm{fppf}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbf G_m)=\operatorname{Br}(k)=H^2_{\text{ét}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbf G_m)$ (comparison of fppf and étale cohomology for the smooth sheaf $\mathbf G_m$), and this vanishes because $k$ is separably closed: the small étale site of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ has only the final object up to isomorphism (every finite separable $k$-algebra is a product of copies of $k$), so its topos is the category of sets and $H^q_{\text{ét}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,-)=0$ for $q\ge1$. Hence the middle map is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Pic}(X)\simeq\mathcal P(k)$; concretely it sends a line bundle to its class in the fibre $\mathcal P(k)=\{\text{line bundles on }X\}/p^*\operatorname{Pic}(k)$, which is already a bijection since $\operatorname{Pic}(k)=0$.
(1b) $P$ is an abelian variety and $P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$. This is the Grothendieck--Kleiman representability theorem (FGA, Théorème 5.2; Kleiman, Toward a numerical theory of algebraic cycles): for $X$ projective over a field, $\mathcal P$ is a group scheme locally of finite type over $k$; for $X$ smooth, projective and geometrically connected its identity component $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k}$ is an abelian variety, $\mathcal P/P$ is étale, and the $k$-points of $P$ are exactly the line bundles on $X$ algebraically equivalent to zero. This is precisely the content of the abbreviation $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X):=P(k)$ in the statement, so no further argument is needed.
(1c) Exactness of $0\to P(k)\xrightarrow{\iota(k)}\operatorname{Pic}(X)\xrightarrow{q}\operatorname{NS}(X)\to0$: $\iota(k)$ is injective because $\iota$ is a monomorphism of sheaves; $q$ is surjective by definition of the quotient group $\operatorname{NS}(X):=\operatorname{Pic}(X)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)$; and $\ker q=\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)=\iota(k)(P(k))$ again by that definition. This is the only place where the geometry of $X$ is used, and it is purely definitional.

STEP 2: IDENTIFYING $P[\ell^n](k)$ WITH THE $\ell^n$-TORSION OF THE GROUP $P(k)$. By definition $P[m]:=\ker([m]:P\to P)$ is the kernel taken in the category of fppf sheaves of abelian groups. Kernels of morphisms of sheaves of groups are computed sectionwise (the presheaf $T\mapsto\ker(P(T)\xrightarrow{[m]}P(T))$ is a sheaf and satisfies the universal property of the kernel), so for every $k$-scheme $T$ one has a canonical equality $P[m](T)=\ker([m]:P(T)\to P(T))=(P(T))[m]$. Taking $T=\operatorname{Spec}k$ gives $P[\ell^n](k)=(P(k))[\ell^n]$, and this identification is compatible with the map $\iota$ of Notation (i). Consequently the sequence whose exactness we must prove is literally
\[0\longrightarrow A[m]\longrightarrow B[m]\longrightarrow C[m]\longrightarrow 0,\qquad A:=P(k),\ B:=\operatorname{Pic}(X),\ C:=\operatorname{NS}(X),\ m:=\ell^n,\]
for the exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ of Step 1(c).

STEP 3: DIVISIBILITY OF $P(k)$, i.e. $[m]:P(k)\to P(k)$ IS SURJECTIVE FOR EVERY $m\ge1$. Let $g:=\dim P$. If $g=0$ then $P=0$ (an abelian variety of dimension $0$ is the trivial group scheme) and the claim is trivial, so suppose $g\ge1$. Standard theorem on abelian varieties (Mumford, Abelian Varieties, §15, Thm 1; equivalently $A[m]$ is finite locally free of rank $m^{2g}$): for every integer $m\ge1$ the multiplication morphism $[m]:P\to P$ is a finite locally free homomorphism of rank $m^{2g}\ge1$ (an isogeny; for $(m,\operatorname{char}k)=1$ it is finite étale, and in general one factors $m=p^r m'$ with $p=\operatorname{char}k$ and uses $[p]=V\circ F_{\mathrm{rel}}$, the relative Frobenius followed by the Verschiebung, both finite locally free of rank $p^{2g}$). Now fix $x\in P(k)$, viewed as a $k$-morphism $\operatorname{Spec}k\to P$, and form the cartesian square defining the scheme-theoretic fibre $Z:=P\times_{[m],P,\operatorname{Spec}k}$. Finiteness and locally free rank are preserved under base change, so $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite locally free of rank $m^{2g}\ge1$; in particular $B:=\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$ is a free $k$-vector space of rank $m^{2g}$, hence a nonzero ring. A nonzero finitely generated algebra over a field has a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ (by Zorn's lemma, or by Noether normalisation), and since $B$ is finite-dimensional over $k$, the field $\kappa(\mathfrak m)=B/\mathfrak m$ is a finite field extension of $k$, hence $\kappa(\mathfrak m)=k$ because $k$ is algebraically closed. The corresponding $k$-morphism $y:\operatorname{Spec}k\to Z\to P$ satisfies $[m](y)=x$. Thus $[m]:P(k)\to P(k)$ is surjective; applying this with $m=\ell^n$ gives the required hypothesis for Step 4. (Equivalently: the group of rational points of an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field is divisible.)

STEP 4: THE GROUP-THEORETIC LEMMA. Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{\pi}C\to0$ be an exact sequence of abelian groups and let $m\ge1$.
(a) The sequence $0\to A[m]\xrightarrow{i}B[m]\xrightarrow{\pi}C[m]$ is exact. Proof. $i$ is injective, so its restriction to $A[m]$ is. The maps land in the torsion subgroups because $mi(a)=i(ma)$ and $m\pi(b)=\pi(mb)$. If $b\in B[m]$ satisfies $\pi(b)=0$, then $b\in\ker\pi=\operatorname{im}i$, so $b=i(a)$ for some $a\in A$; then $i(ma)=mb=0$ and injectivity of $i$ gives $ma=0$, i.e. $a\in A[m]$. Hence $b\in\operatorname{im}(A[m]\to B[m])$, proving exactness at $B[m]$. (This is the "kernel equals image" point, and it needs no hypothesis on $A$.)
(b) If $[m]:A\to A$ is surjective, then $\pi:B[m]\to C[m]$ is surjective. Proof. Let $c\in C[m]$. By surjectivity of $\pi$ choose $b\in B$ with $\pi(b)=c$. Then $\pi(mb)=mc=0$, so $mb\in\ker\pi=\operatorname{im}i$: write $mb=i(a_0)$ with $a_0\in A$ (unique by injectivity of $i$). By the surjectivity hypothesis on $[m]_A$ there is $a_1\in A$ with $ma_1=a_0$. Put $b':=b-i(a_1)$. Then $mb'=mb-i(ma_1)=i(a_0)-i(a_0)=0$, so $b'\in B[m]$, and $\pi(b')=\pi(b)-\pi(i(a_1))=c-0=c$. Hence $c$ is in the image of $B[m]$.

STEP 5: CONCLUSION. Apply Step 4 with $A=P(k)$, $B=\operatorname{Pic}(X)$, $C=\operatorname{NS}(X)$, $m=\ell^n$, using the exact sequence of Step 1(c) and the surjectivity of $[\ell^n]$ on $A=P(k)$ proved in Step 3. Step 4(a) gives exactness of $0\to P(k)[\ell^n]\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]\to\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]$, and Step 4(b) gives surjectivity onto $\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]$. Rewriting $P(k)[\ell^n]$ as $P[\ell^n](k)$ via Step 2 yields exactly
\[0\longrightarrow P[\ell^n](k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0,\]
and the arrows are the natural ones described in the Notation paragraph. This completes the proof.

REMARKS (not used above). (1) The argument never uses $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$ nor any case distinction on $\operatorname{char}k$: Step 3 shows $[m]$ is surjective on $P(k)$ for every $m\ge1$, so the same proof gives exactness of $0\to P[m](k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)[m]\to\operatorname{NS}(X)[m]\to0$ for all $m\ge1$. The hypotheses that $X$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected are used only to have the Picard scheme with abelian-variety identity component (Step 1b) and the identification $\mathcal P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)$ (Step 1a).
(2) The sequence is in general not exact on the right of $\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]$ nor an isomorphism on the left: by (a)-(b) above, $P[\ell^n](k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]$ is an isomorphism if and only if $\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]=0$, and since $A[\ell]\hookrightarrow A[\ell^n]$ for every $n\ge1$ (an element killed by $\ell$ is killed by $\ell^n$) this vanishing for one $n\ge1$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell]=0$, independently of $n$. For instance, for an Enriques surface $S/\mathbb C$ one has $\operatorname{Pic}^0(S)=0$ and a non-trivial canonical bundle $K_S$ with $K_S^{\otimes2}\simeq\mathcal O_S$, so $\operatorname{Pic}(S)[2]\simeq\mathbb Z/2$ while $P[2](\mathbb C)=0$; the exact sequence above correctly predicts the non-zero term $\operatorname{NS}(S)[2]\simeq\mathbb Z/2$.
(3) Useful special cases where the left map is an isomorphism: if $X$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve then $\operatorname{NS}(X)\simeq\mathbb Z$ via the degree map, and if $X$ is an abelian variety then $\operatorname{NS}(X)$ is the group of symmetric homomorphisms $X\to X^\vee$, a subgroup of the torsion-free group $\operatorname{Hom}(X,X^\vee)$; in both cases $\operatorname{NS}(X)[\ell^n]=0$ and $\operatorname{Pic}(X)[\ell^n]=P[\ell^n](k)$. These are separate statements and are not needed here.

lemma_175.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Suppose \(H^{2i+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(i\ge0\), and that for every \(i\ge0\) the space \(H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by cycle classes \(\mathrm{cl}(z)\) of codimension-\(i\) cycles \(z\) on \(X\) each defined over some finite extension of \(\mathbb F_q\). Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_175.proof:
**Conventions.** For each integer \(m\ge 1\) write \(k_m=\mathbb F_{q^m}\subset k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) for the unique subfield with \(q^m\) elements and \(X_m:=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec} k_m\). Saying that a codimension-\(i\) cycle \(z\) on \(X\) is "defined over some finite extension of \(\mathbb F_q\)" means: there are \(m\ge1\) and \(z'\in Z^i(X_m)\) whose flat pullback along \(X_k=X\times_{\mathbb F_q}k\to X_m\) is the cycle on \(X_k\) under consideration; its class is \(\mathrm{cl}(z')\in H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\). Recall \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\).

We prove that \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), treating odd and even \(n\) separately.

**Step 1: odd degrees.** Let \(n=2i+1\ge1\) be odd. By hypothesis \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\). The zero \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space has a single endomorphism, which is also the identity; hence it is annihilated by \(t-1\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\), a squarefree polynomial, so it is semisimple (equivalently: the empty family is a basis of eigenvectors of the empty operator, and \(V=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\ker(T-\lambda)\) holds trivially for \(V=0\)). Thus the claim holds for all odd \(n\).

**Step 2: even degrees.** Fix \(i\ge0\) and put \(V_i:=H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\).

*2a. \(V_i\) is finite dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\).* The variety \(X\) is smooth projective, hence proper over \(\mathbb F_q\). The Tate twist \(\mathbb Q_\ell(i)\), placed in degree \(0\), is a lisse \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaf of finite rank on \(X_k\), hence an object of \(D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). It carries a natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(\varphi_i:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell(i)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(i)\): indeed \(\mathbb Z_\ell(1)=\varprojlim_\nu\mu_{\ell^\nu}\), and because \(\gcd(q,\ell)=1\) the map \(a\mapsto a^q\) is an automorphism of the finite \(\mathbb Z[1/\ell]\)-group scheme \(\mu_{\ell^\nu}\) (its inverse is \(a\mapsto a^{q'}\) with \(qq'\equiv1\bmod \ell^\nu\)); these automorphisms are compatible with the transition maps \(\mu_{\ell^{\nu+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^\nu}\), so they give \(F_X^*\mathbb Z_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Z_\ell(1)\) and hence \(F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\); for \(i\ge0\) take the \(i\)-fold tensor power (for \(i=0\), the constant sheaf with its standard structure). Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell(i)\) with \(\varphi=\varphi_i\) (its hypothesis that \(X\) be proper over \(\mathbb F_q\) is satisfied) gives that \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))=V_i\) is finite dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\).

*2b. A single common field of definition for a finite spanning set.* By the second hypothesis, \(V_i\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by classes \(\mathrm{cl}(z_\lambda)\) with \(z_\lambda\in Z^i(X_{m_\lambda})\) for some \(m_\lambda\ge1\) (index \(\lambda\) running over a possibly infinite set \(\Lambda\)). Since \(V_i\) is finite dimensional by 2a, there are \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\in\Lambda\) such that \(\mathrm{cl}(z_{\lambda_1}),\dots,\mathrm{cl}(z_{\lambda_r})\) span \(V_i\); we allow \(r=0\) when \(V_i=0\). Set \(m:=\mathrm{lcm}(m_{\lambda_1},\dots,m_{\lambda_r})\) if \(r\ge1\), and \(m:=1\) if \(r=0\). Then \(m\ge1\) and each \(m_{\lambda_s}\mid m\), so \(k_{m_{\lambda_s}}\subset k_m\).

For each \(s\), let \(w_s\in Z^i(X_m)\) be the flat pullback of \(z_{\lambda_s}\) along the morphism \(X_m\to X_{m_{\lambda_s}}\) (base change of the field extension \(k_{m_{\lambda_s}}\hookrightarrow k_m\), hence flat). We claim \(\mathrm{cl}(w_s)=\mathrm{cl}(z_{\lambda_s})\) in \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\). Both classes are classes of cycles on the fixed scheme \(X_k\), and the cycle-class map depends only on the cycle on \(X_k\): by transitivity of flat pullback of cycles (both \(X_m\to X_{m_{\lambda_s}}\) and \(X_k\to X_m\) are flat, and their composite is \(X_k\to X_{m_{\lambda_s}}\)), the pullback of \(w_s\) to \(X_k\) equals the pullback of \(z_{\lambda_s}\) to \(X_k\) as elements of \(Z^i(X_k)\). Hence the classes coincide.

Consequently \(V_i=H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by the classes \(\mathrm{cl}(w_s)\) of codimension-\(i\) cycles \(w_s\) on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) that are defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). (When \(r=0\) this reads \(V_i=0\), which is the same statement with the empty spanning family.)

*2c. Applying lemma_158.* All hypotheses of lemma_158 are satisfied with \(j=i\) and the integer \(m\) just constructed: \(X\) is smooth projective over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), \(\ell\ne p\), \(j\ge0\), \(m\ge1\), and \(H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\) is spanned by classes of codimension-\(j\) cycles on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) (Step 2b). Its conclusion says that \(F^m\) acts as the identity on \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\) and that \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(i))\) and on \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). In particular, \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

(For orientation: the mechanism behind 2c is that each \(w_s\) is fixed by the \(q^m\)-power Frobenius, so \(F^m\) fixes each \(\mathrm{cl}(w_s)\), hence \(F^m=\mathrm{id}\) on \(V_i\); the polynomial \(t^m-1\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\) is separable because \(\operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0\), so \(F\) is semisimple on \(V_i\), and the untwisted statement follows since \(F\) on \(H^{2i}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is \(F\) on \(V_i\) multiplied by the scalar \(q^{-i}\), up to the twist identification. lemma_158 supplies all of this, so we do not reprove it.)
