**Step 3: conclusion.** Every \(n\ge0\) is either odd (Step 1) or of the form \(n=2i\) (Step 2c). Hence \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), which is exactly the claim.

**Remark (relation with the conjecture).** Since \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite dimensional and \(F\) is invertible (lemma_6a gives \(F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F^{-1}\)), lemma_4 shows that geometric Frobenius \(F^{-1}\) also acts semisimply, and lemma_5 shows that this is equivalent to diagonalisability of \(F^{-1}\) on \(H^n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Thus the Frobenius semisimplicity conjecture holds for every \(X\) satisfying the two hypotheses of this lemma.

lemma_177.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be semisimple, that is, have squarefree minimal polynomial over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Then for every integer \(n\ge 1\) the induced automorphism \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n}T\) of \(\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) and the induced automorphism \(\mathrm{Sym}^nT\) of \(\mathrm{Sym}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) are semisimple.
lemma_177.proof:
Let $d=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$, and write $V^{\otimes n}$ for the $n$-fold tensor power of $V$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $T^{\otimes n}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\otimes n})$ for the automorphism determined on pure tensors by
$$T^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=Tv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_n,$$
which is well defined because $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto Tv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_n$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-multilinear; it is invertible with inverse $(T^{-1})^{\otimes n}$. Throughout, $n\ge 1$ is fixed.

**Step 1: $T^{\otimes n}$ is semisimple on $V^{\otimes n}$.**
We argue by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ the claim is the hypothesis on $T$. Assume $n\ge 2$ and that $T^{\otimes (n-1)}$ is semisimple on $V^{\otimes (n-1)}$. The spaces $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ and $V$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, $T^{\otimes(n-1)}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\otimes(n-1)})$ and $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ are both semisimple (squarefree minimal polynomial), and
$$V^{\otimes n}\;=\;V^{\otimes(n-1)}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V,\qquad T^{\otimes n}=T^{\otimes(n-1)}\otimes T$$
(the two sides agree on the spanning set of pure tensors). By lemma_147 (tensor product of two semisimple automorphisms is semisimple) applied with $(V,W,T,S)=(V^{\otimes(n-1)},V,T^{\otimes(n-1)},T)$, the operator $T^{\otimes n}$ is semisimple on $V^{\otimes n}$. This completes the induction.

**Step 2: The exterior power as a $T^{\otimes n}$-stable quotient.**
Let $U_\wedge\subseteq V^{\otimes n}$ be the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace spanned by the tensors $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for which $v_i=v_{i+1}$ for some $i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$.

(a) *Identification with $\bigwedge^n V$.* Let $q_\wedge:V^{\otimes n}\twoheadrightarrow V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge$ be the quotient map and put $v_1\bar\wedge\cdots\bar\wedge v_n:=q_\wedge(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$. The resulting $n$-linear map $\varphi:V^n\to V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge$ vanishes whenever two adjacent arguments are equal, by definition of $U_\wedge$. Since $(v+w)\otimes(v+w)\in U_\wedge$, linearity gives $v\otimes w+w\otimes v\in U_\wedge$, so $\varphi$ is skew-symmetric in each pair of adjacent arguments: $\varphi(\dots,v,w,\dots)=-\varphi(\dots,w,v,\dots)$. The adjacent transpositions $s_i$ generate $S_n$, so by induction on the length of a permutation, $\varphi(v_{\sigma(1)},\dots,v_{\sigma(n)})=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\,\varphi(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ for every $\sigma\in S_n$ (the Coxeter relations are consistent with the sign because $\mathrm{sgn}:S_n\to\{\pm1\}$ is a homomorphism). Hence $\varphi$ vanishes whenever two arguments coincide: if $v_i=v_j$ with $i<j$, the transposition $(i\ j)$ fixes the tuple and has sign $-1$, so $\varphi=-\varphi$, i.e. $2\varphi=0$, and $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q_\ell=0$ forces $\varphi=0$. Thus $\varphi$ is alternating.

Conversely, if $f:V^n\to W$ is any alternating multilinear map into a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $W$, the induced linear map $\tilde f:V^{\otimes n}\to W$ kills every generator of $U_\wedge$, hence kills $U_\wedge$, and so factors uniquely through $q_\wedge$. Thus $V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge$, together with $\varphi$, represents the functor of alternating $n$-linear maps out of $V^n$; by uniqueness of the object representing this functor there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\iota_\wedge:\;V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V,\qquad \iota_\wedge\big(q_\wedge(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\big)=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n.$$
(For $n=1$ one has $U_\wedge=0$ and $\iota_\wedge$ is the identity $V\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigwedge^1V$.)

(b) *Stability.* If $x=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ satisfies $v_i=v_{i+1}=v$, then $T^{\otimes n}x=Tv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_n$ has $(Tv_i)=(Tv)=(Tv_{i+1})$, so $T^{\\otimes n}x$ is again one of the spanning tensors of $U_\wedge$. Since $U_\wedge$ is spanned by such tensors, $T^{\otimes n}(U_\wedge)\subseteq U_\wedge$.

(c) *The induced automorphism is $\bigwedge^n T$.* The subspace $U_\wedge$ is also preserved by $(T^{-1})^{\otimes n}$ by the same argument, so the induced map $\bar T$ on $V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge$ is invertible, with inverse induced by $(T^{-1})^{\otimes n}$. Under $\iota_\wedge$,
$$\iota_\wedge\big(\bar T\,(v_1\bar\wedge\cdots\bar\wedge v_n)\big)=\iota_\wedge\big(Tv_1\bar\wedge\cdots\bar\wedge Tv_n\big)=Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_n=(\textstyle\bigwedge^n T)(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n),$$
so $\iota_\wedge\circ\bar T=(\bigwedge^n T)\circ\iota_\wedge$: $\bar T$ corresponds exactly to $\bigwedge^n T$.

**Step 3: Semisimplicity of $\bigwedge^n T$.**
If $n>d$ then $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=0$ and the assertion is vacuous: the unique operator on the zero space is diagonalisable (empty direct-sum decomposition into eigenspaces). Assume $n\le d$, so $V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge\ne 0$. Apply lemma_145 with $V$ there replaced by the finite-dimensional space $V^{\otimes n}$, with $T$ there replaced by the semisimple automorphism $T^{\otimes n}$ (Step 1), and with $W$ there replaced by the stable subspace $U_\wedge$ (Step 2(b)). Lemma_145 states that the automorphism induced by $T^{\otimes n}$ on the quotient $V^{\otimes n}/U_\wedge$ is semisimple. By Step 2(c) this quotient automorphism is $\bigwedge^n T$ transported along the isomorphism $\iota_\wedge$, and semisimplicity is preserved under transport by an isomorphism (it is the statement that the minimal polynomial is squarefree, which is invariant under conjugation). Hence $\bigwedge^n T$ is semisimple on $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$.

**Step 4: The symmetric power as a $T^{\otimes n}$-stable quotient.**
For $1\le i\le n-1$ let $s_i\in S_n$ be the transposition $(i\ i{+}1)$, acting on $V^{\otimes n}$ by permuting tensor factors: $s_i(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n)=x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{i+1}\otimes x_i\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n$. Let $U_{\mathrm{sym}}\subseteq V^{\otimes n}$ be the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace spanned by all $x-s_i x$ with $x\in V^{\otimes n}$, $1\le i\le n-1$.

(a) *Identification with $\mathrm{Sym}^n V$.* Let $q_{\mathrm{sym}}:V^{\otimes n}\twoheadrightarrow V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and write $v_1\bar v\cdots \bar v v_n:=q_{\mathrm{sym}}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$. By construction the $n$-linear map $\psi:V^n\to V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is invariant under each adjacent transposition; since the $s_i$ generate $S_n$, $\psi$ is $S_n$-invariant, i.e. symmetric. Conversely, any symmetric multilinear $f:V^n\to W$ has associated linear map $\tilde f:V^{\otimes n}\to W$ with $\tilde f(x)=\tilde f(s_i x)$ for all $x,i$, so $\tilde f$ kills $U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and factors uniquely through $q_{\mathrm{sym}}$. Hence $V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ represents the functor of symmetric $n$-linear maps out of $V^n$, and so there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}:\;V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\mathrm{Sym}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V,\qquad \iota_{\mathrm{sym}}\big(q_{\mathrm{sym}}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\big)=v_1\cdots v_n.$$
(For $n=1$, $U_{\mathrm{sym}}=0$ and this is the identity $V\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Sym}^1V$.)

(b) *Stability.* For every $\sigma\in S_n$ one has $T^{\otimes n}\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ T^{\otimes n}$, since both send $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ to $Tv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Tv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}$ (applying $T$ to each factor commutes with permuting the factors). Therefore, for a generator $x-s_i x$ of $U_{\mathrm{sym}}$,
$$T^{\otimes n}(x-s_i x)=T^{\otimes n}x-s_i(T^{\otimes n}x)\in U_{\mathrm{sym}},$$
so $T^{\otimes n}(U_{\mathrm{sym}})\subseteq U_{\mathrm{sym}}$. The same holds for $(T^{-1})^{\otimes n}$, so the induced automorphism $\bar T$ of $V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is invertible.

(c) *The induced automorphism is $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$.* Under $\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}$,
$$\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}\big(\bar T\,(v_1\bar v\cdots\bar v v_n)\big)=\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}(Tv_1\bar v\cdots\bar v Tv_n)=Tv_1\cdots Tv_n=(\mathrm{Sym}^n T)(v_1\cdots v_n),$$
so $\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}\circ\bar T=(\mathrm{Sym}^n T)\circ\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}$.

**Step 5: Semisimplicity of $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$.**
If $V=0$ then $\mathrm{Sym}^nV=0$ and there is nothing to prove, as in Step 3. Otherwise $V^{\otimes n}/U_{\mathrm{sym}}\cong\mathrm{Sym}^nV\ne0$ (the image of $v^{\otimes n}$ for $v\ne0$ is nonzero, as follows from the basis description of $\mathrm{Sym}^nV$). Applying lemma_145 to the semisimple $T^{\otimes n}$ on $V^{\otimes n}$ and the stable subspace $U_{\mathrm{sym}}$ (Steps 1 and 4(b)), the induced quotient automorphism $\bar T$ is semisimple; transporting along $\iota_{\mathrm{sym}}$ (Step 4(c)) and using invariance of squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial under conjugation, $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$ is semisimple on $\mathrm{Sym}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$.

**Step 6: Explicit description of the spectra (consistency check / independent argument).**
Let $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $W=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$, $\widetilde T=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$. By lemma_5, $T$ semisimple on $V$ is equivalent to $\widetilde T$ diagonalisable on $W$. Choose a $\widetilde T$-eigenbasis $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $W$, with $\widetilde T e_i=\alpha_i e_i$; the $\alpha_i$ are nonzero since $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$. Extension of scalars commutes with forming exterior and symmetric powers: the natural maps $(\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)\otimes K\to\bigwedge^n_K W$ and $(\mathrm{Sym}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)\otimes K\to\mathrm{Sym}^n_K W$ are isomorphisms, which one checks on the standard bases: if $E=\{e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}:i_1<\cdots<i_n\}$ is the basis of $\bigwedge^n_K W$ and $S=\{e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_n}:i_1\le\cdots\le i_n\}$ that of $\mathrm{Sym}^n_K W$, both sets lie in the image of the base-changed spaces and have cardinality $\binom dn$ and $\binom{d+n-1}{n}$ respectively, which are the dimensions of $(\bigwedge^n V)\otimes K$ and $(\mathrm{Sym}^n V)\otimes K$; hence the maps are isomorphisms. Under these identifications $\bigwedge^n\widetilde T$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^n\widetilde T$ are the base changes of $\bigwedge^n T$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$, and
$$\textstyle\bigwedge^n\widetilde T\,(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n})=\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_n}\;e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n},\qquad \mathrm{Sym}^n\widetilde T\,(e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_n})=\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_n}\;e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_n},$$
so $E$ and $S$ are eigenbases: $\bigwedge^n\widetilde T$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^n\widetilde T$ are diagonalisable over $K$. By lemma_5 in the reverse direction, $\bigwedge^n T$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$ are semisimple over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, in agreement with Steps 3 and 5.

Combining Steps 3 and 5, for every $n\ge1$ both $\bigwedge^n T$ on $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^n T$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ are semisimple. $\blacksquare$

lemma_hom_colimit_fp.statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty directed partially ordered set (every two elements have an upper bound) and let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a direct system of rings with colimit $A=\varinjlim_{i\in I}A_i$. Let $i_0\in I$, let $M$ be a finitely presented $A_{i_0}$-module, and let $(N_i)_{i\ge i_0}$ be a direct system of modules over the directed system of rings $(A_i)_{i\ge i_0}$, with colimit $N=\varinjlim_{i\ge i_0}N_i$. Writing $M_i=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A_i$ and $M_A=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A$, the natural homomorphism\[\varinjlim_{i\ge i_0}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{A}(M_A,N)\]is an isomorphism of abelian groups.
lemma_hom_colimit_fp.proof:
We prove the statement as written, i.e. for a **directed partially ordered set** $I$. Conventions: all rings are commutative with $1$ and all ring maps preserve $1$; all modules are unital. (Nothing in the argument uses commutativity: for non-commutative rings one reads every module as a right module, $M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A_i$ as the usual balanced tensor product, and the same proofs go through verbatim.) For $i\le j$ we write $\iota_{ij}:A_i\to A_j$ for the transition maps, $\mu_{ij}:N_i\to N_j$ for the transition maps of the module system (so $\mu_{ij}(an)=\iota_{ij}(a)\mu_{ij}(n)$), $\kappa_i:A_i\to A$ and $\tau_i:N_i\to N$ for the colimit maps, and $\nu_{ij}:M_i\to M_j$ for $1\otimes\iota_{ij}$.

=====================================================================
STEP 0. Colimits over a directed poset of abelian groups.
Let $(B_i,\beta_{ij})_{i\in J}$ be a direct system of abelian groups over a nonempty directed poset $J$.

(0a) *Explicit construction.* On the disjoint union $\coprod_{i\in J}B_i$ define $x_i\in B_i\sim x_{i'}\in B_{i'}$ iff there is $i''\in J$ with $i''\ge i,i'$ and $\beta_{ii''}(x_i)=\beta_{i'i''}(x_{i'})$. Reflexivity is trivial ($i'':=i$), symmetry is clear. For transitivity, if $x_i\sim x_{i'}$ via $l\ge i,i'$ and $x_{i'}\sim x_k$ via $m\ge i',k$, choose $n\ge l,m$ (directedness); then $\beta_{in}x_i=\beta_{ln}\beta_{il}x_i=\beta_{ln}\beta_{i'l}x_{i'}=\beta_{i'n}x_{i'}=\beta_{mn}\beta_{i'm}x_{i'}=\beta_{mn}\beta_{km}x_k=\beta_{kn}x_k$, so $x_i\sim x_k$. Thus $\sim$ is an equivalence relation; write $[x_i]$ for the class of $x_i$ and $B$ for the quotient set.

(0b) *Group structure.* For $[x_i],[y_{i'}]$ choose $n\ge i,i'$ and set $[x_i]+[y_{i'}]:=[\beta_{in}x_i+\beta_{i'n}y_{i'}]$. This is independent of the choices: if $n'\ge i,i'$ is another choice and $p\ge n,n'$, then $\beta_{np}(\beta_{in}x_i+\beta_{i'n}y_{i'})=\beta_{n'p}(\beta_{in'}x_i+\beta_{i'n'}y_{i'})$ by the system axioms, so the two sums are equivalent; and if $\tilde x_{\tilde i}\sim x_i$, $\tilde y_{\tilde i'}\sim y_{i'}$, choose $q$ simultaneously equalising $x_i,\tilde x_{\tilde i}$ and $y_{i'},\tilde y_{\tilde i'}$ (take an upper bound of the two equalising indices), then the two resulting sums agree at stage $q$. Abelian-group axioms hold (zero is $[0_i]$, $-[x_i]=[-x_i]$), and each $\beta_i:B_i\to B$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a homomorphism with $\beta_j\beta_{ij}=\beta_i$.

(0c) *Elementary properties.* (i) The $\beta_i$ are jointly surjective (every element is some $[x_i]$). (ii) $\beta_i(x_i)=0\iff$ there is $i''\ge i$ with $\beta_{ii''}(x_i)=0$ (since $[x_i]=[0_i]$ means precisely equality at some later stage). (iii) *Universal property:* given homomorphisms $f_i:B_i\to T$ with $f_j\beta_{ij}=f_i$ for all $i\le j$, there is a unique homomorphism $f:B\to T$ with $f\beta_i=f_i$: define $f([x_i]):=f_i(x_i)$; if $\beta_{ii''}x_i=\beta_{i'i''}x_{i'}$ then $f_i(x_i)=f_{i''}\beta_{ii''}x_i=f_{i''}\beta_{i'i''}x_{i'}=f_{i'}(x_{i'})$, so $f$ is well defined; it is a homomorphism by (0b); uniqueness holds by (i).

(0d) *Exactness.* Let $f_\bullet:B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to D_\bullet\to 0$ be a levelwise exact sequence of systems over $J$ (so $C_i\to D_i\to0$ is exact and $\operatorname{im}(B_i\to C_i)=\ker(C_i\to D_i)$), natural in $i$. Then $\varinjlim B\to\varinjlim C\to\varinjlim D\to0$ is exact. Surjectivity of $\varinjlim C\to\varinjlim D$: an element of $\varinjlim D$ is $[d_i]$, lift to $c_i\in C_i$, then $[c_i]\mapsto[d_i]$. Kernel containment: if $[c_i]\mapsto0$, then $[f_i(c_i)]=0$ in $\varinjlim D$, so by (0c)(ii) there is $k\ge i$ with $\beta^D_{ik}f_i(c_i)=0$, i.e. $f_k\beta^C_{ik}(c_i)=0$; hence $\beta^C_{ik}(c_i)=g_k(b_k)$ for some $b_k\in B_k$, and then $[c_i]=[ eta^C_{ik}(c_i)]=[g_k(b_k)]$ is the image of $[b_k]$. Finally, if $g_\bullet:B_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ is levelwise **injective**, then $\varinjlim g$ is injective: $[g_i(b_i)]=0$ gives $g_k\beta^B_{ik}(b_i)=\beta^C_{ik}g_i(b_i)=0$ for some $k\ge i$, so $\beta^B_{ik}(b_i)=0$, so $[b_i]=0$. Combining, $\varinjlim$ is an exact functor on systems of abelian groups over a directed poset.

(0e) *Finite powers.* For each $r\ge1$ the maps $\beta_i^{\oplus r}:B_i^{\oplus r}\to(\varinjlim_jB_j)^{\oplus r}$ induce an isomorphism $\varinjlim_i B_i^{\oplus r}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (\varinjlim_iB_i)^{\oplus r}$. Surjectivity: an element $([x^{(1)}],\dots,[x^{(r)}])$ has representatives $x^{(a)}\in B_{i_a}$; choose $n\ge i_1,\dots,i_r$ (directedness, iterated) and take the class of $(\beta_{i_1n}x^{(1)},\dots,\beta_{i_rn}x^{(r)})\in B_n^{\oplus r}$. Injectivity: if the class of $(x_1,\dots,x_r)\in B_i^{\oplus r}$ maps to $0$, then each $\beta_i(x_a)=0$, so by (0c)(ii) there are $k_a\ge i$ with $\beta_{ik_a}(x_a)=0$; for an upper bound $k$ of the $k_a$'s, $\beta^{\oplus r}_{ik}(x_1,\dots,x_r)=0$, so the class is $0$.

(No equaliser axiom was used anywhere above: only the existence of upper bounds, which is what directedness of a poset supplies. Note also that for a poset there is at most one arrow $i\to j$, so all transition maps and all $A_{i_0}$-algebra structures below are unambiguous.)

=====================================================================
STEP 1. Cofinality of $I_{\ge i_0}$ and reduction to the case where $i_0$ is the least index.
Put $J:=\{i\in I:i\ge i_0\}$. Then $J$ is nonempty ($i_0\in J$) and directed: for $a,b\in J$ choose an upper bound $c\in I$; then $c\ge a\ge i_0$, so $c\in J$. Every $j\in I$ has an upper bound lying in $J$ (take an upper bound of $j$ and $i_0$). We claim the inclusion $J\hookrightarrow I$ induces a canonical isomorphism of rings $u:\varinjlim_{i\in J}A_i\xrightarrow{\sim}A=\varinjlim_{i\in I}A_i$.

Write $\beta_i:A_i\to B:=\varinjlim_{J}A_i$ for the $J$-colimit maps and $\kappa_i:A_i\to A$ for the $I$-colimit maps. The family $(\kappa_i)_{i\in J}$ is compatible, so by (0c)(iii) (applied to underlying sets/groups of rings) there is a unique ring map $u:B\to A$ with $u\beta_i=\kappa_i$ for $i\in J$. For the inverse, define for each $j\in I$ a map $g_j:A_j\to B$ as follows: choose any $i\in J$ with $i\ge j$ and set $g_j:=\beta_i\circ\iota_{ji}$. This is independent of the choice: if $i,i'\in J$ both satisfy $\ge j$ and $i''\in J$ satisfies $i''\ge i,i'$, then $\beta_i\iota_{ji}=\beta_{i''}\iota_{i i''}\iota_{ji}=\beta_{i''}\iota_{ji''}=\beta_{i''}\iota_{i'i''}\iota_{ji'}=\beta_{i'}\iota_{ji'}$ (no cancellation is needed). The family $(g_j)_{j\in I}$ is compatible: for $j\le j'$ in $I$, choose $i\in J$ with $i\ge j'$ (then also $i\ge j$); then $g_{j'}=\beta_i\iota_{j'i}$ and $g_j=\beta_i\iota_{ji}=\beta_i\iota_{j'i}\iota_{jj'}=g_{j'}\iota_{jj'}$. Hence by (0c)(iii) there is a unique ring map $v:A\to B$ with $v\kappa_j=g_j$ for all $j\in I$. Now $v\circ u=\mathrm{id}_B$ because for $i\in J$, $vu\beta_i=v\kappa_i=g_i=\beta_i$ (using $i$ itself as the chosen index above $i$), and the $\beta_i$ ($i\in J$) are jointly surjective by (0c)(i). Similarly $u\circ v=\mathrm{id}_A$ because for $j\in I$, $uv\kappa_j=u g_j=u\beta_i\iota_{ji}=\kappa_i\iota_{ji}=\kappa_j$ for any $i\in J$ with $i\ge j$, and the $\kappa_j$ are jointly surjective. So $u$ is an isomorphism.

Under $u$ the $A_{i_0}$-algebra structures agree: $u\beta_{i_0}=\kappa_{i_0}$. Consequently $M_A:=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A$ is canonically $M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}B$, the modules $M_i=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A_i$ for $i\ge i_0$ are unchanged, the system $(N_i)_{i\ge i_0}$ is unchanged, and $N=\varinjlim_{i\ge i_0}N_i$ is an $A$-module through $u$ exactly as before. Therefore, **replacing $I$ by $J$, we may and shall assume from now on that $I$ has a least element $i_0$**; in particular every $A_i$ ($i\ge i_0$) carries one canonical $A_{i_0}$-algebra structure $\iota_{i_0i}$, and $A$ is an $A_{i_0}$-algebra via $\kappa_{i_0}$. All $A_i$-modules below are $A_{i_0}$-modules by restriction of scalars, and each $\mu_{ij}$ is $A_{i_0}$-linear since $\mu_{ij}(\iota_{i_0i}(c)n)=\iota_{ij}\iota_{i_0i}(c)\mu_{ij}(n)=\iota_{i_0j}(c)\mu_{ij}(n)$.

=====================================================================
STEP 2. The direct system $\big(\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\big)_{i\in I}$.
Each $M_i=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A_i$ is an $A_i$-module, generated as such by the image of $\eta_i:M\to M_i$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$ (an elementary tensor is $\sum_k m_k\otimes a_k=\sum_k(m_k\otimes1)a_k$). For $i\le j$ define $\theta_{ij}:\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{A_j}(M_j,N_j)$ by
$$\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes a):=a\,\mu_{ij}\big(\varphi(m\otimes1)\big)\qquad(m\in M,\ a\in A_j).$$
*Well-definedness.* The map $M\times A_j\to N_j$, $(m,a)\mapsto a\,\mu_{ij}(\varphi(m\otimes1))$, is biadditive and $A_{i_0}$-balanced: for $c\in A_{i_0}$, using $A_i$-linearity of $\varphi$ (with $c$ acting on $M_i$ through $\iota_{i_0i}$) and $A_{i_0}$-linearity of $\mu_{ij}$,
$$\mu_{ij}\big(\varphi(mc\otimes1)\big)=\mu_{ij}\big(c\,\varphi(m\otimes1)\big)=c\,\mu_{ij}\varphi(m\otimes1),$$
so $(mc,a)$ and $(m,ca)$ have the same image. Hence it descends to an additive map $M_j\to N_j$, which is $A_j$-linear by construction ($b\cdot\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes a)=\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes ba)$). It is the unique $A_j$-linear map $\psi$ with $\psi\nu_{ij}=\mu_{ij}\varphi$, because $\nu_{ij}(m\otimes1)=m\otimes1$ and $M_j$ is generated by such elements; existence is what we just built.
*System axioms.* $\theta_{ii}=\mathrm{id}$ because $\theta_{ii}(\varphi)$ and $\varphi$ are $A_i$-linear maps $M_i\to N_i$ with $\theta_{ii}(\varphi)\nu_{ii}=\mu_{ii}\varphi=\varphi$ and $\nu_{ii}=\mathrm{id}$. For $i\le j\le l$, $\theta_{jl}\theta_{ij}(\varphi)$ and $\theta_{il}(\varphi)$ are $A_l$-maps $M_l\to N_l$ and
$$\theta_{jl}\theta_{ij}(\varphi)\,\nu_{jl}\nu_{ij}=\mu_{jl}\theta_{ij}(\varphi)\nu_{ij}=\mu_{jl}\mu_{ij}\varphi=\mu_{il}\varphi=\theta_{il}(\varphi)\nu_{il},$$
with $\nu_{jl}\nu_{ij}=\nu_{il}$; by the uniqueness just noted, $\theta_{jl}\theta_{ij}=\theta_{il}$. Thus $\big(\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i),\theta_{ij}\big)$ is a direct system of abelian groups over the directed poset $I$ (each $\theta_{ij}$ is plainly a group homomorphism). Let $\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i$ denote its colimit maps.

=====================================================================
STEP 3. Stage-wise adjunction, as an isomorphism of systems.
Define
$$\alpha_i:\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i),\qquad \alpha_i(\varphi)=\varphi\circ\eta_i .$$
This is a group homomorphism. Its inverse is
$$\beta_i:\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i),\qquad \beta_i(\psi)(m\otimes a):=a\,\psi(m),$$
which is well defined by the identical balanced-map computation as in Step 2. Then $\beta_i\alpha_i(\varphi)(m\otimes a)=a\,\varphi(m\otimes1)=\varphi\big((m\otimes1)a\big)=\varphi(m\otimes a)$, so $\beta_i\alpha_i=\mathrm{id}$; and $\alpha_i\beta_i(\psi)(m)=\beta_i(\psi)(m\otimes1)=1\cdot\psi(m)=\psi(m)$, so $\alpha_i\beta_i=\mathrm{id}$. Hence $\alpha_i$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups.

*Compatibility with transitions.* Let $\mu_{ij*}:\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_j)$ be post-composition with $\mu_{ij}$ (a group homomorphism, natural in $i,j$). For $\varphi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)$ and $m\in M$,
$$\alpha_j\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m)=\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes1)=1\cdot\mu_{ij}\varphi(m\otimes1)=\mu_{ij*}\alpha_i(\varphi)(m),$$
using $\eta_j=\nu_{ij}\eta_i$. Thus $\alpha_j\theta_{ij}=\mu_{ij*}\alpha_i$ for all $i\le j$: the $\alpha_i$ constitute an isomorphism of direct systems $\big(\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\big)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\big(\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\big)$ over $I$. By the universal property (0c)(iii) applied to the target system, the colimit maps $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\to\varinjlim_k\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_k)$ composed with the $\alpha_i$ give compatible maps, hence a unique homomorphism
$$\overline\alpha:\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\longrightarrow\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i),\qquad \overline\alpha\,\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i=\kappa^{\prime}_i\,\alpha_i ,$$
and since the $\alpha_i^{-1}$ likewise satisfy $\alpha_i^{-1}\mu_{ij*}=\theta_{ij}\alpha_j^{-1}$ (invert the displayed relation), the same construction gives a two-sided inverse $\overline\alpha^{-1}$. Concretely, $\overline\alpha$ is an isomorphism because it is bijective on the explicit models of (0a)-(0b): an element of the source is a class $[\varphi]$ with $\varphi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)$, and $[\varphi]=[\varphi']$ iff $\theta_{ik}(\varphi)=\theta_{i'k}(\varphi')$ for some $k\ge i,i'$, which by the intertwining relation is equivalent to $\mu_{ik*}\alpha_i(\varphi)=\mu_{i'k*}\alpha_{i'}(\varphi')$, i.e. $[\alpha_i\varphi]=[\alpha_{i'}\varphi']$.

=====================================================================
STEP 4. Hom out of a finitely presented module commutes with the filtered colimit.
Because $M$ is **finitely presented** over $A_{i_0}$, there is an exact sequence
$$A_{i_0}^{\oplus p}\xrightarrow{\ u\ }A_{i_0}^{\oplus q}\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0\qquad(p,q<\infty).$$
For each $i$, applying the left-exact contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(-,N_i)$ yields an exact sequence of abelian groups
$$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(A_{i_0}^{\oplus q},N_i)\xrightarrow{\ u^*\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(A_{i_0}^{\oplus p},N_i),$$
where $u^*(f)=f\circ u$. Identifying $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(A_{i_0}^{\oplus r},N_i)\cong N_i^{\oplus r}$ via $f\mapsto(f(e_1),\dots,f(e_r))$, the map $u^*$ becomes $(n_1,\dots,n_q)\mapsto\big(\sum_a n_au_{a1},\dots,\sum_an_au_{ap}\big)$ where $u(e_b)=(u_{1b},\dots,u_{qb})$. These identifications are natural in $i$: $\mu_{ij*}$ corresponds to $\mu_{ij}^{\oplus r}$, because $\mu_{ij}$ is $A_{i_0}$-linear; and $u^*$ then commutes with the transitions. Hence we have an exact sequence of direct systems over $I$
$$0\longrightarrow\big(\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\big)_i\longrightarrow\big(N_i^{\oplus q}\big)_i\xrightarrow{\ u^*\ }\big(N_i^{\oplus p}\big)_i .$$
By (0d) (exactness of filtered colimits over a directed poset) and (0e) (colimit commutes with the finite power $\oplus r$, used to identify $\varinjlim_iN_i^{\oplus r}\cong N^{\oplus r}$), passing to colimits gives an exact sequence of abelian groups
$$0\longrightarrow\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\longrightarrow N^{\oplus q}\xrightarrow{\ u^*\ }N^{\oplus p},$$
where $N$ is an $A_{i_0}$-module via $A_{i_0}\to A$, and the right-hand map is again precomposition with $u$ under $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(A_{i_0}^{\oplus r},N)\cong N^{\oplus r}$. Applying the same left-exactness at the limit to $A_{i_0}^{\oplus p}\to A_{i_0}^{\oplus q}\to M\to0$ gives $\ker(u^*:N^{\oplus q}\to N^{\oplus p})=\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N)$. Therefore there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\gamma:\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N),\qquad \gamma\big([\psi_i]\big)=\big(m\mapsto\tau_i(\psi_i(m))\big),$$
i.e. $\gamma$ is induced by the maps $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N_i)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N)$, $\psi\mapsto\tau_i\psi$; the description of the image of $\gamma$ as the kernel above shows it is an isomorphism, and the explicit formula follows because $\ker(u^*)$ consists exactly of the tuples $([n_1],\dots,[n_q])$ satisfying the relations, which is how $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N)$ sits in $N^{\oplus q}$.

Composing Steps 3 and 4 we obtain an isomorphism of abelian groups
$$\Psi:=\alpha_A^{-1}\circ\gamma\circ\overline\alpha:\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(M_A,N),$$
where $\alpha_A$ is the map of Step 5 next.

=====================================================================
STEP 5. Adjunction at the limit.
With $\eta:M\to M_A=M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, the same proof as in Step 3 gives an isomorphism of abelian groups
$$\alpha_A:\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(M_A,N)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{i_0}}(M,N),\qquad \alpha_A(\varphi)=\varphi\circ\eta,\qquad \alpha_A^{-1}(\psi)(m\otimes a)=a\,\psi(m),$$
where $N$ is an $A$-module (the colimit $N=\varinjlim_iN_i$ over $A=\varinjlim_iA_i$, with $a\cdot[n_i]:=[\,\iota_{ik}(a)\,\mu_{ik}(n_i)\,]$ for $k\ge i$ large enough to represent $a\in A_k$; this is well defined by exactly the same directedness argument as in (0b)).

=====================================================================
STEP 6. Identification of $\Psi$ with the natural homomorphism.
Define the **natural homomorphism** $\Phi:\varinjlim_i\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(M_A,N)$ as follows. At stage $i$, the $A$-algebra map $\iota_{iA}:A_i\to A$ gives the base-change isomorphism $M_A\cong M_i\otimes_{A_i}A$ (both are $M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A$; explicitly $m\otimes_{A_{i_0}}a\leftrightarrow(m\otimes_{A_{i_0}}1)\otimes_A a$). For $\varphi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)$ set
$$\Phi_i(\varphi):\;M_A\cong M_i\otimes_{A_i}A\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\otimes1\ }N_i\otimes_{A_i}A\xrightarrow{\ \rho_i\ }N,\qquad \rho_i(n\otimes a)=a\,\tau_i(n).$$
$\rho_i$ is well defined and $A$-linear: for $b\in A_i$, $\rho_i(nb\otimes a)=a\,\tau_i(nb)=a\,\kappa_i(b)\tau_i(n)$ (because $\tau_i$ is $A_i$-linear with $A$ acting on $N$ through $\kappa_i$) and $\rho_i(n\otimes ba)=(ba)\tau_i(n)=\kappa_i(b)a\,\tau_i(n)$, which agree; $A$-linearity in the second factor is immediate. Each $\Phi_i$ is a group homomorphism, and the family $\Phi_i$ is compatible with the transitions: for $i\le j$ one checks $\Phi_j\theta_{ij}=\Phi_i$ by evaluating on generators — for $m\in M$, $a\in A$,
$$\Phi_j\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes a)=a\,\tau_j\theta_{ij}(\varphi)(m\otimes1)=a\,\tau_j\mu_{ij}\varphi(m\otimes1)=a\,\tau_i\varphi(m\otimes1)=\Phi_i(\varphi)(m\otimes a),$$
where we used $\tau_j\mu_{ij}=\tau_i$ and the definition of $\theta_{ij}$ in Step 2; since $M_A$ is generated as an $A$-module by the elements $m\otimes1$, the two $A$-linear maps agree. By the universal property (0c)(iii) there is a unique homomorphism $\Phi$ with $\Phi\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i=\Phi_i$ for all $i$; this is the natural homomorphism of the statement.

Now take $\varphi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}(M_i,N_i)$. Tracing it through $\Psi$:
$\ \overline\alpha(\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i\varphi)=[\alpha_i\varphi]=[\varphi\eta_i]\ $, then $\ \gamma[\varphi\eta_i]=\big(m\mapsto\tau_i\varphi(m\otimes1)\big)\ $, and finally by Step 5
$$\Psi\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i(\varphi)(m\otimes a)=a\,\tau_i\varphi(m\otimes1)\qquad\text{for all }m\in M,\ a\in A.$$
But the right-hand side is exactly $\Phi_i(\varphi)(m\otimes a)$ computed above. Hence $\Psi\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i=\Phi_i=\Phi\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i$ for every $i$, and since the colimit maps $\kappa^{\mathrm{Hom}}_i$ are jointly surjective by (0c)(i), $\Psi=\Phi$.

(Note that this computation moves strictly forward in the index: an element of $M_A$ is written as $m\otimes a$ with $a\in A_i$ at the *same* stage $i$ at which $\varphi$ lives, and no structure map $A_j\to A_k$ for $k\ge j$ running backwards is ever used.)

=====================================================================
CONCLUSION.
$\Phi=\Psi$ is a composition of isomorphisms of abelian groups, hence is an isomorphism
$$\varinjlim_{i\ge i_0}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_i}\big(M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A_i,\,N_i\big)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{A}\big(M\otimes_{A_{i_0}}A,\,N\big),$$
which is precisely the natural homomorphism of the lemma. The only properties of the index set used are that $I_{\ge i_0}$ is a directed poset (so that $M_i$ and all transition maps are unambiguously defined, and Steps 0–6 apply) and that $I_{\ge i_0}$ is cofinal in $I$ in the sense of Step 1 (so that $\varinjlim_{i\ge i_0}A_i\cong\varinjlim_{i\in I}A_i=A$); finite generation of the relation module is what makes $p,q$ finite, so that (0e) applies, and this is exactly where finite presentation of $M$ is used. This completes the proof.

lemma_181.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime and let \(A\) be a finitely generated abelian group. For \(n\ge 1\) write \(A[\ell^n]=\ker(\ell^n:A\to A)\), and give the groups \(A[\ell^n]\) the structure of an inverse system via the bonding maps \(A[\ell^{n+1}]\to A[\ell^n]\) given by multiplication by \(\ell\). Then \(\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n]=0\).
lemma_181.proof:
We prove the statement from elementary group theory; no external input is needed, so the proof cites no previously proved lemma.

Throughout, \(\ell\) is a fixed prime and \(A\) is a finitely generated abelian group. For an abelian group \(B\) write
\[ T(B):=B[\ell^{\infty}]=\bigcup_{n\ge 1}B[\ell^{n}] \]
for its \(\ell\)-primary torsion subgroup, and write \(\varprojlim_n B[\ell^{n}]\) for the limit of the system whose bonding maps \(B[\ell^{n+1}]\to B[\ell^{n}]\) are multiplication by \(\ell\).

**Step 0 (the system is well defined).** If \(x\in B[\ell^{n+1}]\) then \(\ell^{n}(\ell x)=\ell^{n+1}x=0\), so \(\ell x\in B[\ell^{n}]\); hence multiplication by \(\ell\) really does give a homomorphism \(B[\ell^{n+1}]\to B[\ell^{n}]\). By induction on \(m-n\), the composite transition map
\[ \varphi_{n,m}:B[\ell^{m}]\longrightarrow B[\ell^{n}],\qquad m\ge n\ge 1, \]
obtained by chaining the bonding maps, is multiplication by \(\ell^{\,m-n}\).

**Step 1 (\(T(A)\) is a subgroup).** If \(x,y\in T(A)\) then \(\ell^{r}x=0\) and \(\ell^{s}y=0\) for some \(r,s\ge 1\), so \(\ell^{\max(r,s)}(x\pm y)=0\); thus \(x\pm y\in T(A)\). Also, if \(a\in A\) satisfies \(\ell^{n}a\in T(A)\), say \(\ell^{k}\ell^{n}a=0\), then \(a\in T(A)\); i.e. \(A/T(A)\) has no non-trivial \(\ell\)-power torsion.

**Step 2 (the \(\ell\)-primary torsion of a finitely generated group has bounded exponent).**

*Claim.* If \(A\) is generated by \(m\) elements, there is an integer \(N\ge 1\) with \(\ell^{N}T(A)=0\).

*Proof of the claim,* by induction on \(m\).

- \(m=0\): then \(A=0\), so \(T(A)=0\) and any \(N\ge 1\) works.
- Inductive step, \(m\ge 1\): write \(A=\langle a_1,\dots,a_m\rangle\), let \(A'=\langle a_1,\dots,a_{m-1}\rangle\) and let \(C=A/A'\), which is cyclic, generated by \(\bar a_m\). By induction there is \(N'\ge 1\) with \(\ell^{N'}T(A')=0\).

  The group \(C\) is either \(\mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z\) with \(d\ge 1\). Set
  \[ \nu:=\begin{cases}0,&C\simeq\mathbb Z,\\ v_{\ell}(d),&C\simeq\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z,\end{cases} \]
  where \(v_{\ell}(d)\ge 0\) is the \(\ell\)-adic valuation of \(d\) (so \(\nu=0\) when \(\gcd(d,\ell)=1\)). In both cases \(\ell^{\nu}\) kills \(T(C)\): if \(C\simeq\mathbb Z\) then \(T(C)=0\); if \(C\simeq\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z\) then \(T(C)=C[\ell^{\nu}]\simeq\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu}\mathbb Z\), which is killed by \(\ell^{\nu}\).

  Now take \(t\in T(A)\). Its image \(\bar t\in C\) is \(\ell\)-power torsion, so \(\ell^{\nu}\bar t=0\), i.e. \(\ell^{\nu}t\in A'\). Since also \(\ell^{\nu}t\in T(A)\), we get \(\ell^{\nu}t\in T(A)\cap A'=T(A')\). Hence \(\ell^{N'}\ell^{\nu}t=0\), i.e. \(\ell^{N'+\nu}t=0\). Taking \(N:=N'+\nu\ge 1\) proves the claim. \(\diamond\)

(One may also obtain Step 2 from the structure theorem \(A\simeq\mathbb Z^{r}\oplus F\) with \(F\) finite: then \(T(A)=T(F)\) is killed by \(|F|\). The argument above is included so the proof is self-contained.)

**Step 3 (identification of the levels).** For every \(n\ge 1\) we have
\[ A[\ell^{n}]=T(A)[\ell^{n}]. \]
Indeed, \(A[\ell^{n}]\subseteq T(A)\) by definition of \(T(A)\), and elements of \(T(A)[\ell^{n}]=\{t\in T(A):\ell^{n}t=0\}\) are, a fortiori, elements of \(A[\ell^{n}]\). Thus the system \(\{A[\ell^{n}]\}\) depends only on the \(\ell\)-primary torsion subgroup, which has bounded exponent.

**Step 4 (the transition maps are eventually zero).** Fix \(N\ge 1\) with \(\ell^{N}T(A)=0\) (Step 2). Let \(m\ge n+N\). For any \(x\in A[\ell^{m}]=T(A)[\ell^{m}]\subseteq T(A)\), Step 0 gives
\[ \varphi_{n,m}(x)=\ell^{\,m-n}x=\ell^{\,m-n-N}\big(\ell^{N}x\big)=0, \]
because \(\ell^{N}x=0\) as \(x\in T(A)\) and \(m-n\ge N\). Hence
\[ \varphi_{n,m}=0\quad\text{for all }m\ge n+N,\ \text{all }n\ge 1. \tag{$*$} \]

**Step 5 (vanishing of the limit).** The limit is the subgroup of the product
\[ \varprojlim_{n}A[\ell^{n}]=\Big\{(x_n)_{n\ge 1}\in\prod_{n\ge 1}A[\ell^{n}]:\ \varphi_{n,m}(x_m)=x_n\ \text{for all }m\ge n\ge 1\Big\}. \]
Let \((x_n)\) be an element. Fix \(n\ge 1\) and put \(m:=n+N\). By \((*)\), \(\varphi_{n,n+N}=0\), so
\[ x_n=\varphi_{n,n+N}(x_{n+N})=0. \]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary, \((x_n)=0\). The limit is therefore the trivial group:
\[ \varprojlim_{n}A[\ell^{n}]=0. \]

**Step 6 (edge cases, checked explicitly).**
- If \(A\) has no non-trivial \(\ell\)-power torsion (e.g. \(A=\mathbb Z^{r}\)), then \(T(A)=0\), so \(A[\ell^{n}]=0\) for all \(n\) by Step 3 and the limit is trivially \(0\). This is consistent with Step 4, where one may take \(N=1\).
- If \(A\) is a finite \(\ell\)-group of exponent \(\ell^{N}\) (e.g. \(A=\mathbb Z/\ell^{N}\mathbb Z\)), then the groups \(A[\ell^{n}]\) stabilise to \(A\) for \(n\ge N\), yet the transition maps \(A[\ell^{n+N}]\to A[\ell^{n}]\), i.e. multiplication by \(\ell^{N}\), are zero; so again the limit is \(0\). Note that the bonding maps themselves need not be zero (e.g. for \(A=\mathbb Z/\ell^{2}\mathbb Z\) the map \(A[\ell^{2}]\to A[\ell^{1}]\) is multiplication by \(\ell\neq 0\)); what the argument uses is only that the *sufficiently far* transition maps vanish, which is exactly the Mittag-Leffler condition with trivial stable images.
- If \(A\) is finitely generated but not \(\ell\)-primary torsion, Step 2 still supplies a single uniform bound \(N\) for the whole torsion subgroup, which is why a single \(N\) works simultaneously at every level \(n\) in Step 4.

This completes the proof that \(\varprojlim_{n}A[\ell^{n}]=0\) for every finitely generated abelian group \(A\) and every prime \(\ell\). \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_179.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(G\) be a finite group of \(\mathbb F_q\)-automorphisms of \(Y\) whose order is prime to \(\ell\). Let \(\pi:Y\to Z:=Y/G\) be the quotient morphism, with \(Z\) smooth projective over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), denote the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on the étale cohomology of \(Y_k\) and of \(Z_k\). If \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_179.proof:
Proof. Let k = overline(F_q). Put V = H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l), W = H^n_et(Z_k,Q_l), and let F_Y and F_Z denote the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of V and W. By lemma_45_finite_frob these vector spaces are finite-dimensional, and by lemma_6a the operators F_Y and F_Z are invertible Q_l-linear automorphisms.

1. Finite geometric quotient. We use the standard finite-group quotient theorem for quasi-projective schemes over a field: if a finite group G acts on a quasi-projective scheme Y, then the quotient Z=Y/G exists, the quotient map pi:Y->Z is finite, and pi is a geometric quotient, i.e. for every geometric point z:Spec(Omega)->Z the underlying set of the fibre Y_z is a single G-orbit. For reference, the theorem follows by covering Y by G-stable affine opens Spec(A) (using a G-linearised ample line bundle); on such an open the quotient is Spec(A^G), A is integral and finite over A^G, and the map disjoint union_g Spec(A) -> Spec(A tensor_{A^G} A) is finite and surjective, which gives the orbit statement after arbitrary base change. Applying the theorem to Y_k and the base-changed action gives that pi_k:Y_k->Z_k is finite and geometric.

2. Leray for a finite morphism. Let F = pi_{k,*}Q_l. Since pi_k is finite, R^i pi_{k,*}Q_l=0 for i>0. Indeed, at a geometric point z the stalk of R^i pi_{k,*}Q_l is H^i(Y_z,Q_l), and Y_z is a finite disjoint union of strictly henselian local schemes, whose positive étale cohomology with constant Q_l coefficients vanishes. Hence the Leray edge map gives a canonical G-equivariant isomorphism
lambda: H^n(Z_k,F) -> H^n(Y_k,Q_l)=V.

3. The invariant part of pi_{k,*}Q_l. The unit map u:Q_l -> F is G-invariant. At a geometric point z we have F_z = Map(|Y_z|,Q_l), and u sends a scalar to the corresponding constant function. Since taking stalks commutes with the finite limit defining G-invariants, (F^G)_z = F_z^G. Because Y_z is a single G-orbit, the G-invariant functions on |Y_z| are exactly the constant functions. Thus the map u_z:Q_l -> (F^G)_z is an isomorphism for every geometric point z, and therefore u:Q_l -> F^G is an isomorphism of sheaves on Z_k.

4. Averaging instead of exactness of invariants. Since l does not divide |G|, the element |G| is invertible in Q_l, and e=(1/|G|) sum_{g in G} g is an idempotent endomorphism of the G-sheaf F. Its image is F^G and F = F^G direct sum ker(e) as sheaves of Q_l-vector spaces. Applying H^n gives
H^n(Z_k,F) = H^n(Z_k,F^G) direct sum H^n(Z_k,ker(e)).
The first summand is the e-fixed subspace of H^n(Z_k,F); for a Q_l[G]-module the e-fixed subspace is the G-invariant subspace. Hence H^n(Z_k,F^G) is canonically H^n(Z_k,F)^G. Using the isomorphism u from Step 3, we obtain
W = H^n(Z_k,Q_l) isomorphic to H^n(Z_k,F)^G.
Transporting by lambda identifies W with V^G. Moreover, the composite W -> H^n(Z_k,F) -> V is exactly the pullback pi_k^*:H^n(Z_k,Q_l)->H^n(Y_k,Q_l), by functoriality of the Leray edge map and the adjunction unit. Thus pi_k^* is an isomorphism W -> V^G.

5. Compatibility with Frobenius. The morphism pi is defined over F_q, and the elements of G are F_q-automorphisms. Naturality of étale pullback gives pi_k^* F_Z = F_Y pi_k^*. Also F_Y commutes with each g^* on V, because g is defined over F_q; hence F_Y preserves V^G. Therefore the isomorphism pi_k^*:W -> V^G intertwines F_Z with F_Y|_{V^G}.

6. Semisimplicity. By hypothesis F_Y is semisimple on V. The subspace V^G is F_Y-stable, so lemma_145 implies that F_Y is semisimple on V^G. Since pi_k^*:W -> V^G is an F-equivariant isomorphism, lemma_8 implies that F_Z is semisimple on W. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemma_pic_torsion_limit.statement:
Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\) be a prime, and let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\). Write \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\) for the group of \(k\)-points of the identity component \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\) of the Picard scheme and \(\operatorname{NS}(Y):=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) is finitely generated. For an abelian group \(A\) and \(n\ge1\), let \(A[\ell^n]\) denote the kernel of multiplication by \(\ell^n\), and give the groups \(A[\ell^n]\) the inverse-system structure with bonding maps \(A[\ell^{n+1}]\to A[\ell^n]\) given by multiplication by \(\ell\). Then the inclusion \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\) induces an isomorphism of abelian groups
\[\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n].\]
lemma_pic_torsion_limit.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_pic_torsion_limit",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_173"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_181"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that the inclusion \(\iota:\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\hookrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)\) induces an isomorphism of abelian groups
\[
\varprojlim_{n\ge 1}\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\varprojlim_{n\ge 1}\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n],
\]
where in both systems the bonding map \(A[\ell^{n+1}]\to A[\ell^n]\) is multiplication by \(\ell\). The argument has six steps; it uses only lemma_173 and lemma_181.

**Step 0 (the inverse systems are well defined).** For an abelian group \(A\) and \(n\ge 1\), \(A[\ell^n]=\ker(\ell^n:A\to A)\) is a subgroup of \(A\). If \(a\in A[\ell^{n+1}]\), i.e. \(\ell^{n+1}a=0\), then \(\ell^n(\ell a)=\ell^{n+1}a=0\), so \(\ell a\in A[\ell^n]\). Thus multiplication by \(\ell\) does define a homomorphism of abelian groups \(u^A_n:A[\ell^{n+1}]\to A[\ell^n]\), and \((A[\ell^n],u^A_n)_{n\ge 1}\) is an inverse system of abelian groups indexed by \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\) with its usual order. Its limit is taken in the category of abelian groups; concretely
\[
\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n]=\Big\{(a_n)_{n\ge 1}\in\prod_{n\ge 1}A[\ell^n]\ :\ u^A_n(a_{n+1})=a_n\ \text{for all }n\ge 1\Big\},
\]
a subgroup of the product, with componentwise addition. A homomorphism \(f:A\to B\) of abelian groups restricts to \(f_n:A[\ell^n]\to B[\ell^n]\) (since \(\ell^n a=0\Rightarrow \ell^n f(a)=0\)) and these restrictions satisfy \(u^B_n\circ f_{n+1}=f_n\circ u^A_n\) because both sides send \(a\) to \(\ell f(a)=f(\ell a)\); hence \(f\) induces a group homomorphism \(\varprojlim f_n:\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n]\to\varprojlim_n B[\ell^n]\).

**Step 1 (identifying \(P[\ell^n](k)\) with \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\)).** Write \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\), so that \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)=P(k)\) by the definition used in the statement. The symbol \(P[\ell^n]\) denotes the kernel (as a commutative group scheme, equivalently as a sheaf for the fppf topology) of multiplication by \(\ell^n\) on \(P\). Taking \(k\)-points is the same as taking global sections over the one-point fppf site of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), which is a left-exact functor; applied to the exact sequence of fppf sheaves \(0\to P[\ell^n]\to P\xrightarrow{\ \ell^n\ }P\) it gives an exact sequence \(0\to P[\ell^n](k)\to P(k)\xrightarrow{\ \ell^n\ }P(k)\). Hence \(P[\ell^n](k)=\ker(\ell^n:P(k)\to P(k))=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\), and this identification is compatible with multiplication by \(\ell\), since both are the restriction of the same operation on \(P(k)\).

**Step 2 (a short exact sequence for each \(n\)).** The hypotheses of lemma_173 are satisfied: \(k\) is algebraically closed, \(Y\) is smooth projective and geometrically connected over \(k\), \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\), and \(n\ge 1\). By lemma_173 the natural sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow P[\ell^n](k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0
\tag{1}
\]
is exact. Using Step 1 and writing \(i_n:\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\) for the inclusion and \(q_n:\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\) for the map induced by the quotient \(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{NS}(Y)=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\) (well defined because \(\ell^nx=0\) implies the class of \(x\) in \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) is killed by \(\ell^n\)), (1) reads
\[
0\to\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\;i_n\;}\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\;q_n\;}\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\to 0.
\]

**Step 3 (these form a short exact sequence of inverse systems).** We check that (1) is a morphism of inverse systems over \(n\), i.e. that the squares
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] & \xrightarrow{i_{n+1}} & \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] \\
\ \downarrow \scriptstyle{\ell} & & \downarrow \scriptstyle{\ell}\\
\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^{n}] & \xrightarrow{i_{n}} & \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n}] 
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] & \xrightarrow{q_{n+1}} & \operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}] \\
\ \downarrow \scriptstyle{\ell} & & \downarrow \scriptstyle{\ell}\\
\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n}] & \xrightarrow{q_{n}} & \operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^{n}]
\end{array}
\]
commute. Both bonding maps on all three terms are multiplication by \(\ell\), and \(i_n,q_n\) are group homomorphisms (\(i_n\) is the inclusion of a subgroup, \(q_n\) the restriction of a quotient homomorphism), so \(\ell\, i_{n+1}(x)=i_n(\ell x)\) and \(\ell\, q_{n+1}(x)=q_n(\ell x)\) hold identically. Exactness at each level is Step 2. Thus we have a short exact sequence of inverse systems \(0\to (\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n])\to(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n])\to(\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n])\to 0\).

**Step 4 (left exactness of the limit).** We record and prove the general fact we need: if \(0\to A'_n\xrightarrow{i_n}A_n\xrightarrow{q_n}A''_n\to 0\) is a short exact sequence of inverse systems of abelian groups (bonding maps \(u'_n,u_n,u''_n\) commuting with \(i_n,q_n\)), then
\[
0\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n A'_n \xrightarrow{\ \varprojlim i\ } \varprojlim_n A_n \xrightarrow{\ \varprojlim q\ } \varprojlim_n A''_n
\]
is exact.

*Injectivity.* If \((a'_n)\in\varprojlim A'_n\) maps to \(0\) in \(\varprojlim A_n\), then \(i_n(a'_n)=0\) for every \(n\); since each \(i_n\) is injective, \(a'_n=0\) for every \(n\).

*Exactness in the middle.* Let \(a=(a_n)\in\varprojlim A_n\) with \(q(a)=0\) in \(\varprojlim A''_n\). Then \(q_n(a_n)=0\) for all \(n\), so by exactness at \(A_n\) there is a unique \(a'_n\in A'_n\) with \(i_n(a'_n)=a_n\). It remains to check \((a'_n)\) is a compatible family: for each \(n\),
\[
i_n\big(u'_n(a'_{n+1})\big)=u_n\big(i_{n+1}(a'_{n+1})\big)=u_n(a_{n+1})=a_n=i_n(a'_n),
\]
where the first equality is the commutativity of the left square (Step 3) and the second uses \(i_{n+1}(a'_{n+1})=a_{n+1}\). Injectivity of \(i_n\) gives \(u'_n(a'_{n+1})=a'_n\), so \((a'_n)\in\varprojlim A'_n\) maps to \(a\).

*Surjectivity onto \(\varprojlim A''_n\) is NOT claimed in general* (it can fail; the obstruction is \(\varprojlim{}^{1}\)); we will not need it, because the term \(\varprojlim A''_n\) will turn out to be zero.

Applying Step 4 to the sequence of systems of Step 3 gives an exact sequence of abelian groups
\[
0\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\ \varprojlim i\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\ \varprojlim q\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n].
\tag{2}
\]

**Step 5 (the last term vanishes).** By hypothesis \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) is a finitely generated abelian group. Lemma_181, applied to \(A=\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) and to the prime \(\ell\), says precisely that for the inverse system \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\) with bonding maps multiplication by \(\ell\) one has
\[
\varprojlim_n \operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]=0 .
\tag{3}
\]
(The hypotheses of lemma_181 match exactly: the groups are the \(\ell^n\)-torsion subgroups and the transition maps are multiplication by \(\ell\).) For completeness let us recall why (3) is true in this concrete situation: writing \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\cong \mathbb Z^{r}\oplus T\) with \(T\) finite, one has \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\cong T[\ell^n]\) because the free part is torsion-free, and multiplication by \(\ell\) sends \(T[\ell^{n+1}]\) into \(T[\ell^{n}]\). An element of the limit is a compatible sequence \((t_n)\) with \(t_n=\ell t_{n+1}\) for all \(n\); then \(t_1\) is divisible by \(\ell^{m}\) in the finite group \(T\) for every \(m\ge 0\), i.e. lies in \(\bigcap_{m}\ell^{m}T\). Since multiplication by \(\ell\) is eventually constant on the finite descending chain \(T\supseteq \ell T\supseteq \ell^{2}T\supseteq\cdots\), say \(\ell^{m}T=\ell^{m+1}T=\cdots\), the map \(\ell:\ell^{m}T\to\ell^{m}T\) is surjective, hence an automorphism of the finite group \(\ell^{m}T\); writing \(t_1=\ell^{m}s\) with \(s\in\ell^{m}T\) and using that \(t_1\) is killed by some \(\ell^{N}\) gives \(0=\ell^{N}t_1=\ell^{N+m}s\), whence \(s=0\) as \(\ell^{N+m}\) acts invertibly on \(\ell^{m}T\) (it is a power of the automorphism above, after increasing \(m\)). Thus \(t_1=0\), and similarly every component of a limit element vanishes, so the limit is \(0\). This is exactly the content of lemma_181, which we cite.

**Step 6 (conclusion).** Substitute (3) into the exact sequence (2):
\[
0\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\ \varprojlim i\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0 .
\]
Exactness at the left says \(\varprojlim i\) is injective; exactness at the middle says its image is the kernel of the map \(\varprojlim q\) to the zero group, which is the whole of \(\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\); hence \(\varprojlim i\) is surjective as well. Therefore
\[
\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]
\]
is an isomorphism of abelian groups, as claimed. Concretely: every compatible sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(L_n\in\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\) and \(L_n\simeq L_{n+1}^{\otimes\ell}\) has all \(L_n\) algebraically equivalent to zero (because its image in \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\) is a compatible sequence, hence zero by Step 5), and the lift to the limit of \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\) is unique because each \(i_n\) is injective.

**Explicit description of the map and its inverse.** The map is the one induced by the inclusions \(i_n\): it sends a compatible family \((M_n)\) of \(\ell^n\)-torsion line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero to the same family viewed inside \(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\); it is a homomorphism because the limits are subgroups of the products and \(i_n\) is a homomorphism in each degree. Its inverse sends \((L_n)\) to the unique family \((M_n)\) with \(M_n\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\) and \(i_n(M_n)=L_n\): existence and uniqueness of each \(M_n\) follow from Step 2 (surjectivity of \(q_n\) with kernel \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\)) once one knows \(q_n(L_n)=0\), which is precisely the vanishing of the image of \((L_n)\) in \(\varprojlim_n\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]=0\); compatibility \(\ell M_{n+1}=M_n\) follows by applying the injective map \(i_n\) and using compatibility of the \(L_n\). This inverse is a group homomorphism since it is the inverse of a bijective homomorphism.

**Remarks on what was and was not used.** No \(\varprojlim^{1}\) or Mittag–Leffler argument is needed: the cokernel of \(\varprojlim i\) embeds into \(\varprojlim_n\operatorname{NS}(Y)[\ell^n]\), which is zero by lemma_181, so left exactness of the limit already suffices. Nor is the structure theorem \(P[\ell^n](k)\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z)^{2g}\) required; the statement is purely a consequence of the exactness of lemma_173 together with the vanishing of lemma_181. Geometrically, the isomorphism identifies \(\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\) with the Tate module \(T_\ell(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k})=\varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)\) of the Picard variety.
"
}

lemma_186.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), denote the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on the étale cohomology of \(Z_k\). Suppose \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(i\ge0\) and \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(j\ge0\). Then \(F_{X\times Y}\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_186.proof:
Fix q=p^a, smooth projective F_q-varieties X and Y, k = \overline{F}_q, a prime \ell\neq p, and for a F_q-scheme Z write F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* with \sigma(c)=c^q. Abbreviate
\[ V^i_X:=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad V^j_Y:=H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). \]
We must show that F_{X\times Y} is semisimple on W^n for every n\ge 0.

Step 0 (finite dimensionality and invertibility).
X, Y and X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y are proper over \mathbb F_q, and the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on each of their geometric fibres carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to each of the three varieties gives that V^i_X, V^j_Y and W^n are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces for all i,j,n. Applying lemma_6a to each of them gives that F_X, F_Y and F_{X\times Y} are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of these spaces (with F_Z^{-1} the geometric Frobenius). In particular all the operators appearing below lie in the respective GL of the space concerned, so statements about "semisimple automorphisms" apply.

Step 1 (what the hypotheses give, in minimal-polynomial form).
By hypothesis F_X is semisimple on V^i_X and F_Y is semisimple on V^j_Y for all i,j\ge 0. Whatever of the two equivalent readings of "semisimple" one adopts (squarefree minimal polynomial over \mathbb Q_\ell, or diagonalisability after extending scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell), lemma_5 identifies them; hence we may and shall use the following: for every i\ge 0 the minimal polynomial \mu_i\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t] of T_i:=F_X|_{V^i_X} is squarefree, and for every j\ge 0 the minimal polynomial \nu_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t] of S_j:=F_Y|_{V^j_Y} is squarefree. (Indeed, if semisimplicity is read as diagonalisability over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, then T_i is semisimple on V^i_X by lemma_5, and the definition of semisimplicity used there — cf. also lemma_155 — says exactly that \mu_i is squarefree.)

Step 2 (each K\u00fcnneth tensor factor is semisimple).
Fix i,j\ge 0. The spaces V^i_X and V^j_Y are finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, and T_i\in\mathrm{GL}(V^i_X), S_j\in\mathrm{GL}(V^j_Y) are semisimple automorphisms with squarefree minimal polynomials by Step 1. Lemma_147 therefore applies and yields that
\[ U_{i,j}:=T_i\otimes S_j\in\mathrm{GL}\!\big(V^i_X\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V^j_Y\big) \]
is semisimple. (If one of V^i_X, V^j_Y is the zero space, then V^i_X\otimes V^j_Y=0 and U_{i,j} is the identity of the zero space, whose minimal polynomial is 1, hence trivially squarefree; so the conclusion holds in that case too.)

Step 3 (finite direct sums of semisimple automorphisms are semisimple).
We record and prove the following linear-algebra fact, used with k=\mathbb Q_\ell. Let k be a field of characteristic 0, let V_1,\dots,V_r be finite-dimensional k-vector spaces and let T_m\in\mathrm{GL}(V_m) have squarefree minimal polynomial \mu_m. Put V=\bigoplus_{m=1}^r V_m and T=\bigoplus_{m=1}^r T_m\in\mathrm{GL}(V). Then T is semisimple.

Proof of the fact. Each \mu_m is a non-zero polynomial; extend scalars to \bar k. Since \mu_m is squarefree over k, it is squarefree over \bar k, and over \bar k it splits as \mu_m=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda_m}(t-\lambda) with \Lambda_m a finite set of distinct elements of \bar k. The space V_m\otimes_k\bar k is a module over \bar k[t] via T_m\otimes 1, annihilated by \mu_m. The factors (t-\lambda), \lambda\in\Lambda_m, are pairwise coprime, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives \bar k[t]/(\mu_m)\cong\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda_m}\bar k[t]/(t-\lambda), and the images of the standard orthogonal idempotents e_\lambda=\prod_{\lambda'\in\Lambda_m,\,\lambda'\ne\lambda}(t-\lambda')/(\lambda-\lambda')\in\bar k[t]/(\mu_m) give a decomposition
\[ V_m\otimes_k\bar k=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_m}\ker\big(T_m\otimes 1-\lambda\big), \]
because for v in the \lambda-summand, (t-\lambda) annihilates v, i.e. (T_m\otimes 1)v=\lambda v, and conversely the idempotents sum to 1 and act as the projections. Thus T_m\otimes 1 is diagonalisable over \bar k for each m. Direct summing the decompositions over m shows that
\[ T\otimes 1=\bigoplus_{m=1}^r (T_m\otimes 1) \]
is diagonalisable on V\otimes_k\bar k=\bigoplus_m (V_m\otimes_k\bar k): indeed T\otimes 1 acts as the scalar \lambda on each summand \ker(T_m\otimes 1-\lambda), and grouping equal eigenvalues over all m exhibits V\otimes\bar k as a direct sum of eigenspaces of T\otimes 1. Hence T\otimes 1 is diagonalisable, which by lemma_5 (applied with \mathbb Q_\ell replaced by the characteristic-0 field k; the argument of lemma_5 is exactly the equivalence between squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial and diagonalisability after scalar extension) says that T is semisimple, i.e. its minimal polynomial over k is squarefree. This proves the fact. \quad(\square)

Step 4 (the whole K\u00fcnneth source is semisimple).
Fix n\ge 0. The index set I_n=\{(i,j)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2 : i+j=n\} is finite (it has n+1 elements). For (i,j)\in I_n put U_{i,j}=T_i\otimes S_j on V^i_X\otimes V^j_Y, which is semisimple by Step 2. Applying the fact of Step 3 with r=|I_n| and the family \{U_{i,j}\}_{(i,j)\in I_n} we obtain that
\[ \Theta_n:=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}U_{i,j}=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}\big(F_X|_{V^i_X}\otimes F_Y|_{V^j_Y}\big)\in\mathrm{GL}\!\Big(\bigoplus_{i+j=n}V^i_X\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V^j_Y\Big) \]
is semisimple.

Step 5 (transport across the K\u00fcnneth isomorphism).
By lemma_146, applied to X, Y and n, the K\u00fcnneth map
\[ \kappa:\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*(x)\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*(y), \]
is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, and under it F_{X\times Y} corresponds to F_X\otimes F_Y on the (i,j)-summand for all i,j. In other words
\[ \kappa\circ\Theta_n=F_{X\times Y}\circ\kappa . \]
Both source and target are finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell by Step 0, and both \Theta_n and F_{X\times Y} are invertible by Steps 0 and 4. Hence lemma_8 applies to \alpha=\kappa, T_V=\Theta_n, T_W=F_{X\times Y}, and gives: \Theta_n is semisimple if and only if F_{X\times Y} is semisimple. Since \Theta_n is semisimple by Step 4, F_{X\times Y} is semisimple on W^n.

Step 6 (conclusion and edge cases).
The integer n\ge 0 was arbitrary, and Step 5 covers every n, including n=0 (where I_0=\{(0,0)\} and the argument is the same) and n larger than 2\dim(X\times Y) (where W^n=0 and the summands V^i_X\otimes V^j_Y are all zero by the K\u00fcnneth isomorphism, the zero operator on the zero space being semisimple, as already noted in Step 2). Thus F_{X\times Y}=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* acts semisimply on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0, which is the desired conclusion.

(Remark, not needed for the statement: since F_{X\times Y} is invertible by Step 0 and semisimple by Step 5, lemma_5 identifies this with diagonalisability of its scalar extension to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and lemma_4 would give the same for geometric Frobenius.)

lemma_187.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism of smooth projective varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(n\ge0\). Write \(F_X\) and \(F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Suppose \(f^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f^*\) and that \(f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective. If \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_187.proof:
We prove the statement by reducing it to two elementary facts about semisimple linear operators (restriction to a stable subspace, and transport along an intertwining isomorphism).

Step 1: The cohomology groups are finite-dimensional. Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, they are proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to $X$ (respectively $Y$) with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, the constant complex in degree $0$, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ar}}^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ coming from $\sigma(c)=c^q$. The hypercohomology of the constant sheaf is the étale cohomology, so $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Write
$$W:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad V:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$

Step 2: The Frobenius operators are invertible. By lemma_6a applied to the $\mathbb F_q$-schemes $X$ and $Y$, the pullback by $\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$ with $\sigma(u)=u^q$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (its inverse being the geometric Frobenius, which is finite-dimensional by Step 1). Thus
$$S:=F_X\in \mathrm{GL}(W),\qquad T:=F_Y\in \mathrm{GL}(V)$$
arend are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators. By hypothesis $S$ acts semisimply on $W$.

Step 3: The image of $f^*$ is an $S$-stable subspace. Put $\alpha:=f^*:V\to W$; this is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, and by hypothesis it is injective and satisfies
$$\alpha\circ T=S\circ\alpha .
$$
Let $U:=\alpha(V)\subseteq W$. Then $U$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $W$, and since $\alpha$ is injective the induced map $\alpha:V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }U$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Moreover $U$ is stable under $S$: indeed for $u\in U$ write $u=\alpha(v)$ with $v\in V$; then
$$S(u)=S(\alpha(v))=\alpha(T(v))\in\alpha(V)=U,$$
where the middle equality is the intertwining relation. Hence $S(U)\subseteq U$.

Step 4: Restriction of $S$ to $U$ is semisimple and invertible. Apply lemma_145 to the semisimple operator $S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ on the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $W$ and to the $S$-stable subspace $U\subseteq W$: the restriction $S|_U\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ is semisimple. (For completeness, the fact that $S|_U$ is an automorphism of $U$ is also immediate directly: $S|_U$ is injective because $S$ is, and an injective endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $U$ is surjective.)

Step 5: Transport semisimplicity back along $\alpha$. We have the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\alpha:V\xrightarrow{\sim}U$ between finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, the invertible operator $T$ on $V$, the invertible operator $S|_U$ on $U$, and the intertwining identity $\alpha\circ T=(S|_U)\circ\alpha$ (the same relation as in Step 3, with codomain restricted to $U$). By lemma_8, $T$ is semisimple if and only if $S|_U$ is semisimple. Since $S|_U$ is semisimple by Step 4, $T$ is semisimple.

Step 6: Conclusion. $T=F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, which is exactly the desired conclusion. Note that no property of $f$ beyond the injectivity and $F$-equivariance of $f^*$ in degree $n$ was used, and no hypothesis on the other degrees of cohomology is needed. $\blacksquare$

lemma_top_trace_generically_finite.statement: Let \(q=p^{a}\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge 1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_{q}\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\), and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_{Z}:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_{Z}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q}]\) for every closed point \(z\) of \(Z\), where \(\mathrm{cl}(z)\) is the cycle class of \(z\) on \(Z_{k}\) and \(\kappa(z)\) is its residue field. Then the \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear automorphism \(\operatorname{tr}_{X}\circ f^{*}\circ\operatorname{tr}_{Y}^{-1}\) of \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-D)\) is multiplication by \(d\).
lemma_top_trace_generically_finite.proof:
## 0. Conventions and bookkeeping for the twist

**(0.1) Integrality, function fields, degree.** Since $Y$ is smooth over $\mathbb F_q$, $Y_k:=Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$ is regular; since $Y$ is geometrically connected, $Y_k$ is connected. A connected regular Noetherian scheme is integral, so $Y_k$ is integral; the faithfully flat (even smooth, surjective) map $Y_k\to Y$ then shows $Y$ is integral: surjectivity gives irreducibility (the continuous image of an irreducible space is irreducible), and reducedness descends under faithfully flat quasi-compact morphisms. The same argument applies to $X$. Hence the function fields $k(X),k(Y)$ are defined; $f$ is surjective, hence dominant, so $k(Y)\hookrightarrow k(X)$, and $f$ is quasi-finite at the generic point $\xi$ of $X$ because $k(X)/k(Y)$ is finite. By definition of the degree of a generically finite dominant morphism of integral varieties, $d=[k(X):k(Y)]\ge 1$.

**(0.2) Twisted traces.** Write $\operatorname{tr}_Z^{D}:=(\operatorname{tr}_Z\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ$(canonical contraction $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(D)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$), so $\operatorname{tr}_Z^{D}:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$. Because $\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$ is a $1$-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space and the twist is by a constant coefficient module, $H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))=H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$, and $\operatorname{tr}_Z^{D}$ is again a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism; in particular $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))=1$. For a closed point $z$ of the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$, its cycle class is $\mathrm{cl}(z):=\mathrm{cl}([\{z\}])\in H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))$, and the normalisation of lemma_77(a) (which supplies these trace isomorphisms for smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over a finite field, with $m=1$, $d=D$) reads
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z^{D}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\in\mathbb Q_\ell,$$
where $\kappa(z)$ is the **finite** residue field of the closed point $z$ of $Z$ (a point of the $\mathbb F_q$-model, never of the geometric fibre). This is the reading of the normalisation in the statement of the lemma.

**(0.3) Reduction.** We will prove
$$\qquad (\ast)\qquad \operatorname{tr}_X^{D}\circ f_k^{*}=d\cdot \operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}\quad\text{as maps } H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell,$$
and then deduce the required untwisted identity in Step 6. Note that $(\ast)$ is an identity of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear functionals on a $1$-dimensional space.

## 1. A dense open over which $f$ is finite locally free of rank $d$

**(1a) The quasi-finite locus.** The morphism $f$ is of finite type (it is projective), and for a morphism locally of finite type the set $X_{\mathrm{qf}}\subset X$ of points at which $f$ is quasi-finite is open (Zariski's Main Theorem in the form "the quasi-finite locus is open"). We check $\xi\in X_{\mathrm{qf}}$: the generic fibre is $X_{\eta}:=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}k(Y)$. Covering $Y$ by affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}A_0\subset Y$ with $A_0$ a domain and taking $S=A_0\setminus\{0\}$, the affine pieces of $X_\eta$ are $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A)$ with $A$ a finitely generated domain over $A_0$ with fraction field $k(X)$. Then $S^{-1}A$ is a finitely generated $k(Y)$-algebra, a domain with fraction field $k(X)$, so its Krull dimension is $\operatorname{trdeg}_{k(Y)}k(X)=0$; a $0$-dimensional domain of finite type over a field is a field, hence $S^{-1}A=k(X)$. Thus $X_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}k(X)=\{\xi\}$: the fibre over $\eta$ is a single isolated point, i.e. $f$ is quasi-finite at $\xi$, and $\xi$ is the *only* point of $X$ lying over $\eta$.

**(1b) Removing the non-quasi-finite locus.** Put $E:=X\setminus X_{\mathrm{qf}}$, a proper closed subset (proper since $\xi\notin E$). As $f$ is proper it is a closed map, so $f(E)$ is closed in $Y$; and $\eta\notin f(E)$ because $\xi\notin E$ and $\xi$ is the only point over $\eta$. Hence $Y_0:=Y\setminus f(E)$ is a dense open subscheme of $Y$ and $f^{-1}(Y_0)\to Y_0$ is proper and quasi-finite, hence **finite**.

**(1c) The locally free locus.** The sheaf $\mathcal M:=f_*\mathcal O_{X}$ restricted to $Y_0$ is a coherent $\mathcal O_{Y_0}$-algebra, and by (1a)
$$\mathcal M\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y_0}}k(Y)=\Gamma(X_\eta,\mathcal O)=k(X),\qquad \dim_{k(Y)}k(X)=d,$$
so $\mathcal M$ is generically free of rank $d$. Since $Y_0$ is Noetherian and integral, the locus of points where $\mathcal M$ is free of rank $d$ over the local ring is open (generic freeness / openness of flatness, and the rank is locally constant on the locally free locus over the integral scheme $Y_0$); it contains $\eta$. Let $Z\subset Y_0$ be its complement, a proper closed subset, and set
$$V:=Y_0\setminus Z=Y\setminus\big(f(E)\cup Z\big).$$
Then $V$ is a dense open subscheme of $Y$, and $g:=f|_{U}:U:=f^{-1}(V)\to V$ is finite and $g_*\mathcal O_U=\mathcal M|_V$ is locally free of rank $d$; i.e. **$g$ is finite locally free of rank $d$**. (All the subsets involved are constructed inside the abstract scheme $Y$ from $f$, so $V$ is an open subscheme of $Y$ and inherits the $\mathbb F_q$-structure; no descent statement is needed.)

**(1d) A closed point of $V$.** $V$ is a nonempty scheme of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, hence has a closed point $y$ (every nonempty finite type scheme over a field has a closed point), and by Zariski's lemma $\kappa(y)$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb F_q$; write
$$r:=[\kappa(y):\mathbb F_q]\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.$$
We deliberately do **not** look for a $k$-rational point of $Y_k$; such a point need not descend to $Y$, and the normalisation of the trace is not available for points of the geometric fibre.

## 2. The scheme-theoretic fibre over $y$

Since $g^{-1}(y)=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ is the base change of the finite locally free rank-$d$ algebra $\mathcal M|_V$, it is $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with
$$A:=\kappa(y)\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}(f_*\mathcal O_X)_y,$$
a free $\kappa(y)$-module of rank $d$; in particular $\dim_{\kappa(y)}A=d$. As $A$ is a finite-dimensional algebra over a field it is Artinian, so
$$A\;\cong\;A_1\times\cdots\times A_s,$$
with each $A_i$ Artin local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i$ and residue field $\kappa(x_i):=A_i/\mathfrak m_i$, a finite extension of $\kappa(y)$. The points $x_1,\dots,x_s$ are exactly the points of the fibre $X_y$; each is closed in $X_y$ and the projection $X_y\to X$ is finite (a closed immersion $\{y\}\hookrightarrow V$ base-changed, followed by the open immersion $U\hookrightarrow X$), hence integral and closed, so the $x_i$ are **closed points of the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$**, with residue fields $\kappa(x_i)$ finite over $\mathbb F_q$. Write
$$n_i:=\operatorname{length}_{A_i}(A_i)=\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{X_y,x_i}}\mathcal O_{X_y,x_i}\;\ge 1.$$
**Computation of $d$.** The $A_i$ has a composition series as $A_i$-module of length $n_i$ with all factors $\kappa(x_i)$ (e.g. the filtration by powers of $\mathfrak m_i$, whose graded pieces $\mathfrak m_i^{j}/\mathfrak m_i^{j+1}$ are finite-dimensional $\kappa(x_i)$-vector spaces and which realises $\operatorname{length}_{A_i}A_i=\dim_{\kappa(x_i)}A_i$). Hence $\dim_{\kappa(y)}A_i=n_i\,[\kappa(x_i):\kappa(y)]$, and summing over $i$,
$$\qquad (\dagger)\qquad d=\dim_{\kappa(y)}A=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,[\kappa(x_i):\kappa(y)].\qquad\qquad (*)$$
Note that the $n_i$ are essential: the fibre may be non-reduced (ramification), and we make no claim that it is a disjoint union of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}$ of a field.
Since $\kappa(y)\subset\kappa(x_i)$ are both finite over $\mathbb F_q$, the tower formula for finite fields gives
$$\qquad (\ddagger)\qquad [\kappa(x_i):\mathbb F_q]=[\kappa(x_i):\kappa(y)]\cdot[\kappa(y):\mathbb F_q]=[\kappa(x_i):\kappa(y)]\,r.$$

## 3. The pullback of the cycle $[y]$

**(3a) $f$ is lci of relative dimension $0$.** Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so the graph $\Gamma_f:X\hookrightarrow X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y$ is a regular immersion (it is the inverse image of the diagonal $X\hookrightarrow X\times X$ under $\mathrm{id}\times f$, and the diagonal of a smooth scheme is a regular immersion), of codimension $D$, while the projection $X\times Y\to Y$ is smooth of relative dimension $D$. Thus $f$ factors as "regular immersion followed by smooth" of virtual dimension $D-D=0$: $f$ is a local complete intersection morphism of relative dimension $0$. Consequently the refined Gysin pullback on Chow groups
$$f^{!}:\mathrm{CH}^{k}(Y)\longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}^{k}(X)$$
is defined for every $k$ (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, §6.2). **No tor-independence statement is used**: the pullback is attached to the lci morphism $f$ itself, not to the cartesian square $\{y\}\to Y\leftarrow X$, which need not be tor-independent because $f$ is not flat at every point of $Y$ (a blow-up along a positive-dimensional centre shows $f$ need not even be of relative dimension $0$ everywhere; that is precisely why we shrank to $V$ in Step 1).

**(3b) Evaluation on $[y]$.** The point $y$ lies in $V$, and $f$ is flat in a neighbourhood of the whole fibre $|X_y|=\{x_1,\dots,x_s\}\subset U$. Two standard properties of refined Gysin homomorphisms now apply:
(i) *compatibility with flat base change of the target*: for the cartesian square $U\xrightarrow{\;j'\;}X$, $\downarrow g\;\downarrow f$, $V\xrightarrow{\;j\;}Y$ with $j$ an open immersion (hence flat), one has $f^{!}\,j_{*}=j'_{*}\,g^{!}$ on cycles supported on $V$ (Fulton, I.T., Theorem 6.2 / Proposition 1.7);
(ii) *on a flat morphism of relative dimension $n$ the refined Gysin pullback is the flat pullback* (Fulton, I.T., Proposition 6.2(b)), and flat pullback of the integral closed subscheme $\{y\}$ by $g$ is the fundamental cycle of the scheme-theoretic fibre: with $g^{-1}(y)=\coprod_i\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ and $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ having the single point $x_i$, Fulton I.T., Example 1.7.1 gives
$$g^{!}[y]=g^{*}_{\mathrm{flat}}[y]=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\operatorname{length}_{(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_i}}\!\big((A_i)_{\mathfrak m_i}\big)[x_i]=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i[x_i],$$
the last equality because $A_i$ is already local Artin, so $(A_i)_{\mathfrak m_i}=A_i$.
Since $[y]=j_*[y]$ in $\mathrm{CH}^{D}(Y)$, (i) and (ii) give, in $\mathrm{CH}^{D}(X)$ (the group of $0$-cycles modulo rational equivalence),
$$\qquad (\S)\qquad f^{!}[y]=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,[x_i].\qquad\qquad (\S)$$

## 4. Cycle classes

The $\ell$-adic cycle class map for smooth varieties over $\mathbb F_q$, $\mathrm{cl}_Z:\mathrm{CH}^{k}(Z)\to H^{2k}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(k))$, is contravariant for morphisms of smooth varieties, in the precise sense that for the lci morphism $f:X\to Y$ between smooth $\mathbb F_q$-schemes one has, for every $z\in\mathrm{CH}^{k}(Y)$,
$$\mathrm{cl}_X\big(f^{!}z\big)=f_k^{*}\,\mathrm{cl}_Y(z)\in H^{2k}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(k))$$
(Fulton, I.T., Example 17.4.1; equivalently the standard "compatibility of cycle classes with refined Gysin pullback", SGA 6, Exp. X, or Milne, *Étale Cohomology*, VI, §11).
