Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth over $\mathbb F_q$, so the hypothesis of this property is satisfied. Applying it to $z=[y]$ and using $(\S)$ and the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\mathrm{cl}_X$,
$$\qquad (\S\S)\qquad f_k^{*}\,\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)=\mathrm{cl}_X\!\big(f^{!}[y]\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,\mathrm{cl}_X(x_i).\qquad\qquad (\S\S)$$

## 5. Applying the traces: proof of $(\ast)$

First, $\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\neq0$: by the normalisation of lemma_77(a) and (0.2),
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}\big(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\big)=[\kappa(y):\mathbb F_q]=r,$$
and $r$ is a positive integer, hence non-zero (indeed invertible) in the characteristic-$0$ field $\mathbb Q_\ell$. Since $\operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}$ is an isomorphism, $H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))$ is $1$-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, so $\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)$ is a basis of it.
Now apply $\operatorname{tr}_X^{D}$ to $(\S\S)$ and use $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity, the normalisation for the closed points $x_i$ of $X$, and then $(\ddagger)$ and $(\dagger)$:
$$\operatorname{tr}_X^{D}\big(f_k^{*}\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,\operatorname{tr}_X^{D}\big(\mathrm{cl}_X(x_i)\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,[\kappa(x_i):\mathbb F_q]=\sum_{i=1}^{s}n_i\,[\kappa(x_i):\kappa(y)]\,r=r\,d .$$
On the other hand $d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=d\,r$. Hence
$$\big(\operatorname{tr}_X^{D}\circ f_k^{*}\big)\big(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\big)=d\cdot \operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}\big(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\big)=(\,d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}\big)\big(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)\big).$$
The two maps $\operatorname{tr}_X^{D}\circ f_k^{*}$ and $d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y^{D}$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps out of the $1$-dimensional space $H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))$, and they agree on the basis vector $\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)$; therefore they are equal. This proves $(\ast)$.

## 6. Untwisting and conclusion

Fix a non-zero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$ and identify $H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(D))=H^{2D}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$. The pullback $f_k^{*}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$-linear under this identification, because the twist is by a *constant* coefficient module and the adjunction map $f_k^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell(D)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(D)$ is the identity on the coefficient space; i.e. $f_k^{*}(\alpha\otimes\xi)=f_k^{*}\alpha\otimes\xi$ for all $\alpha\in H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Moreover, writing $\langle-,-\rangle:\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\times\mathbb Q_\ell(D)\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ for the canonical perfect pairing, $\operatorname{tr}_Z^{D}(\beta\otimes\eta)=\langle\operatorname{tr}_Z\beta,\eta\rangle$. Thus $(\ast)$ evaluated at $\alpha\otimes\xi$ reads, for every $\alpha$,
$$\big\langle\,(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^{*}-d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y)(\alpha),\ \xi\,\big\rangle=0 .$$
The map $w\mapsto\langle w,\xi\rangle$ is a non-zero $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ out of a $1$-dimensional space, hence an isomorphism; so
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^{*}=d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y\qquad\text{as maps } H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D).$$
Composing on the right with $\operatorname{tr}_Y^{-1}:\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2D}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ gives
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^{*}\circ\operatorname{tr}_Y^{-1}=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)}.$$
Since $d\ge1$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q_\ell$, this endomorphism is indeed a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism, and it is multiplication by $d$. $\blacksquare$

## 7. Remarks on the points flagged in the previous attempt

* Every residue field appearing above ($\kappa(y)$, $\kappa(x_i)$) is that of a closed point of $Y$ or $X$ **as $\mathbb F_q$-schemes**, so $[\kappa(-):\mathbb F_q]$ is a finite integer and the normalisation of lemma_77(a) legitimately applies; no closed point of a geometric fibre $Z_k$ is ever used.
* No cohomological pushforward $f_*$ is constructed and the false assertion that a proper generically finite morphism has relative dimension $0$ is not used; the only relative-dimension statement is that the *lci* pullback $f^{!}$ (a pullback, defined for any morphism of smooth schemes of the same dimension) preserves codimension, and the multiplicity computation is carried out on the open $V$ where $f$ really is finite locally free of relative dimension $0$.
* The fibre $X_y$ is not assumed reduced or étale: its possible nilpotents are accounted for by the lengths $n_i$ in $(\dagger)$, which is exactly what makes $(\dagger)$ give $d=\operatorname{rank}$ rather than a count of points.
* (Not used above, and deliberately not proved here:) the identity $(\ast)$ formally implies $f^{*}$ is an isomorphism in degree $2D$ and, combined with the perfect pairings of lemma_77(b), gives $\langle f^{*}\alpha,f^{*}\beta\rangle_X=d\,\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_Y$; those consequences belong to the parent lemma.

lemma_picard_frob_pullback.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/\mathbb F_q}\). Write \(F_{Y,k}=\operatorname{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), and let \(\pi_P\) be the \(q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism of \(P\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). Under the canonical identification \(P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)\), the map \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)\to\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)\) induced by pullback along \(F_{Y,k}\) is the map on \(k\)-points induced by \(\pi_P\).
lemma_picard_frob_pullback.proof:
**Notation.** Put $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, and $F_k:=\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ (an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism, since $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$). Write $Y_k=Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, so that $F_{Y,k}=\operatorname{id}_Y\times F_k:Y_k\to Y_k$ is a morphism of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes, $\sigma$-semilinear over $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Let $\pi_P$ denote the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism of the $\mathbb F_q$-group scheme $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$; since $\mathbb F_q$ is pointwise fixed by $x\mapsto x^q$, this is the absolute $q$-power Frobenius $F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}$ of the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $P$ (equivalently, the relative $q$-Frobenius $P\to P^{(q)}$ composed with the canonical identification $P^{(q)}\simeq P$).

The proof has four steps: (1) recall the functor-of-points description of $P(k)$ and the resulting identification $P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)$; (2) record that $\pi_P$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-group endomorphism and prove the naturality of absolute Frobenius; (3) compute the restriction map of the functor $P(-)$ along $F_k$ as pullback by $F_{Y,k}$; (4) combine (2) and (3).

---

**Step 1: The identification $P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)$.**

Since $Y$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, the morphism $f:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ is proper, flat and of finite presentation, is cohomologically flat in dimension $0$ (for every $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $S$ one has $f_{S*}\mathcal O_{Y_S}\simeq\mathcal O_S$, because the geometric fibres are connected and reduced), and its geometric fibres are integral. Hence the Picard functor $\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$ is representable by a separated $\mathbb F_q$-scheme locally of finite type, and its identity component $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q$ (Kleiman, *The Picard scheme*; FGAvI, Exp. 6). Two standard properties of the representing object, both functorial in $S$, will be used:

(1a) *Description of $S$-points over an algebraically closed field.* For $S=\operatorname{Spec}K$ with $K$ algebraically closed, the canonical map $\operatorname{Pic}(Y_K)\to\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}(K)$ factors through an isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Pic}(Y_K)\big/ p^*\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}K)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}(K),\qquad p:Y_K\to\operatorname{Spec}K,$$
and its restriction to $P(K)$ identifies $P(K)$ with the subgroup $\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_K)\subseteq\operatorname{Pic}(Y_K)$ of line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero. (The first statement is the injectivity/surjectivity theorem for the Picard functor: injectivity holds because $f$ is cohomologically flat in dimension $0$, and surjectivity holds because $Y_K\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ admits a section — such a section exists since $Y$ is smooth of finite type over a finite field, so $Y(K)\neq\varnothing$: take any closed point of $Y$, its residue field is a finite extension of $\mathbb F_q$ and embeds in $K$. The second is the definition/characterisation of the identity component of the Picard scheme over an algebraically closed field: it represents the functor of line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero.)

Taking $K=k$ and using that $k$ is a field, hence every line bundle on $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is trivial, i.e. $\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}k)=0$, we obtain a canonical bijection (in fact a group isomorphism)
$$\iota:P(k)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k),\qquad \xi\longmapsto [L_\xi],$$
where $L_\xi$ is the unique (up to unique... up to isomorphism, and the class is unique because the quotient in (1a) is trivial) line bundle on $Y_k$ representing $\xi$. This is the "canonical identification" appearing in the statement. Concretely, $\iota$ is obtained by pulling the universal class back along $\xi$, or equivalently by the identification of presheaves $\operatorname{Pic}(Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}-)$ with the sheaf $\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$ over spectra of algebraically closed fields.

(1b) *Functoriality.* The isomorphism $\iota$ is compatible with restriction along $\mathbb F_q$-morphisms of spectra of algebraically closed fields: if $g:\operatorname{Spec}K'\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism, then the square
$$\begin{array}{ccc} P(K) & \xrightarrow{\;\iota\;} & \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_K)\\ \downarrow{g^*} && \downarrow{(\operatorname{id}_Y\times g)^*}\\ P(K') & \xrightarrow{\;\iota\;} & \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_{K'}) \end{array}$$
commutes. Indeed $\iota$ is induced by the canonical morphism of presheaves $\mathcal F=\operatorname{Pic}(Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}-)\to a\mathcal F=\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$ (fppf sheafification), and a morphism of presheaves commutes with restriction maps by definition; the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ along $g$ is exactly pullback of line bundles along $\operatorname{id}_Y\times g$, and the restriction map of the sheaf $a\mathcal F$ is the map on points induced by the functoriality of $\operatorname{Hom}(-,\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q})$. The compatibility with the subfunctors $P\subseteq\underline{\operatorname{Pic}}_{Y/\mathbb F_q}$ and $\operatorname{Pic}^0\subseteq\operatorname{Pic}$ holds because pullback along an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism of spectra of algebraically closed fields preserves algebraic equivalence: a line bundle $M$ on $Y_K\times_K C$ for a smooth projective geometrically connected $K$-curve $C$ gives, after base change along $g$, a line bundle on $Y_{K'}\times_{K'}C_{K'}$ (with $C_{K'}$ again smooth projective geometrically connected over $K'$), and $g$ carries $K$-points of $C$ to $K'$-points of $C_{K'}$, so families exhibiting algebraic equivalence are carried to families exhibiting algebraic equivalence.

---

**Step 2: $\pi_P$ as an endomorphism, and naturality of absolute Frobenius.**

(a) *$\pi_P$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism.* For an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$, the absolute $q$-power Frobenius $F_X^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the morphism which is the identity on the underlying topological space and acts on sections by $u\mapsto u^q$. The structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ satisfies $F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}^{\mathrm{abs}}=\operatorname{id}$ (because $c^q=c$ for all $c\in\mathbb F_q$), so by (b) below the diagram $X\xrightarrow{F_X^{\mathrm{abs}}}X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ equals $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$; hence $F_X^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$. Thus $\pi_P:=F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is an endomorphism of $P$ as an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme, and $P(k)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_q}(\operatorname{Spec}k,P)$ is stable under post-composition with $\pi_P$.

(b) *Naturality.* For any morphism $h:X\to X'$ of $\mathbb F_p$-schemes one has
$$F_{X'}^{\mathrm{abs}}\circ h\;=\;h\circ F_X^{\mathrm{abs}}. \tag{$\ast$}$$
Proof. On underlying topological spaces both composites equal $|h|$, since $F^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the identity on points. On structure sheaves, take $V\subseteq X'$ open and $u\in\mathcal O_{X'}(V)$. Writing $h^\#:\mathcal O_{X'}(V)\to\mathcal O_X(h^{-1}V)$ for the map of sheaves of rings, the $q$-th-power maps commute with $h^\#$ because $h^\#$ is a ring homomorphism: $(h\circ F_X)^\#(u)=F_X^\#(h^\#u)=(h^\#u)^q=h^\#(u^q)=h^\#(F_{X'}^\#u)=(F_{X'}\circ h)^\#(u)$. This proves $(\ast)$.

(c) *$\pi_P$ is a group homomorphism.* Absolute Frobenius commutes with products over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p$ (it is the identity on the underlying space of a product and the $q$-th power on a tensor product of $\mathbb F_p$-algebras is computed componentwise): $F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_p}X'}^{\mathrm{abs}}=F_X^{\mathrm{abs}}\times F_{X'}^{\mathrm{abs}}$. Applying $(\ast)$ to the multiplication $m_P:P\times_{\mathbb F_q}P\to P$ (a morphism of $\mathbb F_p$-schemes) gives $F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}\circ m_P=m_P\circ(F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}\times F_P^{\mathrm{abs}})$, i.e. $\pi_P(\xi_1\xi_2)=\pi_P(\xi_1)\pi_P(\xi_2)$; similarly $\pi_P(e)=e$. So $\pi_P\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_q\text{-grp}}(P)$ and the induced map on $P(k)$ is a group endomorphism.

---

**Step 3: The restriction map along $F_k$ is pullback by $F_{Y,k}$.**

Apply the commutative square of Step 1b with $K=K'=k$ and $g=F_k=\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$. First observe that $F_k$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism: the induced map on rings $\mathbb F_q\hookrightarrow k\xrightarrow{\sigma} k$ is the inclusion itself, since $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ pointwise.

Second, identify the two copies of the base-changed scheme that occur. The source of $\operatorname{id}_Y\times F_k$ is $Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, where $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the source of $F_k$, i.e. the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$ with its usual structure map; this is literally $Y_k$. The target is $Y\times_{\mathbb{\mathbb F}_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$ with the target's structure map, again literally $Y_k$. Under these identifications
$$(\operatorname{id}_Y\times F_k)=\operatorname{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma=F_{Y,k}.$$
Hence Step 1b gives, for every $\xi\in P(k)$ represented by a line bundle $L_\xi$ on $Y_k$,
$$\iota\big(P(F_k)(\xi)\big)\;=\;F_{Y,k}^{*}L_\xi\quad\text{in }\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k). \tag{3.1}$$

(We also record that $F_{Y,k}$ is an isomorphism of schemes: $F_k$ is an automorphism of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ with inverse $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}$, so $F_{Y,k}^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}$; consequently $L\mapsto F_{Y,k}^*L$ is an automorphism of the abstract group $\operatorname{Pic}(Y_k)$, and (3.1) shows it preserves $\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)$ and restricts to a group automorphism of $\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)$.)

---

**Step 4: The restriction map along $F_k$ is $\pi_P$.**

By the definition of a functor of points, $P(-):(\operatorname{Sch}/\mathbb F_q)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\operatorname{Grp}$ sends a morphism $g:S'\to S$ to precomposition with $g$; thus for $\xi:\operatorname{Spec}k\to P$,
$$P(F_k)(\xi)=\xi\circ F_k.$$
By the naturality $(\ast)$ of Step 2b applied to $h=\xi:\operatorname{Spec}k\to P$ (a morphism of $\mathbb F_p$-schemes), and using $F_{\operatorname{Spec}k}^{\mathrm{abs}}=\operatorname{Spec}(c\mapsto c^q)=F_k$ and $F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}=\pi_P$ (Step 2a),
$$\xi\circ F_k=\xi\circ F_{\operatorname{Spec}k}^{\mathrm{abs}}=F_P^{\mathrm{abs}}\circ\xi=\pi_P\circ\xi=\pi_P(\xi)\in P(k). \tag{4.1}$$

---

**Conclusion.** Combining (3.1) and (4.1): for every $\xi\in P(k)$, represented under $\iota$ by a line bundle $L$ on $Y_k$,
$$\iota\big(\pi_P(\xi)\big)=\iota\big(P(F_k)(\xi)\big)=\big[F_{Y,k}^{*}L\big].$$
Since $\iota$ is a bijection, this says precisely that the following diagram of sets (in fact of abelian groups) commutes:
$$\begin{array}{ccc} P(k) & \xrightarrow{\;\iota\;\sim\;} & \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)\\ \downarrow{\ \xi\mapsto\pi_P\circ\xi\ } && \downarrow{\ L\mapsto F_{Y,k}^{*}L\ }\\ P(k) & \xrightarrow[\;\iota\;\sim\;]{} & \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k). \end{array}$$
That is, under the canonical identification $P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y_k)$, the map induced by pullback along $F_{Y,k}=\operatorname{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ is the map induced on $k$-points by the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi_P$ of $P$. This is exactly the statement to be proved.

---

**Remarks on conventions (verification and warning).**

(i) *Concrete check.* Take $Y=C$ a curve and $\xi=[\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-y)]$ with $x,y\in C(k)$. Writing $a\in C(k)$ for a $k$-point, the composite $F_{C,k}\circ a$ is the $k$-point $a^{(q)}$ obtained by raising the coordinates to the $q$-th power, and on the affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$ of $\mathbb P^1_k$ the map $F_{\mathbb P^1,k}$ is $\sum c_it^i\mapsto\sum c_i^{q}t^i$, so the ideal $(t-a)$ pulls back to $(t-a^{q})$. Hence $F_{C,k}^{*}\mathcal O(x-y)\simeq\mathcal O(x^{(q)}-y^{(q)})$, which is the classical description of the action of the Frobenius endomorphism of the Jacobian on $\operatorname{Pic}^0$. The statement proved above is consistent with this, and with the convention of lemma_abjac_frob.

(ii) *Do not confuse $F_{Y,k}$ with the base change of $\pi_Y$.* The base change to $k$ of the absolute Frobenius $\pi_Y:F_Y^{\mathrm{abs}}\to$ of the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Y$ is $\pi_Y\times\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}k}:Y_k\to Y_k$, which on $\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$ acts by $t\mapsto t^q$ with coefficients fixed, whereas $F_{Y,k}$ acts by $t\mapsto t$ and $c\mapsto c^q$ on coefficients; their composite is $F^{\mathrm{abs}}_{Y_k}$. Pullback by $\pi_Y\times\operatorname{id}$ sends $\mathcal O(a)$ to $\mathcal O(q\cdot a)$ (the divisor of degree $q$), while pullback by $F_{Y,k}$ sends $\mathcal O(a)$ to $\mathcal O(a^{(q)})$. It is the latter — the $k$-point action of $\pi_P$ — that the lemma identifies, as proved above from the functoriality of the Picard functor.

(iii) *No semisimplicity input is used.* The argument is purely the functoriality of the Picard scheme plus the naturality of absolute Frobenius; in particular it does not depend on the Kummer sequence, on Tate modules, or on any of the cohomological lemmas in the list, none of which is cited.

lemma_188.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/\mathbb F_q}\) be the Picard variety with \(q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism \(\pi_P\). Put \(T_\ell(P_k)=\varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)\), with bonding maps multiplication by \(\ell\), and \(V_\ell(P_k)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(P_k)\). Suppose there is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(\alpha:H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\sim}V_\ell(P_k)\) with \(\alpha\circ F=\pi_P\circ\alpha\), where \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), acts on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\) through its action on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\) and on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_188.proof:
Write $V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $V(1):=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$, and denote by $F_0$ (resp. $F_1$) the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $V$ (resp. $V(1)$) induced by $F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$; the hypothesis on $\alpha$ is $\alpha\circ F_1=\pi_P\circ\alpha$. The claim is that $F_1$ and $F_0$ are semisimple.

STEP 0 (finite dimensionality and invertibility). By lemma_6a, $F_0$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $V$. The sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$ carries its arithmetic Frobenius structure (an isomorphism $F^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ of sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces), so the same construction gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism $F_1$ of $V(1)$. Since $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ (each equipped with its Frobenius structure) shows $V$ and $V(1)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

STEP 1 (the Tate module and $\pi_P$). Since $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/\mathbb F_q}$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q$, and $P_k=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X_k/k}$. Apply lemma_tate_rank to the abelian variety $P_k$ over the algebraically closed field $k$ and the prime $\ell\neq p=\operatorname{char}k$: $T_\ell(P_k)=\varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)$ (bonding maps $\times\ell$) is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2\dim P$, hence $V_\ell(P_k)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(P_k)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, of dimension $2\dim P$. The $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi_P$ of $P$ is a homomorphism of group schemes over $\mathbb F_q$; it preserves each finite subgroup $P[\ell^n](k)$ and is compatible with $\times\ell$, so it induces a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear endomorphism of $T_\ell(P_k)$ and a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism, denoted $\pi_P$, of $V_\ell(P_k)$. It is invertible: $\pi_P$ is an isogeny, and its dual (the Verschiebung) $\check\pi_P$ satisfies $\check\pi_P\circ\pi_P=\pi_P\circ\check\pi_P=[q]_P$; functoriality of $V_\ell$ and the fact that $V_\ell([m])=m\cdot\mathrm{id}$ (multiplication by $m$ on $A[\ell^n](k)$ is the $\mathbb Z_\ell$-scalar $m$) give $V_\ell(\pi_P)\circ(q^{-1}V_\ell(\check\pi_P))=\mathrm{id}$. So $\pi_P\in\mathrm{GL}(V_\ell(P_k))$.

STEP 2 (the case $\dim P=0$). Then $T_\ell(P_k)=0$, so $V_\ell(P_k)=0$, and $\alpha$ forces $V(1)=0$. By Step 5's twisting map $\Phi$ below (which exists independently of the argument, since $\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, $1\mapsto\xi$, is an isomorphism of constant sheaves for any $0\ne\xi$), $V\cong V(1)=0$. The zero operator on the zero space has squarefree minimal polynomial (it is $1\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, or vacuously diagonalisable), so both $F_1$ and $F_0$ are semisimple. Henceforth assume $\dim P\ge 1$.

STEP 3 ($\pi_P$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(P_k)$).
3a. By lemma_poincare_reducibility applied to the abelian variety $P$ over the field $\mathbb F_q$, there exist simple abelian $\mathbb F_q$-subvarieties $B_1,\dots,B_r\subseteq P$ ($r\ge1$) such that the addition homomorphism $\sigma:B:=B_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}B_r\to P$, $(b_1,\dots,b_r)\mapsto\sum b_i$, is an isogeny. Let $\pi_i$ be the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism of $B_i$ and $\pi_B$ that of $B$.
3b. Naturality of Frobenius: for every morphism $f:A\to A'$ of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes one has $F_{A'}\circ f=f\circ F_A$, where $F_A=\mathrm{id}_A\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$. (Both sides are the identity on topological spaces, and on structure sheaves both are $\sigma$-semilinear with the same effect on local functions.) Applying this to the closed immersion $\iota_i:B_i\hookrightarrow P$ (defined over $\mathbb F_q$) gives $\pi_P\circ\iota_i=\iota_i\circ\pi_i$; applying it to $\sigma$ (defined over $\mathbb F_q$) gives $\pi_P\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\pi_B$. Moreover $\pi_B=\pi_1\times\cdots\times\pi_r$, since Frobenius on a product of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes is computed componentwise.
3c. $V_\ell(\sigma):V_\ell(B)\to V_\ell(P)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. Let $n=\deg\sigma\ge1$ and $N=\ker\sigma$, a finite group scheme of order $n$ over $\mathbb F_q$. By Lagrange's theorem for finite group schemes, $N\subseteq B[n]$, i.e. $[n]_B$ kills $N$. By the universal property of the quotient abelian variety $P=B/N$, the homomorphism $[n]_B$ factors uniquely through $\sigma$: there is a homomorphism $\tau:P\to B$ with $\tau\circ\sigma=[n]_B$. Then $\sigma\tau\sigma=\sigma[n]_B=[n]_P\sigma$ (as $\sigma$ is a homomorphism), and since $\sigma$ is surjective, hence an epimorphism of fppf sheaves, $\sigma\circ\tau=[n]_P$. Applying $V_\ell$ gives $V_\ell(\sigma)V_\ell(\tau)=n\,\mathrm{id}=V_\ell(\tau)V_\ell(\sigma)$; as $n\ne0$ in the characteristic-$0$ field $\mathbb Q_\ell$, $V_\ell(\sigma)$ is invertible with inverse $n^{-1}V_\ell(\tau)$.
3d. $V_\ell(B)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(B_i)$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell[\pi]$-modules. Let $p_i:B\to B_i$ and $s_i:B_i\to B$ be the projection and the $i$-th section. Then $\sum_i s_ip_i=\mathrm{id}_B$ and $p_is_j=\delta_{ij}\mathrm{id}_{B_i}$. The functor $V_\ell$ is additive on homomorphisms: for $f,g:A\to A'$ one has $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ on $k$-points, so $V_\ell(f+g)=V_\ell(f)+V_\ell(g)$ as $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear maps of $T_\ell$, and $V_\ell(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$. Hence the maps $V_\ell(p_i)$ and $V_\ell(s_i)$ exhibit $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(B_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}V_\ell(B)$, $\oplus x_i\mapsto\sum_i V_\ell(s_i)x_i$. Under this identification, $V_\ell(\pi_B)=\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_i)$: indeed $\pi_Bs_i=s_i\pi_i$ by 3b applied to $s_i$, so $V_\ell(\pi_B)=\sum_i V_\ell(s_i)V_\ell(\pi_i)V_\ell(p_i)$.
3e. Each $\pi_i$ acts semisimply on $V_\ell(B_i)$: this is lemma_92 with $m=1$, applied to the simple abelian variety $B_i$ over $\mathbb F_q$ and its $q$-power Frobenius $\pi_i$; it says the minimal polynomial of $\pi_i$ on $V_\ell(B_i)$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$.
3f. Each $\pi_i$ is invertible on $V_\ell(B_i)$ by the argument of Step 1 (the Verschiebung). Hence by lemma_9, $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_i)$ is semisimple on $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(B_i)$; by 3d, $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(B)$.
3g. The isomorphism $V_\ell(\sigma)$ of 3c satisfies $V_\ell(\sigma)\circ V_\ell(\pi_B)=V_\ell(\pi_P)\circ V_\ell(\sigma)$ by 3b. Both $V_\ell(B)$ and $V_\ell(P_k)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (lemma_tate_rank, and $V_\ell(B)\cong\oplus_iV_\ell(B_i)$), and both operators are invertible. Lemma_8 now implies $V_\ell(\pi_P)=\pi_P$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(P_k)$.

STEP 4 (transfer to $H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$). The map $\alpha:V(1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V_\ell(P_k)$ is an isomorphism of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces intertwining the invertible operators $F_1$ and $\pi_P$ (hypothesis: $\alpha\circ F_1=\pi_P\circ\alpha$). By Step 3, $\pi_P$ is semisimple, so lemma_8 gives that $F_1$ is semisimple on $V(1)=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$. This proves the first assertion.

STEP 5 (removing the Tate twist). Choose $0\ne\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$; since $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is a $1$-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, $m_\xi:\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, $1\mapsto\xi$, is an isomorphism of constant étale sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces on $X_k$, inducing a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\Phi:V\xrightarrow{\sim}V(1)$ on cohomology. By lemma_78, whose setup records the arithmetic Frobenius structure on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ as multiplication by $q^{-j}$; for $j=1$ the structure isomorphism $\theta:F^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ therefore satisfies $\theta(F^*\xi)=q^{-1}\xi$, while the structure isomorphism $\psi:F^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ is the identity. Unwinding the definitions, $F_1\circ\Phi$ is induced on coefficients by $\theta\circ F^*(m_\xi)\circ\psi^{-1}:\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, $1\mapsto q^{-1}\xi$, i.e. by $m_{q^{-1}\xi}=q^{-1}m_\xi$; hence $F_1\circ\Phi=q^{-1}\,\Phi\circ F_0$, equivalently $\Phi^{-1}\circ F_1\circ\Phi=q^{-1}F_0$. (Only the non-vanishing of the scalar is used below, so the argument is independent of the $q$ vs.\ $q^{-1}$ convention.) Since $F_1$ is semisimple (Step 4) and $\Phi$ is an intertwining isomorphism of finite-dimensional spaces with invertible operators, lemma_8 yields that $q^{-1}F_0$ is semisimple on $V$. Finally, $q^{-1}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, and by lemma_64(iv) semisimplicity passes to nonzero scalar multiples (applying it with the scalars $q^{-1}$ and $q$ gives the equivalence: $T$ semisimple $\Leftrightarrow cT$ semisimple for $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$); thus $F_0=q\cdot(q^{-1}F_0)$ is semisimple on $V=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This proves the second assertion, and together with Step 4 completes the proof.

(Remark on the role of the hypotheses: geometric connectedness of $X$ is not used in an essential way beyond guaranteeing that $P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/\mathbb F_q}$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q$; the whole content is the given identification $\alpha$, which reduces the problem to the semisimplicity of the Frobenius endomorphism on the rational Tate module of $P$, proved in Step 3 from the simple case (lemma_92) via Poincaré complete reducibility.)

lemma_194.statement: Let \(q=p^{a}\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a dominant morphism of degree \(d\ge 1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_{q}\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\) and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_{Z}:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism of Poincaré duality normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_{Z}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q}]\), and let \(f^{*}\) denote pullback on cohomology. Then for every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\) there exists a unique \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear map \(f_{*}:H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\) such that \(\operatorname{tr}_{Y}(f_{*}x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_{X}(x\cup f^{*}y)\) for all \(x\in H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\) and \(y\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\).
lemma_194.proof:
**Proof.** Write \(V_Z^m := H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) and \(m\ge 0\), and write \(L:=\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\); note that \(L\) is a one-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space (Tate twisting does not change the underlying \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space dimension).

**Step 1 (finite-dimensionality).** Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are projective over \(\mathbb F_q\), hence proper. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob with \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\), the constant sheaf on \(Z_k\) (which lies in \(D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\)) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\). It gives that \(H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(n\). Thus every \(V_Z^m\) below is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space.

**Step 2 (the trace map and the Poincar\'e pairings).** The varieties \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_{q^1}\). Apply lemma_77 with \(m=1\) and \(d=D\), to \(Z=X\) and to \(Z=Y\). Its part (a) yields a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism
\[\operatorname{tr}_Z:V_Z^{2D}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\qquad \operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q],\]
which is exactly the map whose existence the statement of the present lemma prescribes (it is in fact unique: two such isomorphisms differ by a scalar \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\), and evaluating on \(\mathrm{cl}(z)\) for any closed point \(z\) of \(Z\) — closed points exist because \(Z\) is of finite type over the field \(\mathbb F_q\) — forces \(\lambda[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\), i.e. \(\lambda=1\)). Its part (b) yields, for every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\), a perfect \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear pairing
\[\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z:V_Z^n\times V_Z^{2D-n}\longrightarrow L,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_Z=\operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v).\]

**Step 3 (unwinding perfectness).** Saying that \(\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z\) is perfect means that the two canonical \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear maps
\[\beta_Z^n:V_Z^n\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Z^{2D-n},L),\quad u\longmapsto \big(v\mapsto \operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)\big),\qquad\text{and}\qquad V_Z^{2D-n}\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Z^n,L),\]
are isomorphisms. (Both maps are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear because the cup product is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear and \(\operatorname{tr}_Z\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear; since the spaces are finite-dimensional by Step 1 and \(L\) is one-dimensional, either map being an isomorphism implies the other, so the reading of "perfect" is immaterial here.) We shall use only the first map, for \(Z=Y\): henceforth fix an \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\) and put \(\beta:=\beta_Y^n\), an isomorphism.

**Step 4 (construction of \(f_*\)).** Let \(f_k:X_k\to Y_k\) be the base change of \(f\) to \(k\); by functoriality (contravariance) of \'etale cohomology it induces a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map \(f^*:=f_k^*:V_Y^{j}\to V_X^{j}\) for every \(j\). For \(x\in V_X^n\) define
\[\psi_x:V_Y^{2D-n}\longrightarrow L,\qquad \psi_x(y):=\operatorname{tr}_X\big(x\cup f^*y\big).\]
This is well defined: \(f^*y\in V_X^{2D-n}\), so \(x\cup f^*y\in V_X^{2D}\) by graded-commutativity/compatibility of the cup product with degrees, and \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) is defined on \(V_X^{2D}\). It is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear because it is the composite of the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear maps \(y\mapsto f^*y\), \(y\mapsto x\cup f^*y\) (with \(x\) fixed) and \(\operatorname{tr}_X\). Hence \(\psi_x\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Y^{2D-n},L)=\operatorname{coker? }\) — precisely, \(\psi_x\) lies in the target of \(\beta\). Define
\[f_*x:=(\beta_Y^n)^{-1}(\psi_x)\ \in V_Y^n.\]
By the definition of \(\beta_Y^n\) this element is characterised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\psi_x(y)\) for all \(y\in V_Y^{2D-n}\), i.e.
\[\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\qquad\text{for all }x\in V_X^n,\ y\in V_Y^{2D-n},\]
which is the required identity. This proves existence.

**Step 5 (linearity of \(f_*\)).** Let \(x,x'\in V_X^n\) and \(a,b\in\mathbb Q_\ell\). For every \(y\in V_Y^{2D-n}\),
\[\psi_{ax+bx'}(y)=\operatorname{tr}_X\big((ax+bx')\cup f^*y\big)=a\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)+b\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x'\cup f^*y)=(a\psi_x+b\psi_{x'})(y),\]
using \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinearity of the cup product and \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(\operatorname{tr}_X\). Thus \(x\mapsto\psi_x\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, and since \(f_*=(\beta_Y^n)^{-1}\circ(x\mapsto\psi_x)\) is a composite of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear maps, \(f_*:V_X^n\to V_Y^n\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear.

**Step 6 (uniqueness).** Suppose \(g:V_X^n\to V_Y^n\) is any map (not a priori linear) satisfying \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(g(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\) for all \(x,y\). Fixing \(x\) and subtracting the identity of Step 4 gives \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\big((g(x)-f_*x)\cup y\big)=0\) for every \(y\in V_Y^{2D-n}\), i.e. \(\beta_Y^n(g(x)-f_*x)=0\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Y^{2D-n},L)\). Since \(\beta_Y^n\) is an isomorphism (Step 3), it is injective, so \(g(x)-f_*x=0\). As \(x\) was arbitrary, \(g=f_*\). In particular there is at most one \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with the stated property.

**Step 7 (edge cases and scope of the argument).** The construction uses only that \(0\le n\le 2D\), so that lemma_77(b) supplies a perfect pairing on both \(X\) and \(Y\); it applies verbatim at the extremes \(n=0\) (pairing \(V_Y^0\times V_Y^{2D}\to L\)) and \(n=2D\) (pairing \(V_Y^{2D}\times V_Y^0\to L\)), and no further case has to be considered because the statement asserts existence and uniqueness only for \(0\le n\le 2D\). Note also that the hypotheses that \(f\) is dominant and of degree \(d\) are not needed for this adjointness statement: the argument uses only \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(f^*\), which holds for an arbitrary morphism of \(\mathbb F_q\)-schemes, together with the fact that \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same pure dimension \(D\) so that both pairings take values in the same line \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\). (The degree \(d\) enters the further, separate identity \(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^*=d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y\) on top cohomology, which is not asserted here.)

Combining Steps 4, 5 and 6, for every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\) there exists a unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\) for all \(x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(y\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_196.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge 1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F_X,F_Y\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), of the \(\ell\)-adic cohomology of \(X_k,Y_k\). For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism with \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). Let \(f_{*}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map satisfying \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\) for all \(x\in H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(y\in H^{2D-n}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*\) and \(f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}\).
lemma_196.proof:
Write $H^i(Z):=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, and write $f^*:H^i(Y)\to H^i(X)$ for the pullback of $f_k:=f\times\mathrm{id}_k:X_k\to Y_k$. Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so lemma_77 applies to each of them with $m=1$, $d=D$, and $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q$.

**Step 0 (reduction to $0\le n\le 2D$).** Étale cohomology of a scheme vanishes in negative degrees (it is the right derived functor of a left exact functor), and for a smooth $D$-dimensional variety over the separably closed field $k$ one has $H^i=0$ for $i>2D$ (standard bound on the cohomological dimension of a smooth $D$-fold over a separably closed field, with $\ell\ne\mathrm{char} k$). Hence for $n\notin[0,2D]$ both $H^n(X)$ and $H^n(Y)$ are the zero space, $f_*:0\to 0$ and $f^*:0\to0$, and the two asserted identities $f_*F_X=F_Yf_*$ and $f_*f^*=d\,\mathrm{id}$ hold trivially. Assume from now on $0\le n\le 2D$.

**Step 1 (the trace maps are the canonical ones, and are Frobenius-equivariant).** For $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, lemma_77(a) provides a canonical isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z:H^{2D}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ with $\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$ for every closed point $z$ of $Z$, and it is equivariant for arithmetic Frobenius, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ as multiplication by $q^{D}$; i.e.
\[ \operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z(F_Z u)=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z(u)\qquad\text{for all }u\in H^{2D}(Z). \tag{1}\]
Since $\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z$ is an isomorphism, $H^{2D}(Z)$ is $1$-dimensional; and for any closed point $z$ of $Z$ (such exist, $Z$ being non-empty, as $f$ is surjective of degree $d\ge1$) $\mathrm{cl}(z)\ne0$ because $\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\ge1\ne0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell$. Thus the classes of closed points span the $1$-dimensional space $H^{2D}(Z)$. The map $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ appearing in the hypotheses of the present lemma is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $H^{2D}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ taking the same values $\mathrm{cl}(z)\mapsto[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$ on a spanning set, hence
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Z=\operatorname{tr}^{77}_Z, \tag{2}\]
so (1) holds for $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ as well. (The same uniqueness shows the $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ of the present lemma coincide with those of lemma_77 and of lemma_top_trace_generically_finite, so those results may be applied verbatim.)

**Step 2 (perfectness; the cancellation principle).** By lemma_77(b), for each $i$ with $0\le i\le 2D$ the pairing $H^i(Z)\times H^{2D-i}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)$, is perfect. Consequently we may use the following cancellation rule: if $a,b\in H^i(Z)$ satisfy $\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup v)=\operatorname{tr}_Z(b\cup v)$ for every $v\in H^{2D-i}(Z)$, then $\operatorname{tr}_Z((a-b)\cup v)=0$ for all $v$ (by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of $\cup$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_Z$), and perfectness (injectivity of $H^i(Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2D-i}(Z),\mathbb Q_\ell(-D))$) forces $a=b$. \tag{3}

**Step 3 (functoriality of Frobenius: $F_X\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y$).** Let $p_Z:Z_k\to Z$ and $q_Z:Z_k\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ be the projections. The morphism $\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma:Z_k\to Z_k$ is the unique morphism into the fibre product $Z_k=Z\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ satisfying $p_Z\circ(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=p_Z$ and $q_Z\circ(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=\sigma\circ q_Z$. Compare the two morphisms $X_k\to Y_k$ given by $f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)$ and by $(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)\circ f_k$; using $p_Y\circ f_k=f\circ p_X$ and $q_Y\circ f_k=q_X$:
\[ p_Y\circ f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=f\circ p_X,\qquad q_Y\circ f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=\sigma\circ q_X, \]
\[ p_Y\circ(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)\circ f_k=f\circ p_X,\qquad q_Y\circ(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)\circ f_k=\sigma\circ q_X. \]
By the universal property of $Y_k$ the two morphisms are equal:
\[ f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)\circ f_k. \tag{4}\]
Contravariance of étale cohomology under composition of morphisms of schemes then gives $F_X\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y$. \tag{5}

**Step 4 (Frobenius is a ring automorphism, and is bijective).** Each $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is the pullback by an automorphism of the scheme $Z_k$, hence is a graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra automorphism of $\bigoplus_i H^i(Z)$: $F_Z(u\cup v)=F_Zu\cup F_Zv$. By lemma_6a, $F_Z$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism with inverse $(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*$; in particular $F_Y:H^{2D-n}(Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2D-n}(Y)$ is surjective. \tag{6}

**Step 5 (proof of $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$).** Fix $x\in H^n(X)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$, and put $\tilde y:=F_Y(y)\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$. We compute, indicating the justification of each equality:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*(F_Xx)\cup\tilde y\bigr)
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_Xx\cup f^*\tilde y\bigr) \quad\text{[defining property of }f_*,\text{ applied to }F_Xx\in H^n(X),\ \tilde y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)]}\\
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_Xx\cup F_X(f^*y)\bigr) \quad\text{[by (5), since }f^*\tilde y=f^*F_Yy=F_Xf^*y]}\\
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X(x\cup f^*y)\bigr) \quad\text{[by (4)/(6): }F_X\text{ preserves cup products]}\\
&=q^{D}\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y) \quad\text{[by (1) for }Z=X,\text{ with }u=x\cup f^*y\in H^{2D}(X)]}\\
&=q^{D}\,\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y) \quad\text{[defining property of }f_*]}\\
&=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Y(f_*x\cup y)\bigr) \quad\text{[by (1) for }Z=Y,\text{ with }u=f_*x\cup y\in H^{2D}(Y)]}\\
&=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Yf_*x\cup F_Yy\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Yf_*x\cup\tilde y\bigr) \quad\text{[by (6)]}.
\end{aligned}\]
Here $x\cup f^*y\in H^{n+(2D-n)}(X)=H^{2D}(X)$ and $f_*x\cup y\in H^{2D}(Y)$, so (1) applies in both cases. Thus for every $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$,
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((f_*F_Xx-F_Yf_*x)\cup\tilde y\bigr)=0, \]
and by (6) the element $\tilde y=F_Yy$ runs over all of $H^{2D-n}(Y)$. The cancellation rule (3) with $i=n$, $a=f_*F_Xx$, $b=F_Yf_*x$ yields $f_*F_Xx=F_Yf_*x$. As $x\in H^n(X)$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$ as endomorphisms of the pair $(H^n(X),H^n(Y))$. This proves the first claim.

**Step 6 (proof of $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^n(Y)}$).** Fix $x\in H^n(Y)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$. Then
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*(f^*x)\cup y\bigr)
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*x\cup f^*y\bigr) \quad\text{[defining property of }f_*,\text{ applied to }f^*x\in H^n(X)]}\\
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*(x\cup y)\bigr) \quad\text{[$f^*$ is a graded }\mathbb Q_\ell\text{-algebra map]}\\
&=d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y). \quad\text{[see below]}
\end{aligned}\]
For the last equality: by lemma_top_trace_generically_finite, applied to the proper surjective generically finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ of degree $d$ between smooth projective geometrically connected $D$-folds over $\mathbb F_q$ with the normalised traces, the automorphism $\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^*\circ\operatorname{tr}_Y^{-1}$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ is multiplication by $d$. Taking $u:=x\cup y\in H^{2D}(Y)$ and applying this to $\operatorname{tr}_Y(u)$ gives $\operatorname{tr}_X(f^*u)=d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y(u)$; note $d\cdot(-)$ denotes the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $v\mapsto d\,v$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, so $d\operatorname{tr}_Y(u)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(d\,u)$ as well. Since $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, $d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((d\,x)\cup y\bigr)$. Hence
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*f^*x\cup y\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((d\,x)\cup y\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }y\in H^{2D-n}(Y). \]
By the cancellation rule (3) with $a=f_*f^*x$ and $b=d\,x$, we obtain $f_*f^*x=d\,x$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^n(Y)}$.

**Step 7 (conclusion).** Steps 5 and 6 establish both identities for $0\le n\le 2D$, and Step 0 covers the remaining degrees. This completes the proof. \[
\qed
\]

lemma_195.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/\mathbb F_q}\) be the Picard variety with \(q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism \(\pi_P\), and suppose \(\operatorname{NS}(X_k)=\operatorname{Pic}(X_k)/P(k)\) is finitely generated. Give \(T_\ell(P_k)=\varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)\) the bonding maps \(x\mapsto \ell x\). Then the Kummer isomorphism \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\sim}\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(X_k)[\ell^n]\) composed with the inverse of the map \(T_\ell(P_k)\to\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(X_k)[\ell^n]\) induced by \(P\subset\operatorname{Pic}\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-modules \(\varphi\) satisfying \(\varphi\circ F_{X,k}^*=\pi_P\circ\varphi\), where \(F_{X,k}=\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), acts by pullback of line bundles.
lemma_195.proof:
We prove the statement in seven steps. Throughout, write
\[Y:=X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k,\qquad \operatorname{Pic}:=\operatorname{Pic}(Y),\qquad P_k:=P\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k,\]
and write $\Phi:\operatorname{Pic}\to\operatorname{Pic}$ for the pullback homomorphism $L\mapsto F_{X,k}^{*}L$ induced by $F_{X,k}=\operatorname{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$.

**Preliminaries (identifications and notation).**
(a) Since $X$ is smooth projective (hence proper, flat and of finite presentation over $\mathbb F_q$) and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=\mathbb F_q$ (as $X$ is geometrically connected), the Picard functor commutes with the field extension $\mathbb F_q\subset k$: $\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/k}\simeq \operatorname{Pic}_{X/\mathbb F_q}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$. Taking identity components and $k$-points identifies $P(k)$ with $\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)$, the subgroup of $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$ of line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero; we use this identification silently. In particular $P$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q$ (the Picard variety), so $P_k$ is an abelian variety over $k$; put $g:=\dim P$. Also $\operatorname{NS}:=\operatorname{NS}(X_k):=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/P(k)$ is a finitely generated abelian group by hypothesis.
(b) Because $\sigma(c)=c^q$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ elementwise, the structure morphism $p:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ satisfies $p\circ F_{X,k}=p$; thus $F_{X,k}$ is a morphism of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes.
(c) For an abelian group $A$ we write $A[\ell^n]=\ker(\ell^n:A\to A)$, always with bonding maps $\times\ell$, as in the statement.

**Step 1. Multiplication by $\ell$ on $P(k)$ is surjective.**
Consider $[\ell]:P_k\to P_k$. Its differential at the identity $e$ is multiplication by $\ell$ on the $k$-vector space $T_eP_k$: indeed $[\ell]$ is the $\ell$-fold sum $e+\cdots+e$ of $\operatorname{id}_{P_k}$ under the group law, and the tangent map of a sum of homomorphisms of group schemes is the sum of the tangent maps. Since $\operatorname{char}k=p\neq\ell$, this differential is an isomorphism, so $[\ell]$ is étale at $e$; the identity $[\ell]\circ t_x=t_{\ell x}\circ[\ell]$ for translations $t_x$ then shows $[\ell]$ is étale everywhere, hence an open map. Its image $[\ell](P_k)$ is also closed, because $P_k$ is proper over $k$ and a morphism from a proper $k$-scheme to a separated $k$-scheme is a closed map. Thus $[\ell](P_k)$ is a non-empty (it contains $e$) open-and-closed subset of $P_k$; as $P_k$ is connected (irreducible, being an abelian variety), $[\ell](P_k)=P_k$, i.e. $[\ell]$ is surjective on geometric points. Now let $a\in P(k)$. The scheme-theoretic fibre $Z:=P_k\times_{[\ell],P_k,a}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a non-empty closed subscheme of finite type over $k$; since $k$ is algebraically closed every non-empty finite type $k$-scheme has a $k$-rational point (take a closed point; its residue field is a finite algebraic extension of $k$, hence $k$). Hence there is $b\in P(k)$ with $\ell b=a$, so $\times\ell:P(k)\twoheadrightarrow P(k)$.

**Step 2. The map $\iota:T_\ell(P_k)\to\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}[\ell^n]$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups.**
By definition of $\operatorname{NS}$ there is a short exact sequence of abelian groups
\[0\longrightarrow P(k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(Y)\longrightarrow \operatorname{NS}\longrightarrow 0.\]
For each $n$, since $P[\ell^n]$ is the kernel of the homomorphism of group schemes $[\ell^n]:P_k\to P_k$ and taking $k$-points is left exact on group schemes, $P[\ell^n](k)=\ker(\ell^n:P(k)\to P(k))=P(k)[\ell^n]$; the same holds for $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$. By Step 1, multiplication by $\ell$ on $D:=P(k)$ is surjective. We may therefore apply lemma_limsys_torsion_exact (eoinm/lemma_limsys_torsion_exact) to the above short exact sequence with $D=P(k)$, $G=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$, $Q=\operatorname{NS}$; all torsion systems carry the bonding maps $\times\ell$, exactly as in the statement. It yields an exact sequence
\[0\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)\xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\longrightarrow \varprojlim_n\operatorname{NS}[\ell^n]\longrightarrow 0,\]
where the map labelled $\iota$ is precisely the one induced levelwise by the inclusion $P[\ell^n](k)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$, i.e. the map of the statement. Since $\operatorname{NS}$ is finitely generated, lemma_181 (eoinm/lemma_181) gives $\varprojlim_n\operatorname{NS}[\ell^n]=0$. Exactness then forces $\iota$ to be injective and surjective, hence an isomorphism of abelian groups.

**Step 3. $\iota$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear.**
For any abelian group $A$, $\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n]$ is a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module as follows: for $z\in\mathbb Z_\ell$ and $\mathbf a=(a_n)_n\in\varprojlim A[\ell^n]$ set $z\cdot\mathbf a:=(z_na_n)_n$, where $z_n\in\mathbb Z$ is any integer with $z_n-z\in\ell^n\mathbb Z_\ell$. This is well defined: $\ell^na_n=0$, so $z_na_n$ depends only on $z\bmod \ell^n$; and if $\ell a_{n+1}=a_n$ then $\ell(z_{n+1}a_{n+1})=z_{n+1}a_n=(z_{n+1}-z_n)a_n+z_na_n=z_na_n$ because $\ell^n\mid(z_{n+1}-z_n)$ and $\ell^na_n=0$, so $(z_na_n)_n$ again lies in the limit. With this description, $\iota(z\cdot\mathbf a)=(z_na_n)_n$ computed inside $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)$, which is exactly $z\cdot\iota(\mathbf a)$. Hence $\iota$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Z_\ell$-modules.

**Step 4. The Kummer isomorphism.**
$Y=X_k$ is smooth projective geometrically connected over the algebraically closed field $k$, and $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k=p$. By lemma_kummer_h1 (eoinm/lemma_kummer_h1) applied to $Y$, the connecting homomorphisms of the Kummer sequences $0\to\mu_{\ell^n}\to\mathbb G_m\xrightarrow{\ \ell^n\ }\mathbb G_m\to0$ give canonical isomorphisms $\kappa_n:H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$, compatible with the transition maps $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, and with $\times\ell$ on the right, and inducing a canonical $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module isomorphism
\[\kappa:=\varprojlim_n\kappa_n:\;H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))=\varprojlim_nH^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(X_k)[\ell^n].\]

**Step 5. Equivariance of $\kappa$ with respect to $F_{X,k}$.**
We first equip $H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))$ with the pullback action of $F_{X,k}$ and check that $\kappa$ intertwines it with $\Phi$ on the limit of Picard torsion groups. The sheaves $\mu_{\ell^n}$ and $\mathbb G_m$ on $Y_{\acute et}$ are represented by the base changes $\mu_{\ell^n,\mathbb F_q}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}Y$ and $\mathbb G_{m,\mathbb F_q}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}Y$. For a morphism of schemes $f:Z\to W$, inverse image on the étale topos sends the sheaf represented by $V\to W$ to the sheaf represented by $V\times_WZ\to Z$; applying this to $f=F_{X,k}$ and using $p\circ F_{X,k}=p$ from Preliminaries (b), the projection $(u,x)\mapsto(x,u)$ gives a canonical isomorphism of group schemes over $Y$
\[(\mu_{\ell^n,\mathbb F_q}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}Y)\times_{Y,F_{X,k}}Y\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\mu_{\ell^n,\mathbb F_q}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}Y\]
(and likewise for $\mathbb G_m$): indeed $(F_{X,k}(x),u,x)$ with $u$ over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ matching $F_{X,k}(x)$ satisfies $p(x)=p(F_{X,k}(x))$, so $(x,u)$ is well defined, with inverse $(x,u)\mapsto(F_{X,k}(x),u,x)$. Denote the resulting isomorphisms of étale sheaves of abelian groups by $\theta_{\mu,n}:F_{X,k}^{-1}\mu_{\ell^n}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mu_{\ell^n}$ and $\theta_{\mathbb G}:F_{X,k}^{-1}\mathbb G_m\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb G_m$. Because the inclusion $\mu_{\ell^n}\hookrightarrow\mathbb G_m$, the power morphism $u\mapsto u^{\ell^n}$, the power morphism $u\mapsto u^{\ell}$ and the transition $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, are all defined over $\mathbb F_q$, they are preserved by these identifications; i.e. the squares formed with $\theta_{\mu,n}$, $\theta_{\mu,n+1}$, $\theta_{\mathbb G}$ and the above morphisms commute. Since $F_{X,k}^{-1}$ is exact on abelian sheaves, the inverse image of the Kummer sequence is exact, and the $\theta$'s give an isomorphism from $F_{X,k}^{-1}$ of the Kummer sequence to the Kummer sequence itself. Functoriality of the long exact cohomology sequence then yields, for each $n$, a commutative diagram
\[\begin{CD}H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})@>{\kappa_n}>>\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\\ @V{\Phi_n}VV @VV{\Phi}V\\ H^1_{\acute et}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})@>{\kappa_n}>>\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n],\end{CD}\]
where $\Phi_n$ is the composite $H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{F_{X,k}^{-1}}H^1(Y,F_{X,k}^{-1}\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\theta_{\mu,n,*}}H^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$, i.e. the pullback map of $F_{X,k}$, and the right vertical arrow is the restriction of $\Phi=L\mapsto F_{X,k}^*L$: on the bottom row this is the standard identification of the map $H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m)\to H^1(Y,F_{X,k}^{-1}\mathbb G_m)\xrightarrow{\theta_{\mathbb G,*}}H^1(Y,\mathbb G_m)$ with pullback of line bundles, because a $\mathbb G_m$-torsor $T=L^{\times}$ pulls back to the torsor $T\times_{Y,F_{X,k}}Y=(F_{X,k}^*L)^{\times}$ of the base-changed line bundle, and forming the associated line bundle $-\times^{\mathbb G_m}\mathbb A^1$ is compatible with this. The commutativity with the transition maps in $n$ (already noted) shows the $\Phi_n$ are compatible with the bonding maps $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}$, so they define an endomorphism $\varprojlim_n\Phi_n$ of $H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))=\varprojlim_nH^1(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})$, which is by definition the action of $F_{X,k}$ by pullback on $H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))$ denoted $F_{X,k}^{*}$ in the statement. Passing to the inverse limit over $n$ in the diagram gives
\[\kappa\circ F_{X,k}^{*}=\Phi_{\lim}\circ\kappa,\qquad \Phi_{\lim}:=\varprojlim_n\Phi:\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\to\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n].\]
(Each $\Phi_n$ and $\Phi_{\lim}$ is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear, being induced by the group homomorphism $\Phi$ levelwise, in the sense of Step 3.)

**Step 6. Equivariance of $\iota$: on $T_\ell(P_k)$ the pullback $\Phi$ is $\pi_P$.**
Apply lemma_picard_frob_pullback (eoinm/lemma_picard_frob_pullback) to $Y=X$ over $\mathbb F_q$: under the identification $P(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(X_k)$ of Preliminaries (a), the endomorphism of $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X_k)$ induced by pullback along $F_{X,k}$ is the map on $k$-points induced by the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi_P:P\to P$. Thus $\Phi|_{P(k)}=\pi_P|_{P(k)}$. Consequently, for $L\in P[\ell^n](k)$ one has $\ell^n\Phi(L)=\Phi(\ell^nL)=0$, so $\Phi$ carries $P[\ell^n](k)$ into itself and coincides there with $\pi_P$; and $\Phi$ commutes with the bonding maps $\times\ell$ because pullback is a group homomorphism ($F_{X,k}^*(L\otimes M)=F_{X,k}^*L\otimes F_{X,k}^*M$). Hence $\Phi$ restricts to an endomorphism of $\varprojlim_nP[\ell^n](k)=T_\ell(P_k)$, and this restricted endomorphism is exactly the one induced levelwise by $\pi_P$, which is what $\pi_P$ denotes on $T_\ell(P_k)$ in the statement (it is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear, since $\pi_P$ is a group homomorphism and the $\mathbb Z_\ell$-action is defined levelwise by integral multiples, as in Step 3). By construction of $\iota$ as the map induced by the inclusions $P[\ell^n](k)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]$ we therefore have
\[\iota\circ\pi_P=\Phi_{\lim}\circ\iota.\]

**Step 7. Conclusion.**
Define
\[\varphi:=\iota^{-1}\circ\kappa:\;H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }T_\ell(P_k),\]
i.e. the Kummer isomorphism $\kappa$ of Step 4 followed by the inverse of the isomorphism $\iota$ of Steps 2--3. Both $\kappa$ and $\iota^{-1}$ are isomorphisms of $\mathbb Z_\ell$-modules, hence so is $\varphi$. Finally, using Step 5 and Step 6,
\[\varphi\circ F_{X,k}^{*}=\iota^{-1}\circ\kappa\circ F_{X,k}^{*}=\iota^{-1}\circ\Phi_{\lim}\circ\kappa=\iota^{-1}\circ\iota\circ\pi_P\circ\iota^{-1}\circ\kappa=\pi_P\circ\varphi.\]
This is the required intertwining relation, and it completes the proof. \(\blacksquare\)

(Remark, not used above: tensoring $\varphi$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ identifies $H^1_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$ with $V_\ell(P_k)$ equivariantly for $F$ and $\pi_P$, which is precisely the hypothesis needed to invoke lemma_188.)

lemma_199.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts on \(H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as multiplication by \(q^D\); in particular \(F\) and geometric Frobenius act semisimply on it.
lemma_199.proof:
**Proof.** Write \(V:=H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(F:V\to V\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism \((\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\).

**Step 1 (Frobenius-equivariance of the trace isomorphism).** We apply lemma_77 (Frobenius-equivariant Poincaré duality), part (a), with the following input: the base field of that lemma is \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) with \(m:=1\), i.e. \(\mathbb F_q\) itself; \(Y:=X\), which is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d:=D\) over \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_{q^1}\); \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\); and the prime \(\ell\neq p\). The \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of lemma_77 is then, with \(m=1\), exactly our \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F\). That lemma supplies a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism
\[\operatorname{tr}=\operatorname{tr}_X:\; V \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\ \text{ for every closed point } z\in X,\]
which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where \(F\) acts on the one-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) as multiplication by the scalar \(c=q^{md}=q^{1\cdot D}=q^D\). Written as an identity of maps \(V\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\), this is
\[\tag{1} \operatorname{tr}\circ F=q^D\cdot \operatorname{tr}.\]

**Step 2 (\(F\) is the scalar \(q^D\)).** Let \(x\in V\). By \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(\operatorname{tr}\) we have \(\operatorname{tr}(q^D x)=q^D\operatorname{tr}(x)\), and by (1), \(\operatorname{tr}(Fx)=q^D\operatorname{tr}(x)\). Hence
\[\operatorname{tr}(Fx-q^Dx)=\operatorname{tr}(Fx)-\operatorname{tr}(q^Dx)=q^D\operatorname{tr}(x)-q^D\operatorname{tr}(x)=0.\]
Since \(\operatorname{tr}\) is an isomorphism it is injective, so \(Fx-q^Dx=0\). As \(x\) was arbitrary,
\[\tag{2} F=q^D\cdot \mathrm{id}_V.\]
Two by-products we will use: because \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) is one-dimensional, \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=1\) (so in particular \(V\neq 0\) and \(V\) is finite-dimensional, as required to invoke lemma_6a below); and (2) exhibits \(F\) as an invertible operator since \(q^D=p^{aD}\neq 0\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) (characteristic \(0\)).

**Step 3 (semisimplicity of \(F\) and of geometric Frobenius).** The polynomial \(T-q^D\in\mathbb Q_\ell[T]\) is linear, hence coprime to its derivative \(1\), hence squarefree. By (2) the minimal polynomial of \(F\) divides \(T-q^D\); since \(V\neq 0\) and \(F=q^D\mathrm{id}\neq 0\), the minimal polynomial is exactly \(T-q^D\). Thus \(F\) is semisimple in the sense used throughout (squarefree minimal polynomial); equivalently every nonzero vector of \(V\) is an eigenvector.

For geometric Frobenius: by lemma_6a applied to \(i=2D\) (the space is finite-dimensional by Step 2), the geometric Frobenius \(F_{\mathrm{geo}}:=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*\) satisfies \(F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}=F^{-1}\). By (2), \(F^{-1}=q^{-D}\mathrm{id}_V\). This is again a scalar automorphism, with minimal polynomial \(T-q^{-D}\), which is linear and hence squarefree; so geometric Frobenius is semisimple on \(V\) as well.

Finally, for any field extension \(\Omega/\mathbb Q_\ell\) — in particular \(\Omega=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) — the base-changed operator \(F_\Omega=q^D\mathrm{id}_{V\otimes\Omega}\) is diagonal with respect to every basis, hence diagonalizable; the same holds for \(F_{\mathrm{geo},\Omega}=q^{-D}\mathrm{id}\). This is the equivalent formulation of semisimplicity appearing in the conjecture (cf. lemma_5), and it completes the proof for \(D\ge 1\).

**Step 4 (the case \(D=0\)).** Suppose \(D=0\). A smooth proper \(0\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F_q\)-scheme is finite étale, so \(X=\operatorname{Spec} L\) with \(L\) a finite separable \(\mathbb F_q\)-algebra; \(X\) being geometrically connected forces \(L\) to be a field with \(L\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) connected, and since the latter is \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q^{[L:\mathbb F_q]}\), we get \([L:\mathbb F_q]=1\), i.e. \(X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\). Then \(X_k=\operatorname{Spec} k\) is connected and strictly henselian, so \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\Gamma(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) acts on it through the canonical identification \(F^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\) of constant sheaves, which is the identity on the constant value \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); thus \(F=\mathrm{id}=q^0\cdot\mathrm{id}\), as claimed. (This agrees with Steps 1–2, since lemma_77(a) imposes no restriction on \(d\) and for \(d=0\) gives \(\operatorname{tr}:H^0(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(0)=\mathbb Q_\ell\) with \(F\) acting on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(0)\) as \(q^{1\cdot 0}=1\).) Geometric Frobenius is then also the identity, hence semisimple.

Combining Steps 2–4, \(F\) acts on \(H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as multiplication by \(q^D\), and both \(F\) and geometric Frobenius act semisimply on it. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_abjac_h1_frob_equiv.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}\) be its Jacobian, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. For \(y\in C(k)\) let \(\varphi_y:C_k\to J_k\) be the Abel\(\text{\u2013}\)Jacobi morphism \(x\mapsto[\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-y)]\). Then \[\varphi_y^*\circ F_J=F_C\circ\varphi_y^*\] as maps \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), where \(F_J=(\mathrm{id}_J\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) and \(F_C=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) with \(\sigma(c)=c^q\).
lemma_abjac_h1_frob_equiv.proof:
**Notation.** Write $F_{C,k}:=\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:C_k\to C_k$ and $F_{J,k}:=\mathrm{id}_J\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:J_k\to J_k$, where $\sigma(c)=c^q$ is the $q$-power automorphism of $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. The operators in the statement are the pullbacks $F_C:=F_{C,k}^*$ on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $F_J:=F_{J,k}^*$ on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. We must prove $\varphi_y^*\circ F_J=F_C\circ\varphi_y^*$ as maps $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The argument uses only functoriality of pullback, the Frobenius-compatibility of the Abel–Jacobi map, and the triviality of the action of translations on cohomology; no semisimplicity and no isomorphism property of $\varphi_y^*$ is used.

**Step 0 (the objects of the assertion are well defined).** The Jacobian $J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q$, so $C$ and $J$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is an object of $D^b_c(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for both. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to $X=C$ and to $X=J$ with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\phi=\psi$ the natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$ shows that $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. By lemma_6a, applied to $X=C$ and $X=J$ with $i=1$, the pullbacks $F_C=F_{C,k}^*$ and $F_J=F_{J,k}^*$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of these spaces. Pullback along the $k$-morphism $\varphi_y:C_k\to J_k$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $\varphi_y^*:H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, so both $\varphi_y^*\circ F_J$ and $F_C\circ\varphi_y^*$ are well-defined $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (the former lands in $H^1(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; both are maps $H^1(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$).

**Step 1 (Frobenius compatibility of the Abel–Jacobi map, dualised).** Since $F_{C,k}$ is a morphism $C_k\to C_k$ over $k$, it sends $k$-rational points to $k$-rational points; hence $F_{C,k}(y)\in C(k)$ and $\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}$ is defined. Lemma_abjac_frob, applied to the curve $C/\mathbb F_q$, its Jacobian $J$, and the point $y$, gives an equality of morphisms $C_k\to J_k$:
$$F_{J,k}\circ\varphi_y=\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}\circ F_{C,k}.\qquad (1)$$
\'Etale cohomology is contravariant: $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. Dualising (1) and keeping the order of composition exactly as contravariance dictates,
$$\varphi_y^*\circ F_{J,k}^*=(F_{J,k}\circ\varphi_y)^*=(\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}\circ F_{C,k})^*=F_{C,k}^*\circ\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}^*,$$
that is,
$$\varphi_y^*\circ F_J=F_C\circ\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}^*.\qquad (2)$$
(Reversing the order here would be the standard mistake: the left-hand factor $F_{J,k}$ of (1) becomes the right-hand factor $F_{J,k}^*=F_J$ after pullback.)

**Step 2 (the two Abel–Jacobi maps differ by a translation).** We claim that
$$\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}=t_a\circ\varphi_y\qquad\text{with}\qquad a:=[\mathcal O_{C_k}(y-F_{C,k}(y))]\in J(k),$$
where $t_a:J_k\to J_k$ is translation by $a$.

First, $a$ is a well-defined $k$-point of $J$: the divisor $y-F_{C,k}(y)$ on $C_k$ has degree $1-1=0$, so $\mathcal O_{C_k}(y-F_{C,k}(y))$ is a degree-$0$ line bundle on the smooth projective geometrically connected curve $C_k$, hence an element of $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C_k/k}(k)=J(k)$ (the group law on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_k)$ being given by tensor product of line bundles).

Now take any $x\in C(k)$. By definition of the Abel–Jacobi morphism, $\varphi_y(x)=[\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-y)]$ and $\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}(x)=[\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-F_{C,k}(y))]$. As divisors on $C_k$ we have $(x-F_{C,k}(y))-(x-y)=y-F_{C,k}(y)$, hence a canonical isomorphism of line bundles
$$\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-F_{C,k}(y))\simeq\mathcal O_{C_k}(x-y)\otimes_{\mathcal O_{C_k}}\mathcal O_{C_k}(y-F_{C,k}(y)).$$
Both factors on the right have degree $0$ (the first because $\deg(x-y)=0$), so they lie in $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_k)$, and passing to classes in $J(k)$ with the group law given by tensor product yields
$$\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}(x)=\varphi_y(x)+a=t_a(\varphi_y(x))\qquad\text{for all }x\in C(k).$$
It remains to promote this equality of $k$-point evaluations to an equality of morphisms. Both $u:=\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}$ and $v:=t_a\circ\varphi_y$ are morphisms $C_k\to J_k$, and $J_k$ is separated over $k$ (it is proper, being an abelian variety). Therefore the equaliser $E=\{x\in C_k:u(x)=v(x)\}$, the inverse image of the diagonal $\Delta_{J_k}\subset J_k\times_k J_k$ under $(u,v):C_k\to J_k\times_k J_k$, is closed in $C_k$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed and $C_k$ is of finite type over $k$, the closed points of $C_k$ are exactly $C(k)$, and they are dense in $C_k$ (non-empty, finite type over a field). As $E$ contains $C(k)$, $E=C_k$, so $u=v$. This proves
$$\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}=t_a\circ\varphi_y.\qquad (3)$$

**Step 3 (translations act trivially on $H^1$).** Pulling back (3) gives $\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}^*=\varphi_y^*\circ t_a^*$. Apply lemma_translations_trivial to the abelian variety $A=J$ over $\mathbb F_q$, the point $a\in J(k)$, and the degree $n=1$: $t_a^*=\operatorname{id}$ on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Consequently
$$\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}^*=\varphi_y^*\qquad\text{on }H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\qquad (4)$$

**Step 4 (conclusion).** Substitute (4) into the right-hand side of (2):
$$\varphi_y^*\circ F_J=F_C\circ\varphi_{F_{C,k}(y)}^*=F_C\circ\varphi_y^*.$$
This is exactly the required equality of maps $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, i.e. $\varphi_y^*$ is equivariant for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius. $\blacksquare$

**Remark (independence of $y$, and generality).** The proof shows more: the same reasoning, with $n$ arbitrary, gives $\varphi_y^*\circ F_J=F_C\circ\varphi_y^*$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge 0$, since lemma_translations_trivial holds in every degree. It also shows $\varphi_{y'}^*=\varphi_y^*$ on $H^1$ for any two $y,y'\in C(k)$ (take $a=[\mathcal O(y'-y)]$ in place of the above $a$), so the equivariance does not depend on the choice of base point.

lemma_203.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Suppose that for every \(n\ge 1\) the cup-product homomorphism \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces. Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge 0\).
lemma_203.proof:
Write $V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and write $F_n$ (resp. $F_1$) for the automorphism $F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, of $H^n$ (resp. of $V$). We must show $F_n$ is semisimple for every $n\ge 0$.

Step 0 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility). An abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, hence $A_k$ is proper over $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. The constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $A_k$, placed in cohomological degree $0$, is an object of $D^b_c(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_{A_k}^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell$. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to $X=A$, $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $\varphi=\psi$ gives that for every $n$ the hypercohomology $\mathbb H^n(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space; since $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a sheaf concentrated in degree $0$, the hypercohomology spectral sequence degenerates and identifies $\mathbb H^n(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with the sheaf cohomology $H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Thus every $H^n$, and in particular $V$, is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By lemma_6a (applied to the scheme $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$), for every $n$ the pullback $F_n=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^n$, with inverse $F_n^{\,-1}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$ (geometric Frobenius). Hence $F_n\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n)$, and the induced map $\bigwedge^n F_1$ is an automorphism of $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ with inverse $\bigwedge^n(F_1^{-1})$.

Step 1 (semisimplicity in degree 1). By lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple, which applies verbatim to the abelian variety $A/\mathbb F_q$, the prime $\ell\ne p$ and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is semisimple. That is, $F_1\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ has squarefree minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

Step 2 (semisimplicity on the exterior power). Fix $n\ge 1$. Since $V$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space and $F_1\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is semisimple (Step 1), lemma_177 applied to $T=F_1$ gives that the induced automorphism $\bigwedge^n F_1$ of $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ is semisimple, i.e. has squarefree minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

Step 3 (the cup-product map intertwines $\bigwedge^n F_1$ with $F_n$). Consider
\[
\mu_n:\ \bigwedge{}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\longrightarrow H^n,\qquad x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n\longmapsto x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_n ,
\]\nwhich is exactly the homomorphism that the hypothesis of the lemma assumes to be an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces (for $n\ge 1$). We check that $\mu_n$ is $F$-equivariant. The operator $F$ on $\bigoplus_n H^n$ is pullback on cohomology along the single morphism of $k$-schemes $g:=\mathrm{id}_{A}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:A_k\to A_k$; pullback along a morphism of schemes is a homomorphism of graded rings, i.e. for homogeneous classes $a,b$ one has $g^*(a\cup b)=g^*a\cup g^*b$, and $g^*(1)=1$. By induction on $n$ it follows that $F_n(x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_n)=F_1x_1\cup\cdots\cup F_1x_n$ for all $x_1,\dots,x_n\in V$. On the other hand, by definition of the induced exterior power automorphism, $\bigwedge^nF_1(x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n)=F_1x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge F_1x_n$. Therefore
\[
\mu_n\circ\Big(\bigwedge{}^n F_1\Big)=F_n\circ\mu_n
\]\nfor every $n\ge 1$: the pure tensors $x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n$ span $\bigwedge^nV$, so the two $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps $\mu_n\circ\bigwedge^nF_1$ and $F_n\circ\mu_n$ agree on a spanning set, hence agree everywhere.

Step 4 (transfer of semisimplicity along $\mu_n$). Fix $n\ge 1$. We have finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces $W_1:=\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$ and $W_2:=H^n$, invertible operators $T_{W_1}=\bigwedge^nF_1\in\mathrm{GL}(W_1)$ (Step 0) and $T_{W_2}=F_n\in\mathrm{GL}(W_2)$ (Step 0), and a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\alpha=\mu_n:W_1\xrightarrow{\sim}W_2$ (hypothesis) with $\alpha\circ T_{W_1}=T_{W_2}\circ\alpha$ (Step 3). Lemma_8 applies and yields: $T_{W_1}$ is semisimple if and only if $T_{W_2}$ is semisimple. By Step 2, $T_{W_1}=\bigwedge^nF_1$ is semisimple; hence $F_n$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

(Concretely, the content of lemma_8 here is that $\mu_n$ identifies $\mathbb Q_\ell[F_n]\backslash H^n$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell[\bigwedge^nF_1]\backslash\bigwedge^nV$, so the two operators have the same minimal polynomial; squarefreeness of the latter, established in Step 2, is thus inherited by the former.)

Step 5 (the case $n=0$). An abelian variety is, by definition, proper, smooth and with geometrically connected fibres over the base, so $A_k$ is connected; therefore $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$, generated by the class $1$ of the constant function. Pullback along $g=\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ sends a locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued function to itself, so $F_0=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}$. Its minimal polynomial is $t-1$, which is squarefree, so $F_0$ is semisimple. (Equivalently, $\mu_0:\bigwedge^0V=\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}H^0$ is the isomorphism $1\mapsto 1$, which is $F$-equivariant, and $\bigwedge^0F_1=\mathrm{id}$ is semisimple.)

Step 6 (vanishing in high degrees, for completeness). Since $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=0$ for all $n>\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V$; the hypothesis then forces $H^n=0$ for those $n$, and the (unique) automorphism of the zero space is semisimple, so the conclusion holds trivially there as well. This case is in any event already covered by Steps 2–4, since lemma_177 and lemma_8 apply verbatim to $W_1=W_2=0$.
