Conclusion. Steps 5 and 4 together give: for every integer $n\ge 0$, the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This is exactly the required statement. $\qquad\blacksquare$

lemma_201.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(n\ge 1\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Write \(h=c_1(\mathcal O_{{\mathbb P}^n}(1))\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then the homomorphism \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})\to\bigoplus_{m\ge 0}H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(t^i\mapsto h^i\), is an isomorphism of graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-algebras, where \(F\) acts on \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})\) by \(F(t^i)=q^i t^i\) for \(0\le i\le n\).
lemma_201.proof:
We fix the notation of the statement: $q=p^a$, $n\ge 1$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$, $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, $F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius, and $h=c_1(\mathcal O_{{\mathbb P}^n}(1))\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$. By lemma_6a, $F$ is a ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$; being a pull-back map it is also multiplicative for the cup product, $F(x\smile y)=Fx\smile Fy$, and it preserves cohomological degree. (Multiplicativity is the standard fact that pull-back of sheaves on the small \'etale site is symmetric monoidal, so the cup product, which is defined via the derived tensor product, is functorial in the required sense.)

STEP 1. The ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-cohomology of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ and the Frobenius on it.
Put $X_0=\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb F}_q$; then $(X_0)_k=\operatorname{Spec}(k\otimes_{{\mathbb F}_q}k)=\operatorname{Spec}k$. Since $k$ is separably closed, every $k$-\'etale algebra is a finite product of copies of $k$; hence the small \'etale topos $\operatorname{Sh}((\operatorname{Spec}k)_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ is equivalent to $\mathbf{Sets}$ (evaluation at the final object $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an equivalence). Under this equivalence the constant sheaf ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$ corresponds to the set ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and $\Gamma$ corresponds to the identity functor, which is exact. Therefore
$$H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)={\mathbb Q}_\ell,\qquad H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)=0\ \ (m\ge 1).$$
The morphism $\mathrm{id}_{X_0}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma:(X_0)_k\to (X_0)_k$ is $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$. For the corresponding morphism of topoi $f$, the inverse-image functor satisfies $f^{-1}\circ\Delta=\Delta$ (where $\Delta$ is the constant-sheaf functor, because $\Delta$ is the inverse image of the structure morphism of the topos and inverse images compose); the induced identification $f^{-1}{\mathbb Q}_\ell\cong{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is the canonical one used to define the arithmetic Frobenius on ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-cohomology. On global sections, $\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)={\mathbb Q}_\ell\to\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}k,f^{-1}{\mathbb Q}_\ell)={\mathbb Q}_\ell$ sends the constant section with value $a$ to the constant section with value $a$. Hence
$$F_{X_0}=\mathrm{id}_{{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\ \ \text{on}\ H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell).$$

STEP 2. Applying the Frobenius-equivariant projective bundle formula (lemma_110).
$X_0=\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb F}_q$ is smooth and projective of pure dimension $0$ over ${\mathbb F}_q$. Let $E={\mathcal O}_{X_0}^{\,n+1}$, a vector bundle of rank $r=n+1\ge 1$. With the convention of lemma_110 that $\pi:{\mathbb P}(E)\to X_0$ is the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients, ${\mathbb P}(E)=\mathbf{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}E^\vee)=\mathbf{Proj}{\mathbb F}_q[x_0,\dots,x_n]={\mathbb P}^n_{{\mathbb F}_q}$, and the tautological quotient line bundle ${\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}(E)}(1)$ is the usual ${\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^n}(1)$. The class $\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$ of lemma_110, which corresponds to $c_1({\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}(E)}(1))$ under the same identification of the twisted and untwisted Chow/Chern class conventions used in the statement of that lemma, is therefore exactly $h=c_1({\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^n}(1))$. Lemma_110 then gives, for every $m\ge 0$, an isomorphism
$$\varphi_m:\bigoplus_{j=0}^{n} H^{m-2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell),\qquad (x_j)\longmapsto\sum_{j=0}^{n}\pi^*x_j\smile h^{j},$$\nequivariant for Frobenius, where $F$ acts on the $j$-th summand as $q^{j}F_{X_0}$; and it also states directly that $F\xi=q\xi$, i.e. $Fh=qh$.

STEP 3. Computation of the groups.
By Step 1 the source of $\varphi_m$ is ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (in the summand $j=m/2$) if $m$ is even with $0\le m\le 2n$, and $0$ otherwise: if $m$ is odd, every $m-2j$ is odd and $\ge 1$ or negative, so all terms vanish; if $m=2i$ with $0\le i\le n$, the only non-zero summand is $j=i$, contributing $H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)={\mathbb Q}_\ell$; if $m=2i$ with $i>n$ or $m>2n$, then $m-2j\ge m-2n>0$ for all $0\le j\le n$, so all summands vanish. Hence
$$H^{2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)={\mathbb Q}_\ell\cdot h^{i}\ \ (0\le i\le n),\qquad H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)=0\ \ (m\ \text{odd or}\ m>2n).$$
In particular $h^i\ne 0$ for $0\le i\le n$ (for $i=0$, $h^0=1=\pi^*(1)$ generates $H^0={\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which is non-zero; and $\varphi_{2i}$ is an isomorphism carrying $1\in H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k)$ to $h^i$), each $H^m$ is one-dimensional in even degrees $\le 2n$, and $h^{n+1}=0$ for degree reasons since $H^{2n+2}=0$.

STEP 4. Frobenius weights.
Since $F$ is multiplicative and $Fh=qh$, for every $0\le i\le n$
$$F(h^{i})=F(h)^{i}=(qh)^{i}=q^{\,i}h^{i}.$$
(Equivalently, this is the $i$-th case of the equivariance of $\varphi_{2i}$ in Step 2 together with $F_{X_0}=\mathrm{id}$ from Step 1.) Thus $F$ acts on $H^{2i}$ by the scalar $q^i$, and on $H^m=0$ trivially; in particular $F$ preserves each homogeneous piece.

STEP 5. The graded ring structure.
Consider
$$\Phi:{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{m\ge 0}H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell),\qquad \overline{t^{\,i}}\longmapsto h^{i}.$$
(a) $\Phi$ is well defined: the relation $t^{n+1}=0$ maps to $h^{n+1}=0$, which holds by Step 3; hence the assignment extends the unique ring homomorphism ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]\to\oplus_m H^m$, $t\mapsto h$ (which exists because the cup product is commutative/associative and ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$ maps to $1\in H^0$), and this homomorphism kills the ideal $(t^{n+1})$.
(b) $\Phi$ is a ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear isomorphism: ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})$ has basis $\overline{1},\overline t,\dots,\overline{t^{n}}$, and by Step 3 $\oplus_m H^m$ has basis $1,h,\dots,h^n$; $\Phi$ carries basis to basis.
(c) $\Phi$ is multiplicative: $\Phi(\overline{t^{\,i}}\cdot\overline{t^{\,j}})=\Phi(\overline{t^{\,i+j}})=h^{i+j}=h^i\smile h^j=\Phi(\overline{t^{\,i}})\smile\Phi(\overline{t^{\,j}})$, where for $i+j\ge n+1$ both sides are $0$ (left because $t^{i+j}\in(t^{n+1})$, right because $h^{i+j}$ is a product of classes whose total degree $2(i+j)>2n$ lands in $H^{2(i+j)}=0$; more precisely $h^{i+j}=h^{n+1}h^{i+j-n-1}=0$).
(d) $\Phi$ is graded: put on ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})$ the grading with $t$ of degree $2$, i.e. $({\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1}))^m={\mathbb Q}_\ell\overline{t^{\,m/2}}$ for $m$ even, $0\le m\le 2n$, and $0$ for $m$ odd. Then $\Phi$ sends degree $m$ into $H^m$ and is an isomorphism in each degree by (b) and Step 3.

STEP 6. The $F$-action on ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})$ and $F$-equivariance.
Define $T:{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})\to{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})$ ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linearly by $T(\overline{t^{\,i}})=q^{i}\overline{t^{\,i}}$ for $0\le i\le n$. This is well defined: $T(t^{n+1})=q^{n+1}\overline{t^{\,n+1}}=0$ in the quotient, so the ideal $(t^{n+1})$ is $T$-stable. It is a ring homomorphism since $T(\overline{t^{\,i}}\,\overline{t^{\,j}})=T(\overline{t^{\,i+j}})=q^{i+j}\overline{t^{\,i+j}}=q^{i}\overline{t^{\,i}}\,q^{j}\overline{t^{\,j}}=T(\overline{t^{\,i}})\,T(\overline{t^{\,j}})$ (both sides are $0$ if $i+j\ge n+1$), it is ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear by definition, and it is an automorphism with inverse $\overline{t^{\,i}}\mapsto q^{-i}\overline{t^{\,i}}$ ($q\in{\mathbb Z}_{>0}\subset{\mathbb Q}_\ell^\times$). It preserves the grading of Step 5(d). By Step 4,
$$\Phi\bigl(T(\overline{t^{\,i}})\bigr)=\Phi(q^{i}\overline{t^{\,i}})=q^{i}h^{i}=F(h^{i})=F\bigl(\Phi(\overline{t^{\,i}})\bigr)$$\nfor all $0\le i\le n$, and by ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linearity for all elements. Thus $\Phi$ is $F$-equivariant, where $F$ acts on the left as $T$, i.e. by $F(t^i)=q^i t^i$ as required.

STEP 7. Conclusion.
Steps 5 and 6 show that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of graded rings which is ${\mathbb Q}_\ell$-linear and intertwines the automorphism $t^i\mapsto q^i t^i$ of ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^{n+1})$ with the arithmetic Frobenius $F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ on $\oplus_{m\ge0}H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}({\mathbb P}^n_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)$. That is precisely an isomorphism of graded ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[F]$-algebras. \quad($\blacksquare$)

Remark on edge cases. For $n=1$ the conclusion reads $H^0={\mathbb Q}_\ell$, $H^1=0$, $H^2={\mathbb Q}_\ell h$ with $Fh=qh$ and $h^2=0$ in the ring ${\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]/(t^2)$, which is exactly the content of Steps 3-4 with $0\le i\le 1$; no separate argument is needed. The argument also uses $n\ge1$ only through $r=n+1\ge1$, the rank condition of lemma_110.

lemma_205.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\), let \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\) denote the group of \(k\)-points of the identity component \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\) of the Picard scheme of \(Y\) over \(k\), and let \(\operatorname{NS}(Y):=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\). Then \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) is a finitely generated abelian group.
lemma_205.proof:
We prove that NS(Y) := Pic(Y)/Pic^0(Y) is a finitely generated abelian group. No lemma from the provided list is used: lemma_173, lemma_pic_torsion_limit and lemma_195 all take the finite generation of a Néron–Severi group as a HYPOTHESIS, so they would be circular here. The argument is: (1) identify Pic(Y)/Pic^0(Y) with the group of line bundles modulo algebraic equivalence, using the Picard scheme; (2) apply the theorem of the base (a standard external theorem of Néron–Severi, valid over any algebraically closed field), with the hypothesis check made explicit. A self-contained proof of the characteristic-zero case is added at the end.

STEP 0 (preliminaries). Since Y is geometrically connected over k, H^0(Y, O_Y) = k; in particular Y ≠ ∅. As k is algebraically closed, every closed point of the finite-type k-scheme Y has residue field k, so Y(k) ≠ ∅; fix y ∈ Y(k). (If one's convention allowed Y = ∅, then Pic(∅) = 0 and NS(∅) = 0, trivially finitely generated; so assume Y ≠ ∅.)

STEP 1 (the Picard scheme). Because Y is projective, flat and of finite presentation over k with H^0(Y,O_Y) = k, the Picard functor
   Pic_{Y/k} : (Sch/k)^op → Ab,   S ↦ Pic(Y ×_k S)/pr_2^* Pic(S)
(is the fppf sheafification, which for projective Y is already a sheaf in the étale topology) is representable by a k-scheme Pic_{Y/k}, separated and locally of finite type over k. Since Y has the k-point y, the rigidified Picard functor (rigidified at y) coincides with the above quotient functor and is represented by the same scheme; taking S = Spec k, pr_2^* Pic(Spec k) = 0 because Pic(Spec k) = 0, so we get a canonical bijection
   Pic_{Y/k}(k)  --~-->  Pic(Y),
which is an isomorphism of abelian groups (tensor product of line bundles is the group law on the Picard scheme). By definition Pic^0(Y) is the subgroup Pic^0_{Y/k}(k) of k-points of the identity component. The identity component Pic^0_{Y/k} is an open-and-closed subgroup scheme of Pic_{Y/k} (connected components of a scheme locally of finite type over a field are open). Because Y is smooth projective, Pic^0_{Y/k} is an abelian variety: it is a connected group scheme of finite type over k, smooth (Y smooth) and proper (standard theorem: Pic^0 of a smooth projective variety is an abelian variety, the dual of the Albanese variety); in particular it is integral and proper over k. The quotient A := Pic_{Y/k}/Pic^0_{Y/k} = π_0(Pic_{Y/k}) is an étale k-group scheme, and from the exact sequence of étale sheaves 1 → Pic^0_{Y/k} → Pic_{Y/k} → A → 1 (exact because Pic^0_{Y/k} is smooth, hence the quotient map is étale-locally split) we obtain an injection
   NS(Y) = Pic_{Y/k}(k)/Pic^0_{Y/k}(k)  ↪  A(k).
Thus NS(Y) is the group of k-points of the component group, modulo nothing; concretely it is Pic(Y) modulo the subgroup Pic^0(Y).

STEP 2 (Pic^0(Y) = line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero).
Definition. A line bundle L on Y is algebraically equivalent to zero, written L ≡_alg 0, if there exist a connected variety T over k, k-rational points t_0, t_1 ∈ T(k), and a line bundle M on T ×_k Y such that M|_{t_0 × Y} ≅ O_Y and M|_{t_1 × Y} ≅ L.

(⊆) Suppose L ≡_alg 0 via (T, t_0, t_1, M). By representability, M ∈ Pic(T ×_k Y) determines a k-morphism φ_M : T → Pic_{Y/k} whose value at a k-point t is the class of M|_{t × Y}. The map φ_M is continuous, and T is connected, so φ_M(T) ⊂ |Pic_{Y/k}| is a connected subset containing φ_M(t_0) = [O_Y] = e, the identity element. A connected subset containing e lies in the connected component of e, which is the underlying set of Pic^0_{Y/k}; since Pic^0_{Y/k} is an open-and-closed subscheme, the morphism φ_M factors through Pic^0_{Y/k}. Evaluating at t_1 gives L = φ_M(t_1) ∈ Pic^0_{Y/k}(k) = Pic^0(Y).

(⊇) Conversely let L ∈ Pic^0(Y) = Pic^0_{Y/k}(k). Write A^0 := Pic^0_{Y/k}, which by Step 1 is an abelian variety, hence a connected, proper variety over k with identity element e ∈ A^0(k). Take T := A^0, t_0 := e, t_1 := L (viewed as a k-point of A^0). Since Y is projective over k and Y(k) ≠ ∅ (the point y of Step 0 rigidifies the universal family), a Poincaré bundle P exists on Pic_{Y/k} ×_k Y; restrict it to A^0 ×_k Y. By the universal property of the Poincaré bundle, for every k-point x of Pic_{Y/k} the restriction P|_{x × Y} is a representative of the class x ∈ Pic(Y). Hence P|_{e × Y} ≅ O_Y and P|_{L × Y} ≅ L, which exhibits L ≡_alg 0. Note that the witnessing T = A^0 may be taken proper, so the same conclusion holds for the variant definition of algebraic equivalence in which T is required to be proper (and, by the standard curve-chain argument, for the definition via chains of complete curves).

Combining the two inclusions, Pic^0(Y) = {L ∈ Pic(Y) : L ≡_alg 0}. In particular this shows the algebraically trivial line bundles form a subgroup, and gives a canonical identification of abelian groups
   NS(Y) = Pic(Y)/Pic^0(Y)  =  Pic(Y)/{≡_alg} =: Pic(Y)/Pic^a(Y),
the classical Néron–Severi group defined via algebraic equivalence.

STEP 3 (theorem of the base; conclusion). We invoke the following standard external theorem.

Theorem of the base (Néron–Severi; Néron's theorem in arbitrary characteristic, in the form given by Kleiman's numerical theory of ampleness). Let Ω be an algebraically closed field and let V be a scheme which is projective of finite type over Ω. Then the group Pic(V)/Pic^a(V) of isomorphism classes of line bundles on V modulo algebraic equivalence is a finitely generated abelian group.

Hypothesis check for the theorem, applied to V := Y and Ω := k:
 (i) k = overline{F}_q is algebraically closed — true by construction;
 (ii) Y is a smooth projective variety over k, hence of finite type and separated over k, and the structure morphism Y → Spec k is projective; so Y is a scheme projective of finite type over the algebraically closed field k — true by the hypotheses of the lemma (smoothness is not needed for the theorem, only projectivity and finite type).
Therefore the theorem applies and Pic(Y)/Pic^a(Y) is a finitely generated abelian group. By the identification of Step 2 this group is canonically NS(Y) = Pic(Y)/Pic^0(Y). Hence NS(Y) is a finitely generated abelian group, which is the claim.

SUPPLEMENT (self-contained proof in the case where k embeds into C, showing the theorem of the base is not a bare citation there). Assume given an embedding ι : k → C (e.g. k = C or k = overline{Q}; this forces char k = 0).
(a) Descent. Y is of finite presentation over k, so there is a finitely generated extension K_0/Q inside k and a smooth projective K_0-scheme Y_0 with Y_0 ×_{K_0} k ≅ Y (take K_0 generated over Q by the coefficients of homogeneous equations cutting out Y ⊂ P^n_k; smoothness and projectivity are then already satisfied over K_0). For each intermediate field K_0 ⊂ K ⊂ k write Y_K := Y_0 ×_{K_0} K and A^0_K := Pic^0_{Y_K/K}, A_K := π_0(Pic_{Y_K/K}).
(b) Injectivity under field extension. For K_0 ⊂ K ⊂ K' ⊂ k, base change gives A_K ×_K K' ≅ A_{K'}: indeed Pic_{Y_K/K} ×_K K' ≅ Pic_{Y_{K'}/K'}, and since char = 0 the identity component Pic^0 is an abelian variety, which is geometrically connected, so it commutes with the base change. As A_K is étale and separated over K and Spec K' → Spec K is faithfully flat, A_K(K) → A_{K'}(K') is injective (two sections of a separated scheme agreeing after faithfully flat base change agree). Together with the injection NS(Y_K) ↪ A_K(K) of Step 1 this shows NS(Y_K) → NS(Y_{K'}) is injective for all K ⊂ K'.
(c) Every class comes from a finitely generated subfield. By the limit theorem for Picard groups of proper finitely presented schemes, Pic(Y_k) = colim_K Pic(Y_K) as K runs over the finitely generated extensions of K_0 inside k. Hence, using (b), NS(Y_k) = colim_K NS(Y_K) = ⋃_K NS(Y_K) inside NS(Y_k), where the union is taken via the injective transition maps NS(Y_K) ↪ NS(Y_C) obtained from ι : K → C.
(d) The case of C. For X := Y_C(C)^an, a compact Kähler manifold, GAGA identifies Pic(Y_C) with H^1(X, O_X^*). The exponential sequence 0 → Z → O_X → O_X^* → 0 gives an exact sequence H^1(X,O_X) → H^1(X,O_X^*) → H^2(X,Z). The kernel of c_1 : Pic(Y_C) → H^2(X,Z) is the image of H^1(X,O_X), which is precisely the group of line bundles parametrised by the identity component Pic^0_{Y_C/C}(C) of the Picard scheme (the classical identification of topologically trivial with algebraically trivial line bundles). Hence c_1 induces an injection NS(Y_C) ↪ H^2(X,Z). Since X has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, H^2(X,Z) is a finitely generated abelian group, so NS(Y_C) is finitely generated.
(e) Conclusion in this case. By (c), NS(Y_k) is a subgroup of the finitely generated abelian group NS(Y_C); subgroups of finitely generated abelian groups are finitely generated (Z^n is noetherian). Hence NS(Y_k) is finitely generated. This recovers, without the theorem of the base, the statement proved in Step 3 whenever k embeds into C; in the remaining cases (in particular char k = p > 0) Step 3 gives the result via Néron's theorem of the base, whose hypotheses were verified explicitly above. ∎

Remark (not used in the proof): the finite generation just established is exactly the hypothesis that other results in the library (e.g. lemma_173, lemma_pic_torsion_limit, lemma_195) assume about the Néron–Severi group; this lemma supplies it, and none of them was used here.

lemma_hc_affine_space.statement: Let $q=p^{a}$ be a prime power, let $k=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}$, let $\ell\neq p$ be prime, and let $m\ge 0$. For $\mathbb{A}^{m}_{k}=\operatorname{Spec}k[t_{1},\dots,t_{m}]$ with structure morphism $f:\mathbb{A}^{m}_{k}\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, write $H^{n}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{m}_{k},\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}):=H^{n}(\operatorname{Spec}k,Rf_{!}\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})$ for the etale cohomology with compact supports. Then $H^{n}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{m}_{k},\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})=0$ for every $n\neq 2m$, and $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}}H^{2m}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{m}_{k},\mathbb{Q}_{\ell})=1$.
lemma_hc_affine_space.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_hc_affine_space.

=== 0. Notation and the standard facts that are cited (not reproved) ===

For a scheme S of finite type over k = overline(F_q) with structure morphism f: S -> Spec k we write
  H^n(S, Q_l) := H^n(Spec k, Rf_* Q_l)  and  H^n_c(S, Q_l) := H^n(Spec k, Rf_! Q_l).
We use three standard facts of etale cohomology, quoted as such:

(F1) Localisation in compact supports (SGA 4, Exp. XVI, Th. 2.3.5; equivalently, the distinguished triangle Rj_! Q_l -> Q_l -> Ri_* Q_l -> in D^b_c(X, Q_l) attached to an open immersion j: U -> X of a noetherian scheme with closed complement i: Z -> X, to which one applies RGamma(X, -)). It yields a long exact sequence
  ... -> H^n_c(U, Q_l) -> H^n(X, Q_l) -> H^n(Z, Q_l) -> H^{n+1}_c(U, Q_l) -> ...,
where the middle arrow is the pullback i^*: H^n(X, Q_l) -> H^n(Z, Q_l) (under the identification H^n(X, Ri_* Q_l) = H^n(Z, Q_l), valid because i is a closed immersion, hence finite, hence i_* is exact on etale sheaves and Gamma(X, i_* -) = Gamma(Z, -)). The identification of H^n(X, Rj_! Q_l) with H^n_c(U, Q_l) used in (F1) comes from compatibility of R_! with composition: RGamma_c(U, Q_l) = Rf_{U,!} Q_l = Rf_{X,!} Rj_! Q_l = RGamma(X, Rj_! Q_l).

(F2) For a proper morphism the canonical map Rf_! -> Rf_* is an isomorphism (SGA 4, Exp. XVII, 3.2.4 / Exp. XVIII, 3.2.5). Hence H^n_c = H^n on proper k-schemes and on Spec k.

(F3) k is separably closed, so every finite etale k-scheme is a disjoint union of copies of Spec k; the small etale topos of Spec k is equivalent to the category of sets, Gamma(Spec k, -) is exact, and therefore H^0(Spec k, Q_l) = Q_l and H^n(Spec k, Q_l) = 0 for all n >= 1.

We also record that for every S of finite type over k one has H^n(S, Q_l) = 0 and H^n_c(S, Q_l) = 0 for n < 0: sheaf cohomology is a right derived functor, hence concentrated in degrees >= 0, and RGamma_c(S, Q_l) = RGamma(Spec k, Rf_! Q_l) is computed by the spectral sequence E_2^{p,q} = H^p(Spec k, R^q f_! Q_l) => H^{p+q}_c(S, Q_l) with p, q >= 0.

=== 1. The two preliminary claims ===

Claim 1 (cohomology of projective space over k). For every r >= 0,
  H^n(P^r_k, Q_l) = Q_l * h_r^s  for n = 2s with 0 <= s <= r, and H^n(P^r_k, Q_l) = 0 otherwise,
where h_r := c_1(O_{P^r}(1)) in H^2(P^r_k, Q_l). In particular dim H^{2s}(P^r_k) = 1 for 0 <= s <= r, and H^n(P^r_k) = 0 for n odd or n > 2r.
Proof of Claim 1. For r >= 1 this is exactly lemma_201 (eoinm), which asserts that Q_l[t]/(t^{r+1}) -> (+)_{m>=0} H^m(P^r_k, Q_l), t^i -> h_r^i, is an isomorphism of graded Q_l[F]-algebras, where the grading is the cohomological one (deg t = deg h_r = 2, since h_r lies in H^2). Comparing the homogeneous piece of degree n gives: it is Q_l * h_r^{n/2} when n = 2s is even with 0 <= s <= r, and 0 when n is odd, and 0 when n = 2s > 2r because t^{r+1} = 0 in the source (the source has no component in degrees 2s > 2r). For r = 0 one has P^0_k = Spec k, and the assertion H^0 = Q_l, H^n = 0 for n >= 1 is (F3) (together with the vanishing in negative degrees).

Claim 2 (restriction to a linear hyperplane). Let r >= 1 and let i: P^{r-1}_k -> P^r_k be the closed immersion onto a linear hyperplane. Then i^* h_r = h_{r-1}; consequently i^*: H^{2s}(P^r_k, Q_l) -> H^{2s}(P^{r-1}_k, Q_l) is an isomorphism for 0 <= s <= r-1, its target is 0 for s >= r, and in odd degrees i^* is the (zero) map between zero groups.
Proof of Claim 2. Because the hyperplane is linear, i^* O_{P^r}(1) = O_{P^{r-1}}(1); the first Chern class (etale cycle class) is compatible with pullback, hence i^* h_r = h_{r-1}, and therefore i^*(h_r^s) = h_{r-1}^s. For 0 <= s <= r-1 both Q_l * h_r^s = H^{2s}(P^r_k) and Q_l * h_{r-1}^s = H^{2s}(P^{r-1}_k) hold by Claim 1, so i^* is an isomorphism there. For s >= r one has 2s > 2(r-1), so H^{2s}(P^{r-1}_k) = 0 by Claim 1. Odd groups vanish on both sides by Claim 1.

=== 2. The case m = 0 ===

A^0_k = Spec k and f = id is proper, so by (F2) H^n_c(A^0_k, Q_l) = H^n(Spec k, Q_l), which by (F3) and the negative-degree vanishing equals Q_l for n = 0 = 2*0 and 0 for every n != 0. This is the statement for m = 0.

=== 3. The case m >= 1: the set-up ===

Identify A^m_k = Spec k[t_1,...,t_m] with the standard affine open D_+(T_0) of P^m_k = Proj k[T_0,...,T_m] via t_i = T_i/T_0. Its complement is V_+(T_0) = P^{m-1}_k. Write j: A^m_k -> P^m_k for the open immersion and i: P^{m-1}_k -> P^m_k for the closed immersion. By (F1), with X = P^m_k, U = A^m_k, Z = P^{m-1}_k, there is a long exact sequence, for all n in Z:

(L)  ... -> H^{n-1}(P^m_k, Q_l) --i^*--> H^{n-1}(P^{m-1}_k, Q_l) --delta--> H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) --> H^n(P^m_k, Q_l) --i^*--> H^n(P^{m-1}_k, Q_l) -> ...

We now chase (L) degree by degree. Throughout, h denotes h_m on P^m_k and h_{m-1} on P^{m-1}_k.

(a) n = 0. The exact piece 0 = H^{-1}(P^{m-1}_k) -> H^0_c(A^m_k) -> H^0(P^m_k) --i^*--> H^0(P^{m-1}_k) applies: by Claim 1 both H^0 groups are Q_l * 1 and by Claim 2 (s = 0) the map i^* is an isomorphism. Exactness says im(H^0_c -> H^0(P^m_k)) = ker(i^*) = 0, and the map H^0_c -> H^0(P^m_k) is injective (its kernel is the image of H^{-1}(P^{m-1}_k) = 0). Hence H^0_c(A^m_k, Q_l) = 0.

(b) n = 1. The exact piece H^0(P^m_k) --i^*--> H^0(P^{m-1}_k) --delta--> H^1_c(A^m_k) -> H^1(P^m_k). The map i^* is an isomorphism by (a), hence surjective, so ker(delta) = im(i^*) is everything and delta = 0. Exactness then makes H^1_c(A^m_k) -> H^1(P^m_k) injective, and H^1(P^m_k) = 0 by Claim 1 (odd degree). Hence H^1_c(A^m_k, Q_l) = 0.

(c) 2 <= n <= 2m - 1 (this range is empty when m = 1). Consider the exact piece
  H^{n-1}(P^m_k) --i^*--> H^{n-1}(P^{m-1}_k) --delta--> H^n_c(A^m_k) -> H^n(P^m_k) --i^*--> H^n(P^{m-1}_k).
Here 1 <= n-1 <= 2m-2. If n-1 = 2u+1 is odd, both groups H^{n-1} are 0 by Claim 1, so i^* is (trivially) an isomorphism. If n-1 = 2u with 1 <= u <= m-1, then i^*: H^{2u}(P^m_k) -> H^{2u}(P^{m-1}_k) is an isomorphism by Claim 2. In either case i^* is an isomorphism, so delta = 0 and H^n_c(A^m_k) injects into H^n(P^m_k). Now: if n is odd, H^n(P^m_k) = 0 by Claim 1, so H^n_c(A^m_k) = 0; if n = 2u with 1 <= u <= m-1, the following map i^*: H^{2u}(P^m_k) -> H^{2u}(P^{m-1}_k) is an isomorphism by Claim 2, so the kernel through which H^n_c injects is 0, and again H^n_c(A^m_k) = 0. Thus H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) = 0 for 2 <= n <= 2m-1.

(d) n = 2m. The exact piece H^{2m-1}(P^{m-1}_k) -> H^{2m}_c(A^m_k) -> H^{2m}(P^m_k) --i^*--> H^{2m}(P^{m-1}_k). By Claim 1 the left group is 0 (degree 2m-1 is odd, and also 2m-1 > 2(m-1)) and the right group is 0 (2m > 2(m-1) = top degree of P^{m-1}_k). Hence H^{2m}_c(A^m_k, Q_l) -> H^{2m}(P^m_k, Q_l) is an isomorphism, and by Claim 1 the target is Q_l * h^m, of dimension 1 over Q_l.

(e) n >= 2m+1. The exact piece H^{n-1}(P^{m-1}_k) -> H^n_c(A^m_k) -> H^n(P^m_k). For n >= 2m+1 we have n-1 >= 2m > 2(m-1), so H^{n-1}(P^{m-1}_k) = 0 by Claim 1, and n > 2m, so H^n(P^m_k) = 0 by Claim 1. Exactness gives H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) = 0.

=== 4. Conclusion ===

Collecting (a)-(e) for m >= 1: H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) = 0 for n = 0, for 1 <= n <= 2m-1 (by (b),(c)) and for n >= 2m+1 (by (e)), while H^{2m}_c(A^m_k, Q_l) is isomorphic to H^{2m}(P^m_k, Q_l) = Q_l * h^m, of dimension 1 (by (d)). Together with Section 2 this proves the lemma for every m >= 0.

(Remark on finiteness, needed only to make the dimension statement meaningful: at every step H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) is the kernel, cokernel or an extension of subquotients of H^n(P^m_k, Q_l) and H^{n-1}(P^{m-1}_k, Q_l), each of which has dimension <= 1 by Claim 1; hence all H^n_c(A^m_k, Q_l) are finite-dimensional. No Frobenius-equivariance is claimed or used here; that refinement is a separate statement.)

lemma_208.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge 1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(0\le n\le 2D\). Write \(F_X,F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), and let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map characterised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\), where \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). Then \(\operatorname{im}(f^*)\) and \(\ker(f_*)\) are \(F_X\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspaces with \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\operatorname{im}(f^*)\oplus\ker(f_*)\), and \(f^*\) is an isomorphism \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{im}(f^*)\) intertwining \(F_Y\) with the restriction of \(F_X\).
lemma_208.proof:
Notation. Put $V_X:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $V_Y:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and write $a:=f_k=f\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,k}:X_k\to Y_k$ for the base change of $f$; then $f^*=a^*:V_Y\to V_X$. Write $\Phi_X:=\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$ and $\Phi_Y:=\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$, so that $F_X=\Phi_X^*$ on $V_X$ and $F_Y=\Phi_Y^*$ on $V_Y$. For $Z\in\{X,Y\}$ let $\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ be the trace isomorphism with $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$.

Step 1: The map $f_*$ exists and satisfies the two key identities.
The morphism $f$ is proper, surjective and generically finite of degree $d\ge 1$; in particular it is a dominant morphism of degree $d$ between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension $D$. Hence lemma_194 applies: for our $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ there exists a unique $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $f_*:V_X\to V_Y$ such that $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\smile y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\smile f^*y)$ for all $x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This is exactly the map denoted $f_*$ in the statement (uniqueness shows the two definitions agree). Applying lemma_196 to this $f_*$ (its hypotheses are the same as ours: proper surjective generically finite of degree $d\ge1$, smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$, the same normalised traces, and the defining identity of $f_*$) we obtain the two identities
\[ f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{V_Y}. \tag{1}\]
Since $d\ge1$ is an integer and $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, $d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$.

Step 2: Pullback commutes with Frobenius, $F_X\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y$.
Consider the two morphisms $X_k\to Y_k$ given by $a\circ\Phi_X$ and $\Phi_Y\circ a$. Both are the product morphism $f\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$: on the $X$-factor the first is $f\circ\mathrm{id}_X=f$ and the second is $\mathrm{id}_Y\circ f=f$, and on the $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$-factor both are $\mathrm{id}_k\circ\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma=\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma\circ\mathrm{id}_k=\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$. Explicitly, on the affine model $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal O_U\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k)$ over an affine open $U\subseteq Y$, both morphisms are induced by the ring map $u\otimes c\mapsto f^{\#}(u)\otimes c^{q}$. Hence
\[ a\circ\Phi_X=\Phi_Y\circ a. \tag{2}\]
\'Etale cohomology is contravariant for morphisms of $k$-schemes, so from (2),
\[ F_X\circ f^*=\Phi_X^*\circ a^*=(a\circ\Phi_X)^*=(\Phi_Y\circ a)^*=a^*\circ\Phi_Y^*=f^*\circ F_Y. \tag{3}\]

Step 3: $f^*$ is injective, $f_*$ is surjective, and $V_X=\operatorname{im}(f^*)\oplus\ker(f_*)$.
Injectivity of $f^*$: if $y\in V_Y$ with $f^*y=0$, then by (1) $d\,y=f_*f^*y=f_*(0)=0$, and since $d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$ we get $y=0$.
Surjectivity of $f_*$: given $w\in V_Y$, (1) gives $w=f_*(d^{-1}f^*w)$, so $w$ is in the image of $f_*$.
Sum: for any $x\in V_X$ write
\[ x=\underbrace{f^*\!\big(d^{-1}f_*x\big)}_{=:u\,\in\,\operatorname{im}(f^*)}+\underbrace{\big(x-f^*(d^{-1}f_*x)\big)}_{=:v}. \]
Using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $f_*$ and $f_*f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$,
\[ f_*v=f_*x-f_*f^*(d^{-1}f_*x)=f_*x-d\cdot d^{-1}f_*x=0, \]
so $v\in\ker(f_*)$. Thus $V_X=\operatorname{im}(f^*)+\ker(f_*)$.
Intersection: if $x\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)\cap\ker(f_*)$, write $x=f^*y$; then $0=f_*x=f_*f^*y=d\,y$, so $y=0$ and $x=0$. Hence the sum is direct:
\[ V_X=\operatorname{im}(f^*)\oplus\ker(f_*). \tag{4}\]

Step 4: Both summands are $F_X$-stable.
For $\operatorname{im}(f^*)$: take $x=f^*y\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$. By (3), $F_Xx=F_Xf^*y=f^*(F_Yy)\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$, using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $f^*$. So $\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ is $F_X$-stable.
For $\ker(f_*)$: take $x\in\ker(f_*)$. By the first identity in (1), $f_*(F_Xx)=F_Y(f_*x)=F_Y(0)=0$, using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $F_Y$. So $\ker(f_*)$ is $F_X$-stable.
Both are thus $F_X$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspaces of $V_X$. Moreover, by lemma_6a, $F_X$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $V_X$; the restrictions $F_X|_{\operatorname{im}(f^*)}$ and $F_X|_{\ker(f_*)}$ are then automorphisms of the respective summands: injectivity is inherited, and if $x\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ and $x=F_Xx'$ with $x'=u+v$ the decomposition (4) with $u\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$, $v\in\ker(f_*)$, then $x=F_Xu+F_Xv$ is a decomposition of $x$ with $F_Xu\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ and $F_Xv\in\ker(f_*)$; by uniqueness in (4) and $x\in\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ we get $x=F_Xu$. So $F_X$ preserves each summand in the strong (invertible) sense, and $F_X$ is the direct sum of its two restrictions.

Step 5: $f^*$ identifies $V_Y$ with $\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ equivariantly.
By definition of the image, $f^*:V_Y\to\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ is surjective; by Step 3 it is injective; it is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear (functoriality of $\ell$-adic cohomology gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear pullback). Hence it is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space isomorphism $V_Y\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{im}(f^*)$. Equation (3) says precisely that for every $y\in V_Y$,
\[ f^*(F_Yy)=F_X(f^*y), \]
where the right-hand side is computed in $V_X$ and, by Step 4, lies in $\operatorname{im}(f^*)$; thus $f^*$ intertwines $F_Y$ with the restriction $F_X|_{\operatorname{im}(f^*)}$. In other words $f^*$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules.

Steps 3, 4 and 5 together give exactly the assertions of the lemma: $\operatorname{im}(f^*)$ and $\ker(f_*)$ are $F_X$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspaces with $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\operatorname{im}(f^*)\oplus\ker(f_*)$, and $f^*$ is an $F$-intertwining isomorphism $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{im}(f^*)$. This completes the proof.

lemma_207.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) with \(\dim X=D\) and \(\dim Y=E\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F_X,F_Y\) denote the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), on the \(\ell\)-adic cohomology of \(X_k\) and \(Y_k\). For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2d_Z}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d_Z)\), \(d_Z=\dim Z\), be the trace isomorphism with \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\), and for \(0\le n\le 2D\) let \(f_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2E-2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the Gysin homomorphism characterised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_!x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\). Then \(f_!\circ F_X=q^{D-E}\,F_Y\circ f_!\).
lemma_207.proof:
We fix the following shorthand throughout: $d_X:=D=\dim X$, $d_Y:=E=\dim Y$, and for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$ we write $H^*(Z):=H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $F_Z$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_Z\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, and $\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2d_Z}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d_Z)$ for the trace of the statement. Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth, projective and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$; since a smooth scheme over a field is regular, and a connected Noetherian regular scheme is irreducible (its irreducible components are open and closed), each of $X_k,Y_k$ is integral, so $X,Y$ are of pure dimension $D,E$ and lemma_77 applies to each of them with $m=1$.

STEP 0 (reading of the adjunction identity, and independence of the reading).
The two sides of the defining identity $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_!x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)$ a priori live in the different one-dimensional spaces $\mathbb Q_\ell(-E)$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$; the identity is therefore to be read after identifying both with $\mathbb Q_\ell$. Fix once and for all a nonzero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ and put $\mathbb Q_\ell(-m):=\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)^{\otimes m}$ with basis element $\xi^m$; define the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued trace
$$t_Z:H^{2d_Z}(Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}_Z(w)=t_Z(w)\cdot \xi^{d_Z}.$$
We read the characterising property as
$$t_Y(f_!x\cup y)=t_X(x\cup f^*y)\qquad\text{for all }x\in H^n(X),\ y\in H^{2D-n}(Y),\tag{$*$}$$
where $y$ is taken in degree $2D-n$ precisely so that both cup products have top degree ($n+(2D-n)=2D$ on $X$, and $(n+2E-2D)+(2D-n)=2E$ on $Y$). This is legitimate: nothing in the argument below depends on the choice of $\xi$, and in any case a different choice $\xi'=\lambda\xi$ ($\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$) gives $t'_Z=\lambda^{-d_Z}t_Z$, so that $(*)'$, the identity $(*)$ read with $t'$, reads $\lambda^{-E}t_Y(f'_!x\cup y)=\lambda^{-D}t_X(x\cup f^*y)$, hence $f'_!=\lambda^{E-D}f_!$ by non-degeneracy of the pairing of Step 1(d). Since the desired conclusion $f_!\circ F_X=q^{D-E}F_Y\circ f_!$ is homogeneous in $f_!$, it holds for $f_!$ if and only if it holds for $f'_!$. Thus it suffices to prove it for the map defined by $(*)$ for our fixed $\xi$.

We set $a:=n+2E-2D$ (the degree of the target of $f_!$) and $b:=2D-n$ (the degree of $y$); then $a+b=2E$, and from $0\le n\le 2D$ we get $b\ge 0$.

STEP 1 (preliminary facts).
(a) *$F_Z$ is an invertible graded algebra automorphism.* By lemma_6a, for each $i\ge0$ the pullback $F_{\mathrm ar}=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^i(Z)$ (its inverse being geometric Frobenius). Being pullback along a morphism of $k$-schemes, it preserves cup products: $F_Z(u\cup v)=F_Zu\cup F_Zv$, and preserves cohomological degree.

(b) *$f^*$ commutes with Frobenius.* Let $p_X:X_k\to X$, $p_Y:Y_k\to Y$ be the projections; $f_k:=f\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,k}=p_Y^{-1}$-lift of $f$ satisfies $f_k=F$-square: as morphisms $X_k\to Y_k$,
$$F_Y\circ f_k=(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)\circ(f\times\mathrm{id})=(f\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=(f\times\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)=f_k\circ F_X,$$
where we used $\mathrm{id}_Y\circ f=f=f\circ\mathrm{id}_X$ and $\sigma\circ\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}\circ\sigma$. Taking contravariant pullbacks gives $F_X\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y$ on every $H^i(Y)$, and hence, applying $F_X^{-1}$ on the left (which exists by (a)),
$$F_X^{-1}\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y^{-1}.\tag{1}$$

(c) *Frobenius behaviour of the traces.* By lemma_77(a) with $m=1$, applied to $Z=X$ and to $Z=Y$, the canonical trace isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}^{\mathrm{can}}_Z:H^{2d_Z}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d_Z)$, normalised by $\operatorname{tr}^{\mathrm{can}}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$, is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d_Z)$ as multiplication by $q^{d_Z}$. Our $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ has exactly the same normalisation; since $H^{2d_Z}(Z)$ is one-dimensional (it is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d_Z)$) and $\mathrm{cl}(z)\ne0$ for any closed point $z$ (its trace is the positive integer $[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$; closed points exist because $Z_k$ is a nonempty scheme of finite type over $k$), the two isomorphisms coincide. Hence
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z w)=q^{d_Z}\operatorname{tr}_Z(w)\quad(w\in H^{2d_Z}(Z)).$$
Since $F(\xi)=q\xi$ (the case $d_Z=1$ above, or equivalently the definition of the Tate twist), we obtain, writing $\operatorname{tr}_Z(u)=t_Z(u)\xi^{d_Z}$,
$$t_Z(F_Z w)\,\xi^{d_Z}=\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Zw)=F(\operatorname{tr}_Z w)=t_Z(w)F(\xi^{d_Z})=q^{d_Z}t_Z(w)\xi^{d_Z},$$
so
$$t_Z\circ F_Z=q^{d_Z}\,t_Z\ \text{ on } H^{2d_Z}(Z).\tag{2}$$
Combining (2) with the fact that $F_Z$ is a ring map gives, for all $u\in H^r(Z)$, $v\in H^{2d_Z-r}(Z)$,
$$t_Z(F_Zu\cup F_Zv)=t_Z(F_Z(u\cup v))=q^{d_Z}t_Z(u\cup v),\tag{3}$$
which is the scalar form of lemma_77(b).

(d) *Perfectness.* By lemma_77(b) with $m=1$, for every $r$ with $0\le r\le 2E$ the pairing $H^r(Y)\times H^{2E-r}(Y)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-E)$, $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup v)$, is perfect. Composing the target with the isomorphism $\mathbb Q_\ell(-E)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$, $c\,\xi^E\mapsto c$, we get that
$$(u,v)\longmapsto t_Y(u\cup v)\quad\text{on } H^r(Y)\times H^{2E-r}(Y)\tag{4}$$
is a perfect pairing; in particular it is non-degenerate in $u$, so two classes of $H^r(Y)$ that pair equally with all $v\in H^{2E-r}(Y)$ are equal.

STEP 2 (the case $a<0$). If $n+2E-2D<0$ then $H^a(Y)=H^{<0}(Y)=0$, so $f_!=0$ (and then $(*)$ is vacuous, as $b=2D-n>2E$ forces $H^b(Y)=0$). Both $f_!\circ F_X$ and $q^{D-E}F_Y\circ f_!$ are the zero map $H^n(X)\to0$, and the required identity holds.

Henceforth assume $a\ge0$. Then $a=n+2E-2D\le 2E$ (as $n\le 2D$) and $b=2E-a\in[0,2E]$, so (4) applies with $r=a$.

STEP 3 (the main computation). Let $x\in H^n(X)$ and $y\in H^b(Y)$ be arbitrary. We compute in $\mathbb Q_\ell$:

(i) Since $F_Xx\in H^n(X)$, applying $(*)$ to the pair $(F_Xx,\,y)$ gives
$$t_Y\big(f_!(F_Xx)\cup y\big)=t_X\big(F_Xx\cup f^*y\big).$$

(ii) By (a), $F_X$ is an algebra automorphism, and $F_X(F_X^{-1}f^*y)=f^*y$; hence
$$F_Xx\cup f^*y=F_Xx\cup F_X(F_X^{-1}f^*y)=F_X\big(x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y\big).$$
Note $x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y\in H^{n+b}(X)=H^{2D}(X)$, so it is in the domain of $t_X$.

(iii) By (2) applied to $Z=X$, $d_X=D$,
$$t_X\big(F_X(x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y)\big)=q^{D}\,t_X\big(x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y\big).$$

(iv) By (1), $F_X^{-1}f^*y=f^*F_Y^{-1}y$, with $F_Y^{-1}y\in H^b(Y)$ (degree-preserving automorphism), so
$$q^{D}\,t_X\big(x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y\big)=q^{D}\,t_X\big(x\cup f^*(F_Y^{-1}y)\big).$$

(v) Applying $(*)$ to the pair $(x,\,F_Y^{-1}y)$ (valid since $F_Y^{-1}y\in H^b(Y)$) gives
$$q^{D}\,t_X\big(x\cup f^*F_Y^{-1}y\big)=q^{D}\,t_Y\big(f_!x\cup F_Y^{-1}y\big).$$

(vi) Finally, apply (3) with $Z=Y$, $d_Y=E$, $u=f_!x\in H^a(Y)$, $v=F_Y^{-1}y\in H^b(Y)$ (note $a+b=2E$): $t_Y(F_Yu\cup y)=t_Y(F_Yu\cup F_Yv)=q^{E}t_Y(u\cup v)$, i.e.
$$q^{D}\,t_Y\big(f_!x\cup F_Y^{-1}y\big)=q^{D-E}\,t_Y\big(F_Y(f_!x)\cup y\big)=t_Y\big(q^{D-E}F_Y(f_!x)\cup y\big),$$
the last step being $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of the pairing ($q^{D-E}\in\mathbb Q^\times\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^\times$).

Chaining (i)--(vi) we obtain, for every $y\in H^b(Y)$,
$$t_Y\big(f_!(F_Xx)\cup y\big)=t_Y\big(q^{D-E}F_Y(f_!x)\cup y\big).$$
Both $f_!(F_Xx)$ and $q^{D-E}F_Y(f_!x)$ lie in $H^a(Y)$ (degree-preserving maps), and by (4)/non-degeneracy in the first argument the pairing $H^a(Y)\times H^b(Y)\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ separates points of $H^a(Y)$. Hence
$$f_!(F_Xx)=q^{D-E}F_Y(f_!x)\quad\text{in }H^a(Y).$$
As $x\in H^n(X)$ was arbitrary, $f_!\circ F_X=q^{D-E}\,F_Y\circ f_!$ as maps $H^n(X)\to H^{n+2E-2D}(Y)$.

STEP 4 (conclusion). Steps 2 and 3 cover all $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ (the only two possibilities for $a=n+2E-2D$), so the identity is established in every case. By Step 0 the identity is independent of the auxiliary choice of $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)^\times$ used to read the characterising adjunction, so it holds for the Gysin homomorphism as stated. This completes the proof.

(Remark, not used above: when $D=E$ the factor is $q^0=1$ and the statement reduces to the ordinary Frobenius-equivariance of proper push-forward for a dominant morphism of smooth projective varieties of the same dimension, as expected.)

lemma_abjac_picard_kernel_torsion.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus \(g\ge 1\) over \(k\), let \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k}\) be its Jacobian, let \(y\in C(k)\), and let \(\varphi_y:C\to J\), \(x\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(x-y)]\), be the Abel\u2013Jacobi morphism. If \(L\) is a line bundle on \(J\) whose class lies in \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(J)(k)\) and \(\varphi_y^*L\cong\mathcal O_C\), then \(L^{\otimes g!}\cong\mathcal O_J\).
lemma_abjac_picard_kernel_torsion.proof: Proof. We first record a norm lemma. Let π:X→Y be a finite dominant morphism of integral normal varieties over k, and let d=[k(X):k(Y)]. If N∈Pic(Y) and π^*N≅O_X, then N^{⊗d}≅O_Y. Choose a nonzero rational section s of N, let D=div(s), so N≅O_Y(D). Since π^*N is trivial, π^*D=div(f) for some f∈k(X)^×. For a codimension-one point η of Y, put R=O_{Y,η}, K=Frac(R), L=k(X), B=Γ(π^{-1}(Spec R),O_X). Then B is a finite torsion-free R-module, hence free of rank d. If a is a local equation for D at η, the coefficient of η in π_*π^*D is length_R(B/aB)=d length_R(R/aR), so π_*π^*D=dD. If π^*D=div(f), the coefficient of η in π_*div(f) is the valuation of the determinant of multiplication by f on the R-lattice B, which equals ord_η(Nm_{L/K}(f)) after clearing denominators if necessary; hence π_*div(f)=div(Nm(f)). Therefore dD=div(Nm(f)) is principal, so O_Y(dD)≅O_Y. This proves the norm lemma. Now define s:C^g→J by s(x_1,...,x_g)=Σ_i φ_y(x_i), and let σ_g:J^g→J be the addition map, so s=σ_g∘(φ_y×...×φ_y). By the cited lemma lemma_mult_pic0, for the binary addition σ:J×J→J and any M∈Pic^0(J) one has σ^*M≅pr_1^*M⊗pr_2^*M. Induction on g gives σ_g^*L≅⊗_{i=1}^g pr_i^*L. Hence s^*L≅⊗_{i=1}^g φ_y^*L≅O_{C^g}. Let S_g act on C^g by permuting the factors and let C^{(g)}=C^g/S_g be the symmetric product, with quotient map π:C^g→C^{(g)}. The map s is S_g-invariant, so it factors uniquely as s=u∘π with u:C^{(g)}→J. On k-points u sends an effective divisor D of degree g to the class of O_C(D-gy). The variety C is smooth and geometrically connected over the algebraically closed field k, hence integral; C^g is smooth connected, hence integral normal. On affine S_g-stable opens the quotient is Spec A^{S_g} for a normal domain A, and A^{S_g} is again a normal domain: it is a subring of A, and if x∈Frac(A^{S_g}) is integral over A^{S_g}, then x∈Frac(A) is integral over A, so x∈A, and x is fixed by S_g, hence x∈A^{S_g}. Thus C^{(g)} is integral normal. The quotient map π is finite because A is integral over A^{S_g}, and it is dominant. Its function field is K(C^g)^{S_g}. The action of S_g on K(C^g) is faithful; by Artin's theorem on fixed fields, [K(C^g):K(C^g)^{S_g}]=|S_g|=g!. Indeed, for α in a field E acted on by a finite group G, the polynomial ∏_{g∈G}(T-gα) has coefficients in E^G, so α has degree at most |G|, while the |G| distinct G-embeddings over E^G give [E:E^G]≥|G|. Applying the norm lemma to π with N=u^*L and d=g!, and using π^*N=s^*L≅O_{C^g}, we obtain (u^*L)^{⊗g!}≅O_{C^{(g)}}. Equivalently, if M=L^{⊗g!}, then u^*M≅O_{C^{(g)}}. We next prove that u is proper, surjective, and birational, and that u_*O_{C^{(g)}}≅O_J. The symmetric product C^{(g)} is projective, for example because the tensor product of the pullbacks of an ample line bundle on C^g over all elements of S_g descends to an ample line bundle on the quotient; hence u is proper. For surjectivity, take any N∈J(k) and set L_N=N⊗O_C(gy), a line bundle of degree g. Riemann-Roch gives h^0(C,L_N)-h^0(C,K_C⊗L_N^{-1})=deg(L_N)+1-g=1, so h^0(C,L_N)≥1. A nonzero section defines an effective divisor D of degree g with O_C(D)≅L_N, and then u(D)=N. Let W⊂J be the locus of N such that h^0(C,N⊗O_C(gy))=1. If g=1, Riemann-Roch and deg(K_C⊗(N⊗O_C(y))^{-1})=-1 show W=J. If g≥2, the complement Z={N:h^0(C,N⊗O_C(gy))≥2} is described as follows. Riemann-Roch gives h^0(C,N⊗O_C(gy))≥2 iff h^0(C,K_C⊗N^{-1}⊗O_C(-gy))≥1. A nonzero section of this line bundle of degree g-2 is equivalent to an effective divisor E of degree g-2 with K_C⊗N^{-1}⊗O_C(-gy)≅O_C(E), i.e. N≅K_C⊗O_C(-E)⊗O_C(-gy). Thus Z is the image of the morphism C^{(g-2)}→J, E↦[K_C(-E-gy)]. This image is closed because C^{(g-2)} is proper and J is separated, and it has dimension at most g-2<dim J=g, so Z is a proper closed subset. Hence W is a nonempty open subset of J. The reduced effective divisors form an open dense subset R⊂C^{(g)}: the complement of the diagonals in C^g is open dense, and the quotient map π is open. Since u is surjective and C^{(g)} is irreducible, u^{-1}(W)∩R is nonempty; choose D_0 in it. Write N_0=u(D_0). Because D_0 is reduced, C^{(g)} is smooth at D_0: locally a length-g subscheme near D_0 splits uniquely into g length-1 subschemes near the distinct points of D_0, so the completed local ring is a product of the local rings of C at those points. The tangent space is T_{D_0}C^{(g)}≅H^0(C,O_{D_0}(D_0)), which has dimension g. The tangent space to J at N_0 is T_{N_0}J≅H^1(C,O_C), also of dimension g. The differential du_{D_0} is the boundary map δ:H^0(C,O_{D_0}(D_0))→H^1(C,O_C) associated to 0→O_C→O_C(D_0)→O_{D_0}(D_0)→0. Since N_0∈W, h^0(C,O_C(D_0))=1; the long exact cohomology sequence shows δ is injective. Riemann-Roch for O_C(D_0) gives h^0(C,O_C(D_0))-h^1(C,O_C(D_0))=1, hence h^1(C,O_C(D_0))=0, so δ is surjective. Thus du_{D_0} is an isomorphism, and u is étale at D_0. Let U be the étale locus of u. Then U is open and contains D_0, and u(U) is open because étale morphisms are open. Set V=W∩u(U); this is a dense open subset of J. For v∈V, the fibre u^{-1}(v) is the complete linear system |v⊗O_C(gy)|≅P(H^0(C,v⊗O_C(gy))). Since v∈W, this projective space is a single reduced point. Since v∈u(U), that point lies in U. Therefore u^{-1}(V)→V is étale and proper, and its fibres are finite; hence it is quasi-finite. A proper quasi-finite morphism is finite, so u^{-1}(V)→V is finite étale of degree one, hence an isomorphism. Thus u is birational. Since u is proper and birational, C^{(g)} is integral, and J is normal, we have u_*O_{C^{(g)}}≅O_J. Indeed, for an affine open Spec R⊂J with R normal, Γ(Spec R,u_*O) is a finite R-algebra contained in the common function field k(J), because u is birational and C^{(g)} is integral; every element is integral over R, hence lies in R. Finally, by the projection formula, M≅M⊗u_*O_{C^{(g)}}≅u_*(u^*M)≅u_*O_{C^{(g)}}≅O_J. Therefore L^{⊗g!}≅O_J. QED.

lemma_211.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(k\), let \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) be its group of line bundles, let \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\) denote the subgroup of line bundles of degree \(0\) (the \(k\)-points of the Jacobian \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k}\)), and let \(\operatorname{NS}(C):=\operatorname{Pic}(C)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\). Then the degree homomorphism \(\deg:\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to\mathbb Z\) is surjective with kernel \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\), and it induces an isomorphism of abelian groups \(\operatorname{NS}(C)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Z\) under which the class of \(\mathcal O_C(x)\) maps to \(1\) for every closed point \(x\in C\).
lemma_211.proof:
Let \(k\) be algebraically closed and \(C/k\) a smooth projective geometrically connected curve. We write \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) for the group of isomorphism classes of line bundles on \(C\) under \(\otimes\), \(J:=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k}\) for the Jacobian (the identity component of the Picard scheme, whose existence is recalled in Step 6), and \(\operatorname{NS}(C):=\operatorname{Pic}(C)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\). The proof has seven steps.

=== Step 1. Elementary geometry of \(C\). ===
(1a) \(C\neq\varnothing\): \(C\) is connected, and by the standard convention a connected scheme is non-empty. A non-empty scheme of finite type over a field has a closed point, so \(C^{(0)}\neq\varnothing\).
(1b) Closed points are \(k\)-rational: for \(x\in C^{(0)}\) the field \(k(x)\) is a finitely generated algebraic extension of \(k\) (Zariski's lemma, since \(x\) is closed in a finite-type \(k\)-scheme), hence \(k(x)=k\) because \(k\) is algebraically closed. In particular \(C(k)\neq\varnothing\).
(1c) \(C\) is integral. Smoothness over \(k\) makes \(C\) regular, and \(\dim\mathcal O_{C,x}=\dim_x C=1\) (\(C\) has pure dimension 1), so each \(\mathcal O_{C,x}\) is a regular local ring of dimension 1, hence a discrete valuation ring, hence a domain. Thus \(C\) is locally integral; being noetherian and connected it is integral: reducedness is clear, and if \(Z\) is an irreducible component and \(x\in Z\), an integral open neighbourhood \(V\ni x\) is irreducible, so \(V\subseteq Z'\) for a unique component \(Z'\) (necessarily \(Z'=\overline V\)); if \(Z\neq Z'\) then \(V\cap (C\setminus\bigcup_{j\neq i}Z_j)\) is a non-empty open subset of \(V\) contained in \(Z\), forcing \(V\subseteq Z\) and hence \(Z'=\overline V\subseteq Z\), a contradiction. So every component is open, and connectedness gives exactly one component: \(C\) is irreducible, hence integral. So the function field \(k(C)\) and Weil divisors make sense.
(1d) Since \(C\) is integral, noetherian, and every local ring \(\mathcal O_{C,x}\) is a DVR with uniformiser \(t_x\), the usual dictionary holds: the free abelian group \(\operatorname{Div}(C)=\bigoplus_{x\in C^{(0)}}\mathbb Z\cdot x\) maps onto the Cartier divisors, \(D\mapsto\mathcal O_C(D):=\{f\in k(C)^*: \operatorname{ord}_x(f)+n_x\ge 0\ \forall x\}\) is an invertible sheaf (locally \(\mathcal O(D)=t_x^{-n_x}\mathcal O_{C,x}\)), \(\mathcal O(D)\otimes\mathcal O(E)\simeq\mathcal O(D+E)\), and \(\mathcal O(D)\simeq\mathcal O(E)\iff D-E=\operatorname{div}(g)\) for some \(g\in k(C)^*\) (an isomorphism is multiplication by \(g\in k(C)^*=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(D),\mathcal O(E))\)). Finally every line bundle is of the form \(\mathcal O(D)\): \(L\) is trivial on some non-empty open \(U\), a trivialising section there is a non-zero rational section \(s\) of \(L\), and \(L\simeq\mathcal O(\operatorname{div}(s))\) via \(f\mapsto fs\) (locally \(s=t^{n}e\) with \(e\) a generator, so \(f\mapsto fs\) identifies \(\{f:\operatorname{ord}(f)\ge -n\}=t^{-n}\mathcal O\) with \(L\)).

=== Step 2. Degree of divisors. ===
Define \(\deg:\operatorname{Div}(C)\to\mathbb Z\), \(D=\sum n_x x\mapsto\sum n_x\,[k(x):k]=\sum n_x\) (by (1b) all \([k(x):k]=1\)). This is a group homomorphism, and \(\deg\mathcal O_C=0\).

=== Step 3. Principal divisors have degree 0. ===
Let \(0\neq g\in k(C)^*\). If \(g\in k^*\) then \(\operatorname{div}(g)=0\). Otherwise \(g\) is non-constant and defines a dominant \(k\)-morphism \(f:C\to\mathbb P^1_k\) (the rational map extends because \(C\) is a smooth curve and \(\mathbb P^1\) is proper). It is finite: dominant and non-constant \(\Rightarrow\) image is a closed irreducible subset of dimension 1, i.e. all of \(\mathbb P^1\); the fibres are \(0\)-dimensional, so \(f\) is quasi-finite, and \(f\) is proper since \(C\) is proper over \(k\); proper + quasi-finite \(\Rightarrow\) finite. Put \(n:=\deg f=[k(C):k(\mathbb P^1)]=[k(C):k(g)]\).
View \(g=f^{\#}(T)\) for the standard coordinate \(T\in k(\mathbb P^1)^*\). For \(x\in C^{(0)}\), \(y=f(x)\), the DVR \(\mathcal O_{C,x}\) dominates \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1,y}\) with ramification index \(e_x:=\operatorname{ord}_x(\pi_y)\) for a uniformiser \(\pi_y\); hence \(\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=e_x\operatorname{ord}_y(T)\). Therefore
\[\sum_{x\in C^{(0)}}\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^1(k)}\operatorname{ord}_y(T)\Big(\sum_{x\mapsto y}e_x\Big).\]
By the fundamental equality \(\sum_{x\mapsto y}e_x f_x=n\) with \(f_x=[k(x):k(y)]\); all residue fields are \(k\) by (1b), so \(f_x=1\) and \(\sum_{x\mapsto y}e_x=n\) for every \(y\). Thus \(\deg\operatorname{div}(g)=n\sum_{y}\operatorname{ord}_y(T)\).
Finally \(\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^1}\operatorname{ord}_y(T)=0\): writing \(h=c\,T^{m}\prod_i (T-a_i)^{m_i}/\prod_j (T-b_j)\in k(T)^*\) with \(a_i,b_j\in k^*\) pairwise distinct and \(m_i\ge1\), one has \(\operatorname{ord}_a(h)=v_a\) (exponent of \(T-a\)) for \(a\in k^*\), \(\operatorname{ord}_0(h)=m\), \(\operatorname{ord}_\infty(h)=-\big(m+\sum_i m_i-s\big)\); summing gives \((m+\sum_i m_i-s)-(m+\sum_i m_i-s)=0\). Hence \(\deg\operatorname{div}(g)=0\).

=== Step 4. \(\deg:\operatorname{Pic}(C)\to\mathbb Z\) is a well-defined surjective homomorphism. ===
For \(L\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) choose a divisor \(D\) with \(L\simeq\mathcal O(D)\) (Step 1d) and set \(\deg L:=\deg D\). By Step 3 and Step 1d (\(\mathcal O(D)\simeq\mathcal O(E)\Rightarrow D-E\) principal) this is independent of \(D\). If \(L\simeq\mathcal O(D)\), \(M\simeq\mathcal O(E)\), then \(L\otimes M\simeq\mathcal O(D+E)\), so \(\deg(L\otimes M)=\deg L+\deg M\): a group homomorphism. Surjectivity: for \(x\in C(k)\) (non-empty by (1b)), \(\mathcal O_C(x)\) has degree 1, so \(\deg\) is onto.

=== Step 5. \(\deg L=\chi(C,L)-\chi(C,\mathcal O_C)\). ===
Since \(C\) is proper over \(k\), Grothendieck's finiteness theorem gives \(\dim_k H^i(C,\mathcal F)<\infty\) for every coherent \(\mathcal F\), so \(\chi(\mathcal F):=\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_k H^i(C,\mathcal F)\) is defined, and it is additive on short exact sequences (long exact cohomology sequence).
For \(x\in C(k)\) and any line bundle \(L\), tensoring \(0\to\mathcal O_C\to\mathcal O_C(x)\to k(x)\to0\) by \(L\) (exact, \(L\) locally free) gives \(0\to L\to L(x)\to L\otimes k(x)\to0\); the quotient is \(L_x/\mathfrak m_xL_x\cong k\), one-dimensional. Hence \(\chi(L(x))=\chi(L)+1\), and applying \(0\to L(-x)\to L\to L|_x\to0\) gives \(\chi(L(-x))=\chi(L)-1\). (Here \(\mathcal O_C(x)/\mathcal O_C\cong k(x)\) because locally \(\mathcal O(x)=t^{-1}\mathcal O\) and \(t^{-1}\mathcal O/\mathcal O\cong\mathcal O/(t)=k(x)\).) Starting from \(L=\mathcal O_C\) and adding the points of a divisor \(D=\sum n_xx\) one at a time with their signs yields \(\chi(\mathcal O(D))=\chi(\mathcal O_C)+\sum n_x=\chi(\mathcal O_C)+\deg D\). Thus \(\deg L=\chi(L)-\chi(\mathcal O_C)\) for all \(L\). In particular the degree of a flat family of line bundles on \(C\) over a connected base is locally constant (cohomology and base change / Grauert: \(R^ip_{2*}\mathcal M\) are coherent and their fibres compute the cohomology of the fibres), so this \(\deg\) agrees with the usual "degree in families" used to define the components of the Picard scheme.

=== Step 6. Identification of the kernel with \(J(k)\). ===
We use the following standard theorem on the Picard scheme of a curve (Kleiman/GRO; the hypotheses — proper, flat, finitely presented, geometrically integral fibres — hold here).

(Pic) \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}\), the fppf-sheafification of \(T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(T\times_k C)/p_2^*\operatorname{Pic}(T)\), is represented by a scheme which is smooth, separated and locally of finite type over \(k\); the natural map \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) is a group isomorphism (indeed \(\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}k)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Br}(k)=0\) for \(k\) separably closed, so the Leray sequence for \(\mathbb G_m\) gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)\)). It decomposes as a disjoint sum of open-and-closed subschemes \(\operatorname{Pic}^d_{C/k}\), \(d\in\mathbb Z\), where \(\operatorname{Pic}^d_{C/k}\) represents \(T\)-families of line bundles all of whose geometric fibres have degree \(d\) (equivalently \(\chi\)-degree \(d\), cf. Step 5). The identity component \(J:=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k}\) is an abelian variety over \(k\) (the Jacobian), and \(\operatorname{Pic}^d_{C/k}\) is a \(J\)-torsor; the group law on \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}\) corresponds to \(\otimes\) on \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\).

Under the isomorphism \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) we view \(J(k)\) as a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\); this subgroup is what the statement calls \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\).

(6a) \(J(k)\subseteq\ker\deg\). Let \(L\in J(k)\). For each \(n\ge1\), the multiplication-by-\(n\) morphism \([n]:J\to J\) is an isogeny of an abelian variety over the algebraically closed field \(k\): finite, flat of rank \(n^{2g}\), surjective. Hence the scheme-theoretic fibre over \(L\) is a non-empty finite \(k\)-scheme, which has a closed point whose residue field is finite algebraic over \(k\), i.e. \(k\) itself. So there is \(M\in J(k)\) with \(M^{\otimes n}=L\). Then \(\deg L=n\deg M\in n\mathbb Z\). As this holds for every \(n\ge1\) and \(\deg L\in\mathbb Z\), \(\deg L=0\).

(6b) \(\ker\deg\subseteq J(k)\). First we show: for \(p,q\in C(k)\) one has \(\mathcal O_C(q-p)\in J(k)\). Fix \(p\in C(k)\). On \(C\times_k C\) with projections \(p_1,p_2\), the three closed subschemes \(\Delta\), \(p_1^{-1}(p)=\{p\}\times C\), \(p_2^{-1}(p)=C\times\{p\}\) are effective Cartier divisors (\(C\times C\) is smooth of dimension 2 over \(k\); the diagonal of a smooth morphism is a regular immersion of codimension 1; \((p)\subset C\) is an effective Cartier divisor since \(\mathcal O_{C,p}\) is a DVR, and pullbacks of effective Cartier divisors are effective Cartier). Set
\[\mathcal M:=\mathcal O_{C\times C}\big(\Delta-\{p\}\times C-C\times\{p\}\big).\]
For \(x\in C(k)\), restricting to the fibre \(\{x\}\times C\simeq C\): \(\mathcal O(\Delta)|\) is \(\mathcal O_C(x)\) (the intersection \(\Delta\cap(\{x\}\times C)=\{(x,x)\}\)), \(\mathcal O(C\times\{p\})|\) is \(\mathcal O_C(p)\) (as \(C\times\{p\}=p_2^*(p)\)), and \(\mathcal O(\{p\}\times C)|\) is trivial (as \(\{p\}\times C=p_1^*(p)\) restricts to the pullback of a line bundle on \(\operatorname{Spec}k\)). Hence \(\mathcal M|_{\{x\}\times C}\simeq\mathcal O_C(x-p)\), which has degree \(1-1=0\). Thus \(\mathcal M\) is a \(C\)-valued point of the degree-0 Picard functor, i.e. a \(k\)-morphism \(u_p:C\to J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/k}\) (the Abel–Jacobi morphism based at \(p\)) with \(u_p(x)\) corresponding to \(\mathcal O_C(x-p)\) under \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(C)\). Taking \(x=q\) gives \(\mathcal O_C(q-p)\in J(k)\).
Now let \(L\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)\) with \(\deg L=0\). Write \(L\simeq\mathcal O(D)\) with \(D=\sum_x n_x x\) and \(\sum_x n_x=0\). Let \(r:=\sum_{n_x>0}n_x=\sum_{n_x<0}(-n_x)\) (finite support since \(D\) is a divisor). Choose \(k\)-points \(p_1,\dots,p_r,q_1,\dots,q_r\) listing each \(x\) with \(n_x>0\) exactly \(n_x\) times and each \(x\) with \(n_x<0\) exactly \(-n_x\) times. Then \(D=\sum_{i=1}^r(p_i-q_i)\) and
\[L\simeq\mathcal O(D)\simeq\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\mathcal O_C(p_i-q_i)\]\nby Step 1d. Each factor lies in \(J(k)\) by the case just proved (with \(p=q_i\), \(q=p_i\)), and \(J(k)\) is a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Pic}(C)\); hence \(L\in J(k)\). (If \(r=0\) then \(D=0\) and \(L\simeq\mathcal O_C\), the identity element of \(J(k)\).)

Combining (6a) and (6b): \(\ker(\deg)=J(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\), which is exactly the parenthetical identification in the statement, and \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\) is the subgroup of degree-0 line bundles.

=== Step 7. Conclusion. ===
Steps 4 and 6 give an exact sequence of abelian groups
\[0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)=J(k)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\ \deg\ }\mathbb Z\longrightarrow 0,\]\nwith surjectivity from Step 4 (\(\deg\mathcal O_C(x)=1\)). By the first isomorphism theorem, \(\deg\) induces an isomorphism
\[\overline{\deg}:\operatorname{NS}(C):=\operatorname{Pic}(C)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Z.\]
For every closed point \(x\in C\), Step 1b gives \(k(x)=k\), so Step 4 gives \(\overline{\deg}([\mathcal O_C(x)])=\deg\mathcal O_C(x)=1\). Equivalently, \(\overline{\deg}\) is the unique isomorphism sending the class of \(\mathcal O_C(x)\) to \(1\) for every closed point \(x\) (and then \(\overline{\deg}([L])=\deg L\) for all \(L\)). This proves all the claims. (As a by-product, \(\operatorname{NS}(C)\cong\mathbb Z\) is free of rank 1.)

None of the lemmas listed as already proved is needed for this result: they concern Frobenius actions on \(\ell\)-adic cohomology, whereas the present statement is a purely geometric fact about the Picard group of a curve over an algebraically closed field, proved above from first principles together with the standard existence theorem for the Picard scheme/Jacobian of a curve (quoted in Step 6).

lemma_213.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as multiplication by \(q\); in particular \(F\) and the geometric Frobenius act semisimply on it.
lemma_213.proof:
**Step 1 — The curve $C$ has pure dimension $D=1$, and $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite dimensional.**

By hypothesis $C$ is a curve over $\mathbb F_q$, i.e. $\dim C=1$; in particular $C\neq\varnothing$. Since $C$ is smooth over the field $\mathbb F_q$, every local ring $\mathcal O_{C,x}$ is regular, hence a domain, so $C$ is locally integral; for a locally integral Noetherian space the irreducible components are pairwise disjoint and each is open and closed. Geometric connectedness of $C$ implies connectedness (the base-change projection $C_k\to C$ is surjective, and the image of a connected space is connected), so $C$ has a single irreducible component; hence $C$ is irreducible and equidimensional of dimension $1$, i.e. of pure dimension $D=1$. Also, $C$ being geometrically connected, smooth and projective over $\mathbb F_q$ means exactly that $C$ satisfies the hypotheses of the quoted lemmas with $X=C$ and $D=1$, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$.

Since $C$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, we may apply lemma_45_finite_frob to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_C^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$: for every $n$, $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, and $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is a well-defined $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of it (this is also the content of lemma_6a). Thus it makes sense to speak of the minimal polynomial and of semisimplicity of $F$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Step 2 — $F$ acts on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by $q$.**

*Direct derivation.* Take $m=1$, $Y=C$ (a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over $\mathbb F_{q^1}=\mathbb F_q$) and $d=1$ in lemma_77(a). Part (a) gives a canonical $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism (the trace/cycle-class isomorphism)
\[
\operatorname{tr}:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-1),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\ \ \text{for every closed point }z\in C,
\]
and asserts that $\operatorname{tr}$ is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ as multiplication by the positive rational number $q^{md}=q^{1\cdot 1}=q$. Writing $F_{-1}$ for this action on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$, equivariance means $\operatorname{tr}\circ F=F_{-1}\circ\operatorname{tr}=q\cdot\operatorname{tr}$. Hence for every $x\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(Fx)=q\,\operatorname{tr}(x)=\operatorname{tr}(qx),
\]
and since $\operatorname{tr}$ is injective, $Fx=qx$. Thus $F=q\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. (Moreover $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\neq 0$, so $\operatorname{tr}$ being an isomorphism shows $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=1$; concretely, $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\neq 0$ for any closed point $z$, so the space is nonzero and the scalar $q$ is genuinely the eigenvalue.)

*Consistency check via a proved lemma.* The same conclusion is exactly the case $D=1$ of lemma_199, whose hypotheses were verified in Step 1 ($C$ smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension $1$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$): it gives that $F$ acts on $H^{2D}=H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by $q^D=q$. Either argument yields
\[
F=q\cdot \mathrm{id}_{H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}.
\]

**Step 3 — $F$ acts semisimply.**

By Step 2, $F=q\,\mathrm{id}$ with $q\in\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $q\neq 0$ (characteristic of $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is $0$). Since $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\neq 0$ (Step 2), the minimal polynomial of $F$ is $t-q$, a degree-one polynomial, which is separable/squarefree over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (its derivative is $1$, so it is coprime to $t-q$). By the definition of semisimplicity used here (squarefree minimal polynomial, as in lemma_177), $F$ is semisimple. Equivalently, after any extension of scalars — in particular after $-\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ — the operator is still $q\cdot\mathrm{id}$, which is diagonal in every basis; so its action is diagonalizable.

**Step 4 — The geometric Frobenius acts semisimply.**

Let $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*$ be the geometric Frobenius, the inverse of the arithmetic Frobenius $F_{\mathrm{ar}}=F$ (matching the conjecture's convention that geometric Frobenius is the inverse of $x\mapsto x^q$). By lemma_6a, $F_{\mathrm{geo}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{ar}}$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of the finite-dimensional space $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}$. Since $F_{\mathrm{ar}}=q\,\mathrm{id}$ and $q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, we obtain
\[
F_{\mathrm{geo}}=q^{-1}\,\mathrm{id}_{H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)},
\]
again a scalar operator. Its minimal polynomial is $t-q^{-1}$, which is squarefree over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ it is $q^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{id}$, diagonal in every basis. Hence $F_{\mathrm{geo}}$ acts semisimply.

**Conclusion.** $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ acts on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by $q$, and consequently both the arithmetic and the geometric Frobenius act semisimply (equivalently, diagonably after $-\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$) on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This is precisely the statement of the lemma. (Note that no case distinction is needed: $C$ is non-empty and connected by hypothesis, $H^2$ is $1$-dimensional by Step 2, and $q$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q_\ell$ because $\ell\neq p$ and $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q_\ell=0$.)

lemma_alb_h1_geometric.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\) with a point \(x_0\in X(k)\), let \(A=\operatorname{Alb}_{X/k}\) be the Albanese variety of \(X\) and \(\alpha:X\to A\) the Albanese morphism with \(\alpha(x_0)=0\). For every prime \(\ell\neq p\), the pullback \(\alpha^*:H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
lemma_alb_h1_geometric.proof:
Proof. Let k = overline(F_q). Write P = Pic^0_{X/k}, so P(k) = Pic^0(X). For an abelian variety B over k, write B^vee = Pic^0_{B/k}. Choose a Poincare line bundle L_B on B × B^vee, rigidified along {0} × B^vee and B × {0}. We use the standard universal property of the Picard scheme: a line bundle M on S × B, rigidified along {s_0} × B and S × {0}, defines a unique morphism f:S -> Pic_{B/k} such that (id_B × f)^*L_B ≅ M. If S is connected and the fiber over s_0 is trivial, then f lands in Pic^0_{B/k}=B^vee. Indeed, the component group of Pic_{B/k} is NS(B), which is finitely generated by lemma_205, hence discrete; a connected S maps into one component, and the rigidification at s_0 puts that component equal to the identity component.

1. The induced map α^#: A^vee -> P is an isogeny.

Let M be the Poincare bundle on X × P, rigidified along {x_0} × P and X × {0}. By the preceding paragraph applied to S=X and B=P, the family M on X × P defines a morphism α_P:X -> P^vee with α_P(x_0)=0 and
(id_P × α_P)^*L_P ≅ τ^*M
as rigidified line bundles on P × X, where τ swaps the factors.

By the Albanese universal property, since α_P:X -> P^vee is a morphism to an abelian variety with α_P(x_0)=0, there is a unique homomorphism h:A -> P^vee such that α_P = h ∘ α.

Let λ_P:P -> (P^vee)^vee be the canonical biduality isomorphism. For p ∈ P(k), λ_P(p) is the line bundle on P^vee whose fiber at q ∈ P^vee(k) is L_P(p,q). Pulling it back by α_P gives the line bundle on X whose fiber at x is L_P(p,α_P(x)). By the defining property of α_P, this equals M(x,p). Hence α_P^#(λ_P(p)) is exactly the point p of P(k)=Pic^0(X). Thus α_P^# ∘ λ_P = id_P on k-points, and therefore as homomorphisms of abelian varieties.

Functoriality of pullback gives α_P^# = α^# ∘ h^#, where h^#:P -> A^vee is pullback along h. Therefore
α^# ∘ (h^# ∘ λ_P) = id_P,
so α^# is surjective.

It remains to prove that ker(α^#) is finite. Let B ⊂ A^vee be an abelian subvariety contained in ker(α^#), and let i:B -> A^vee be the inclusion. Put G = (id_A × i)^*L_A on A × B. By the Picard-scheme component argument applied to G, each fiber G|_{a × B} lies in Pic^0(B)=B^vee; define ψ:A -> B^vee by ψ(a) = [G|_{a × B}] for a ∈ A(k).

Put H = (α × id_B)^*G on X × B. For β ∈ B(k), the line bundle G|_{A × {β}} corresponds to i(β) ∈ A^vee(k)=Pic^0(A). Since i(β) ∈ ker(α^#), we have α^*i(β) ≅ O_X, hence H|_{X × {β}} ≅ O_X. Also H|_{ {x_0} × B} = G|_{ {0} × B} ≅ O_B by the rigidification of L_A along {0} × A^vee. Apply lemma_seesaw_slices to τ^*H on B × X: its restrictions to {β} × X are trivial for every β ∈ B(k), and its restriction to B × {x_0} is trivial. Hence H ≅ O_{X × B}.

Consequently G|_{α(x) × B} ≅ O_B for every x ∈ X(k), so ψ(α(x))=0.

We now show that ψ is a homomorphism. Let σ:A × A -> A be addition, and define
M = (σ × id_B)^*G ⊗ pr_{13}^*G^{-1} ⊗ pr_{23}^*G^{-1}
on A × A × B, where pr_{13}(a,a',b)=(a,b) and pr_{23}(a,a',b)=(a',b). For β ∈ B(k), G|_{A × {β}} = i(β) ∈ Pic^0(A). By lemma_mult_pic0, σ^*i(β) ≅ pr_1^*i(β) ⊗ pr_2^*i(β), so M|_{A × A × {β}} ≅ O. Also M|_{ {(0,0)} × B} ≅ O because G|_{ {0} × B} ≅ O. Apply lemma_seesaw_slices to τ^*M on B × (A × A): its restrictions to {β} × (A × A) are trivial for all β ∈ B(k), and its restriction to B × {(0,0)} is trivial. Hence M ≅ O. Restricting to (a,a') × B gives G|_{a+a',B} ≅ G|_{a,B} ⊗ G|_{a',B}, so ψ(a+a')=ψ(a)+ψ(a'). Thus ψ is a homomorphism of abelian varieties.

Next, α(X) generates A. If B_0 ⊂ A is an abelian subvariety containing α(X), then α factors through B_0. By the Albanese universal property applied to α:X -> B_0, there is a homomorphism g:A -> B_0 such that the composite X -> B_0 -> A equals α. Uniqueness for α:X -> A gives that B_0 -> A is surjective; since it is a closed immersion, B_0=A.

Consider the sum maps s_n:X^n -> A, (x_1,...,x_n) ↦ Σ α(x_i). Their images Y_n are closed irreducible subsets, contain 0, and satisfy Y_n ⊂ Y_{n+1}. For some N, Y_N=Y_{N+1}; then Y_N+α(X) ⊂ Y_N, and by induction Y_N=Y_m for all m ≥ N. In particular Y_N+Y_N ⊂ Y_{2N}=Y_N. Let Stab(Y_N)={a ∈ A | a+Y_N=Y_N}; it is a closed subgroup. For y ∈ Y_N, translation by y preserves Y_N by dimension, so Y_N ⊂ Stab(Y_N). Since Y_N is connected and contains 0, Y_N lies in the identity component Stab(Y_N)^0. This is an abelian subvariety containing α(X), hence equals A. Therefore Y_N=A, so s_N is surjective.

Since ψ is a homomorphism and ψ∘α=0, the surjectivity of s_N on k-points implies ψ=0 on A(k), hence ψ=0. Thus G|_{a × B} ≅ O_B for every a ∈ A(k). Also G|_{A × {0}} ≅ O_A by rigidification. Apply lemma_seesaw_slices directly to G on A × B: its restrictions to {a} × B are trivial for all a ∈ A(k), and its restriction to A × {0} is trivial. Hence G ≅ O_{A × B}.

For β ∈ B(k), the fiber G|_{A × {β}} corresponds to i(β) ∈ A^vee(k). Since G is trivial, i(β)=0 for all β ∈ B(k), so i=0 and B=0. Thus ker(α^#) has trivial identity component, hence is finite. Together with surjectivity, α^# is an isogeny.

2. Comparison with étale cohomology.

For any smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y over k, let P_Y=Pic^0_{Y/k}. By lemma_kummer_h1, Kummer theory gives a functorial isomorphism
H^1_et(Y,Z_ℓ(1)) ≅ lim_n Pic(Y)[ℓ^n],
where the inverse limit uses the maps L ↦ L^{⊗ℓ}. By lemma_205, NS(Y) is finitely generated, and lemma_pic_torsion_limit identifies lim_n Pic(Y)[ℓ^n] with lim_n Pic^0(Y)[ℓ^n]=T_ℓ(P_Y). Hence
H^1_et(Y,Z_ℓ(1)) ≅ T_ℓ(P_Y).
Choose compatible ℓ-power roots of unity in k; this trivializes Z_ℓ(1) and Q_ℓ(1). Tensoring with Q_ℓ gives a functorial isomorphism
θ_Y:H^1_et(Y,Q_ℓ) ≅ V_ℓ(P_Y).
Functoriality for pullback follows from the functoriality in lemma_kummer_h1 and the fixed choice of roots of unity.

Apply this to Y=A and Y=X. Since A^vee=Pic^0_A and P=Pic^0_X, the square
H^1_et(A,Q_ℓ) --α^*--> H^1_et(X,Q_ℓ)
    | θ_A                         | θ_X
    v                             v
V_ℓ(A^vee) --V_ℓ(α^#)--> V_ℓ(P)
commutes. The map α^#:A^vee -> P is an isogeny by Step 1. By lemma_120, V_ℓ(α^#) is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. The vertical maps θ_A and θ_X are isomorphisms, so α^* is an isomorphism.

Thus α^*:H^1_et(A,Q_ℓ) -> H^1_et(X,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. QED.

lemma_215.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\). Then \(T\) is semisimple if and only if the transpose automorphism \(T^{\vee}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})\) of \(V^{\vee}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) defined by \(T^{\vee}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T\) is semisimple.
lemma_215.proof:
Throughout, write $F:=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $N:=\dim_F V<\infty$. By "semisimple" we use the same meaning as in the rest of this development (cf. the definition invoked in lemma_177): $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is semisimple if its minimal polynomial over $F$ is squarefree. In Step 6 below we check that this is equivalent to $\overline{F}$-diagonalisability, so the statement also covers the "diagonalizable after scalar extension" formulation.

**Step 1. $T^\vee$ is an automorphism, and the two minimal-polynomial ideals.**
Since $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the map $T^\vee:V^\vee\to V^\vee$, $\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ T$, is $F$-linear, and $(T^{-1})^\vee$ is its inverse: for all $\varphi$, $(T^\vee\circ (T^{-1})^\vee)(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T^{-1}\circ T=\varphi$ and $((T^{-1})^\vee\circ T^\vee)(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T\circ T^{-1}=\varphi$. So $T^\vee\in\mathrm{GL}(V^\vee)$.
