For any $S\in\mathrm{End}_F(V)$ (or $\mathrm{End}_F(V^\vee)$) the set $I_S:=\{f\in F[t]: f(S)=0\}$ is an ideal of $F[t]$: it is an $F$-subspace, and if $f(S)=0$ and $g\in F[t]$ then $(gf)(S)=g(S)f(S)=0$. Since $N^2+1$ endomorphisms $\mathrm{id},S,\dots,S^{N^2}$ of the $N^2$-dimensional space $\mathrm{End}_F(V)$ are $F$-linearly dependent, $I_S\neq 0$. As $F[t]$ is a principal ideal domain, $I_S=(m_S)$ for a unique monic polynomial $m_S$, the minimal polynomial of $S$. In particular $f(S)=0\iff m_S\mid f$.

**Step 2. Powers and polynomials commute with duality.**
We claim $(T^i)^\vee=(T^\vee)^i$ for every $i\ge 0$. For $i=0$ both sides are $\mathrm{id}_{V^\vee}$. If it holds for $i$, then $(T^{i+1})^\vee(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T^{i+1}=(\varphi\circ T^i)\circ T=(T^i)^\vee(\varphi)\circ T=T^\vee\bigl((T^i)^\vee(\varphi)\bigr)=(T^\vee)^{i+1}(\varphi)$. Hence by induction, for every $f(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}a_i t^i\in F[t]$,
\[
f(T^\vee)=\sum_{i=0}^r a_i (T^\vee)^i=\sum_{i=0}^r a_i (T^i)^\vee=\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^r a_i T^i\Bigr)^\vee=f(T)^\vee,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad f(T^\vee)(\varphi)=\varphi\circ f(T)\ \ \text{for all }\varphi\in V^\vee.\tag{$\ast$}
\]

**Step 3. Vanishing of $f(T)$ is equivalent to vanishing of $f(T^\vee)$.**
First, if $f(T)=0$ then $(\ast)$ gives $f(T^\vee)(\varphi)=\varphi\circ 0=0$ for all $\varphi$, so $f(T^\vee)=0$.
Conversely, suppose $f(T^\vee)=0$. We use that linear functionals separate points of $V$: if $w\in V$, $w\neq0$, extend $\{w\}$ to a basis $\{w,e_2,\dots,e_N\}$ of $V$ and define $\varphi_w\in V^\vee$ on that basis by $\varphi_w(w)=1$, $\varphi_w(e_j)=0$; then $\varphi_w(w)\neq0$.
Now put $w:=f(T)v$ for an arbitrary $v\in V$. By $(\ast)$, for every $\varphi\in V^\vee$ we have $\varphi(w)=\varphi(f(T)v)=f(T^\vee)(\varphi)(v)=0$, since $f(T^\vee)=0$ as an endomorphism of $V^\vee$. Taking $\varphi=\varphi_w$ shows $w=0$. Thus $f(T)v=0$ for all $v\in V$, i.e. $f(T)=0$.

**Step 4. The minimal polynomials coincide.**
Step 3 says exactly $I_{T^\vee}=I_T$ as subsets of $F[t]$. Their unique monic generators are therefore equal:
\[
m_{T^\vee}=m_T.\tag{$\dagger$}
\]
(Explicitly: in a basis $\{v_1,\dots,v_N\}$ of $V$ and the dual basis $\{v_1^\vee,\dots,v_N^\vee\}$ of $V^\vee$, $T^\vee(v_j^\vee)=\sum_i (v_j^\vee\circ T)(v_i)\,v_i^\vee=\sum_i a_{ji}\,v_i^\vee$ if $T(v_i)=\sum_j a_{ji}v_j$; so $T^\vee$ is represented by the transpose matrix, and $(\dagger)$ is the familiar statement that a matrix and its transpose have the same minimal polynomial. The basis-free argument above proves this without choosing bases.)

**Step 5. Conclusion of the equivalence.**
By definition $T$ is semisimple $\iff m_T$ is squarefree in $F[t]$, and $T^\vee$ is semisimple $\iff m_{T^\vee}$ is squarefree in $F[t]$. By $(\dagger)$ these two conditions are literally the same condition. Hence
\[
T\text{ is semisimple}\iff T^\vee\text{ is semisimple}.\]
This proves the lemma. (Note that neither direction used $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ beyond ensuring $T^\vee$ is invertible; the argument is valid for any $T\in\mathrm{End}_F(V)$.)

**Step 6. Compatibility with the "diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$" formulation.**
For completeness we justify that the hypothesis of Step 5 is the same as diagonalisability after extending scalars to $\overline F$, which is the form appearing in the conjecture.

(6a) *Minimal polynomials are unchanged by field extension.* Let $K/F$ be a field extension and $S\in\mathrm{End}_F(V)$; write $S_K:=\mathrm{id}_K\otimes S\in\mathrm{End}_K(K\otimes_F V)$ and let $d:=\deg m_S$. The $d$ endomorphisms $\mathrm{id},S,\dots,S^{d-1}$ are $F$-linearly independent (otherwise a nonzero polynomial of degree $<d$ would kill $S$). Identifying $\mathrm{End}_F(V)\simeq F^{N^2}$ via a basis, independence means that the $N^2\times d$ matrix of coordinates has rank $d$, i.e. some $d\times d$ minor is nonzero; that minor is an element of $F$ and its nonvanishing is unchanged in $K$, so $\mathrm{id},\dots,S_K^{d-1}$ are $K$-linearly independent. Since $m_S(S_K)=0$, the minimal polynomial $m_{S_K}\in K[t]$ divides $m_S$ and has degree $\ge d=\deg m_S$; both are monic, so $m_{S_K}=m_S$.

(6b) *Squarefreeness is unchanged by field extension.* $m_S$ is squarefree in $F[t]$ iff $\gcd(m_S,m_S')=1$ in $F[t]$ (with $m_S'$ the formal derivative). The Euclidean algorithm computing this gcd uses only the coefficients of $m_S$, which lie in $F$; running it in $K[t]$ performs the identical arithmetic and yields the same gcd. Hence $m_S$ is squarefree in $F[t]$ iff it is squarefree in $K[t]$.

(6c) *Over an algebraically closed field, squarefree minimal polynomial $\iff$ diagonalisable.* Let $K$ be algebraically closed and $U\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$ with $W$ finite dimensional. If $U$ is diagonalisable with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$, then $\prod_{i}(t-\lambda_i)$ kills $U$, so $m_U$ divides the squarefree polynomial $\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)$ and is itself squarefree. Conversely, if $m_U=\prod_{i=1}^r (t-\lambda_i)$ with the $\lambda_i\in K$ pairwise distinct, set $P_i:=m_U/(t-\lambda_i)$. The $P_i$ have no common irreducible factor, so $\gcd(P_1,\dots,P_r)=1$ and there exist $a_i\in K[t]$ with $\sum_i a_iP_i=1$. Define $\pi_i:=a_i(U)P_i(U)\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$. Then $\sum_i\pi_i=\mathrm{id}_W$; for $i\ne j$ the product $P_iP_j$ is divisible by $m_U$ (it contains both factors $t-\lambda_i$ and $t-\lambda_j$), so $\pi_i\pi_j=a_i(U)a_j(U)(P_iP_j)(U)=0$; and $(U-\lambda_i\,\mathrm{id})\pi_i=a_i(U)m_U(U)=0$, so $\mathrm{im}\,\pi_i\subseteq\ker(U-\lambda_i\,\mathrm{id})$. Hence $W=\sum_i\mathrm{im}\,\pi_i\subseteq\sum_i\ker(U-\lambda_i\,\mathrm{id})$, and the sum of distinct eigenspaces is direct, so $W$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces of $U$, i.e. $U$ is diagonalisable.

Combining (6a), (6b), (6c) for $S=T$ and $S=T^\vee$ over $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ shows that the semisimplicity of $T$ used above is equivalent to diagonalisability of $T\otimes_F\overline F$, and likewise for $T^\vee$; and $V^\vee\otimes_F\overline F\simeq (V\otimes_F\overline F)^\vee$ identifies $(T^\vee)_{\overline F}$ with the dual of $T_{\overline F}$. Thus the proved equivalence is exactly the one needed to pass between $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and its dual in arguments about Frobenius semisimplicity.

lemma_214.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(f:X\to Y\) be a morphism of schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\). For a scheme \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) write \(Z_k=Z\times_{\mathbb F_q}k\) and \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then for every \(n\ge0\) the pullback \(f_k^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) satisfies \(f_k^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_k^*\).
lemma_214.proof:
We prove the statement directly from the definitions of the Frobenius endomorphism of a base-changed scheme and of pullback in $\ell$-adic \'etale cohomology; no finiteness or properness of $X,Y$ is used, so the argument is valid for all schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$.

**Step 1: Notation.** For a scheme $Z$ of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ we write $Z_k=Z\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, with projections $\pi_Z:Z_k\to Z$ and $p_Z:Z_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Since $\sigma(c)=c^q$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ elementwise, $\sigma$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb F_q$-algebras $k\to k$, hence $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, and
$$\Phi_Z:=\mathrm{id}_{Z}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:Z_k\longrightarrow Z_k$$\nis a well-defined endomorphism of the scheme $Z_k$; it is an isomorphism (inverse $\mathrm{id}_Z\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}$). The operator denoted $F_Z$ in the statement is the pullback $F_Z:=\Phi_Z^{*}$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The morphism $f:X\to Y$ over $\mathbb F_q$ base-changes to $f_k:=f\times\mathrm{id}_k:X_k\to Y_k$, and $f_k^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the usual pullback. The claim is the identity of maps $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$
$$f_k^{*}\circ\Phi_Y^{*}=\Phi_X^{*}\circ f_k^{*}.\qquad(\ast)$$

**Step 2: The Frobenius square commutes.** We show
$$f_k\circ\Phi_X=\Phi_Y\circ f_k\quad\text{as morphisms }X_k\to Y_k.\qquad(1)$$

*Proof via the universal property of the fibre product.* Both composites are morphisms $X_k\to Y=Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, so by the universal property of $Y_k$ they are determined by their two components (i.e. their composites with $\pi_Y:Y_k\to Y$ and $p_Y:Y_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$). Using $\pi_Y\circ f_k=f\circ\pi_X$, $p_Y\circ f_k=p_X$, $\pi_Z\circ\Phi_Z=\pi_Z$ and $p_Z\circ\Phi_Z=\sigma\circ p_Z$ (valid for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, by the defining property of the product morphism $\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$), we compute
$$\pi_Y\circ(f_k\circ\Phi_X)=(f\circ\pi_X)\circ\Phi_X=f\circ\pi_X=\pi_Y\circ(\Phi_Y\circ f_k),$$
$$p_Y\circ(f_k\circ\Phi_X)=p_X\circ\Phi_X=\sigma\circ p_X=p_Y\circ f_k=p_Y\circ(\Phi_Y\circ f_k),$$\nwhere in the last chain we used $p_Y\circ\Phi_Y=\sigma\circ p_Y$. Equal components imply equality of the morphisms into the fibre product, proving (1).

*Explicit affine check (same computation at the level of rings).* Take affine opens $V=\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq Y$, $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq X$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$, and put $C=A\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k$, $D=B\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k$. Then $f_k|_{U_k}^{V_k}$ is induced by $f_k^{\#}:D\to C$, $b\otimes\lambda\mapsto f^{\#}(b)\otimes\lambda$, and $\Phi_X,\Phi_Y$ are induced by $\Phi_X^{\#}(a\otimes\lambda)=a\otimes\lambda^{q}$ and $\Phi_Y^{\#}(b\otimes\lambda)=b\otimes\lambda^{q}$. For a generator $b\otimes\lambda\in D$:
$$(f_k^{\#}\circ\Phi_Y^{\#})(b\otimes\lambda)=f_k^{\#}(b\otimes\lambda^{q})=f^{\#}(b)\otimes\lambda^{q},\qquad (\Phi_X^{\#}\circ f_k^{\#})(b\otimes\lambda)=\Phi_X^{\#}(f^{\#}(b)\otimes\lambda)=f^{\#}(b)\otimes\lambda^{q}.$$
The two ring homomorphisms $D\to C$ agree on generators, hence are equal; this is exactly (1) on affine opens, and the opens cover, so (1) holds globally.

**Step 3: Contravariant functoriality of $\ell$-adic \'etale cohomology, with the coherence needed.** We record precisely the fact to be applied, and justify it.

(a) For a morphism $g:Z'\to Z$ of schemes, base change $W\mapsto W\times_Z Z'$ sends \'etale $Z$-schemes to \'etale $Z'$-schemes and defines a morphism of \'etale topoi $\varepsilon_g:(Z'_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\to(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ with exact inverse-image functor $g^{-1}:=\varepsilon_g^{-1}$. For composable morphisms $Z''\xrightarrow{h}Z'\xrightarrow{g}Z$ the canonical isomorphism of functors on $Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$
$$(W\times_Z Z')\times_{Z'}Z''\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;W\times_Z Z'',\qquad ((w,z'),z'')\longmapsto (w,z''),$$\nwith inverse $(w,z'')\mapsto((w,h(z'')),z'')$, is an isomorphism of \'etale $Z''$-schemes and yields a canonical isomorphism of inverse-image functors
$$\alpha_{g,h}:(g\circ h)^{-1}\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;h^{-1}\circ g^{-1}.\qquad(2)$$
These isomorphisms are associative: for a triple $Z'''\to Z''\to Z'\to Z$ the two ways of identifying $((g\circ h)\circ k)^{-1}$ with $k^{-1}h^{-1}g^{-1}$ agree, because both are induced by the single set-theoretic/scheme-theoretic reassociation $((w,z''),z''',z''')\rightsquigarrow(w,z''')$ of iterated fibre products (the standard pentagon coherence for fibre products).

(b) Let $\Lambda_\nu:=\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu}$. The constant sheaf $\Lambda_{\nu,Z}$ on $Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ is the coproduct of $\Lambda_\nu$ copies of the terminal sheaf $*_{Z}$. Since $g^{-1}$ is left exact (hence preserves the terminal object) and is a left adjoint (hence preserves all colimits), there is a *canonical* identification
$$\iota_g:g^{-1}\Lambda_{\nu,Z}\;=\;\coprod_{\Lambda_\nu}g^{-1}*_{Z}\;=\;\coprod_{\Lambda_\nu}*_{Z'}\;=\;\Lambda_{\nu,Z'},$$\nwhich is the identity on the index set $\Lambda_\nu$. By construction of $\alpha_{g,h}$ in (2) — it acts as the identity on the index of a coproduct of terminal sheaves — the coherence
$$\iota_{h}\circ\alpha_{g,h}(\Lambda_{\nu,Z})=\iota_{g\circ h}\qquad\text{as identifications }(g\circ h)^{-1}\Lambda_{\nu,Z}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{\nu,Z''}$$\nholds: both sides send a local section, i.e. a locally constant $\Lambda_\nu$-valued function, to the same locally constant $\Lambda_\nu$-valued function on $Z''_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ obtained by precomposition with the structure map. In words: the pullback identifications of constant sheaves compose strictly.

(c) The derived functor $R\Gamma(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}},-)$ applied to $\Lambda_{\nu,Z}$ gives $H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu})$, and the pair $(\varepsilon_g,\iota_g)$ is a morphism of ringed topoi $(Z'_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\Lambda_{\nu,Z'})\to(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\Lambda_{\nu,Z})$. Hence it induces $\mathbb Z/\ell^\nu$-linear maps $g^*:H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu)\to H^n(Z',\Lambda_\nu)$ (equivalently, via $H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\Lambda_\nu)}(\Lambda_{\nu,Z},\Lambda_{\nu,Z}[n])$, the map $u\mapsto g^{-1}u$ under the identifications in (b)). Because $g^{-1}$ is exact, and by the strict composition of the identifications proved in (b) together with the associativity (2), we obtain, for composable $Z''\xrightarrow{h}Z'\xrightarrow{g}Z$,
$$(g\circ h)^*=h^*\circ g^*:H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu)\to H^n(Z'',\Lambda_\nu),\qquad \mathrm{id}^*=\mathrm{id}.\qquad(3)$$
This is the usual contravariant functoriality, spelled out with the coherence that the structural identifications of constant sheaves compose strictly (no sign, no twist, no choice).

(d) The transition maps $\Lambda_{\nu+1}\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda_\nu$ induce the standard maps $H^n(Z,\Lambda_{\nu+1})\to H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu)$, and $H^n(Z,\mathbb Z_\ell):=\varprojlim_\nu H^n(Z,\Lambda_\nu)$, $H^n(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}H^n(Z,\mathbb Z_\ell)$. Since $g^{-1}$ is compatible with the reduction maps (base change commutes with the coefficient sequence $\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu+1}\to\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu}$ termwise, as $g^{-1}$ is $\mathbb Z/\ell^{\nu+1}$-linear and the quotient sheaves are computed objectwise), the maps $g^*$ are compatible with the transition maps; hence $g\mapsto g^*$ is a contravariant functor also on $H^n(-,\mathbb Z_\ell)$ and, after $\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}(-)$ (which is a functor, so it preserves the equalities (3)), on $H^n(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Thus (3) holds verbatim with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ coefficients:
$$(g\circ h)^*=h^*\circ g^*\quad\text{on }H^n(-,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad\text{all }n\ge0.\qquad(4)$$
(No finiteness of the groups is needed for (4); it is an identity of homomorphisms.)

**Step 4: Conclusion.** Apply (4) to the equality of composites (1) with $g=f_k$, $h=\Phi_X$, and also to the same equality read with $g=\Phi_Y$, $h=f_k$. For every $n\ge0$:
$$F_X\circ f_k^{*}=\Phi_X^{*}\circ f_k^{*}\overset{(4)}{=}(f_k\circ\Phi_X)^{*}\overset{(1)}{=}(\Phi_Y\circ f_k)^{*}\overset{(4)}{=}f_k^{*}\circ\Phi_Y^{*}=f_k^{*}\circ F_Y.$$
Each equality is justified: the first and last are the definition $F_Z=\Phi_Z^*$, the second and fourth are the contravariance (4), and the third is the commutativity of the Frobenius square (1), which is Step 2. Rearranging gives exactly $f_k^{*}\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_k^{*}$, the required intertwining relation. $\blacksquare$

**Step 5: Edge cases and remarks on the hypotheses.**
- $n=0$: $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space of locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued functions on the set of geometric connected components of $Z_k$; $\Phi_Z^*$ and $f_k^*$ are precomposition with the corresponding maps on components, and (1) says precisely that the two ways of precomposing agree. So the identity holds also in degree $0$ (and the general argument in Steps 2--4 already covers it).
- $X_k=\varnothing$ (or $Y_k=\varnothing$): then $H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ (the \'etale topos of the empty scheme is the terminal topos, whose cohomology in all degrees is $0$), and both sides of $(\ast)$ are the zero map $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to 0$. No exception is needed.
- Non-proper/non-smooth $X,Y$: the proof uses only functoriality of pullback, never finiteness of the cohomology groups nor Poincar\'e duality, so the hypotheses "of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$" are more than sufficient (in fact the statement holds for arbitrary $\mathbb F_q$-schemes).
- $\ell\neq p$ is not used in the proof of the intertwining identity either; it is part of the standing convention ensuring $\mathbb Q_\ell$-coefficients are the good ones for \'etale cohomology in characteristic $p$.
- Linearity: all maps involved are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, since pullback along a morphism of $\mathbb Z_\ell$-ringed topoi is $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear after tensoring; hence $(\ast)$ is an identity in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))$.

**Step 6: Companion statement for geometric Frobenius (same proof).** Replacing $\sigma$ by $\sigma^{-1}$ (which also fixes $\mathbb F_q$) in Step 2 gives $f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})=(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})\circ f_k$: indeed $p_Y\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^{-1})=\sigma^{-1}\circ p_Y$, and the component computation of Step 2 goes through unchanged with $\sigma$ replaced by $\sigma^{-1}$. Step 4 then yields $f_k^{*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_Y\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^{*}=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^{*}\circ f_k^{*}$, i.e. the geometric Frobenius also commutes with pullback. (Equivalently, this follows from the present lemma together with $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}$, since $\sigma\circ\sigma^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_k$ and Step 4 applied to $\Phi_Z\circ\Phi_Z^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$ gives $F_{\mathrm{ar},Z}\circ F_{\mathrm{geo},Z}=\mathrm{id}$.)

lemma_212.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and also on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\).
lemma_212.proof:
Let F_X = (id_X × Spec σ), σ(c)=c^q. Denote by F_1 the induced automorphism of H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), and by Φ_1 the arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ(1)) induced by the canonical arithmetic Frobenius structure on the Tate twist. Under the Kummer identification, Φ_1 is pullback of line bundles. We prove Φ_1 is semisimple and then compare it with F_1.

1. Reduction to the Picard variety. Put P = Pic^0_{X/F_q}, and let π_P be its q-power Frobenius endomorphism. Since X is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_q, X_k is smooth projective geometrically connected over k. The Picard scheme commutes with this base change, so Pic^0_{X_k/k} = P_k and Pic^0(X_k)=P(k). By lemma_205, NS(X_k)=Pic(X_k)/P(k) is finitely generated. Hence lemma_195 applies. It gives a Z_ℓ-linear isomorphism φ: H^1_et(X_k,Z_ℓ(1)) → T_ℓ(P_k) such that φ ∘ Φ_Z = π_P ∘ φ, where Φ_Z is the operator induced by pullback of line bundles. By functoriality of the Kummer isomorphism (lemma_kummer_h1), Φ_Z is the arithmetic Frobenius operator on H^1(X_k,Z_ℓ(1)) induced by the canonical structure on Z_ℓ(1).

The Tate module T_ℓ(P_k) is a finite free Z_ℓ-module (rank 2 dim P; if P=0 the rank is 0). Therefore H^1(X_k,Z_ℓ(1)) is finite free, and tensoring φ with Q_ℓ gives a Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism α: H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ(1)) → V_ℓ(P_k) satisfying α ∘ Φ_1 = V_ℓ(π_P) ∘ α.

2. Semisimplicity of V_ℓ(π_P). If P=0, then V_ℓ(P_k)=0 and the zero operator is semisimple. Assume dim P>0. By lemma_poincare_reducibility, there are simple abelian F_q-subvarieties B_1,...,B_r of P such that the addition morphism σ:B_1×...×B_r→P is an isogeny over F_q. For any isogeny f:A→B of abelian varieties over k, V_ℓ(f) is a Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism: if g:B→A and n≥1 satisfy g∘f=[n]_A and f∘g=[n]_B, then V_ℓ(g)V_ℓ(f)=n id and V_ℓ(f)V_ℓ(g)=n id, so V_ℓ(f)^{-1}=n^{-1}V_ℓ(g). Applying this to σ gives V_ℓ(σ):V_ℓ(B_1×...×B_r)→V_ℓ(P_k) an isomorphism.

The rational Tate module of a product is the direct sum of the rational Tate modules of the factors, V_ℓ(B_1×...×B_r) ≅ ⊕ V_ℓ(B_i). Under this identification the q-power Frobenius on the product is the direct sum of the q-power Frobenii π_{B_i}. By lemma_92, each V_ℓ(π_{B_i}) acts semisimply on V_ℓ(B_i). By lemma_9, the direct sum ⊕ V_ℓ(π_{B_i}) acts semisimply on V_ℓ(B_1×...×B_r). Because σ is defined over F_q, it commutes with Frobenius: σ∘π_B=π_P∘σ. Applying V_ℓ gives V_ℓ(σ)∘V_ℓ(π_B)=V_ℓ(π_P)∘V_ℓ(σ). All Frobenius operators here are invertible (Frobenius is an isogeny), so lemma_8 transfers semisimplicity across the intertwining isomorphism V_ℓ(σ). Hence V_ℓ(π_P) acts semisimply on V_ℓ(P_k). In particular V_ℓ(P_k) is finite-dimensional.

3. Semisimplicity on the twisted cohomology. The operator Φ_1 is invertible because F_X is an automorphism of X_k and the coefficient structure on Q_ℓ(1) is an isomorphism. The isomorphism α intertwines Φ_1 with V_ℓ(π_P), and both spaces are finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ. By lemma_8, Φ_1 acts semisimply on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ(1)). This proves the statement for the canonical Tate-twist Frobenius.

4. Comparison with untwisted Frobenius. Let Λ=Z_ℓ(1)(k)=lim_n μ_{ℓ^n}(k). This is a free Z_ℓ-module of rank 1; put L=Q_ℓ⊗Λ. Since k is separably closed, Q_ℓ(1) is the constant sheaf with value L. Choose a Z_ℓ-basis e of Λ and let s_e:L→Q_ℓ be the Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism sending e to 1. It induces τ:H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ(1))→H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ).

The operator Φ_1 is induced by the canonical isomorphism θ:F_X^{-1}Q_ℓ(1)→Q_ℓ(1). Under the identifications by s_e, the transported θ is an automorphism of the constant sheaf Q_ℓ. Since X_k is connected, every automorphism of a constant sheaf of Q_ℓ-vector spaces is multiplication by a unique λ∈Q_ℓ^×. Indeed, such an automorphism is given stalkwise by a Q_ℓ-linear endomorphism, hence by a locally constant function to Q_ℓ, and this function is constant on the connected space. The untwisted arithmetic Frobenius F_1 is induced by the identity automorphism of the constant sheaf Q_ℓ. Naturality of cohomology with respect to sheaf isomorphisms therefore gives τ ∘ Φ_1 ∘ τ^{-1} = λ F_1.

Since Φ_1 is semisimple, λF_1 is semisimple. Multiplication by a nonzero scalar preserves semisimplicity: if the minimal polynomial of an operator T is squarefree, then the minimal polynomial of cT is obtained by scaling the variable and is again squarefree. Thus F_1 acts semisimply on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ).

Finally, if the Frobenius on H^1(X_k,Q_ℓ(1)) is defined by the alternative convention F_1⊗id under the identification H^1(X_k,Q_ℓ(1))≅H^1(X_k,Q_ℓ)⊗Q_ℓ(1), then that operator is λ^{-1}Φ_1, a nonzero scalar multiple of the semisimple operator Φ_1, and is therefore also semisimple. Hence the arithmetic Frobenius acts semisimply on both H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) and H^1_et(X_k,Q_ℓ(1)).

lemma_218.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of the \(\ell\)-adic cohomology of \(X_k\). For every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le D\), \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if it acts semisimply on \(H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_218.proof:
We prove that for every $0\le n\le 2D$ (a fortiori for $0\le n\le D$) the operator $F$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if it is semisimple on $H^{2D-n}_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The whole argument is Poincar\'e duality plus elementary linear algebra; no semisimplicity is assumed anywhere.

Recall the working definition: an automorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $U$ is \emph{semisimple} if $T\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable, equivalently if $U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}=\bigoplus_{\lambda} U_\lambda(T)$ is the direct sum of the eigenspaces of $T$.

\textbf{Step 1 (Notation).} Put
\[
 V:=H^n_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H^{2D-n}_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad L:=\mathbb Q_\ell(-D),
\]
and write $F_V,V\to V$, $F_W:W\to W$ for the maps induced by $F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$; these preserve cohomological degree because $F$ is the pullback of a morphism of $X_k$.

\textbf{Step 2 (Finite-dimensionality and invertibility).} $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, and the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. Applying lemma\_45\_finite\_frob to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$ and $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W<\infty$. Applying lemma\_6a (with $i=n$ and $i=2D-n$) gives that $F_V$ and $F_W$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear \emph{automorphisms}, with inverses the corresponding geometric Frobenius maps. Thus $F_V\in \mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F_W\in \mathrm{GL}(W)$.

\textbf{Step 3 (Frobenius-equivariant Poincar\'e duality).} We apply lemma\_77 with $m=1$, $Y=X$, $d=D$ (all its hypotheses hold: $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_{q^1}=\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$, and $F$ is the $q^1$-power arithmetic Frobenius). Its part (a) gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}:H^{2D}_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }L=\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ on which $F$ acts as multiplication by the positive rational number $q^{1\cdot D}=q^D$; i.e.
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(F z)=q^D\operatorname{tr}(z)\quad\text{for all }z\in H^{2D}_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
Its part (b), applied to the degree $n$ (note $0\le n\le 2D$ and $0\le 2D-n\le 2D$), gives the pairing
\[
 \langle x,y\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\ \in L,\qquad x\in V,\ y\in W,
\]
which is a \emph{perfect} pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and satisfies
\[
 \langle F_V v,\,F_W w\rangle=q^D\langle v,w\rangle\qquad\text{for all }v\in V,\ w\in W.\tag{$\ast$}
\]

\textbf{Step 4 (The adjoint identification $W\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(V,L)$).} Define
\[
 \iota:W\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,L),\qquad \iota(w)(v):=\langle v,w\rangle .
\]
Since the pairing is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear, $\iota$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear; since it is perfect, $\iota$ is an isomorphism. We compute the operator transported by $\iota$ from $F_W$. For $w\in W$ and $v\in V$,
\[
 \iota(F_W w)(v)=\langle v,F_W w\rangle .
\]
Because $F_V$ is invertible (Step 2), write $v=F_V u$ with $u=F_V^{-1}v$. Then by $(\ast)$,
\[
 \langle v,F_W w\rangle=\langle F_V u,F_W w\rangle=q^D\langle u,w\rangle=q^D\,\iota(w)(F_V^{-1}v).
\]
Hence, with
\[
 A:=\Big(\varphi\longmapsto q^D\cdot(\varphi\circ F_V^{-1})\Big)\ \in\ \mathrm{GL}(\operatorname{Hom}(V,L)),
\]
we have proved the intertwining relation
\[
 \iota\circ F_W=A\circ\iota .\tag{4.1}
\]
($A$ is invertible, with inverse $\varphi\mapsto q^{-D}\varphi\circ F_V$; it is also conjugate to the invertible $F_W$ by (4.1).)

\textbf{Step 5 (Transport to the plain dual $V^{\vee}$).} $L$ is one-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, so choose a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\psi:L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$. Conjugation by $\psi$ gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
 \Theta:\operatorname{Hom}(V,L)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V^{\vee}:=\operatorname{Hom}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \varphi\longmapsto \psi\circ\varphi,
\]
whose inverse is $\alpha\mapsto\psi^{-1}\circ\alpha$. For $\alpha\in V^{\vee}$,
\[
 \Theta A\Theta^{-1}(\alpha)=\psi\circ A(\psi^{-1}\circ\alpha)=\psi\circ\big(q^D\,\psi^{-1}\circ\alpha\circ F_V^{-1}\big)=q^D\,\alpha\circ F_V^{-1},
\]
because $q^D\in\mathbb Q^{\times}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ is a scalar and $\psi$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear. In the notation of lemma\_215, $T^{\vee}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T$, this says
\[
 \Theta A\Theta^{-1}=q^D\cdot (F_V^{-1})^{\vee}\ \in\ \mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee}).\tag{5.1}
\]

\textbf{Step 6 (Two elementary linear-algebra facts).}

\emph{Fact S1 (nonzero scalar multiples).} Let $S\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(U)$ with $U$ finite dimensional, and $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. Then $S$ is semisimple if and only if $cS$ is. Indeed, for $\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ one has $S_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}u=\lambda u\iff (cS)_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}u=c\lambda u$, and multiplication by $c$ is a bijection of $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; hence $U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}$ is the direct sum of the eigenspaces of $S$ if and only if it is the direct sum of the eigenspaces of $cS$ (the two eigenspace decompositions are literally the same decomposition, re-labelled by $\lambda\mapsto c\lambda$).

\emph{Fact S2 (inverses).} Let $T\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ with $U$ finite dimensional. Then $T$ is semisimple if and only if $T^{-1}$ is. First note that if $T$ is semisimple then every polynomial in $T$ is semisimple: $U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}=\bigoplus_\lambda U_\lambda(T)$ and $p(T)$ acts on $U_\lambda(T)$ as the scalar $p(\lambda)$, so $U_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}=\bigoplus_\mu\big(\bigoplus_{\lambda:\,p(\lambda)=\mu}U_\lambda(T)\big)$ is an eigenspace decomposition for $p(T)$. Now let $m(t)=t^r+a_{r-1}t^{r-1}+\cdots+a_1t+a_0\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ be the minimal polynomial of $T$. Then $a_0\ne0$: if $a_0=0$ then $0=m(T)=T\,(T^{r-1}+a_{r-1}T^{r-2}+\cdots+a_1)$ and invertibility of $T$ forces $T^{r-1}+\cdots+a_1\cdot 1$ to annihilate $U$, contradicting minimality of $m$ (and $T\ne0$ since $T$ is invertible). Hence
\[
 T^{-1}=-a_0^{-1}\big(T^{r-1}+a_{r-1}T^{r-2}+\cdots+a_1\cdot \mathrm{id}\big),
\]
obtained by dividing $m(T)=0$ by $T$. So $T^{-1}$ is a polynomial in $T$, and is semisimple whenever $T$ is. Applying this implication to $T^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$, whose inverse is $T$, gives the converse.

\textbf{Step 7 (Chain of equivalences).} All operators below are invertible and all spaces finite dimensional, so lemma\_8 (transport of semisimplicity along an intertwining isomorphism) applies at each step.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $F_W$ is semisimple on $W$ $\iff$ $A$ is semisimple on $\operatorname{Hom}(V,L)$, by lemma\_8 applied to the isomorphism $\iota$ and the intertwining relation (4.1).
\item[(ii)] $A$ semisimple on $\operatorname{Hom}(V,L)$ $\iff$ $\Theta A\Theta^{-1}=q^D(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}$ semisimple on $V^{\vee}$, by lemma\_8 applied to the isomorphism $\Theta$ and (5.1).
\item[(iii)] $q^D(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}$ semisimple $\iff$ $(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}$ semisimple, by Fact S1 with $c=q^D\in\mathbb Q^{\times}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$.
\item[(iv)] $(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}$ semisimple on $V^{\vee}$ $\iff$ $F_V^{-1}$ semisimple on $V$, by lemma\_215 applied to $T=F_V^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ (whose transpose $T^{\vee}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ F_V^{-1}$ is exactly $(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}$).
\item[(v)] $F_V^{-1}$ semisimple $\iff$ $F_V$ semisimple, by Fact S2 with $T=F_V$.
\end{enumerate}
Chaining (i)--(v) yields: $F$ acts semisimply on $W=H^{2D-n}_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if $F$ acts semisimply on $V=H^n_{\text{\'et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

\textbf{Step 8 (Edge cases).} If $D=0$ then $X\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$, $V=W=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $L=\mathbb Q_\ell(0)=\mathbb Q_\ell$, and $F$ is the identity on both, so the statement holds; the argument above also covers it verbatim. If $n>2D$ both groups vanish and both operators are trivially semisimple; in the range $0\le n\le D$ under consideration this cannot occur. The hypothesis $n\le D$ is used nowhere except to avoid stating the same equivalence twice (with $n$ and $2D-n$ interchanged); the proof actually gives the equivalence for all $n$.

This completes the proof of lemma\_218. \qed

lemma_h1_zl_free.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(k\), and let \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\) be the identity component of the Picard scheme of \(Y\). Then the inverse limit \(\varprojlim_n H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\), taken over the transition maps induced by \(\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}\), \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}\), is a free \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module of rank \(2\dim P\).
lemma_h1_zl_free.proof:
We write \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y):=P(k)\) for the group of \(k\)-points of \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\), and \(\operatorname{NS}(Y):=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\).

**Preliminaries (the \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-structures).**

(a) Since \(Y\) is smooth projective over the algebraically closed field \(k\), the Picard scheme \(\operatorname{Pic}_{Y/k}\) is locally of finite type over \(k\) and its identity component \(P=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{Y/k}\) is proper, hence an abelian variety over \(k\). Put \(g:=\dim P\).

(b) We fix the following standard way of putting a \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module structure on an inverse system. Let \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) be an inverse system of abelian groups whose bonding maps \(\varphi_n:A_{n+1}\to A_n\) are multiplication by \(\ell\), and suppose each \(A_n\) is killed by \(\ell^n\). Then each \(A_n\) is a \(\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z\)-module, and for \(\lambda=(\lambda_n)_n\in\mathbb Z_\ell=\varprojlim_n\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z\) and \(a=(a_n)\in\varprojlim_n A_n\) the formula \((\lambda a)_n:=\lambda_n a_n\) defines an element of \(\varprojlim_n A_n\): indeed
\[
\varphi_n\big((\lambda a)_{n+1}\big)=\ell\,(\lambda_{n+1}a_{n+1})=\lambda_n\,(\ell a_{n+1})=\lambda_n\varphi_n(a_{n+1})=\lambda_n a_n=(\lambda a)_n,
\]
where \(\ell\lambda_{n+1}=\lambda_n\) in \(\operatorname{End}(A_n)\) because \(\lambda_{n+1}\equiv\lambda_n\pmod{\ell^n}\) and \(\ell a_{n+1}\in A_n\) is annihilated by \(\ell^n\). This makes \(\varprojlim_n A_n\) a module over \(\varprojlim_n\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z_\ell\). Moreover, if \(f_\bullet:(A_n)\to(B_n)\) is a morphism of two such systems (i.e. a compatible family of group homomorphisms), the induced \(\varprojlim f_n\) is \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear, because a homomorphism of abelian groups commutes with multiplication by integers, hence with the action of every \(\lambda_n\in\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z\) defined through integers.

In our situation each of the three systems below is of this form:
\(A_n=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\) (via \(\theta_n\) of Step 1, it is killed by \(\ell^n\), and its transition maps are the ones corresponding to \(L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}\)), \(A_n=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\), and \(A_n=\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]=P[\ell^n](k)\); in each case the bonding maps are multiplication by \(\ell\) by definition, and each term is by definition annihilated by \(\ell^n\). We give each limit this canonical \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module structure; by (b) every map constructed below, being induced by a morphism of systems, is \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear.

**Step 1 (Kummer identification).** Apply lemma_kummer_h1 with the algebraically closed field \(k\) (of characteristic \(p\neq\ell\)) and the smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Y\). It gives canonical isomorphisms
\[
\theta_n:\;H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
which are compatible with the transition morphisms \(\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^n}\), \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}\) on the left and \(L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}\) on the right. Passing to inverse limits we obtain a \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module isomorphism
\[
\Theta:\;\varprojlim_n H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n].
\]
Note that the transition maps on the left are exactly the ones occurring in the statement of the present lemma.

**Step 2 (\(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) is finitely generated).** The base field here is \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(Y\) is smooth projective geometrically connected over \(k\), so lemma_205 applies verbatim and yields that \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)=\operatorname{Pic}(Y)/\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\) is a finitely generated abelian group.

**Step 3 (Removing the Néron–Severi part).** By Step 2 the hypothesis of lemma_pic_torsion_limit is satisfied for the algebraically closed field \(k\), the prime \(\ell\neq p=\operatorname{char}(k)\) and the variety \(Y\). That lemma gives an isomorphism, induced by the inclusion \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(Y)\),
\[
\Psi:\;\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n],
\]
both sides carrying the bonding maps \(x\mapsto\ell x\). By (b), \(\Psi\) is \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear.

**Step 4 (Identification with the Tate module).** Since \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)=P(k)\) and \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]=P[\ell^n](k)\), the left-hand side of Step 3 is, by definition and with bonding maps \(x\mapsto\ell x\), exactly the Tate module
\[
\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Pic}^0(Y)[\ell^n]=\varprojlim_n P[\ell^n](k)=T_\ell(P).
\]

**Step 5 (Tate module of an abelian variety).** Apply lemma_tate_rank to the abelian variety \(B:=P\) of dimension \(g\) over the algebraically closed field \(k\) and the prime \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\): \(T_\ell(P)\) is a free \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module of rank \(2g=2\dim P\).

**Conclusion.** The composite
\[
T_\ell(P)\;\xrightarrow{\ \Psi\ }\;\varprojlim_n\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\;\xrightarrow{\ \Theta^{-1}\ }\;\varprojlim_n H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})
\]
is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-modules by Steps 1, 3, 4 and (b). Since \(T_ell(P)\) is free of rank \(2\dim P\) over \(\mathbb Z_\ell\) by Step 5, so is \(\varprojlim_n H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mu_{\ell^n})\): being free of a given rank is transported by module isomorphisms (a \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-basis of \(T_\ell(P)\) maps to a \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-basis of the limit). This is precisely the claim. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

(Remarks on what was *not* used, in view of the traps flagged in the guidance: we never asserted surjectivity of the maps \(\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^{n+1}]\to\operatorname{Pic}(Y)[\ell^n]\), nor torsion-freeness of \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\); only the finite generation of \(\operatorname{NS}(Y)\) from lemma_205, as required by lemma_pic_torsion_limit.)

lemma_220.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of the graded ring \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), which satisfies \(F(x\cup y)=Fx\cup Fy\). For a homogeneous class \(v\) of degree \(r\), write \(V_v=\langle F^n v : n\ge 0\rangle_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\subseteq H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and call \(v\) Frobenius\(-\)semisimple when \(F|_{V_v}\) is semisimple. Then the unit \(1\in H^0\) is Frobenius-semisimple, and the cup product of two homogeneous Frobenius-semisimple classes is Frobenius-semisimple.
lemma_220.proof:
## Proof of lemma_220

Throughout write $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $\bar K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and $H^*=H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. By hypothesis $F$ is an automorphism of the graded ring $H^*$ with $F(x\cup y)=Fx\cup Fy$; in particular $F$ maps $H^r$ into $H^r$ for each $r$.

### 0. Finiteness, and a few linear-algebra facts

**(Finiteness.)** Since $X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$ it is proper. Apply **lemma_45_finite_frob** (eoinm) with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf on $X_k$, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$: for every $n\ge 0$ the space $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

**(Well-definedness of $V_v$.)** Let $v\in H^r$ be homogeneous. Since $F$ preserves the grading, $F^nv$ is homogeneous of degree $r$ for all $n\ge 0$, so $V_v\subseteq H^r$; being a subspace of a finite-dimensional space, $V_v$ is finite-dimensional. It is $F$-stable because $F(F^nv)=F^{n+1}v\in V_v$. Hence $F|_{V_v}$ is an injective, hence bijective, endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $V_v$, and "semisimple" for it is the usual notion: $V_v$ is a semisimple $K[t]$-module with $t$ acting as $F|_{V_v}$.

If $X=\varnothing$ then $H^*=0$, every $V_v=0$, and the identity of the zero space is semisimple; both assertions are then trivial. We may (and need not) assume $X\neq\varnothing$ below; the arguments are valid in either case.

We record three elementary facts.

**(L1) Minimal-polynomial criterion.** For a finite-dimensional $K$-space $U$ and $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(U)$ with minimal polynomial $m_A$, $A$ is semisimple if and only if $m_A$ is a product of pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) If $U$ is a direct sum of simple $K[t]$-submodules $U_j$, the annihilator of $t$ on $U_j$ is a maximal ideal $(p_j)$ with $p_j$ irreducible, so $U_j\simeq K[t]/(p_j)$ and $m_A=\mathrm{lcm}_j(p_j)=\prod_{\text{distinct }p_j}p_j$, squarefree. ($\Leftarrow$) If $m_A=\prod_{i=1}^m p_i$ with the $p_i$ distinct irreducibles, the Chinese remainder theorem gives $K[t]/(m_A)\simeq\prod_{i=1}^m K[t]/(p_i)$, a product of fields. Since $m_A(A)=0$, $U$ is a module over this ring; the orthogonal idempotents $e_i$ give $U=\bigoplus_i e_iU$, and each $e_iU$ is a vector space over the field $K[t]/(p_i)$, hence a direct sum of $1$-dimensional (thus simple, $A$-stable) $K[t]$-subspaces. So $U$ is semisimple. $\square$

**(L2) Inheritance.** If $A$ is semisimple on $U$ and $U'\subseteq U$ is $A$-stable, then $A|_{U'}$ and the operator induced by $A$ on $U/U'$ are semisimple. Indeed $m_{A|_{U'}}\mid m_A$ and $m_{A,U/U'}\mid m_A$ (both make sense exactly because $U'$ is stable), and a divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree; conclude with (L1). $\square$

**(L3) Tensor products.** If $T\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$ and $S\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$ are semisimple with $V,W$ finite-dimensional, then $T\otimes S\in\mathrm{End}_K(V\otimes_K W)$ is semisimple.

*Proof.* By **lemma_5** (eoinm), a finite-dimensional operator is semisimple over $K$ if and only if its scalar extension to $\bar K$ is semisimple, equivalently (as $\bar K$ is algebraically closed) diagonalizable. Applying this to $T$ and $S$, the operators $\bar T=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $\bar V=V\otimes_K\bar K$ and $\bar S=S\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $\bar W$ are diagonalizable. Choose eigenbases $\{e_i\}$, $\{f_j\}$ with $\bar Te_i=\lambda_ie_i$, $\bar Sf_j=\mu_jf_j$. The canonical isomorphism $(V\otimes_KW)\otimes_K\bar K\xrightarrow{\sim}\bar V\otimes_{\bar K}\bar W$ carries $(T\otimes S)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ to $\bar T\otimes\bar S$, and $\{e_i\otimes f_j\}$ is a $\bar K$-basis of $\bar V\otimes_{\bar K}\bar W$ with $(\bar T\otimes\bar S)(e_i\otimes f_j)=\lambda_i\mu_j\,(e_i\otimes f_j)$. Thus $(T\otimes S)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalizable, and by lemma_5 again $T\otimes S$ is semisimple. $\square$

### 1. The unit $1\in H^0$ is Frobenius-semisimple

Let $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ be the structure morphism; it is a morphism of schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ (as $X$ is projective). We show $F(1)=1$.

(a) The base change $f_k:X_k\to(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q)_k=\operatorname{Spec}k$ satisfies $f_k^*(1_{\operatorname{Spec}k})=1_{X_k}$: pullback of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is the constant sheaf, and the adjunction map $\mathbb Q_\ell\to f_{k*}\mathbb Q_\ell$ sends the constant section $1$ to the constant section $1$. Thus the unit of $H^*(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, which is by definition the image of $1\in H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$, is $f_k^*(1)$.

(b) The operator $F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ on $H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ is induced by the $k$-morphism $\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma):\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Pullback of the constant sheaf along it is the constant sheaf, and the induced $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map on global sections $\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ sends the constant function $1$ to the constant function $1$; being $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear it is the identity. Hence $F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}(1)=1$.

(c) By **lemma_214** (eoinm) applied to $f$ and $n=0$, $f_k^*\circ F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}=F_X\circ f_k^*$. Therefore
$$F(1)=F_X\bigl(f_k^*(1)\bigr)=f_k^*\bigl(F_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}(1)\bigr)=f_k^*(1)=1.$$

Consequently $V_1=\langle F^n\cdot 1:n\ge0\rangle_K=K\cdot 1$, and $F|_{V_1}=\mathrm{id}$, whose minimal polynomial is $t-1$, squarefree. By (L1), $1$ is Frobenius-semisimple.

### 2. The cup product of two homogeneous Frobenius-semisimple classes is Frobenius-semisimple

Let $u\in H^r$ and $w\in H^s$ be homogeneous and Frobenius-semisimple. Put
$$V:=V_u\subseteq H^r,\qquad W:=V_w\subseteq H^s,\qquad T:=F|_{V},\qquad S:=F|_{W}.$$
By the finiteness paragraph and the discussion of $V_v$, $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional and $F$-stable, and $T$, $S$ are semisimple by the hypothesis on $u$ and $w$.

**(2a) The image of the restricted cup product is $F$-stable, and the product map intertwines.** Consider the $K$-linear map
$$\mu:V\otimes_K W\longrightarrow H^{r+s},\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto x\cup y,$$
and let $M:=\mathrm{im}(\mu)$, a finite-dimensional subspace of $H^{r+s}$. For a simple tensor, using the multiplicativity of $F$ from the statement,
$$\mu\bigl((T\otimes S)(x\otimes y)\bigr)=\mu(Fx\otimes Fy)=Fx\cup Fy=F(x\cup y)=F\bigl(\mu(x\otimes y)\bigr).$$
Both sides are $K$-linear in the argument of $\mu$, and simple tensors span $V\otimes W$, hence
$$\mu\circ(T\otimes S)=F\circ\mu.\qquad(\ast)$$
It follows that $M$ is $F$-stable: $F(M)=F(\mu(V\otimes W))=\mu((T\otimes S)(V\otimes W))\subseteq\mu(V\otimes W)=M$. Also $\ker\mu$ is $(T\otimes S)$-stable, since $\mu(z)=0\Rightarrow\mu((T\otimes S)z)=F(\mu(z))=0$, and $\mu$ induces an $F$-equivariant isomorphism $(V\otimes W)/\ker\mu\xrightarrow{\sim}M$.

**(2b) $F|_M$ is semisimple.** By (L3), $T\otimes S$ is semisimple on $V\otimes W$. Let $P(t)\in K[t]$ be its minimal polynomial; by (L1), $P$ is squarefree. From $(\ast)$ one gets by induction $\mu\circ(T\otimes S)^n=F^n\circ\mu$ for all $n\ge0$, hence by linearity $\mu\circ P(T\otimes S)=P(F)\circ\mu$. Therefore for $m=\mu(z)\in M$,
$$P(F)(m)=\mu\bigl(P(T\otimes S)z\bigr)=\mu(0)=0,$$
so $P(F|_M)=0$. Thus $m_{F|_M}\mid P$ is squarefree, and by (L1) $F|_M$ is semisimple. (Equivalently: by (L2) applied to the stable subspace $\ker\mu$, the induced operator on $(V\otimes W)/\ker\mu$ is semisimple, and the intertwining isomorphism above transfers this to $M$.)

**(2c) Conclusion.** The class $u\cup w$ is homogeneous of degree $r+s$. For each $n\ge0$, using $(\ast)$-type computation with $F^n$ (which is again multiplicative),
$$F^n(u\cup w)=F^nu\cup F^nw\in M,$$
since $F^nu\in V$ and $F^nw\in W$. Hence $V_{u\cup w}=\langle F^n(u\cup w):n\ge0\rangle_K\subseteq M$. This subspace is $F$-stable, and $F|_M$ is semisimple by (2b); by (L2) applied to the inclusion $V_{u\cup w}\subseteq M$, the operator $F|_{V_{u\cup w}}$ is semisimple. That is exactly the assertion that $u\cup w$ is Frobenius-semisimple.

### 3. End

Step 1 shows the unit of $H^0$ is Frobenius-semisimple, and Step 2 shows the cup product of two homogeneous Frobenius-semisimple classes is Frobenius-semisimple. This is the desired statement. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* Combined, the two parts say the homogeneous Frobenius-semisimple classes together with $0$ form a graded sub-semiring of $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ containing $1$; in particular every class expressible as a polynomial with $\mathbb Q_\ell$-coefficients in cup products of homogeneous algebraic-cycle classes is Frobenius-semisimple.

lemma_generic_fiber_integral.statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(u:X\to Y\) be a dominant morphism of integral varieties over \(k\), let \(K=\kappa(Y)\) be the function field of \(Y\), and let \(W\subset X\) be an integral closed subscheme with function field \(\kappa(W)\). Then \(W_\eta:=W\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K\) is empty if \(W\) does not dominate \(Y\), while if \(W\) dominates \(Y\) it is an integral scheme whose generic point is \(\xi_W\), with function field \(\kappa(W)\) and dimension \(\dim W-\dim Y\); in particular, when \(\dim W=\dim Y\), the scheme \(W_\eta\) is the spectrum of a finite field extension of \(K\) of degree \([\kappa(W):K]\).
lemma_generic_fiber_integral.proof:
## Conventions and setup

A *variety over k* means an integral scheme of finite type over k (separatedness is never used). For an integral scheme $Z$ we write $\xi_Z$ for its generic point and $\kappa(Z):=\kappa(\xi_Z)$ for its function field. Recall the following elementary facts, which we use freely:

(a) An integral scheme is non-empty (it has a generic point), is irreducible and reduced, every non-empty open subset of it is integral with the *same* generic point and the same function field, and every non-empty open subset is dense.

(b) In a scheme, the closure of a point is irreducible; a topological space is $T_0$, so two distinct points have distinct closures. (Proof of $T_0$: given $x\neq y$ in a scheme $T$, take an affine open $U\ni x$; if $y\notin U$ then $U$ separates them; if $y\in U$, write $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $x=\mathfrak p$, $y=\mathfrak q$; some $f$ lies in exactly one of $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q$, and the corresponding $D(f)$ separates them.)

(c) For $U$ open in $T$ and $F\subset U$, one has $\operatorname{cl}_U(F)=\operatorname{cl}_T(F)\cap U$: the inclusion $\subset$ holds because $\operatorname{cl}_T(F)\cap U$ is closed in $U$ and contains $F$; conversely if $u\in\operatorname{cl}_T(F)\cap U$ and $W\subset U$ is open with $u\in W$, then $W$ is open in $T$, so $W\cap F\neq\varnothing$, whence $u\in\operatorname{cl}_U(F)$.

We are given: $u:X\to Y$ a dominant morphism of integral varieties over $k$; $\eta:=\xi_Y$ the generic point of $Y$ and $K=\kappa(Y)=\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}$, with canonical morphism $j:\operatorname{Spec}K\to Y$; and $W\subset X$ an integral closed subscheme with generic point $\xi_W$ and function field $\kappa(W)$. Write $f:=u|_W:W\to Y$. Then $W_\eta:=W\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K$.

---

## Preliminary 1 (points of the base change to the generic point)

**Statement.** Let $f:T\to Y$ be any morphism and $T_\eta:=T\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K$, with projection $\mathrm{pr}_1:T_\eta\to T$. Then $\mathrm{pr}_1$ identifies $|T_\eta|$ homeomorphically with the subspace $f^{-1}(\eta)\subset|T|$, and for $z\in T_\eta$ lying over $t\in f^{-1}(\eta)$ one has $\kappa(z)=\kappa(t)$.

**Proof.** *Affine computation.* Let $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be a non-empty affine open of $Y$ (it contains $\eta$, and $B$ is a domain because $Y$ is integral, with $(0)\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ the point $\eta$; $S^{-1}B=K$ for $S=B\setminus\{0\}$). Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be an affine open of $T$ with $f(U)\subset V$; then $U$ factors through $V$ and
$$U_\eta:=U\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K=U\times_V\operatorname{Spec}K=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_BK)=\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A).$$
Localisation identifies $|\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A)|$ homeomorphically (with the subspace topology) with $\{\mathfrak a\in\operatorname{Spec}A:\mathfrak a\cap S=\varnothing\}$. For such $\mathfrak a$ the contraction $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a\cap B$ satisfies $\mathfrak b\cap S=\varnothing$, i.e. $\mathfrak b\subset B\setminus S=\{0\}$, so $\mathfrak b=(0)$, which is $\eta$; conversely a prime of $A$ lying over $(0)$ is disjoint from $S$. Hence $|U_\eta|$ is exactly $U\cap f^{-1}(\eta)$, mapped homeomorphically. Moreover for $\mathfrak a\in|U_\eta|$ with contraction $\mathfrak a^c\in|U|$,
$$\kappa(\mathfrak a)=\operatorname{Frac}\big((S^{-1}A)/\mathfrak a\big)=\operatorname{Frac}\big(S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak a^c)\big)=\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak a^c)=\kappa(\mathfrak a^c),$$
localising a domain at non-zero elements not changing its fraction field.

*Gluing.* Every $t\in T$ has an affine open neighbourhood $U_t$ with $f(U_t)$ contained in an affine open $V_t$ of $Y$: take any affine open $W_0\ni t$, put $y=f(t)$, choose an affine open $V_t\ni y$, and then an affine open $U_t$ with $t\in U_t\subset W_0\cap f^{-1}(V_t)$. The $U_t$ cover $T$, and since $\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(U_t)=(U_t)_\eta$ (base change), the $(U_t)_\eta$ cover $T_\eta$ (a point of $T_\eta$ maps into some $U_t$). Injectivity of $|\mathrm{pr}_1|$: two points with the same image $t$ lie in $(U_t)_\eta$, where $\mathrm{pr}_1$ is injective. Surjectivity onto $f^{-1}(\eta)$: for $t\in f^{-1}(\eta)$, $t\in U_t$, and $t$ lies in the image of $|(U_t)_\eta|$. Finally a subset $\Omega\subset T_\eta$ is open iff each $\Omega\cap (U_t)_\eta$ is open, iff each $\mathrm{pr}_1(\Omega)\cap(U_t\cap f^{-1}(\eta))$ is open in $U_t\cap f^{-1}(\eta)$, and since the $U_t\cap f^{-1}(\eta)$ form an open cover of $f^{-1}(\eta)$ (subspace topology), this says $\mathrm{pr}_1(\Omega)$ is open in $f^{-1}(\eta)$. So $\mathrm{pr}_1$ is a homeomorphism onto $f^{-1}(\eta)$. The residue-field claim follows from the affine computation. $\dashv$

---

## Preliminary 2 (dimension of an integral scheme of finite type over a field)

**Statement.** If $Z$ is integral and of finite type over a field $\kappa$, then $\dim Z=\operatorname{trdeg}_\kappa\kappa(Z)$.

**Proof.** *Affine case* $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $A$ a finitely generated $\kappa$-domain: by the Noether normalisation lemma there are algebraically independent $y_1,\dots,y_d\in A$ such that $A$ is integral (finite) over $P:=\kappa[y_1,\dots,y_d]$. Then $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ is algebraic over $\operatorname{Frac}(P)=\kappa(y_1,\dots,y_d)$, so $d=\operatorname{trdeg}_\kappa\operatorname{Frac}(A)=\operatorname{trdeg}_\kappa\kappa(Z)$. For an integral extension $P\subset A$ one has $\dim A=\dim P$: lying-over lets every chain of primes of $P$ be lifted to a chain of $A$ (so $\dim A\ge\dim P$), and incomparability (two primes of $A$ with the same contraction to $P$ are equal) makes every chain of primes of $A$ contract to a strictly increasing chain of $P$ (so $\dim A\le\dim P$). Finally $\dim P=d$: the chain $(0)\subsetneq(y_1)\subsetneq(y_1,y_2)\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq(y_1,\dots,y_d)$ gives $\ge d$, and Krull's principal ideal theorem (applied inductively: a prime minimal over $r$ elements has height $\le r$, and every maximal ideal of $P$ is generated by $d$ elements, e.g. by the standard form of the theorem $\dim P\le d$) gives $\le d$.

*General case.* We show $\dim Z=\dim U$ for every non-empty affine open $U\subset Z$. First $\dim U\le\dim Z$: a chain $F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r$ of irreducible closed subsets of $U$ has closures $\operatorname{cl}_ZF_i$ which are irreducible closed in $Z$ and still strict, since $\operatorname{cl}_ZF_i=\operatorname{cl}_ZF_{i+1}=G$ would force $F_i=G\cap U=F_{i+1}$ by (c). Conversely, given a chain $Z_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_r$ in $Z$, choose a non-empty affine open $U$ meeting $Z_0$ (possible: $Z_0\neq\varnothing$ and affine opens form a basis). Then each $Z_i\cap U$ is non-empty (it contains $Z_0\cap U\neq\varnothing$), irreducible and closed in $U$, and the inclusions are strict: $Z_i\cap U=Z_{i+1}\cap U$ would give $Z_i=\operatorname{cl}_Z(Z_i\cap U)=\operatorname{cl}_Z(Z_{i+1}\cap U)=Z_{i+1}$, using that $Z_i\cap U$ is a non-empty open of the irreducible $Z_i$, hence dense. So $r\le\dim U$. Thus $\dim Z=\dim U=\operatorname{trdeg}_\kappa\kappa(U)=\operatorname{trdeg}_\kappa\kappa(Z)$, the middle equality being the affine case and $\kappa(U)=\kappa(Z)$ because $U$ is a non-empty open of the integral $Z$. $\dashv$

---

## Preliminary 3 (zero-dimensional integral schemes of finite type over a field)

**Statement.** Let $T$ be integral, of finite type over a field $K$, with $\dim T=0$. Then $T=\operatorname{Spec}L$ with $L/K$ a finite field extension.

**Proof.** (1) $T\neq\varnothing$ and has a generic point $\xi$ with $\overline{\{\xi\}}=T$.

(2) $|T|=\{\xi\}$. Let $y\in T$ with $y\neq\xi$. Then $\overline{\{y\}}\neq T$: equality would mean $y$ and $\xi$ have the same closure, contradicting $T_0$ (fact (b)). Hence $\overline{\{y\}}\subsetneq\overline{\{\xi\}}=T$ is a chain of two distinct irreducible closed subsets of $T$ (closures of points are irreducible; $T$ is irreducible), so $\dim T\ge1$, contradiction. Thus $y=\xi$.

(3) $T$ is affine: the whole space $T=\{\xi\}$ is an open neighbourhood of $\xi$, and a scheme is covered by affine opens, so $T$ itself is affine, $T=\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $C=\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$. Since $T$ is integral, $C$ is a domain. Since $\operatorname{Spec}C$ has exactly one point, $(0)$ is its only prime ideal, hence its only maximal ideal. If $0\neq a\in C$ were not a unit it would lie in a maximal ideal, and the only maximal ideal is $(0)$, contradiction; so every non-zero element is a unit and $C=L$ is a field.

(4) $T\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ of finite type with $T=\operatorname{Spec}L$ means $L$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra. By **Zariski's lemma** $L/K$ is then finite algebraic; for completeness: write $L=K[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ and induct on $n$. For $n=0$, $L=K$. For $n\ge1$ put $L':=K[a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}]$, a field by induction (it is a $K$-subalgebra of the field $L$ generated by elements... more precisely $L'$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra which is a domain, and by induction applied to the field of fractions argument — instead argue directly: $L'$ is a domain finite type over $K$; since $L$ is algebraic over $L'$ (as $a_n$ is, see below) and $L$ is a field, $L'$ is a field: for $0\ne b\in L'$, $1/b\in L$ is algebraic over $L'$, so $1/b$ satisfies $t^m+c_1t^{m-1}+\dots+c_m=0$ with $c_i\in L'$, $c_m\ne0$, giving $1/b=-(c_m)^{-1}(c_1+\dots+c_{m-1}b^{1-m})\in L'$ — this uses only that $L'/K$ is a domain of finite type and $L$ is a field algebraic over $L'$). Now $L=L'[a_n]$: if $a_n$ were transcendental over $L'$, then $L'[a_n]\cong L'[t]$ is not a field ($1/t\notin L'[t]$), contradicting $L=L'[a_n]$; so $a_n$ is algebraic over $L'$ and $L/L'$ is finite. By induction $L'/K$ is finite, hence $L/K$ is finite. $\dashv$

---

## Step 1: $W_\eta$ is of finite type over $K$

$W$ is a closed subscheme of $X$, which is of finite type over $k$; hence $W$ is of finite type over $k$ (and noetherian). The morphism $f=u|_W$ is a $k$-morphism from a $k$-scheme of finite type to $Y$. To see $f$ is of finite type, let $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be an affine open of $Y$; then $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $W$, hence of finite type over $k$, hence (being noetherian and quasi-compact) a finite union of affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ with each $A_i$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Since $f$ is a $k$-morphism, $k\to A_i$ factors as $k\to B\to A_i$, so $A_i=B[a_1,\dots,a_m]$ is a finitely generated $B$-algebra. Thus $f$ is of finite type. Base change preserves finite type, so $W_\eta=W\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is of finite type.

## Step 2: $W_\eta\neq\varnothing$ if and only if $W$ dominates $Y$

By Preliminary 1, $|W_\eta|\cong f^{-1}(\eta)$, so $W_\eta\neq\varnothing\iff\eta\in f(|W|)$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $\eta\in f(|W|)$ then $Y=\overline{\{\eta\}}\subset\overline{f(|W|)}$, so $f$ is dominant, i.e. $W$ dominates $Y$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $f$ dominant. Since $W$ is integral it is non-empty; pick $t_0\in W$ and, as in Preliminary 1, a non-empty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\ni t_0$ with $f(U)\subset V:=\operatorname{Spec}B$ for some affine open $V\subset Y$. As $U$ is a non-empty open of the irreducible $W$, $U$ is dense in $W$, so by continuity $f(U)$ is dense in $f(W)$ (indeed $f(W)=f(\overline{\{U\}})\subset\overline{f(U)}$), hence dense in $Y$; since $f(U)\subset V$ and $V$ is open, $\overline{f(U)}\cap V=V$, so $U\to V$ has dense image. The closure of the image of $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}B$ is $V(\ker(B\to A))$, so $\ker(B\to A)\subset\operatorname{nil}(B)=(0)$; thus $B\to A$ is injective. With $S=B\setminus\{0\}$, its image in $A$ avoids $0$, so $S^{-1}A$ is a localisation of the domain $A$ at a set not containing $0$: it is a non-zero domain. Hence $U_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A)\neq\varnothing$, and its points map to $\eta$, so $W_\eta\neq\varnothing$. $\dashv$

In particular, if $W$ does **not** dominate $Y$, then $W_\eta=\varnothing$, which is the first claim of the lemma.

## Step 3: in the dominating case $W_\eta$ is integral, with generic point $\xi_W$ and function field $\kappa(W)$

Assume $W$ dominates $Y$.

*(The affine opens of $W_\eta$.)* Consider the family $\mathcal U$ of pairs $(U,V)$ with $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset W$ a non-empty affine open and $V=\operatorname{Spec}B\subset Y$ an affine open with $f(U)\subset V$. Such $U$ cover $W$ (argument at the end of Preliminary 1), so the $U_\eta:=U\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}K$ cover $W_\eta$ (since $\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(U)=U_\eta$). Each $U\in\mathcal U$ is a non-empty open of the irreducible $W$, hence dense, and the argument of Step 2 ($\Leftarrow$) applies verbatim: $B\to A$ is injective and
$$U_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A),\qquad S=B\setminus\{0\}\subset A\setminus\{0\},$$
with $S^{-1}A$ a non-zero domain. So every $U_\eta$ is a **non-empty integral affine** open of $W_\eta$.

*(A common generic point.)* Since $f$ is dominant, $f(\xi_W)=\eta$: indeed $f(W)\subset\overline{\{f(\xi_W)\}}$ (because $W=\overline{\{\xi_W\}}$ and $f$ is continuous), so $\overline{\{f(\xi_W)\}}\supset\overline{f(W)}=Y$, and $\eta$ is the unique point of the irreducible $Y$ with closure $Y$. Thus $\xi_W\in f^{-1}(\eta)=|W_\eta|$; let $\xi_\eta$ be the corresponding point of $W_\eta$ (unique by Preliminary 1). For each $U\in\mathcal U$, $\xi_W\in U$ (non-empty open of irreducible $W$), so $\xi_\eta\in U_\eta$, and under $|U_\eta|\xrightarrow{\sim}U\cap f^{-1}(\eta)$ the generic point of $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}A)$, namely $(0)$, maps to $(0)\in\operatorname{Spec}A=\xi_U=\xi_W$. Hence $\xi_\eta$ is the generic point of every $U_\eta$.

*(Irreducible.)* Let $\Omega\subset W_\eta$ be a non-empty open. Some $U_\eta$ meets $\Omega$ (else $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $U_\eta$ covering $W_\eta$), and $\Omega\cap U_\eta$ is a non-empty open of the irreducible $U_\eta$, so it contains $\xi_\eta$. Thus every non-empty open of $W_\eta$ contains $\xi_\eta$; any two non-empty opens therefore intersect, so $W_\eta$ is irreducible, and $\overline{\{\xi_\eta\}}=W_\eta$ (otherwise $W_\eta\setminus\overline{\{\xi_\eta\}}$ is a non-empty open not containing $\xi_\eta$), i.e. $\xi_\eta$ is the generic point of $W_\eta$. Under the homeomorphism of Preliminary 1 this generic point *is* the point $\xi_W$ of $W$.

*(Reduced and the function field.)* Being reduced is local on any open cover, and each $U_\eta$ is reduced (a domain), so $W_\eta$ is reduced. Hence $W_\eta$ is integral. Its function field is the residue field at its generic point, and Preliminary 1 gives $\kappa(\xi_\eta)=\kappa(\xi_W)$, so $\kappa(W_\eta)=\kappa(W)$.

## Step 4: $\dim W_\eta=\dim W-\dim Y$

By Step 1 and Step 3, $W_\eta$ is integral of finite type over $K$, so by Preliminary 2 and Step 3
$$\dim W_\eta=\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(W_\eta)=\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(W).$$
Dominance of $f:W\to Y$ makes the pullback $K=\kappa(Y)\hookrightarrow\kappa(W)$ an injective homomorphism of fields. For the tower $k\subset K\subset\kappa(W)$ the transcendence degrees add: if $S_1$ is a transcendence basis of $K/k$ and $S_2$ a transcendence basis of $\kappa(W)/K$, then $S_1\cup S_2$ is algebraically independent over $k$ (an algebraic relation over $k$ among elements of $S_2$ with coefficients in $k(S_1)$ would give one over $K$) and $\kappa(W)$ is algebraic over $k(S_1\cup S_2)$ (transitivity of algebraicity), hence
$$\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)=\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(W)+\operatorname{trdeg}_k K.$$
Applying Preliminary 2 to the integral $k$-schemes of finite type $W$ and $Y$ gives $\dim W=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)$ and $\dim Y=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)=\operatorname{trdeg}_kK$. Substituting,
$$\dim W_\eta=\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(W)=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)-\operatorname{trdeg}_kK=\dim W-\dim Y,$$
as claimed (this also shows $\dim W\ge\dim Y$ in the dominating case).

## Step 5: the case $\dim W=\dim Y$

Assume now that $W$ dominates $Y$ and $\dim W=\dim Y$. Then Step 4 gives $\dim W_\eta=0$; by Steps 1 and 3, $W_\eta$ is integral and of finite type over the field $K$. Preliminary 3 therefore applies: $W_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}L$ with $L/K$ a finite field extension. Since $\operatorname{Spec}L$ has one point, its function field is $L$ itself, and Step 3 identifies it with $\kappa(W)$. Hence $W_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(W)$ with $[\kappa(W):K]=[L:K]<\infty$, which is exactly the last clause. (The dominance hypothesis is genuinely needed here: if $W$ does not dominate $Y$ then $W_\eta=\varnothing$ by Step 2, and the empty scheme is not the spectrum of a field; in the statement the "in particular" sits inside the dominating branch.)

## Conclusion

Steps 2, 3, 4 and 5 establish, respectively: $W_\eta=\varnothing$ when $W$ does not dominate $Y$; $W_\eta$ integral with generic point $\xi_W$ and function field $\kappa(W)$ when it does; $\dim W_\eta=\dim W-\dim Y$; and $W_\eta=\operatorname{Spec}L$ for a finite field extension $L/K$ of degree $[\kappa(W):K]$ when moreover $\dim W=\dim Y$. This is precisely the stated lemma. No result from the list of previously proved lemmas (all of which concern $\ell$-adic cohomology) is required.

lemma_222.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\pi_A:A\to A\) be its \(q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(V_\ell(A_k)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A_k)\) with \(T_\ell(A_k)=\varprojlim_m A[\ell^m](k)\), the inverse system taken with bonding maps multiplication by \(\ell\). Then the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A\) of \(V_\ell(A_k)\) is semisimple.
lemma_222.proof:
We write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$; this is algebraically closed of characteristic $p$, and $\ell\neq p$. For an abelian variety $G$ over $\mathbb F_q$ we write $G_k=G\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$ and $T_\ell(G):=\varprojlim_m G[\ell^m](k)$ (bonding maps $x\mapsto \ell x$), $V_\ell(G):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(G)$; thus $V_\ell(G)=V_\ell(G_k)$ as in the statement. Note $\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ is also an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_q$ in the sense of the lemmas we cite.

**Step 0: Functoriality of $V_\ell$.** Let $f:G\to H$ be a homomorphism of abelian varieties over $\mathbb F_q$. Since $\ell^m f(x)=f(\ell^m x)$, $f$ carries $G[\ell^m](k)$ into $H[\ell^m](k)$, and this is compatible with the bonding maps because $f(\ell x)=\ell f(x)$. Hence $f$ induces a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear map $T_\ell(f):T_\ell(G)\to T_\ell(H)$, and we set $V_\ell(f):=\mathrm{id}\otimes T_\ell(f)\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_\ell(G),V_\ell(H))$. From the definitions, $V_\ell(\mathrm{id}_G)=\mathrm{id}$ and $V_\ell(g\circ f)=V_\ell(g)\circ V_\ell(f)$. Moreover the group law on each $G[\ell^m](k)$ is the one inherited from $H$, so for homomorphisms $f,g:G\to H$ one has $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ pointwise, hence $T_\ell(f+g)=T_\ell(f)+T_\ell(g)$ and $V_\ell(f+g)=V_\ell(f)+V_\ell(g)$. In particular, with $f=\pi_A$, the operator whose semisimplicity is asserted in the statement is exactly $V_\ell(\pi_A)$: the symbol $\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ means $\mathrm{id}\otimes T_\ell(\pi_A)=V_\ell(\pi_A)$.

**Step 1: The zero-dimensional case.** If $\dim A=0$ then $A$ is the trivial group scheme over $\mathbb F_q$, so $A[\ell^m](k)=0$ for all $m$, $T_\ell(A_k)=0$, $V_\ell(A_k)=0$, and $\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A=\mathrm{id}_{0}$, which is semisimple (its minimal polynomial is $1$, which is squarefree; equivalently the zero space is the direct sum of the empty family of eigenspaces). Henceforth assume $\dim A\ge 1$.

**Step 2: Finite-dimensionality and invertibility.** Since $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $p$ and $\ell\neq p$, lemma_tate_rank (applied over $k$ to $A_k$ and to the factors constructed below) gives that $T_\ell(A_k)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2\dim A$, so $V_\ell(A_k)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space of dimension $2\dim A$.

The $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi_A:A\to A$ is an isogeny: the absolute Frobenius of a scheme of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ is a finite universal homeomorphism (it is integral, since every local section $s$ satisfies $s^{q^b}\in\mathbb F_q\cdot s$-type relations, i.e. is a root of $T^{q}-T$-type equations over the prime field; concretely on an affine $\mathbb F_q$-algebra $R$, $R$ is generated over $R^q$ by the roots of $T^q-r$, so $\mathrm{Frob}$ is finite), hence surjective with finite kernel, and it is a group homomorphism because the addition map $m:A\times A\to A$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism and $\mathrm{Frob}$ is natural for such morphisms. Therefore lemma_120, applied to the isogeny $\pi_A:A\to A$ over the field $\mathbb F_q$ (where $\ell$ is invertible), shows that $V_\ell(\pi_A)=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $V_\ell(A_k)$.

**Step 3: Poincaré complete reducibility over $\mathbb F_q$.** Apply lemma_poincare_reducibility with the base field equal to $\mathbb F_q$ and the abelian variety $A$. It yields an integer $r\ge 1$ and abelian $\mathbb F_q$-subvariets $B_1,\dots,B_r\subseteq A$, each simple over $\mathbb F_q$ (no nonzero proper abelian $\mathbb F_q$-subvariety), such that the addition homomorphism
$$\mu:B:=B_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}B_r\longrightarrow A,\qquad (b_1,\dots,b_r)\longmapsto \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^r b_i,$$
is an isogeny over $\mathbb F_q$. By lemma_120 applied to the isogeny $\mu$, the map $V_\ell(\mu):V_\ell(B)\to V_\ell(A)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism; and by lemma_tate_rank each $V_\ell(B_i)$ and $V_\ell(B)$ is finite-dimensional.

**Step 4: Identifying $V_\ell(B)$ with $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(B_i)$.** Let $\mathrm{pr}_i:B\to B_i$ be the projection and $\sigma_i:B_i\to B$, $x\mapsto(0,\dots,x,\dots,0)$, the inclusion into the $i$-th factor; both are homomorphisms over $\mathbb F_q$. In the category of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes, $B$ is the product of the $B_i$, so a homomorphism into $B$ is determined by its composites with the $\mathrm{pr}_i$. Since $\mathrm{pr}_j\circ\sigma_i=\mathrm{id}_{B_i}$ if $i=j$ and $=0$ otherwise, we get $\mathrm{pr}_j\circ\big(\sum_i\sigma_i\circ\mathrm{pr}_i\big)=\sum_i(\mathrm{pr}_j\sigma_i)\mathrm{pr}_i=\mathrm{pr}_j$ for every $j$, hence $\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i\circ\mathrm{pr}_i=\mathrm{id}_B$. Define
$$\alpha:V_\ell(B)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(B_i),\quad v\mapsto\big(V_\ell(\mathrm{pr}_i)v\big)_{i},\qquad \beta\big((w_i)_i\big)=\textstyle\sum_i V_\ell(\sigma_i)w_i.$$
Using the functoriality and additivity from Step 0: $\alpha\beta((w_i))$ has $j$-th component $\sum_i V_\ell(\mathrm{pr}_j\sigma_i)w_i=V_\ell(\mathrm{id})w_j=w_j$, and $\beta\alpha(v)=\sum_i V_\ell(\sigma_i\mathrm{pr}_i)v=V_\ell(\mathrm{id}_B)v=v$. So $\alpha$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism with inverse $\beta$.

**Step 5: Frobenius on the product, and its transport.** For a scheme $Z$ of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism over $\mathbb F_q$ coincides with the absolute Frobenius $\mathrm{Frob}_Z$: the structure morphism $Z\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ satisfies $\mathrm{Frob}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q}=\mathrm{id}$ because $c^q=c$ for all $c\in\mathbb F_q$, so $\mathrm{Frob}_Z$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, and on $\mathbb F_q$-algebras it is exactly $u\mapsto u^q$. Absolute Frobenius is natural for morphisms of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes: if $f:X\to Y$ is such a morphism then $f\circ\mathrm{Frob}_X=\mathrm{Frob}_Y\circ f$, because both sides are the identity on underlying topological spaces and on sections over $V\subseteq Y$ both send $s$ to $f^\sharp(s)^q$ (using $f^\sharp(s^q)=f^\sharp(s)^q$). Applying this to the projections $\mathrm{pr}_i:B\to B_i$ gives $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ\mathrm{Frob}_B=\mathrm{Frob}_{B_i}\circ\mathrm{pr}_i$, i.e. $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ\pi_B=\pi_{B_i}\circ\mathrm{pr}_i$ where $\pi_B,\pi_{B_i}$ are the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphisms; by the universal property of the product this says $\pi_B=\pi_{B_1}\times\cdots\times\pi_{B_r}$. Applying the naturality to the $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $\mu$ gives
$$\mu\circ\pi_B=\pi_A\circ\mu .$$
Applying $V_\ell$ (functoriality, Step 0) yields the intertwining relation
$$V_\ell(\mu)\circ V_\ell(\pi_B)=V_\ell(\pi_A)\circ V_\ell(\mu).\tag{5.1}$$
Moreover, under the isomorphism $\alpha$ of Step 4, the operator $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is carried to the block-diagonal operator $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$: indeed the $i$-th component of $\alpha\big(V_\ell(\pi_B)v\big)$ is $V_\ell(\mathrm{pr}_i)V_\ell(\pi_B)v=V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})V_\ell(\mathrm{pr}_i)v$. Equivalently,
$$\alpha\circ V_\ell(\pi_B)\circ\alpha^{-1}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(\pi_{B_i}).\tag{5.2}$$
Each $\pi_{B_i}:B_i\to B_i$ is an isogeny (Step 2 applies verbatim), so by lemma_120 each $V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ is invertible; likewise $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is invertible.

**Step 6: The simple case.** Fix $i$. The abelian variety $B_i$ is simple over $\mathbb F_q$, and $\pi_{B_i}\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb F_q}(B_i)$ is its $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism. Apply lemma_92 with $m=1$ (so that $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q$) and $B=B_i$, $\pi=\pi_{B_i}$: it states that the minimal polynomial of $\pi_{B_i}$ on $V_\ell(B_i)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(B_i)$ is squarefree in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, equivalently that $\pi_{B_i}$ acts semisimply on $V_\ell(B_i)$. Thus each $V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ is a semisimple $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of the finite-dimensional space $V_\ell(B_i)$.

**Step 7: Assembling the direct sum.** The spaces $V_\ell(B_1),\dots,V_\ell(B_r)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (lemma_tate_rank) and the operators $V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ are invertible (Step 5) and semisimple (Step 6). By lemma_9, the direct-sum operator $\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ on $\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(B_i)$ is semisimple. By (5.2) and the fact that semisimplicity is preserved under transport by a linear isomorphism (conjugate operators have the same minimal polynomial), $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(B)$.

**Step 8: Conclusion.** We apply lemma_8 with $V=V_\ell(B)$, $W=V_\ell(A_k)$, $T_V=V_\ell(\pi_B)$, $T_W=V_\ell(\pi_A)=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ and $\alpha=V_\ell(\mu)$. Its hypotheses are satisfied: $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces (Step 2 and lemma_tate_rank), $T_V$ and $T_W$ are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators (Step 2, lemma_120), $\alpha$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism (Step 3), and $\alpha\circ T_V=T_W\circ\alpha$ by (5.1). Since $T_V$ is semisimple by Step 7, lemma_8 gives that $T_W=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(A_k)$. Together with Step 1 this covers all cases, and the proof is complete. $\blacksquare$

(Remark, not used above: since $\pi_A$ is invertible on $V_\ell(A_k)$ and semisimplicity is preserved under taking inverses, the same argument gives semisimplicity of the geometric Frobenius $\pi_A^{-1}$ on $V_\ell(A_k)$.)

lemma_225.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, and let \(T_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\) be automorphisms whose base changes to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) are diagonalizable. Then the tensor product automorphism \(T_V\otimes T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W)\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_225.proof:
Write $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $L=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; $L$ is an algebraically closed field containing $K$. For a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $U$ and $S\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ write $U_L:=U\otimes_K L$ and $S_L:=S\otimes \mathrm{id}_L\in\mathrm{GL}(U_L)$. The hypothesis is that $T_{V,L}$ and $T_{W,L}$ are diagonalizable $L$-linear automorphisms, and the conclusion is that $(T_V\otimes T_W)_L\in\mathrm{GL}((V\otimes_K W)_L)$ is diagonalizable.

**Step 0 (degenerate case).** If $\dim_K V=0$ or $\dim_K W=0$ then $V\otimes_K W=0$, and $\mathrm{GL}(0)$ is the trivial group; the unique operator on the zero space is diagonalizable (the empty set is a basis, hence a basis of eigenvectors). There is nothing to prove. In the sequel assume $\dim_K V=m\ge 1$ and $\dim_K W=n\ge 1$.

**Step 1 (extension of scalars commutes with tensor products).** There is a canonical $L$-linear isomorphism
$$\Phi:(V\otimes_K W)\otimes_K L\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\; (V\otimes_K L)\otimes_L (W\otimes_K L)=V_L\otimes_L W_L,\qquad \Phi\big((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\big)=(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1),$$
with inverse
$$\Psi\big((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes\mu)\big)=(v\otimes w)\otimes_K(\lambda\mu).$$
Construction and verification of well-definedness:

(a) *Definition of $\Phi$.* The map $V\times W\times L\to V_L\otimes_L W_L$, $(v,w,\lambda)\mapsto (v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1)$ is $K$-trilinear: additivity in each slot is immediate, and for $a\in K$ one has $(av\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1)=(v\otimes a\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1)$ and $(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(aw\otimes 1)=(v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes a\cdot 1)$, where in the second identity we used $aw\otimes 1 = w\otimes a$ in $W\otimes_K L$ and then $L$-balancedness of $\otimes_L$ (moving the scalar $a\in L$ from the left factor to the right factor). Hence it factors through a $K$-linear map $(V\otimes_K W)\otimes_K L\to V_L\otimes_L W_L$, which is in fact $L$-linear when $L$ acts on the source on the last factor and on the target through the first factor, because
$$\Phi\big((v\otimes w)\otimes(a\lambda)\big)=(v\otimes a\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1)=a\cdot\big((v\otimes\lambda)\otimes_L(w\otimes 1)\big)=a\,\Phi\big((v\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\big).$$

(b) *Definition of $\Psi$.* First consider the $K$-quadrilinear map $V\times L\times W\times L\to (V\otimes_K W)\otimes_K L$, $(v,\lambda,w,\mu)\mapsto (v\otimes w)\otimes_K\lambda\mu$; $K$-bilinearity in the pair $(v,\lambda)$ (resp. $(w,\mu)$) holds since $(av\otimes w)\otimes\lambda\mu=(v\otimes w)\otimes a\lambda\mu=(v\otimes aw)\otimes\lambda\mu$. It therefore descends to a $K$-linear map $\overline\Psi:(V\otimes_K L)\otimes_K(W\otimes_K L)\to (V\otimes_K W)\otimes_K L$.
