**Step 5 (the minimal polynomial of $T$ is squarefree).** For $P\in K[X]$, we claim
$$P(T)=0\text{ on }V\iff P(T_i)=0\text{ on }U_i\ \text{ for all }i.\tag{5.1}$$
The forward implication is restriction. Conversely, if each $P(T_i)=0$, then $P(T)$ annihilates each $U_i$ (as $U_i$ is $T$-stable, $P(T)|_{U_i}=P(T_i)$), and since $V=U_1+\cdots+U_r$ (the $v_i$ span $V$) every $v\in V$ is a sum $v=\sum_i u_i$ with $u_i\in U_i$, whence $P(T)v=\sum_i P(T)u_i=0$.

Let $M\in K[X]$ be the least common multiple of $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$ (a monic polynomial, well defined since $r\ge 1$). By construction $\mu_i\mid M$ for all $i$, so $M(T_i)=0$ for all $i$, and (5.1) gives $M(T)=0$. Hence the minimal polynomial $\mu_T$ of $T$ divides $M$ (again by the division-algorithm argument used in Step 2). Finally, each $\mu_i$ is a product of distinct monic irreducibles by (4.1), say $\mu_i=\prod_{f\in F_i}f$ with $F_i$ a finite set of monic irreducibles without repetition; then $M=\prod_{f\in\bigcup_iF_i}f$ is likewise a product of distinct monic irreducibles, i.e. squarefree. A monic divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree (its irreducible factorisation uses the same irreducibles with exponents $\le 1$). Therefore
$$\mu_T\ \text{is squarefree in }K[X].\tag{5.2}$$

**Step 6 (squarefree minimal polynomial $\Rightarrow$ diagonalisable after base change).** Assume (5.2) and prove that $T_\Omega=T\otimes 1\in\mathrm{End}_\Omega(V_\Omega)$ is diagonalisable. Write
$$\mu_T=\prod_{j=1}^{s}f_j\qquad(s\ge 1)$$
with the $f_j\in K[X]$ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles ($s\ge1$ because $V\neq0$, so $\mu_T$ is nonconstant).

*(6a) Each $f_j$ splits over $\Omega$ into distinct linear factors.* Since $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$, $f_j'\neq 0$; if $\deg f_j=1$ then $f_j'=1$ and trivially $\gcd(f_j,f_j')=1$. If $\deg f_j\ge2$, then $\deg f_j'=\deg f_j-1<\deg f_j$, so any common divisor of $f_j$ and $f_j'$ has degree $<\deg f_j$ and cannot be an associate of the irreducible $f_j$; hence $\gcd(f_j,f_j')=1$, and B\'ezout gives $u,v\in K[X]$ with $uf_j+vf_j'=1$. If $f_j$ had a repeated root $\beta\in\Omega$, then $f_j=(X-\beta)^2g$ in $\Omega[X]$ and $f_j'=2(X-\beta)g+(X-\beta)^2g'$, so $X-\beta$ would divide both $f_j$ and $f_j'$ in $\Omega[X]$, contradicting the B\'ezout identity (viewed in $\Omega[X]$). Thus all roots of $f_j$ in $\Omega$ are simple, and since $\Omega$ is algebraically closed, $f_j=\prod_{l}(X-\beta_{jl})$ with the $\beta_{jl}$ pairwise distinct.

*(6b) The root sets are disjoint for different $j$.* For $j\neq k$, $\gcd(f_j,f_k)=1$ in $K[X]$ (distinct monic irreducibles), so $af_j+bf_k=1$ with $a,b\in K[X]$; the same identity in $\Omega[X]$ shows $f_j,f_k$ have no common root in $\Omega$.

Combining (6a) and (6b), the image $\bar\mu\in\Omega[X]$ of $\mu_T$ factors as
$$\bar\mu=\prod_{i=1}^{t}(X-\lambda_i)\qquad\text{in }\Omega[X],\tag{6.1}$$
with the $\lambda_i\in\Omega$ pairwise distinct and $t=\deg\mu_T\ge1$. (No statement is made about the minimal polynomial of $T_\Omega$; only the polynomial $\bar\mu$ is used.)

*(6c) $\bar\mu$ annihilates $T_\Omega$.* Writing $\mu_T=\sum_j a_jX^j$ with $a_j\in K$, we have $\bar\mu(T_\Omega)=\sum_ja_j(T\otimes1)^j=\sum_ja_j(T^j\otimes1)=(\sum_ja_jT^j)\otimes1=\mu_T(T)\otimes1=0$.

*(6d) Primary decomposition.* Let $S:=\Omega[X]/(\bar\mu)$ and let $\mathrm{ev}:\Omega[X]\to\mathrm{End}_\Omega(V_\Omega)$, $P\mapsto P(T_\Omega)$, the $\Omega$-algebra homomorphism; by (6c), $(\bar\mu)\subseteq\ker\mathrm{ev}$, so $\mathrm{ev}$ factors through $S$.

In $S$, the principal ideals generated by the classes of $X-\lambda_i$ are pairwise comaximal, because $(X-\lambda_i)-(X-\lambda_k)=\lambda_k-\lambda_i\in\Omega^{\times}$, and their product is $0$ in $S$ by (6.1). By the Chinese remainder theorem (proved by induction from the comaximality: $I\cap J=IJ$ and $R/(IJ)\simeq R/I\times R/J$ for comaximal ideals $I,J$),
$$S\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \prod_{i=1}^{t}\Omega[X]/(X-\lambda_i).$$
Let $\varepsilon_i\in S$ be the element mapping to $(0,\dots,0,1,0,\dots,0)$ and choose a lift $e_i\in\Omega[X]$. In $S$ one has $\sum_i\varepsilon_i=1$, $\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_k=0$ for $i\neq k$, $\varepsilon_i^2=\varepsilon_i$, and $(X-\lambda_i)\varepsilon_i=0$ (in the $i$-th coordinate $X=\lambda_i$, and in every other coordinate $\varepsilon_i=0$). Applying the factored homomorphism $S\to\mathrm{End}_\Omega(V_\Omega)$ and writing $p_i:=e_i(T_\Omega)$, we obtain endomorphisms $p_i$ of $V_\Omega$ with
$$\textstyle\sum_i p_i=\mathrm{id},\qquad p_ip_k=0\ (i\neq k),\qquad p_i^2=p_i,\qquad (T_\Omega-\lambda_i\,\mathrm{id})\,p_i=0.\tag{6.2}$$

*(6e) Conclusion of Step 6.* Set $W_i:=\mathrm{im}\,p_i\subseteq V_\Omega$. By the first relation in (6.2), $V_\Omega=\sum_iW_i$. The sum is direct: if $0=\sum_iw_i$ with $w_i=p_iv_i$, applying $p_j$ and using the second and third relations gives $0=p_j(\sum_iw_i)=\sum_ip_jp_iv_i=p_j^2v_j=w_j$. By the fourth relation, $T_\Omega$ acts on $W_i$ as the scalar $\lambda_i$: for $w=p_iv$, $T_\Omega w=T_\Omega p_iv=\lambda_ip_iv=\lambda_iw$. Hence every nonzero vector of $W_i$ is an eigenvector of $T_\Omega$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, and any $\Omega$-basis of $W_i$ consists of eigenvectors. Taking a basis of each $W_i$ (finitely many, $V_\Omega$ finite-dimensional), their union is an $\Omega$-basis of $V_\Omega$ consisting of eigenvectors of $T_\Omega$. Thus $T_\Omega$ is diagonalisable.

**Step 7 (conclusion).** By Step 6, $T\otimes1$ is diagonalisable on $V\otimes_K\Omega$. Lemma_5 (with $V$, $T$ as here) states that a $K$-linear operator on a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space is semisimple if and only if its base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable. Applying the "if" direction, $T$ is semisimple on $V$. Together with Step 0 this covers all cases, and the proof is complete.

**Remark.** The hypothesis $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ was used nowhere: the argument only needs $T\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$. The role of $c\in K^{\times}$ is to make $X^{m}-c$ squarefree (Step 3), which fails for $c=0$, where $X^m$ is not squarefree for $m\ge2$ — matching the fact that non-semisimple unipotent-type operators are exactly the obstruction.

lemma_230.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\). Let \(V_1,\dots,V_m\) be \(T\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspaces of \(V\) whose sum is all of \(V\). If the restriction \(T|_{V_j}\) is semisimple for every \(j=1,\dots,m\), then \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\).
lemma_230.proof:
Write $k=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\bar k=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; both have characteristic $0$. We use the standard notion: $T$ is *semisimple* on $V$ when $V$ is a sum of $T$-stable irreducible subspaces (irreducible = minimal among nonzero $T$-stable subspaces). Step 1 below shows this is equivalent to the minimal polynomial of $T$ being square-free, to $T_{\bar k}$ being diagonalisable, and to the complement property, so the argument works verbatim with any of these usual definitions.

STEP 0 (reductions). If $V=\{0\}$ then $T$ is trivially semisimple, so assume $V\neq 0$. Discard any $V_j=\{0\}$; the remaining subspaces (still denoted $V_1,\dots,V_r$, $r\ge 1$) are $T$-stable, nonzero, finite-dimensional over $k$, and $V=V_1+\cdots+V_r$. Write $T_j=T|_{V_j}\in\mathrm{End}_k(V_j)$ and $m_j\in k[t]$ for its (monic) minimal polynomial; $m_j\neq 1$ since $V_j\neq 0$. Note that nowhere do we use invertibility of $T$; only $T$-stability of the $V_j$ and that they span $V$.

STEP 1 (four linear-algebra facts).

1.1 (square-free $\Leftrightarrow$ derivative criterion, in characteristic $0$). Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $0\neq g\in F[t]$, with factorisation $g=u\prod_{a=1}^{r}q_a^{e_a}$, $u\in F^{*}$, the $q_a$ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles and $e_a\ge 1$. Then $g$ is square-free (all $e_a=1$) if and only if $\gcd(g,g')=1$ in $F[t]$.
Proof. By the product rule applied to $\prod_a q_a^{e_a}$, differentiating one factor at a time,
$$g'=u\sum_{b=1}^{r}\Big(e_b\,q_b^{\,e_b-1}\,q_b'\prod_{c\neq b}q_c^{\,e_c}\Big),\qquad(\ast)$$
i.e. the $b$-th summand is the derivative $e_bq_b^{e_b-1}q_b'$ of the $b$-th factor times the product of all the *other* factors $q_c^{e_c}$ ($c\neq b$).
If some $e_a\ge 2$: the $b=a$ summand of $(\ast)$ is divisible by $q_a^{e_a-1}$, hence by $q_a$ (as $e_a-1\ge 1$); each summand with $b\neq a$ contains the factor $q_a^{e_a}$, hence is also divisible by $q_a$. Thus $q_a\mid g'$, and since $q_a\mid g$ we get $\gcd(g,g')\neq 1$.
Conversely suppose all $e_a=1$, so $g=u\prod_c q_c$ and $(\ast)$ reads $g'=u\sum_b q_b'\prod_{c\neq b}q_c$. Fix $a$ and reduce modulo $q_a$: every summand with $b\neq a$ contains the factor $q_a$ and vanishes, while the $b=a$ summand becomes $q_a'\prod_{c\neq a}q_c$. Now $\deg q_a\ge 1$ (irreducibles are nonconstant), and since $\operatorname{char}F=0$ the integer $\deg q_a$ is nonzero in $F$, so the leading term $q_a=\alpha t^{d}+\cdots$ ($\alpha\neq 0$, $d=\deg q_a\ge 1$) differentiates to $q_a'=d\alpha t^{d-1}+\cdots\neq 0$ of degree $d-1<d$; hence $q_a\nmid q_a'$ (every nonzero multiple of $q_a$ has degree $\ge d$). Each $q_c$ with $c\neq a$ is irreducible and not associate to $q_a$, so $q_a\nmid q_c$. Since $q_a$ is irreducible in the UFD $F[t]$, the ideal $(q_a)$ is prime and $F[t]/(q_a)$ is a domain; therefore $q_a$ divides neither $q_a'$ nor any $q_c$ nor their product, so $q_a\nmid g'$. As $a$ was arbitrary, no irreducible factor of $g$ divides $g'$. Any common divisor of $g$ and $g'$ of positive degree would have an irreducible factor dividing $g$, contradiction; hence $\gcd(g,g')=1$. $\square$

1.2 (gcd's are unchanged by extending the field). Let $F\subseteq\Omega$ be fields and $f,g\in F[t]$ not both zero. Then the monic gcd of $f,g$ computed in $F[t]$ equals the monic gcd computed in $\Omega[t]$.
Proof. If $g=0$ (or $f=0$) the monic gcd in both rings is the monic associate of the other polynomial, so assume both nonzero. Run the Euclidean algorithm in $F[t]$: $r_{-1}=f$, $r_0=g$ (after swapping, $\deg r_{-1}\ge\deg r_0$, which is a statement about degrees, the same in both rings), and $r_{i-1}=q_{i+1}r_i+r_{i+1}$ with $r_{i+1}=0$ or $\deg r_{i+1}<\deg r_i$; the algorithm terminates because the degrees strictly decrease. At each step the pair $(q,r)$ is *uniquely determined* by $r_{i-1}=qr+r_{i+1}$, $\deg r_{i+1}<\deg r_i$, and since the leading coefficient of $r_i$ lies in $F^{*}$ the long division producing $q,r$ uses only arithmetic in $F$. The pair computed in $F[t]$ is therefore also a valid quotient/remainder pair in $\Omega[t]$, where it is again unique; so the sequence of remainders in $\Omega[t]$ starting from the same inputs is identical, terminates at the same step, and its last nonzero remainder, made monic, is the same polynomial in both rings. That polynomial is the monic gcd in each ring. $\square$

1.3 (square-freeness is preserved and reflected by field extension, char $0$). Let $F\subseteq\Omega$ be fields of characteristic $0$ and $0\neq g\in F[t]$. Then $g$ is square-free in $F[t]$ if and only if it is square-free in $\Omega[t]$.
Proof. The formal derivative of $g$ is computed coefficientwise, so it is the same polynomial whether regarded in $F[t]$ or $\Omega[t]$. By 1.1 applied over $F$, $g$ is square-free in $F[t]$ iff $\gcd_{F[t]}(g,g')=1$; by 1.2 these gcds agree; and by 1.1 applied over $\Omega$, $\gcd_{\Omega[t]}(g,g')=1$ iff $g$ is square-free in $\Omega[t]$. Chaining gives the claim. $\square$

1.4 (minimal polynomial is unchanged by extension of scalars). Let $F\subseteq\Omega$ be fields, $W$ a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space, $S\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)$, and $S_\Omega=\mathrm{id}_\Omega\otimes S\in\mathrm{End}_\Omega(\Omega\otimes_F W)$. Then $m_{S_\Omega}=m_S$.
Proof. Identify $\Omega\otimes_F W$ with the scalar-extended space and $w\otimes 1$ with $1\otimes w$. First, $m_S(S_\Omega)=\mathrm{id}_\Omega\otimes m_S(S)=0$, so $m_{S_\Omega}\mid m_S$ in $\Omega[t]$.
Conversely we show: every $h\in\Omega[t]$ with $h(S_\Omega)=0$ is divisible by $m_S$ in $\Omega[t]$. Divide $h$ by $m_S$ **in $\Omega[t]$** — legitimate because $m_S$ is monic — obtaining $h=m_SQ+R$ with $Q,R\in\Omega[t]$ and $R=0$ or $\deg R<\deg m_S$. Then $R(S_\Omega)=h(S_\Omega)-m_S(S_\Omega)Q(S_\Omega)=0$. Write $R=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\beta_jt^j$ with $\beta_j\in\Omega$, choose an $F$-linearly independent set $c_1,\dots,c_s\in\Omega$ spanning the $\beta_j$ over $F$, say $\beta_j=\sum_i a_{ji}c_i$ with $a_{ji}\in F$, and put $R_i=\sum_j a_{ji}t^j\in F[t]$; then $R=\sum_i c_iR_i$ with $\deg R_i\le\deg R<\deg m_S$. Extend $\{c_1,\dots,c_s\}$ to an $F$-basis $\{c_1,\dots,c_s\}\cup\{d_j\}_{j\in J}$ of $\Omega$. The map $\bigoplus_{b}(b\otimes_F W)\to\Omega\otimes_FW$, $(w_b)_b\mapsto\sum_b b\otimes w_b$, is an $F$-linear isomorphism, so
$$\Omega\otimes_FW=\Big(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}c_i\otimes_FW\Big)\oplus\Big(\bigoplus_{j\in J}d_j\otimes_FW\Big)$$
is a *direct* sum of $F$-subspaces. For $w\in W$,
$$0=R(S_\Omega)(1\otimes w)=\sum_j\beta_j\otimes S^{j}w=\sum_i c_i\otimes R_i(S)w.$$
By directness each component $c_i\otimes R_i(S)w$ vanishes, and since $c_i\otimes-$ is an $F$-linear isomorphism $W\xrightarrow{\sim}c_i\otimes_FW$, we get $R_i(S)w=0$. As $w$ varies, $R_i(S)=0$, so $m_S\mid R_i$ in $F[t]$; combined with $\deg R_i<\deg m_S$ this forces $R_i=0$ for all $i$, hence $R=0$ (the $c_i$ are linearly independent). Thus $m_S\mid h$ in $\Omega[t]$. Taking $h=m_{S_\Omega}$ gives $m_S\mid m_{S_\Omega}$; with the reverse divisibility and both polynomials monic, $m_{S_\Omega}=m_S$. $\square$

1.5 (the equivalences for $T$). For $S\in\mathrm{End}_k(W)$, $W$ finite-dimensional over $k=\mathbb Q_\ell$, the following are equivalent:
 (a) $W$ is a sum of $S$-stable irreducible subspaces;
 (b) $m_S$ is square-free in $k[t]$;
 (c) $S_{\bar k}$ is diagonalisable on $\bar k\otimes_k W$;
 (d) every $S$-stable subspace of $W$ has an $S$-stable complement.

(b)$\Rightarrow$(a): write $m_S=\prod_{i=1}^{\rho}q_i$ with the $q_i$ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles. By the Chinese remainder theorem (the ideals $(q_i)$ are pairwise comaximal, since distinct monic irreducibles are coprime) there are $e_i\in k[t]$ with $e_i\equiv 1\pmod{q_i}$ and $e_i\equiv 0\pmod{q_j}$ for $j\neq i$. Then $e_ie_j-\delta_{ij}e_i$ and $\sum_ie_i-1$ are congruent to $0$ modulo every $q_l$, hence lie in $\bigcap_l(q_l)=(\prod_lq_l)=(m_S)$ (coprimality gives intersection $=$ product). Evaluating $t\mapsto S$ (well defined since $m_S(S)=0$) gives operators $E_i=e_i(S)$ with $E_iE_j=\delta_{ij}E_i$ and $\sum_iE_i=\mathrm{id}_W$. Hence $W=\bigoplus_i W_i$ with $W_i=E_iW$; each $W_i$ is $S$-stable because $S$ commutes with $E_i$. Moreover $q_ie_i\equiv 0\pmod{q_l}$ for all $l$, so $q_ie_i\in(m_S)$ and $q_i(S)E_i=0$, i.e. $q_i(S)|_{W_i}=0$. Thus $W_i$ is a vector space over the field $k[t]/(q_i)$ via $\bar f\cdot x=f(S)x$, and choosing a $k[t]/(q_i)$-basis $\{x_\alpha\}$ of $W_i$, each line $k[t]/(q_i)\,x_\alpha$ is $S$-stable and is isomorphic as $k[t]$-module to $k[t]/(q_i)$ (annihilator exactly $(q_i)$: it contains $(q_i)$, and any $f$ with $f(S)x_\alpha=0$ has $q_i\mid f$ by irreducibility of $q_i$ and maximality of $(q_i)$). Being a $1$-dimensional vector space over a field, it has no nontrivial $k[t]/(q_i)$-subspaces, hence no nontrivial $S$-stable $k$-subspaces: it is $S$-irreducible. So $W_i$ is a sum of irreducible $S$-stable subspaces, and so is $W$.

(a)$\Rightarrow$(b): take finitely many irreducible $S$-stable subspaces $U_1,\dots,\overset{\circ}{U}_s$ spanning $W$ (possible since $W$ is finite-dimensional; $s\ge 1$ if $W\neq 0$, and if $W=0$ there is nothing to prove). For $U_a$, pick $0\neq u\in U_a$; the map $k[t]\to U_a$, $f\mapsto f(S)u$, is surjective because its image is a nonzero $S$-stable subspace of the irreducible $U_a$, and its kernel is a proper ideal, maximal because $k[t]/\ker\cong U_a$ is a simple $k[t]$-module. Hence $\ker=(q_a)$ with $q_a\in k[t]$ monic irreducible. For any $u'=f(S)u\in U_a$ we have $q_a(S)u'=f(S)q_a(S)u=0$, so $q_a(S)|_{U_a}=0$, i.e. $m_{S|U_a}\mid q_a$; as $U_a\neq 0$ this minimal polynomial is not $1$, so $m_{S|U_a}=q_a$ is irreducible. Let $L=\mathrm{lcm}(q_1,\dots,q_s)$: it is a product of the *distinct* members of the finite list $\{q_a\}$, hence square-free, and $L(S)|_{U_a}=0$ for each $a$ because $L$ is a multiple of $q_a=m_{S|U_a}$. Since the $U_a$ span $W$, $L(S)=0$ on $W$, so $m_S\mid L$ in $k[t]$. Finally, a monic divisor of a square-free polynomial is square-free: in the UFD $k[t]$, writing $L=\prod_{b\in B}p_b$ with the $p_b$ distinct monic irreducibles, every irreducible factor of $m_S$ divides $L$ (Euclid's lemma, applied to $m_S\mid L$), hence is associate to — i.e. equal to — some $p_b$, and no $p_b$ can occur with exponent $\ge 2$ in $m_S$ because it occurs with exponent $1$ in $L$. So $m_S=\prod_{b\in B'}p_b$ with $B'\subseteq B$, square-free.

(b)$\Rightarrow$(c): by 1.4, $m_{T_{\bar k}}=m_S$, and by 1.3 square-freeness over $k$ is equivalent to square-freeness over $\bar k$. Since $\bar k$ is algebraically closed, $m_S=\prod_{i=1}^{\rho}(t-\lambda_i)$ with the $\lambda_i\in\bar k$ pairwise distinct. Applying (b)$\Rightarrow$(a) over the field $\bar k$ (characteristic $0$) to $S_{\bar k}$ gives $\bar k\otimes_kW=\bigoplus_i W_i'$ with $W_i'=E_i'W$ and $(t-\lambda_i)(S_{\bar k})|_{W_i'}=0$, i.e. $W_i'=\ker(S_{\bar k}-\lambda_i)$. Any basis of $\bar k\otimes_kW$ obtained by concatenating bases of the $W_i'$ is an eigenbasis, so $S_{\bar k}$ is diagonalisable.

(c)$\Rightarrow$(b): if $S_{\bar k}$ is diagonalisable with (finite) set of eigenvalues $\Lambda$, then $\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(t-\lambda)$ annihilates $S_{\bar k}$, so $m_{S_{\bar k}}$ is a product of distinct linear factors over $\bar k$, hence square-free in $\bar k[t]$; by 1.4 $m_S=m_{S_{\bar k}}$, and by 1.3 $m_S$ is square-free in $k[t]$.

(a)$\Leftrightarrow$(d): (a)$\Rightarrow$(d): write $W=\sum_{i\in I}U_i$ with the $U_i$ irreducible $S$-stable, and let $U\subseteq W$ be $S$-stable. Choose $J\subseteq I$ maximal with $U\cap\sum_{j\in J}U_j=\{0\}$ (maximum exists by finite-dimensionality). If $U+\sum_{j\in J}U_j\neq W$, some $U_i$ is not contained in it; then $U'=U+\sum_{j\in J}U_j$ is $S$-stable, $U_i\cap U'$ is an $S$-stable subspace of the irreducible $U_i$ and is proper (as $U_i\not\subseteq U'$), hence $U_i\cap U'=\{0\}$, contradicting maximality of $J$. So $W=U\oplus\sum_{j\in J}U_j$ with $\sum_{j\in J}U_j$ $S$-stable. (d)$\Rightarrow$(a): let $U$ be the sum of all irreducible $S$-stable subspaces. If $U\neq W$, then by (d) $W=U\oplus U'$ with $U'$ $S$-stable and $U'\neq 0$; a nonzero $S$-stable subspace of minimal dimension inside $U'$ (exists by finite-dimensionality) is $S$-irreducible and contained in $U'$, hence $\subseteq U\cap U'=\{0\}$, contradiction. So $W=U$. (In particular (a) and (d) define the same class of operators, so the argument applies whichever of them is taken as the definition.)

STEP 2 (the restrictions have square-free minimal polynomials). Each $T_j=T|_{V_j}$ is semisimple by hypothesis, i.e. (a) holds for $S=T_j$ on $W=V_j$. By 1.5, $m_j=m_{T_j}$ is square-free in $k[t]$.

STEP 3 (the lcm of the $m_j$ annihilates $V$). Let $M=\mathrm{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_r)$ in the PID $k[t]$, taken monic; explicitly, if $\{p\}$ runs over the finitely many monic irreducibles dividing some $m_j$, then $M=\prod_p p^{e_p}$ with $e_p=\max_j v_p(m_j)$. For each $j$, $M$ is a multiple of $m_j$, so $M(T)|_{V_j}=M(T_j)=0$. Since $V=\sum_jV_j$, every $v\in V$ is $\sum_jv_j$ with $v_j\in V_j$, and $M(T)v=\sum_jM(T)v_j=0$. Hence $M(T)=0$ on $V$.

STEP 4 (the minimal polynomial of $T$ divides $M$). The set $\mathfrak A=\{f\in k[t]:f(T)=0\}$ is an ideal of $k[t]$ generated by the monic minimal polynomial $m_T$; by Step 3, $M\in\mathfrak A$, so $m_T\mid M$ in $k[t]$.

STEP 5 ($m_T$ is square-free). Each $m_j$ is square-free by Step 2, so $M=\prod_p p^{e_p}$ has all $e_p\in\{0,1\}$, i.e. $M$ is a product of pairwise distinct monic irreducibles. As shown in Step 1 (a)$\Rightarrow$(b), a monic divisor of such a product is again a product of a sub-collection of those irreducibles: if $M=m_T\cdot Q$ and $m_T=\prod_a s_a^{f_a}$ is a factorisation into monic irreducibles, each $s_a\mid M$, so $s_a=p$ for some $p$ in the support of $M$ (Euclid's lemma applied to $p\mid\prod_pp$), and $f_a\le 1$ because $p$ occurs with exponent $1$ in $M$. Hence $m_T$ is square-free in $k[t]$.

STEP 6 (conclusion). By 1.5, (b)$\Rightarrow$(a), the square-freeness of $m_T$ implies that $V$ is a sum of $T$-stable irreducible subspaces, i.e. $T$ is semisimple on $V$. Equivalently, by the other parts of 1.5, $T_{\bar k}$ is diagonalisable on $V\otimes_k\bar k$.

Remark. The hypothesis $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ was used only in that $T$ is a $k$-linear endomorphism: the proof needs just the $T$-stability of the $V_j$ and the fact that their sum is $V$.

lemma_235.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism of Poincar\u00e9 duality. For every \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\) there exists a unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) such that \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*(y))\) for all \(x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(y\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), where \(f^*\) is pullback.
lemma_235.proof:
Notation. Write $V_Z^{m}:=H^{m}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$ and $m\ge 0$, and $L:=\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$. Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so all the results quoted below apply with $m=1$ and $d=D$ in the notation of those statements.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality). $X$ and $Y$ are proper varieties over $\mathbb F_q$, and the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $Z_k$ carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$. Hence lemma_45_finite_frob, applied to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, shows that each $V_Z^{m}$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.

Step 2 (the Poincar\'e pairings and the adjunction isomorphism). By lemma_77(a) there are trace isomorphisms of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces $\operatorname{tr}_Z:V_Z^{2D}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }L$ (the ones appearing in the statement, normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$). By lemma_77(b), for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ the pairing
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z:V_Z^{n}\times V_Z^{2D-n}\longrightarrow L,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_Z:=\operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)$$
is perfect. Concretely, this gives $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps
$$\Phi_{Z,n}:V_Z^{n}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Z^{2D-n},L),\qquad \Phi_{Z,n}(u)(v)=\langle u,v\rangle_Z ,$$
and the analogous $\Phi'_{Z,n}:V_Z^{2D-n}\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Z^{n},L)$, and we claim both are isomorphisms. Indeed, non-degeneracy on the left (part of perfectness) says $\Phi_{Z,n}$ is injective, whence $\dim V_Z^{n}\le\dim V_Z^{2D-n}$; non-degeneracy on the right says $\Phi'_{Z,n}$ is injective, whence $\dim V_Z^{2D-n}\le\dim V_Z^{n}$. By Step 1 both dimensions are finite and equal, so $\Phi_{Z,n}$ is an isomorphism. (If one reads "perfect" as already meaning that $\Phi_{Z,n}$ and $\Phi'_{Z,n}$ are isomorphisms, the preceding sentence may be skipped.)

$\Phi_{Z,n}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear: for $a,b\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $u_1,u_2\in V_Z^{n}$, $v\in V_Z^{2D-n}$, the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of the cup product and the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ give
$$\Phi_{Z,n}(au_1+bu_2)(v)=\operatorname{tr}_Z\big((au_1+bu_2)\cup v\big)=a\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(u_1\cup v)+b\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(u_2\cup v)=(a\Phi_{Z,n}(u_1)+b\Phi_{Z,n}(u_2))(v),$$
where $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_Z^{2D-n},L)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space via the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-structure of $L$.

Step 3 (the functional attached to a class on $X$). Fix $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$. Pullback along the $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $f$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear homomorphism $f^*:V_Y^{2D-n}\to V_X^{2D-n}$ preserving cohomological degree. For $x\in V_X^{n}$ define
$$\lambda_x:V_Y^{2D-n}\longrightarrow L,\qquad \lambda_x(y):=\operatorname{tr}_X\big(x\cup f^*(y)\big).$$
This makes sense because $x\cup f^*(y)\in V_X^{n+(2D-n)}=V_X^{2D}$, to which $\operatorname{tr}_X$ applies. The map $\lambda_x$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, being the composite of the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps $f^*$, $v\mapsto x\cup v$, and $\operatorname{tr}_X$. Moreover the assignment $x\mapsto\lambda_x$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear: for $a,b\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, $x_1,x_2\in V_X^{n}$ and $y\in V_Y^{2D-n}$,
$$\lambda_{ax_1+bx_2}(y)=\operatorname{tr}_X\big((ax_1+bx_2)\cup f^*y\big)=a\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x_1\cup f^*y)+b\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x_2\cup f^*y)=(a\lambda_{x_1}+b\lambda_{x_2})(y),$$
again by bilinearity of the cup product and linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_X$.

Step 4 (existence). Since $\Phi_{Y,n}$ is an isomorphism by Step 2, for each $x\in V_X^{n}$ there is a unique element of $V_Y^{n}$ mapped to $\lambda_x$; define
$$f_*(x):=\Phi_{Y,n}^{-1}(\lambda_x).$$
By construction $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\Phi_{Y,n}(f_*x)(y)=\lambda_x(y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)$ for every $y\in V_Y^{2D-n}$, which is exactly the required identity. The map $f_*=\Phi_{Y,n}^{-1}\circ\,(x\mapsto\lambda_x)$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear as a composite of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps (Steps 2 and 3). This proves existence.

Step 5 (uniqueness). Let $g:V_X^{n}\to V_Y^{n}$ be any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map with $\operatorname{tr}_Y(g(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)$ for all $x,y$. Fixing $x$, the element $g(x)$ satisfies $\Phi_{Y,n}(g(x))=\lambda_x=\Phi_{Y,n}(f_*(x))$; since $\Phi_{Y,n}$ is an isomorphism (in particular injective), $g(x)=f_*(x)$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $g=f_*$. Equivalently: the difference $z=g(x)-f_*(x)$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_Y(z\cup y)=0$ for all $y\in V_Y^{2D-n}$, and non-degeneracy on the left of the pairing of Step 2 forces $z=0$.

Step 6 (edge cases). No case distinction is needed, but we record the extremes explicitly. For $n=0$ the construction uses the perfect pairing $V_Y^{0}\times V_Y^{2D}\to L$; for $n=2D$ it uses $V_Y^{2D}\times V_Y^{0}\to L$; both are covered by lemma_77(b) since $0\le n\le 2D$. If $V_Y^{2D-n}=0$ (which can happen, e.g. for $Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$-like low-dimensional ranges outside $[0,2D]$), then $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,L)=0$ and $\Phi_{Y,n}$ is the unique map $V_Y^{n}\to 0$, which is an isomorphism by Step 2; the construction then yields $f_*=0$, and the identity $\operatorname{tr}_Y(0\cup y)=0=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)$ holds because $f^*:0=V_Y^{2D-n}\to V_X^{2D-n}$ forces $\lambda_x=0$. The hypotheses that $f$ is proper, surjective and generically finite are not needed for existence and uniqueness of $f_*$; they only ensure $X$ and $Y$ have the same dimension $D$, so that the characterising identity involves groups in the same degree on both sides.

Step 7 (identification, for later use). Since $\dim X=\dim Y=D$, the Gysin homomorphism $f_!:V_X^{n}\to V_Y^{n+2D-2D}=V_Y^{n}$ of lemma_207 is characterised by exactly the same identity $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_!x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)$; by the uniqueness just proved, $f_!=f_*$. In particular lemma_207 (with $D=E$, so $q^{D-E}=1$) gives $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$, i.e. the pushforward is Frobenius-equivariant; this is not needed for the present statement but shows the characterisation is the right one.

Conclusion: for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ there exists a unique $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $f_*:H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ satisfying $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*(y))$ for all $x$ and $y$. QED.

lemma_236.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for \(Z\in\{X,Y,X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y\}\). If \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(r\ge0\) and \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^s_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(s\ge0\), then \(F_{X\times Y}\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_236.proof:
Fix data as in the statement: $q=p^a$, $X,Y$ smooth projective geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, and $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$, for $Z\in\{X,Y,X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y\}$. Write $H^r(X):=H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $H^s(Y):=H^s_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n(X\times Y):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. We must show: for every $n\ge 0$, $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n(X\times Y)$, assuming $F_X$ semisimple on every $H^r(X)$ and $F_Y$ semisimple on every $H^s(Y)$.

Step 0 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of the operators). The schemes $X$, $Y$ and $X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$: for each of the three varieties $Z$ and each $m\ge0$, $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space. Next, $\sigma:k\to k$, $c\mapsto c^q$, is a field automorphism with inverse $\sigma^{-1}$, so by lemma_6a (applied to $Z$) the pullback $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (indeed $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}$). Thus each $F_Z|_{H^m}$ is an element of $\mathrm{GL}$ of the corresponding space, so the hypotheses about invertible operators occurring in lemma_5, lemma_8, lemma_9 and lemma_225 are satisfied everywhere below.

Step 1 (K"unneth as an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules). Fix $n\ge0$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, lemma_226 applies to the pair $(X,Y)$ and to this $n$: the cup-product homomorphism
\[
\kappa^n:\bigoplus_{r+s=n}H^r(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^s(Y)\;\longrightarrow\;H^n(X\times Y),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*x\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*y,
\]
where $r,s$ range over all integers $\ge0$ with $r+s=n$, is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules, with $F$ acting on the summand $H^r(X)\otimes H^s(Y)$ by $x\otimes y\mapsto F_Xx\otimes F_Yy$. Note the direct sum has exactly $n+1$ summands, hence is finite. Set $W_n:=\bigoplus_{r+s=n}H^r(X)\otimes H^s(Y)$ and denote by $T_n:=\bigoplus_{r+s=n}\bigl(F_X|_{H^r(X)}\otimes F_Y|_{H^s(Y)}\bigr)$ the resulting operator on $W_n$. Being an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules means precisely that
\[
\kappa^n\circ T_n=F_{X\times Y}\circ\kappa^n .
\tag{1}
\]

Step 2 (each tensor-product summand is semisimple). Fix a pair $(r,s)$ with $r+s=n$, and put $V_1:=H^r(X)$, $V_2:=H^s(Y)$, $T_1:=F_X|_{V_1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_1)$, $T_2:=F_Y|_{V_2}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_2)$. By hypothesis $T_1$ is semisimple on $V_1$ and $T_2$ is semisimple on $V_2$. Both $V_1,V_2$ are finite-dimensional by Step 0, so lemma_5 applies: $T_1\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalizable on $V_1\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and likewise $T_2\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ on $V_2\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

If $V_1=0$ or $V_2=0$, then $V_1\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_2=0$ and the assertion that $T_1\otimes T_2$ is semisimple on it is vacuous. Otherwise $V_1\otimes V_2$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space and $T_1\otimes T_2\in\mathrm{GL}(V_1\otimes V_2)$ (the tensor product of two invertible maps is invertible, with inverse $T_1^{-1}\otimes T_2^{-1}$). We may therefore apply lemma_225 with $V=V_1$, $W=V_2$, $T_V=T_1$, $T_W=T_2$: it gives that $T_1\otimes T_2$, viewed as an automorphism of $V_1\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_2$, is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e. $(T_1\otimes T_2)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalizable on $(V_1\otimes V_2)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By lemma_5 in the reverse direction, $T_1\otimes T_2$ is semisimple on $V_1\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_2$.

(Concretely, this is the usual statement that if $\{v_i\}$, $\{w_j\}$ are eigenbases of $T_1$, $T_2$ after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, with eigenvalues $\alpha_i,\beta_j\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\times}$, then $\{v_i\otimes w_j\}$ is an eigenbasis of $T_1\otimes T_2$ with eigenvalues $\alpha_i\beta_j$; lemma_225 is exactly the formalisation of this step, and the eigenvalues are nonzero because $T_1,T_2$ are invertible.)

Thus $T|_{r,s}:=T_1\otimes T_2$ is semisimple on each summand $H^r(X)\otimes H^s(Y)$ of $W_n$.

Step 3 (the direct sum is semisimple). The space $W_n$ is the direct sum of the finitely many ($n+1$) finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces $H^r(X)\otimes H^s(Y)$, and $T_n$ is the direct-sum operator $\bigoplus_{r+s=n}T|_{r,s}$ (this is exactly how $F$ acts on the direct sum, by Step 1). By Step 2 each $T|_{r,s}$ is semisimple. Applying the "if" direction of lemma_9 to the family $\{H^r(X)\otimes H^s(Y)\}_{r+s=n}$ with operators $\{T|_{r,s}\}_{r+s=n}$, we conclude that $T_n$ is semisimple on $W_n$.

Step 4 (transport across the K"unneth isomorphism). We have $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphisms and an intertwining relation (1): $\kappa^n\circ T_n=F_{X\times Y}\circ\kappa^n$, where $T_n\in\mathrm{GL}(W_n)$ and $F_{X\times Y}\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n(X\times Y))$ by Step 0, and both spaces are finite-dimensional. Apply lemma_8 with $V=W_n$, $W=H^n(X\times Y)$, $T_V=T_n$, $T_W=F_{X\times Y}$, $\alpha=\kappa^n$: since $T_n$ is semisimple (Step 3), $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n(X\times Y)$.

Step 5 (conclusion). The integer $n\ge0$ was arbitrary, and Step 4 establishes semisimplicity of $F_{X\times Y}$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$. This is exactly the required conclusion. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Remark on the scope of the argument: no input beyond the K"unneth decomposition (lemma_226) and the linear-algebraic facts that semisimplicity is preserved under tensor products (lemma_225), direct sums (lemma_9) and conjugation (lemma_8) is used; in particular the hypothesis is needed for all degrees $r,s$ only insofar as the pairs with $r+s=n$ enter, and the vanishing of $H^r$ for $r>2\dim X$ (a consequence of Step 0 together with standard dimension bounds, but not needed here) plays no role.

lemma_231.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of the graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). For each \(j\ge0\) fix a nonzero \(\xi_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)\), and for a codimension-\(j\) cycle \(z\) on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) let \(c_z\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the class with \(\mathrm{cl}(z)=c_z\otimes\xi_j\) under \(H^{2j}(\mathbb Q_\ell(j))=H^{2j}(\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j)\). If \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is generated as a graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-algebra by \(1\) and by such classes \(c_z\), then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(i\ge0\).
lemma_231.proof:
We prove that under the stated generation hypothesis the arithmetic Frobenius $F$ acts on each $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as a SCALAR, hence semisimply. Write $H^i=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^i(j)=H^i\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, and write $\Phi=\mathrm{id}_X\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma:X_k\to X_k$, so that $F=\Phi^*$.

STEP 0 (edge case and finiteness).
If $X=\varnothing$ then every $H^i=0$ and there is nothing to prove, so assume $X\neq\varnothing$. Since $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell$ carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, lemma_45_finite_frob (applied to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$) gives that each $H^i$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By lemma_6a, $F=\Phi^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^i$, i.e. $F|_{H^i}\in\mathrm{GL}(H^i)$; this is the operator whose semisimplicity we must establish.

STEP 1 (two formal properties of $F$ as a pullback).
(a) $F$ is a graded ring homomorphism preserving the unit: $F(1)=1$ and $F(x\cup y)=Fx\cup Fy$ for homogeneous $x,y$. Indeed $\Phi$ is a morphism of schemes and étale pullback $\Phi^*$ on cohomology with constant coefficients is induced by the symmetric-monoidal functor $\Phi^{-1}$ (equivalently, by the adjunction map $\mathbb Q_\ell\to R\Phi_*\mathbb Q_\ell$ together with $R\Phi_*$ being symmetric monoidal on the derived category of sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-modules, since $\Phi^{-1}$ is symmetric monoidal); hence it carries the cup product to the cup product and the fundamental class $1\in H^0$ to $1$. (The same multiplicativity is recorded in the setup of lemma_220.)
(b) Functoriality for $\mathbb F_q$-morphisms: if $f:Y\to Z$ is a morphism of schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, then $f_k^*\circ F_Z=F_Y\circ f_k^*$ on cohomology; this is exactly lemma_214.

STEP 2 (reduction of $X$ to pure-dimensional pieces).
$X$ is smooth, hence regular, over $\mathbb F_q$; a regular locally Noetherian scheme has all local rings domains, whence its irreducible components are open; since $X$ is Noetherian they are also closed. Thus $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in\pi_0(X)}X_\alpha$ is a finite disjoint union of its connected components, each $X_\alpha$ open-and-closed, irreducible, and (being a connected regular locally Noetherian scheme) integral. Each $X_\alpha$ is open in $X$, hence smooth over $\mathbb F_q$; and $X_\alpha$ is the closed subscheme cut out by the idempotent ideal $\mathcal O_X e_\alpha$ for a global idempotent $e_\alpha\in H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)$, so $X_\alpha$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$ and is a closed subscheme of $X$; since $X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$, so is $X_\alpha$. Being integral of finite type over a field, $X_\alpha$ is of pure dimension, say $d_\alpha$. (If one's convention already makes "variety" irreducible, or if $X$ is known pure-dimensional, this step is vacuous and there is a single component.)
Base change preserves finite coproducts, so $X_k=\coprod_\alpha X_{\alpha,k}$ with $X_{\alpha,k}=X_\alpha\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$. The étale topos of a finite disjoint union is the product of the étale topoi, so for every $n$ and every $j$
\[\bigl(i_{\alpha,k}^*\bigr)_\alpha:\;H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\bigoplus_\alpha H^n(X_{\alpha,k},\mathbb Q_\ell(j)\]
is an isomorphism (finite products of abelian groups are exact, so derived global sections over the union are the direct sum). By Step 1(b) applied to the $\mathbb F_q$-morphisms $i_\alpha:X_\alpha\hookrightarrow X$, each $i_{\alpha,k}^*$ intertwines $F_X$ with $F_{X_\alpha}$.

STEP 3 (the key eigenvalue identity for the generators).
Claim: for every $j\ge 0$ and every codimension-$j$ cycle $z$ on $X$ defined over $\mathbb F_q$, one has
\[ F(c_z)=q^{\,j}\,c_z\qquad\text{in }H^{2j}. \tag{$\ast$}
]
Proof of the claim. Write $z=\sum_{W}n_W[W]$ with the $W$ integral closed subschemes of $X$ of codimension $j$. Each $W$ is contained in a unique component $X_\alpha$ (the components are open and closed), so $z=\sum_\alpha z_\alpha$ with $z_\alpha=\sum_{W\subset X_\alpha}n_W[W]$ a cycle on $X_\alpha$. Since the components $X_\alpha$ are defined over $\mathbb F_q$ and $z$ is a cycle on the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X$, each $z_\alpha$ is a cycle on the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $X_\alpha$, i.e. is defined over $\mathbb F_q$. Moreover $\mathrm{codim}_{X_\alpha}(W)=\mathrm{codim}_X(W)=j$: indeed any $W'\supset W$ irreducible closed in $X$ satisfies $\varnothing\neq W\subset W'\cap X_\alpha$, an open subset of the irreducible $W'$; as $X_\alpha$ is also closed, $W'\cap X_\alpha$ is clopen nonempty in $W'$, hence $W'=W'\cap X_\alpha\subset X_\alpha$, so chains from $W$ in $X$ and in $X_\alpha$ coincide. Thus $z_\alpha$ is a codimension-$j$ cycle on $X_\alpha$ defined over $\mathbb F_q$.
By the functoriality of $\ell$-adic cycle class maps for flat pullback (an open-and-closed immersion is flat of relative dimension $0$, and codimension is preserved, as just shown),
\[ i_{\alpha,k}^*\,\mathrm{cl}_X(z)=\mathrm{cl}_{X_\alpha}(z_\alpha)\quad\text{in }H^{2j}(X_{\alpha,k},\mathbb Q_\ell(j)). \]
Pullback on twisted cohomology is $i_{\alpha,k}^*\otimes\mathrm{id}$ under $H^{2j}(j)=H^{2j}\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ (the twist is by a constant coefficient object and the identification is natural in the variety), so with $\mathrm{cl}_X(z)=c_z\otimes\xi_j$ we get $\mathrm{cl}_{X_\alpha}(z_\alpha)=(i_{\alpha,k}^*c_z)\otimes\xi_j$. Since $\xi_j\neq 0$ and $v\mapsto v\otimes\xi_j$ is an isomorphism, uniqueness in the definition of $c_{z_\alpha}$ gives $c_{z_\alpha}=i_{\alpha,k}^*(c_z)$.
Now apply lemma_78 to the smooth projective $\mathbb F_q$-variety $X_\alpha$, which is of pure dimension $d_\alpha$: its "equivalently" clause, whose convention for $c_{z_\alpha}$ (fix $0\ne\xi_j\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, $\mathrm{cl}=c\otimes\xi_j$) and whose operator $F_*=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ are verbatim those of the present lemma, yields
\[ F_{X_\alpha}(c_{z_\alpha})=q^{\,j}c_{z_\alpha}. \]
Combining, for every $\alpha$,
\[ i_{\alpha,k}^*\bigl(F_Xc_z-q^{\,j}c_z\bigr)=F_{X_\alpha}i_{\alpha,k}^*c_z-q^{\,j}i_{\alpha,k}^*c_z=F_{X_\alpha}c_{z_\alpha}-q^{\,j}c_{z_\alpha}=0, \]
where the first equality is Step 1(b). Since $\bigl(i_{\alpha,k}^*\bigr)_\alpha$ is injective (Step 2), $F_Xc_z=q^{\,j}c_z$. The claim $(\ast)$ is proved.

STEP 4 (monomials in the generators are eigenvectors).
Let $S=\{1\}\cup\{c_z:z\ \text{a codimension-}j\ \text{cycle on }X\text{ over }\mathbb F_q,\ j\ge 0\}$ be the given set of homogeneous generators, $\deg c_z=2j$. Let $m=c_{z_1}\cup\cdots\cup c_{z_r}$ be a monomial of length $r\ge 0$ (the case $r=0$ is $m=1$) lying in $H^i$, so $\sum_{s=1}^r 2j_s=i$ where $z_s$ has codimension $j_s$. By Step 1(a) and Step 3, inductively on $r$,
\[ F(m)=\prod_{s=1}^r F(c_{z_s})=\prod_{s=1}^r q^{\,j_s}\,c_{z_s}=q^{\,j_1+\cdots+j_r}m=q^{\,i/2}m, \]
with the convention $q^{0/2}=1$ for $m=1$, consistent with $F(1)=1$.

STEP 5 (each $H^i$ is a scalar $F$-space).
Let $A\subseteq H^*$ be the graded subalgebra generated by $S$; by definition $A^i$ is the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-span of the monomials of total degree $i$. The hypothesis says $A=H^*$, i.e. $A^i=H^i$ for all $i$. Since every element of $S$ has even degree, there are no monomials of odd total degree, so $A^i=0$ and hence $H^i=0$ for $i$ odd. For $i=2j$ even, $H^{2j}$ is spanned by monomials $m$ with $F(m)=q^{\,j}m$ by Step 4; by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity, $F(v)=q^{\,j}v$ for every $v\in H^{2j}$, i.e.
\[ F|_{H^{2j}}=q^{\,j}\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^{2j}}. \tag{$\ast\ast$}
]
(In particular $H^{2j}=0$ is allowed, in which case $(\ast\ast)$ is the empty statement.) Note $q^{\,j}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^*$, so $(\ast\ast)$ is consistent with Step 0's invertibility of $F$.

STEP 6 (semisimplicity).
Fix $i\ge 0$. If $H^i=0$ there is nothing to prove: the zero space is the (empty) direct sum of eigenspaces, so $F|_{H^i}$ is semisimple by definition. If $H^i\ne 0$ then $i=2j$ is even and by $(\ast\ast)$ the minimal polynomial of $F|_{H^i}\in\mathrm{GL}(H^i)$ is $\mu(t)=t-q^{\,j}\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, which is irreducible of degree $1$ and hence squarefree ($\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$). Lemma_60, equivalence (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii), applied to the nonzero finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $H^i$ and the automorphism $F|_{H^i}$, gives that $F|_{H^i}$ is semisimple.

This proves the lemma for every $i\ge 0$.

STEP 7 (relation with the conjecture's formulation; remark).
By Step 5 the geometric Frobenius $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F^{-1}$ (lemma_6a) equals $q^{-j}\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{2j}$ and $H^{2j+1}=0$; it is scalar, hence semisimple by the same appeal to lemma_60, and after extension of scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ it is diagonal (already a scalar matrix). Lemma_5 confirms that the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-semisimplicity just proved is equivalent to diagonalisability of the base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which is the second formulation in the conjecture. Thus the conjecture holds for every smooth projective $X/\mathbb F_q$ whose $\ell$-adic cohomology ring is generated by classes of cycles defined over $\mathbb F_q$ (in particular, for products of projective spaces, complete intersections, toric varieties, etc., whenever that generation is known). No use is made of the standard conjectures, hard Lefschetz, the Künneth theorem, or semisimplicity for abelian varieties.

lemma_237.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be semisimple (diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)). Then \(T\) is semisimple on every \(T\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace \(W\subseteq V\), on the automorphism of the quotient \(V/W\) induced by \(T\), and hence on every subquotient \(W/W'\) with \(W'\subseteq W\) both \(T\)-stable.
lemma_237.proof:
Write $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\Omega=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Throughout, for a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $U$ and $S\in\mathrm{End}_K(U)$ we say that $S$ is *semisimple* when $S_\Omega:=S\otimes_K\mathrm{id}_\Omega\in\mathrm{End}_\Omega(U\otimes_K\Omega)$ is diagonalizable; by lemma_5 (applied over $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$) this is exactly the usual notion of semisimplicity of $S$ on $U$, and it is the equivalence stated in the parenthetical of the lemma's hypothesis. We prove four claims and then deduce the three statements.

**Claim 1 (the minimal polynomial is unchanged by an arbitrary base change).** Let $U$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, $S\in\mathrm{End}_K(U)$, let $L/K$ be any field extension, $U_L:=U\otimes_K L$, $S_L:=S\otimes\mathrm{id}_L$. Then $\mu_{S_L}=\mu_S$ as elements of $L[t]$ (both monic).

*Proof.* Put $A:=K[t]$, and let $\varphi:A\to\mathrm{End}_K(U)$ be the $K$-algebra homomorphism $t\mapsto S$. Since $\dim_K\mathrm{End}_K(U)=n^2<\infty$, the $n^2+1$ operators $1,S,\dots,S^{n^2}$ are $K$-linearly dependent, so $\ker\varphi\neq(0)$; as $A$ is a PID, $\ker\varphi=(\mu_S)$ for a unique monic polynomial $\mu_S$ (with the convention $\mu_S=1$ when $U=0$, in which case $\varphi=0$ and $\ker\varphi=A$). Note $\mu_S\neq 0$ in every case, since it is monic.

Because $U$ is a finite *free* $K$-module (every vector space over a field is free), there is a canonical $L$-linear isomorphism
$$\Phi:\mathrm{End}_K(U)\otimes_K L\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\mathrm{End}_L(U_L),\qquad f\otimes\lambda\longmapsto\big(u\otimes\mu\mapsto f(u)\otimes\lambda\mu\big).$$
For completeness we check it: choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $U$; then $e_1\otimes1,\dots,e_n\otimes1$ is an $L$-basis of $U_L$, $\mathrm{End}_K(U)$ has basis the matrix units $E_{ab}$, and $\Phi(E_{ab}\otimes1)$ is the $L$-linear endomorphism of $U_L$ with matrix $E_{ab}$ in that basis; so $\Phi$ sends a $K$-basis of the source to an $L$-basis of the target, hence is an isomorphism, and the formula is basis-free so the isomorphism is canonical.

Identify $A\otimes_K L$ with $L[t]$ by $\sum_j p_j\otimes\lambda_j\mapsto\sum_j\lambda_j p_j(t)$ (an isomorphism of $K$-algebras, both sides free on the monomials $t^m$). Under these two identifications, $\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_L$ is precisely $\psi:L[t]\to\mathrm{End}_L(U_L)$, $t\mapsto S_L$: indeed $\Phi((\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_L)(t\otimes1))=\Phi(S\otimes1)=S_L$, and both maps are $L$-algebra homomorphisms.

Now $L$ is a vector space over $K$, hence a free $K$-module, hence flat over $K$. Tensor the short exact sequence of $K$-vector spaces $0\to(\mu_S)\xrightarrow{\ i\ }A\to A/(\mu_S)\to0$ with $L$ over $K$; flatness gives an exact sequence $0\to(\mu_S)\otimes_K L\xrightarrow{i\otimes1}A\otimes_K L\to (A/(\mu_S))\otimes_K L\to0$. By exactness, $\ker(\varphi\otimes\mathrm{id}_L)=\mathrm{im}(i\otimes1)$, and the image is the $L$-subspace, equivalently the ideal, generated by $\mu_S$, namely $\mu_S\cdot L[t]$. Thus
$$\ker\psi=\mu_S\cdot L[t].$$
Since $\mu_S$ is monic, it is the monic generator of $\ker\psi$, and by definition of the minimal polynomial over $L$ that generator is $\mu_{S_L}$. Hence $\mu_{S_L}=\mu_S$ in $L[t]$. (If $U=0$ the same argument reads $\ker\psi=L[t]=(1)$, so $\mu_{S_L}=1=\mu_S$.) $\square$

A useful reformulation: for $g\in L[t]$, $g(S_L)=0$ if and only if $g\in\mu_S L[t]$, if and only if $\mu_S$ divides $g$ in $L[t]$. Divisibility by the monic $\mu_S$ is computed by the ordinary division algorithm coefficientwise in $K$, so no choice of basis of $L/K$ is involved.

**Claim 2 (square-free criterion in characteristic $0$).** Let $U$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space and $S\in\mathrm{End}_K(U)$. Then $S$ is semisimple (i.e. $S_\Omega$ is diagonalizable) if and only if $\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_S,\mu_S')=1$.

*Proof.* If $U=0$, then $S_\Omega$ is the operator on the zero space, whose empty family of vectors is a basis of eigenvectors, so it is diagonalizable; and $\mu_S=1$, $\mu_S'=0$, $\gcd(1,0)=1$. Both sides hold, so assume $U\neq0$. Then $\mu_S$ is nonconstant, and since $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$ its formal derivative $\mu_S'$ is nonzero of degree $\deg\mu_S-1$; the Euclidean algorithm below is legitimate.

First observe that the monic gcd of two polynomials of $K[t]$ is the same whether it is computed in $K[t]$ or in $\Omega[t]$: every division step in the Euclidean algorithm is division by a monic polynomial, and that division is performed coefficientwise in $K$, so the successive quotients and remainders in $K[t]$ coincide with those computed in $\Omega[t]$. Hence the final nonzero remainder, made monic, is the same in both rings.

$(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_S,\mu_S')=1$, hence also $\gcd_{\Omega[t]}(\mu_S,\mu_S')=1$. Factor $\mu_S$ in $\Omega[t]$: since $\Omega$ is algebraically closed, $\mu_S=c\prod_{i\in I}(t-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$ with $\lambda_i\in\Omega$ distinct, $e_i\ge1$, and $c=1$ as $\mu_S$ is monic. If some $e_i\ge2$, then $(t-\lambda_i)$ divides both $\mu_S$ and $\mu_S'$ (each term of the derivative contains $\prod_{j\ne i}(t-\lambda_j)^{e_j}$ times $e_i(t-\lambda_i)^{e_i-1}$), contradicting $\gcd=1$. So every $e_i=1$: writing $\Lambda=\{\lambda_i:i\in I\}$, $\mu_S=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(t-\lambda)$ with the $\lambda$ pairwise distinct. By Claim 1, $\mu_{S_\Omega}=\mu_S$ is the same polynomial. The ideals $((t-\lambda))\subset\Omega[t]$, $\lambda\in\Lambda$, are maximal (linear, hence irreducible) and pairwise distinct, hence pairwise comaximal; the Chinese remainder theorem gives an isomorphism of $\Omega$-algebras
$$\Omega[t]/(\mu_{S_\Omega})\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\Omega[t]/(t-\lambda)\cong\Omega^{\Lambda}.$$
Via $t\mapsto S_\Omega$, the space $U_\Omega$ is an $\Omega[t]$-module annihilated by $\mu_{S_\Omega}$, hence a module over $\Omega[t]/(\mu_{S_\Omega})$. Let $\varepsilon_\lambda\in\Omega^{\Lambda}$ be the idempotent supported at $\lambda$ and let $e_\lambda\in\Omega[t]/(\mu_{S_\Omega})$ be its preimage. Then $\sum_\lambda e_\lambda=1$, $e_\lambda e_{\lambda'}=0$ for $\lambda\ne\lambda'$, so $U_\Omega=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}e_\lambda U_\Omega$; and $(t-\lambda)$ annihilates $e_\lambda\cdot\Omega[t]/(\mu_{S_\Omega})$ because $(t-\lambda)$ kills the $\lambda$-component and $e_\lambda$ is supported there. Thus $S_\Omega$ acts on $e_\lambda U_\Omega$ as the scalar $\lambda$, i.e. $e_\lambda U_\Omega\subseteq\ker(S_\Omega-\lambda)$. So $U_\Omega$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces of $S_\Omega$, and choosing a basis of each $e_\lambda U_\Omega$ gives a basis of $U_\Omega$ of eigenvectors: $S_\Omega$ is diagonalizable.

$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $S_\Omega$ diagonalizable. Let $\Lambda\subset\Omega$ be the finite set of its eigenvalues (nonempty, since $U_\Omega\ne0$ and $\Omega$ is algebraically closed), and put $P(t):=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(t-\lambda)$. We show $\mu_{S_\Omega}=P$. On one hand $P(S_\Omega)=0$, because $U_\Omega=\bigoplus_{\lambda}E_\lambda(S_\Omega)$ and $P(S_\Omega)$ acts on $E_\mu$ as multiplication by $P(\mu)=0$; hence $\mu_{S_\Omega}\mid P$ in $\Omega[t]$. On the other hand, if $Q\in\Omega[t]$ satisfies $Q(S_\Omega)=0$ and $0\ne v\in E_\lambda$, then $0=Q(S_\Omega)v=Q(\lambda)v$, so $Q(\lambda)=0$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$; by the linear-factor theorem each $(t-\lambda)$ divides $Q$, and as these are pairwise non-associate primes in the UFD $\Omega[t]$ their product $P$ divides $Q$. Taking $Q=\mu_{S_\Omega}$ gives $P\mid\mu_{S_\Omega}$; with the reverse divisibility and both monic, $\mu_{S_\Omega}=P$. By Claim 1, $\mu_S=P$ in $\Omega[t]$, so $\mu_S$ splits in $\Omega$ with pairwise distinct roots. Then $\mu_S'(\lambda)=\prod_{\mu\in\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}}(\lambda-\mu)\ne0$ for every root $\lambda$ of $\mu_S$, so $\mu_S$ and $\mu_S'$ have no common root in the algebraically closed field $\Omega$, i.e. $\gcd_{\Omega[t]}(\mu_S,\mu_S')=1$. By the observation on gcds, $\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_S,\mu_S')=1$. $\square$

**Claim 3 (restriction to a stable subspace).** Let $W\subseteq V$ be a $T$-stable $K$-subspace. Then $T(W)\subseteq W$ induces $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$, and $\mu_{T|_W}$ divides $\mu_T$ in $K[t]$; consequently, if $T$ is semisimple then so is $T|_W$.

*Proof.* $T|_W:W\to W$ is $K$-linear and injective (as $T$ is injective on $V$); since $W$ is finite-dimensional, injectivity implies bijectivity, so $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$. Now $\mu_T(T)=0$ in $\mathrm{End}_K(V)$, so a fortiori $\mu_T(T)(w)=0$ for all $w\in W$, i.e. $\mu_T(T|_W)=0$ in $\mathrm{End}_K(W)$. By the reformulation at the end of Claim 1 (with $L=K$, $S=T|_W$), $\mu_{T|_W}\mid\mu_T$ in $K[t]$; write $\mu_T=\mu_{T|_W}\cdot h$ with $h\in K[t]$ monic. Differentiating, $\mu_T'=\mu_{T|_W}'\,h+\mu_{T|_W}\,h'$. Let $d:=\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_{T|_W},\mu_{T|_W}')$. Then $d\mid\mu_{T|_W}\mid\mu_T$ and $d\mid\mu_{T|_W}'$, and from the displayed identity $d\mid\mu_T'$ as well; hence $d\mid\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_T,\mu_T')$. If $T$ is semisimple, Claim 2 gives $\gcd_{K[t]}(\mu_T,\mu_T')=1$, so $d=1$, and Claim 2 applied to $S=T|_W$ shows $T|_W$ is semisimple. $\square$

**Claim 4 (quotient by a stable subspace).** Let $W\subseteq V$ be a $T$-stable $K$-subspace. Then $T$ induces an automorphism $\overline T\in\mathrm{GL}(V/W)$, $\mu_{\overline T}\mid\mu_T$ in $K[t]$, and if $T$ is semisimple then $\overline T$ is semisimple.

*Proof.* First we check that $\overline T$ is invertible, not merely injective/surjective as an endomorphism. By Claim 3, $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$, i.e. $T$ maps $W$ bijectively onto $W$. If $v\in V$ satisfies $Tv\in W$, choose $w\in W$ with $Tw=Tv$; injectivity of $T$ gives $v=w\in W$. Hence $T^{-1}W\subseteq W$, so $T^{-1}$ also induces a map $V/W\to V/W$, and the two induced maps are mutually inverse. Thus $\overline T\in\mathrm{GL}(V/W)$ is well defined.

For the minimal polynomial: $\mu_T(T)=0$ on $V$, so the induced endomorphism $\mu_T(\overline T)$ of $V/W$ is also $0$ (a polynomial in $T$ that vanishes on $V$ descends to the zero map on the quotient). By the reformulation of Claim 1 applied to $S=\overline T$ on $U=V/W$ with $L=K$, $\mu_{\overline T}\mid\mu_T$. The divisor argument of Claim 3 then applies verbatim: writing $\mu_T=\mu_{\overline T}h$, any common divisor of $\mu_{\overline T}$ and $\mu_{\overline T}'$ divides $\mu_T$ and $\mu_T'$, so semisimplicity of $T$ (i.e. $\gcd(\mu_T,\mu_T')=1$, Claim 2) forces $\gcd(\mu_{\overline T},\mu_{\overline T}')=1$, hence $\overline T$ is semisimple by Claim 2. $\square$

**Conclusion of the lemma.** Let $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ be semisimple.

(i) *Stable subspaces.* For a $T$-stable $W\subseteq V$, $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ is semisimple by Claim 3. The two degenerate cases are covered: if $W=V$ this is the hypothesis; if $W=0$ then $T|_W$ is the operator on the zero space, which Claim 2 (and its edge-case remark) identifies as semisimple, consistently with Claim 3's proof, where $\mu_{T|_0}=1$ divides $\mu_T$.

(ii) *Quotients.* By Claim 4 the induced $\overline T\in\mathrm{GL}(V/W)$ is semisimple. Again $W=V$ gives the zero space (semisimple) and $W=0$ gives $V/W=V$ with $\overline T=T$ (semisimple by hypothesis).

(iii) *Subquotients.* Let $W'\subseteq W\subseteq V$ be $T$-stable. Then $W'$ is stable under $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$, and by (i) $T|_W$ is semisimple. Applying (ii) to the semisimple operator $T|_W$ on $W$ and its stable subspace $W'$, the automorphism $\widetilde T$ of $W/W'$ induced by $T|_W$ is semisimple. It remains to note that $\widetilde T$ coincides with the automorphism of $W/W'$ induced directly by $T$: for $w+W'\in W/W'$, since $T|_{W'}=T|_W|_{W'}$, one has $\widetilde T(w+W')=(T|_W)w+W'=Tw+W'$, which is exactly the map induced by $T$; both are well-defined automorphisms of $W/W'$ by the argument in Claim 4.

Finally, by lemma_5, for each of the operators just produced ($T|_W$ on $W$, $\overline T$ on $V/W$, $\widetilde T$ on $W/W'$) semisimplicity in the sense used above is equivalent to diagonalizability of its base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. This is precisely the threefold assertion of the lemma. $\blacksquare$

lemma_234.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of the graded ring \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), which acts on \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) through the induced action. Fix \(n\ge1\), and suppose the cup-product homomorphism \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is surjective. Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_234.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_234",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_45_finite_frob"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_6a"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_225"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_9"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_8"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_220"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_228"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "**Proof of lemma_234.**

Notation. Write \(V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(W:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and denote by \(F_V\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\), \(F_W\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W)\) the operators \((\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Write \(F_{\wedge}\) for the induced automorphism of \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\), i.e. \(F_{\wedge}(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)=F_Vv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge F_Vv_n\).

**Step 0 (finite-dimensionality, invertibility).** An abelian variety is proper over \(\mathbb F_q\), so lemma_45_finite_frob applied to \(X=A\) and \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) (with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) shows that \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(m\); in particular \(V\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional. By lemma_6a, \(F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of each \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), with inverse the geometric Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*\). Hence \(F_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(F_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\); consequently \(F_{\wedge}\in\mathrm{GL}(\wedge^n V)\) as well, its inverse being the map induced by \(F_V^{-1}\).

**Step 1 (semisimple \(\Longleftrightarrow\) diagonalisable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)).** We record the general fact, used to feed lemma_225, that for a finite-dimensional vector space \(U\) over a field \(F\) of characteristic \(0\) and \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(U)\), \(T\) is semisimple if and only if \(T_{\overline F}:=\overline F\otimes_F T\) is diagonalisable. Indeed, let \(\mu_T\in F[t]\) be the minimal polynomial. Semisimplicity of \(T\) is equivalent to \(\mu_T\) being a product of pairwise distinct irreducibles. Since \(\mu_T\) is monic, the division algorithm in \(F[t]\) shows that \(f(T)=0\) for \(f\in F[t]\) iff \(\mu_T\mid f\); applying this in \(\overline F[t]\) shows the minimal polynomial of \(T_{\overline F}\) is again \(\mu_T\) (viewed in \(\overline F[t]\)). As \(F\) has characteristic \(0\), every irreducible of \(F[t]\) is separable, so over \(\overline F\) it splits into pairwise distinct linear factors. Hence \(\mu_T\) is squarefree in \(F[t]\) iff it splits in \(\overline F[t]\) into distinct linear factors, and the latter is exactly diagonalisability of \(T_{\overline F}\). Thus the two notions coincide, and we use whichever is convenient.

**Step 2 (\(F_V\) is semisimple).** An abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\) is, by definition, proper, smooth and geometrically integral, so lemma_h1_abelian_semisimple applies to \(A/\mathbb F_q\) and gives: the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is semisimple, i.e. \(F_V\) is semisimple. By Step 1, \((F_V)_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\) is diagonalisable.

**Step 3 (\(F_V^{\otimes n}\) is semisimple on \(V^{\otimes n}\)).** We argue by induction on \(n\ge1\). For \(n=1\) this is Step 2. For the induction step, \(V^{\otimes(n+1)}=V^{\otimes n}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) and \(F_V^{\otimes(n+1)}=F_V^{\otimes n}\otimes F_V\); both \(V^{\otimes n}\) and \(V\) are finite-dimensional and both operators have diagonalisable base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) (induction hypothesis, Step 2). lemma_225 then gives that \(F_V^{\otimes(n+1)}\) is diagonalisable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). Hence \(F_V^{\otimes n}\) is semisimple on \(V^{\otimes n}\) by Step 1.

**Step 4 (\({\textstyle\bigwedge^n}V\) is an \(F\)-stable direct summand of \(V^{\otimes n}\)).** For \(\rho\in S_n\) let \(\tau_\rho\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\otimes n})\) be \(\tau_\rho(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\rho^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\rho^{-1}(n)}\), and define the alternator
\[\mathrm{Alt}=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\rho\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,\tau_\rho\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^{\otimes n})\]
(this makes sense since \(n!\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) is invertible in the characteristic-\(0\) field \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)).

*Alt is idempotent.* For each \(\sigma\in S_n\), \(\tau_\sigma\mathrm{Alt}=\frac1{n!}\sum_\rho\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\tau_{\sigma\rho}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\rho'}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma^{-1}\rho')\tau_{\rho'}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\mathrm{Alt}\). Therefore \(\mathrm{Alt}^2=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\tau_\sigma\mathrm{Alt}=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)^2\mathrm{Alt}=\mathrm{Alt}\). Hence \(V^{\otimes n}=\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}\oplus\ker\mathrm{Alt}\).

*Both summands are \(F_V^{\otimes n}\)-stable.* \(F_V^{\otimes n}\tau_\rho=\tau_\rho F_V^{\otimes n}\) for every \(\rho\) (both send \(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\) to \(F_Vv_{\rho^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_Vv_{\rho^{-1}(n)}\)), so \(F_V^{\otimes n}\) commutes with \(\mathrm{Alt}\); thus \(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}\) and \(\ker\mathrm{Alt}\) are stable under \(F_V^{\otimes n}\) and under its inverse, and the decomposition is one of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t,t^{-1}]\)-modules for \(t\mapsto F_V^{\otimes n}\).

*Identification with the exterior power.* Let \(q:V^{\otimes n}\to{\textstyle\bigwedge^n}V\), \(q(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n\). Define \(\iota:{\textstyle\bigwedge^n}V\to V^{\otimes n}\) on decomposable wedges by \(\iota(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n):=\mathrm{Alt}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\). This is well defined: \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto\mathrm{Alt}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\) is \(n\)-linear, and it is alternating because if \(v_i=v_{i+1}\) then for \(\rho=(i\;i{+}1)\) the tensor \(w=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\) satisfies \(\tau_\rho w=w\), whence \(\mathrm{Alt}(w)=\mathrm{Alt}(\tau_\rho w)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\mathrm{Alt}(w)=-\mathrm{Alt}(w)\), so \(\mathrm{Alt}(w)=0\). Next, using \(q(\tau_\rho w)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)q(w)\),
\[q(\iota(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n))=\tfrac1{n!}\sum_\rho\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,q(\tau_\rho(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=\tfrac1{n!}\sum_\rho\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)^2\,(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n,\]
so \(q\circ\iota=\mathrm{id}_{{\bigwedge^n}V}\). Also \(\iota\circ q=\mathrm{Alt}\), since both are linear and agree on pure tensors. Consequently \(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}=\operatorname{im}(\iota\circ q)\subseteq\operatorname{im}\iota\subseteq\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}\), so \(\iota\) identifies \({\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\) isomorphically with \(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}\subset V^{\otimes n}\), with inverse \(q|_{\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}}\).

*\(\iota\) is Frobenius-equivariant:* \(\iota(F_{\wedge}(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n))=\mathrm{Alt}(F_Vv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes F_Vv_n)=\mathrm{Alt}(F_V^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=F_V^{\otimes n}\iota(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)\), i.e.
\[\iota\circ F_{\wedge}=F_V^{\otimes n}\circ\iota .\]

**Step 5 (\(F_{\wedge}\) is semisimple on \({\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\)).** By Step 3, \(F_V^{\otimes n}\) is semisimple on \(V^{\otimes n}\). The decomposition \(V^{\otimes n}=\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}\oplus\ker\mathrm{Alt}\) of Step 4 is a direct sum of \(F_V^{\otimes n}\)-stable subspaces, so lemma_9 (the "only if" direction) gives that \(F_V^{\otimes n}|_{\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt}}\) is semisimple. Transporting along the intertwining isomorphism \(\iota^{-1}:(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{Alt},F_V^{\otimes n})\xrightarrow{\sim}({\bigwedge^n}V,F_{\wedge})\) and using lemma_8, \(F_{\wedge}\) is semisimple on \({\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\).

**Step 6 (the cup product is Frobenius-equivariant).** The arithmetic Frobenius on the graded ring \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is multiplicative: \(F(x\cup y)=Fx\cup Fy\). This is exactly the ring-automorphism property stated for a smooth projective \(\mathbb F_q\)-variety in lemma_220, which applies because \(A\) is smooth projective over \(\mathbb F_q\). By induction on \(n\), \(F_Vv_1\cup\cdots\cup F_Vv_n=F_V(v_1\cup\cdots\cup v_n)\) for \(v_i\in V\).

The target lemma supplies the cup-product homomorphism \(\mu:{\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\to W\); for completeness we note it is the map determined by \(\mu(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)=v_1\cup\cdots\cup v_n\): the multiplication map \(m:V^{\otimes n}\to W\), \(m(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\cup\cdots\cup v_n\), satisfies \(m\circ\tau_\rho=-m\) for each adjacent transposition \(\rho=(i\;i{+}1)\), because graded commutativity of the cup product gives \(y\cup x=-x\cup y\) for \(x,y\in H^1\); hence \(m\) vanishes on tensors having two equal adjacent factors, and since \(\ker q\) is spanned by those tensors (from \((x+y)\otimes(x+y)-x\otimes x-y\otimes y=x\otimes y+y\otimes x\) one gets \(x\otimes y\equiv -y\otimes x\) modulo their span \(I\), so \(\tau_\rho\equiv-1\) on \(V^{\otimes n}/I\) and the universal property of the exterior power gives \(I=\ker q\)), \(m\) factors as \(m=\mu\circ q\). Combining with Step 6's multiplicativity,
\[\mu\big(F_{\wedge}(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)\big)=\mu(F_Vv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge F_Vv_n)=F_Vv_1\cup\cdots\cup F_Vv_n=F_V(v_1\cup\cdots\cup v_n)=F_W\big(\mu(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)\big),\]
that is,
\[\mu\circ F_{\wedge}=1\cdot F_W\circ\mu\qquad\text{with }1\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}.\]

**Step 7 (conclusion).** We apply lemma_228 to the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \(V'=\,{\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\) and \(W'=W\), to \(T_{V'}=F_{\wedge}\in\mathrm{GL}(V')\) and \(T_{W'}=F_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W')\) (Step 0), to the scalar \(c=1\), and to \(\varphi=\mu\). The identity \(\mu\circ F_{\wedge}=1\cdot F_W\circ\mu\) of Step 6 is precisely the required intertwining relation; \(F_{\wedge}\) is semisimple by Step 5; and \(\mu\) is surjective by the hypothesis of the lemma. The "in particular" part of lemma_228 then yields that \(F_W\) is semisimple on \(W=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

This is exactly the desired conclusion: the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}_A\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). \(\blacksquare\)

(Remark on the role of the hypothesis: the only place surjectivity of \(\mu\) is used is the final application of lemma_228; the argument shows in any case that \(F\) is semisimple on the image \(\mu({\bigwedge^n}V)\subseteq H^n\), which is all of \(H^n\) when the cup product is surjective.)
}

lemma_240.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\). For \(v\in V\) write \(V_v=\langle T^{n}v : n\ge 0\rangle_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\). Suppose \(V\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by those vectors \(v\) for which the restriction \(T|_{V_v}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_v)\) is semisimple. Then \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\).
lemma_240.proof:
We prove: if a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $V$ with $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is spanned by the vectors $v$ whose cyclic subspace $V_v=\langle T^nv:n\ge0\rangle_{\mathbb Q_\ell}$ carries a semisimple restriction of $T$, then $T$ is semisimple on $V$.

CONVENTION. For an automorphism of a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, "semisimple" means diagonalisable after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; by lemma_5 (eoinm) this is equivalent to semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ itself, and it is the notion appearing in both the hypothesis and the conclusion of the present lemma.

STEP 0 (trivial case). If $V=\{0\}$ then $T=\mathrm{id}_0$, whose matrix in the empty basis is the empty matrix, diagonalisable; there is nothing to prove. Assume $V\ne\{0\}$ from now on.

STEP 1 (each $V_v$ is $T$-stable and $T$ restricts to an automorphism of it). Fix $v\in V$. An arbitrary element of $V_v$ has the form $w=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_nT^nv$ with $a_n\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, and $Tw=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_nT^{n+1}v\in V_v$; so $V_v$ is $T$-stable. Since $V_v\subseteq V$ and $V$ is finite-dimensional, $V_v$ is finite-dimensional; and $T|_{V_v}$ is injective because $T$ is. An injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is bijective, hence $T|_{V_v}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_v)$, as the statement of the lemma asserts.

STEP 2 (reduce the spanning hypothesis to finitely many vectors, and expand to the cyclic subspaces). Put $S=\{v\in V: T|_{V_v}\ \text{is semisimple}\}$. By hypothesis $\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(S)=V$. Because $V$ is finite-dimensional, some finite subset $\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}\subset S$ spans $V$, with $m\ge1$: $V=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb Q_\ell v_j$. Each $v_j$ lies in $V_{v_j}$ (the term $n=0$), so
$$V=\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbb Q_\ell v_j\ \subseteq\ \sum_{j=1}^m V_{v_j}\ \subseteq\ V,$$
hence $V=\sum_{j=1}^m V_{v_j}$. By Step 1 each $V_{v_j}$ is a $T$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace, and by construction ($v_j\in S$) each restriction $T|_{V_{v_j}}$ is semisimple.

STEP 3 (conclusion). Lemma_230 (eoinm) states: if $V_1,\dots,V_r$ are $T$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspaces of $V$ whose sum is all of $V$, and $T|_{V_j}$ is semisimple for every $j$, then $T$ is semisimple on $V$. Applying it with $V_j:=V_{v_j}$ and $r:=m$ yields that $T$ is semisimple on $V$. This proves the lemma.

STEP 4 (self-contained verification of the aggregation step, for completeness). We spell out the linear algebra behind Step 3, which also shows no hypothesis was used vacuously.

Claim (square-free minimal-polynomial criterion). Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $W$ a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space, $U\in\mathrm{End}_F(W)$. Then $U\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable over $\overline F$ if and only if the minimal polynomial $\mu_U\in F[t]$ is a product of distinct monic irreducibles.

Proof of the claim. Choose a basis of $W$ and let $M$ be the matrix of $U$; the same $M$ is the matrix of $\overline U:=U\otimes\mathrm{id}$ in the induced basis of $\overline W=W\otimes_F\overline F$. For $f\in F[t]$, $f(U)=0\iff f(M)=0$ in $\mathrm{Mat}_d(F)\iff f(M)=0$ in $\mathrm{Mat}_d(\overline F)\iff f(\overline U)=0$. Hence $\{f\in\overline F[t]:f(\overline U)=0\}=(\mu_U)\cdot\overline F[t]$, and since $\mu_{\overline U}$ is the monic generator of that ideal, $\mu_{\overline U}=\mu_U$ as a polynomial in $\overline F[t]$.

Separability input: if $p\in F[t]$ is monic irreducible of degree $\ge1$, then $p'\ne0$ (characteristic $0$) and $\deg p'<\deg p$, so $\gcd(p,p')=1$ in $F[t]$ (any common divisor of positive degree would be a multiple of the irreducible $p$, impossible by degree). Hence every root $\lambda\in\overline F$ of $p$ is simple, i.e. $p=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda_p}(t-\lambda)$ in $\overline F[t]$ with $\Lambda_p$ a set of distinct elements.

($\Leftarrow$) Write $\mu_U=\prod_{i=1}^rp_i$ with the $p_i$ distinct monic irreducibles. Their root sets $\Lambda_i\subset\overline F$ are pairwise disjoint: a common root would make $\gcd_{\overline F[t]}(p_i,p_{i'})$ nonconstant, and the gcd computed by the Euclidean algorithm is the same over $F$ and over $\overline F$, contradicting irreducibility/distinctness of $p_i,p_{i'}$. Set $M_i=\prod_{i'\ne i}p_{i'}$. No irreducible divides all of $M_1,\dots,M_r$, so the ideal $(M_1,\dots,M_r)=F[t]$; choose $a_i\in F[t]$ with $\sum_ia_iM_i=1$. Evaluating at $\overline U$ gives $e_i:=a_i(\overline U)M_i(\overline U)$ with $\sum_ie_i=\mathrm{id}$, and for $i\ne j$, $e_ie_j=a_i(\overline U)a_j(\overline U)(M_iM_j)(\overline U)=0$ because $M_iM_j$ is divisible by $\mu_U=\mu_{\overline U}$ and $\mu_{\overline U}(\overline U)=0$. Also $p_i(\overline U)e_i=a_i(\overline U)\mu_{\overline U}(\overline U)=0$, so $e_i(\overline W)\subseteq\ker p_i(\overline U)=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_i}\ker(\overline U-\lambda)$ (the direct-sum decomposition of the kernel follows by the same Bézout argument applied to the pairwise coprime linear factors of $p_i$). Therefore $\overline W=\sum_ie_i(\overline W)$ is contained in, hence equal to, the sum of the eigenspaces $E_\lambda=\ker(\overline U-\lambda)$, and the sum is direct; so $\overline U$ is diagonalisable.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\overline U$ diagonalisable, with (finite) spectrum $\Lambda\subset\overline F$. Then $P:=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(t-\lambda)\in\overline F[t]$ satisfies $P(\overline U)=0$, so $\mu_{\overline U}\mid P$ in $\overline F[t]$; thus $\mu_{\overline U}$ is a product of distinct linear factors. If $\mu_U=\prod_ip_i^{e_i}$ in $F[t]$ had some $e_i\ge2$, take a root $\lambda\in\overline F$ of $p_i$, which is simple by the separability paragraph; then $(t-\lambda)^{e_i}\mid\mu_U=\mu_{\overline U}$ in $\overline F[t]$ with $e_i\ge2$, a contradiction. Hence all $e_i=1$. $\square$ (Claim)

Now apply the claim with $F=\mathbb Q_\ell$, which has characteristic $0$. For each $j$, $T|_{V_{v_j}}$ is semisimple, i.e. diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (this is exactly the content of lemma_5 used in the convention), so $\mu_j:=\mu_{T|_{V_{v_j}}}$ is square-free. Let $\mu\in\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ be the monic least common multiple of $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$. In the UFD $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$ write $\mu_j=\prod_\pi\pi^{e_{j,\pi}}$ with $\pi$ running over monic irreducibles and $e_{j,\pi}\in\{0,1\}$; then $\mu=\prod_\pi\pi^{\max_je_{j,\pi}}$ with $\max_je_{j,\pi}\in\{0,1\}$, so $\mu$ is again square-free. Since $\mu_j\mid\mu$, the operator $\mu(T)$ restricts to $\mu(T|_{V_{v_j}})=0$ on each $V_{v_j}$; as $V=\sum_jV_{v_j}$, $\mu(T)=0$ on all of $V$. Hence $\mu_T\mid\mu$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, and a monic divisor of a square-free polynomial is square-free (its exponents are $\le$ those of $\mu$, hence $\le1$). By the claim, $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e. $T$ is semisimple on $V$, which is the desired conclusion. (The case $V_{v_j}=\{0\}$ causes no trouble: then $\mu_j=1$ and the restriction is semisimple by convention.)

Both Step 3 and Step 4 give the result, so the lemma is proved. $\blacksquare$

lemma_241.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and let \(m\ge 1\) be an integer. Then \(T\) is semisimple (that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)) if and only if the power \(T^{m}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) is semisimple.
lemma_241.proof:
Throughout, $\ell$ is a prime, $V$ a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $m\ge 1$ an integer, and $K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$). For $A\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$ write $A_K:=A\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{End}_K(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K)$. Note the elementary identity $(T^m)_K=(T_K)^m$, which holds because $(A\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(B\otimes\mathrm{id})=(AB)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ for all $A,B$, giving $(T_K)^m=(T^m)_K$ by induction on $m$.

**Step 0 (the zero space).** If $V=\{0\}$, then $T=\mathrm{id}_0$ and $T^m=\mathrm{id}_0$; the empty set is a basis of $V_K=\{0\}$ consisting of eigenvectors for both, so both are diagonalizable and the equivalence holds trivially. Assume henceforth $V\ne\{0\}$; then $\dim_K V_K=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\ge 1$, so $V_K\ne\{0\}$ and minimal polynomials over $K$ of operators on $V_K$ have degree $\ge 1$.

**Step 1 (two linear-algebra facts over $K$, an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$).** Let $W$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, $W\ne\{0\}$, and $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$; let $\mu_A\in K[t]$ be the minimal polynomial of $A$ (the monic generator of $\{p\in K[t]:p(A)=0\}$; it divides every polynomial annihilating $A$).

*Fact 1 (diagonalizability criterion).* $A$ is diagonalizable over $K$ if and only if $\mu_A$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors of $K[t]$.

*Proof of Fact 1.*
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $A$ diagonalizable, and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ be the *distinct* eigenvalues of $A$, with eigenspaces $E_i:=\ker(A-\alpha_i)$.
