Diagonalizability means $W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r E_i$. Put $p(t):=\prod_{i=1}^r(t-\alpha_i)$. For $w=\sum_i w_i$ with $w_i\in E_i$, $p(A)w=\sum_i p(\alpha_i)w_i=0$ since $p(\alpha_i)=0$; hence $p(A)=0$ and $\mu_A\mid p$. Every monic divisor of a product of distinct linear factors over a field is a product of a subset of those factors, so $\mu_A$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\mu_A=\prod_{i=1}^r(t-\alpha_i)$ with the $\alpha_i\in K$ pairwise distinct. For each $i$ set $e_i(t):=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{t-\alpha_j}{\alpha_i-\alpha_j}\in K[t]$; this is well defined because $\alpha_i-\alpha_j\ne 0$ for $i\ne j$. By construction $e_i(\alpha_k)=\delta_{ik}$. We record three properties.
(i) $\sum_{i=1}^r e_i(t)-1$ is a polynomial of degree $\le r-1$ vanishing at the $r$ distinct points $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, hence it is the zero polynomial: $\sum_i e_i=1$ in $K[t]$.
(ii) For $i\ne j$, $e_ie_j$ vanishes at every $\alpha_k$ (at $k=i$ because $e_j(\alpha_i)=0$, at $k=j$ because $e_i(\alpha_j)=0$, at $k\ne i,j$ because both factors contain the term $t-\alpha_k$). By the factor theorem, a polynomial vanishing at $\alpha$ is divisible by $t-\alpha$; iterating over the distinct $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ (after dividing out $t-\alpha_1$, the quotient still vanishes at $\alpha_2\ne\alpha_1$, etc.) shows $e_ie_j$ is divisible by $\mu_A$.
(iii) $(t-\alpha_i)e_i(t)=\big(\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)\big)^{-1}\mu_A(t)$, a scalar multiple of $\mu_A$.
Now put $E_i:=e_i(A)\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$. From (i), $\sum_i E_i=\mathrm{id}_W$; from (ii), $E_iE_j=0$ for $i\ne j$; from (iii), $(A-\alpha_i)E_i=0$, so $E_iW\subseteq\ker(A-\alpha_i)$. Every $w\in W$ equals $\sum_i E_iw$ with $E_iw\in\ker(A-\alpha_i)$, so $W$ is spanned by eigenvectors of $A$, i.e. $A$ is diagonalizable. This proves Fact 1. $\triangleleft$

*Fact 2 (repeated roots detected by the derivative).* Let $0\ne h\in K[t]$, $h(t)=c\prod_{i=1}^{s}(t-\gamma_i)^{d_i}$ with $c\ne 0$, the $\gamma_i\in K$ pairwise distinct and $d_i\ge 1$. Then $\gamma_i$ is a root of $h'$ if and only if $d_i\ge 2$. Indeed, differentiating the product,
$$h'(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{s} d_i (t-\gamma_i)^{d_i-1}\prod_{j\ne i}(t-\gamma_j)^{d_j},$$
and evaluating at $t=\gamma_i$: the $i$-th summand is $0$ if $d_i\ge2$, is $\prod_{j\ne i}(\gamma_i-\gamma_j)^{d_j}\ne0$ if $d_i=1$ (all $\gamma_i-\gamma_j\ne0$), and every other summand ($i'\ne i$) contains the factor $t-\gamma_i$ and vanishes at $\gamma_i$. Hence $h'(\gamma_i)=0$ iff $d_i\ge2$ (note $\mathrm{char}\,K=0$ is used to conclude $d_i\cdot(\text{unit})\ne0$ when $d_i=1$). Consequently $h$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors if and only if $h$ and $h'$ have no common root in $K$. $\triangleleft$

**Step 2 (proof of $\Rightarrow$).** Assume $T$ is semisimple. By lemma_5 (applied to $T$), $T_K$ is diagonalizable on $W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$. Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $W$ with $T_Ke_j=\lambda_je_j$, $\lambda_j\in K$. Then $T_K^me_j=\lambda_j^me_j$ for every $j$, so $T_K^m$ is diagonal in the same basis, hence diagonalizable. Since $T_K^m=(T^m)_K$, lemma_5 applied to $T^m$ gives that $T^m$ is semisimple on $V$.

**Step 3 (proof of $\Leftarrow$).** Assume $T^m$ is semisimple. By lemma_5, $S:=T_K$ satisfies: $S^m=(T^m)_K$ is diagonalizable on $W$.

*Claim 3a.* Let $f:=\mu_{S^m}\in K[t]$. Then $f$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors, and $f(0)\ne0$.
*Proof.* The first statement is Fact 1 applied to the diagonalizable operator $S^m$. For the second, write $f(t)=a_0+a_1t+\cdots+a_dt^d$ with $a_d\ne0$ and $d=\deg f\ge1$ (possible since $W\ne\{0\}$). If $a_0=0$, then $f(t)=t\,q(t)$ with $q(t)=a_1+\cdots+a_dt^{d-1}$ a nonzero polynomial of degree $<d$, and $0=f(S^m)=S^m\circ q(S^m)$. But $S^m$ is invertible ($S=T_K\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$), so $q(S^m)=0$, contradicting the minimality of $f$. Hence $a_0=f(0)\ne0$. $\triangleleft$

*Claim 3b.* The polynomial $g(t):=f(t^m)\in K[t]$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors.
*Proof.* Writing $f=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jt^j$ we have $g=\sum_j a_jt^{mj}$, so $g\ne0$ (its leading coefficient is $a_d\ne0$), and $g(0)=f(0)\ne0$ by Claim 3a. Differentiating,
$$g'(t)=\sum_{j\ge1} mj\,a_j\,t^{mj-1}=m\,t^{m-1}\sum_{j\ge1} j\,a_j\,t^{m(j-1)}=m\,t^{m-1}f'(t^m).$$
Let $\gamma\in K$ be a common root of $g$ and $g'$. Then $f(\gamma^m)=0$, and $0=g'(\gamma)=m\gamma^{m-1}f'(\gamma^m)$. Since $\mathrm{char}K=0$, $m\ne0$ in $K$. If $\gamma=0$, then $0=g(0)=f(0)$, contradicting Claim 3a; so $\gamma\ne0$, whence $f'(\gamma^m)=0$. Thus $\gamma^m$ is a common root of $f$ and $f'$, and by Fact 2 (applied to $h=f$) that would mean $f$ has a repeated root, contradicting Claim 3a. So $g$ and $g'$ have no common root in $K$, and Fact 2 applied to $h=g$ shows $g$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors. $\triangleleft$

*Claim 3c.* $S=T_K$ is diagonalizable over $K$, hence $T$ is semisimple on $V$.
*Proof.* Since $g(S)=f(S^m)=0$ (as $f=\mu_{S^m}$ annihilates $S^m$), the minimal polynomial $\mu_S$ divides $g$ in $K[t]$. By Claim 3b, $g$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors, and so is every monic divisor of $g$ over the field $K$. Thus $\mu_S$ is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors, and Fact 1 applied to $A=S$ shows $S$ is diagonalizable on $W=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$. By lemma_5 (the direction: diagonalizable after scalar extension $\Rightarrow$ semisimple), $T$ is semisimple on $V$. $\triangleleft$

**Step 4 (conclusion).** Step 2 gives semisimplicity of $T\Rightarrow$ semisimplicity of $T^m$, and Step 3 gives the converse. Both implications were proved for every $m\ge1$ (the case $m=1$ is included: then $g=f$ and the argument is tautological). This establishes the equivalence stated in the lemma. $\blacksquare$

lemma_242.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the Poincar\u00e9 duality trace isomorphism normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). For \(0\le n\le 2D\) let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*(y))\) for all \(x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(y\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_242.proof:
We fix the notation of the statement: $q=p^a$, $f:X\to Y$ proper surjective generically finite of degree $d\ge 1$ between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$, $n$ an integer with $0\le n\le 2D$, and $f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ the map whose defining identity is
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*(x)\cup y\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(x\cup f^*(y)\bigr)\qquad\bigl(x\in H^n(X_k),\ y\in H^{2D-n}(Y_k)\bigr).\tag{$*$}
$$
We must prove $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Step 0 (Poincar\u00e9 duality input: the traces are the ones of the statement, and the pairings are perfect).**
Apply lemma_77 with $m=1$ (so $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q$) and $d=D$, to the variety $Y$ and, separately, to the variety $X$; both are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. Its part (a) yields, for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, a canonical isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$$
normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$ for every closed point $z$ of $Z$. This is precisely the normalisation demanded in the present statement (and in lemma_235 and lemma_top_trace_generically_finite), so the three uses of $\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y$ below refer to the same maps. Its part (b) yields that for every $r$ with $0\le r\le 2D$ the pairing
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z:H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2D-r}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\qquad \langle a,b\rangle_Z=\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup b),$$
is a PERFECT pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces.

From perfectness for $Z=Y$ we extract the following cancellation criterion, which is the only consequence of Step 0 we use.

(0.1) *If $u\in H^r_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup w)=0$ for every $w\in H^{2D-r}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, then $u=0$.*

*Proof of (0.1).* Perfectness means that the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map
$$\Phi:H^r(Y_k)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2D-r}(Y_k),\ \mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\bigr),\qquad \Phi(u)(w):=\operatorname{tr}_Y(u\cup w),$$
is an isomorphism; in particular it is injective. The hypothesis says exactly $\Phi(u)=0=\Phi(0)$, hence $u=0$. $\square$

(We also record, for later reference, that $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear and that $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear; these are part of the content of lemma_77(a),(b), the cup product being a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear graded-commutative product on $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.)

**Step 1 (functoriality of the cup product with respect to pullback; no finiteness input needed).**
For every morphism $f:X\to Y$ of schemes, every prime $\ell$ inverted on the base, and every $r,s\ge 0$, one has
$$f^*(a\cup b)=f^*a\cup f^*b\qquad\bigl(a\in H^r(Y_{\bar\eta},\mathbb Q_\ell),\ b\in H^s(Y_{\bar\eta},\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr),$$
i.e. $f^*:H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{\bar\eta},\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\bar\eta},\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a homomorphism of graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebras. This is a basic functoriality property of the cohomology theory, to be quoted rather than derived, and it involves no limit argument and no finiteness hypothesis: the inverse-image functor $f^{-1}$ of the morphism of small \u00e9tale topoi induced by $f$ is exact and strong monoidal ($f^{-1}(\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal G)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }f^{-1}\mathcal F\otimes f^{-1}\mathcal G$, checked on geometric stalks, and $f^{-1}\underline{\mathbb Z}_\ell=\underline{\mathbb Z}_\ell$), while the cup product is the Yoneda product on $\operatorname{Ext}^*$; an exact strong-monoidal functor induces a homomorphism of $\operatorname{Ext}$-algebras, so pullback preserves the product. Passing from the integral $\mathbb Z_\ell$-theory to $\mathbb Q_\ell$-coefficients is by $-\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell$, which is exact and compatible with the product by construction; hence the identity holds in $\mathbb Q_\ell$-cohomology formally. In particular, applied to $Y_k$ and $X_k$ over $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, for all $y\in H^n(Y_k)$ and $w\in H^{2D-n}(Y_k)$,
$$f^*(y\cup w)=f^*y\cup f^*w\quad\text{in } H^{2D}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{1.1}$$

**Step 2 (behaviour of the top-degree trace under $f^*$).**
The hypotheses of lemma_top_trace_generically_finite are satisfied verbatim by the present data: $q=p^a$, $f:X\to Y$ proper surjective generically finite of degree $d\ge1$ between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$, and the traces $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$ (the same normalisation as in Step 0). That lemma states that $\operatorname{tr}_X\circ f^*\circ\operatorname{tr}_Y^{-1}$ is multiplication by $d$ on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$. Rewriting this without inverses: for every $u\in H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*(u)\bigr)=d\cdot \operatorname{tr}_Y(u)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\tag{2.1}$$
where $d$ is viewed as an element of $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$ acting by scalar multiplication on the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$.

**Step 3 (the computation).**
Fix an arbitrary class $y\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. We claim that $f_*(f^*y)=d\cdot y$. By the cancellation criterion (0.1) applied with $r=n$ to $u:=f_*(f^*y)-d\cdot y\in H^n(Y_k)$, it suffices to prove
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((f_*(f^*y)-d\cdot y)\cup w\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for every } w\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{3.0}$$
So let $w\in H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be arbitrary. Note first that $f^*y\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, since $f^*$ preserves cohomological degree; hence $f^*y$ is an admissible first argument $x$ in the defining identity $(*)$ of $f_*$ (the existence and uniqueness of the map $f_*$ satisfying $(*)$ is the content of lemma_235, and $(*)$ is exactly the property assumed in the present statement). Applying $(*)$ with $x=f^*y$ and with $w$ in the role of its second argument gives
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*(f^*y)\cup w\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*y\cup f^*w\bigr).\tag{3.1}$$
Now we transform the right-hand side in two steps:
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*y\cup f^*w\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*(y\cup w)\bigr)\qquad\text{by }(1.1),\tag{3.2}$$
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f^*(y\cup w)\bigr)=d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y(y\cup w)\qquad\text{by }(2.1)\text{ with }u=y\cup w\in H^{2D}(Y_k),\tag{3.3}$$
where $y\cup w\in H^{n+(2D-n)}(Y_k)=H^{2D}(Y_k)$, so that $u$ really lies in the degree to which $(2.1)$ applies. Finally, by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of the cup product, $(d\cdot y)\cup w=d\cdot(y\cup w)$, and by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$,
$$d\cdot\operatorname{tr}_Y(y\cup w)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((d\cdot y)\cup w\bigr).\tag{3.4}$$
Chaining $(3.1)$, $(3.2)$, $(3.3)$, $(3.4)$ and using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ once more to subtract, we obtain
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((f_*(f^*y)-d\cdot y)\cup w\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f_*(f^*y)\cup w\bigr)-\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl((d\cdot y)\cup w\bigr)=0.$$
Since $w$ was arbitrary, $(3.0)$ holds, and $(0.1)$ yields $f_*(f^*y)=d\cdot y$. As $y\in H^n(Y_k)$ was arbitrary,
$$f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}.$$
This is the desired identity; note that the composite is an endomorphism of $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, since $f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Step 4 (case-by-case checks and edge conditions).**
- *Range of $n$.* The statement only concerns $0\le n\le 2D$, and the argument uses the pairing $H^n(Y_k)\times H^{2D-n}(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, which is perfect for exactly these $n$ by lemma_77(b). No other $n$ is claimed.
- *$n=0$.* Then $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (as $Y$ is geometrically connected) and the pairing is $\mathbb Q_\ell\times H^{2D}(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, $\ (\lambda,u)\mapsto\lambda\,\operatorname{tr}_Y(u)$, which is perfect because $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ is an isomorphism; the argument above applies verbatim and gives $f_*f^*=d$ on $\mathbb Q_\ell$, which is the familiar statement that the pushforward of the fundamental class has degree $d$.
- *$n=2D$.* Dually the pairing $H^{2D}(Y_k)\times H^0(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ is perfect by lemma_77(b), and the argument applies verbatim; no separate computation of $f_*$ on top-degree classes is needed.
- *$D=0$.* Then $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension $0$, hence each isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$, $f$ is an isomorphism and $d=1$; the only value of $n$ is $0$, the pairing $H^0(Y_k)\times H^0(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ is perfect, and the argument gives $f_*f^*=1\cdot\mathrm{id}$, which is correct. (Consistently, $\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]=1$ for the unique point $z$.)
- *The prime $\ell$ and possible divisibility of $d$.* At no point is $d$, or any power of $\ell$, inverted: $d$ only ever appears as a scalar $d\in\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$ multiplying classes in the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$. The only cancellation used is the injectivity of $\Phi$ in $(0.1)$, which is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and holds regardless of how $\ell$ sits relative to $d$. Hence the proof is valid even when $\ell\mid d$, where $f_*$ is not a multiple of a section of $f^*$ in any integral model.
- *Dependence on the normalisation.* The identity $(2.1)$ from lemma_top_trace_generically_finite is asserted for the trace maps normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$; by Step 0 the maps $\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y$ of the present statement are exactly those (uniqueness in lemma_77(a) is part of its statement, which constructs the map with that normalisation). Thus the normalisations on the two sides of the chain of equalities in Step 3 agree, and no scalar ambiguity arises.

This completes the proof of $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$... rather, on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, the composite being an endomorphism of $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as noted at the end of Step 3. $\blacksquare$

lemma_245.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(f:A\to B\) be an isogeny of abelian varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\). For \(Z\in\{A,B\}\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\), \(F_A\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(F_B\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_245.proof:
Fix a prime power q = p^a, a prime \ell \neq p, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, an isogeny f : A \to B of abelian varieties over \mathbb F_q, and an integer n \ge 0. Write k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q and \sigma : k \to k, \sigma(c) = c^q, and denote F_A = (\mathrm{id}_{A_k}\times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* on H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and F_B = (\mathrm{id}_{B_k}\times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* on H^n_{\acute et}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). We prove that F_A is semisimple if and only if F_B is semisimple, by showing that the two operators are conjugate via the pullback f^*.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality of the cohomology spaces). An abelian variety over \mathbb F_q is proper, so both A and B are proper varieties over \mathbb F_q. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to X = A and to X = B with K = \mathbb Q_\ell the constant sheaf, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi : F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell (which exists because \mathbb Q_\ell is the constant sheaf and F_X = \mathrm{id}_X \times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma covers the identity on X). The conclusion of lemma_45_finite_frob is that H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. Hence
  V_B := H^n_{\acute et}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)  and  V_A := H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.

Step 2 (the Frobenius maps are invertible). By lemma_6a, for any scheme X over \mathbb F_q the pullback (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^i_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every i (its inverse being (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*). Thus F_A \in \mathrm{GL}(V_A) and F_B \in \mathrm{GL}(V_B).

Step 3 (the isogeny induces a linear isomorphism on cohomology). By lemma_isogeny_cohom_finite_field, since f : A \to B is an isogeny of abelian varieties over \mathbb F_q, for every n \ge 0 the pullback
  f^* = f_k^* : H^n_{\acute et}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. Set \alpha := f^* : V_B \xrightarrow{\sim} V_A.

Step 4 (the pullback intertwines the two Frobenius operators). The morphism f is defined over \mathbb F_q, hence is a morphism of schemes of finite type over \mathbb F_q. Therefore lemma_214, applied with X = A, Y = B and this n, gives exactly
  f_k^* \circ F_B = F_A \circ f_k^*,
that is \alpha \circ F_B = F_A \circ \alpha.
For completeness, let us recall why this identity holds at the level of maps on the base change: the graph of \sigma-equivariance gives a commutative square of \mathbb F_q-schemes
  A_k \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}_{A_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma\ } A_k
  \ \downarrow f_k \qquad\qquad\qquad \downarrow f_k
  B_k \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}_{B_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma\ } B_k,
commutative because f is defined over \mathbb F_q (so f_k \circ (\mathrm{id}_{A_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma) = (\mathrm{id}_{B_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma) \circ f_k as morphisms of k-schemes, both being the base change to k of f along \sigma). Contravariance of \acute etale cohomology turns this commutative square into the claimed operator identity.

Step 5 (conjugate operators have the same semisimplicity status). We now have finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces V_B, V_A, invertible operators F_B, F_A, and a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \alpha : V_B \xrightarrow{\sim} V_A with \alpha \circ F_B = F_A \circ \alpha. This is precisely the hypothesis of lemma_8 (with V = V_B, T_V = F_B, W = V_A, T_W = F_A), whose conclusion is that F_B is semisimple if and only if F_A is semisimple.

For full transparency we spell out the mechanism that lemma_8 encapsulates, so that no step is hidden. From \alpha \circ F_B = F_A \circ \alpha one gets by induction \alpha \circ F_B^{m} = F_A^{m} \circ \alpha for all m \ge 0, hence for every polynomial P(t) \in \mathbb Q_\ell[t], \alpha \circ P(F_B) = P(F_A) \circ \alpha. Taking P to be the minimal polynomial \mu_B of F_B gives P(F_A)\circ\alpha = \alpha\circ P(F_B) = 0, and since \alpha is an isomorphism, P(F_A) = 0; so \mu_A \mid \mu_B. Reversing the roles using \alpha^{-1}\circ F_A = F_B\circ\alpha^{-1} gives \mu_B \mid \mu_A, so \mu_A = \mu_B =: \mu. Base-changing to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, the operators \overline{F}_B and \overline{F}_A are conjugate (by \overline{\alpha} = \alpha\otimes\mathrm{id}), so they are simultaneously triangularisable/diagonalisable and share the same minimal polynomial \mu. By the standard criterion, an operator over a field is diagonalisable if and only if its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct irreducible factors; this criterion depends only on \mu. Hence \overline{F}_A is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell if and only if \overline{F}_B is, i.e. (by the definition of semisimplicity used here, cf. lemma_5) F_A is semisimple on V_A if and only if F_B is semisimple on V_B.

Step 6 (conclusion). Since n \ge 0 was arbitrary, the equivalence holds in every degree: F_A acts semisimply on H^n_{\acute et}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) if and only if F_B acts semisimply on H^n_{\acute et}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). This is exactly the statement of the lemma.

(Remark on scope: the argument used nothing about the isogeny other than that f^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear cohomology isomorphism and that f is defined over \mathbb F_q; in particular the same proof shows the statement for geometric Frobenius as well, since geometric Frobenius is the inverse of arithmetic Frobenius by lemma_6a and inversion preserves semisimplicity.)

lemma_248.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and let \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\). Then \(T\) is semisimple (that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)) if and only if the scalar multiple \(c\,T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) is semisimple.
lemma_248.proof:
We prove: for a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $V$, $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, $T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ if and only if $cT$ is.

**Step 0 (Setup and edge case).** Put $K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$, a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space. Write $A:=T\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ and $A_c:=(cT)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$. Since $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\subset K^{\times}$, for every elementary tensor we have $A_c(v\otimes 1)=(cT v)\otimes 1=c\,(Tv\otimes 1)=c\,A(v\otimes 1)$, and both $A_c$ and $cA$ are $K$-linear, so $A_c=c\,A$ on all of $W$. Note $cT\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ because $c\neq0$ and $T$ is invertible. If $V=0$ then $W=0$ and both operators are (vacuously) diagonalizable, so the statement holds; assume below that eigenspace sums are taken in $W$ (the argument is literally the same when $W=0$).

**Step 1 (Reduction to the algebraically closed field $K$).** Apply lemma_5 to the operator $T$ on $V$: $T$ is semisimple over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ if and only if $A=T\otimes\mathrm{id}_K$ is diagonalizable on $W$. Apply lemma_5 again to the operator $cT$: $cT$ is semisimple over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ if and only if $A_c=(cT)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K=cA$ is diagonalizable on $W$. Hence it suffices to prove the following purely linear-algebraic statement over the algebraically closed field $K$: for $B\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)$ and $c\in K^{\times}$, $B$ is diagonalizable if and only if $cB$ is diagonalizable. (Invertibility of $B$ plays no role in what follows.)

**Step 2 (Two standard facts about eigenspaces).** For $\lambda\in K$ write $W_\lambda(B):=\ker(B-\lambda\,\mathrm{id}_W)$.

*Fact 2a (independence).* If $v_1,\dots,v_r$ are nonzero with $v_j\in W_{\lambda_j}(B)$ for pairwise distinct $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\in K$, then $\{v_1,\dots,v_r\}$ is linearly independent. Proof by induction on $r$. For $r=1$ this is clear. Suppose $r\ge2$ and $\sum_{j=1}^r a_jv_j=0$. Apply $P:=(B-\lambda_2\mathrm{id})\cdots(B-\lambda_r\mathrm{id})$. For $j\ge2$, $(B-\lambda_j\mathrm{id})v_j=0$, and $P$ is a product of commuting factors, so $Pv_j=0$ for $j\ge2$. Also $Pv_1=\prod_{j=2}^r(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)v_1$. Hence $0=\sum a_jPv_j=a_1\prod_{j=2}^r(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)v_1$, and the product is a nonzero element of the field $K$ since $\lambda_1\ne\lambda_j$; thus $a_1=0$. Then $\sum_{j=2}^ra_jv_j=0$ and the induction hypothesis gives $a_2=\dots=a_r=0$. Consequently the sum $\sum_{\lambda\in K}W_\lambda(B)$ is direct, and only finitely many $\lambda$ have $W_\lambda(B)\ne0$ (otherwise Fact 2a would produce linearly independent sets of arbitrarily large size in the finite-dimensional space $W$).

*Fact 2b (criterion).* $B$ is diagonalizable over $K$ if and only if $W=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in K}W_\lambda(B)$. Proof: if $B$ is diagonalizable, $W$ has an eigenbasis, and each basis vector lies in some $W_\lambda(B)$, so $W=\sum_\lambda W_\lambda(B)$, which is direct by Fact 2a. Conversely, if $W=\bigoplus_\lambda W_\lambda(B)$, then only finitely many summands are nonzero, and concatenating a $K$-basis of each nonzero $W_\lambda(B)$ yields a basis of $W$ consisting of eigenvectors, i.e. $B$ is diagonalizable.

**Step 3 (The eigenspaces of $B$ and of $cB$ coincide, up to relabelling).** Fix $\mu\in K$. Since $c\neq0$ we have, as endomorphisms of $W$,
$$cB-\mu\,\mathrm{id}_W=c\,\bigl(B-\mu c^{-1}\mathrm{id}_W\bigr),$$
and multiplication by the nonzero scalar $c$ is a $K$-linear automorphism of $W$, hence an isomorphism $\ker(B-\mu c^{-1}\mathrm{id})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ker(cB-\mu\,\mathrm{id})$ whose inverse is multiplication by $c^{-1}$. Therefore
$$W_\mu(cB)=\ker(cB-\mu\,\mathrm{id}_W)=\ker(B-\mu c^{-1}\,\mathrm{id}_W)=W_{\mu/c}(B).$$
The map $\mu\mapsto\mu/c$ is a bijection $K\to K$ (inverse $\lambda\mapsto c\lambda$). It follows that the two families of subspaces $\{W_\mu(cB)\}_{\mu\in K}$ and $\{W_\lambda(B)\}_{\lambda\in K}$ are the same family, indexed bijectively, and hence
$$\bigoplus_{\mu\in K}W_\mu(cB)=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in K}W_{\lambda}(B)$$
as subspaces of $W$: directness on each side is Fact 2a, and the two internal sums are termwise equal under the bijection. (Note also that $\mu=0$ gives $W_0(cB)=W_0(B)$, so the kernel is treated correctly as well.)

**Step 4 (Conclusion of the reduction).** Applying Fact 2b to $B$ and to $cB$, and using the equality of Step 3,
$$B\text{ diagonalizable}\iff W=\textstyle\bigoplus_{\lambda}W_\lambda(B)\iff W=\bigoplus_{\mu}W_\mu(cB)\iff cB\text{ diagonalizable}.$$
Taking $B=A$ and using $A_c=cA$ together with Step 1 gives exactly: $T$ semisimple $\Leftrightarrow cT$ semisimple. This completes the proof.

**Step 5 (Independent cross-check via minimal polynomials).** Over the algebraically closed field $K$, write the minimal polynomial of $A$ as $m_A(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(t-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$ with the $\lambda_i$ pairwise distinct and $d:=\sum_i e_i=\deg m_A$. Set $q(t):=\prod_{i=1}^s(t-c\lambda_i)^{e_i}$; then $q(cA)=\prod_i(cA-c\lambda_i)^{e_i}=c^{d}\prod_i(A-\lambda_i)^{e_i}=c^{d}m_A(A)=0$, so $m_{cA}\mid q$. Reversing the roles of $A$ and $cA$ with the scalar $c^{-1}$ gives $m_A\mid t\mapsto m_{cA}(ct)/\text{leading coeff.}$, hence $\deg m_A\le\deg m_{cA}$ and therefore $m_{cA}=q$. In particular $m_{cA}$ is squarefree (all $e_i=1$) if and only if $m_A$ is squarefree; and over the algebraically closed field $K$ an operator is diagonalizable exactly when its minimal polynomial is squarefree. This again yields $A$ diagonalizable $\Leftrightarrow$ $cA$ diagonalizable, in agreement with Steps 2--4, and also shows the eigenvalues are exactly $\{c\lambda_i\}$, matching the eigenspace computation of Step 3.

lemma_249.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(A\) be an abelian variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(T_\ell(A_k)=\varprojlim_m A[\ell^m](k)\) with bonding maps \(x\mapsto \ell x\), let \(V_\ell(A_k)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(A_k)\), and let \(\pi_A:A\to A\) be the \(q\)-power Frobenius endomorphism over \(\mathbb F_q\), which induces an automorphism of \(T_\ell(A_k)\) and hence a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A\) of \(V_\ell(A_k)\). Then \(\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A\) is semisimple, that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_249.proof:
We prove that $\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A\in\mathrm{GL}(V_\ell(A_k))$ is semisimple (equivalently diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$), by reducing along a Poincaré complete-reducibility isogeny to the case of a simple abelian variety, where it is lemma_92.

STEP 0 (Notation, functoriality, finite dimensionality). For an abelian variety $Z$ over $\mathbb F_q$ write $T_\ell(Z):=\varprojlim_m Z[\ell^m](k)$ with bonding maps $x\mapsto \ell x$, and $V_\ell(Z):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(Z)$; these are the modules of the statement when $Z=A$. A homomorphism $f:Z\to Z'$ over $\mathbb F_q$ maps $Z[\ell^m](k)$ into $Z'[\ell^m](k)$ compatibly with the bonding maps, hence induces a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-linear map $T_\ell(f)$ and a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $V_\ell(f):=\mathrm{id}\otimes T_\ell(f)$; clearly $V_\ell(f\circ g)=V_\ell(f)\circ V_\ell(g)$ and $V_\ell(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$. In particular $V_\ell(\pi_Z)=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_Z$ is the operator of the statement for $Z=A$.
By lemma_tate_rank applied to the abelian variety $Z_k$ over the algebraically closed field $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ (with $\ell\neq p=\mathrm{char}\,k$), $T_\ell(Z_k)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2\dim Z$; hence $V_\ell(Z)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space, $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V_\ell(Z)=2\dim Z$. For $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ (the trivial abelian variety) the modules are $0$.

STEP 1 (The zero-dimensional case). If $\dim A=0$ then $A_k=\operatorname{Spec}k$, $A[\ell^m](k)=\{0\}$ for all $m$, so $T_\ell(A_k)=0$ and $V_\ell(A_k)=0$. The only automorphism of the zero space is diagonalisable with respect to the empty basis. Henceforth assume $g:=\dim A\ge 1$.

STEP 2 (Poincaré complete reducibility over $\mathbb F_q$). Apply lemma_poincare_reducibility with the field $\mathbb F_q$: there are an integer $r\ge 1$ and abelian $\mathbb F_q$-subvarieties $B_1,\dots,B_r\subseteq A$, each simple over $\mathbb F_q$ (no nonzero proper abelian $\mathbb F_q$-subvariety), such that the addition homomorphism
$$\sigma:B:=B_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}B_r\longrightarrow A,\qquad (b_1,\dots,b_r)\longmapsto \textstyle\sum_i b_i,$$
which is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$ (the group law of $A$ and the inclusions are defined over $\mathbb F_q$), is an isogeny. Since $\sigma$ is surjective with finite kernel, $\dim B=\sum_i\dim B_i=\dim A=g$.

STEP 3 (Frobenius is natural, commutes with products, and is a homomorphism). For an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ let $F^q_Z$ denote the absolute $q$-Frobenius (identity on the underlying topological space, $a\mapsto a^q$ on $\mathcal O_Z$). Because the $q$-power Frobenius of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ is the identity, the $q$-power Frobenius endomorphism $\pi_Z$ is exactly $F^q_Z$.
(a) Naturality: if $f:Z\to W$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, then $f\circ F^q_Z=F^q_W\circ f$. Indeed both composites induce the same continuous map $|f|$ (each $F^q$ is the identity on points), and for $V\subseteq W$ open, $s\in\mathcal O_W(V)$, $U=f^{-1}V$, the two pullbacks of $s$ to $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ are $(f^\#s)^q$ and $f^\#(s^q)=f^\#(s)^q$, which agree since $f^\#$ is a ring homomorphism.
(b) Products: applying (a) to the projections $\mathrm{pr}_i:B\to B_i$ gives $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ F^q_B=F^q_{B_i}\circ\mathrm{pr}_i=\mathrm{pr}_i\circ\bigl(\prod_i F^q_{B_i}\bigr)$; by the universal property of the product, $F^q_B=\prod_i F^q_{B_i}$, i.e.
$$\pi_B=\pi_{B_1}\times\cdots\times\pi_{B_r}.\tag{3.1}$$
(c) Applying (a) to $\sigma$ (a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$) gives $\sigma\circ\pi_B=\pi_A\circ\sigma$.\tag{3.2}
(d) Group homomorphism: applying (a) to the group law $m_Z:Z\times Z\to Z$ and using (b) for $Z\times Z$, $m_Z\circ(\pi_Z\times\pi_Z)=\pi_Z\circ m_Z$; so every $\pi_Z$ is a homomorphism of group schemes.

STEP 4 (Each $\pi_Z$ is an isogeny, and $V_\ell(\pi_Z)$ is invertible). Let $Z/\mathbb F_q$ be any abelian variety. (i) $\pi_Z=F^q_Z$ is the identity on the underlying topological space, hence surjective. (ii) It is finite: take an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq Z$; since $F^q$ is the identity on points, $(F^q)^{-1}U=U$, and the corresponding ring map is $R\to R$, $r\mapsto r^q$, exhibiting $R$ as an algebra over itself via the subring $R^q$ of $q$-th powers. Now $R$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb F_q$-algebra, say $R=\mathbb F_q[x_1,\dots,x_s]$; since $\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_q^q\subseteq R^q$, $R=R^q[x_1,\dots,x_s]$, and because $x_i^q\in R^q$ this is generated as an $R^q$-module by the finitely many monomials $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_s^{e_s}$ with $0\le e_i<q$. Thus $R$ is a finite $R^q$-module and $\pi_Z$ is a finite morphism. (iii) $\ker\pi_Z=\pi_Z^{-1}(e)$ (with $e:\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\to Z$ the identity section) is a fibre of a finite morphism, hence a finite $\mathbb F_q$-scheme. By (i)--(iii) and (d) of Step 3, $\pi_Z$ is a surjective homomorphism with finite kernel, i.e. an isogeny.
Apply lemma_120 to the isogeny $\pi_Z:Z\to Z$ (the field is $\mathbb F_q$, in which $\ell\neq p$ is invertible, and its algebraic closure is our $k$): there exist a homomorphism $g:Z\to Z$ and an integer $n\ge1$ with $\pi_Z\circ g=[n]_Z$ and $g\circ\pi_Z=[n]_Z$, and $V_\ell(\pi_Z)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism with inverse $\tfrac1n V_\ell(g)$. Thus $V_\ell(\pi_Z)\in\mathrm{GL}(V_\ell(Z))$ for $Z=A$ and for each $B_i$.

STEP 5 ($V_\ell$ of a product is the direct sum of the $V_\ell$'s, compatibly with Frobenius). For each $m\ge1$: $k$-points commute with finite products, so $B(k)=\prod_i B_i(k)$; and $[\ell^m]_B=\prod_i[\ell^m]_{B_i}$, since $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ[\ell^m]_B=[\ell^m]_{B_i}\circ\mathrm{pr}_i$ (naturality of $[\ell^m]$ for the homomorphisms $\mathrm{pr}_i$) and the universal property of the product applies as in Step 3(b). Hence $y\in B(k)$ satisfies $\ell^m y=0$ if and only if each component does, giving a canonical isomorphism of abelian groups $\prod_i B_i[\ell^m](k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }B[\ell^m](k)$. These isomorphisms are compatible with the bonding maps $x\mapsto\ell x$ (again because $[\ell]$ on a product is the product of the $[\ell]$'s). Passing to $\varprojlim_m$ (limits commute with finite products, and a finite product of abelian groups is their direct sum) gives a $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module isomorphism $\bigoplus_i T_\ell(B_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }T_\ell(B)$; tensoring with $\mathbb Q_\ell$, which commutes with finite direct sums, gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
$$\theta:\bigoplus_{i=1}^r V_\ell(B_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V_\ell(B).$$
Under $\theta$, the automorphism $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ corresponds to $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$: indeed by (3.1) $\pi_B=\prod_i\pi_{B_i}$, and the map this induces on $B[\ell^m](k)=\prod_i B_i[\ell^m](k)$ acts on the $i$-th factor as $\pi_{B_i}$ and preserves each factor's torsion subgroup. That is,
$$\theta\circ\Bigl(\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})\Bigr)=V_\ell(\pi_B)\circ\theta.\tag{5.1}$$

STEP 6 (Semisimplicity on $V_\ell(B)$). Fix $i$. The variety $B_i$ is a simple abelian variety over $\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_{q^1}$ and $\pi_{B_i}$ is its $q^1$-power Frobenius endomorphism. Applying lemma_92 with $m=1$ (so that $\overline{\mathbb F_{q^1}}=k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and the Tate module of lemma_92 is exactly $V_\ell((B_i)_k)$ with bonding maps $x\mapsto\ell x$) we obtain that $V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_{B_i}$ is semisimple on the finite-dimensional space $V_\ell(B_i)$ (finite-dimensionality: Step 0). By Step 4 each $V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ is invertible. Lemma_9, applied to the family $\{V_\ell(B_i),V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})\}_{i=1}^r$, gives that $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$ is semisimple on $\bigoplus_i V_\ell(B_i)$. Transporting along the intertwining isomorphism (5.1) by means of lemma_8 (with $V=\bigoplus_i V_\ell(B_i)$, $T_V=\bigoplus_i V_\ell(\pi_{B_i})$, $W=V_\ell(B)$, $T_W=V_\ell(\pi_B)$, $\alpha=\theta$; all hypotheses — finite dimensionality, invertibility, intertwining — are available from Steps 0, 4, 5) we conclude that $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is semisimple on $V_\ell(B)$.

STEP 7 (Descent along the isogeny $\sigma$). By lemma_120 applied to the isogeny $\sigma:B\to A$ of Step 2, $V_\ell(\sigma):V_\ell(B)\to V_\ell(A)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. Functoriality of $V_\ell$ together with the relation (3.2), $\sigma\circ\pi_B=\pi_A\circ\sigma$, yields
$$V_\ell(\sigma)\circ V_\ell(\pi_B)=V_\ell(\pi_A)\circ V_\ell(\sigma).$$
Now apply lemma_8 with $V=V_\ell(B)$, $T_V=V_\ell(\pi_B)$, $W=V_\ell(A_k)$, $T_W=V_\ell(\pi_A)=\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$, $\alpha=V_\ell(\sigma)$ (finite-dimensionality by Step 0, invertibility by Step 4). Since $V_\ell(\pi_B)$ is semisimple by Step 6, so is $\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ on $V_\ell(A_k)$.

STEP 8 (Conclusion). By Step 0, $V_\ell(A_k)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, and lemma_5 states that for such a space a linear operator is semisimple if and only if its base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable. The semisimplicity obtained in Step 7 therefore says exactly that $\mathrm{id}\otimes\pi_A$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which is the claim. Together with Step 1 this covers all abelian varieties $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$. $\blacksquare$

lemma_250.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_X\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_250.proof:
Let U = H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell) and V = H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell(1)). We prove that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius F_V on V is semisimple, and then remove the Tate twist.

1. Picard variety. Since X is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_q, X_k is smooth projective geometrically connected over k. Let P = Pic^0_{X/F_q} be the Picard variety, an abelian variety over F_q, and let pi_P be its q-power Frobenius endomorphism. By lemma_205 applied to X_k, NS(X_k) = Pic(X_k)/P(k) is finitely generated.

2. Integral Kummer identification. By lemma_195, there is a Z_ell-linear isomorphism phi: H^1_et(X_k, Z_ell(1)) -> T_ell(P_k) such that phi o F_Z = pi_P o phi, where F_Z is the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^1_et(X_k, Z_ell(1)).

3. Rationalization. By lemma_tate_rank, T_ell(P_k) is a free Z_ell-module of finite rank; hence H^1_et(X_k, Z_ell(1)) is finite free. By the usual definition of rational ell-adic cohomology, H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell(1)) is H^1_et(X_k, Z_ell(1)) tensor Q_ell. Tensoring phi with Q_ell gives a Q_ell-linear isomorphism phi_Q: V -> V_ell(P_k) = Q_ell tensor T_ell(P_k), and it satisfies phi_Q o F_V = (id tensor pi_P) o phi_Q.

4. Semisimplicity on V. By lemma_249, id tensor pi_P is semisimple on V_ell(P_k). By lemma_8, because phi_Q intertwines F_V with id tensor pi_P, F_V is semisimple on V.

5. Relation with the untwisted cohomology. The convention for arithmetic Frobenius on Tate twists used in the library is recorded in lemma_78: for every j, F acts on Q_ell(j) by q^{-j}. In particular, for j=1, F acts on Q_ell(1) by q^{-1} id. Cohomology with a constant finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space is obtained by tensoring cohomology with Q_ell coefficients with that vector space, and the Frobenius acts diagonally. Choose a nonzero vector e in Q_ell(1). The map U -> V, u -> u tensor e, is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism, and under this identification F_V(u tensor e) = F_U(u) tensor q^{-1} e = q^{-1}(F_U(u) tensor e). Therefore, transported to U, F_V = q^{-1} F_U. Since ell != p, q is a unit in Q_ell, so q^{-1} is a nonzero scalar.

6. Scalar multiple. By lemma_248, an operator T is semisimple if and only if cT is semisimple for any c in Q_ell^times. Applying this with T = F_U and c = q^{-1}, the semisimplicity of F_V = q^{-1}F_U implies the semisimplicity of F_U. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemma_good_quotient_finite_surjective.statement: Let k be a field, let G be a finite group acting by k-automorphisms on a k-scheme Y of finite type, and let pi: Y -> Z be a good quotient for this action, that is, pi is affine, satisfies pi \circ g = pi for every g \in G, and the induced homomorphism \mathcal{O}_Z \to (\pi_*\mathcal{O}_Y)^G of sheaves of rings is an isomorphism. Then pi is finite and surjective.
lemma_good_quotient_finite_surjective.proof:
PROOF. The statement is purely local-on-the-base commutative algebra plus the definition of a good quotient; none of the Frobenius-semisimplicity lemmas in the corpus is used. We first collect the needed algebraic facts (Part I), then prove the claim (Part II).

================================================================
PART I. PRELIMINARIES
================================================================

Standing conventions. All rings are commutative with 1 and all homomorphisms preserve 1; S_f denotes the localisation of S at f. For an affine scheme X = Spec S and h \in S we use the standard identification D(h) = Spec S_h and hence \Gamma(D(h), O_X) = S_h. Saying that elements f_1,...,f_s of a ring S \"generate the unit ideal\" means (f_1,...,f_s) = S; for s = 0 this reads 1 = 0, i.e. S = 0, equivalently Spec S = \emptyset. We use the following concrete formulation of the hypotheses: \"Y is of finite type over k\" means that Y is a k-scheme admitting a FINITE affine open cover Y = \cup_{i=1}^{m} Spec R_i with each R_i a finitely generated k-algebra (this is the usual definition of a morphism of finite type, specialised to S = Spec k: locally of finite type plus quasi-compact). A morphism f: X \to S is called FINITE if S has an affine open cover by U with f^{-1}U affine, say f^{-1}U = Spec T, and \Gamma(U, O_S) \to T making T a finite \Gamma(U,O_S)-module (the usual definition; it is local on the target by construction).

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1 (patching with coefficients in the small ring).
Let C \subseteq B be subrings (with the same 1) and let f_1,...,f_s \in C. Suppose
 (i) the f_t generate the unit ideal of C;
 (ii) for each t the canonical map C_{f_t} \to B_{f_t} is surjective;
 (iii) if s = 0 then B = 0.
Then C = B.

Proof. If s = 0, (iii) gives B = 0, and a subring C \subseteq 0 with 1_C = 1_B is 0, so C = B. Assume s \ge 1. Since C \subseteq B it suffices to show every b \in B lies in C. Fix t. By (ii), b/1 \in B_{f_t} is the image of some c_t/f_t^{n_t} with c_t \in C, n_t \ge 0. Equality in B_{f_t} means, by the definition of localisation, that there is r_t \ge 0 with f_t^{r_t}(f_t^{n_t} b - c_t) = 0 in B. Put N_t := r_t + n_t \ge 0 and c'_t := f_t^{r_t} c_t \in C. Then
   (*)            f_t^{N_t} b = c'_t \in C        for each t = 1,...,s.
Claim: f_1^{N_1},...,f_s^{N_s} generate the unit ideal of C. Indeed, by (i) 1 = \sum_t e_t f_t with e_t \in C, hence 1 = 1^M = (\sum_t e_t f_t)^M with M := N_1 + ... + N_s. Expanding, 1 is a C-linear combination of monomials \prod_t (e_t f_t)^{a_t} of total degree \sum_t a_t = M; since M = \sum_t N_t, some a_t \ge N_t, and such a monomial equals (\prod_u e_u^{a_u} f_u^{a_u - N_t} \cdot [f_t^{N_t}]), i.e. is divisible by f_t^{N_t} for that t. Hence 1 = \sum_t \varepsilon_t f_t^{N_t} with \varepsilon_t \in C. Therefore, using (*),
   b = 1 \cdot b = \sum_t \varepsilon_t (f_t^{N_t} b) = \sum_t \varepsilon_t c'_t \in C,
as all summands lie in the ring C. So C = B. \square

(Remarks on what is NOT used: no Reynolds/averaging operator, and no hypothesis on char k relative to |G|; and B/C is never treated as a B-module — the coefficients used are the \varepsilon_t \in C.)

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 2 (finite generation patches over a principal cover).
Let A \to B be a ring map, and let f_1,...,f_s \in B generate the unit ideal of B. If each B_{f_t} is a finitely generated A-algebra, then B is a finitely generated A-algebra.

Proof. If s = 0 then 1 = 0 in B, i.e. B = 0, and B is generated over A by the empty set (the image of A in 0 is 0 = B). Assume s \ge 1. Finite generation of B over A depends only on the image of A in B, so we may replace A by that image and assume A \subseteq B. For each t choose A-algebra generators \xi_{t,1},...,\xi_{t,n_t} of B_{f_t}; write \xi_{t,u} = a_{t,u}/f_t^{m_{t,u}} with a_{t,u} \in B, m_{t,u} \ge 0. Choose g_t \in B with 1 = \sum_{t=1}^{s} g_t f_t, and set
   C := A[f_1,...,f_s, (a_{t,u})_{1\le t\le s,1\le u\le n_t}, g_1,...,g_s] \subseteq B.
Then f_t \in C and the relation 1 = \sum_t g_t f_t holds inside C (all g_t were adjoined), so the f_t generate the unit ideal of C: hypothesis (i) of Lemma 1. Also C_{f_t} \to B_{f_t} is surjective, because its image is an A-subalgebra of B_{f_t} containing 1/f_t and every a_{t,u}, hence containing \xi_{t,u} = a_{t,u}/f_t^{m_{t,u}} for all u, and these generate B_{f_t} over A: hypothesis (ii). Hypothesis (iii) is void since s \ge 1. Lemma 1 gives C = B, and C is generated over A by the finitely many elements f_t, a_{t,u}, g_t. \square

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 3 (quasi-compact opens of an affine scheme).
If X = Spec R and U \subseteq X is a quasi-compact open, then U = D(r_1) \cup ... \cup D(r_t) for some r_1,...,r_t \in R.

Proof. For each p \in U choose r_p \in R with p \in D(r_p) \subseteq U (principal opens form a basis). {D(r_p)}_{p \in U} is an open cover of U, and U is quasi-compact, so finitely many, D(r_1),...,D(r_t), cover U. \square

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 4 (Hilbert basis theorem; opens of noetherian affines).
(a) If R is noetherian then R[x] is noetherian. (b) If R is noetherian then every open subset of Spec R is quasi-compact. (c) Every finitely generated k-algebra is noetherian.

Proof of (a). Let I \lhd R[x]. For n \ge 0 set L_n := {a \in R : a = 0, or a is the leading coefficient of some f \in I with deg f = n}.
* L_n is an ideal. Take a, b \in L_n and r \in R. If a \ne 0, a = LC(f) with f \in I, deg f = n; then rf \in I and LC(rf) = ra if ra \ne 0 (else ra = 0 \in L_n), so ra \in L_n. Similarly, if a, b \ne 0 come from f, g of degree n, then f + g, f - g \in I; if LC(f \pm g) \ne 0 it has degree n and equals a \pm b, and if it is 0 then a \pm b = 0; in both cases a \pm b \in L_n. Hence L_n is an ideal.
* L_0 \subseteq L_1 \subseteq ... : if a \in L_n is LC(f) with deg f = n, then xf \in I has degree n+1 and leading coefficient a, so a \in L_{n+1}.
Thus L := \cup_n L_n is an ideal, and the chain stabilises: there is N with L_n = L_N for all n \ge N.
* L is finitely generated: L = (a_1,...,a_r) with a_\ell = LC(f_\ell), f_\ell \in I, deg f_\ell = n_\ell. Let d := max(N, n_1,...,n_r). Then L = L_d: L_d \subseteq L trivially, and each generator a_\ell \in L_{n_\ell} \subseteq L_d, with L_d an ideal.
* For each n < d, L_n is an ideal of the noetherian ring R, so L_n = (b_{n,1},...,b_{n,t_n}) with b_{n,h} = LC(g_{n,h}) for suitable g_{n,h} \in I of degree n (by definition of L_n).
Claim: I = (f_1,...,f_r, g_{n,h} : n < d, 1 \le h \le t_n) R[x]. The \supseteq is clear. For f \in I, induct on n := deg f. If n \ge d, then LC(f) =: a \in L_n = L_d = L = \sum_\ell R a_\ell, so a = \sum_\ell c_\ell a_\ell, and f' := f - \sum_\ell c_\ell x^{n - n_\ell} f_\ell \in I (note n \ge d \ge n_\ell, so the exponents are \ge 0) has deg f' < n. If n < d, then a \in L_n = \sum_h R b_{n,h}, a = \sum_h d_h b_{n,h}, and f' := f - \sum_h d_h g_{n,h} \in I has deg f' < n. In both cases the induction gives f' in the right-hand side, hence f as well. So I is finitely generated, and R[x] is noetherian.

Proof of (b). Let U \subseteq Spec R be open; write U = \cup_{\alpha} D(f_\alpha) with principal opens. The ideal J := (f_\alpha : \alpha) is finitely generated, J = (f_{\alpha_1},...,f_{\alpha_t}). Then Spec R \ U = \cap_\alpha V(f_\alpha) = V(J) = V(f_{\alpha_1},...,f_{\alpha_t}) = Spec R \ \cup_{\ell=1}^{t} D(f_{\alpha_\ell}), so U = \cup_{\ell=1}^{t} D(f_{\alpha_\ell}) is a finite union of principal opens, hence quasi-compact.

Proof of (c). A field k is noetherian (its only ideals are 0 and k). By (a) and induction on m, k[x_1,...,x_m] is noetherian. A finitely generated k-algebra is a quotient k[x_1,...,x_m]/I, and a quotient of a noetherian ring is noetherian (ideals of the quotient correspond to ideals containing I). \square

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 5 (global sections of an affine open of a finite type k-scheme).
Let Y be a k-scheme of finite type and let V \subseteq Y be an open subscheme which is affine, V = Spec B. Then B is a finitely generated k-algebra.

Proof. If V = \emptyset then B = 0, generated over k by the empty set. Assume V \ne \emptyset.
(1) Take a finite affine open cover Y = \cup_{i=1}^{m} Y_i with Y_i = Spec R_i and R_i a finitely generated k-algebra.
(2) By Lemma 4(c) and 4(b), every open subset of Y_i is quasi-compact. Hence W_i := V \cap Y_i is quasi-compact, and by Lemma 3, W_i = \cup_{j=1}^{n_i} D_{Y_i}(f_{ij}) for some f_{ij} \in R_i. Put W_{ij} := D_{Y_i}(f_{ij}) = Spec S_{ij} with S_{ij} = (R_i)_{f_{ij}} = R_i[T]/(f_{ij}T - 1), a finitely generated k-algebra. The W_{ij} (i = 1..m, j = 1..n_i) form a FINITE cover of V, because V \subseteq \cup_i Y_i and V = \cup_i W_i.
(3) Each W_{ij} is affine, hence quasi-compact; as a quasi-compact open subset of the affine scheme V = Spec B, Lemma 3 gives W_{ij} = \cup_{u=1}^{t_{ij}} D_V(b_{ij,u}) with b_{ij,u} \in B. These principal opens cover V, so the finite family {b_{ij,u}} generates the unit ideal of B.
(4) Fix (i,j,u) and write C := B_{b_{ij,u}} = \Gamma(D_V(b_{ij,u}), O_Y). The open D_V(b_{ij,u}) is quasi-compact (it is affine) and is contained in W_{ij} = Spec S_{ij}; by Lemma 3, D_V(b_{ij,u}) = \cup_{v=1}^{w} D_{W_{ij}}(s_v) for some s_v \in S_{ij}. Let \bar s_v be the image of s_v in \Gamma(D_V(b_{ij,u})) = C. As subsets of Spec C, D_C(\bar s_v) = D_V(b_{ij,u}) \cap D_{W_{ij}}(s_v) = D_{W_{ij}}(s_v), so the D_C(\bar s_v) cover Spec C and the \bar s_v generate the unit ideal of C. Moreover
      C_{\bar s_v} = \Gamma(D_C(\bar s_v)) = \Gamma(D_{W_{ij}}(s_v)) = (S_{ij})_{s_v},
which is a finitely generated k-algebra (a localisation of a finitely generated k-algebra). Lemma 2 applied to k \to C and the \bar s_v shows that C is a finitely generated k-algebra.
(5) Finally apply Lemma 2 to k \to B and the elements b_{ij,u}: they generate the unit ideal of B by (3), and B_{b_{ij,u}} = C is a finitely generated k-algebra by (4). Hence B is a finitely generated k-algebra. \square

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 6 (integral + finitely generated = finite).
Let A \subseteq B be rings with B = A[\beta_1,...,\beta_r] and each \beta_i integral over A. Then B is a finite A-module.

Proof. First, if D = C[\gamma] with \gamma integral over C, say \gamma^d = c_0 + c_1\gamma + ... + c_{d-1}\gamma^{d-1}, then D = \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} C\gamma^j: every element of D is P(\gamma) with P \in C[T], and by induction on deg P the relation rewrites T^m (m \ge d) as \sum_{j<d} c_j T^{j+m-d}, a combination of strictly smaller degrees. Now induct on i: A[\beta_1] is a finite A-module by the preceding paragraph; \beta_{i+1} is integral over A, hence over A[\beta_1,...,\beta_i] (the same monic polynomial has coefficients in A \subseteq A[\beta_1,...,\beta_i]), so A[\beta_1,...,\beta_{i+1}] is a finite A[\beta_1,...,\beta_i]-module; and a module finite over a module-finite algebra is module finite (products of finite generating sets generate). Thus B is a finite A-module. \square

----------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 7 (lying over).
Let A \subseteq B be an integral extension of rings with B \ne 0. Then Spec B \to Spec A is surjective.

Proof. Let p \in Spec A and S := A \ p (which contains 1, so S \ne \emptyset). First, S^{-1}B \ne 0: if 1 = 0 in S^{-1}B there is s \in S with s \cdot 1_B = 0 in B; since A is a SUBRING of B with the same 1, s = 0 in A, but 0 \in p, contradicting s \in S. Choose a maximal ideal m of the nonzero ring S^{-1}B (Zorn's lemma). Localisations of integral extensions are integral: b/s = (b/1)\cdot(s/1)^{-1}, where b/1 is integral over A_p (same monic equation, coefficients now in A_p) and (s/1)^{-1} \in A_p, and the elements of S^{-1}B integral over A_p form a subring containing A_p and all b/1. Let q := m \cap A_p. Then A_p/q \hookrightarrow (S^{-1}B)/m is an integral extension with the right-hand side a field; a domain D integral over which a field K is integral is itself a field: for 0 \ne d \in D, d^{-1} \in K is integral over D, so (d^{-1})^n + a_{n-1}d^{-(n-1)} + ... + a_0 = 0 with a_i \in D, and multiplying by d^{n-1} gives d^{-1} = -(a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}d + ... + a_0 d^{n-1}) \in D. Hence A_p/q is a field, q is maximal; as A_p is local with maximal ideal pA_p and q \subseteq pA_p \ne A_p, we get q = pA_p. Finally Q := {b \in B : b/1 \in m} is a prime of B with Q \cap A = {a \in A : a/1 \in pA_p} = p (contraction of pA_p to A is p, as p is saturated for S). So p is in the image. \square

================================================================
PART II. THE GOOD QUOTIENT IS FINITE AND SURJECTIVE
================================================================

Notation. Write the action as G \ni g \mapsto \varphi_g \in Aut_k(Y), with \varphi_{gh} = \varphi_g \circ \varphi_h. For a ring S with a group action we write S^G for the subring of invariants.

Step 1 (invariants of \pi_*O_Y are computed sectionwise). Let U \subseteq Z be open. Since \pi \circ \varphi_g = \pi, a point y with \pi(y) \in U satisfies \pi(\varphi_g(y)) = \pi(y) \in U, so \varphi_g(\pi^{-1}U) \subseteq \pi^{-1}U; applying this to g^{-1} gives equality, hence each \varphi_g restricts to an automorphism of the open subscheme \pi^{-1}U. Pullback therefore gives a left action of G on the ring O_Y(\pi^{-1}U) = (\pi_*O_Y)(U), namely g \cdot s := \varphi_{g^{-1}}^{*}(s). The presheaf U \mapsto (\pi_*O_Y)(U)^G is a sheaf: it is the equaliser in presheaves of the two maps \prod_{g \in G}\pi_*O_Y \rightrightarrows \prod_{g\in G}\pi_*O_Y, and an equaliser of sheaves computed sectionwise is a sheaf (compatibility on a cover is tested after applying the two maps, which are defined sectionwise). Hence it is the sheaf-theoretic invariant subsheaf: (\pi_*O_Y)^G(U) = O_Y(\pi^{-1}U)^G.

Step 2 (the affine-local description of the rings). Let U = Spec A \subseteq Z be an affine open. Since \pi is affine, V := \pi^{-1}U is affine; write V = Spec B, so B = \Gamma(V, O_Y) = (\pi_*O_Y)(U). The hypothesis that O_Z \to (\pi_*O_Y)^G is an isomorphism of sheaves of rings, on taking \Gamma(U, -), gives a ring isomorphism
      A = \Gamma(U, O_Z) \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\; (\pi_*O_Y)^G(U) = B^G,
and this isomorphism is induced by \pi^{\#}: O_Z \to \pi_*O_Y, so under it the structure map A \to B is the inclusion B^G \subseteq B. We thus identify A = B^G as a subring of B. Note also that V is G-stable (Step 1), so G acts on B, and A = B^G is exactly the invariant subring for that action.
If B = 0 then A = B^G = 0, so U = Spec A = \emptyset, and V = Spec B = \emptyset: the map V \to U is the empty map \emptyset \to \emptyset, which is finite and surjective. In the sequel assume B \ne 0.

Step 3 (B is a finitely generated A-algebra). V = Spec B is an affine open subscheme of the finite type k-scheme Y, so Lemma 5 applies: B is a finitely generated k-algebra, B = k[\beta_1,...,\beta_r]. Because each \varphi_g is a k-morphism, \varphi_{g^{-1}}^{*}: B \to B is the identity on the image of k; since B \ne 0 the map k \to B is injective (its kernel is a proper ideal of the field k), hence k \subseteq B^G = A. Therefore
      B = k[\beta_1,...,\beta_r] = A[\beta_1,...,\beta_r],
a finitely generated A-algebra.

Step 4 (B is integral over A; orbit polynomials). Let b \in B and consider
      P_b(T) := \prod_{g \in G} (T - g \cdot b) \;\in\; B[T].
The coefficients are, up to sign, the elementary symmetric polynomials in the finite multiset {g \cdot b : g \in G}. For h \in G, applying h to the coefficients sends this multiset to {hg \cdot b : g \in G} = {g' \cdot b : g' \in G}, the same multiset (left translation is a bijection of G); hence h fixes every coefficient, i.e. P_b(T) \in B^G[T] = A[T]. The polynomial is monic, and P_b(b) = 0 because the factor for g = e is (T - b) and b = e \cdot b. Thus b is integral over A. This argument is valid in every characteristic and uses no averaging. Since b was arbitrary, A \subseteq B is an integral extension, and by Step 3 it is also generated by finitely many elements; Lemma 6 gives:
      B is a FINITE A-module.

Step 5 (\pi is finite). Let z \in Z and choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec A as in Step 2. If B = 0 then U = \emptyset, impossible; so B \ne 0 and Step 4 applies. Thus \pi^{-1}U = Spec B is affine and \Gamma(U,O_Z) = A \to B is finite. This exhibits an affine open cover of Z over which \pi is given by finite ring maps, i.e. \pi is a finite morphism.

Step 6 (\pi is surjective). Let z \in Z, choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec A, and write \pi^{-1}U = Spec B. As in Step 5, B \ne 0 (else U = \emptyset). Let p \subseteq A be the prime corresponding to z. By Step 4, A = B^G \subseteq B is integral, and B \ne 0, so Lemma 7 gives a prime Q \in Spec B with Q \cap A = p, i.e. a point of V = \pi^{-1}U mapping to z. Hence z is in the image of \pi, and \pi is surjective.

(For completeness: if Y = \emptyset then every affine open U \subseteq Z satisfies \pi^{-1}U = \emptyset, so A = B^G = 0 and U = \emptyset; hence Z = \emptyset and \pi = id_\emptyset is finite and surjective, as Steps 2, 5, 6 already account for.)

Steps 5 and 6 together say that \pi is finite and surjective, which is the claim. \square

SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT: on an affine open U = Spec A of Z, affineness of \pi gives \pi^{-1}U = Spec B with A = B^G; V = Spec B is an affine open of the finite type k-scheme Y, hence B is a finitely generated k-algebra (Lemma 5, which is where the corrected patching Lemma 1/Lemma 2 and the Hilbert basis Lemma 4 are used, applied twice: first to the rings B_{b_{ij,u}} covered by principal opens of the W_{ij}, then to B covered by the D_V(b_{ij,u})); k \subseteq A because the action is by k-automorphisms, so B is generated over A by finitely many elements, each integral over A by the orbit polynomial \prod_g (T - g b) \in A[T]; hence B is a finite A-module (\pi finite) and lying over applies (\pi surjective). No characteristic hypothesis on |G| and no Reynolds operator are used.

lemma_252.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism with \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). For \(0\le n\le 2D\) let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*(y))\) for all \(x,y\). Write \(F_X,F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Then \(f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*\).
lemma_252.proof:
Write $H^i(Z):=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, and write $F_X,F_Y$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$. Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so they satisfy the hypotheses of lemma_77 with $m=1$, $d=D$, and with the same normalisation of the trace ($\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$).

We fix $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ and prove $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$ as maps $H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)$.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 0. The four input facts.

(0a) $F_Z$ is a graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra automorphism of $H^*(Z)$. Indeed $\varphi_Z:=\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:Z_k\to Z_k$ is a morphism of schemes over $\mathbb F_q$ (because $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$), and $\varphi_Z^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}$, so $\varphi_Z\circ\varphi_Z^{-1}=\varphi_Z^{-1}\circ\varphi_Z=\mathrm{id}$. Pullback of \'etale sheaves is a tensor (monoidal) functor, hence for homogeneous $u,v$ one has $\varphi_Z^*(u\cup v)=\varphi_Z^*u\cup\varphi_Z^*v$; i.e. $F_Z(u\cup v)=F_Zu\cup F_Zv$, and $F_Z$ preserves cohomological degree. By lemma_6a, $F_Z$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^i(Z)$ with inverse $F_Z^{-1}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$. Thus $F_Z$ is an invertible graded algebra endomorphism, and $F_Z^{-1}$ also preserves degrees and cup products.

(0b) (lemma_214, applied to $f:X\to Y$) For every $i\ge0$, $f^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f^*$ on $H^i(Y)$. In particular, since $F_X,F_Y$ are invertible and degree preserving, applying $F_X^{-1}$ on the left and $F_Y^{-1}$ on the right gives
$$F_X^{-1}\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_Y^{-1}\qquad\text{on every }H^i(Y).\tag{$*$}$$
(Explicitly: $f^*F_Y=F_Xf^* \Rightarrow F_X^{-1}f^*F_Y=F_X^{-1}F_Xf^*=f^* \Rightarrow F_X^{-1}f^*=f^*F_Y^{-1}$.)

(0c) (lemma_77(a) with $m=1$, $d=D$, applied to $Z=X$ and to $Z=Y$) $\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ as multiplication by $q^{1\cdot D}=q^D$. Concretely, for every $u\in H^{2D}(Z)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z u)=q^D\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(u).\tag{$\dagger$}$$

(0d) (lemma_77(b) with $m=1$, $d=D$) For each $i$ with $0\le i\le 2D$ the pairing
$$H^i(Z)\times H^{2D-i}(Z)\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\qquad (u,v)\longmapsto \operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)$$
is a PERFECT pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. In particular it is nondegenerate on the left: if $a\in H^i(Z)$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup v)=0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ for every $v\in H^{2D-i}(Z)$, then $a=0$.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1. A formal identity for the top-degree pairing.

Claim. For $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, every $i$ with $0\le i\le 2D$, every $a\in H^i(Z)$ and every $b\in H^{2D-i}(Z)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z a\cup b)=q^D\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup F_Z^{-1}b).\tag{1}$$
Proof of the claim. By (0a), $F_Z^{-1}$ preserves degrees, so $F_Z^{-1}b\in H^{2D-i}(Z)$ and $a\cup F_Z^{-1}b\in H^{2D}(Z)$. Using again that $F_Z$ is a graded algebra homomorphism,
$$F_Z a\cup b=F_Z a\cup F_Z(F_Z^{-1}b)=F_Z\big(a\cup F_Z^{-1}b\big).$$
Applying $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ and then $(\dagger)$ from (0c) to the top-degree class $a\cup F_Z^{-1}b$ gives
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Z\!\big(F_Z(a\cup F_Z^{-1}b)\big)=q^D\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup F_Z^{-1}b),$$
which is (1). $\square$

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2. The main computation.

Let $x\in H^n(X)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$ be arbitrary. Note $F_Xx\in H^n(X)$ (degree preserving), and $f^*y\in H^{2D-n}(Y\to X)$, i.e. $f^*y\in H^{2D-n}(X)$, so both are admissible inputs for the defining property of $f_*$, which says: for all $x'\in H^n(X)$ and all $y'\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\big(f_*(x')\cup y'\big)=\operatorname{tr}_X\big(x'\cup f^*(y')\big).\tag{2}$$
We compute, chaining equalities in the one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$:

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{tr}_Y\big(f_*(F_Xx)\cup y\big)
&=\operatorname{tr}_X\big(F_Xx\cup f^*y\big) \qquad &&\text{by (2) with }x'=F_Xx,\ y'=y,\\[2pt]
&=q^D\,\operatorname{tr}_X\big(x\cup F_X^{-1}f^*y\big) \qquad &&\text{by (1) with }Z=X,\ a=x,\ b=f^*y,\\[2pt]
&=q^D\,\operatorname{tr}_X\big(x\cup f^*(F_Y^{-1}y)\big) \qquad &&\text{by }(*)\text{ from (0b)},\\[2pt]
&=q^D\,\operatorname{tr}_Y\big(f_*x\cup F_Y^{-1}y\big) \qquad &&\text{by (2) with }x'=x,\ y'=F_Y^{-1}y\ (\in H^{2D-n}(Y)),\\[2pt]
&=\operatorname{tr}_Y\big(F_Y(f_*x)\cup y\big) \qquad &&\text{by (1) with }Z=Y,\ a=f_*x,\ b=y,\text{ read right-to-left.}
\end{align*}
Each step is an equality of elements of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$; no cancellation of a scalar is needed (and $q^D\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ anyway). Hence, for all $x\in H^n(X)$ and all $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y\Big(\big(f_*(F_Xx)-F_Yf_*(x)\big)\cup y\Big)=0,$$
by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $f_*$, of $F_Y$, of the cup product in the first variable, and of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3. Conclusion by nondegeneracy.

Put $u(x):=f_*(F_Xx)-F_Y(f_*x)\in H^n(Y)$. Step 2 shows $\operatorname{tr}_Y(u(x)\cup y)=0$ for every $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$. By the perfectness of the pairing of (0d) for $i=n$, the map $H^n(Y)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2D-n}(Y),\mathbb Q_\ell(-D))$, $a\mapsto\big(y\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup y)\big)$, is injective; therefore $u(x)=0$. Since $x\in H^n(X)$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$ as maps $H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)$, which is the desired identity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Remarks on the hypotheses and edge cases. (i) The range $0\le n\le 2D$ is exactly the range in which Poincar\'e duality (0d) is stated; outside it both $H^n(Z)$ vanish for a smooth projective pure-dimensional $Z$, but no such statement is needed here. (ii) Geometric connectedness and purity of dimension are used only to ensure that $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ is the isomorphism of lemma_77(a) (a single copy of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ in the top degree) and that the pairing of lemma_77(b) is perfect; both are hypotheses of the present lemma. (iii) The argument never uses the degree of $f$ nor the relation $f_*f^*=d$; only the defining duality property (2) of $f_*$, the Frobenius-equivariance of $f^*$ (lemma_214), the Frobenius-equivariance of the traces (lemma_77(a)) and the perfectness of the duality pairing (lemma_77(b)). Since $F_X,F_Y$ are the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius, this proves $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$. (Equivalently, inverting both sides, $f_*$ also intertwines the geometric Frobenii, by lemma_6a.)

lemma_254.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), and let \(F_1=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\). Then \(F_1\) is semisimple, that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_254.proof:
Notation. Write k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^q, and
\[ f:=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma : X_k\longrightarrow X_k .\]
Since $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ pointwise, $f$ is a morphism of $X_k$ over $\mathbb F_q$; since $\sigma$ is an automorphism of $k$, $f$ is an automorphism of the scheme $X_k$, with inverse $\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1}$. Put
\[ V:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1)),\]
let $F:=f^*\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ be the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (the operator of lemma_250), and let $F_1:=f^*\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ be the operator of the present statement, i.e. the automorphism induced by pullback along $f$ together with the standard arithmetic Frobenius structure on $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$. The proof has four steps: (1) understand the coefficient space $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$; (2) identify $W$ with $V\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$; (3) compute the operator $F_1$ on that tensor product (this is where the twist contributes a scalar $q^{-1}$); (4) conclude by lemma_250, lemma_248 and lemma_8.

Use of the hypotheses, recorded once and for all. $X$ projective over $\mathbb F_q$ implies $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, which is what is needed to apply lemma_45_finite_frob for finiteness of $V$; $\ell\neq p=\mathrm{char}(k)$ is what makes $\mu_{\ell^n}$ finite \'etale over $k$; $k$ algebraically closed is what makes $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ cyclic of order $\ell^n$ and makes every locally constant constructible sheaf on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$ constant; and "smooth, projective, geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$" is exactly the hypothesis list of lemma_250, which we invoke verbatim.

STEP 1. The $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is one-dimensional, and the sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$ is the constant sheaf with that value.

By definition $\mathbb Z_\ell(1):=\varprojlim_n \mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ with transition maps $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, and $\mathbb Q_\ell(1):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$. Because $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $p\neq\ell$, $k^\times$ contains all $\ell^n$-power roots of unity and they are distinct, so $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ is a cyclic group of order $\ell^n$, and the map $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}(k)\to\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$, is surjective. Choosing inductively elements $\zeta_n\in\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ with $\zeta_{n+1}^{\ell}=\zeta_n$ and $\zeta_1$ a primitive $\ell$-th root of unity (possible by surjectivity) gives an element $(\zeta_n)_n\in\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$; the homomorphism $\mathbb Z_\ell\to\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$, $a\mapsto a\cdot(\zeta_n)_n$, is an isomorphism (it is an isomorphism modulo $\ell^n$ for every $n$, hence an isomorphism by the defining limit). Thus $\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$ is free of rank $1$ over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is a one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.

For the sheaf-theoretic form of the same statement: the group scheme $\mu_{\ell^n}$ over $k$ is the constant group scheme $\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z}$ (all its geometric points are $k$-rational), so $\mu_{\ell^n}$ is the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z}$ on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$. Limits of sheaves of sets are computed objectwise, so the sheaf $\varprojlim_n\mu_{\ell^n}$ is the constant sheaf with value $\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$; filtered colimits of sheaves of sets are likewise computed objectwise (filtered colimits commute with finite limits in $\mathbf{Set}$), so $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)=\varinjlim_m \frac{1}{\ell^m}\mathbb Z_\ell(1)$ is the constant sheaf with value the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$.

STEP 2. Canonical identification $\Phi:V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W$.

Take an injective resolution $0\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to I^\bullet$ in the category of sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces on $X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$. For any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $E$ let $\underline E:=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}E$ (the constant sheaf of Step 1 when $E=\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$). Since $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is a free $\mathbb Q_\ell$-module of rank $1$, $I^n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong I^n$ is injective for each $n$, and $0\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}\to I^\bullet\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is exact because tensoring with the flat module $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is exact on sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-modules (exactness is checked on stalks). Hence $\Gamma(X_k,I^\bullet\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=\Gamma(X_k,I^\bullet)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ computes $R\Gamma(X_k,\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)})$.

Now take any complex $C^\bullet$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and any free $\mathbb Q_\ell$-module $E$ of rank $1$. Flatness of $E$ gives $Z^n(C^\bullet\otimes E)=Z^n(C^\bullet)\otimes E$ and $B^n(C^\bullet\otimes E)=B^n(C^\bullet)\otimes E$, and exactness of $-\otimes E$ applied to $0\to B^n\to Z^n\to H^n(C^\bullet)\to0$ gives $H^n(C^\bullet\otimes E)\cong H^n(C^\bullet)\otimes E$. Applying this to $C^\bullet=\Gamma(X_k,I^\bullet)$ yields a canonical isomorphism
\[ \Phi:\;H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1)). \]
Concretely, $\Phi$ is characterised as follows: for $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, the homomorphism of constant sheaves $\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}$ sending $1\mapsto\xi$ induces a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $(1\mapsto\xi)_*:V\to W$, and $\Phi(v\otimes\xi)=(1\mapsto\xi)_*(v)$. In particular, for each nonzero $\xi$, writing $\varphi_\xi:V\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W$ for $v\mapsto\Phi(v\otimes\xi)$, the map $\varphi_\xi$ is an isomorphism (it is the composite of $v\mapsto v\otimes\xi$, an isomorphism since $\xi$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, with $\Phi$).

STEP 3. Finite-dimensionality and invertibility of the operators.

$X$ is projective, hence proper, over $\mathbb F_q$; the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ lies in $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. Lemma_45_finite_frob therefore gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty$ for every $n$, in particular $\dim V<\infty$. By Step 2, $\dim W=\dim V<\infty$.

$F$ is an automorphism of $V$: this is part of the statement of lemma_250, which calls $F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ the arithmetic Frobenius *automorphism* of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (equivalently, pullback along the automorphism $f$ of $X_k$ is invertible, with inverse pullback along $f^{-1}=\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1}$).

$F_1$ is an automorphism of $W$: by definition $F_1$ is the composite
\[ W=H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\;f^*\;}H^1(X_k,f^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\;H^1(\varphi_1)\;}H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=W, \]
where $\varphi_1:f^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is the arithmetic Frobenius structure on $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$. The first arrow is an isomorphism because $f$ is an automorphism of $X_k$ (functoriality of pullback gives $f^{*-1}\circ f^*=\mathrm{id}$ and conversely), and the second is an isomorphism because $\varphi_1$ is an isomorphism of sheaves. Hence $F_1\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$.

STEP 4. Computation of $F_1$ on $V\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$: the twist contributes the scalar $q^{-1}$.

(a) For every $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $E$, pullback along $f$ identifies $f^*\underline E$ with $\underline E$ canonically. Indeed, writing $\gamma_Y:Y_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ for the global-sections geometric morphism, the constant-sheaf functor on $Y$ is $\Delta_Y=\gamma_Y^{-1}$; for $f:X_k\to X_k$ we have $\gamma_{X_k}\circ f=\gamma_{X_k}$, hence $f^{-1}\Delta_{X_k}=\Delta_{X_k}$, and since $f^*M=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell}f^{-1}M=f^{-1}M$ for sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-modules, $f^*\underline E=\underline E$.

(b) Under $\Phi$, the map $f^*:W\to H^1(X_k,f^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=W$ corresponds to $F\otimes\mathrm{id}$. To see this, use the resolution $I^\bullet\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ of Step 2. The morphism of complexes representing $f^*$ is built from $I^\bullet\to f_*I^\bullet$, and for $E=\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ free of rank $1$ the projection formula holds trivially: $f_*(A\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\underline E)\cong f_*A\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}E$, because $A\otimes\underline E\cong A^{\oplus 1}$ and $f_*$ is additive. Thus the representing map is $f^*\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $\Gamma(X_k,I^\bullet)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, which on $H^1$ is $F\otimes\mathrm{id}$.

(c) The endomorphisms of the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}$ are exactly the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of the vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ (the constant-sheaf functor is fully faithful: it is left adjoint to $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma\Delta=\mathrm{id}$). Hence the Frobenius structure $\varphi_1:f^*\mathbb Q_\ell(1)=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}$ is $\underline{F^{(1)}}$ for a unique $F^{(1)}\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$, the arithmetic Frobenius on the coefficient space; by (b) and functoriality in $E$ of the construction of Step 2, the map $H^1(\varphi_1)$ corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V\otimes F^{(1)}$. Combining,
\[ F_1\circ\Phi=\Phi\circ(F\otimes F^{(1)}). \tag{$*$}\]

(d) Value of $F^{(1)}$.
