Lemma_78 fixes and uses the convention that, for $F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$, the arithmetic Frobenius acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ as multiplication by $q^{-j}$ (that is precisely the convention under which lemma_78 states $F_*c_z=q^{j}c_z$ for the untwisted vector attached to the class of an $\mathbb F_q$-rational codimension-$j$ cycle). Taking $j=1$, $F^{(1)}=q^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell(1)}$.

Substituting (d) into $(*)$ and using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\Phi$, for every $v\in V$ and every nonzero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$:
\[ F_1(\varphi_\xi(v))=F_1\Phi(v\otimes\xi)=\Phi(Fv\otimes q^{-1}\xi)=q^{-1}\Phi(Fv\otimes\xi)=q^{-1}\varphi_\xi(Fv)=\varphi_\xi\big((q^{-1}F)v\big), \]
that is,
\[ F_1\circ\varphi_\xi=\varphi_\xi\circ(q^{-1}F). \tag{$**$} \]
This is the whole content of the twist: on the tensor-product model, $F_1$ is the operator $q^{-1}F$ transported by the isomorphism $\varphi_\xi$.

STEP 5. Conclusion.

(i) By lemma_250, whose hypotheses ($q=p^a$ a prime power, $X$ smooth projective geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, $F=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$) are exactly those of the present lemma, $F$ is semisimple on $V$.

(ii) The number $q^{-1}$ is a nonzero element of $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$, hence $c:=q^{-1}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. Lemma_248 (applied to the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $V$ and $T=F$) gives: $F$ semisimple $\iff$ $q^{-1}F$ semisimple. So $q^{-1}F$ is semisimple on $V$.

(iii) The map $\varphi_\xi:V\xrightarrow{\sim}W$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism between finite-dimensional spaces (Step 3), $q^{-1}F\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $F_1\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ are invertible (Step 3), and they satisfy the intertwining relation $(**)$, i.e. $\varphi_\xi\circ(q^{-1}F)=F_1\circ\varphi_\xi$. By lemma_8, $q^{-1}F$ is semisimple if and only if $F_1$ is semisimple. Hence $F_1$ is semisimple on $W=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))$.

(iv) Finally, lemma_5 states that for a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space and a linear operator, "semisimple" is equivalent to "diagonalizable after base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$". Thus $F_1$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which is exactly the required conclusion.

(Convention check: had one chosen the opposite convention for the arithmetic Frobenius on $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, namely multiplication by $q$, the relation $(**)$ would read $F_1\varphi_\xi=\varphi_\xi(qF)$, and the identical argument with $c=q$ in lemma_248 would give the same conclusion; the proof is insensitive to that choice.)

lemma_247.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) of pure dimensions \(D\ge E\), put \(r=D-E\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) with first Chern class \(c_1(L)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\). For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\deg_Z:H^{2\dim Z}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(\dim Z))\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the degree map sending the class of a closed point \(z\) to \([\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). Then there exists a positive integer \(d\) such that \(\deg_X\!\bigl(c_1(L)^{r}\cup f^{*}u\bigr)=d\,\deg_Y(u)\) for every \(u\in H^{2E}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(E))\).

lemma_258.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts as multiplication by the scalar \(q\).
lemma_258.proof:
We prove that the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, acts on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by the scalar $q$.

**Step 0: The hypotheses of the input lemmas are satisfied.**
$C$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over $\mathbb F_q$. Being smooth of finite type over the field $\mathbb F_q$ and geometrically connected, $C$ is geometrically integral, hence irreducible; being of finite type over a field with all local rings regular of dimension $1$ (a curve), it follows that $C$ is of pure dimension $d=1$. It is projective (hence proper) and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$. By lemma_6a, the pullback $F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (with inverse $F_{\mathrm{geo}}$), so it makes sense to speak of the scalar by which it acts; this $F_{\mathrm{ar}}$ is exactly the operator $F$ of the statement. Likewise the $F$ occurring in lemma_77 with $m=1$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius, i.e. the same operator.

**Step 1: Apply Frobenius-equivariant Poincar\u00e9 duality (lemma_77) with $m=1$, $Y=C$, $d=1$.**
Part (a) of lemma_77, applied to the structure morphism $f\colon C\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^1}$, gives a canonical $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism (the Poincar\u00e9 duality trace)
\[
\operatorname{tr}\colon H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-1),
\]
which is equivariant for $F$, where $F$ acts on the target $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)=\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ as multiplication by the positive rational number $q^{md}=q^{1\cdot 1}=q$. Writing this equivariance out explicitly:
\[
\text{for all } x\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(Fx)=q\,\operatorname{tr}(x). \tag{$\ast$}
\]
(In particular $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=1$, since $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ is one-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.)

**Step 2: Conclude that $F$ is the scalar $q$.**
Let $x\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Since $\operatorname{tr}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, $q\,\operatorname{tr}(x)=\operatorname{tr}(q\,x)$. Hence by $(\ast)$,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(Fx-qx)=\operatorname{tr}(Fx)-\operatorname{tr}(qx)=q\operatorname{tr}(x)-q\operatorname{tr}(x)=0 .
\]
As $\operatorname{tr}$ is an isomorphism it is injective, so $Fx-qx=0$, i.e. $Fx=qx$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $F=q\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This is the desired conclusion.

**Step 3: Independent derivation of the equivariance $(\ast)$ from the perfect pairing of lemma_77(b) (cross-check).**
Lemma_77(b) with $d=1$, $m=1$, $n=2$ says that
\[
\langle-,-\rangle\colon H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-1),\qquad \langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y),
\]
is a perfect pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and that $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^{md}\langle x,y\rangle=q\langle x,y\rangle$. Since $C$ is geometrically connected, $C_k$ is connected, so $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1$ (locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued functions on the connected space $C_k$). Moreover the morphism $\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ is the identity on the underlying topological space of $C_k$ (the map $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ is the identity on the one-point space $\operatorname{Spec}k$, and the underlying set of $C_k=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is $C\times\{\ast\}$), so pullback of locally constant functions is the identity; hence $F(1)=1$. Therefore for every $x$,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(Fx)=\langle Fx,1\rangle=\langle Fx,F1\rangle=q\langle x,1\rangle=q\operatorname{tr}(x),
\]
which is exactly $(\ast)$, and Step 2 applies. (This shows the scalar is forced by the pairing and needs no semisimplicity input.)

**Step 4: Compatibility with the cycle-class normalisation (second cross-check).**
Let $z\in C$ be any closed point, of degree $n=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\ge 1$; as a $0$-cycle on the $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $C$ it is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, and it has codimension $j=1$. Fix $\xi_1\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ nonzero and write $\mathrm{cl}(z)=c_z\otimes\xi_1$ with $c_z\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. By lemma_78 (equivalently, by the second sentence of lemma_77, using that $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ as $q^{-1}$), $F c_z=q^{1}c_z=q\,c_z$. On the other hand the normalisation of the trace in lemma_77(a) gives $\operatorname{tr}(c_z)=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]=n\neq 0$, so $c_z\neq 0$; since $H^2$ is one-dimensional (Step 1), $c_z$ spans $H^2$, and $F=q\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on all of $H^2$. This agrees with Step 2 and confirms that the scalar is $q$ (and not, say, $-q$ or $1$).

**Conclusion.** The $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ acts on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by the scalar $q$. In particular it is semisimple there, and by lemma_6a the same holds for geometric Frobenius, which acts as multiplication by $q^{-1}$.

lemma_260.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2\).
lemma_260.proof:
Write $V^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and let $F_n\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V^n)$ denote the operator from the statement, $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$. We must show $F_n$ is semisimple, i.e.\ diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, for $n=0,1,2$. These three values are the only cases in the range $0\le n\le 2$.

Step 0 (two preliminaries, used in all cases).
(a) \emph{Invertibility of the operator named in the statement.} Apply lemma_6a with $X=C$ and the $q$-power automorphism $\sigma(c)=c^q$: for every $i\ge 0$ the pullback $F_{\mathrm{ar}}:=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_{\mathrm{geo}}:=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}$. The operator $F$ of the statement is exactly $F_{\mathrm{ar}}$; hence $F_n\in\mathrm{GL}(V^n)$ for every $n\ge 0$.
(b) \emph{Finite-dimensionality.} The curve $C$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob with $X=C$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, the prime $\ell\ne p$, $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ (the constant sheaf, viewed as a complex concentrated in degree $0$; it is an object of $D^b_c(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$), and $\phi=\psi\colon F_C^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ the canonical arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism of the constant sheaf. The lemma states that for every integer $n$ the hypercohomology $H^n(C_k,K)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$; since $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ is concentrated in degree $0$ with no higher terms, this hypercohomology is by definition $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V^n$. Thus each $V^n$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space. (We use this lemma only for the finite-dimensionality, not for any assertion about which automorphism it produces.)

Step 1 (the case $n=0$). By definition of the constant sheaf, $V^0=H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\Gamma(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space of locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued functions on the underlying topological space $|C_k|$ of $C_k$. Because $C$ is geometrically connected, $|C_k|$ is connected, so every locally constant function on it is constant; and $C_k\ne\varnothing$ (a smooth projective curve has a closed point, whose residue field is finite over $\mathbb F_q$ and embeds into $k$, giving a $k$-point). Hence $V^0=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1$, of dimension $1$. By (a), $F_0$ is the pullback along $\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$; on the constant sheaf this pullback is the canonical identification of the constant sheaf with itself, and the induced map on global sections is precomposition with the underlying homeomorphism $|\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma|\colon|C_k|\to|C_k|$. Therefore $F_0(f)=f\circ|\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma|$, which sends $a\cdot 1$ to $a\cdot 1$ for every $a\in\mathbb Q_\ell$. Thus $F_0=\mathrm{id}_{V^0}$; its matrix in the basis $\{1\}$ is the $1\times1$ diagonal matrix $(1)$, so $F_0$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e.\ semisimple.

Step 2 (the case $n=1$). The hypotheses of lemma_250 hold verbatim with $X=C$: $q=p^a$ is a prime power, $C$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$ is prime, and $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Its conclusion is precisely that $F$ is semisimple on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V^1$.

Step 3 (the case $n=2$). By Step 0(b), $V^2$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and by Step 0(a), $F_2\in\mathrm{GL}(V^2)$. The hypotheses of lemma_258 hold verbatim ($q=p^a$; $C$ a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over $\mathbb F_q$; $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$; $\ell\ne p$; $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^q$), and its conclusion is that $F$ acts on $H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by the scalar $q$: $F_2=q\cdot\mathrm{id}_{V^2}$.
Now the identity operator $\mathrm{id}_{V^2}$ is semisimple: in any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $V^2$ (the empty basis, if $V^2=0$) its matrix is the identity matrix, which is diagonal, hence diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. The number $q=p^a$ is a strictly positive integer, and since $\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb Q_\ell=0$ its image in $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is non-zero, hence $q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. Apply lemma_248 with $V=V^2$ (finite-dimensional), $T=\mathrm{id}_{V^2}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^2)$ and $c=q\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$: since $T$ is semisimple, the scalar multiple $c\,T=q\cdot\mathrm{id}_{V^2}=F_2$ is semisimple.

Step 4 (conclusion). The cases $n=0$, $n=1$, $n=2$ established in Steps 1--3 exhaust all integers $n$ with $0\le n\le 2$, and in each case $F=(\mathrm{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This is exactly the statement to be proved.

lemma_262.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism with \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\). For \(0\le n\le 2D\) let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the map with \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*y)\), and let \(F_X,F_Y\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Then \(e:=d^{-1}f^*\circ f_*\) is an idempotent of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) satisfying \(e\circ F_X=F_X\circ e\), its image equals \(\operatorname{im} f^*\), and \(f^*\) induces an \(F\)-equivariant \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{im} e\).
lemma_262.proof:
Fix integers q = p^a, d ≥ 1, D ≥ 0, n with 0 ≤ n ≤ 2D, and a prime ℓ ≠ p, and set k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q. Write
  V_X := H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, \mathbb Q_\ell),  V_Y := H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k, \mathbb Q_\ell),
  V_X' := H^{2D-n}_{\acute et}(X_k, \mathbb Q_\ell),  V_Y' := H^{2D-n}_{\acute et}(Y_k, \mathbb Q_\ell),
and write F_X, F_Y for the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms (id × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^q, of V_X and V_Y respectively. By lemma_6a (applied to the schemes X and Y over \mathbb F_q, whose étale cohomology groups are finite-dimensional by lemma_45_finite_frob since X and Y are proper), F_X and F_Y are indeed invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operators on V_X and V_Y.

Since d ≥ 1 is a nonzero integer it is invertible in \mathbb Q_\ell, so e := d^{-1} f^* ∘ f_* : V_X → V_X is a well-defined \mathbb Q_\ell-linear endomorphism: f_* : V_X → V_Y and f^* : V_Y → V_X are both maps of degree 0, and both are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear (for f^* this is functoriality of étale cohomology, the pullback being a homomorphism of graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebras; for f_* see Step 0 below).

Step 0 (linearity of f_*). By lemma_77(b) with m = 1, the pairing V_Y × V_Y' → \mathbb Q_\ell(-D), (u, v) ↦ tr_Y(u ∪ v), is perfect. Let λ ∈ \mathbb Q_\ell, x, x' ∈ V_X. For every y ∈ V_Y', using the \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinearity of the cup product, the \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of f^* and of tr_X, and the defining property of f_*,
  tr_Y(f_*(λx + x') ∪ y) = tr_X((λx + x') ∪ f^* y) = λ\, tr_X(x ∪ f^* y) + tr_X(x' ∪ f^* y) = λ\, tr_Y(f_* x ∪ y) + tr_Y(f_* x' ∪ y) = tr_Y((λ f_* x + f_* x') ∪ y).
Perfectness of the pairing forces f_*(λx + x') = λ f_* x + f_* x'. So f_* is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear, as claimed. (This is exactly the map whose existence lemma_242 and lemma_252 assert, with the same normalisation tr_Z(cl(z)) = [κ(z):\mathbb F_q] of the trace; the hypotheses of those two lemmas — proper, surjective, generically finite of degree d ≥ 1, X and Y smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension D over \mathbb F_q — are precisely ours.)

Step 1 (the key relation f_* ∘ f^* = d·id). By lemma_242, applied verbatim with our f, X, Y, D, d, n, we have
  f_* ∘ f^* = d · id_{V_Y}.
In particular f^* is injective: if f^* y = 0 then d·y = f_* f^* y = 0, and d^{-1} ∈ \mathbb Q_\ell gives y = 0. Also d^{-1} f_*|_{V_Y} is a left inverse of f^*.

Step 2 (e is idempotent). Using Step 1,
  e^2 = (d^{-1} f^* ∘ f_*) ∘ (d^{-1} f^* ∘ f_*) = d^{-2} f^* ∘ (f_* ∘ f^*) ∘ f_* = d^{-2} f^* ∘ (d · id_{V_Y}) ∘ f_* = d^{-1} f^* ∘ f_* = e.
So e is a projection (idempotent \mathbb Q_\ell-linear endomorphism) of V_X.

Step 3 (image of e equals image of f^*). Both inclusions are elementary.
  (⊆) For x ∈ V_X, e(x) = f^*(d^{-1} f_* x) ∈ im f^*. Hence im e ⊆ im f^*.
  (⊇) For y ∈ V_Y put x := f^* y ∈ V_X. Then, using Step 1,
     e(x) = d^{-1} f^*(f_* f^* y) = d^{-1} f^*(d·y) = f^*(y) = x,
  so x ∈ im e. Hence im f^* ⊆ im e.
Thus im e = im f^*.
(For later use we record the complementary description of the kernel: since f^* is injective, e(x) = 0 ⇔ f^*(f_* x) = 0 ⇔ f_* x = 0, so ker e = ker f_*. Together with Step 3 this exhibits V_X = im f^* ⊕ ker f_* and shows e is the projection onto im f^* along ker f_*; in particular e|_{im e} = id_{im e}, which is also immediate from the computation above.)

Step 4 (e commutes with Frobenius). By lemma_214 applied to the \mathbb F_q-morphism f : X → Y (a morphism of schemes of finite type over \mathbb F_q), pullback is Frobenius-equivariant:
  f^* ∘ F_Y = F_X ∘ f^*   on V_Y.
By lemma_252 applied to f (same hypotheses as above), the trace-dual push-forward is also Frobenius-equivariant:
  f_* ∘ F_X = F_Y ∘ f_*   on V_X.
Therefore, as endomorphisms of V_X,
  e ∘ F_X = d^{-1} f^* ∘ f_* ∘ F_X = d^{-1} f^* ∘ F_Y ∘ f_* = d^{-1} F_X ∘ f^* ∘ f_* = F_X ∘ e.

Step 5 (F_X-stability of im e). Let x ∈ im e, so x = e(x') with x' ∈ V_X. Then by Step 4, F_X x = F_X e(x') = e(F_X x') ∈ im e. Hence F_X(im e) ⊆ im e. Since F_X is invertible (Step 0/lemma_6a) and commutes with e, the same argument with F_X^{-1} (which also commutes with e: from F_X e = e F_X we get e = F_X^{-1} e F_X, hence F_X^{-1} e = e F_X^{-1}) gives F_X^{-1}(im e) ⊆ im e, so F_X(im e) = im e. Thus F_X restricts to an automorphism F_e of im e, and by construction F_e is the restriction of F_X.

Step 6 (f^* identifies V_Y with im e, F-equivariantly). Consider the corestriction
  φ : V_Y → im e,  φ(y) := f^*(y),
which is well defined by Step 3 and \mathbb Q_\ell-linear because f^* is.
  Injectivity: φ(y) = 0 means f^* y = 0, whence y = 0 by Step 1.
  Surjectivity: every element of im e is, by Step 3, of the form f^*(y) for some y ∈ V_Y.
Equivalently, an explicit inverse is ψ : im e → V_Y, ψ(x) := d^{-1} f_*(x): indeed ψ ∘ φ = d^{-1} f_* ∘ f^* = id_{V_Y} by Step 1, and φ ∘ ψ(x) = d^{-1} f^* f_*(x) = e(x) = x for x ∈ im e by Step 2/Step 3 (e acts as the identity on its image). So φ is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism V_Y \xrightarrow{\sim} im e.
  F-equivariance: for y ∈ V_Y, using the relation f^* ∘ F_Y = F_X ∘ f^* from Step 4 and the fact that F_e is the restriction of F_X to im e,
     φ(F_Y y) = f^*(F_Y y) = F_X(f^* y) = F_e(φ(y)),
  i.e. φ ∘ F_Y = F_e ∘ φ.

Steps 2, 3, 4 and 6 are exactly the four assertions of the lemma: e is an idempotent of H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, \mathbb Q_\ell), it commutes with F_X, its image is im f^*, and f^* induces an F-equivariant \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} im e. This completes the proof.

lemma_263.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Fix an integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D\). If \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_263.proof:
We write $V_X:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $V_Y:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and we use "semisimple" in the sense of the hypotheses and conclusion: the operator is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of the Frobenius operators). Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, they are proper. Equip the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:\mathcal F_{X}^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ (resp. for $Y$), where $\mathcal F_X=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ to $X$ and to $Y$ shows that $V_X$ and $V_Y$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and that the induced automorphisms are exactly the pullbacks $F_X=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ and $F_Y=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$. By lemma_6a, $\sigma:c\mapsto c^q$ is an automorphism of $k$, so $\mathcal F_X,\mathcal F_Y$ are isomorphisms of $k$-schemes and hence $F_X\in\mathrm{GL}(V_X)$, $F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}(V_Y)$ are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators.

Step 2 (the degree of $f$ is defined and $\ge 1$). Both $X$ and $Y$ are smooth, projective and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, hence integral, of pure dimension $D$. A proper surjective generically finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ between integral varieties of the same dimension $D$ induces a finite extension of function fields $k(X)/k(Y)$; set $d:=[k(X):k(Y)]$. Since $k(Y)\subseteq k(X)$, $d\ge 1$. Thus $f$ is a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree $d\ge 1$, as required in the hypotheses of lemma_242 and lemma_252.

Step 3 (existence of the pushforward with $f_*f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$). All hypotheses of lemma_242 are satisfied by $q$, $f:X\to Y$, $D$, $k$, $\ell$, and the trace normalisation there. Lemma_242 therefore provides a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map (the trace-duality pushforward)
$$f_*:V_X\longrightarrow V_Y$$
satisfying $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{V_Y}$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V_Y$, where $f^*:V_Y\to V_X$ is the pullback.

Step 4 ($f^*$ is injective and identifies $V_Y$ with $W:=\mathrm{im}(f^*)$). Since $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$ and $d\ge 1$, the scalar $d$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q_\ell$. The identity $f_*\circ f^*=d\,\mathrm{id}$ shows that $\frac1d f_*:V_Y\to V_X$... precisely: $\big(\tfrac1d f_*\big)\circ f^*=\mathrm{id}_{V_Y}$. Hence $f^*$ admits a left inverse, so $f^*$ is injective. Let $W:=f^*(V_Y)\subseteq V_X$. Then $f^*:V_Y\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism, with inverse $\frac1d f_*|_W:W\to V_Y$ (for $w=f^*y$ one has $\frac1d f_*(w)=y$, which is independent of the chosen $y$ by injectivity).

Step 5 ($W$ is $F_X$-stable). The morphism $f$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, so lemma_214 applied to $f:X\to Y$ and to the degree $n$ gives
$$f^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f^*.$$
Consequently, for $w=f^*y\in W$ we have $F_X(w)=F_X f^*(y)=f^*(F_Y y)\in W$, so $W$ is $F_X$-stable and $F_X|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ (stability under the invertible operator $F_X$ together with $F_X^{-1}f^*=f^*F_Y^{-1}$, also from the intertwining relation, gives stability under $F_X^{-1}$; in any case $W$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell[F^{\pm1}]$-submodule).

Step 6 (descent of semisimplicity to $W$). Assume $F_X$ acts semisimply on $V_X$. Since $V_X$ is finite-dimensional (Step 1), $W\subseteq V_X$ is $F_X$-stable (Step 5), and $F_X\in\mathrm{GL}(V_X)$ is semisimple, lemma_237 applied with $V=V_X$, $T=F_X$, $W=W$ yields that $F_X|_W$ is semisimple.

Step 7 (transport back to $V_Y$). We now apply lemma_8 with $V=V_Y$, $T_V=F_Y$, $W'=W$, $T_{W'}=F_X|_W$, and $\alpha=f^*:V_Y\xrightarrow{\sim}W$ (an isomorphism by Step 4). The intertwining property $\alpha\circ T_V=T_{W'}\circ\alpha$ is exactly the identity $f^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f^*$ of Step 5, restricted to $W$ as target. Lemma_8 then gives: $F_Y$ is semisimple on $V_Y$ if and only if $F_X|_W$ is semisimple on $W$. By Step 6 the latter holds, hence $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

This is precisely the desired conclusion. (Remark on the mechanism: Steps 3–5 in fact give a Frobenius-equivariant decomposition $V_X=W\oplus\ker f_*$, since $\ker f_*$ is $F_X$-stable by the equivariance $f_*F_X=F_Yf_*$ and every $x\in V_X$ decomposes as $x=f^*(\tfrac1d f_*x)+(x-f^*(\tfrac1d f_*x))$; the argument above only uses the summand $W$, which is $F_X$-equivariantly isomorphic to $V_Y$.)

lemma_264.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). For every integer \(i\) with \(0\le i\le 2d\), \(F\) is semisimple (diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)) on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if it is semisimple on \(H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_264.proof:
We prove that for each $0\le i\le 2d$ the operator $F$ is semisimple on $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if it is semisimple on $H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The argument is Poincar\'e duality plus three elementary linear-algebra facts (semisimplicity is preserved by passing to the dual operator, by inverting, and by multiplying by a nonzero scalar).

**Step 0 (Notation, finite-dimensionality, invertibility, convention on \"semisimple\").**
Put
$$V:=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),$$
and write $F_V,V\ni x\mapsto F_Vx$ and $F_W$ for the operators $F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, on $V$ and on $W$ respectively.

*Finite-dimensionality.* $X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper. The constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, so lemma_45_finite_frob (with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$) gives that $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space for every $n$; in particular $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$ and $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W<\infty$.

*Invertibility.* By lemma_6a, for every scheme over $\mathbb F_q$ the pullback $F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (its inverse being $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$). Thus $F_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $F_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$; in particular $F_V^{-1}$ and $F_W^{-1}$ make sense.

*Convention.* We use \"semisimple\" in the sense of the statement, i.e. diagonalisable of $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on $U\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By lemma_5 this is equivalent, for a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $U$ and $T\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$, to $T$ being semisimple over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ in the sense used in lemma_4 and lemma_64 (squarefree minimal polynomial); so the lemmas quoted below apply verbatim to the notion of the statement.

*The zero case.* If $V=0$, then the perfect pairing of Step 1 identifies $W$ with $V^{\vee}=0$, so $W=0$; on the zero space the (unique) operator is diagonalisable with the empty basis, so both sides of the desired equivalence are true. Symmetrically $W=0\Rightarrow V=0$. Henceforth we assume $V\ne 0$ (and therefore $W\ne 0$); all spaces below are then nonzero and finite-dimensional.

**Step 1 (The geometric input: Frobenius-equivariant Poincar\'e duality).**
Apply lemma_77 with $m=1$, $Y=X$ and $n=i$. Its hypotheses are satisfied: $q=p^a$, $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_{q^1}=\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\ne p$, and $F$ is the $q^1$-power arithmetic Frobenius. Part (a) supplies the trace isomorphism
$$\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$$
which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, $F$ acting on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by $q^{md}=q^d$ (a positive rational number, hence an element of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$). Part (b) then says that
$$\langle x,y\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\in \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad x\in V,\ y\in W,$$
is a PERFECT pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and that
$$\langle F_Vx,\,F_Wy\rangle=q^d\,\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x\in V,\ y\in W.\tag{1}$$
(Perfectness means that both induced maps $V\xrightarrow{\sim}W^{\vee}$, $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle$, and $W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^{\vee}$, $y\mapsto\langle -,y\rangle$, are isomorphisms.)

**Step 2 (Rewriting the pairing as an isomorphism $\gamma:W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^{\vee}$).**
Fix once and for all a nonzero vector $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ (possible since $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is a $1$-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space, and nonzero as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space). Every $u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is uniquely of the form $u=\lambda\xi$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$; define $\delta(u):=\lambda$. Then $\delta:\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism ($\delta$ is linear because $\lambda\mapsto\lambda\xi$ is a linear parametrisation, and it is bijective because $\xi\ne0$ spans).

Define
$$\gamma:W\longrightarrow V^{\vee}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \gamma(y)(x):=\delta\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle\bigr).$$
$\gamma$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear: for $a,b\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, $y_1,y_2\in W$ and $x\in V$, $\gamma(ay_1+by_2)(x)=\delta(a\langle x,y_1\rangle+b\langle x,y_2\rangle)=a\delta\langle x,y_1\rangle+b\delta\langle x,y_2\rangle=(a\gamma(y_1)+b\gamma(y_2))(x)$, using bilinearity of $\langle-,-\rangle$ over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and linearity of $\delta$. Moreover $\gamma$ is the composite
$$W\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))\xrightarrow{\ \delta\circ-\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V^{\vee},\qquad y\mapsto (x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle)\mapsto(x\mapsto\delta\langle x,y\rangle),$$
where the first arrow is an isomorphism by perfectness of the pairing (it is exactly the map $W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^{\vee}$ above, after identifying $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))$ with the space of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$-valued linear forms, which is what $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle$ is), and the second is an isomorphism because $\delta$ is one and $V$ is finite-dimensional. Hence $\gamma$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism.

**Step 3 (The intertwining relation).**
Let $D\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})$ be the dual (transpose) of $F_V^{-1}$:
$$D(\lambda):=\lambda\circ F_V^{-1}\qquad(\lambda\in V^{\vee}).$$
$D$ is invertible, with inverse $\mu\mapsto\mu\circ F_V$, because $F_V$ is.

**Claim.** $\gamma\circ F_W=(q^d D)\circ\gamma$, i.e. $\gamma F_W\gamma^{-1}=q^d D$.

*Proof of the claim.* Take $y\in W$ and $x\in V$. Apply identity (1) with $x$ replaced by $F_V^{-1}x$ (legitimate, since $F_V^{-1}x\in V$ and (1) holds for all pairs):
$$\langle F_V(F_V^{-1}x),\,F_Wy\rangle=q^d\langle F_V^{-1}x,\,y\rangle,$$
and the left-hand side is $\langle x,F_Wy\rangle$ because $F_VF_V^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_V$. Thus
$$\langle x,F_Wy\rangle=q^d\,\langle F_V^{-1}x,y\rangle.\tag{2}$$
Now apply $\delta$ and use its $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity together with $q^d\in\mathbb Q_\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$:
$$\gamma(F_Wy)(x)=\delta\langle x,F_Wy\rangle=\delta\bigl(q^d\langle F_V^{-1}x,y\rangle\bigr)=q^d\,\delta\langle F_V^{-1}x,y\rangle=q^d\,(\gamma(y)\circ F_V^{-1})(x)=q^d\,D(\gamma(y))(x)=\bigl((q^dD)(\gamma(y))\bigr)(x).$$
Since this holds for every $x\in V$, $\gamma(F_Wy)=(q^dD)(\gamma y)$; since $y\in W$ was arbitrary, $\gamma F_W=(q^dD)\gamma$, and composing with $\gamma^{-1}$ on the right gives $\gamma F_W\gamma^{-1}=q^dD$. $\square$

**Step 4 (Duals and inverses preserve semisimplicity).**
**Claim.** $D$ is semisimple on $V^{\vee}$ if and only if $F_V$ is semisimple on $V$.

*Proof.* (i) By lemma_64(iv) (the \"companion facts, valid over every field\" clause), semisimplicity of an operator passes to the dual operator. Apply this to the invertible operator $F_V^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ over the field $\mathbb Q_\ell$: $F_V^{-1}$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if its dual $(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda\circ F_V^{-1}$, is semisimple on $V^{\vee}$. By definition $(F_V^{-1})^{\vee}=D$, so
$$D\ \text{semisimple on }V^{\vee}\iff F_V^{-1}\ \text{semisimple on }V.\tag{3}$$
(ii) By lemma_4, for a finite-dimensional vector space over a field and an invertible linear operator, $T$ is semisimple if and only if $T^{-1}$ is semisimple (equivalently, by the last companion fact in lemma_64(iv)); applied to $T=F_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$,
$$F_V^{-1}\ \text{semisimple on }V\iff F_V\ \text{semisimple on }V.\tag{4}$$
Chaining (3) and (4) proves the claim. $\square$

**Step 5 (Assembly).** All of $F_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$, $q^dD\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})$, $D\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})$, $F_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ act on finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-spaces, and $q^d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$.

(a) Apply lemma_8 with $V$ of that lemma $:=W$, $T_V:=F_W$, $W$ of that lemma $:=V^{\vee}$, $T_W:=q^dD$, and $\alpha:=\gamma$. Its hypotheses hold: $\gamma$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^{\vee}$, both operators are invertible, and $\gamma\circ F_W=(q^dD)\circ\gamma$ by Step 3. Hence
$$F_W\ \text{semisimple on }W\iff q^dD\ \text{semisimple on }V^{\vee}.$$

(b) Apply lemma_248 to the space $V^{\vee}$, the operator $D$, and the scalar $c=q^d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$:
$$q^dD\ \text{semisimple on }V^{\vee}\iff D\ \text{semisimple on }V^{\vee}.$$

(c) Step 4: $D$ semisimple on $V^{\vee}\iff F_V$ semisimple on $V$.

Concatenating (a), (b), (c) yields
$$F_W\ \text{is semisimple on }W\iff F_V\ \text{is semisimple on }V,$$
in the sense of diagonalisability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (the equivalences are all in that sense: lemma_248 and lemma_8 are stated over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ with this notion, and the compatibility for lemma_4/lemma_64 is the remark at the end of Step 0).

**Step 6 (Conclusion).** Unwinding the notation, Step 5 says precisely that $F$ is semisimple (diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$) on $H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if it is semisimple on $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Every hypothesis used was verified: $0\le i\le 2d$ is exactly the range in which lemma_77(b) provides the perfect pairing between $H^i$ and $H^{2d-i}$; the case $V=0$ (equivalently $W=0$) was disposed of in Step 0. This completes the proof of the lemma. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* No semisimplicity statement is used anywhere: only the perfectness and the Frobenius compatibility $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^d\langle x,y\rangle$ of Poincar\'e duality, which are content of lemma_77(b). The result is manifestly symmetric in $i\leftrightarrow 2d-i$, as the pairing of Step 1 is.

lemma_265.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then \(F\) acts as the identity on \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and as multiplication by the scalar \(q^d\) on \(H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\); in particular \(F\) is semisimple on both of these spaces.
lemma_265.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: $q=p^a$, $X$ smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, and $F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$.

Preliminary remarks on the space $X_k$. Since $X$ has pure dimension $d\ge 1$, every irreducible component of $X$ has dimension $d\ge 1$; in particular $X$ is non-empty. Since $X$ is geometrically connected, $X_k$ is connected, and since $X$ is non-empty and of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ it has a closed point, so $X_k$ is non-empty. Also, $g:=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma:X_k\to X_k$ is a morphism of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes which is an isomorphism (its inverse is $\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1}$), hence its underlying map $|g|:|X_k|\to|X_k|$ is a homeomorphism; in particular $|g|$ induces the identity on the one-point set $\pi_0(X_k)$. By lemma_6a, $F=g^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and $F^{-1}=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*$ is geometric Frobenius.

=====================================================================
PART I.  The action on $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Step I.1 (identification of $H^0$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$).  Fix $m\ge 1$. On the small \'etale site of $X_k$, the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}$ is represented by the finite \`etale $X_k$-scheme $E_m=\coprod_{a\in\mathbb Z/\ell^m}X_k$ (a disjoint union of $\ell^m$ copies of $X_k$, which is finite \`etale over $X_k$). For a scheme represented by an \`etale cover, global sections of the represented sheaf are morphisms from the base, so
$$H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)=\mathrm{Hom}_{X_k}\bigl(X_k,\coprod_{a}X_k\bigr).$$
A morphism $X_k\to\coprod_a X_k$ is precisely a decomposition of $X_k$ into a finite disjoint union of open-and-closed subschemes indexed by $a\in\mathbb Z/\ell^m$, i.e. a continuous map $\pi_0(X_k)\to\mathbb Z/\ell^m$ with the discrete target. Since $X_k$ is connected, $\pi_0(X_k)$ is a single point, and therefore the only such maps are the constant ones. Thus the map
$$\mathbb Z/\ell^m\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m),\qquad a\longmapsto (\text{constant section }a)$$
is a bijection (of rings, and of $\mathbb Z/\ell^m$-modules).

Step I.2 (the inverse system).  For each $m$ we have a morphism of constant sheaves $\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1}}\to\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}$ given by the quotient map of sets $\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1}\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb Z/\ell^m$; it sends the constant section $a$ to the constant section $a\bmod \ell^m$. Hence under the identifications of Step I.1 the transition map $H^0(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1})\to H^0(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)$ is the natural reduction $\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1}\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb Z/\ell^m$, which is surjective. Taking the inverse limit (and using that a surjective tower has $R^1\varprojlim=0$) gives
$$H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell):=\varprojlim_m H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\mathbb Z_\ell,$$
sending the constant section $1$ to $1\in\mathbb Z_\ell$. By the definition of \`etale cohomology with $\mathbb Q_\ell$-coefficients,
$$H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Z_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1,$$
a one-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space (this agrees with the finiteness given by lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $X$ proper and $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$).

Step I.3 ($F$ fixes $1$).  The operator $F=g^*$ is the map on global sections induced by inverse image of sheaves along $g$. Inverse image of sheaves of rings is a functor to sheaves of rings and preserves the unit section, so $g^*(1)=1$; equivalently, under the description of $H^0$ as locally constant functions, $g^*$ acts by precomposition with $|g|$, and a constant function composed with any map is the same constant function (recall $|g|$ induces the identity on $\pi_0(X_k)$, which is a point anyway). Since $F$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear (lemma_6a), for every $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ we obtain
$$F(c\cdot 1)=c\cdot F(1)=c\cdot 1.$$
Hence $F=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This proves the first assertion.

=====================================================================
PART II.  The action on $H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Step II.1 (apply the Frobenius-equivariant trace).  We apply lemma_77 with $m=1$ and $Y=X$ (so $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q$, and $q^m=q$), which is exactly our situation: $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\ell\neq p$, and $F$ is the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius. Part (a) of lemma_77 provides a canonical isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces
$$\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$$
(normalised by $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]$ for closed points $x$) which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by $q^{1\cdot d}=q^d$.

Step II.2 (conclusion).  Equivariance means precisely that for every $x\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(Fx)=q^d\,\operatorname{tr}(x)=\operatorname{tr}(q^d x),$$
the second equality being $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}$. Since $\operatorname{tr}$ is an isomorphism, it is injective, and therefore $Fx=q^d x$ for all $x$. That is, $F$ acts on $H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by the scalar $q^d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. (Note $q^d\neq 0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell$: $q=p^a$ with $p\neq\ell$, so $q$ is a unit of $\mathbb Z_\ell$. This is consistent with $F\in\mathrm{GL}$, as in lemma_6a.) As a by-product, $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)=1$, so the space is non-zero and the statement is not vacuous. This proves the second assertion.

=====================================================================
PART III.  Semisimplicity.

Both operators computed above are scalar multiplications: $F=1\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^0$ and $F=q^d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{2d}$. Let $V$ be either of these $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces and $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ the corresponding scalar. After extending scalars, $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is a $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-vector space on which $F\otimes\mathrm{id}=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{id}$; for any $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-basis $\mathcal B$ (e.g. the basis obtained from a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $V$) every element of $\mathcal B$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$, so the matrix of $F\otimes\mathrm{id}$ in $\mathcal B$ is the diagonal matrix $\lambda\,\mathrm{Id}$. Hence $F\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, i.e. $F$ is semisimple on $V$ in the sense of lemma_5, which asserts exactly that semisimplicity over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and diagonalizability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ are equivalent. Applying this to $V=H^0$ and to $V=H^{2d}$ gives the claimed semisimplicity in both degrees.

(For completeness: by lemma_4 and lemma_6a, geometric Frobenius $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=F^{-1}$ is semisimple whenever $F$ is; here explicitly $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=\mathrm{id}$ on $H^0$ and $F_{\mathrm{geo}}=q^{-d}\cdot\mathrm{id}$ on $H^{2d}$, again scalar, hence semisimple.)

This completes the proof of the lemma. \hfill $\blacksquare$

lemma_266.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and write \(F_X,F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Fix \(n\ge0\) and suppose \(f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective. If \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_266.proof:
Write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$. Abbreviate
\[
V:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad u:=f_k^*:W\longrightarrow V,
\]
\[
T:=F_X=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V),\qquad S:=F_Y=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W),
\]
and put $U:=\mathrm{im}(u)\subseteq V$. The hypothesis on $f$ that we use is precisely that $u$ is injective; the goal is to prove that $S$ is semisimple (diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$), assuming $T$ is.

**Step 1: $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces.**
$X$ and $Y$ are projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply lemma_45_finite_frob to $X$ with $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X_k}$ the constant sheaf, viewed as an object of $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and with $\varphi=\psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ the natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. The lemma gives that the hypercohomology $\mathbb H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$; since the constant sheaf is concentrated in degree $0$, its hypercohomology is its sheaf cohomology, i.e. $\mathbb H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=V$. Thus $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V<\infty$. The identical argument applied to the proper $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Y$ gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W<\infty$. (Only the finiteness conclusion of lemma_45_finite_frob is used here; the operators $T,S$ are the ones named in the statement of the present lemma.)

**Step 2: $T$ and $S$ are invertible.**
By lemma_6a, for any $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ the pullback $(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $i$; taking $Z=X$ and $Z=Y$ (and $i=n$) shows $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $S\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$. These are exactly the operators appearing in the statement, so no identification issue arises.

**Step 3: $u$ is Frobenius-equivariant.**
$f:X\to Y$ is a morphism of schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ (it is a morphism of projective $\mathbb F_q$-schemes). Lemma_214 applied to $f$ and to $n$ gives
\[
f_k^*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_k^*,\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad u\circ S=T\circ u.\tag{3.1}
\]

**Step 4: $U$ is $T$-stable.**
Let $w\in U$. By definition of $U$ there is $y\in W$ with $w=u(y)$. Then by (3.1), $T(w)=T(u(y))=u(S(y))\in\mathrm{im}(u)=U$. Hence $T(U)\subseteq U$, so $T$ restricts to a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $T|_U:U\to U$.

**Step 5: $U$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear direct summand of $V$.**
$U$ is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space $V$, hence itself finite-dimensional; let $e_1,\dots,e_r$ be a basis of $U$. By the basis-extension theorem for vector spaces over a field, $e_1,\dots,e_r$ extends to a basis $e_1,\dots,e_r,e_{r+1},\dots,e_m$ of $V$. Define $p:V\to U$ on a vector $v=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i e_i$ ($\lambda_i\in\mathbb Q_\ell$) by $p(v):=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i e_i$. Then $p$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, $p|_U=\mathrm{id}_U$, and $V=U\oplus\ker p$ (every $v$ decomposes as $p(v)+(v-p(v))$ with $v-p(v)=\sum_{i>r}\lambda_ie_i\in\ker p$, and the sum is direct because $v\in U\cap\ker p$ gives $v=p(v)=0$). Thus $U$ is a direct summand of $V$ as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.

**Step 6: $T|_U$ is semisimple.**
We now apply lemma_35(ii) with the space $V$, the invertible operator $T$ (Step 2), and the subspace $U$: Step 4 gives $T$-stability and Step 5 gives that $U$ is a direct summand, and by hypothesis $T$ is semisimple on $V$. Lemma_35(ii) concludes that $T|_U$ is semisimple on $U$. (Note also that $T|_U$ is invertible: it is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and injective because $T$ is, and $U$ is finite-dimensional by Step 5, so $T|_U$ is bijective.)

**Step 7: descend semisimplicity from $U$ to $W$ along $u$.**
The corestriction $u:W\to U$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, surjective by the definition of $U=\mathrm{im}(u)$, and injective by the hypothesis of the lemma; hence it is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. Equation (3.1) says precisely that $u\circ S=(T|_U)\circ u$, i.e. $u$ identifies the operator $S$ on $W$ with the operator $T|_U$ on $U$. Both $W$ (Step 1) and $U$ (Step 5) are finite-dimensional, and both $S$ (Step 2) and $T|_U$ (Step 6 parenthetical) are invertible. Therefore lemma_8 applies with $V:=W$, $T_V:=S$, $W:=U$, $T_W:=T|_U$, $\alpha:=u$, and yields
\[
S\ \text{is semisimple on } W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T|_U\ \text{is semisimple on } U.
\]
By Step 6 the right-hand side holds, so $S=F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Edge cases.** If $W=0$ then $S$ is the identity on the zero space, which is semisimple, and the argument above still applies verbatim ($u$ is then the zero isomorphism $0\xrightarrow{\sim}0$, and Steps 4--6 give $U=0$). If $U=V$ there is nothing to check in Steps 5--6 beyond what is written. No case distinction is needed: the proof covers every $n\ge 0$ uniformly, including $n>2\dim X$, where the groups vanish.

This proves: whenever $f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is injective and $F_X$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, the operator $F_Y$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. $\quad\blacksquare$

(Remark on the role of the hypotheses: properness of $X$ and $Y$ over $\mathbb F_q$ is used only to make the cohomology groups finite dimensional, Step 1, and to know Frobenius acts invertibly, Step 2; surjectivity of $f$ and geometric connectedness of $X$ and $Y$ are not used at all, because the injectivity of $f^*$ is assumed explicitly. This is exactly the point at which the present lemma extends lemma_263, where injectivity of $f^*$ was derived from $f$ being generically finite of degree $d\ge1$ via $f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$.)

lemma_270.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\). Write \(V^{\vee}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and let \(T^{\vee}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})\) be the contragredient automorphism \(T^{\vee}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T^{-1}\). Then \(T\) is semisimple (that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)) if and only if \(T^{\vee}\) is semisimple.
lemma_270.proof:
**Notation and standing conventions.** Write \(k:=\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(\bar k:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). For a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector space \(W\) and \(A\in\mathrm{End}_k(W)\), let \(\mu_A\in k[t]\) denote the minimal polynomial of \(A\), i.e. the monic generator of the ideal \(\{p\in k[t]:p(A)=0\}\) (this ideal is nonzero because \(\dim_k\mathrm{End}_k(W)<\infty\), and it is principal because \(k[t]\) is a PID; it is generated by \(\mu_A\) by the division algorithm).

For a monic polynomial \(f=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_i t^i\in k[t]\) of degree \(n\ge 1\) with \(b_0=f(0)\neq 0\), define its **reciprocal polynomial**
\[
f^{\#}(t):=b_0^{-1}\,t^{n}f(t^{-1})=b_0^{-1}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{n} b_i t^{n-i}\Big)\in k[t].
\]
Its leading coefficient is \(b_0^{-1}b_0=1\), so \(f^{\#}\) is monic of degree \(n\), and its constant term is \(f^{\#}(0)=b_0^{-1}b_n=b_0^{-1}\neq 0\).

---

**Step 0 (the zero-dimensional case, and non-constancy of minimal polynomials).** If \(V=0\), then \(V^{\vee}=\mathrm{Hom}_k(0,k)=0\), both \(T\) and \(T^{\vee}\) are the (unique) operator on the zero space, and the zero space has the empty eigenbasis, so both are diagonalizable. Henceforth assume \(d:=\dim_k V\ge 1\). Then \(\dim_k V^{\vee}=d\ge 1\) as well (a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(V\) yields the dual basis \(e_1^{\vee},\dots,e_d^{\vee}\) of \(V^{\vee}\)). Consequently, for every \(A\in\mathrm{End}_k(V)\) or \(A\in\mathrm{End}_k(V^{\vee})\) that is invertible, \(\mu_A\) is non-constant (\(\mu_A=1\) would force \(\mathrm{id}=0\) on a nonzero space) and, by Step 3(a) below, \(\mu_A(0)\neq 0\); so \(\mu_A^{\#}\) is defined and of degree \(\ge 1\).

---

**Step 1 (transpose: \(\mu_{T^{t}}=\mu_T\)).** Define \(T^{t}\in\mathrm{End}_k(V^{\vee})\) by \(T^{t}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T\). For \(A,B\in\mathrm{End}_k(V)\) and \(c\in k\) we have \((A+B)^{t}=A^{t}+B^{t}\), \((cA)^{t}=cA^{t}\), and
\[
A^{t}\circ B^{t}(\varphi)=A^{t}(\varphi\circ B)=(\varphi\circ B)\circ A=\varphi\circ(B\circ A)=(B\circ A)^{t}(\varphi),
\]
so \(A\mapsto A^{t}\) is a \(k\)-linear anti-homomorphism \(\mathrm{End}_k(V)\to\mathrm{End}_k(V^{\vee})\). By induction on \(i\), \((T^{t})^{i}=(T^{i})^{t}\). Hence for every \(p=\sum_i a_i t^i\in k[t]\),
\[
p(T^{t})=\textstyle\sum_i a_i (T^{t})^{i}=\sum_i a_i (T^{i})^{t}=\big(\sum_i a_i T^{i}\big)^{t}=p(T)^{t}.
\]
Next, \(p(T)^{t}=0\iff p(T)=0\): the forward implication holds because if \(p(T)\neq 0\) there is \(v\in V\) with \(w:=p(T)v\neq 0\); extending \(w\) to a basis of \(V\) and defining \(\varphi\) on that basis by \(\varphi(w)=1\) gives \(\varphi\circ p(T)\neq 0\), i.e. \(p(T)^{t}\neq 0\). The reverse implication is immediate. Thus
\[
\{p\in k[t]:p(T)=0\}=\{p\in k[t]:p(T^{t})=0\},
\]
and these ideals have the same monic generator: \(\mu_{T^{t}}=\mu_T\).

---

**Step 2 (\(T^{\vee}\) is the inverse of \(T^{t}\)).** Since \(T\) is invertible, so is \(T^{t}\), and its two-sided inverse is exactly \(T^{\vee}\): for all \(\varphi\in V^{\vee}\),
\[
(T^{t}\circ T^{\vee})(\varphi)=T^{t}(\varphi\circ T^{-1})=(\varphi\circ T^{-1})\circ T=\varphi,\qquad
(T^{\vee}\circ T^{t})(\varphi)=(\varphi\circ T)\circ T^{-1}=\varphi.
\]
So \(T^{\vee}=(T^{t})^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})\).

---

**Step 3 (minimal polynomial of an inverse).** Let \(S\in\mathrm{GL}_k(W)\) with \(\dim_k W\ge 1\), and write \(\mu=\mu_S=\sum_{i=0}^{e}a_i t^i\) with \(a_e=1\) and \(e=\deg\mu\ge 1\).

*(a) \(a_0\neq 0\).* If \(a_0=0\), then \(\mu(t)=t\,q(t)\) with \(q(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{e}a_i t^{i-1}\), a nonzero polynomial of degree \(e-1<e\). From \(0=\mu(S)=S\,q(S)\) we obtain \(q(S)=S^{-1}S\,q(S)=0\), contradicting the minimality of \(\mu\). Hence \(a_0=\mu(0)\neq 0\), and \(\mu^{\#}\) is defined.

*(b) \(\mu^{\#}(S^{-1})=0\).* Multiply the relation \(0=\sum_{i=0}^{e}a_i S^{i}\) on the right by \(S^{-e}\) (all \(S^i\) commute with \(S^{-e}\)):
\[
0=\sum_{i=0}^{e}a_i S^{i-e}=\sum_{i=0}^{e}a_i (S^{-1})^{e-i}=a_0 (S^{-1})^{e}+a_1(S^{-1})^{e-1}+\cdots+a_{e-1}S^{-1}+a_e=a_0\,\mu^{\#}(S^{-1}).
\]
Since \(a_0\neq 0\), \(\mu^{\#}(S^{-1})=0\). Letting \(\nu:=\mu_{S^{-1}}\), the definition of the minimal polynomial gives \(\nu\mid\mu^{\#}\), hence \(\deg\nu\le\deg\mu^{\#}=e\).

*(c) Reverse inequality.* Apply part (b) to the invertible operator \(S^{-1}\). Its minimal polynomial \(\nu\) satisfies \(\nu(0)\neq 0\) by (a), and \((S^{-1})^{-1}=S\); part (b) gives \(\nu^{\#}(S)=\nu^{\#}\big((S^{-1})^{-1}\big)=0\). Hence \(\mu=\mu_S\mid\nu^{\#}\), so \(e=\deg\mu\le\deg\nu^{\#}=\deg\nu\).

*(d) Conclusion.* From (b) and (c), \(\deg\nu=e=\deg\mu^{\#}\) and \(\nu\mid\mu^{\#}\); two monic polynomials with the same degree and a divisibility between them are equal. Thus
\[
\mu_{S^{-1}}=\mu=\ \mu_S^{\#},\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad \mu_{S^{-1}}(t)=\mu_S(0)^{-1}\,t^{\deg\mu_S}\mu_S(t^{-1}).
\]

---

**Step 4 (the minimal polynomial of \(T^{\vee}\)).** Apply Step 3 to \(S:=T^{t}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee})\) (valid since \(\dim_k V^{\vee}=d\ge 1\)), using Step 2:
\[
\mu_{T^{\vee}}=\mu_{(T^{t})^{-1}}=(\mu_{T^{t}})^{\#}=(\mu_T)^{\#},
\]
the last equality being Step 1. Write \(\mu:=\mu_T\); by Step 3(a) applied to \(S=T\) (which is invertible) we have \(\mu(0)\neq 0\), so \(\mu^{\#}\) is defined and monic of degree \(e:=\deg\mu\ge 1\).

---

**Step 5 (\(\mu^{\#}\) is squarefree if and only if \(\mu\) is).** First record two formal properties of \(\#=^{\#}\) on the set \(\mathcal M\) of monic polynomials of degree \(\ge1\) with nonzero constant term.

*Multiplicativity.* For monic \(f,g\) with \(f(0)g(0)\neq0\): \((fg)(0)=f(0)g(0)\) and \(t^{\deg f+\deg g}(fg)(t^{-1})=[t^{\deg f}f(t^{-1})]\,[t^{\deg g}g(t^{-1})]\); dividing gives \((fg)^{\#}=f^{\#}g^{\#}\).

*Involutivity.* With \(f=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_it^i\) as above, \(f^{\#}(0)=b_0^{-1}\) and \((f^{\#})^{\#}(t)=(b_0^{-1})^{-1}t^{n}f^{\#}(t^{-1})=b_0\,t^{n}\,b_0^{-1}t^{-n}f(t)=f(t)\). So \(\#\) is a bijection of \(\mathcal M\) with inverse itself; in particular \(f^{\#}\) is monic of degree \(\deg f\ge1\) and \(f^{\#}\in\mathcal M\).

*Irreducibility is preserved.* If \(f\in\mathcal M\) is monic irreducible and \(f^{\#}=uv\) with \(u,v\) monic of degree \(\ge1\), then \(u(0)v(0)=f^{\#}(0)\neq0\), so \(u,v\in\mathcal M\) and \(f=(f^{\#})^{\#}=u^{\#}v^{\#}\) with \(\deg u^{\#}=\deg u\ge1\), \(\deg v^{\#}=\deg v\ge1\), contradicting the irreducibility of \(f\). Hence \(f^{\#}\) is irreducible.

Now factor \(\mu=\prod_{j=1}^{r}p_j^{e_j}\) in \(k[t]\), with the \(p_j\) distinct monic irreducibles and \(e_j\ge1\). Since \(\mu(0)=\prod_j p_j(0)^{e_j}\neq0\), each \(p_j(0)\neq0\), so \(p_j\in\mathcal M\). By multiplicativity,
\[
\mu^{\#}=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\big(p_j^{\#}\big)^{e_j},
\]
where each \(p_j^{\#}\) is monic irreducible of degree \(\ge1\), and \(p_i^{\#}=p_j^{\#}\Rightarrow p_i=(p_i^{\#})^{\#}=(p_j^{\#})^{\#}=p_j\Rightarrow i=j\) by involutivity and distinctness. Thus the right-hand side is the factorisation of \(\mu^{\#}\) into distinct monic irreducibles, with exactly the same exponents \(e_1,\dots,e_r\) (uniqueness of factorisation in the UFD \(k[t]\)). Therefore
\[
\mu^{\#}\ \text{squarefree}\iff e_j=1\ \forall j\iff\mu\ \text{squarefree}.
\]

---

**Step 6 (semisimplicity criterion over a perfect field).** Let \(K\) be a perfect field, \(W\) a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, \(A\in\mathrm{End}_K(W)\), \(\bar K\) an algebraic closure, \(\bar W:=W\otimes_K\bar K\) and \(\bar A:=A\otimes\mathrm{id}\). Then \(\bar A\) is diagonalizable if and only if \(\mu_A\in K[t]\) is squarefree.

*6.1 Base change of the minimal polynomial: \(\mu_{\bar A}=\mu_A\).* If \(W=0\) both sides equal \(1\). Otherwise: make \(W\) a \(K[t]\)-module by \(t\cdot w=A w\); then \(\mathrm{Ann}_{K[t]}(W)=\{p:p(A)=0\}=(\mu_A)\). By the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over the PID \(K[t]\), and since \(W\) is finite-dimensional over \(K\) (so there is no free summand and no torsion prime-power ambiguity),
\[
W\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}K[t]/(f_i),\qquad f_1\mid f_2\mid\cdots\mid f_s,\quad f_i\ \text{non-constant},\ s\ge1,
\]
as \(K[t]\)-modules. Annihilators commute with finite direct sums (\(p\) kills the sum iff it kills every summand), so \(\mathrm{Ann}_{K[t]}(W)=\bigcap_i (f_i)=(\mathrm{lcm}_i f_i)=(f_s)\), the last equality using the divisibility chain; hence \(\mu_A=f_s\). Now \(\bar K[t]\cong\bar K\otimes_K K[t]\) as \(K[t]\)-algebras, and \(\bar W\cong\bar K\otimes_K W\cong\bar K[t]\otimes_{K[t]}W\) as \(\bar K[t]\)-modules, where \(t\) acts as \(\bar A\) (indeed \(t\cdot(a\otimes w)=a\otimes Aw\)). Tensoring the exact sequence \(K[t]\xrightarrow{\ \cdot f\ }K[t]\to K[t]/(f)\to0\) (right exactness of \(\otimes\)) gives \(\bar K[t]\otimes_{K[t]}K[t]/(f)\cong\bar K[t]/(f)\). Therefore
\[
\bar W\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}\bar K[t]/(f_i)\quad\text{as }\bar K[t]\text{-modules},
\]
and the same annihilator computation over the PID \(\bar K[t]\) (the divisibility chain is preserved) yields \(\mathrm{Ann}_{\bar K[t]}(\bar W)=(f_s)\), i.e. \(\mu_{\bar A}=f_s=\mu_A\).

*6.2 Over an algebraically closed field.* Let \(L\) be algebraically closed, \(U\) a finite-dimensional \(L\)-vector space, \(B\in\mathrm{End}_L(U)\). Then \(B\) is diagonalizable iff \(\mu_B\) is a product of distinct linear factors. (If \(U=0\) there is nothing to prove; assume \(U\neq0\), so \(\mu_B\) is non-constant.)

\(\Longleftarrow\): suppose \(\mu_B=\prod_{j=1}^{r}(t-\lambda_j)\) with the \(\lambda_j\in L\) pairwise distinct, \(r\ge1\). For each \(j\), the Chinese remainder theorem (applicable since the ideals \((t-\lambda_i)\) are pairwise coprime) gives \(\eta_j\in L[t]\) with \(\eta_j\equiv1\pmod{t-\lambda_j}\) and \(\eta_j\equiv0\pmod{t-\lambda_i}\) for \(i\ne j\). Set \(P_j:=\eta_j(B)\). Since \(\sum_j\eta_j\equiv1\pmod{\mu_B}\) we get \(\sum_j P_j=\mathrm{id}_U\); since \(\eta_i\eta_j\equiv0\pmod{\mu_B}\) for \(i\ne j\) and \(\eta_j^2\equiv\eta_j\pmod{\mu_B}\) we get \(P_iP_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\) and \(P_j^2=P_j\). Since \((t-\lambda_j)\eta_j\equiv0\pmod{\mu_B}\), \((B-\lambda_j)P_j=0\), so \(\mathrm{im}\,P_j\subseteq E_{\lambda_j}:=\ker(B-\lambda_j)\). Conversely, if \(u\in E_{\lambda_j}\), write \(\eta_j=1+(t-\lambda_j)h_j\) and \(\eta_i=(t-\lambda_j)g_i\) for \(i\ne j\); then \(P_ju=u+(B-\lambda_j)h_j(B)u=u\) and \(P_iu=(B-\lambda_j)g_i(B)u=0\). Hence \(E_{\lambda_j}=\mathrm{im}\,P_j\) and \(U=\sum_j\mathrm{im}\,P_j=\bigoplus_j E_{\lambda_j}\) (the sum is direct because \(P_j\) is the identity on \(\mathrm{im}\,P_j\) and zero on \(\mathrm{im}\,P_i\), \(i\ne j\)): \(B\) is diagonalizable.

\(\Longrightarrow\): if \(U=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda\) with \(\Lambda\subset L\) the finite set of eigenvalues used, then \(\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(B-\lambda)=0\), so \(\mu_B\mid\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(t-\lambda)\); a monic divisor in \(L[t]\) of a product of distinct linear factors is itself such a product.

*6.3 Conclusion of the criterion.* By 6.1 and 6.2 with \(L=\bar K\), \(\bar A\) is diagonalizable iff \(\mu_A=\mu_{\bar A}\) is squarefree in \(\bar K[t]\). Factor \(\mu_A=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q_j^{e_j}\) in \(K[t]\) with \(q_j\) distinct monic irreducibles, \(e_j\ge1\). In \(\bar K[t]\), \(q_j=\prod_a (t-\alpha_{j,a})^{f_j}\) where \(f_j\ge1\) is the inseparability degree of \(q_j\); since \(K\) is perfect, \(f_j=1\) and the \(\alpha_{j,a}\) are pairwise distinct. Hence \(\mu_A=\prod_{j,a}(t-\alpha_{j,a})^{e_j}\) in \(\bar K[t]\), which is squarefree iff \(e_j=1\) for all \(j\), i.e. iff \(\mu_A\) is squarefree in \(K[t]\). This proves Step 6.

---

**Step 7 (conclusion).** Take \(K=k=\mathbb Q_\ell\) (characteristic \(0\), hence perfect) and \(\bar K=\bar k=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). By the definition in the statement, \(T\) is semisimple means \(\bar T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalizable on \(V\otimes_k\bar k\); likewise \(T^{\vee}\) is semisimple means \(\bar T^{\vee}\) is diagonalizable on \(V^{\vee}\otimes_k\bar k\). Applying Step 6 to \((W,A)=(V,T)\) and to \((W,A)=(V^{\vee},T^{\vee})\), and chaining with Steps 5 and 4:
\[
T\ \text{semisimple}\ \overset{6}{\Longleftrightarrow}\ \mu_T\ \text{squarefree}\ \overset{5}{\Longleftrightarrow}\ \mu_T^{\#}\ \text{squarefree}\ \overset{4}{\Longleftrightarrow}\ \mu_{T^{\vee}}\ \text{squarefree}\ \overset{6}{\Longleftrightarrow}\ T^{\vee}\ \text{semisimple}.
\]
(The middle equivalence uses \(\mu_{T^{\vee}}=\mu_T^{\#}\) from Step 4, and Step 5 applies because \(\mu_T(0)\neq0\) by Step 3(a).) Together with the trivial case \(V=0\) settled in Step 0, this establishes the lemma. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_271.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of each \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincar\u00e9 duality trace, \(F\) acting on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) as multiplication by \(q^d\), and let \(\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\) be the perfect pairing \(H^n\times H^{2d-n}\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\). Fix \(0\le n\le 2d\), a nonzero \(\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), and let \(\Psi:H^{2d-n}\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^n,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the isomorphism determined by \(\langle x,y\rangle=\Psi(y)(x)\,\xi\). Then \(\Psi\circ F=q^{d}\,(F^{-1})^{\vee}\circ\Psi\), where \((F^{-1})^{\vee}\) is the dual of \(F^{-1}\) on the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear dual.
lemma_271.proof:
## Notation and conventions

Write $V:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $W:=H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and denote by $F$ the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism on each of $V$, $W$, and $H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. For a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $U$ write $U^{*}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and for a linear map $T:U\to U'$ let $T^{\vee}:(U')^{*}\to U^{*}$, $T^{\vee}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T$, be its (ordinary) dual/transpose; since $F^{-1}:V\xrightarrow{\sim}V$ is an automorphism, $(F^{-1})^{\vee}:V^{*}\to V^{*}$ is the automorphism $\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ F^{-1}$. (Remark on conventions: if one uses instead the contragredient convention $T^{\vee}_{ctr}(\varphi)=\varphi\circ T^{-1}$, then the operator appearing in the statement is $F^{\vee}_{ctr}$, because $\varphi\circ F^{-1}=T^{\vee}_{ctr}(\varphi)$ with $T=F$. The identity proved below is the same statement in either notation.)

## Step 1. Finite-dimensionality and invertibility of $F$

$X$ is projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence proper. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell\in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $i$; in particular $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional. By lemma_6a, $F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of each $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, so $F^{-1}$ (on both $V$ and $W$) is defined.

## Step 2. The target $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is one-dimensional, so $\Psi$ is well defined and an isomorphism

$\mathbb Q_\ell(1)=\bigl(\varprojlim_m\mu_{\ell^m}(k)\bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a free $\mathbb Q_\ell$-module of rank $1$ (over the algebraically closed field $k$ the $\ell^m$-torsion of $\mathbb G_m$ is cyclic of order $\ell^m$, so the Tate module of $\mathbb G_m$ has $\mathbb Z_\ell$-rank $1$), and $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(d),\mathbb Q_\ell)$ likewise has $\mathbb Q_\ell$-dimension $1$; the Frobenius action on it is by the scalar $q^d$ (as the statement of the lemma also assumes, and as lemma_77(a) confirms). Hence for the given nonzero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ the map
$$\iota_\xi:\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad t\longmapsto t\,\xi$$
is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism, and so is
$$\iota_\xi^{V}:V^{*}\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)),\qquad \varphi\longmapsto\bigl(x\mapsto\varphi(x)\,\xi\bigr).$$
By lemma_77(b) (with $m=1$) the pairing $\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)$, $V\times W\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, is perfect; therefore the map
$$\theta:W\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)),\qquad \theta(y)(x)=\langle x,y\rangle,$$
is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. The map of the statement is $\Psi=(\iota^{V}_\xi)^{-1}\circ\theta$: for each $y$ there is a unique $\Psi(y)\in V^{*}$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=\Psi(y)(x)\,\xi$ for all $x$ (uniqueness uses $\xi\neq0$), $\Psi$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear because the pairing is linear in $y$, and $\Psi$ is an isomorphism as a composite of isomorphisms. This establishes all the claims made about $\Psi$ in the statement; the identity to be proved only uses its defining relation.

## Step 3. Frobenius equivariance of the pairing

We claim
$$\langle F a, F b\rangle=q^{d}\langle a,b\rangle\qquad\text{for all }a\in H^{i},\ b\in H^{2d-i},\ 0\le i\le 2d.\tag{$*$}$$
Indeed, $F$ is the pullback on cohomology along the morphism of schemes $\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma:X_k\to X_k$, and pullback along a morphism of (ringed) topoi is a homomorphism of the graded étale cohomology ring, so $F(a\cup b)=Fa\cup Fb$. Moreover, by lemma_77(a) (with $m=1$) the Poincaré duality trace $\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, normalised by $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$, is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where $F$ acts on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ as multiplication by $q^{d}$; that is, $\operatorname{tr}(F c)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}(c)$ for all $c\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Combining, with $c=a\cup b$:
$$\langle Fa,Fb\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(Fa\cup Fb)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(F(a\cup b)\bigr)=q^{d}\operatorname{tr}(a\cup b)=q^{d}\langle a,b\rangle.$$
(If the trace of the statement differs from the normalised one of lemma_77(a) by a scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ — it does not, since the normalisation fixes it uniquely — then both $\langle-,-\rangle$ and $\Psi$ are multiplied by $\lambda$, and $(*)$ and the final identity are unchanged; so nothing depends on this choice.)

## Step 4. Rewriting with $F^{-1}$

Apply $(*)$ with $a=F^{-1}x\in V$ and $b=y\in W$. Then $Fa=x$ and $Fb=Fy$, so
$$\langle x,Fy\rangle=q^{d}\langle F^{-1}x, y\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x\in V,\ y\in W.\tag{$**$}$$

## Step 5. Proof of the operator identity

Fix $y\in W$. For every $x\in V$, using the defining relation of $\Psi$ on the vector $Fy\in W$, then $(**)$, then the defining relation of $\Psi$ on $y$ applied to $F^{-1}x$, and finally the definition of the dual map,
$$\Psi(Fy)(x)\,\xi=\langle x,Fy\rangle=q^{d}\langle F^{-1}x,y\rangle=q^{d}\,\Psi(y)(F^{-1}x)=q^{d}\bigl((F^{-1})^{\vee}\Psi(y)\bigr)(x).$$
Thus $\bigl(\Psi(Fy)-q^{d}(F^{-1})^{\vee}\Psi(y)\bigr)(x)\,\xi=0$ for all $x\in V$; since $\xi\neq0$ in the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$, $\bigl(\Psi(Fy)-q^{d}(F^{-1})^{\vee}\Psi(y)\bigr)(x)=0$ for all $x$, hence $\Psi(Fy)=q^{d}(F^{-1})^{\vee}\Psi(y)$. As $y\in W$ was arbitrary,
$$\Psi\circ F=q^{d}\,(F^{-1})^{\vee}\circ\Psi$$
as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps $W\to V^{*}$, which is the claim. (Both sides are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, and $q^d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, so no division issue arises.)

## Step 6. Consistency check in an extremal case

Take $n=2d$, so $W=H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $V=H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. By lemma_265, $F$ is the identity on $H^0$ and is multiplication by $q^d$ on $H^{2d}$; hence $F^{-1}$ on $V$ is multiplication by $q^{-d}$. For $y\in W$, $x\in V$: the left side gives $\Psi(Fy)(x)=\Psi(y)(x)$, while the right side gives $q^{d}\bigl((F^{-1})^{\vee}\Psi(y)\bigr)(x)=q^{d}\Psi(y)(q^{-d}x)=\Psi(y)(x)$, using the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\Psi(y)$. The identity holds, as predicted. The same check for $n=0$ is the mirror image of this one. Both extreme cases are covered by the general argument of Steps 3–5, which needed only $(*)$; the general argument is valid for every $0\le n\le 2d$, including $d=0$ (where $q^{d}=1$ and $(*)$ reads $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, which is again what lemma_77 gives with $m=1$, $d=0$).

This completes the proof of the lemma.
